Lets focus on the bad first.
Most games already on steam aren't optimised for the controller so I personally have little use for it for any games outside audiosurf. Also the Steam Controller, in most cases, doesn't best the console controllers for games like "Rocket League" or FPS games due to the two giantgantic touchpads being above the important single thumbstick and buttons making it very tricky to manouver your hands around the controller if you're use to console controllers.
It does also take some getting use to since it is such a unquie design and it will throw off a few people if they don't give it a chance. It's taken me probably a day and a bit to just get familar with the button placements on the controller.
However, I do really like the controller. I use it quite a bit for surfing the web and it works really well with simple tasks that usually only need a mouse. It feels like a much better replacement than and keyboard and mouse in that sense.
Also the little details like making a custom sound and name for your own controller makes it feel like it's not just a normal souless controller which I adore. It's such a nice touch that makes it so nice to have.
As for typing with the controller. The GUI is top notch! At first I wasn't adjusted to having the GUI keyboard split in two and then using each touchpad to type on both sides. It did grow on me though and I definately think it has made typing with a controller 5 times easier than console controllers.
All in all though, I think as of now, it's  definately worth waiting to buy it just for the lack of games you cam play with it. I think if developers build their games around the controller though, then I believe the controller will be a joy to use. It stands out from the rest and can be the next evolution in controllers.
Final Verdict = Will recommend but more games need to be built with the controller in mind.
TL:DR = Tis really good but not a lot of games to use it with hurts it re-useability.

I pre-ordered this controller. I was really excited to use it. The very first game I launched and tried to play with the controller was GTA5. I don't know if it was because I was so used to the keyboard or the controller itself, but I was a little let down. If you are used to another controller (Xbox or PS) this may be a little awkward at first. The hardware itself is very nice. At first I didn't like how it fit in my hand, but after giving the controller some time I actually really enjoy using it on some titles. Overall, if you are looking for a good controller and arent married to either the xbox or ps controllers already, this is a great option for PC gaming. It uses the same button layout as the xbox so many games "just work" right out of the box. (Even non-steam games) Battery life is as you'd expect for a controller that uses AA batteries. There is a mini USB to USB cable included so you don't have to use battery or you can switch over if your batteries die. Would have loved to see a rechargable option. I also haven't looked into a rechargable option so it's possible it already exists.
TL;DR
Good controller. Buy it if you don't already have a Xbox or PS controller hooked to your PC.

I know there's been a ton of negative reviews and disparaging remarks about the Steam Controller (I've read many of them) but here's the rub...in most cases what others say about something often doesn't sway me heavily and I try to think and experience for myself in most cases - i.e. I like to try something to see if I like it...not if you or you or you like it.  Because when it comes right down to it...it doesn't matter if YOU like it...it only matters if I like it.
Found a Steam Link and Steam Controller from my wife under the tree for Christmas yesterday...and while I've only had a few hours of use with the Stream Controller...at this point I love it.  Oh I know there's a steep learning curve and reprogramming of my 'muscle memory' and my right thumb is going to hurt like hell...blah blah blah (seems like every review says this) but that's the same for ANY new thing you try out.  Frankly, as a primarily PC gamer (sure - the Xbox comes into play now and then for some platform specific game like Gears or Destiny but really nearly all my gaming is PC) ANYTHING that takes away my mouse and keyboard takes a "learning curve, muscle memory, and sore thumbs."  What the Steam Controller is IM not-so HO is, and should be, is a nice pairing to the Steam Link (or Steam console if you popped for one).  It means I can sit back on my couch and get my laptop off my lap...and not have a mouse on the arm of my armchair...and I can play around all day with my PC games on the big screen in the living room.  And the Steam Controller lets me do that, and do it well.
Not just shooters...but all my games.  The customization is awesome...and I can play a little Civ or and RPG like Sword Coast or maybe fire up some Dawn of War.  Dare I say a little Talos Principle would be nice with the Steam Controller?  I can now waste time with these games from the couch...and the Steam Controller does it nicely.
Is it perfect?  No.  Is anything?  No.  Simple enough.  What the Steam Controller is...is innovative and new.  Not the same as the past 20 years of standardized game controllers, nor should it be.  Don't get me wrong the classic two-handed game controller setup has been tried and true and there's the giant trumpeting of "if it's not broke don't fix it" mentality coming down from the ivory towers of gamer haters and trolls.  But to me those complaints fall on deaf ears...and have a very luddite feel to them.  It's been disappointing to see the gaming and tech crowd disparge innovation (and we've had damn too little innovation of late).  Maybe we shouldn't hide down in the cold basement clutching our Xbox controller lovingly as if we'll be using that same form factor 50 years from now (and hopefully we'll move out of mom's basement by then too)...maybe we should try new things and embrace creativity a bit.  Maybe the Steam Controller isn't quite the 100% final evolution of gaming controllers...but at least it's a creative step toward the future.  Do you use your Playstation controller to play Rock Band?  No...you got the drumset (with the cymbals I hope).  Do you zip around in Flight Simulator with your Xbox controller?  No...you plug in your HOTAS.  So now...when I fire up (most of) my PC games on my TV...I grab my Steam Controller.
My best advice...try something new once in awhile...you might find you like it...or even love it.

Any item can be created at any time if the blueprints for it have been found and the items in the player's inventory. It is important to note that when leveling the character, Nick Ramos, any point put into unlocking crafting options does not unlock blueprints. Instead investing points in a crafting category will let the player use any item of a particular type to craft an item. For example, the "Laser Sword" is a combination of a flashlight (electronic item) and gems (thrown item). If the player invests in the "electronic item" category then they can use any electronic item and gems to make a laser sword. The game also features combination vehicles that can be made anywhere.
Survivors are no longer useless like they were in the previous games. Now survivors have half decent A.I., aren't restricted to escort/babysitting missions, and can be used to create a "posse" that can be given basic orders (attack/follow/scavenge).
I recommend not using any DLC weapons or vehicles during normal gameplay as it can unbalance the game quickly.

I really wish I could give an 'average' rating. Because I would like to recommend the game based on the fact that there is currently no Vietnam era FPS offering similiar gameplay. The battles are fun and the weapons look, feel, and sound amazing. The gameplay is challenging, though when you get the hang of it, you'll die a lot less, but still a lot.
I love the team-based effort of reaching objectives, the leveling system, the achievments, getting a kill feel well earned, etc. But there are also some major drawbacks. Bugs and random crashes aside, the primary drawback is that quality games rely on quality communication for teamwork.. Yet, 80% of the community does not communicate in game. This can make some games seem extremely dull. If there was a level of communication like in a game like Squad, then the gameplay of Rising Storm 2 would be outstanding.
Gameplay aside, It is very hard to recommend this game when the online community is so small. Only a handful of servers are going at a time. Unfortunately, the same handful of servers are typically maxed unless you happen to catch it at a good time. Or you join a 1/3 populated server and wait. Im on the west coast USA, and ping is also an issue. there are maybe 2-3 populated servers I can join where I can get under 100 ping. This is all a major concern because the game is MP only. So if you cant access a server, or ping is too high, you're screwed.
So in short, yes I would recommend this game to a select few. Especially if they still have an interest after learning about the cons.

Short Review: A reasonably priced game that gives you a lot of bang for its buck. More 'realistic' multiplayer shooter with heavy emphasis on teamwork and asymmetric warfare. Gameplay includes optional piloting of helicopters as well as being a commander for your entire team, but for the most part is heavily infantry combat. Realistic weapons handling (damage, recoil, penetration, trajectory, etc.). One of few games made for 64 players. Initially high learning curve that may frustrate impatient players, but once you get into the hang of things it becomes very fun experience. Refreshing and different than most mainstream shooters. If you're looking for a MP shooter that's a bit similar to the old Battlefield and Red Orchestra series (64 players, small amount of vehicles, strong emphasis on teamwork to take objectives), requires a little more thought than your arcadey Call of Duties (no run-and-gun, realistic weapons handling), but is a bit less hardcore than shooter sims like the ArmA series, this is up your alley.
Long Review:
Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is a multiplayer shooter set in the Vietnam war era. Like its predecessor, it is made by the same guys who developed the Red Orchestra series. Unlike the last game which was asymmetric warfare in World War 2, this game moves up the timeline to the 70's. And it's a blast.
There are several differences. Veterans of the RO and RS series will still find the same features that made those older games appealing: 64 players, asymmetric warfare, heavy emphasis on teamwork, squad creation and spawning mechanics, a commander to lead both sides alongside their special abilities, etc. However, being a new game in a new timeline, there are many differences. Instead of land vehicles like tanks, the Southern Forces here have access to piloting helicopters and using devasting commander airstrikes. The Northern Forces have access to unique mechanics like Squad Tunnels and various nasty traps.
If you've never played any of the previous Red Orchestra/Rising Storm games, essentially this game is similar to the Battlefield series (specifically the older ones like BF2), but is more realistic and with heavier emphasis on teamwork. There are tons of mechanics to learn and get the hang of if you're a new player. In terms of infantry combat, weapons are handled completely differently than most shooters. Things are more realistic: Players often die in as little as 1-2 shots to the torso, weapons have differing levels of penetration through various materials, long ranged combat must take into account trajectory and bullet drop, and much more. Suppression is a thing too - receiving sustained gunfire towards you will slow your character down, blur your vision, and worsen your accuracy through lots of shakiness. This gives machine guns and covering fire a larger role than would be seen in most games. There are a lot of other minor mechanics as well, like stamina (your sprint eventually slows down to a mediocre jogging pace), you can hold breath to steady aim, there are features with certain classes, etc.
As with strategy games, once you get past the initial overwhelming amounts of mechanics to learn, it all comes together into a cohesive, satisfying package. And like the recent battle royale genre games like PUBG, once you start dying less often and get better at working with your team, each little victory gives a surge of satisfaction.
Each player chooses a side and a class to play as. Each class offers different weapons, but for the most part every soldier is the same - no one soaks more bullets than another. In fact, nothing really stops you from simply picking up a dropped weapon and using it the same as anyone else. The majority of players will play as the standard Grunt classes, equipped with the popular rifles of the time along with frag grenades. Other classes offer differing specializations, allowing some to spawn with smoke grenades, different traps, sniper rifles, RPGs, etc. Combat and Transport Pilots on the Southern side can fly helicopters in from 'off-map' airbases. The only infanty class with special powers is the Pointman/Scout, as they can detect traps much more easily as it will be highlighted for them (whereas everyone else would need to spot them without any visual aid).
The game is asymmetric, meaning both sides have different weapons, commander abilities, and exclusive mechanics that reflect history. Southern Forces have technologies like helicopters and airstrikes - they tend to be bombastic, with more advanced weaponry (including flamethrowers) and air superiority. Their squad members also spawn directly on their squad leaders. This all might seem unfair, but the Northern Forces have some tricks too. While they don't have any vehicles, they have multiple ways of countering Southern detection and air traffic. Their squad leaders can also build Squad Tunnels to allow squadmates to spawn from them. This results in a sort of guerilla warfare where the Northern forces want to be dastardly sneaky by setting up traps and spawning from flanks. Meanwhile the Southern forces try to flank by landing transport helicopters, and want to actively hunt for enemy tunnels.
If you don't fancy infantry combat, flying helicopters (exclusive to the Southern side) is also a blast. As one would expect, the helicopter controls are a little more advanced than in Battlefield, offering collective controls and generally realistic physics and handling. While these are powerful, especially the attack cobra, they are by no means invulnerable - pilots routinely can be shot out by small arms fire, and the RPG class can, well, shoot rockets that are of paramount danger to helos everywhere. However, inexperienced pilots can be very detrimental so it is recommended to practice first before flying in real sessions.
Lastly, a single player on both sides may lead as a Commander. The Commander can access stationary radios, or Radiomen soldiers, to utilize unique abilities to help out their team, including recon and artillery. Commanders generally are the ones that keep a constant look at the state of the map, inform teammates of abilities, communicate what's going on and order soldiers to do things. As such voice chat is pretty important, and obviously there's a lot of pressure especially if one is new. Being a Commander isn't really hard - the hard part is the strategy and communication really. Squad Leaders must also place marks down on the map for the commander to use many abilities, so teamwork goes both ways.
The main mode is Supremacy, where multiple capture points need to be taken and held down to tick away to victory. There are limited number of pooled lives that start off in the hundreds or even a thousand, but over the course of the match these can dwindle down until respawns are out if the match hasn't ended yet. Other modes are available for less players or further attack/defend simplicity.
Overall, once you get the hang of things, the game can be quite fun. Really the only con is the lack of a good tutorial. Initially the curve can be a bit annoying (dying frequently can be a bummer) and sometimes you just get bad luck with teammates who won't work together, but the vast majority of the time everyone's nice and plays the way the game was meant to be played. The community is small but dedicated, and despite a supposedly small playerbase, it is not difficult to find full servers to play in at all. One side note is that if you're sensitive to racial/political/whatever jokes, you may be turned off. A lot of players like to say funny things with terrible accents and stereotypes ('casual racism role play' as I call it) as they 'role play' their side. Obviously vast majority of the time this is all in jest and multiple people get in with the jokes, but hey, just a warning. As someone whose parents fled to Canada from the Vietnam War, this stuff doesn't faze me, and in fact it's actually pretty entertaining.

I've been holding onto this one for about two years before I actually decided to sit down an play the darn thing.  Holy cow, why did I delay?
While Bioshock Infinite still holds my place for the best story that I've gone through in a game this year, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, were it released this year, would be a very close second.  And in terms of the actual gameplay, this one *blows* out Bioshock Infinite (and any other first-person shooters I've played recently).
The great thing about the gameplay is the multitude of choices on how to approach different scenarios.  Want to punch through a wall to access a room?  How about hacking a keypad to access it?  Or maybe you want to access it via a hidden duct system?   All can be done.
Or, how do you approach enemies?  Want to do it guns ablazing?  Check.  Or silently sneak behind each one and take them down?  Check.
How to get down a ladder?  Climb down it?  Okay, or you could enhance your abilities to just fall/jump down without taking any damage.
And yes, the story, as mentioned before, is great.  If you've played any of the Mass Effect series, the conversations take place with the same type of interface and allow you to make choices that do affect the outcome.  The variances in story, admitedly, aren't as wide as what Bioware might provide, for example, and you don't have the ability as much to affect your relationships with others.  But nevertheless, you do get a sense that you are in control to some degree.  And with a game like this, that's enough.
The graphics are solid but are nothing to write home about (compared to, say, Battlefield 3).  Frame rates were smooth but I have a pretty beefy rig so I can't say how it will perform with a relatively older machine.
Voice acting is solid as well, although I confess that the actor that portrayed Jensen (the main character) sounded a little too much like Clint Eastwood.  Also, it sounded as if he were recorded in a different studio than the other actors; you can notice a difference in overall "volume/tone" between characters when conversations take place.  Not a deal breaker, of course.
The music is fantastic; it's very much in the style of what you would hear with Daft Punk's score for Tron Legacy but even a little more nuanced.  Very well done.  In many games, I get tired of the tracks that repeat over and over again as you explore - *ahem Assassin's Creed Revelations ahem* - but I can't that say that for this game.
I have only one legitimate complaint - it's the inventory system.  For OCD'ish people like me, the inability for the game to do an "automatic rearranging" of your items in a way that *I* would like drove me nuts.   You can manually rearrange the inventory but geez, it's a lot of work to get it just right.   I guess this is more my problem than the games' problem. :-)
Anyway, 9/10 without question.  A must play - get it ASAP if you haven't.

Ok, so I have been playing this game annually for over 20 years now, and I still enjoy it as much as when I was a kid.
This game is the DEFINITIVE point&click game to me. It literally embodies everything the modern game-industry is missing, and you can feel the passion the developers had for this game when they were making it.
It might not be packed with action, but as it stands it can not only keep up with modern games, but absolutes wrecks many of it's modern day opponents. All of the characters feel believable in a whacky way, yet achieve to fit into the world around them. The Plot is incredibly immersive, and the protagonist will forever stay in your mind as  "Guybrush Threepwood, Mighty Pirate." From the first second of dialog to the last cutscene, every second is filled with hilarious jokes - some of which even break the fourth wall (remember this game released in 1990). Additionally the graphics have been reworked, and the ENTIRE GAME has spoken dialog, and monologues.
If you (like me) are old as ♥♥♥♥, and would like to take a stroll down memory lane, or you'd like to experience the game that started it all - I HIGHLY RECOMMEND YOU BUY THIS GAME.

Okay, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.
It's the kind of game you play once every few weeks, but for the rest of your life. Great if you randomly feel like immersing yourself in a richly aurally-textured half-axon half-multiverse tunnel with a pace ranging from narcoleptic to highly spasmodic.
The actual goal is collecting glyphes embodying tiered concepts, with a final one marking a progression we'll get back to; all while avoiding obstacles as your speed slowly increases with each level.
For instance, level 1 is the nasal ganglia, with concepts such as "peculiar insight" or "nervous laugh" and the final glyph being Awareness.
The gameplay also involves the ability to, holy ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥
. The game really has a particular relation to time in general, as you slow down the sound environment as well and pausing temporally stucks you in one audio piece. Said pieces otherwise naturally flow with the game.
While all golden glyphes make you "progress", and the general goal is to collect everything, the game has one and only one condition for winning : collecting the very final glyph, Unhumanity. Completing a playthrough rewards you with the ability to choose an in-game avatar from a variety of monsters. As for what happens when you miss the glyph... I'll let you see for yourself.
So in short, exceedingly fun, love the overall feel of the game, EXTREMELY underrated on steam. It's one of those little games that have a special place in my heart. Maybe literally given the environment.

$9.99 is a rather steep price tag for such a simple game, though. I'm glad that I bought this on sale and only shelled out $2.50. It wouldn't have been worthwhile to spend any more money than that.

I give it a strong 9/10.

Monster Loves You! is a charming text based, choose your own adventure game. You live the life of a monster, from conception to old age (if you make it that far!).  The game has 14 possible endings, all with their own achievements. Each stage of life offers you different, randomized scenarios. These plot points can add or subtract points to your personality traits and overall village respect rating.
Two hours in, and five monster lives lived, I find myself impressed with the number of scenarios that exist in the game. I keep coming upon ones I haven't seen before in all of the different stages of life. I feel as if I'm truly a different monster each time, which leads me to be pleasantly surprised by the replay value.
$10 may be a little much for a game that requires nothing more than some clicking, but I would encourage anyone to pick it up during a sale. What kind of monster will you be? Will you dissolve into a vat of slime? Or will you lead a revolution? Either way, you'll have a fun time doing it.

I've been using it for a couple of weeks and I can see the potential for this to be an essential piece of PC hardware for any gamer. Just not yet. Unless you're prepared to get your hands dirty and have a bucket load of free time you might find yourself frustrated with the controller.
Quick Summary - Buy it if you don't mind spending a fair bit of time getting each game to feel right for you and don't mind doing a lot of the setup yourself. Steer clear for now if you're expecting a plug and play experience or don't have a lot of time.
Detailed review -
First off, prepare for an almost vertical learning curve. This is unlike anything you've used before. You will need to spend time with the controller to get your muscle memory used to the unique feeling of the touchpads.
Configuration can take a long time to get right for each game. There's no single profile that will work. Often the community/developer created profiles were of no use to me. I used some of them as a baseline and tweaked from there.
The configuration options are insane and not all are clearly explained. It's intimidating at first but essential to have these options to ensure you get the controller feeling just right. This needs to be streamlined with better presets from valve and developers.
Still feels like a beta product to me as valve are constantly making tweaks and adding new features (which is ace as every update has made the product better).
Recent beta feature to store your controller config is a godsend if you plan to take your controller to a friends to play.
Best features are having almost perfect mouse like input on the touchpad. When you set it up right it feels amazing to move around (especially in FPS games). The gyro is also an excellent addition to make those finer movements when sniping/zoomed in possible. The haptic feedback of the touchpads are also damn near perfect.
I had very mixed feelings with the controller after a couple of days and found myself going back to my xbox one controller instead. However, I stuck with it for a few weeks and spent a lot of time getting my presets perfect and it's now a joy to use which is why I'm recommending it.

My first attempt:

And here comes the Steam controller!
Much more easy now.

The best thing of this controller is that its almost completely symmetrical, the 2 halves are nearly identical, the only thing that differ is the stick VS the buttons. This makes it much more easier to control 2 charachters at the same time in the game.
And a bonus: The XYAB buttons can be configured to be a D-PAD for movement if you want that. Big plus to Valve for that.

A really good game to be completely honest.  This game is perfect if you like games like "The Isle" and so on because its a human vs dino game where you can either play as one of the 5 human classes, Pathfinder (Shotgunner), Scientist (Sniper/Immobilizer), Commando (Assault Rifle Dude), Pyro (Flamwthrower Guy) and finally the Trapper (Nets Things).  Or you can play as the dinos where there are 10 dinos, T-Rex, Spinosaurus, Acrocanthysaurus (hope i spelt that correctly xD), Novaraptor, Oviraptor, Dilophosaurus, Cryolophosaurus, Carnotaurus, Pteradon and finally the Tupandactylus (hope i spelt that correctly too xD).
Each dino is split into 5 groups, Tyrants (T-Rex, Spino, Acro), Predators (Nova, Ovi), Spittters (Dilo, Cryo), Bruisers (Carno) and finally, Flyers (Ptera, Tupa).
The game does have its issues like for example most games of freemode (when you can have unbalanced teams of the 2 factions with no time or score limit) which include about 23 people playing as dinos and 2 people playing as humans, TDM isn't all that great because you are not allowed to switch team and there is a time limit and it almost feels like a Call Of Duty but one team are dinos.  However there are also 2 other gamemodes that are ok but aren't seen that often on the servers list and those are "Hunt" and "Dino Deathmatch". Hunt is a Stalker/The Hidden gamemode from Gmod where one player is randomly selected as an almost invisible raptor who can pounce and attack and has about 1000 health (i think) which is the same as the carno. The other players must find and kill it while the "Hunt Raptor" as it's called tries to hunt them down, whoever kills the raptor becomes is next round. Dino Deathmatch is basically TDM but no humans instead it's a gamemode where every dino can harm eathother, raptors can pounce other raptors and spitters (im not sure about the flyers), flyers can pick up raptors and spitters and so on.
Finally the maps are actually really good, there are a few safe zones for humans if they are eing chased by a tyrant and need to go into a tight space, raptors can feel like super predators hiding in long grass while waiting for some foolish human to walk by so that they can pounce them, Bruisers can charge and bash enemies sending them flying, flyers can pick up or bash enemies and drop them leaving them to fall to their death and finally tyrants can feel like kings while chasing down helpless prey that have hardly enough bullets left to take them down.
In my opinion this game is very good and would deserve an 8/10 in my opinion but does lack a few things such as new dinos added and so on.
In order to make this game better, the creators NEED to add more dinos because this game is slowly dying and i really want to keep playing it.

Learning to bird:
Yet another indie game I've had the honor of playing a little early and this one is SO beautiful! Have you ever wanted to be a bird, flitting from tree to tree, gathering twigs and building a nest? Ever wanted to do it in a politically unstable city? Well now's your chance!
Honestly, I think you could quite happily enjoy the game by just pretending to be a bird for hours and not paying too much attention to the story if politics doesn't interest you, but the story and depth are there for those who want it!
A beautiful musical score and incredibly uplifting and relaxing game play, I highly recommend you try out Copoka!

Absolutely loved this game. Being the silent observer and having no real hand in the events going on in the city was an interesting change of pace. Basically, you are a bird, and your involvement in listening to or ignoring the story is entirely on you (though I highly recommend following it. Its interesting). You can stay and listen to conversations between NPCs, or just drop in, collect your trinket, and fly off.
Basically, the general story is that you are a bird building a nest in the city of Copoka, which is in the beginning stages of people getting ready to stage a rebellian against their "Great Leader". Some of the dialogue hints at people disappearing after speaking against the leader, some hint at medicine and food shortages. As you progress by building your nest, so does the story. Through all of it, your only involvment is picking up trinkets to build your nest (everything from broken glasses, twigs, military medals, etc...), and listening in on conversations between people. In between collecting trinkets and listening to NPCs, there are feathers to collect which give you a speed increase.
Graphically, the game has a colorful, cartoony style. The store page screenies are pretty accurate. No real complaints there, though itd have been cool if the NPC's faces were detailed even a little.
Audio is solid. The music scores were very relaxing, and the voice acting was done very well. Pretty much every conversation had some solid voice acting behind it. You might not be able to recognize NPCs by face, but after awhile certain NPCs stand out from the voice acting alone (Most notable, "John", his guard buddy, and the artist).
Only real complaint I had was texture pop ins. I didnt notice it too much until I collected most of the feathers. If you fly too fast, some of the tree textures pop in. There was also an odd FPS drop near the harbor. Other than that, I didnt find any crashes or glaring bugs.
Overall, the game is pretty enjoyable if youre looking for sort of a zen game. Going into this game, I was expecting to fly around collecting junk for my nest, and that to be about all I did. I wasnt expecting to actually get into the story (as much as you can as an observer anyway), or to actually look forward to certain NPCs conversations (Mostly "John" and his partner). And I certainly wasnt expecting the world to be nearly as detailed or large as it was. Really recommend it, especially if you find it on sale somewhere.

Set roughly 80 years after Fallout 1, the world once again needs the aid of an individual to overcome a great evil. Originally you're sent out from your tribe, founded by the original Vault Dweller from F1, to retrieve a GECK that will help them survive as their village is dying. Needless to say, a lot more than that is going on which you will uncover soon enough.
The world of Fallout 2 feels similliar to Fallout 1's (from here F1). The very south of F2's map is actually connected to F1's top, making it possible for the player to revisit a few of the old locations, such as Vault 13 and 15, as well as the NCR, which used to be Shady Sands. Other than that's there's a lot of new places to discover, including personal favorite of mine such as New Reno and a locationIreallycan'tnamewithoutspoilingthegame.
As for the combat and levelling mechanics, these are the same as in F1, meaning you start the game by picking your SPECIAL and tag skills and as you defeat enemies in turn based combat and levelling up, you get to spend more skill points on various skills. The use of AP for moves in combat is a really neat system.
As for F2 as a sequel, it's pretty great. The mechanics from F1 are re-used but other than that, it's a direct continuation on the lore with new events, a (mostly) new setting, all new story line and great characters.
The massive downside of Fallout 2, however, is the start. The game starts in an insanely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tutorial, and the first few hours are annoying as♥♥♥♥♥♥ The SPECIAL you pick at the start wil also really influence the game a *ton*. I, for example, went with 4 strenght, leaving me unable to use 90% of the weapons untill much later on, which was a major♥♥♥♥♥♥off. Amongst that the enemies suddenly go from easy to kill to pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and if you're not prepared for that you're having a hard time. A good companion team is basically a must at that point.
Before I wrap this up, I must say Fallout 2 has some absolutely hilarious moments to make up for some of the rage it might cause, such as the Café of Broken Dreams, the Bridge Guardian, conversations with certain NPCs and...SERGEANT DORNAN.
Overall, 8.5/10.

Having played around with this and the Steam Link for well over a month now, to say I'm extremely disappointed is an understatement.
For a start the haptic feedback often seems to go off when I'm not even touching it even after the firmware update, and the pad is only really useful for certain genres. For other genres the use of the right touch pad for camera movement for example feels totally out of place, and the 'dead zone' is far too restrictive in that the thumb has to travel a much greater distance from one end to the other than a player would otherwise have had to using a conventional analogue stick.
I know my controllers and have to say that this is the new JogCon of the controller world (in other words a gimmick). Don't be fooled by the number of positive reviews you find on here, for they are shrills that have been sent to bolster what is essentially a flawed product. Apologies to Valve for not acquiescing and giving this a positive review but f*ck you, I say it as it is.
Put another way, the Xbox and Playstation controllers have largely remained the same over the last 3-4 generations (since PSX's first analogue pad and the original Xbox's S-Type pad) because they WORK. If there was any room to implement what Steam have attempted to do, then Microsoft and Sony would have done so years ago. Valve on the other hand believe they can re-invent the wheel on their first attempt, and have failed.
What I can say about the Steam Link however is a different story entirely, but you'll have to wait for that until Steam allow me to review it - noticing that there are far fewer reviews for the Link than there are for their controller.

This isn't the kind of game I usually play. I wasn't sure what to expect, but I took a chance on it anyway. Boy was I disappointed. I could nitpick this game for hours, but I'll try to keep it focused on three main gripes.
I haven't seen a professional game with such terrible affordances since the 90's. I put up with it then, but today I expect better.
The game developers had some interesting story ideas, and explored some interesting themes, but the implementation is awful. The script sounds like it was written by schoolboys. The dialogue is a long sequence of non-sequiters and statements that don't actually mean what they should. As a mundane example, at one point the sidekick with the map says "just keep going forwards"... and the
only has doors to the side. Sure, outside-the-screen I know that the writer meant "the level design is completely linear and boring", but in-character that line is nonsense.
The game acts like it wants to be taken seriously, but that's nigh impossible. It tries numerous times to explain how backups/restores/teleportation work, but it still doesn't make sense. How does every vending machine have a copy of my body? with my weapons and pod? even when I'm
. Just how many fusion reactors are lying around in these vending machines, anyway? Not to mention the ridiculous story elements, from
to
, and
to
.
The game is fairly difficult in the beginning, with extremely limited healing and an awful ranged attack (that gets less accurate when it's locked on target...). As soon as you get a heal-over-time chip and the pod with homing rockets, the rest of the game can be completed trivially by standing as far as possible from your target while holding down the ranged attack button, dodging occasionally. Not only is there no difficulty anymore, but this optimal strategy is boring as can be. The hardest "boss fight" is a random gold-plated machine that you encounter early on, is next-to-impossible to engage in melee, and takes hardly any damage from attacks. I was kiting it in circles for a good half hour before it died. I guess you're supposed to hack into it - but you meet it as a character who can't hack :\
To make battles drag on even more, the pod upgrade costs are completely skewed as well. In the natural course of playing the game, you'll obtain all you need to upgrade a pod from level 2 to max, long before you obtain the parts to level it from 1 to 2. So unless you dedicate a lot of time to farming the materials early on, you'll play the whole game with level 1 pods.
As a closing note, the game's developers consider looking up the main character's skirt to be an achievement. Take that as you will.

The most recent choose-your-own-adventure, (primarily) text-based game I have played is Dark Scavenger. I was interested in this game after discussing it with my brother, who had seen a playthrough by YouTube personalities Game Grumps. A few days later, this game was the Steam Daily Deal.
If you like super casual gameplay, choose-your-own-adventures, and text-based games, then you will enjoy Monsters Loves You!
The game is extremely short - I completed one playthrough in less than 45 minutes. Keep in mind, however, that I read A LOT and can read considerably quickly.
The aesthetics (like most other elements of this game) are fairly casual with a small pool of recycled pictures and text. The detail in the scenery is good, and your monster's appearance varies greatly and seems to be determined by the initial options you select. The music is suprisingly good, and the ending background music in particular adds a majestic, urgent feel to the gameplay.
The controls just involve you to click, and the learning curve is minimal. There is no apprent tutorial, however, many of the options have a "help" button that you can click, allowing things to be explained without progressing the story - in dialogue options, this is usually presented as the top/first option (clicking it will provide you with additional situational information without continuing the story).
I have to stress that gameplay is extremely casual, and since this is a text-based game, you will have to really rely on your imagination to fill in the details. Readers interested in the theme will probably like this game, however, if you do not read regularly (especially for recreational purposes) you may find this game to be very boring.
Almost every decision you make in the game will result in you obtaining (or even losing) different stat points like bravery, respect, ferocity, honesty, etc. For example, fighting a bear and winning may give you points in bravery, ferocity, and respect. Besides respect, every monster stat is represented on the bottom of the screen in the form of different icons, and you can click each one to give you additional information. You can level all stats to a maximum of 100.
The stats are important for the end-game, where many of your actions are dependent on your stat scores (ex: to successfully fught off an opponent you need a high bravery/ferocity rating). Furthermore, respect is extremely important for getting other monsters on your side, especially in political situations. While the "politics" element really interested me, remember that this is an extremely casual game, and the politicial intrigue is reflectively minimal. Most of the politics involves your interactions with both the human and monster communities, and the end-game (if you get that far) will add two new gauges - the "how humans view monsters" and "how monster view humans" meters (maximum value of 100).
Respect is critical for the end-game, where your decisions will determine which particular ending you receive.
Each "phase" of the monster's life cycle is broken up, and you have a fixed amount of turns before you advance to the next stage of life. The last stage requires you to have a high respect rating and/or high character stats.
During each "phase," you can go adventuring. I really liked this part, because you only have enough "turns" (represented by days) in each "phase" to go on adventures. When selecting an adventure, you must click on different icons to activate a mission - you are not given any information besides the pictures on each adventure icon. I loved this mechanic because it made things less predictable and also more exciting. I am not sure if the available adventures are randomized for each playthrough, but I have noticed that they can be different each time (it may depend on the initial options you pick right when you start playing).
For achievement hunters, you will have to do A LOT of playthroughs, since you need to unlock every possible ending. After doing enough playthroughs, you should be able to progress through the game fairly quickly, especially once each adventure icon becomes more and more familiar to you.
That being said, it is very, very easy for you to become bored of this game if you try to get all the achievements in one (or few) sittings, since all of the decision tree consequences will be known to you. Instead, I strongly suggest you only do one playthrough per sitting, and try to spread the playtime for this game around to keep things fresh. Remember, there is A LOT of text in this game, so avoid it if you do not like reading.
For choose-your-own-adventure buffs and text-based game lovers, this casual game will fit very well in your libraries. For anyone not interested in those things, you might want to avoid playing this.
Recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

So this is a stat based adventure game. There are different endings you achieve by boosting the right stats and making decisions. The art is lively but the majority of the game is text-based. The events that take place are randomized with each playthrough making it practically impossible to see every outcome. I feel that is a good thing.
The choices you make often give surprising results making it easy to construct your own highly personal narrative.
I particularly like the deceptively dense lore of the world. Different paths give you amazing insights into the nature of the monster species.
Compared to other games of its kind, it is very easy. There are no failstates nor do you have to keep track of laberynthine event trees. It is suitable for younger and/or inexperienced players. That said there is a fair amount of violence so discretion is advised.
Overall it is enjoyable, surprising and often touching with at least 5 hours of play.

A brilliant, beautiful piece that can really be good. But it isn't. At first I worried that my decisions could wound, if not destroy, my character - such as life is. However, there was no threat. I was worried that a lot of decisions might have flip-side effects that make decisions far more difficult than they seem, but they're not.
I was really looking forward to fleshing out my character and choosing between eating children, becoming an outcast creature or building friendships and skills such as Alter Ego that this game, I am guessing, is heavily built from. But it's not.
I played through the whole thing - including reading and considering every decision - in an hour. Yes, there's replay value to be sure, but for no other reason than to get achievements and a pat on the back for clicking the right, very terribly obvious, buttons.
It's a shame that the developers didn't do more with this. There was such a great possibility here.
In the last stage of the game, you're offered two icons with a %. One is how much monsters like humans, and the other how much humans like monsters. You just have to press some buttons to get these in the direction you want, for the outcome you want. If you balanced your character throughout the game - which isn't very difficult, I wound up with 90%+ in all on the first go, you've got no problems with this "Grand Finale".
It's fun to play for the first couple of stages, and the dialogue is actually very well written, and the graphics are comically wonderful - however, this only reaches out to the child side of me. I felt no threat, no worry, no challenge.

Very good game, I understand that a lot of people are having crash issues, which is unfortunate. I am lucky to have a AMD FX 8350 Eight core processer, 16GB RAM, and a AMD 980 3GB Video card, so I feel I can write a fair review ignoring these crashes.
EDIT: I was going through reviews and noticed that people were explaining what their graphics settings were set to.... I want to say mine were all set to the maximum, even having 1920x1080 resolution.
The Pros:
ROOM TO ROAM!
Very open world, many of the buildings are open for exploration, to at least some degree.
ZOMBIES!!!!
HUNDREDS of zombies on screen at the same time...... and I mean hundreds. There's nothing more scary than trying to get to your next quest marker, than having to go over a freeway filled with quite possibly over a thousand zombies, and ohh wait! all you have is a brick in your hand!
WEAPONS!!!!!!
Yeah, when this game says anything is a weapon, it means it..... I have even found a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥as a weapon (Was part of a side mission, but yeah, you get the point, this game has it all). The combo weapons are also very creative, combining a scythe with a katana to make the "Grim Reaper"? Or a Broadsword with Motor Oil to make a burning blade that not only slices and dices, but to add insult to injury, sets zombies on fire?! Yessir!
VEHICLES!!!
Now, I love a game that has vehicles and the ability to run stuff over, ever since my childhood days of sneaking onto Carmageddon..... now that I'm a big boy, I don't see it often anymore. This game right here..... it satiates my longing for it! The standard vehicles are fun to drive, very responsive, even with the limiting of keyboard bindings... but when you start getting combivehicles..... GOOD GOD! Prepare to unleash a can of♥♥♥♥♥whoop on these zombies. My personal favourite so far (Which is a DLC vehicle, and therefore is one you can access from the start) Is the Sawblade Motorcycle (not completely sure of the name right now). It's a motorcycle, with sawblades for wheels. It has a mechanism that shoots sawblades from the front of it, to slice zombies in your path.... and much to my great delight...... if you hold on the break, and do a burnout, any zombie dumb enough to get close to the spinning, burning saw blade on the back instantly gets roasted alive... er... dead.
Combat:
What else is there to say about the combat? It's a literal hack and slash combat system, with many different weapons and ways to sew chaos in this game world, with weapons ranging from a katana that slices zombies apart, to using a combo sawnoff shotgun with a machette strapped to it for blasting and hacking your foes. (Let's not even start with the DLC weapons.... I've tried a few of those, and they deserve a whole paragraph to themselves for how fun they are..... just leave it with this.... think the best weapons in the game (Auto Shotgun, plus chainsaw) and combine them, to make them even better).
Graphics:
I'd say this game has as good of graphics as I have seen on a game (Mainly PC gamer here, have not been exposed to PS4 nor XBone yet, waiting for Ryze; Son of Rome to test full graphics capability). I'd give the graphics a solid 9. 9/10 because simply...... the character's facial features seem much too "Arcade-ish" when they move their features.
The CONS:
Followers:
Now, having a posse to go around killing zombies is fun, and I mean good fun. But when they start dying, and can't even figure out to KEEP F@!$ING SMACKING THOSE UNDEAD IDIOTS, then something is wrong with the AI...... I think the followers are more annoyance than help, as they consistantly kill zombies that you need in certain spots for missions, blowing them up too close to themselves, or even worse, yourself, and thus, killing each other with splash damages. Ohh, did I mention? They are too dumb to pick up food themselves off the ground to heal themselves. Yeah. Cause it's so hard to stuff your face full of all this food just laying around -_-
Overall:
I'd give this game a solid 8.5/10. It's fun, it's addictive, and you can really just lose yourself for hours in the desperate survival that a "true" zombie apocalypse game should demand.

Windows 7 review (Prepare for a messy review) - Over 100 hours non-steam:
Dungeon siege is an old series of 3d hack and slash games,very fast paced this one being from 2002 that made me start gaming on pc and brought me here where I am today. Of course the graphics are out dated but who really cares when the game brings you so much content that's enjoyable. There are A LOT of items in this game with different rarities ,there are 2 shops in every town and area so you can get better gear. You can be a warrior,an archer,a mage (nature or combat magic) or a hybrid determined by strength - warrior,dexterity - archer and intelligence - mage. You have the option to take other characters with you but I think they're a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(you can steal items from the ones you get for free then leave them there hue hue hue), I like to be alone and strong. I always play as a warrior because that's what I did back in the day. A playthrough will last way more than 15 hours if you actually take a look at the game because it actually has secrets , easter eggs and puzzles that are pretty fun and they reward you with rare items. It actually has co-op multiplayer but I don't have much to say about it since I only tried it like 2 times and I didin't get to finish the game, it may not work. If you're playing for the first time you may want to play on medium because it's the most enjoyable difficulty. The game has different mobs and bosses for each area  you are in so you don't have to fight the same creatures for the entire game, you don't go back so you'll only see new places. You can play at 1920x1080 there are guides on steam about how to do it, also there is a DLC for this game called legends of the aranna and you can find guides for it as well easily, I really recommend the DLC because it's another campaign that lasts A LONG TIME as well, more than 7-10 hours anyway. The review is more for the game than the steam version but you can get this game on sale for less than 3 dollars.. just buy it.
And remember... ALWAYS SAVE THE GAME EVERY 10 MINUTES!

Way back in 1999 a PC Game was released by Eidos that redefined not only what an FPS could be, but also what an RPG could be. It's sequel was, for want of a better word, forgettable. When DE:HR came out originally, I remember it being plagued with problems ranging from glitchy, stupid AI and baffling game mechanics to dodgy textures and other worldly physics.
DE:HR - Director's Cut manages to fix a lot of these problems. One good example is when in a firefight with multiple assailants in a crowded area, the AI no longer responds like some suicidal maniac running either directly into your crosshairs or running away, twitching and shooting at where you were a good 20 seconds ago. They actually hide, plan, shoot from behind cover, throw grenades to flush you out etc.
The graphics have also improved somewhat; they're still a bit dodgy in places, but there's certainly discernible differences. There's more realistic lighting indoors, proper fogging and better reflections.
Throughout the game you'll find that the music will quite often grab you and remind you of the game's musical influences from people like Coil, Vangelis and Gary Numan. The quality of sound effects are as one would expect from a high-end developer, top-notch, and of course the voice-acting remains some of the best out there, too.
I suppose the most important element of all this is of course that you are no longer obliged to have to engage in boss fights, as with this version it's now possible to kill them without direct confrontation (plus, killing them doesn't count against your pacifist rating).
The two DLCs The Missing Link and the Pre-Order Bonus Mission where you rescue Tong's son, are now seamlessly integrated into the game, along with another extra - the Commentary by the makers of the game, included as an optional, much like in the HL2 games.
Bottom Line : If you've not yet had the chance, or if you've not played it in a couple years, this is a fantastic package. It offers better graphics, improved gameplay and a genuinely fun commentary from the makers of the game.
The game's intriguing cyberpunk meets rennaissance italy aesthetic, clever open-ended gameplay mechanics and thought provoking storyline are as fresh as ever, and now that so many bugs have been fixed, there's now no reason not to play this fantastic foray into the life of rogueish, augmented anti-hero, Adam Jensen.

Aura Kingdom is a free to play (mmo) game licensed by Aeria Games. During my first week into the game, I was greeted with the traditional anime esc story about how you are the main character and the world revolves around you. Now this being an MMO I grew tired of reading through everyones dialouge and skipped most of the story until I found myself in Navea. Navea is the main hub for players to sell their items, fight players, window shop, etc. Having made my way to lvl 20 and viewing everyone elses cool costumes and items, I found myself looking through the Auction House. I will say this right now... DO NOT spend any money on this game. Every item can be obtained by completing quests or dungeon running, although it will take far longer your wallet will be thanking you in the end.
Now that the fancy costumes are out of the way, we can begin talking about the combat system. Combat in Aura Kingdom is very... spammy? Without knowing any better, you will soon be allocating all your combat points into speed which will reduce the cooldown on all of your abilities. Now with infinite ability spamming, the bosses in this game are a lot easier and reduce the amount of time you spend in dungeons. All in all, the combat system is nice but very broken with the cooldown on all of your abilities... especially the bard class.
Would I recommend the game? Yes. Aura Kingdom is a free to play game with a lot potential but is wasted on broken builds and abilities. However, the world is very fruity and with new patches being released every month or so it makes up for the mistakes that it clearly made.

I only picked this up today and I can't seem to put it down. I've tried a few free-to-play MMOs in the past (even stuck around on one), but while this game's still got all the similar elements I'm used to in the genre, it's nevertheless the best one I've encountered so far. It's just so enjoyable that I mowed through several hours without realizing it; somehow the seeminly run of the mill repetitive questing wasn't even remotely tedious. But even without that in mind I find that even the battling feels different; it's just so smooth, and the characters are engaging enough to make me invested.
Not only that, but as a customization drunkard I thrive off of the opportunity to dress up my character, and Aura delivers early on with costume alternatives available with in-game coin. There's that and the fact that there are so many classes to satisfy my needs for mulling over options for way too long.
From what I've experienced so far gameplay-wise, it's like the MMOs I used to like--only polished, improved, and just generally more friendly. And I'm not talking about the community; the game itself just lets you play in whichever way makes you the most comfortable. That's not to say the community's bad, I just tend to solo due to shyness and the like, and the thing about several other games in this family is that keeping to yourself is indirectly frowned upon. You'll realize that it's harder, not as enjoyable--sometimes impossible--to play without teaming up at least once. So far, while still not holding my hand, Aura's given me free reigns to solo to my heart's content.
Incidentally, that even led me to join guilds and initiate interactions, so go figure. All they had to do was to let me go at it if I wanted to, not because I had to, and suddenly it was more appealing and more enjoyable in equal measure.
These thoughts are kind of all over the place, I realize, but I just have to say I'm glad I came across an MMORPG that's both relaxing, enjoyable and manageable for someone like me. Of course, I'm certain there are plenty of titles like it, but this is definitely the first for me that ended up being just right. It's a rare occasion for someone so bone-numbingly picky.

PLEASE NOTE WHEN PURCHASING:

Perfect for controller supported games. Don't have an Xbox Controller? Get this.

What I Expected:
I was immediately interested in any controller made by Valve because I trusted them to do come up with a driver support and controll configuration that would JUST WORK.  I've been frustrated for years trying to use drivers that would support my PS3 controllers.
What I Got:
I was not dissapointed.  Most games work brilliantly with no need for custom configurations at all.  A lot of games that don't even have controller support STILL work well because the track pad and on-screen steam keyboard work really well for general PC use.  I've got a custom built HTPC and I have traditionally been using a wireless keyboard and mouse on a lapdesk from my couch.  Now I feel like I can use the Steam controller for everything that I'll be doing on an HTPC anyway.
When custom configuration was needed, Valve exceeded my expectations by providing reccommended and community shared configs.  So for most popular games, I usually STILL don't have to do the custom configuration myself, I just install somebody elses.  Even if there are no configs available, there's also the option to start from a configuration template.
It is what it is and not what it isn't:
Some people may complain that it's not as good as a mouse and keyboard, some people may also complain that it's not as good as an XBox controller, but for those of us who are looking for something that is a little of both and want to be in FULL control of how the controls are mapped, the Steam Controller delivers flawlessly.
Multi-Player Support:
I'll start by saying the the multi-player support out-of-the-box on several games is far easier to set up than it EVER has been using PS3 controllers.  People using XBox controllers may not have had as many problems with this in the past as I have due to better driver support.  In my case at any rate, it was a marked improvement for MOST games.
That said, there were still some games where it seemed I just could not get multiple controllers working.  The one benefit of the doubt I'll give here is, these are the same games I had to muck around a lot with the settings to get to work with my PS3 controllers.  So it could just be that my settings are now causing problems with the Steam Controllers.
In spite of that, for the most part it really was a breaze to have multiple controllers, even one's registered to different accounts worked just fine.  My brother came over with his control and could plug in his dongle, turn his controller on and just play, no hassle with guest controllers at all.
Cons?:
The only con, and it's not really a con after all, is that in order to get the best support you absolutlely should be in Big Picture mode.  I tried to play Dirt 3 with multiple steam controllers while not in Big Picture mode and the controller key mapping was oddly split between the two controllers.  So watch out for that.  The reason this is not REALLY a con though, is that I was bery pleasantly surprised with all of the improvements valve has made to Big Picture mode, and honestly, they've tailored it quite well to the Steam Controller so that using them together is a really good user experience.  There are still some things I haven't been able to figure out how to do in the Big Picure mode, like install games to a specific steam folder/drive for example.
Conclusion:
I am more than pleased with this controller and would strongly recommended it to anyone who is not happy with their current controller and multi-player support on PC games.  You may find, as I did, that is just a really good general purpose input device for HTPCs as well.

This game is KOTOR in Little big Chinatown. It's more homage to the Chinese Marital-art house asthetic than an RPG set in a faithflly re-created Ancient China, which will hit you as soon as the Steampunk technology comes into play.
If you've played the Bioware Knights franchise, this game will feel right at home to you. The dialogue system, the alignment system, the influence over companions, etc. is all inherited from the 1st game.
The only serious deviation is askewing of realtime-turn-based combat, for 3rd person combat. You click, and your character attacks, you can move and manuever your character at will.
There is also a shoot-em' up mini-game which, at times I think clashes with the rest of the game in tone, but otherwise is memorable where most of BIoware's mini games were either boring or insufferable.
Perhaps the most memorable feature to this game? The Cast. Alot of star power arrived for this outing, Nathan Fillion, Brian Doyle Murray, Armin Shimerman, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly John Cleese, and anyone whose played adapation titles like Devil May Cry or Final Fantasy 9 or Armored Core 4 will recognize Kari Wahlgren.
I honestly can't recommend this game enough, but be warned, Imperfect Customer has it right, you do need to mess with some files inorder to get the game both to work, and for your cursor (the mouse pointer) to appear.
If you're experiencing this problem download this file and put it into your Jade Empire directory:
It's an old Jade Empire exe renamed "JadeEmpireLauncher" so steam will launch it instead of the launcher which can end in error. You still need to launch the game from Steam though, clicking on it won't do anything.
Your Jade Empire Directory can be found in Steam-> SteamApps -> Common-> Jade Empire.

-Pros:
Pretty fun when teams are balanced
Great Nam' feeling
New bandaging system is a huge improvement over the red orchestra one
Guns feel right
Some maps are amazing especially the new ones added in the Anzac update
Gunplay feels pretty damn good and tense, where one mistake or unchecked corner can lead to a horrible death (well that when the hitreg is working)
Sound design is pretty great, guns sound distinct
-Cons:
Best strategy in game is getting to a good spot, seriously while checking corners, gunplay and strategy still play a big part the fact is doing well is 90% based on getting to cheeky spots where you can headglitch people and avoid being GL'd
There is almost no communication or supressing fire use since popping on a mg and laying in supressive fire is inviting a instant sniper bullet/GL since tracers give your position away and accomplishing nothing by your troubles since it's hard to coordinate an advance with teammates (use a smoke for advancing through firelanes it's way easier)
Hitreg is horrible (the default for servers is a tickrate of 20) if you have any latency (believe me there aren't many servers with people so depending where you live you are SOL in that department)
Maps are very crowded and way too easy to cover all the aproachs, because of that I recomend playing on 32 man servers, avoiding Hue city and Hill 937 or playing supremacy since those spread people out more and allow for more tactical play rather than meatgriding on the frontlines the entire match (just beware that sometimes it turns into a cluster♥♥♥♥ of people running everywhere without any battlelines but those can be fun in it's own right)
Some maps have issues that still aren't patched (like the fact when the americans run out of tickets in Hill 937 the spawn protection isn't disabled
Tied to the hitreg is that damage is location based, wich is fine on itself but tied to the inconsistent hitreg it leads to strange situations where you can shoot someone two times in the upper chest with a 7.62x39 and they run to safety while in others you shoot a enemy once in the shoulder or abdomen with a pistol and they drop instantly
Material penetration is also inconsistent, I've dropped people shooting through concrete walls with a shotgun while other times I had them survive being shot by a 7.62x51mm because some straw bale wall was in the way
Tied with the above explosions and flames interact pretty weirdly with the game geometry, sometimes people can survive grenades and being showered with napalm because a thin wooden wall was in the way and deflected everything, other times they get turned into red paste by a explosion happening on the other side of a wall or burned to a crisp by napalm being spewed from a corner 3 meters away (on that note stay away from teamates with flamethrowers unless you want to be burned to death by some lick of flame bouncing from a wall and hitting you)
Like I said before lack of communication makes any coordination impossible, some spots and important positions become deathtraps because you can't coordinate with people to hold multiple angles, so if possible get some friends to play with you, the game is massively better with them
Overall I had a lot of fun playing it but I just can't recommend it to everyone because it's too darn inconsistent, so if you got a good consistent internet connection, live in the EU or the continental US and has some friends to play with you then yes, get this game since while you're still going to run into some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (mostly by the hitreg) it won't be as annoying if you have low ping and a squad you can communicate with, otherwise it might be better looking elsewhere for this kind of action.

In the current video game market, there seems to be a massive overflow of "gun games". Anyone who has played Borderlands, Team Fortress 2, or Call of Duty knows what I am talking about. Games that are just one massive setpiece moment full of guns and explosions with a flimsy story, if any. Games where the only choices are "Should I kill this guy with this gun, or that gun?"
I can proudly say that Deus Ex is not one of those games.
Before Mass Effect and Dishonored took the approch of having a good storyline while introducing permanent choices, Deus Ex and its sequels have been pefecting this formula for more than ten years. The latest of these games, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, is continuing this tradition started out by its predecessors. In this game, almost anything is fair game. Do you want to play a stealth game? This game's got it. How about a crazy run-and-gun? Got that too. You can choose not to kill anyone at all. However, the biggest point this game has to offer is the choices. Once you make a choice, it is permanent, and you can very rarely take it back. And these are not small things like whether or not I should upgrade this. There are bigger choices here. For example, later in the game you have to choose to either kill off the one person who could testify against the bad guys, or kill off all the innocent people that they were experimenting on. Its choices like this that make you think long and hard about your humanity-and during the final choice, the humanity of the world.
In short, this game has so much to offer that one playthrough is not enough to cover it all. I highly reccomend this game to any one with a spare twenty dollars. It is a must-have.

Details:
I decided to play this with the modern graphics throughout, which look great. You can toggle back to classic version graphics anytime if you prefer. The only thing I disliked was that hot spots on the map (in bird's eye view) can be difficult to locate unless you try hovering your cursor over a small, specific set of pixels. The story is fresh and full of humour, although dialogue can be draggy. I was able to skip whole cutscenes by hitting backspace. However, I couldn't find any way of fast-forwarding conversations on a sentence by sentence basis even though I read the dialogue text before the voice-over was done. That really killed any incentive for me to replay the game. The voice-overs were fantastic by the way. They gave the characters personality and made the whole experience more enjoyable. Also love all the music, which changes depending on the scene.
Many puzzles require examining every item in your inventory carefully, or trying different combinations of actions. Some puzzles have completely out-of-the-box solutions which players may have trouble figuring out on your own. Fortunately, there is a hint system that gives you clues on how to solve puzzles and eventually specific instructions. I have no idea how players in the past completed the game without a guidebook, short of applying trial and error for hours. The hint system is the best feature and a solid selling point of the remastered version.

Wow, what a product. Let me start by saying that i was on the fence about this controller BUT after reading through pages of mixed reviews, I decided to give it a try. So glad that i did. For a first time controller from Valve I believe they did an excellent job and let me tell you why.
Customization - Is extremely detailed. You can literally customize every single button and click of the controller for each individual game or you can scroll through some community user customized templates and just automatically use the template you think is best for you!
Comfort - The controller feels very good in the hands. Its very light-weight and the smooth curves just gives it an overall comfortable feel.
Battery Life - From what I can tell so far, the controller doesnt hardly consume much battery power during use. The 2 AA batteries that come included seem to still be fully charged even after several days of use. A bug/glitch? time will tell.
Automatic gamepad support  - For games that do not support controllers, the steam controller automatically simulates a mouse/keyboard so you can play ANY game with the steam controller. I do however recommend using an xbox controller for certain games. Fighting games or platformers. This controller seems to really shine with top down view games/Shooters.
Plug and Play - The controller requires absolutely no setup what so ever. I got a pop up box to install a firmware update so the controller would be up to date. Took less than 10 seconds.
Track Pad - Is very responsive and does a great job at simulating a mouse. Sometimes a little too responsive. I have to keep sensitivity pretty low on most games because I tend to move my thumbs a little too far too fast.
Ok now on to some Cons. Yes there are a few flaws BUT mainly due to it being a new product and most users just arent Pre-trained for a controller like this. Ill make a Short list and do an overall description at the end because they are self explanatory.
1. Button Layout/Size
2. The D-Pad is (in my opinion too large) for what its needed for.
3. Learning Curve is pretty high.
4. The D-Pad and Trackpad are very loud when pressed. (Thats just me being picky though). You can be heard from a good distance pressing buttons lol. So good luck trying to be quiet during those late night gaming sessions.
Overall the bad points can be eventually overcome with practice. This is a new product that users just arent use to but I assure you, time will make this controller feel like an absolute dream to play with. Think of the N64 when we saw one oddly placed thumbstick and a weird button layout, the we hit the Dual shock controllers and was like WTF now we got 2 thumbsticks AND a bunch of buttons lol. Ok enough with the references, im sure you get the point im trying to make. Practice makes perfect.
Final Thoughts - For those not sure about the purchase. Just Do It! The negative reviews are mainly users that tried the controller out for a day or two and just didnt get the hang of it and now they are mad because they felt like they threw $50 away.
From a rating of 1-10, I give this controller a very solid 8 !

A solid controller IF you use "Big Picture Mode". The main attraction tot eh controller is the fully customizable touch pads. These works great as long as the games you're going to use have 2 things in common. First, they need to use the steam overlay in game. If not, then most games wont read the updated mapping and will switch to defaults. Games that recognize it as an xbox controller have no issues however since the auto-mapping is very tight in those cases. Second, if the game can't be launched through Big Picture Mode, then the settings of the controller can't be changed on the fly and the games have no updated mappings. For these reasons things like Binding of Isaac (original) don't work with the controller without external app support which more or less defeats the purpose. Also, many games that run through DosBox will be hit or miss. Something like SW Dark Forces that has fixed controls will again, not work without external app supoort.  A game like Thief Gold however, with fully mappable controls, works fine with some patience and tweaking.
All in all I do recommend the controller to anyone with an extensive library of mouse games that wants a universal contorller to handle gamepad games and mouse games alike. There is one major gripe I have as well that I have to mention since it's such an irritating circumstance. The preorder bonuses for the controller would have been great but I bought the controller right after it came out with no preorder. At that point I understand that there would have been no free content but now that I own one, there is suddenly a Christmas pack-in that includes LFD2 and Counter-strike, While it shouldn't be a deal breaker either way, it is a very irritating move to make deals before and after that have now cheated any consumers who bought it between 24 after launch and a few days ago.
All in all, as I said before, the controller is great but you need to have patience and a library that will play nicely. With time though, I'm sure this will a PC necessity for most gamers in today's market.

April 2014.   I always wanted to play this game a long time ago ~2008...now I see it still selling on steam, so I give it a try since I have time now (2014)...It did not work for me recently in April 2014 and on windows 8 but still selling on steam.   Renaming the file to fix does not work either.
But I found a fix on the net in one for the steam forum somewhere and related to other older games... Like the renaming fix, only the main exe works as workaround.    To fix, you need to add "steam" to your win8 environment PATH variable.
Here's how for windows 8:
1. control panel -> system icon -> Advanced system settings -> (this launch windows system properties)
2. Advanced tab -> click on "environment variables" button.  (this launch environment variables user interface)
3. on bottom section, inside system variables, select "PATH" variable from list.
4. click edit button at bottom to edit PATH variable that you select above (3).
5. append to variable value the text ";C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam;"  Make notice semicolon before and after and no blank space outside of ;
click cancel to abort anytime.
step 5 is important, do not mess up.  Or you may have to reinstall your computer.  Do not click okay until you are sure you did not mess up.   You can always come back and fix if you can retype the whole entire  string content from memory.   Click cancel to abort anytime.   Click okay when you are sure you did it right.  FYI: the entire string content is similar on most computer...you are fine if you make typo, just go back and edit.   Deleting and forgot entry is where re-install windows is a fix.  Here is what entire string content looks like on mine minus qoutes minus ":
"C:\WINDOWS\system32;C:\WINDOWS;C:\WINDOWS\System32\Wbem;C:\WINDOWS\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\;C:\Program Files (x86)\ATI
Files (x86)\Steam;"
6. reboot computer to get environment path variable updated.?  play.

Live the life of a Monster, from birth to elderhood and beyond, making decisions that affect the world of Monsters and Humans.
You live in the village of Omen, and your favorite snack is the fingers of small children. As a Monster, you pop up in the most interesting places — what do you do when three angry bears discover a young child in their cabin? Or when you spy a wolf hunting down that woman with the red cloak?
As a Monsterling, your choices are simple ones. Do you chase those poor little mice (+1 Ferocity) or protect them from the dogs (+1 Kindness)? Do you come clean about that fungus your friends ate (+1 Honesty) or cover for them (+1 Bravery)? As a youth, your choices determine your personality.
But all youngins must grow up. Monsters and Humans have been at odds for centuries, and there are Human villages on the other side of the enchanted woods. When Human children get lost in those dark and winding thickets, do you terrorize them for fun (+1 Ferocity)? Do you help return them to Human civilization to prove that not all Monsters are to be feared and hated (+1 Kindness)? Or do you fatten them up for Human foie gras — a Monster delicacy? All this, to the backdrop of increasing tensions between Monster- and Humankind.
