From the unparalled ingenuity behind Drakengard comes a cleverly crafted noir-steampunk masterpiece embellished with a uniquely cynical storyline and has some pretty gratifying hack-and-slash mechanics thrown in for good measure. Set in a post-apocalyptic, dystopian environment, NieR:Automata's visceral depiction of the desperate struggle between androids and machines accompanied by its raw social implications make it more than just a game in many aspects. While NieR isn't meant to be psychologically "fun" by any length (though fighting machines can be potentially therapeutic to some), it certainly brings about a fresh new take on the genre by sporting one of the most impressive and meaningful plots I've ever seen dedicated to a game, a defining element which sets it well apart from most other conventional action games in the market. One could even classify it as more of a rather-interactive narrative device to bridge the gaps of the prequels and to extend upon the trilogy that was brought to life by the NieR series. However, if you've never had a chance to experience the prequels such as Gestalt or Replicant, this is a good place to start as the campaign is likened to a reboot while still retaining some relevant intricacies to the original lore. Though you'll most likely be left with a bunch of post-completion questions that can only be answered with prior events. Getting to the end by acquiring all the story endings is one thing, uncovering the deeper secrets buried within the game and following the characters' personalities as they weave into greater mythos are an entirely different endeavour altogether. As with any Yoko Taro creation, be prepared for an emotional roller-coaster ride of your lifetime riddled with insidious plot twists and painful decisions to contend with.
If you're looking to acquire the game right now, I highly recommend that you check out the
mod. This essential third-party mod is designed to simultaneously rectify any screen resolution anomalies while optimizing overall performance considerably (by selectively reducing negligible graphic features for improved framerates). Do take note that this port has received widespread controversy with respect to performance stability and startup issues are rampant for most systems. For my case however, playing NieR without a controller was really something to get used to for me due to the abnormally sticky camera movements delivered by the mouse (I had to eventually forgo the use of it in favour of the arrow keys for camera manipulation).

Jade Empire is a game that was originally made for the Xbox in 2005, and even now, nearly a decade after realease, it's still a popular, enjoyable, and fantastic video game.
Set in a fantastical version of Eastern Asia, you play as a student under the martial arts master, Master Li. During your days of training, your village is beset by a group of assassins who seem to be targetting you and Li specifically. What follows is an epic, sprawling adventure that takes you across the whole of the Empire. Along the way you gather up party members and characters, each with their own memorable (and evolving) personalities.
A fluid, if slightly clunky, combat system holds this game together, and the addition of enjoyable scenery and complementing music only make the game more fun to play. This is something you want to spend hours, days, even weeks playing. As well, the game is (and has before) easily moddable, so combat can become even more varied without breaking game pace or focus.
Buy this game. Even if it's not on sale, buy this game. It's exceedingly fun, and one of the few games that made me want to play it again.

Fallout 2 is the sequel to one of my favorite RPG's of all time and it does a superb job of the lifting the mantle of the original Fallout even if it does have it's flaws.
Fallout 2 sets you as the descendant of the original Vault Dweller who we now learned founded a small tribe near the Californian coast following the events of the original. This tribe has now fallen on hard times and as the direct descendant of the Vault Dweller you are charged with going out into the world and finding a mythical Vault device known as the G.E.C.K. This device, the elder of your village believe, have the power to turn the part of the wasteland into an utopia and ensure the tribe's future.
You start off the game with a somewhat lackluster tutorial that introduces you to the basic elements of the game however it is only once you leave this initial area and are ready to depart your childhood village for the first time that the game truly comes into it's own. The massive world map at your feet with no restrictions on where to go and who to see.
The mechanics are much the same as the original. Isometric turn-based role playing game using the S.P.E.C.I.A.L system for character development. It is however in the open nature of the game that you find it's soul. Made a female character with high charisma? You might be able to charm, or sleep, your way past several encounters. Made a character with incredibly low intelligence? All of the sudden your dialog responses are just various grunts and the people you encounter will treat you as a freak of nature.
Even most of the storyline can be skipped if you know where to go and almost every task you are given in the game can be solved in a myriad of ways, many options not even becoming apparent to you unless you have the needed skills or made some particular choices beforehand.
The game does have some shortcomings. The 4th wall breaking that was rare in the original are much more commonplace and several characters and areas just feel out of place with the rest of the game.
New Reno in particular, a gambling town complete with mafia families fighting for control and a working porn studio takes you completely out of the game and makes for a rather disappointing experience.
Fallout 2 has all the qualities that made the original one of the greatest RPG's ever and it improves on many aspects of it with better companion AI and a much larger map. It's faults however do weight heavily and keep it from surpassing it's predecessor. It is still one of the greatest RPG's ever to be made and if you are a fan of open ended RPG games and intelligent story and dialog then it should be a definite purchase.

The first video game I played was GTA3, all the way back in 2001, on the PS2. I didn't enjoy it very much (and still don't enjoy GTA-style games in general). The second game I ever played was much better - Age of Empires 2, on the PC. Why do I bring this up? Because it's important to note that I started playing video games well beyond the era of the text-based adventures and RPG's of the 80's. Which is important to note because Monster Loves You! is essentially a text-based adventure game, albiet one that doesn't require typing and has a graphical interface.
It's definitely a solid game, with a clearly defined goal that you're working towards, and it's probably the right length for a modern text-based adventure. The graphical interface is cutesy enough, and is very effective in capturing the player's interest. The game also successfully incorporates some clever RPG-like stat-building, with a series of stats that can be raised or lowered depending on the conversation options the player chooses. All these elements combine into a lighter game that will be enjoyed more by casual gamers than those that play more seriously.
Which is why I can't recommend this game; most people on Steam simply won't enjoy it for long enough to get their money's worth. While I enjoyed it, that was only for 51 minutes; I have no desire to play through the game again. That's not the fault of the game, moreso the fault of the genre. Gamers have simply moved on from the days of the text-based adventure, and now prefer their RPG stats to be accomponied by a 3-dimensional world that they experience through the eyes of a character they make. If you enjoy text-based adventures or more casual games, than this is a game that you'll get multiple hours of enjoyment from. Otherwise, the stat-building and graphical depiction of the story simply won't be enough to keep you captivated beyond the first playthrough.

Are you old enough to remember Alter Ego? The mid-eighties life-sim is a major influence over this quirky title.
Essentially entirely text-based, you click your way through multiple-choice scenarios, which determine the personality of your monster, as you guide it through the life-cycle. It's certainly charming, but quickly became dull, and didn't (to my mind) hold much replay value. There are some stats being tracked 'under the hood' and achievement chasers might care to spend time there, but for me a couple of playthroughs was more than enough. Younger players will probably revel in the fantasy, but it might be more wordy then their patience will stand?
The major CON compared to Alter Ego is that the events (or specifically, their outcomes) are even more random: the authors have tried to give 'Monster World' a consistent logic, but it can be pretty hard to second-guess. Perhaps life is like that?

Monster Loves You! is a text-based choose your own adventure game. You guide your monster through stages of its life, your actions determining your monster's attributes, such as ferocity, cleverness, and bravery.
While each stage of life has multiple short adventures to take your monster on, they rarely influence each other, beyond some of them becoming easier depending on which 'stats' you've leveled up beforehand. It isn't until the latter of the game, which you may or may not reach due to your decisions in game, where you begin having an influence on anything beyond your monster village and the woods around it.
Monster society is darkly humour- black comedy abounds. You meet many different fairytale creatures and have an opportunity to try and befriend or viciously murder and eat all of them. The soundtrack and visuals are bright and cartoonish, and fit perfectly.
Each play-through will take you about twenty to thirty minutes, depending on how fast of a reader you are, and getting most of the endings is pretty intuitive. It's a good game to pass the time.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a combination of everything that is good about videogame storytelling. It displays extraordinary depth, meaningful choices, and most of all, only the bare minimum of exposition.
As a game, it's not perfect. It's severely held back by its engine, which looks dated even for 2011. Limitations in its mechanical capabilities often prevented the dev team from implementing their vision. The controls are every so slightly awkward, especially the cover system and item management controls. The game mechanics have their share of imperfections as well, such as the stamina system which is strangely divided between energy and breath, and the very limited opportunities that you will get to use the long-range weapons in the game.
Time and budget constraints caused major parts of the storyline and setting to be cut. We only got one of them back, in the form of the Missing Link DLC, now seamlessly integrated into this Director's Cut release.
But the juice of the game is in the setting, the backstory, the characters, the art style and the music. And now, with Director's Cut, you can add hours and hours of developer commentary to that list.
Much like the original 2011 release, the DX:HR Director's Cut release had issues on launch. Bugs related to performance, texturing, audio, and game crashes were widely reported across different PC configurations. These problems were patched by Eidos Montreal, and at least for me, the game now runs well. Terrible mouse lag was also present on Windows 8.1 machines, but Microsoft fixed this problem with the KB2908279 update, downloadable from their website.
The value of your Director's Cut purchase will be in the commentary track. The gameplay improvements are concentrated in very specific areas, not worth the purchase price. The graphical improvements are arguably a half-step backwards, since the new release tones down the distinctive yellow hue of the original, leaving the rest of the graphics engine largely untouched.
Nitpicks aside, make no mistake: the immersive nature of DX:HR makes it a must-have. It's so cheap there's no reason not to make the purchase.

I'm sure many will disagree, but I believe this to be the best in the DS Series. DS 2 just didn't do it for me. I didn't like the story at all. The game was boring and tedious. DS 3, same thing, I just didn't like it. Just goes to show you that sometimes, the originals are the best, and that is certainly true with DS 1, for it kicks major booty. For a game that is from 2002, the graphics are excellent. I personally love the outdoor scenery. It's so vivid and colorful, and was nicely done. I sometimes find myself traveling along and stopping my party just to gaze at the wonderful detailed world. The game has a Night/Day Cycle, weather effects, an awesome sound track and superb ambient sounds. The game world really comes alive. But the best part of DS 1 is the story. It's one of the best I've played in a game, and the narrated cut-scenes are just great.
Some like to compare this to Diablo II, but there is no comparison. Although Diablo II is one of the best games ever made, DS is nothing like it, at all. Diablo II is a dark fantasy hack and slash with very little RPG element. DS is an action fantasy RPG. There is much more than just hack and slash in this game. Diablo II gets very boring, very fast. It's just a click-fest with some quests, that's it.
Some of the things I love about DS 1 is how (unlike Diablo), you don't need to keep clicking on an enemy to attack. I about wore my index finger out on Diablo II from clicking the mouse so much. The drop system is also good. Not too much, not too little. It's just right. And if you have the stand alone expansion, LOA (Legends of Aranna), the game is even better.
The Original Campaign is quite long, consisting of 9 Chapters to keep you well entertained. You will meet and talk to tons of people which have unique personalities. Many are voiced extremely well. The game also has a nice modding community.

I cannot recommend the Steam version in its current state, simply because it's broken (i.e. "non-working") beyond belief. This seems to not only be because of a "we don't care" attitude on Bioware's part, but also on Valve/Steam parts for letting things into the Steam shop that obviously haven't been QA'd AT ALL. This basically forces users to "jumping through hoops" like resorting to running Steam as Administrator, "registry hacking", manipulating broken config game files, renaming game executables and so on, without any guarantee that the game will run in the end anyway. Most of the problems are well-known (i.e. mentioned numerous times on forums here at Steam and Bioware), but there seem to be neither official solutions nor statements nor any signs of pressure from Steam towards Bioware to fix it.
* "Can't Find Steam error" : The most blatant proof that Steam didn't QA the Steam Version. The initial setup will throw this error message at your face unless you start the STEAM CLIENT itself in Administrator Mode (!). As the game requires admin privileges, and Interprocess Communcation between game and steam (with Steam_api.dll for Overlay / DRM) requires both executables to have admin privileges. Basic programming mistake on Biowares part? Non-existing QA on Steam's part?
* Verify integrity of the game cache throws you into a loop: Got "2 files failed and will be reaquired" every time you try from the steam client? In this case: Good luck. (Steam's fault)
* Crashing Game Configuration Dialog: The game configuration laucher crashes while trying to discover your hardware? You're out of luck unless you start renaming files / editing the registry / create a valid xml config file. (Bioware's fault)
* Dead-locking game right at the beginning: You only get the initial loading screen where you only see a background image? Afaik, there is no known solution to this problem at this time. (Bioware's fault)
There are speculations that the last 2 points might be caused by the "Optimus" technology from NVidia (modern Laptops with dedicated graphics cards have 2 cards: One integrated HDxxxx Intel version inside your CPU and one dedicated NVidia / ATI card). If that were true, it would mean that most laptops with dedicated graphic hardware (from NVidia) won't run this game at all. This is only *speculation* though.

I got my Steam Controler with my purchase of the Steam Machine.  The controller started out with a few bugs but throughout the whole process of getting the controler and using it I have had a mostly positive experience.  It's the middlepath of controlers.  Depending on the game you are playing it will be like settling.  You can use it for games that use controller or keyboard.  However, it doesn't excel at each of those input methods.
Irritating, because the vast majority of controller supported games are exclusively of the Xbox variety.

Good and bad.  As a controller for using Windows on your TV, it rocks.  I adapted very quickly to using the touch pad as a mouse and it's replaced my actual mouse for casual-TV controlling.
As a gamepad, it's comfortable, INSANELY customizable, and has cool features like the bottom paddles (which I love).
There's one very basic downside: for games designed for normal controllers (Xbox 360), as most action-platformers are, the thumb pad just doesn't compare to a second joystick.  It takes forever to get used to, no matter how I configured it.  Resetting my thumb to the center of the pad every time I lift off is awkward, and it just can't be as responsive as a physical stick.  No amount of haptic feedback (which I always disable as it just annoys me) can compensate for the tactile feedback of the stick hitting the edges of its range.
As for mouse-designed games like FPSs, don't ask me.  I messed with it for a bit and decided that, you know, wireless mice already exist.
Basically, it ALMOST accomplishes what it set out to do, and I applaud the effort and innovation.  But if I ask my brother to play a game with me, he demands my old 360 controller before he'll even consider it.  For a console-only gamer like him, the learning curve simply isn't worth it.

A classic tale of a Hero, The Chosen One, who collects his band of companions on the way to defeat the Bad Guy. When you think of Bioware, you usually either associate the company with either hilariously over the top fantasy romance, gritty bloody or D&D Fantasy and sci-fi moral guided RPG shoot from cover games.
But there was a time where they worked on a game with a very different setting and combat system. This is the game, and the settling is the sadly rarely used Chinese Fantasy. Jade Empire is a very different beast for what we now expect from modern Bioware games. Originally for the first Xbox and ported to the PC around 2007 back in the days where STEAM was also very different and oddly enough not well remembered.
I had fun playing Jade Empire. It was something new, despite the now dated graphics. It was something fresh despite the system limitations like being limited to a single companion and being one of the shorter Bioware games I have played. A good game always has a rock solid foundation. Very few games bother to cover China at all.  The combat system in this game is very unique and reminds me a lot of the more modern but quite different open world game Sleeping Dogs. You fight with WASD, general movement and using techniques (spells) that are fueled by a chi (mana) meter. This makes fighting a lot more fluid and interesting that the usual turn based stuff older RPG games are associated with and there is a simple wonder of going all Bruce Lee (and yes, one of the male main character models pretty much is a tribute to Bruce Lee) and kicking♥♥♥♥♥while staying mobile.
You aren't limited to your fists, there is the usual slightly bland array of metal weaponry and Chinese Magic style techniques some of which transform you into mythical fantasy beasts of the era. The companions themselves, whilst limited in combat are quite interesting like with all Bioware games. There is even the token 'Drunken Style Master' who helps boost you with buffs of well wine really. One of my personal favourite quests in the game is a much more interesting Arena quest that makes the younger Oblivion one seem hilariously bland and boring in comparism. Oh and John Cleese has a cameo too in which he plays an Arrogant♥♥♥♥♥♥of an Elizbethan Explorer who debates and fights you.
Sadly there are some flaws. Like I mentioned before the game is short, I played it one and off for an hour or two for the last few weeks and just shaved past the eighteen hour mark before completing it. Once you finish the Imperial City portion of the game pacing gets incredibly rushed and the scant quest based hub areas vanish completely. The storyline demands you to get it done and over with.
And the Gem system really could have done with some more thought. But these things are pretty minor. The most disturbing issue was the fact this game is one of the older titles that is broken due to STEAM constantly changing but I found a player bashed up fix in the STEAM community forums which was easily to install and get working in about a minute.
So final opinion really, if you are looking for something new and interesting in both setting and combat system RPG wise and don't mind the length and the age of the game you will enjoy Jade Empire. If you don't click with Martial Arts, Fantasy China or would rather have a more relaxed combat system I might suggest looking into amazingly well written Planescape Torment instead which is different enough to take a break from the more boring old school RPG games.
Worth picking up in a sale if it sparks your interest? Go ahead. Even outside the sale, the price is still pretty cheap and it will run like a charm now even on what we would consider old hardware in space year 2013/14.

Dungeon Siege was the first game created by Gas powered games. Founded by Chris Taylor, who created such beloved games like Total Annihilation.
Dungeon Siege is a party based rpg. You play as a humble farmer who has his/her farm attacked by an evil race called the "Krug". Taking it upon themselves, you then go from town to town ridding the land of whatever evil you find on a journey to destroy the source of it. The plot to Dungeon Siege isn't particularly interesting nor particularly fleshed out or focused upon. It's a background distraction that serves to get you from place to place.
What Dungeon Siege excels at is in the gameplay department. The entirety of the experience of Dungeon Siege is unabridged. It takes place in a world completely without loading screens. Even while transitioning from the overworld to dungeons. This is by far the most impressive thing the game does and it feels very authentic. Dungeon Siege feels like an odyssey, where you are constantly moving forward on a trek. It is also absurdly long and has an enormous amount of content with its optional multiplayer campaign (which is double the length of the singleplayer) and has an expansion pack which adds even more to the playtime.
The levelling system is very similar to something like Elder Scrolls, all of your stats level up based on using them. And levelling itself is automatic. Indeed the only real thing you can directly control with your character is what equipment they have and what spells they can use. This makes gameplay very fast and aside from fiddling with your inventory in shops, you spend little time outside of combat.
Dungeon Siege is a kind of mindless game at times. A lot of the combat feels very automated and you mostly just run in and watch your guys smack the enemies around for a little while and then loot bodies, very similar to older rpgs like Ultima. But this is one of the most memorable aspects of the game overall. It's a very comfy game where you just move forward on a journey as your guys pummel the crap out of everything.
Despite its age, still playable and fun!

This game is colorful in its own way. Its much like a virtual novel or a interactive story. You pick your daily actitives and gain points in various skills along the time. Those skills that you gain depend on how you do in various situtations throughout the entire game and determine if you die an old spinster monster, or a great warlord, or a human lover.

Overall, Monster Loves You! was never going to capture the gaming audience that chews through shooters, but that wasn’t the target audience here. Whilst it’s easy to discount it as a child’s game, given it is based around a colourfully-lit interactive story, the truth is that the complexity of the narrative is as apparent or discreet as you allow it to be. You can take the time to think out your responses with an end goal in sight, or just haphazardly click on whatever sounds good at the time and get a result. With roots in storytelling and even text-based adventure games, Monster Loves You! is a charming and unique title that will take most gamers 30-45 minutes to play through, but getting all the endings will take more than a little thought and time.

That said, if you've ever enjoyed books that allowed you to choose your own adventure, you're bound to love this. There are a lot of options and outcomes, all done in a cartoonish and clever style. Don't be fooled by the presentation though, this is not quite what you'd call a "kid's game".
While there is no voice acting, the options you're presented with all have distinct feeling to them, which plays great with idea of shaping your monster from a morsel to an Elder. The various personality traits - such as bravery, ferocity, kindness - increase or decrease depending on your choices. Your options for the final outcome are determined by how high or how low these traits actually are. This also gives MLY plenty fo replaybility, as there are plenty of different outcomes each granting an in-game emblem as well as an achievement. Great for trophy hunters.
I definitely recommend getting this if you're looking for something mellow and relaxing to pass time with. Each "run" is about 30-60 minutes long, depending on what scenarios you receive and how fast you read.
However,
. I cannot stress this enough. Do not get this if you're looking to jump on platforms, or shoot things, or race vehicles - or do anything other than read and choose reactions to the situations presented. It does just this one thing, but it does it really well.

Although I've played DXHR back when it first came out, recently I got into Almost Human and felt the urge to replay the game...especially since the Director's Cut version had come out recently.  And now that I've finished it, I must say that I consider this is easily one of my most favorite games of all time.
Is it perfect?  Of course not.  But what this game *does* have is, interesting settings, compelling and very possible vision of a world in the near future, fascinating storyline and memorable characters....and all of that will stay with you long after the game's done.  There are multiple ways of going through each area to suit just about any playstyle out there; nooks and crannies to explore, secret areas to discover, emails to read, people to talk to, and sidequests to complete.  The game does not lock you into a specific playstyle, but rather makes it possible, through giving the player the ability to pick and choose their augmentations, to cater to and enhance, various ways of play.  Like to sneak around, hack into things and be virtually undetectable?  You can do that.  Like to just mow everyone down with explosions and heavy weapons?  You can do that too.  Don't like killing anyone?  Yes, you can be a pacifist and just knock people out.
One of the most interesting themes the game offers is the subject of the progress of technology and how it relates to us as humans.  Refreshingly, the game doesn't have a pre-determinted opinion on this and doesn't clobber you over the head with whatever it thinks is the right answer.  Rather, throughout the game, it allows you various glimpses and insights into different views from people you interact with, which affect your perception of the matter at hand, and, ultimately, play a huge role in how it all plays out in the end.
TL;DR - highly recommended, buy it and play it if you haven't already! :D

This game is far from perfect, but I'm sure we've all heard that before.
What this game offers is similar to the original Primal Carnage, yet there are many pros and cons.
Now the original had fantastic gameplay. The controls were great (For those of you who use controllers), the community is alright except for the lack of skill in everyone pouncing as raptor for most of the time, the classes are well balanced while the fighting is fair, and the skins were neat, realistic, and as simple as can be.
Primal Carnage Extinction? This game was supposed to be a 'better' version of the original. The game has come a long way from being absolutely terrible. It started out as just a game to buy fancy skins and show them off to people in Free Roam game-mode. But now the devs are at least making the playing-field fair. The gameplay is smooth for the most part; a little fast but hey it can't be perfect. The community has gotten better but it is still filled with cheap kids who just want to buy this game for the cool skins and walk around as a dinosaur. The classes though aren't really balanced imo. Sure they're the same from last time, but just tweak the humans in making them a lot stronger and a lot faster with not so great animations in some areas(humans). The dinos are also a bit op (raptor-wise), other than that I'd say the tyrants are completely useless. A human can walk around behind a 2500 hp spino and kill it in under a minute and the spino wouldn't  even be able to touch him from behind. The PCE Market is full of decent skins but some are for like $200. Like c'mon. $200 for a dang Acro skin? Imo I think this game is revolved more around how the dinos look and what you can do with them. Their skins are labeled with a rare status. The lowest being common, the highest being legendary. I personally like how the original did their skins. They had no rare label, they were just there and you wore whichever skin you liked the best. On this game people want nothing but the "rare" skins, and will act like they rule the world if you've got let's say an uncommon compared to their legendary. This isn't in all cases though. They've also added these new animations or "taunts", an animation where the dino/human does some sort of a victory taunt whenever they kill someone. It's sort of futile to me seeming, whenever you take the time to taunt someone, another dino or human will come along the next second and take advantage of your inability and kill you.
So I think they should definitely improve the fairness when it comes to the classes and damage overall but this game is pretty fun. It isn't a game on skill, just a game on who can slash the human the quickest or who can explode the raptor the farthest. Pretty much anyone can be a pro in this game. I honestly think the original Primal Carnage is better in most areas where this game isn't but it's still pretty good. I personally have had some fun times in this game though, and it isn't bad. I feel like it will get better(hopefully), so if there were an option for an in-between recommendation for a review, that would be my pick. But there isn't so I'm going to have to go with a thumbs up and recommend you get it to try it for yourself.

Very brief but well-designed metroidvania. The game doesn't pad out the length at all, but upgrades come at a steady pace, and there is a fair amount of hidden rooms and items to find in the short playtime.

Space, a portal gun, a rapid fire machine gun and tons of rooms to traverse through will create this very excitig adventure. MiniBoss has created a short, pixalated adventure/platformer game where you control Yuri, a well-known space police offcier that has to escape the planet he's on in order to save humanity.
Pros
- Clever Level Design
A good chunk of these levels can be solved in a multitude of ways. These ways will make you think outside of the box because if you don't, there is a good chance you might be stuck for a while. You can find ways to get through the levels quicker than before or find other ways to avoid doing the levels. You just have to find the secrets and tricks of each room, and like I said, they are very clever.
- Challenging Levels
Alongside clever level design, there are some that require a bit of patience and brainstorming before completing. The game has some rather difficult levels that stops you from speedrunning it through. Of course, if you beat it already it would be easier to do a second run, but the game offers both side of the spectrum in each of its levels, easy and hard.
- Retro Soundtrack
The music actually goes well with the game. It has a pixelated feeling to it and it changes to match each level setting. Reminds me when I use to play the original Mario Bros, it bring great memories to me.
- Smooth Controls
To me, I thought the controls were smooth and reactive, which save me a couple times during the game. It may take awhile to get use to, but you'll get use to it and continue forward. Your main concern will be getting used to the portal mechanics because there are some levels that you have to use the portal gun and it reacts differently to different objects in the game. In the end, the controls are crisp and quick.
Other than those, this game does have its fair share of cons, but most of them can relate to each other.
Cons
- Repetitive Gameplay
The first time through is fun, but going back and doing a second run may cause some problems. There is no extras things when beating the game, it takes you back through everything again with no change. It makes sense if your trying to get all the secrets hidden in each levels, but then after a while it becomes a chore going through each level again and again.
- Short Game
The game can be completed in under an hour or even in twenty minutes (these are achievements by the way). It sucks that if your really good at platforming game, you can rush probably through this game and be done with it. Really, its a very short game, even when finding all of its secrets.
- Minimal Content
There isn't to much to offer in the game, all you get is a few item that will help you get through the game and that' it. The game has some unique gamelevel mechanics, but other than that, there isn't much that will be remembered after you finished the game.
- Other Minor Problems
There are some achievements that require you to go out of your way and spend quite a bit of time to complete them. I had to use a couple of walkthroughs to help me get them, which took me a while.
My Verdict Of The Game
8/10

I'd rate this device a 3.75 out of 5 stars.
My personal opinion of my experience with it so-far:
The touch-input areas don't necessarily have "desired" texture. It feels like there was more emphasis on building the "possibility" for a versitle controller, however, at the last second they threw-on an actual controller.
Personally, this device would function BETTER (if not be THE "end-all" design for all future controllers) if it's multi-touch input regions were in the location that the default joystick and buttons have been placed.
On a side-note, the bottom buttons (paddles?) feel like they could've been down-played a lot more... the total-loss of grip at the cost of laziness... not a really good selling point for me. I feel like we should have the option to utilize those features instead of struggle to play even a simple side-scroller (Battle Block Thatre) with such a cumbersome device.
P.S.
Putting-aside the shape and weight/balance of the controller... The interface through the big-screen mode allows you to fully-customize ALL possible configurations (for any possible game you'd use it with and load said profile at your disgression) - but that alone would set you aside at-least 30 min. Granted, you've now designated the radius for which the touch sensors can/will detect but you've spent as-much time setting this up as you would building an Armored Core.

Pros: Comfortable, many buttons, fully customizable, batteries last a long time.
Cons:
The stick and XYAB buttons are small and positioned in such a manner that they are more difficult to use with the trigger buttons than compared to say the old Xbox 360 controller.
The pads are a neat gimmick but not that useful, The right pad works well enough for games where you need to aim a camera, but for shooters or any fast paced strategy game, there is just no way this could keep up. Also, the left pad is just bad, and should have been redesigned before they started making these. It doesn't sit right in the controler which makes using it difficult nearly all the time. Thankfully the thumbstick works well so it can be used instead.
Sometimes the controller has issues when running a game outside of steam.  It's a little maddening because I don't think it would be very difficult for them to make this controller work regardless of what client you are launching your games out of.
There are other problems, like the price, but this review is already starting to ramble.
Overall, I would recommend it to anyone who doesn't have a controller and wants one for console ports or other single player games. I would not recommend to anyone with a decent controller already, there were many questionable design calls that should have been caught and addressed when they were developing this thing. If you have a controller already, wait for the second generation steam controller, if they make one, hopefully by then they will have fixed the most glaring issues like those mentioned above.

When you think of the heist genre you think of things like Payday or GTA V, but
provides a new way to play this kind of game and I am happy to say, it's a lot of fun.
Each level begins with a flyby overview of the map and an explanation of what objectives need to be completed. Pay attention to this as it's very important to get a good idea of the best approach to each heist. This is also where you will need to think about what characters to bring with you. The characters are fantastic and all have their own personality and fit with the obvious 1970's theme of the game.
You can select a character and move them around the map via way points that you place down on the map. Think of it like other isometric games like The Sims where you point and click to have your character move. In
however, you can pause the game, plan out a series of moves for each of your characters, place down multiple waypoints and then unpause to have them all move.
As you progress of course the levels get bigger and more difficult and from what I played, I had a lot of fun and this game does a great job of building the difficulty so you are prepared for the later levels. You won't be thrown right in the deep end and have the difficulty spike to ridiculous levels suddenly.
is an interesting take on the heist genre and provides plenty of challenge and plenty of fun to keep you coming back for more. I completed some of the missions while being seen but I really want to go back to see if I can complete them without being seen and that's more than I can say about a lot of other games released today.

The steam controller is definitely a fun piece of hardware to use. It's by far not my favorite controller and when i first saw its design i was very skeptical of it. So lets jump into it.
1. The touchpads... The controller is designed with two touchpads on each side of it. One of which has a cross shape on it, that can be used as a Dpad and the other is just a flat surface touch pad. Both touchpads can be pushed down and it's almost like using a trackpad on a laptop. I love the idea behind it. It's almost like putting the precision from a mouse into a controller.... HOWEVER... while i tested it on shooters i noticed that the aiming would seem a bit wobbly. Maybe it's "just my" controller but i honestly didn't feel comfortable playing shooters in it as much as i did with a PS4 controller or Xbox one controller.
2. The joy stick... its a joy stick, nothing to great about it.. it's precise and although you only get 1 it's used very often on the controller.
3. Shape and design... honestly, it feels a little strange at first, but then you tend to adapt to it. Although i have mixed feelings with the trackpad i personally feel the controller is great with it's functionality. The bottom buttons give it an added bonus. Gives the fingers that are unused something to be used for.
4. interface- Although this isn't exactly the controller- how the controller reacts to the big screen mode on steam is very seamless and easy. It really makes it a console-like experience with a power of a pc.
So overall i think the steam controller is definitely worth the money. It's cheaper than the ps4 and xbox one controllers (i have both). I do however still enjoy the xbox controller more than the steam controller.

Crookz – The Big Heist is a game about a group of trained thieves, as the game title implies. The game introduces you to six professional crooks who were betrayed by their boss and ended up in jail. Upon release from prison, the crew reunites and is bent on exacting revenge against their traitor. The game is a tactical stealth strategy game played from a third person isometric perspective. Each heist mission begins with a preview of what the venue for the upcoming heist looks like. You choose four of six members of your crew, buy tools from the workshop from your income earned from previous missions. There are some members who must be used for certain heists, but you get to choose the other members according to their unique skills.
The brains of the crew is a female who runs like the wind and can hide in floor hatches. Other members include a professional locksmith, a contortionist who can crawl through vents to reach other areas of a venue much faster than walking, a technician who can turn off security cameras and manipulate switchboxes, a muscleman/pro wrestler who can knock out guards, and a robot that can be cloak in front of cameras and guards. Although the brains of the crew is fast and stealthy, I used her less than I thought I would, especially as the missions became more complex since her skills were not as useful as the skills of the other crew members.
There are 18 missions in the main story set in San Francisco, CA in the 1970s with lots of funky music. The missions begin in a straightforward manner, teaching you how to unlock doors using your professional locksmith or find the proper key throughout the mission. The missions become more complex since there are more doors that can only open by finding the proper switches and there are laser barriers protecting the rooms. There are switches that open doors in the immediate area, but at the same time close doors in other areas. These intricacies require you to move your crooks so that they end up separated from each other. For example, you may have one crook toggle a switch to open a door while another crook is in separate room toggling a different switch to open another door. The game is designed to be very slow paced and you will have to pause many times so that you can execute commands to each crook by marking waypoints. Venues for heists include a museum, a mansion, the Federal Reserve bank, and the famous San Quentin prison. The crew actually plans to get arrested on purpose at the end of one mission that leads to a mission in which they must escape from the prison. Each mission ends with a score and how much “heat” you picked up. Any heat will result in bribe money to be deducted from your earnings.
The use of commands and waypoints is part of the game interface. The interface is pretty easy to learn, although it took a little time for me to learn the basics in the beginning. There is a context sensitive menu that you can use to make a crook use his/her specialized skill. In the case of the locksmith, you can right click on a security/steel door to bring up the menu that displays a key to indicate that he can lockpick that door. It is important to know each crook’s skills in order to choose them properly for a specific heist mission. This require a lot of planning before the mission begins. The planning phase also includes a look at the locations of the guards and their patrol routes. Therefore, the planning phase in this game provides ample opportunity for you to know how to approach a heist mission. You can also see the vision cones for each guard and camera so that you know when you can be detected.
There are useful tools that you can find in each mission and they can be purchased from the workshop. Tools include blowtorches to open safes and steel doors, dynamite to destroy to cracked walls, noise emitters to distract guards, and door blockers that can cement doors to trap guards in a room. Some missions have enough tools of a certain kind such as keys and crowbars, so that would allow you to choose a crook that would not include a locksmith. I think that skill for skill the locksmith was the most reliable crook of the crew because of his ability to unlock doors. The game requires access to many different rooms.
Completing main story missions unlocks challenges and there are ten of them. Challenges are based on some of the venues from the main story, but are all on a timer. You will have to complete the main objective, then head for the exit before time runs. One challenge begins with each crook in separate rooms and they must find a way to help each other reach the exit. This requires some serious puzzle solving with doors, barriers, cameras and guards. The challenges made my brain work so much since they require quicker coordination than main story missions and there is less margin for error.
The save system is one that is uncommon for games of today. You can save wherever you want and whenever you want. The game also seems to auto save every few seconds. However, there are technical problems with save files. There were times when I tried to load the game, but it would crash to my desktop. There were also times when I tried to manually save the game, but I would receive notification that an error occurred. These technical issues were more apparent when playing the challenges.
I would conditionally recommend Crookz because it is designed to be a slow paced, tactical stealth strategy game and it is a decent one. If you like tactical strategy games that require a lot of pausing before issuing commands to multiple characters I would recommend it. If you like fast paced games that don’t require much pausing, you may want to consider another game. In essence, it comes down to your taste in game genre.

So I'm here to tell it like it is, because honestly I doubt anyone will; this game is OK. No, it's not "great," but it's extremely good at what it does; you feel flighty and free in combat. So let's do a simplified list because otherwise people won't read past the first sentence:
Pros:
1) A variety of both martial and magical styles in the vanilla version -- this allows for several concepts to take shape with each different playthrough, such as a sword-wielding maniac that uses fire to immolate his foes
2) Pleasing visual styles -- the forms look graceful or rough as it is appropriate. Dodging is one of the most enjoyable aspects of the game due to how light your character will feel; it is almost as if you have wings in combat. The lighting is also gorgeous in several areas, and that really brings out the beauty of the pseudo-Chinese architecture.
3) Replayability -- if you beat the game, you have the option of doing a new game + through the Jade Master mode.
4) Intriguing lore and setting -- Jade Empire has beautiful bestiary entires and journals scattered throughout the world in the form of culture-appropriate scrolls or books. Much of the history inside the game, including that of the creatures, is highly stimulating.
Cons (buckle up):
1) Extremely repetitive gameplay -- while the game looks and feels fantastic, the simplistic combat mechanics become almost laborous after a few hours into the game, ESPECIALLY against some of the mush more difficult opponents. Eventually it boils down to mashing on an enemy for several seconds until they die, which in Jade Master mode becomes minutes. The only saving grace to this is the ability to swiftly slaughter small-scale enemies with the Harmonic Combos in the game. Unfortunately, this also means that everything eventually guides you towards taking a few specific styles just to progress in a sane way.
2) Copy and Paste enemies -- this is a tiny con. You'll find yourself running into the same enemies using the same styles and the same heads but on slightly different bodies. BioWare games are notorious for this re-use of content to fill gaps, but here it feels quite coarse; enemies are far too similar, even into the latter half of the game. When you see elite guards using the same poking spear that the peasents wielded in the start of the game, we have a problem.
3) Strength of styles -- it's obvious the team did a ton of balance before they finished this (not), so you'll be left tossing your favorite style in the trash if it's not one of the top tier, otherwise you'll run into a ton of issues in the harder fights or in Jade Master (which is seriously going to test how well you know your combos and styles).
4) Lack of character development/Lack of interesting characters -- I'll be honest here, I thought almost every companion you could get turned out to be 1-dimensional. At least in KotOR I cared about several of the allies working with me, but here everything feels far too stiff. The only character I found interesting was the ridiculous comedic relief. It just feels so forced.
The game is fun if you can look past some of the defects and appreciate it for what it is: a kung-fu beat-em-up with a paper-thin story and paper-thin characters. People put this game near the bottom of the BioWare list and it definitely earns its spot, however...
A certain modder (may she be blessed) has created one of the most fantastic modifications for this game I have ever seen: Jade Empire in Style. It does everything right; character skins, new styles, new combat mechanics, better combos, more combos, more enemies, etc. It's fantastic. It doesn't try to fix anything broken with the story or characters, it builds on the game's strength--the Kung Fu. And holy cow does it do it well! Dungeon Siege is a classic RPG and I always get nostalgic playing it. When I first played Dungeon Siege I was really taken by the simplicity of the skills mechanic and the fact that once you are in the world there are no loading screens - you just constantly walk through one giant map. There's not much story to the game, just some serious grindy RPG action with some side quests thrown in for the completionists like myself.
One thing I originally liked about the game was that there aren't any confusing skill trees, just specialisations and attributes in which you can level up simply by doing things - hitting things with a stick gives you melee skill and mostly strength, while casting spells gives you magic skill and mostly intelligence, etc. This is now the very thing I dislike about the game. While it's nice and simple it does kind of make combat slightly boring as you don't have an array of special abilities to manage (well, none unless you have a mage). Sure, mages have spells which they can switch between, but only being able to actively switch between two spells without some complicated process and having no autocasts just gets tiresome. I still really love this game, but I think if it weren't for the nostalgia I probably wouldn't be enjoying as much as I am today.
If you played Dungeon Siege on its initial release and enjoyed it back then, then it might be worthwhile getting for another play through, but if you're new to the series I would recommend skipping over this one and starting with Dungeon Siege II, which has much better gameplay. Now, back to the grindstone.

Problem with Dungeon Siege is that it is DEATHLY BORING - after a few hours.
The first few hours I thought, "hey, this is OK"..... but I soon tired of the absolute PUSHOVER easy combat. So I tried "medium" difficulty, only to find that was A THOUSAND FOLD harder..... TOTALLY AND UTTERLY IMPOSSIBLE!
So it was either too easy and boring, or impossible!
Edit: Until I tried again, on "normal" later. Then the difficultly *did* seem "normal" as you'd expect. The difficulty levels had become about right.
I also soon got fed up with the constant combats, often they were big closeup toe to toe melee brawls. Not many tactic needed, especially ranged tactics. Unless also oppenents are ranged attackers, then you can have ranged vs ranged fight. If they have melee attackers you are pretty much forced to switched to melee as well.
The maps can be claustraphobic, and often they are heavily cluttered with needless trees and bushes, often reducing your visibility to near zero.
The game world is NOT open world, despite it's best attempts at giving the illusion it is! It is thoroughly linear, linear as a book!
There's constant little nooks and crannies to explore that usually have more goodies, or rather junk, but the constant side-tracking to explore those gets tedious too! Those are optional of course.
You collect WAY too much junk as well. But again you can avoid doing this yourself.
You also end up with too large a party..... I've already got six people and two packmules! Looks like the party managment part of UI has space to handle another 8 members at least! It becomes exponentially more cumbersome as you add more beyond five or so members! Again you could choose to only maintain a small party. But I don't think the game allow that to be feasable. Later on I imagine you will NOT get far without your own personal horde!
Graphics, sounds, music and storyline are all thoroughly humdrum!
The game's pattern is you just go from village to village, those villages being just checkpoints where you sell your junk, buy new junk, and get a few more pointless side quests, and progress the main storyline quest. You then embark, following a linear, long-winded, tedious, twisting turning path to the next village..... being assailed constantly on the way with boring, pointless combats.
At first I was deeming Dungeon Siege to be a 7/10 (B-), but I've since reconsired it a 5/10 (C-).
I should've saved whatever I spent on this for a beer or two.
All the reviews are raving 10/10ers. Appears this is another poor game, yet with a rabid fanboi element!
I only hope Dungeon Siege 2 and 3 are better - I have bought those too!
After one session, I was finding myself, after one hour, not being able to even bear another minute. And when you have a game you cannot wait to STOP playing..... well, then there's a major issue with quality, isn't there?

This is a worthy successor to the original Deus Ex game. In my opinion it is not as good as the original. But it certainly comes very close.
It certainly feels like a true Deus Ex game. While it has a mostly linear story, you get lots of freedom moving around in hub areas and how you take on different missions. There are always more ways to get around a certain problem. You can go guns blazing into a firefight. You can be silent as the night and sneak by guards without killing a single soul.
The graphic style is very appealing. The story and voice acting are great and the combat is solid.
On the downside though, the game has a few problems. Chief among these are the boss fights. Though the Director's Cut does feature improved boss fights. They are still not as strong as the rest of the game and there is no way around them.
When compared to the original Deus Ex, there are also a few things that could have been done more elegantly. The way the experience works kinda works against exploring different solutions to certain problems. For example: Hacking a terminal will always give you more experience than finding the code for the same terminal. There is also little difference between nonlethal and lethal takedowns. With an arbitrairy push of a button you can choose between life and death without much difference in consequence. There are also times when the level design feels a little gamey and could have been a little more elegant (though I am nitpicking here).
The Director's Cut is definitely worth it compared to the normal version of Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
As I mentioned earlier the bossfights have been improved. There is now much more freedom in how the bosses are defeated. So you won't find yourself being underpowered because you chose a certain build.
All the original DLC is now also fully integrated into the game by default. The DLC was worth it to begin with. But this change just makes the whole thing just a little more smooth. There were a number of bugs before, but as far as I know most of these have been ironed out by now.
To conclude, if you like Cyberpunk and are looking for a shooter RPG that provides lots of freedom in play styles. I wholeheartedly recommend this games. Because dispite some minor flaws, it really is a fantastic game and I enjoyed it immensly.

Ironically, while DE: HR is a mix between cRPG and an FPS, it is much more cRPG-ish than most modern games described as computer role playing games. Virtually every quest can be solved in more than one way. You can sneak your way through, talk you way out of tight situations or simply enter the room guns blazing. The character development system allows you to tailor you protagonist to whatever playstyle you wish to choose.
The plot is, at least for me, truly attention riveting - even if you will be able to get to all clues hidden in e-mails, pocket secretaries and eavesdrop on various dialogues, you still shouldn't fully figure out what is going on until late game (say, till somewhere around Singapore). The game has four different endings, each of which has "three" flavours depending on how you played the game.
All of this is dressed in pretty neatly designed graphics.
Only downsides? The AI could use a little work and sometimes it's simply too easy to sneak through, but for me that wasn't that much of a concern since I was focused on plot anyway. And there is a bit too much of backtracking in the Missing Link DLC, but these two faults seem meaningless when compared with the amount of good stuff this game has to offer.

Where to start? Cyber punk games are really interesting because of the philosophy of the cultures. The factions of people who are for augmentations and those who are against it because they think its inhuman to do and against nature itself. A society always questioning the benefits and tradeoffs of disregarding some of your flesh in order to speed ahead of those around you in competitive areas.
+ Dynamic Navigation from point to point
+ Upgrades contribute to navigation
Game is very dynamic with many interesting ways to get from Point A to Point B. The way you move around the environment depends up to you and what upgrades you get. The stealth in the game is great, and so are the ways you can sneak past enemies or use an object in order to lure them away from their defensive post.

+ Multiple ways to take down bosses
The bosses in Director's cut actually have multiple ways to take them down instead of just shooting and running and more shooting. You can actually use hacking and stealth to take down your enemies and there is various different ways to do it. This was a huge improvement over the original game and the main flaw it "used" to have now this game is easier to recommend thanks to the upgrade.

Please note this review is aimed at people who own or have played Primal Carnage and are considering whether or not to buy it. Also I will be reviewing the tech or graphics side only the gameplay and enjoyment elements.
Primal Carnage: Extinction is the sequel to the 2012 game Primal carnage. (well duh)
So what do I think of this game? Well there is so so much to say being a veteran player of the original game. So I'll start by letting this game stand alone and not compare it to anything. Its decent fun enjoyable for a half hour to hour playtime in a session depending on the server. It has a few flaws of being a bit buggy and annoyingly difficult but its fun.
Now lets compare it to when it first was released. *clears throat* ITS FRICKEN FANTASTIC. So in my opinon when it came out it was extremely and I mean EXTREMELY opted towards humans or as some players call them, 'hoomans'. As a dino you would fell very powerful until you actually went into combat, then you felt weak and kinda noobish. It was the total opposite for humans though as you felt insanely tiny but really badass with a slight nauseating feeling. Now however its much more balanced but at times i feel dinos have an annoying advantage. Still its very fun.
Now for the big one, comparing it to the original. The short answer: Primal Carnage by a long shot. The long answer: Ehh both bring stuff to the table. My inspirations for writing this review is while playing Extinction a moment ago I realized that even on fire pteranadons still pick you up and if in mid pounce and shot raptors still pounce. This really ticked me off. like really. LIKE RE-♥♥♥♥♥♥-ALLY. Another thing is that with the original dions had a huge advantage, yes, but when together as a group the humans can destroy two t-rexes easily. Its rather like that in Extinction but without the destroying t-rexes part. You feel powerful but nope you ain't. It may seem like I'm picking on Extinction because I am but don't get me wrong Extinction is better in many ways like how everything is better balanced and it's smoother and not as buggy (oh yeah its buggy but like i said, not as) the maps are refined and slightly more interesting though I don't like the new marsh. it has fun hidey holes and what-not and a great community. taunts are a fun bonus you do get friendly servers where dinos and 'hoomans' co-exist...for a while. But the one thing THE ONE THING I can not get past...is...the...MICRO TRANSACTIONS! No more 'dlc' you can vote for stuff on the workshop and you get crate drops but whats that? YOU NEED A TWO DOLLAR FRICKEN KEY TO GET A RANDOM MOST LIKELY, COMMON, SKIN. yes you get skin drops from time to time and when you level up but its not enough. i don't have 2 bucks everytime I get a crate so deal with it.
All in all both are good but the original, is and forever will but unless they do something drastic, better.

Okay. So, I love dating sims - but I'm pretty sensitive about mature content in games. I'm in it for the story more than anything else. That's why I'm happy to have found Hustle Cat.
The game itself actually isn't very long - you can easily finish each character route in about two hours or less - but you get plenty of enjoyment out of it. I also really appreciate that the game gives you the option to pick your appearance and gender right at the start, so you can play as either a boy or a girl (there is also a non-binary option).
I quickly found myself becoming attached to every single one of the characters, even the ones I didn't like at first. Everyone is given a pretty interesting - and sometimes kind of depressing - backstory that makes you really end up empathizing with them. (For example, Reese, who I initially disliked, ended up being my favorite character after I played his route.) As for the romance and mature content, there's nothing in the game that would get a YouTube video flagged, if you know what I mean. There's some kissing (Reese and Hayes have some rather adorable blushing scenes) and a bit of language, but that's it, really. Just a lot of tender moments.
Oh, and did I mention that this game has some pretty decent music? Most of the tunes are actually pretty catchy. The piano/love theme was just downright beautiful, and has even made me consider buying the soundtrack.
The only thing I disliked about the game was that even once you've finished all the routes, including the secret one, you're still left with questions about the story. I'm not sure if the developers intended to leave loose ends or if they're planning on releasing more content,
but I just hate being left hanging!!
All in all, if you're looking for a somewhat lighthearted dating sim with a little bit of mystery - and not to mention cats - then you'll probably enjoy this wonderful charmer of a game.

Hustle Cat is a super great game and I'd definitely reccomend it to anyone who likes cats, story-rich games, dating sims, or all three. Also, huuuge kudos to the developer for letting you choose your pronouns!! Loved that!! Anyways Hustle Cat is really good and I'd die for all of the characters and its just. Super good. You should totally play it.

There is a lot of repetitive dialogue but there is a fast forward feature so that helps out. You can also save multiple files and at any point - there are two auto save slots as well, though there aren't that many decisions that you would need to save for. Routes get locked in fairly early and once you are locked into a route, I don't remember there being any other choices. Once your romantic interest is locked in, the story sort of just plays out from there.
The story itself is a pretty straightforward set up - you're working your first job at a cat cafe with cute coworkers (both male and female romantic options, as well as you can decide what pronouns your character goes by). There's witchcraft involved and the same basic beats are hit in each route. But what I really enjoyed about this game was the writing - it's very modern, with very distinct character tones throughout. This is definitely not the normal stiff otome writing which I quite enjoyed. Your character has a very set personality, for better or worse. Personally I liked it but I could see that it would annoy some people.
The low points - the game is repetitive and maybe a bit short, the music wasn't that great (I never used headphones), nothing is voiced. But the high points - the writing, the stylization, the characters, I think out weight the bad and I definitely enjoyed this game.

I was sent this game as a christmas present by a friend.
I like playing these visual novels (though mostly on mobile apps) and was looking forward to playing this one, but its not the best out there.
Like all these VN that let your pick a route I didn't feel that there were enough choices, the ones that were there became repected down every character route you take.
Another issue was that I was really looking forward to playing as a cat, but that route was never an option. If you run away from the cafe the games ends with you being stuck as a cat forever because you never go back. Err, sorry, but if I was suddenly a cat and the only way of being human was to be at the cafe and break my curse I would do that before storming out. How dumb.
Considering that the all the character routes were reparted it would have been a way to mix things up a little, maybe on the Hayes route, he prefers being a cat and it would have been esier to get to know him if you were both the same, and as the magic book is discovered at work it wouldn't be a problem for them to study it together at the cafe.
It was also very unsatisfactory to discover that the MC broke the cat curse before it took hold simply because you started playing with a stolen magic book and began teaching yourself spells; your don't even get some challanges to help your discover your magic or a choice of what that magic should be. Its just trash because the MC is a disgusting pig who can't pick up after herself and clean her apartment.
A plus point is that all the characters are different and have distinct personalities and problems, but the varity of the routes is ruined by the the script, which is lazy with each route having the same lay out; a date, a day at work, and the assult on the street by Nacht, and all of them using the same dialogues in placed between choices. Seriously, the fast forward button is just not fast enough in skipping through these sections. (Plus I discovered that using the fast forward button to frequently caused the game to crash.)
The images are inconsistant as well, in the Reese route the MC 'cleans' her place before letting her guest in, but the next morning the image goes back to the messy one, seems like the dev's picked the wrong image.
The endings were also the same with Nacht disposing of all the characters who you aren't dating while the MC does something stupid which results in your date coming to your rescue. Even timid little Hayes breaks character to come to your rescue. I realise this is all fiction but I found it hard to suspend my disbelieve here; the MC was supposed to have had the magic book, broken her curse, and been praticing for weeks yet is completely useless. While your date manages to break their curse and become a better witch in just a couple of days. We can forgive Landry and Reese to some extent because we discover that they are inheeritly magical anyway, but for the others it just doesn't work.
All of the endings are capped off with a little epilogue that doesn't explain why Nacht is after Graves, plenty of hints are given that it is not just about witches claiming new territory but you don't get a proper explaination. Not even at the end of the Graves route, when I expected all the answers and got nothing. You don't even get a proper epilogue with Graves about how they move their relationship on, you kiss after the fight with Nacht and the game ends. Where the devs are stretching bounderies with gay and non-binary options for the MC, it seems a relationship with a older guy was just too hard for them work with, so why bother offering it? Disappointing.
Time was also a problem for me of Graves's route, in all the other routes he is turned to rust instantly, but in his route he is able to resist the effects of it to come to the MC's rescue for over 24 hours. Yawn, backing tracking on five previous plotlines just to make his ending the same as the others makes no sense.
I loved the artwork and the concept, its just a pity that the devs didn't take some more time to write different cut scenes or offer more choices, after six routes all following the same patterns and choices the game ended up feeling repetative and samey.
Less is more, as they say, and with more effort being placed into a smaller 'dating pool' this could have been more amusing than it was.
I had so much fun playing this game, I recommend it!

The game itself is brilliant, unfortunately, Valve is distributing it in a broken, unplayable state for most windows Vista/7/8 users. This requires users to hack the install directory by renaming files, or to seek to resolve the problem by more convoluted and risky means.
It is of course BioWare's responsibility to fix this, but Valve is still selling it, and it's unacceptable that people feel the need to download anonymous executables off the internet in order to play a game they purchased.
If you feel like dealing with the head ache of trying to get this broken product to work, it's actually a very good game. It starts a little slow but you encounter lots of interesting characters, make lots of decisions that impact how things turn out, develop relationships with party members, get multiple endings, and can unlock a lot of cool powers. It's a very good game, it's like a pre-cursor to Mass Effect but JadeEmpireConfig.exe is broken and results in a Can't Find Steam error.
Oh the solution to the Can't Find Steam error? Simple
Make a backup of JadeEmpireLauncher.exe, create a copy of JadeEmpire.exe, and rename that copy to JadeEmpireLauncher.exe. Then run it in XP Compatibility Mode with Run as Administrator checked. For most people, this solves the problem. I'm sorry you had to look for a work around like this to make a game you spent money on playable.

Jade Empire is Bioware's most forgetable RPG.  That doesn't make it bad, but there is a reason the developer turned Mass Effect and Dragon Age into trilogies and we haven't heard a word about Jade Empire 2.
Paradoxically, this is also Bioware's most unique RPG.  It is a martial arts RPG set in a high fantasy world inspired by Chinese folklore.  The combat animations are very good, creating using motion capture technology of actual martial arts professionals.
Here's the problem: the combat is bad.  For a game with a heavy focus on combat, that is very problematic.  The animations look great, but as a player all you do is push a few buttons to either: quick attack, power attack, block, or area attack.  While the player can obtain other styles, almost everything combat has to offer in the game is experienced in the tutorial.  Combat then becomes a routine affair of whitling down enemy health while jumping around trying to avoid damage.  Pro tip: don't use the "Thousand Cuts" style, as a result of its animation timing (seriously), it is notably inferior to the other starting styles.
More problematic: character creation is incredibly linear.  As you level up, your Health, Chi, and Focus increase.  You then can assign 3 points to either Health, Chi, or Focus.  Pro Tip: Chi is probably the best option.  Meaning, multiple playthroughs will feel very similar to each other.
Still, the game does have a story similar to other Bioware hits.  If you liked Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect for the story, you will enjoy this game for the story alone.  It is suitably epic, has a pretty big twist towards the end, and frankly there is nothing else quite like this game. My main issue with this game is the shoddy player identification. The only way a teammate will be identified is if they are in full view and within 50 meters away, so tk'ing is rampant. Enemies aren't identified at all, unless this is just a glitch. An example is that I was lying near a door way and saw feet and a torso enter, but thought it was friendly because it came from behind, but I had not way of telling it was an enemy because of not seeing the face/helmet, and no player tag.
The game is hardcore, so you have to rely heavily on your senses to identify and locate enemies, but the sound design and graphics are pretty crappy so it's very hard to do so. You'll find yourself getting killed by the same sniper over and over, with no indication of where he is because there is no locational hit detection, you can't hear the shot, and there is no scope glint. I play a lot of Arma King of the Hill and have no issues with that game because the sound design makes sense and the bullet cracks provide a general location of the enemy, perpendicular to the spot of the bullet crack.
The maps are not that big, although they have great design. I was pretty disappointed in this since aircraft are a pretty big highlight of the game. Many bushes can't be run through, so they are pretty much just walls. This means you can't use them for cover, and that's extremely annoying in a game that is themed in the jungle.
Another thing, movement feels like you are constantly running through a foot of mud. I understand Rising Storm isn't trying to be AAA but it feels like it's 10 years old and the graphics and animations are rather terrible and overhyped-this coming from someone who also plays games on console.
When you kill someone, you aren't notified for 3-5 seconds after the kill, so you spend time trying to take out someone that is already dead when you could be moving on. This makes it really hard to know if you shot that head glitching s-o-b or if he has ducked for cover. It's really annoying when you think you got him and he pops back up and gets you after you've looked away.
My final straw that made me request a refund was when I vaulted over something and got stuck between an umbrella and the wall. I couldn't cook a grenade to kill myself, and when I threw it under myself, it didn't kill me. So I got stuck for the rest of the match bc my team wouldn't kill me.
I was more than biased that I would love this game, and somehow it managed to kill my bias AND make me hate it. Sad to say it, but this game is a huge disappointment. Honestly don't understand why it gets so many good reviews, although now I understand why very few people make videos of it on YouTube.
