The sequel to Fallout (reviewed
if you're curious), released a year afterwards in 1998. It's bigger and more ambitious than the first game, with more quests, more items and more locations. Even the tone of the game is lighter: more 'epic quest with comedic elements' than 'save your home from doom in the dystopian wasteland', although that element is certainly still there. The wasteland is even starting to rebuild in places - a theme that
would revisit.
Of course, not every writer consistently strikes gold. Fallout 2's writing contains more scattershot comedy, with less of an emphasis on your quest to save your village from starvation. Which might not hit the mark with everyone, this being a relatively hardcore niche title released in 1998 and developed by a team that was almost entirely if not 100% male. But don't despair: there's a solid game here for RPG fans nevertheless.
Base gameplay is much the same as in Fallout: gaining XP to level up and allocating skill points/choosing perks, turn-based combat that uses Action Points, hex-based movement in locations, and wasteland travel between settlements - this time with an optional car!
The interface and companion management is definitely improved from Fallout's. Among other things, the inventory menu isn't tedious to use, you can now trade money in sums containing five figures, and you have much greater control over your companions' battle tactics/equipment. Your companions also level up with you.
Graphics are obviously the same style as Fallout, and FO2 even uses some of the first game's music. Good thing the new tracks are also excellent and evocative. You can download all of the remastered classic Fallout music
.
Much like Fallout, the patched Steam release is pretty buggy, up to and including serious bugs in main quests that can pretty much prevent you from finishing the game. I would suggest downloading killap's Unofficial Patch from
. For those of you interested, he also made the Restoration Project mod, which adds a bunch of cut content.
Fallout 2's early game is more difficult than Fallout's. The first game gave you a gun right from the beginning, and pointed you in a relatively easy direction. Fallout 2 starts with the Temple of Trials, which is an overly lengthy, somewhat implausible and definitely annoying tutorial-by-fire that is ten times more frustrating if your character isn't skilled at Melee Weapons or any of the other tested skills. If you picked any of the less-than-optimal skills, the whole game gets that much harder. Its only saving grace is that it lets you level up a few times. Most of the rest of the game afterwards is much better.
After that ordeal, there are a few quests you can do in your home village before you set out, which are usually a good idea. It'll be several more XP levels and a couple of towns before you find a firearm worth anything. Your options will expand from there, although you're still kind of vulnerable until you find good armor and good weapons you're skilled with. It'll be another while yet before you can clear rooms by yourself, and even in the late game that's not always possible unless you explicitly made a character to do so.
It's worth noting that there are many more high-tier weapons in each class to choose from, as opposed to Fallout where the turbo plasma rifle and gatling laser reigned supreme. True, the pulse rifle does the most damage, but now you have more options across multiple weapon skills and styles for when focusing on DPS doesn't quite cut it.
Overall, it's a good game and a worthy sequel, but watch out for Lynnette.

Perhaps my favorite RPG ever...perhaps. The stat system offers unparalleled variety. This might be the only RPG, for example, where having a low Intelligence actually changes the way your character talks and how NPCs respond (you haven't truly played until you've tried a character with a level 1 INT and watched him bumble about like a cartoon Neanderthal). Also, the game is huge and, best of all, you can do all the things that RPGs usually shy away from: go on a mass child killing spree, get addicted to speed, become a gay porn star (provided your "endurance" score is high enough, of course), contract venereal diseases, become a pimp or a slave trader. What's not to love? Plus, everything's given a sort of "Gee Whiz!," "Leave it to Beaver" sheen so the contrast between the main character's wide eyed naiveté and the often terrible stuff he's duped into doing (often with the best intentions) is always amusing and can provide a good deal of comedy (depending on how you play).

Follow orphan Nick Ramos on his quest to chat up a qt alternative girl in the middle of a zombie apocalypse, rescue other survivors and begrudgingly give them your favourite weapon so that they can fight off hordes of zombies with you before you take it back and leave them to die.

Completed once, as a female dating Finley.  Took 4 hours approx. Found it to be a short, but pretty enjoyable romantic visual novel.  Plenty of replay value for all the different endings (including at least 2 bad endings).
The story is fairly cute... it does have a lot of cats after all.  Although there are some serious elements, which I suspect change based on which character you date.  Finley's arc for example
, and of course there is some body horror that the main story revolves around, which was unexpected, although fairly lightweight, and if you avoid the bad endings it all seems to end of a happy note.
Although on that body horror part, strangely the player character took it a lot better than I as the player did.  Guess they had to to keep the story on a cheerful note
. But then again its not exactly going for serious grimdark.
Was a little disappointed that the various dialogue options largley end at the half way point, once your love interest has established.  After this its pretty much a straight visual novel playing itself out, but I enjoyed where the story went and it based itself around my relationship with said love interest, so can't complain.
Also, the ending for my once through left some big plot holes, specifically
.  But as there is a secret ending after you complete it with everyone else, I'm assuming all will be revealed then, and so its one of those games where you need to play through several routes before everything falls into place.
Overall, I'm definitely going to replay this dating Mason.  And normally I wouldn't bother with dating male characters, but the game's trick of not revealing those plot holes in my until the secret end (I'm assuming) has cleverly forced my hand.  And yes, I want to know that plot hole.  So, yes, I will be playing this several more times, pleny of replace value.
I'd certainly recommend, and be interested to see what else the developer is working on.

I nominated this game for the "Test of Time" award, and isn't it obvious why? The original game was released in 1990 and it's hard to find an earlier game that still holds up so well, or even among newer games! The graphics (well, the original ones) are beautiful, the music is some of the most memorable in any game, (yes, I hum it regularly!) the puzzles flow perfectly, and are pretty hard to forget, well most of them, the great care taken to ensure playability, which was almost unheard of in 1990! (Only other game that was out at the time, that took such care to ensure the player is so well treated and can just have fun... is Mixed-Up Mother Goose.) And one really great thing is the many ways there are to play certain portions! I'm still finding little dialogues and alternative ways to solve the game's puzzles to this day. It's so rare for a game, in any time period, to feel so much like the developers poured their hearts and souls into it, and well, they did! Possibly literally, if you believe the rumours. (And yes, it does feel like it's more rare these days, whatever.)
Oh, I hear the game doesn't exactly work very well if you don't play it on Windows XP, Vista, or 7, and well, Microsoft's doing a pretty good job trying to erase those from the face of the earth. (Thanks guys!) So, if you do get this Special Edition of the game, and I do still recommend it, I recommend you get the "Ultimate Talkie Edition" patch. With it, you'll be able to play on any version of Windows, OS X, pretty much any free operating system, (whatever flavour of Linux, or BSD, or whatever else) Android, and lots of other things, and even DOS like in the Good Old Days! (You kept your old computer, right?!) You don't get the fancy new Special Edition HD graphics but well... look at the screenshots. You aren't missing out too badly.

Saints Row 2 is in my opinion a very enjoyable game, best in the series in my opinion. I love the story and it's full of stuff to do. The map is very good. Theres alot of variety in enviroment, from skyscrapers and downtown to calm suburbs and chinatown. It has alot of memorable places, like the Ultor building, The University and downtown. Its a good map and its fun to explore. There are however a few negatives. The first and probably most obvious one is the graphics. Personally i dont mind, but it's no masterpiece. For me it looks alright, but i can see why some people wont like it. Another is that there are a few bugs here and there. These are mostly wedging stuck in vehicles and other small issues, but they're worth noting. The weapon sounds are also pretty bad to be honest. Some guns have alright sounds, while others sound like airsoft guns. If you enjoyed Saints Row 3 im very, very sure you will enjoy this. The character creation is one of my favourite things about the game, next to the story. The character creation is very good and allows for tons of various sliders and options. Its very fun indeed. The characters in this game are also well made in my opinion and don't feel stock or generic. The story is also fun and interesting. It also features great vehicle customization, as well as the ability to customize cribs and your gang. The music for this game is also great. I love it. There is a nice variety in vehicles, and they have nice customization. I feel that the transition between the first Saints Row and this is very well done and smooth, another plus to the story. Without spoiling it, it has a very brilliant secret mission that i really enjoyed. Its definetly worth checking out. If its on sale you should buy it immediatly.
If you're tired of the vanilla game you should definetly get IdolNinja's Gentlemen Of The Row mod. Its like a giant free DLC. There are also several other game improving, and in the case of the speedup bug game fixing, mods for it, so they're worth checking out.
Worth noting: The game servers for this are down, but online over LAN or Virtual LAN through Evolve for example is still possible. Co-op is fun and you can do the entire campaign in it. Definetly reccomended trying out with a friend.

Great Game.
A choose your own adventure game based off the best selling game: Minecraft.
I don't know about you but i think this game goes well as you play as an animated minecraft player.
The story's really great with the different dimensions and the new mob: THE WITHERSTORM.
SPOILER ALERT!
Minecraft story mode has some sad parts (Rueben) and some extremely hard and exciting parts within.

I played all five episodes that are available so far. Due to the long interval between the 4th and 5th episodes, I had forgotten that the main storyline was actually resolved in the 4th episode, leaving the 5th as a tacked-on standalone. A nice standalone, to be fair, but still -- I originally paid for a five-episode Telltale game, which ultimately became a four-episode Telltale game that suddenly decided to be a longer series, prompting (at least) three DLCs to come out later this year. So, yeah, not sure how I should feel good about that bait-and-switch...
On the plus side, I enjoyed the story and its characters. All of it is relatively simplistic, yes, but simple in my opinion does not equal bad or lazy. If you care to invest a little emotion, some of the choices and consequences can be quite dramatic. A couple of important side characters do not make it to the end of the storyline, which in at least one occasion was actually quite tragic and sad.
The game is getting a lot of bad reviews, some of which -- those related to the bait-and-switch -- are justified. Others, in my personal opinion, are a bit over the top. Minecraft: Story Mode is an interactive story, just like all recent Telltale games were. It is not Minecraft and it was never meant to be. That does not make it a bad game, though.
I had a very good 10 hours of fun with some characters that I cared about and a story that was simplistic, but not necessarily predictable. Will I remember the details in a year from now? Probably not. Will I regret playing the game or paying for it? Highly unlikely.
Verdict: Recommended for people interested in (mostly) light-hearted interactive stories, who also either do not care about the Minecraft look or (like me) enjoy the little references and side jokes that come out of it.

I give this a thumbs-up with some reservations.
It is an under-rated game in that there is a surprising lack of players for what is a competent (but sadly not exceptional) stealth game.
One thing that Crookz does very well is having a planning stage, where you can watch the guards patrol and examine the level in detail prior to picking a team and initial equipment to tackle it. This changes the feel of the game somewhat: Instead of a scrappy sneaky thief making things up as you go along, you are a master criminal crafting and then executing a devious master plan. Or something like that anyway.
You have several characters with mutually exclusive skills only some of which can come with you. In practice however, you almost certainly need the only character who can pick locks, the only character who can cut cameras, and the only character who can take out [most] guards. Item choices can partially mitigate this, but once you have found a team that fits your style, the other characters aren't really involved much.
The other big drawback to the game is that the skill development is not terribly exciting. For example, one character can sneak through light barriers. Except later on the higher security complex have laser barriers instead. Except that later on, your character gets a new skill allowing her to sneak through laser barriers as well. Yawn.
There are some challenge levels that are much harder -- and force you to use a particular set of team members and equipment. However, I did not have enough interest to want to continue once I completed the main campaign.
Overall, a decent game. But not an exceptional one. I bought it on sale, and suggest you do too.

Deus Ex Human Revolution The Director's Cut is a worthy and recommended classic game to pick up if you've not dipped into its delights already and like a bit of thinking man's stealth gameplay. There is a lot of fluff to wade through though, so a bit of patience is required. That said, if you "get it" and become engrossed in the dark foreboding futuristic world, then there's a lot on offer here. For those who already played the original, then the extras don't make too much of a difference and really boils down to how big a fan of the game you are as the extra audio is pretty neat and changed boss fights simply add more options. The missing link is a neat inclusion to add to an already long story, and the graphical upgrades aren't that impacting unless you run the two versions side by side. If you're after the definitive version of the game then this is one to grab, and if you're not bothered, then you won't have missed much if you pass on this. Judging the game as a whole though, and it's still a lovable gem that deserves as much spotlight as it can get.

Still, the journey's a great one and the game deserves to be played

Crookz is a strategy game with some light stealth elements, where the player takes control of a gang of career criminals who are trying to pull off a series of heists, with the ultimate goal of stealing a valuable artefact called the Luna Stone.
Each heist starts with a briefing where your crew explains the mission objectives and gives advice on how to complete them. You can see a detailed map of the building, complete with guard patrol routes and vision cones, plus the locations of security cameras, laser sensor alarms and locked doors.
Most heists allow you to bring four out of the six available crew members, each of whom have their own unique skills. There's a specialist lockpicker, a thug who can temporarily knock out guards (you can't kill anybody) and punch through weak walls, a technician who can disable electronic security devices, a contortionist who can squeeze through air vents, a runner who can move much faster than everyone else, and one other who I won't mention because of story spoilers.
You can also find items during a heist, or buy them during the planning stage, that can allow non-specialists to perform certain actions. For example crowbars will let anyone open a locked door, and anyone can KO guards by using chloroform. Other items that I found really useful include noise makers which can draw guards out of position, and door blockers (basically some kind of industrial strength super glue) that can trap guards in a room so they don't interrupt you later.
Map layouts are really intelligently designed to allow multiple solutions, by bringing different team members and using different items. Once you start the heist, the action is in real time, but you can pause to issue commands. You can save at any time and there are frequent auto saves, so if you make any mistakes they're easy to undo.
Crookz' biggest weakness - and I seem to be saying this about alot of games lately - is that the AI is dumb as a brick. If a guard sees one of your people they will chase after them, and if they catch them its an instant mission failure. However, if you can break line of sight, the guard will go to the last place they saw you, look around for a few seconds, say something like "must have been my imagination", and just go back to their normal patrol route. They won't keep searching or alert the other guards.
And as long as the guards don't actually see your people, they won't react to alot of suspicious situations. They don't care about most doors opening and closing before their eyes, or laser grids shutting off unexpectedly. There was one heist where a guard heard me use dynamite to blow up a weak wall, they came running over to investigate, but I had just enough time to get out of sight. He examined the massive hole in the wall for a few seconds, shrugged his shoulders and went back to his normal route. On another heist I KO'd one awkwardly placed guard half a dozen times as I travelled back and forth across the level, and he never called for backup, or raised the alarm. I can also remember one time I trapped a guard in a room, he was banging on the door calling for help, another guard walked past the door and just ignored it. I actually started to feel bad for exploiting their stupidity.
Heists are linked together by a fairly decent story, although they tried to make too many jokes with the dialogue that I didn't really find very funny. It took me 24 hours to complete the game and there are some additional challenge modes that I haven't tried yet. Controls work fine with mouse and keyboard and the only bug that I can remember was when I tried to order my lockpick guy to use a door blocker on a locked door, the only option I was given was to pick the lock, which I didn't want to do. I had to give the door blocker to another team member and have them use it.
Overall Crookz is a fun game which rewards tactical planning, and I think its worth playing, although hardcore stealth fans might find it a bit too casual.

I see a lot of people complaining about this game or trying to boycott DR3 but for little reason.
They say it is crashes or graphics/frames lag, and i can agree i have had my fair share of crashes, but it was never during the playing of the game, only when i tried to close it. Now that the crash on exit has been fixed i have no issues.
For the frames complaint, i had zero issues with a mid range computer playing on the highest settings (bar shadows because it always tanks a system no matter what). Even when multiplayer, apart from connection lag due to the host running to much programs. The real issue lay with those who have epic rigs which are most likely not yet supported or optimized yet for this game. Crossfire if you are lucky, will work but your best bet like with every new game is to avoid using cross/disable it for the time being.
The zombie variety and difficulty ramps over every day and psycho you fight, with main mission also adding to the crazy amount of new zombie types; from big bulky prison zombies who can take a beating but have the fatal flaw of combo fire or electric weapons, swat and police zombies who can still randomly shoot their gun!(swat with extra armor), firemen zombies who are immune to fire and hold a melee weapon to wreck your butt if you aren't armed well enough, bee zombies who have an extra pop when eliminated (and much more!).
This added variety really helps stop your epic power and can give you a challenge even when fully leveled!
Combo-weapons, the combo system in this sequel is off the charts. From basic weapon combos with small punch and limited use. To the absurdly powerful but hard to pull off weapons in dire straights ( Microwave cannon, Death scythe for some of the more difficult to use if you hit the wrong button). These combo systems really add to that greedy side as you run around picking up both blueprints and new items every room or street you enter, making you make all those goodies only to notice you have no more space left to craft more!! Once you get your durability book, you will contemplate turning off durability because you keep those weapons so long later in the game!
Biggest issue with these combo-weapons is that the crafting of them if done to much in a hurry can cause problems if you have items which also match together, making that metal masher accidentally into a pipe assault rifle which made a 500 bullet minigun into a 120 bullet assault rifle, which could cause some epic disappointment as you now have to destroy the weapon through full use before you can get that material again.
Adding to that problem is the one where if you accidentally drop an epic made item or normal (more annoying with the epic ones), you will have to find the weapon again if you want the items from the location you picked up and made it from to re-spawn their loot, the items need to be FULLY used to re-spawn which is also an issue with cars.(which most time people are gentle with trying not to blow them up.)
Car combo. This was a huge step in the right direction and a massive step in the right direction for this franchise. Some of the car combos are useless and even in the right hands *sweeper zombie chew*, so i am sure you all will pick that car which suits you best.
Cons with the car system. Some of the roads if not most in some areas are blocked, which forces you to either get on foot or find the detour, which are fast learned. But you will notice that the map changes with its road blocks though out the progress of the missions. This can be a huge annoyance if you immerse heavily into the game then wake up out of your daze of zombie mashing prowess to notice that whole route you took, only made you hit a dead end. Now with what i said up above about the cars needing to blow up to re-spawn, you can see how this gets annoying if you only just built it and now are blocked off, now you have a car out there useless till the next time you stumble on its beauty.
Yet another annoyance but an easy one to get over, is that zombies get stuck on your car, tips say swerve or stop sharply to get them off your car. Which works with the non-combo, apart from some combo-cars, but most they will stick on to with the force of a dead star. A helpful tip is to just stop the car and get out making the zombie jump off and not damage the car further.
The skill up tree is amazing, and refreshing. As by the level 25-30 i had already maxed out my storage capacity and partly increased health and weapon durability. A feature annoying in the other two but still exciting once leveled the static form it took was just horrible if you wanted to start again fresh with a friend. Now with this new system allowing you to choose where to allocate your hard earned levels brings back a smile to something so hated amongst those like me who play this game to death for hundreds of hours.
Another note is that you can unlock category options. This feature is one which allows you to match similar item types with an opposite which is also different to make the same item. Example- Shock hammer, takes a battery(computer item) and a sledgehammer. Now, with this skill unlocked i can build shock hammer with - 2x4 wood + keyboard/monitor/flashlight to make the same amazing item. That feature, blew me the F away. Seriously DEV's that was the best move ever *wipes tears*
Guns- They just feel amazing. I am not lying, even i now use the auto aim (without aim down sight) to shoot hordes. Just hold the trigger and Nick will aim loosely at the zombies trying to at least land a fast kill blow if not, glancing them and others. I know people don't usually like this stuff, and i am the same. But by god it came in handy.
Overall this game is just a massive step up from the second and OTR. Adding features and a really nice setting. With only one real huge gripe which is that of Nick being such a total wuss and crying at the drop of a hat. I rate this game a solid 10/10. And i don't think i have ever said that about a game since WC3 frozen throne.
Huge recommend. Hope you guys found this helpful!

Dungeon Siege is an old isometric action-RPG. It was quite original for the wanna-beat-Diablo game of year 2003, but now it can attract only a small group of players with the taste for "old-school games". With the slight remark that DS is not as much old-school, being just an Arpg (with emphasis on Action and not RPG).
However, for an action-rpg it has very promising setting, with the story based on the heritage of the legion of a great empire, lost in the world of magic, and, the most noticeable - the clever system of character grading, where you "levelling" your heroes only when using specific skills. Shoot the bow - become dexterous archer, cast spells - and take a gain in "intelligence" and magic power. Or, well, just bash'em all with a stick or shovel - as you start your adventure with the "child of farmer lost his home" background.
Other than character evolution, Dungeon Siege "key features" are not likely to take your interest, as following the story turns out too thankless task. Well, unless we return to the levelling system - as there you can hire companions (up to 7) and train them to fit your tactics. So you can gather a somewhat standard band, like 2 melee, 2 archers, 2 mages, 2 healers... or to mix all the roles at your leasure. You can even hire 7 mules to carry your stuff, and fight your way all alone... if you that attracted to the DS, which I doubt.
Oh, well. Do I like Dungeon Siege? Sure, it brings some memories, and it is still not bad, if you know the drill. The interface was fine back in time, and it is still quite easy to get along. Although... the gameplay not aged that well, for my tastes. What was quite alright in time between Diablo 1 and 2, now feels... too plain. Bland even.
Can I recommend it to the people who are new to the plethora of games, made more than 10 years back? Barely. People, who started to play in time of Mass Effect rising, certainly will be having hard times motivating themselves to play Dungeon Siege I. It was good back then, but now... now it's worth buying only if you know already what you're getting yourself into.
Nostalgia project, with personal mark 7/10 - for the fun time back in the days. It was nice while it lasted.

Jade Empire - An often over-looked gem
Thrown into a chaotic world full of different factions, you choose which path will you follow: the open palm or the closed fist. Before you uncover the truth about what goes on and what's your role in it, you will have to travel through cities, valleys, forests, swamps, caves and mountains, meeting interesting characters on every corner.

If you recall the old "Choose Your Own Adventure" or perhaps the "Lone Wolf" game books from the '70's and '80's, then you're on the right track for this game.
After a few playthroughs, you'll probably start to recognize some of the options.  This is partially offset by the fact that there appear to be more options that will appear in a single playthrough, and that you won't be able to ever pick all of the options every time either.  The inclusion of Achievements and Cards give some added depth, but some of the Achievements appear to be based on failing in some scenarios so it's not always apparent what might need to be done for the Achievement Hunter.
The soundtrack is minimalist, but the solo accoustic guitar  is pleasant and quite nice, and matches the style of the artist very well.  A glaring omission, here, is the lack of a purchaseable soundtrack (at the time of this writing).  The artwork is quite lovely, and the whimsical nature of it nicely matches the intent of the game.  It is static, with only a few things that move -- mostly the clickable hotspots so that it's apparent what will actually give a response from the game -- but it feels like a callback to old adventure or even the old solely text-based games so I don't find that a bad thing.
The writing is excellent, though you'll most likely find yourself skipping some sectiions as the become more familiar.  It may be a good game to play with your developing reader, though I highly recommend you play it a few times, yourself, as some of the game can wander to the dark or violent (You ARE a monster, after all.) and your mileage may vary as to what's appropriate for your own child.

An absolute amazing prequel to the first Deus Ex. The game takes place in a futuristic cyberpunk world where corporations hold the power and human augmentation are a matter of debate. The game has a profound and very good story that lets you make decisions and live with the consequences either good or bad. The side quests are one of the best aspects of the game. You can choose how you play that game be stealth or shoot and kill everybody with your augmentations. The A.I. is the "worst" aspect of the game, not well programmed but still, not that big of a problem. The conversation between characters and the morality choices of the game are another good aspect, not to mention the good VA of the main character played by Elias Toufexis. Deus Ex Human Revolution is one of the few FPS games that doesn't feel like a straight shoot/run/kill game.

This game is one of Bioware's earlier RPGs before Mass Effect and Dragon Age modern fame.  Like a lot of developers, all their works share similar themes.  Good characterization, good humor, binary good / evil (although in this case its styled differently), good voice acting, etc.  The setting and music are characterization are all good and very well enjoyable, and quite amusing at times.  Bioware is very good at that, and I applaud them.
The problem with the game is that the actual -game- portion is just not very fun.  The combat is downright awful because there is no balance or flow.  Most enemies could be button-mashed to death, and those that can't usually have some sort of rediculous advantage over the player such as no hitstun, extremely high damage, or extremely high health.  There are two types of MP, one for magic + healing and the other for weapons + bullet time... but considering that there is no other way to restore your health aside from generous cutscenes I can't see magic being useful.  Leveling up a weapon style makes it use almost no MP but bullet time drains MP like pouring water out of a cup.  Animations are VERY clunky and often uncancelable, and each style only has one combo and one guardbreak attack.  Controlling your character in fights is a pain because being locked on to an enemy makes you extremely slow, and free camera makes it impossible to hit enemies reliably.
Levelling up gives points to spend in combat styles and other points to spend on stats, but there's no way to really know if you're going to get a good style later down the line and spent points are permanent.  Its a pitfall of RPGs, not knowing how well-spent your resources are because of a lack of transparency in the system.  Luckily stats are more easily corrected as you can swap equipment to boost the little used conversation stats and your primary stats, but nothing boosts your damage or defense directly.
There are scant few puzzles in the game that really only pad or are otherwise obnoxious (get out a pen and paper because you'll need to memorize), and a seemingly pointless Galaga minigame that occurs often and produces no non-Galage related rewards.
The game runs fine on Win7 / HD6850 / 3.2GHz * 6 / 8gb RAM system.  Its was made for the original XBOX and it shows, but the game controls perfectly fine on PC as a port even in the few fixed camera scenes.
I'd say pass on the game unless you like Bioware titles or the asian setting.  The combat in the game holds the whole package back far too much to be a robust title.  It's not worth suffering through for the story, which is only okay, even if well presented.

This was an unexpected surprise. I went in expecting a cheap little platforming game and what I got was an adventure game that was short and very sweet.
The story is quite basic, but you start out in a scrolling shooting game and wind up stranded after the battle on a planet. From there you explore with the use of a teleport gun, all to find your nemesis and escape.
The teleoprt gun is pretty slick, and I honestly can't think of a lot of games off the top of my head that emulated this type of 'metroidvania' style game play using such an item. I'm sure they're
but I haven’t seen them. That said, it is a slick mechanic executed flawlessly in this game. The gun fires a beam that reacts differently depending on whether or not it hits a solid surface, crosses beams of different colors, or passes through bars. There's not a lot to explain here, it all becomes very evident as you play.
Mastering the use of the teleport gun and jumping becomes essential, and then second nature. The game trains the player through elegant and simple level design that will show newcomers a way through and experienced players a lot of previously missed shortcuts.
The games graphics are really excellent.
Once I had the visuals working right I could make out all the little details that had before been a terrible blur.
Graphically this is like a really well made Sega Master System game. I really enjoyed the style and felt just a little nostalgic for the old 8-bit era games. The game play falls into this category as well, being both clever and classic.
Sound effects and music are also well done, and in the same vein of those 8-bit era games.
The game is very short and can be completed in under 20 minutes (my record is 16 minutes), but has a good amount of replay value if you want to explore, discover a handful of hidden areas, and maybe see how fast you can complete the game itself. The game makes no mistakes, the player does. When I kept getting killed it was my fault for not paying attention to what was going on, or for goofing off. The game doesn't punish the player, but it totally rewards good skill and timing.
I only used my controller to play this and found absolutely no problems.
I've clocked over 8 hours and enjoyed every hour spent here. I would love to see more, even a sequel, but as it stands this is a solid platforming game worthy of your time.
Short but brilliant experience. Recommended, especially if on sale.

I'm a bit iffy on this one, to be honest.  Overall, it's a nice enough little game - the graphics are pretty (particularly once you figure out how to get them scaled back from 640x480 pixels) and the story, while linear as all get-out, is pretty easy to follow.  The community, such as I could see of it (bearing in mind I'm an Australian in time zone GMT+8, so I'm effectively about 8 hours out of synch with most of the English-speaking world) seemed friendly enough.  It's an MMO you can just as easily play solo - while there are some parts where you need to be part of a group, they're not compulsory.
All that said, it has one big problem - botting.  If you go into the game, you will see a lot of characters who look remarkably similar - all male, all wearing the first face, first hairstyle, and first hair colour (in other words, short purple hair) and all Grenadiers.  They'll all have the same guardian spirit (usually Sigrun, after about level 25) and they'll turn up at certain spots
.  Their names will be random strings of characters, because they're bots.  If you happen to be trying to level in a spot which has been botted, you're going to find yourself struggling to find the mob you're supposed to be killing, or the item you're supposed to be looking for, or the character you're supposed to be escorting, because the bots are there knee deep, and all you can do is wait for them to move on, and hope everything re-spawns before the next bot wave comes through.
The game also suffers from what appears to be a common problem to many MMO  games - a single spawn point, a single storyline, and as a result the whole thing gets incredibly boring when you're running through the whole thing again in order to try out a different character class (really, though, the only MMOs I've run across which don't have this problem are World of Warcraft, and to a lesser extent, Dark Age of Camelot and City of Heroes).  This is only exacerbated by the highly linear storyline, which doesn't have many side quests available.
Plus, of course, there's the standard anime problem of what the female characters are almost wearing.  One day a game design company is going to realise approximately 50% of the world's population isn't overwhelmingly interested in looking at characters with improbably bouncy breasts (either because breasts just don't do it for them, or because they have a set of breasts themselves, or both) and they're going to realise there's an un-tapped market for eye-candy just waiting to be exploited.  The designers of this game have got part of the way there - the male character models are very pretty, very bishie, and very cute to look at.  But quite frankly, when the female version of an outfit regularly comes to a packet of dental floss, three sequins and a cork (you figure out where each goes) while the male version of the same outfit covers the character from chin to toes, it gets a bit annoying.  Speak to the designers at Square Enix, for crying out loud - they at least accept there are more people playing games out there than just heterosexual men, and they provide some eye candy for the gay men and heterosexual women as well!
Really, it isn't a bad game.  But then again, it doesn't really stand out in my mind as particularly good either.  If Steam had an option for "eeeehhhh..." I'd probably choose that.  But as it stands, it's getting approximately 4.99/10, and voted down.

Nothing bad, but nothing great or unique about it.
This is a top down platformer aimed at children 5-10 years old. It's difficulty level is around Kirby (excluding bosses), Drawn to Life, or the Lego games. Experienced players won't have problems and will probably find it boring. Get it only during a good sale.
There are 16 stages that can be completed in about 10 minutes each. There are several hidden bonus rooms if the player searches or deviates from the main path. There are 3 weapons: a mallet with spring-loaded boxing glove, anvil dropper, and umbrella that slows falling and protect against anvils. Hazards include moving platformers, trampolines, dropping platforms (Donut Lifts), collasping bridge, catwalks, very tiny platforms, crushers (Thwomps), fast conveyer belts, and all of the above over bottomless pits. Death results in being spawned in a nearby location and the loss of some coins.  There are 2 maze levels, some switch puzzles, and 3 bosses. The bosses requires some pattern memorization or tell/cue recognition.
There is a moderate level of character customization. You can be a dog, cat, horse, or chicken. Each has 8 skin pallets. There are about 20 clothes for hats/wigs, gloves, shirts, pants, shoes, and backpacks. There are male and female casual clothes as well as costumes such as princess, priate, vampire, scientist, and more; referecing Warner Brothers cartoons. All of these are purchased with coins or found randomly in stages. (I purchased this game mainly because I like paper dolls, (guilty pleasure). I was pleased with the selection. My only dissapointedment is the lack of pallets for clothing.)
Graphics - looks nice, cartoony with Merry Melodies aesthetics.
Sound - about 5 jazzy songs consisting of apporpriate but not memorable music
Controls - controls are solid but the player moves rather slowy
Misc. - I have no experience of the closed broswer MMO "Cartoon Universe". Credits state that this was developed by Wayforward, but there are several other departments such as marketing, and Warner Brothers staff, etc.

tl;dr version: Do you remember games like Commandos and Desperados?  Did you like those games?  If you answered yes to both those questions then this game is for you.
Full review: Crookz is an isometric, real time with pause, tactical stealth game set in the 70s that follows the exploits of a group of professional thieves.
Pros:
* 70s setting
* 70s style funk soundtrack
* Strong tactical gameplay
* Missions play out differently depending on your chosen team members and tools you brought with you
* Great difficulty curve
* Elegant and user friendly UI
* Game autosaves every 30 or so seconds
Cons:
* Less than stellar visuals
* Mediocre writing
* Enemy AI is a bit too easy to exploit
* Rare pathing issues
Crookz plays a bit like the old Commandos and Desperados games, except even less combat focused.  The idea is to break into a facility, steal or plant something, take any other goodies you can along the way, and get out without being caught.  To achieve this you have a team of thieves, each with their own unique skills.  Most of the time you can't bring the whole team along, so you much choose carefully who to bring for the job.  There are tools available which can make up for skills you lack, covering areas that other teammembers that got left behind would have taken care of, but these tools are consumable (1 use) and you have very limited inventory space.
One of the best things about this game is how good the UI is.  You can pause the game at any time and give out a set of instructions to your team members, including multiple waypoints and multiple commands at each waypoint.  Furthermore you can delete any individual command at any waypoint or any individual waypoint and the game will connect the remaining waypoints for you, making adjusting plans on the fly rather user friendly.
The game starts out very easy with rather straightforward missions and easy to bypass security.  Missing skills can be easily accounted for with tools found in the levels themselves or by taking a different approach.  The game difficulty definitely ramps up though and the missions get more and more complicated and it become almost impossible to cover all bases with team member skills and tools, so you have to improvise in some areas to get past obstacles.  The missions have some replayability to as you can go back to them later when you have access to other team mebers and skills at your disposal (each character has multiple skills that unlock as the story progresses) and try to beat your previous best score.
There is also a challenge mode with particularly difficult missions that you need to attempt with specific team members and tools on hand.  These can be real tricky.
For the most part, pathing is pretty good, though once in a long while weird issues arise, like a character trying to take the long way around through a hole in the wall when there's an open door right in front of them.  These can be worked around by doing smaller steps with your waypoints and happen quite rarely.  Also, the enemy AI seems a little too easy to exploit and to get away from when they spot you.  You need to be able to exploit the enemy AI to some degree to get past some obstacles, but it seems a bit too easy to trick them or lose them when they pursue you.
Overall, this is a game I very much enjoy playing.  The gameplay is really solid and the game can get quite challenging with a lot of moving parts to try to keep track of and complicated security systems to try to bypass.  If you're looking for a tactical stealth game then you owe it to yourself to try this game out.

I am pleased I bought this game as it is challenging and fun to play, with 18 missions in the campaign and a seperate challenge mode where you race the clock with a predetermined team and set of tools.
The missions start off easy to allow you to learn the game mechanics, then it gets more difficult which requires more planning and time to think which makes the pause and plan feature come in handy.
There are six characters to choose from all with unique skills, for example there is the acrobat who can slip through vents and laser barriers and a electronics expert who can disable security systems. The characters can form a maximum team size of 4 which you can decide on in the planning phase to decide your favoured approach as there are many methods to complete the jobs. It is possible to complete the heists with any team combo with the use of tools found on the mission map itself and the choice of three tools for each character you can decide on and carry from the planning phase.
Your job is to steal something or setup conditions to make the next heist possible. There is a "heat meter" for gauging how many times the guards and cameras have spotted you which should you max out will end the mission, the heat meter can be lowered by using a tool on a camera security box if the meter gets too high.
Guards are either stationary or on a route which you can observe through the use of a hotkey, you can either sneak past them by avoiding their cone of vision, distract them away from their route or knock the guard out with your thug or other character who has the chloroform tool if possible. Some guards can not be knocked out.
There are plenty of tools and tactics which allow for a creative solution to each heist and I am giving this game a thumb up as I am enjoying the experience.

This controller is PERFECT. Honestly I don't know why the controller has such a bad reputation. Ok, may look cheap but IT IS NOT cheap. The plastics are exactly the same as my xbox 360 controller. You may not like the design but it has nothing to do with the quality of the controller. Everything works like a charm, the controller activates instantly when you switch it on.
The possibilities with this controller are ENDLESS. You can set whatever you like, the profile configuration tool (you have to access it through big picture mode OR from the games library under the game properties) is incredibly 'complicated' to use and you can fine tune whatever you like, create/save/share profiles, button combinations and so on. Through constant updates they are implementing new functions all the time. Basically you can have hundreds of virtual buttons through combinations or long / multiple presses of hardware buttons, as I said the possibilities are practically endless and now they added support for multiple sub-profiles on the same game profile (you can switch between them). In an open world game you could have different profiles for flying, driving, riding, shooting etc, for instance, and switch between them in a fraction of a second.
To be short:
PROS
- incredible range of customizations, you can play anything you like and yes, it can really replace a mouse (but not be as good) in FPS games. Would not play competitive with it but it would be no problem to play a single player FPS on max difficulty.
- long battery life
- more available buttons compared to a traditional xbox controller
- gyroscope
- haptic feedbacks (customizable as well, and they implemented rumble and sounds through haptic motors)
CONS
- triggers have a very short stroke (a bit uncomfortable when driving), but it's just something to get used to.
I really recommend it, if you can find it in a shop (retail) just get it there and save on the shipping from steam which is quite expensive in Europe. It CANNOT be a substitute for mouse+keyboard obviously for competitive games, but it can really get pretty close. Nothing compared to a traditional dual analog stick controller....I'm sad to see it didn't get a good welcome from the PC community, I think this controller is the product of a genius.

It's a great game, but after playing sixteen hours total on this game for a straight week.. I've realized that I am bored.
There is a variety of great classes (you get to choose one in the beginning and then a secondary once you level up) and lots and lots of skills, and the characters are cute. There isn't a lot of customization choices, but you get to choose an Eidolon when customizing your character. Those are companions that follow you around and can even fight with you.
This game is extremely repetitive, especially if you start to ignore the storyline and simply hit 'Skip' to get to the objectives and rewards of each quest. Most of the quests are, "go here and get this item" or "kill a certain number of this mob." It is a game that you grind for levels and XP.
The combat and skills aspect of the game is interesting. It isn't so easy that you can simply stand there and hit your '1' key repeatedly, as you can move as you charge your abilities and try to avoid attacks. There are many combat skills to obtain in the game, and each one has a different affect on you, your Eidolon, or your enemy. I found that as I continued playing I'd have a routine of what skills I'd go through when in combat.
I realized that the game is much more exciting if you decided to find friends and play with a guild. There are many other side activities that are exciting, but most groups of friends tend to all go to the main server, Navea. Most people there are interested in obtaining rare items, which do not impact gameplay so largely that you'd be missing out if you decided not to explore that aspect of the game.
Overall, it's a fun game to play with friends, but can quickly become boring if you stick to questing for long periods of time. I became bored of the quests quickly and had a hard time continuing to play, but ended up not knowing much about the game besides quests. I also didn't have friends that played & I only did quests during my time in the game, so I'd reccomend you try it out and see for yourself.

Monster Loves You! is a cute new look at the coming of age story
told from the perspective of a newly born monster and the many trials that face them as they come of age
Players are given the fluff of a situation and presented with a number of responses to choose from, these choices reflect certain traits that the players monster can grow stronger in and several choices require a certain amount of these stats to unlock as the monster develops and grows
However this stat system often rewards simply selecting actions based on what stat will be improved, rather than making each decision uniquely
Irregardless, Monster Loves You! is a simple, text based life sim with a unique perspective and style worth at least checking out and good for a few play throughs

Grade: 92/100
Difficulty: Very easy to play; moderately difficult to get the different end-game outcomes.

Cons: Not as engaging as it could be story-wise; many choices are very non-intuitive if you are attempting to reach a particular end-game goal.

Hustle Cat is a very enjoyable VN with an interesting story and very likeable characters. I suck at writing proper reviews so here's some pros and cons:
Pros:
- You can choose the gender of your main character, or leave it ambiguous.
- There's love interests of both genders.
- The MC actually has a personality and actively takes part in the story, unlike so many other games where it feels like the MC just passively observes what's going on around them.
- All the characters are well written.
- The story is very entertaining and contains a lot of mystery, suspense and comedy.
- There's cats. Lots of cats.
Cons:
- It's a bit shorter than your average dating sim. I completed all routes in about 14 hours.
- Some of the relationships between the MC and their chosen love interest could've been fleshed out a little more.
- There's a few minor bugs in the game, but nothing that would impede gameplay.
I definitely recommend this game to any fans of the dating sim genre. And if you're new to these types of games it's definitely worth a try.

Its a shooter dinosaurs against humans (obviously the dinosaurs dont have guns). So the idea is pretty unique

The special abilities use up endurance without endurance you are a sitting duck and to get health back you need to eat bodies of dead dinosaurs wich are also scattered across the whole map.
This game has microtransactions but only skins and cosmetics so nobody needs that in addition: you get drops sometimes.
Finally, i enjoyed this game pretty much but it has a low amount of servers so you got to live with that.

Adventure Capitalist has come a long way since its May 30th release. I acquired the game a couple months after release and played the death out of it. The game does have a microtransaction element which does not affect the game at all as it is a single player game; I will talk more indepth about this later on in the review.
Being a clicker game graphics aren't the main focus by any stretch of the imagination, but this game goes beyond the pixelated and cheap graphics seen in other clicker games and establishes its own bright and colourful scheme with interesting graphics.
This game genre has it easy, customers don't expect flashy and fancy Unreal Engine graphics or Michael Bay sound effects, however this game delivers both with a good effect. Ofcouse their are an abundence of sound effects as that would be a waste of production time. The key part of this section is the music, the melodic singular tune repeating over and over in an endless loop never bothered me whatsoever (whilst being an individual that normally plays with the ingame music mutes) I particularly enjoyed this games music and it kept me whistling the tune weeks after I'd stopped playing the game!
The basic premise of this game is that you are here to make some serious cash, starting with the basics you aim to dominate the lemon industry whilst branching out to many other industrys in the meantime. The simple yet addictive feeling of watching your bank balance rise like the middle of a Skrillex song is massively fascinating to me and the 27,000 other people with positive review of this game as of now. The game does not require you to be on the game to make money, you will be raking in them $ whilst enjoying a long deserved rest or even in your work hours. Overall the gameplay fails to get boring and stale instead it becomes bigger and better as you progress through the game.
I felt like this needed it's own section as some people will be wondering how the microtransaction system works. Yes the game has microtransactions, but hold your horses. Don't leave yet as the game is single player and in no way competitive, so in reality their is little need to actually purchase the microtransactions at all. There's 4 different types of microtransaction in this game and I am going to go through each one.
1. Getting angels without resetting - if you reset you can get to the same stage at about 10 minutes, maybe a little longer.
2. Skipping 1 day - if you don't play this game for 1 day you will have the same effect.
3. Getting x3 multiplier - you get money 3 times faster, and it stacks with multiple buys (x3, x6, x9, ...).
4. New suit for your character - only visual change.
Now having briefly explaining the types of microtransaction the term P2W can't be used for this game as there is no way to win, you aren't competing against anyone and your purchases won't affect anyone but yourself. A positive for these transactions is that you can use them as a term of tipping the developers for the great game supplied for no cost whatsoever.
To conclude this review, this game is definately worth picking up and giving a try; its not coming to any expense to you or your hard-drive being free and less than 1 GB in storage usage. The graphical art style is fun and creative mixed with funky musical backing track and impecible gameplay mechanics. This game is not affected by the microtransactions at all and if anything should be used to tip the developer.

Before I say anything it needs to be mentioned that I started using a controller for an actual action game 2 weeks before the steam controller arrived. Sure there was the once a year fifa duke down with friends but almost exclusively I used the mouse and keyboard, and always felt this was too much in my blood to change. Now this sounds a bit too good to be true but literally one of my first thoughts after installing it and going through steam with it was " Wow, this feels just like my mouse"
This is important because I also realized the Steam controller is trying to achieve more than just playing action video games with it. I can comfortably use it from my bed or chair, being feet away from my computer ,without feeling many restraints on my speed and accuracy, it was build  to be a desktop controller which can replace the mouse. And by god it's doing it better than anything I have hoped.
The Pros:
** It's accurate and very efficient when it comes to replacing activities you would previously use a mouse for
** Easy to get used to if you don't usually use controllers
**Light and easy to hold
**It's highly customizable, you can set up hotkeys and macros for anything from a button push, to button combos, to specific swipes on the touch pads, you can even set up the speed and response times of the swipe pad,
** Has tactile feedback on the touch pads, this helps a lot in getting a better feeling of the speed and accuracy of the touch pad
**Has a gazillion buttons which turn out to be quite handy, most notable analog two stage R 1 and L1 and  the grip buttons under it are also very well placed, I found them ideal for twitch simple commands like healing in Dark Souls 1 and 2
**You can actually download a setting profile for it and have the ideal set up made by other players, and only use it for the game itself. Yes you can set up a controller profile to activate only when you enter a game
**this thing is convenience incarnate, there is no limit to how deep a can bury myself into my cozy bed and still play the games I want without getting punished that I have been using a mouse a keyboard for so long
The cons:
**A bit more pricey than other controllers that are out there like X box and various others
**You need to take time and set it up for some games, especially if you want to be competitive within them. Don't get me wrong the controller will have default settings but the touch pads are not always that ideal for fast camera movement.  You need to adjust the mode and speed or you will end up swiping 5 times for a full 360 turn.
Overall I am amazed with how well it managed to achieve in replacing the mouse and keyboard, it felt like home from the first time I tried it and this is coming from 27 year  old gamer who started using controllers 2 months ago. It is indeed a worthy controler for the PC master race. Gaming wise it's a sound investment and I honestly recommend it if you are looking to play more casually away from your desk.

It is either a great controller or a useless, funny-looking piece of plastic. There is no in-between.
For games that use mouse and keyboard, or even better, M+K and Gamepad simultaneously, it can work wonders. For games with heavy d-pad usage it can bring out your inner scotsman's vocabulary.
It's functionally useless for fighting games, but amazing for flight sims. There's a fine line to how much mouse is too much mouse for a game to use it. Inventory management is a pain in a lot of CRPGs.
Its strongest ability is its customization. You can map so many things to the haptics and the buttons, add modifiers so holding another button essentially unlocks an alternate mapping on the controller. You can tweak sensitivity until it's perfect (Though trackball mode leaves a bit to be desired on the tweaking front).
You can make this controller your perfect tool for I would say 40% of games. 20% of games it makes a passable handle, but is beat by either controller or M+K. Another 20% of games, it's beat by both, but still a nifty way to control it, and for the last 20% of games, it's just flat out not an option, either for technical, comfort, or speed reasons.
Also it's designed for folks with large hands. It's not quite an original xbox pad, but it's definitely on the large size, so people with small hands, beware.
Also, the haptic on the right has nothing in the way of locational feedback, so you can't tell where your thumb is on the pad until you hit the edge, where there is a small band of no detection.
Battery life and connectivity is PHENOMINAL, but my haptics started to make a worrying sound as my AA batteries got lower in charge, so mind that.
The over/under on this controller is that if you love tweaking control settings, it's for you. If you find it to be a chore, don't buy this. I personally love the dang thing.

I was drawn to Aura Kingdom after re-watching Sword Art Online (which has a charming world, despite being pretty awful overall), and I've now put more than a few hours into the game. It's a free-to-play JMMORPG, but how does it compare to its competition?
+++The free-to-play model for this game is really excellent, definitely one of the best I've played. The game never harasses you about paying money, in fact it rarely comes up at all. In addition, you can only pay for cosmetic items or faster leveling, neither of which hinders players who choose not to pay.
+++The environments in this game are first rate. They really did an excellent job with level design, and you never stay in one place for too long. Each area has a mission hub (usually a town) and then several areas branching off of increasing difficulty, then you move on to the next area. All of the areas cover very different biomes and settings, so it mixes up pretty well.
++Even without spending money, there is a ton of cosmetic customization available. None of the classes or genders are pay-locked like in The Old Republic, and you frequently get new outfits in the story.
++The classes are really great. There are 11 classes in total, and they vary pretty well. Whether you prefer melee combat, gunslinging, archery, or magic; you have plenty of options to choose from. In addition, at level 40, you get to choose an offhand class to specialize even more.
++In a DPS class (EVA or DEF), the game is easily solo'able. The story tops off at level 60, but you can play until level 75. I'm currently at level 50 and I believe I have only died twice. Very little content is group-locked, so I hardly ever feel bad about playing alone. Some dungeons require parties, but there is usually a solo option.
++Unlike TERA, this game doesn't try to trick you with a hook. In TERA, you level up really quickly in the beginning and get a lot of new gear, and the quests are pretty fast and fun, but, once you're hooked, the game really slows down. In Aura Kingdom, though, the game barely slows down at all.
++The main game is not complicated at all. Crafting confused me at first, but it's really simple (especially compared to TERA), completely optional, and very benificial. If you have any MMO experience at all, specializing your class is simple and you shouldn't have too many regrets.
++The game runs really well; I'm pretty sure you could hit 60fps on a toaster. I've been playing at 60fps on my laptop's Intel graphics, and hitting the 120fps cap on my desktop. On that note, the graphics settings, despite the engine's simple visuals, are really excellent. There's nothing amiss in the settings, so you can pretty much tune the game to your liking.
++The gameplay settings are highly customizable, it seems like the developers actually know what people want in an MMO. You can auto-block requests and messages, disable and enable all of the UI, toggle manual and automatic functions, and pretty much set the game how you like it.
++If you click on an objective, the game's autorouting will walk you to it. I cannot express how great that is. If I'm a 5 minute walk away from an objective, I can set my character on autopilot and go do something for that time period. Most of the time I choose to move myself, especially because flying is a lot of fun, but it's a very handy feature.
+The game really kindles my love for the anime Sword Art Online. Many aspects of the game are similar to SAO, as well as environments and equipment. The developers must have realized this, because I noticed you can buy near-clones of the outfits from Sword Art Online on the game's store. In addition, there is an area that functions just like SAO, in that it's a tower and each floor is its own dungeon with a boss you have to clear before moving up.
+While unoriginal, the combat in the game is pretty fun and attractive. The animations vary greatly from attack to attack, and each class feels really special on the battlefield.
+The game has a surprisingly large number of references to pop-culture and literature, especially for a Japanese game. While running a dungeon today, an NPC snuck some "Can You Feel The Love Tonight" lyrics into the dialogue. Many of the "hidden quests," as they call unmarked quests, are shoutouts to books, movies, and other games. One of the daily missions this week, even, was a recreation of an Adventure Time episode.
--While the environments are attractively designed, the graphics engine is sub-par. Objects are fairly low-poly, textures are simple, and FX are certainly not of modern quality. If you want a more modern and attractive engine, play TERA.
--Some classes are definitely better than others. I played the Duelist and picked up the Ranger as my offhand, but the Ravager, for example, is absolutely devestating compared to the other classes. I have not tried, but I feel that it would be difficult to solo the game as a support class. It is my opinion that all classes should have the ability to solo in every MMO.
-Flying as a game mechanic is great fun, but it's heavily hindered by the terrible object clip boxes. When you're walking around, it doesn't affect you, but while flying there are invisible walls galore.
-The combat system does not inovate at all. Aura Kingdom uses the same hotkey-based combat you see in World of Warcraft, The Old Republic, and pretty much every other MMO.
-The story is not particularly intriguing, especially compared to The Old Republic. I easily forget what's happening, because I just don't feel engaged, and I find myself skipping dialogue from time to time.
-The dialogue doesn't usually feel immersive. A lot of the characters use throw modern language in, despite the fantasy setting, and it can be pretty hard to be attached to the story. It's not terrible, and the grammar is seldom (but occasionally) incorrect, but it's certainly not beautiful.
*Some people might not like the very anime art style. The game does feature its fair share of bikini-armor, and I'm pretty sure every female armor in the game uses high heels. It's no where near as bad as TERA, which high level female armor is pretty much synonymous with nudity (although they absolutely sexualize males, too). Aura Kingdom is a lot better in that regard, but you'll still see female knights in short shorts.

MLY isn't so much a game as it's an interactive story, like a Choose Your Own Adventure book. That doesn't mean it's bad, but if you're looking for frenetic gameplay, you won't find it here. Instead, everything in this game hinges on your decisions and how you live your life as a monster.
If I had to compare MLY to a video game, the closest thing would be a very, very old game called Alter Ego (from 1986, not the 2010 game of the same name). The similarities are striking, with the exception that in MLY you play a monster in a fictional world whereas in AE you were a male or female human in the real world.
Although MLY's interface is better than AE's, it lacks the same depth. In AE, you didn't just make decisions and get older, but you could get an education, hold down a job, get married, get pregnant (if you were female), die prematurely, and so on.
I wish MLY had included something like those options as it would've increased the replay value a lot.  That said, it's still an entertaining and unusual experienceand, so if you get it on sale (which I did) then you'll get your money's worth.

Once a member of a group of sassy 70's thieves you were tasked with stealing Kryptonite(at least that's what it looks like to me). Alas, as an alien much greater than me once said "It's a Trap!".
Having disbanded after the last heist and down to two members of the original gang you set off to steal this rare moonstone again, years later. Only this time, it's personal.
Crookz The Big Heist is at it's core a simulation heist game. You start with two thieves each with their own "Particular set of skills". With more of the old gang coming back as you progress through the 18 heist scenarios.
The game starts off with a great introduction to the story by making this first "trap" heist act as the tutorial. Explaining the basics of how to unlock doors, read guards, and collect precious loots.
Each level is a little more story and the actual heist itself. You start with an overview of the level where you can select what crew you're bringing with you and purchase any tool you think you may need or want to have just in case.
Delivered in a sweeping look of the map, the narrator explains what you are doing there, what your target is, and things to look out for. During this phase you can zoom in and out, watch guards pathing, and you can see what switches open which doors, etc... You can then start setting commands for your crew. You set waypoints for each member of the crew, which can be edited on the fly.
You progress through each stage by setting these waypoints, having crew members unlock doors, knock out guards, and clear out without anyone getting caught. Precision is key here. Knowing when to set members to wait and taking advantage of the pause button will go along way in a successful heist.
Overall, Crookz is a well designed top-down heist game with a great single player campaign, challenge mode, and enough 70's music to keep you shakin' your groove thing for hours.

There are several playable characters to choose a team from which for most levels allows you to select four to take on a job. Each character has a set of specific skills for example Cleopatra runs faster than all other and can also run through laser beams whereas Bishop as the locksmith is the only one who can pick locks without tools. The characters are all useful in certain levels and selecting your crew comes down to your own play style as well as the various puzzles that will be faced.
Something which I personally enjoyed was the planning phase for a level which works similar to the old rainbow six games in which you can carefully view the blueprints of the level to see what you’ll be up against. In this phase you can scout the level, select your crew and then equip them. There is a variety of equipment available to outfit your thieves with, each costs money from the pool of cash you earn from each successful heist. Each character can only carry three items at any one time which forces you to plan ahead but equipment can also be found in the level. Items range from crowbars to unlock doors and strongboxes, to chloroform for taking out guards. As the game progresses you’ll gain access to more characters and equipment to play around with which then you can take to the challenge mode to replay older missions with new characters.
Once done with planning, the level will start in paused mode in which you can path out your first moves. While the pathing sounds like it makes the game easy, you will often have to pause to make quick changes due to changing guard patterns. One of the key difficulty mechanics is timing, timing your movements, flicking of switches and lock picking of doors is crucial which makes the levels tenser. With patrolling guards, cameras, lasers, switch doors and more, timing and the team work of your crew is essential for not getting caught. Each level has two failure states, first is the heat bar which increases each time you are seen by a guard or device. The second is being arrested by a guard which results in an instant game over.
The levels are fairly enjoyable and there is a decent progression of difficulty in the puzzles. The pathing suffers some problems occasionally with mis-clicks and it can become a little finicky when setting up various actions. The art style of the game works well, its 70’s style is reinforced with the use of vibrant colors. There’s some nice art assets in the game however I personally disliked the use of large icons for items in levels. While the game certainly is not graphically impressive it does a decent job of looking attractive, some animations like walking through doors are odd and could have been much better.
The games soundtrack has a good mix of 70’s style music that’s fun to listen too. Like I’ve said the voice acting isn’t too bad the major issues with both audio and graphically is that there is a host of bugs, while I have not encountered anything game breaking, the audio has bugged out on almost every level with frequent pops or turning on and off. There are frequent graphically problems with clipping, lighting issues, paths being showing even after you’ve deleted them and more. It’s pretty buggy but theres little in the way of game hampering stuff.
Overall Crookz is a decent stealth tactical heist game, I feel it’s over simplistic in places and could have done with being a lot more difficult especially when there is only 18 levels. I personally would have liked larger levels with more emergent gameplay and fewer of the more linear levels however the range the game offers is not bad. While the challenge mode offers the game a little life line in terms of longevity I think a map editor for players to create and play each other’s maps would have been a really beneficial mode for this game. There’s around 10+ hours of game to play if you’re terrible at the game like me however I imagine you could get the single player campaign completed in just less than 10. The game is of a good quality and at $30 the game will satisfy fans of tactical stealth games however if you’re unsure at what you’ve seen I would certainly wait for a sale.

This game is a gem. It might not look like much at first look, but it's everything an otome should be.
First, a relatable main character. With an actual personnality. Bonus points : you can choose whether you want Avery to be a she, a he or a they - not something you see often in otomes (there are also a few customization options, including skin color). Second, the datable characters are all lovable and interesting in their own way, and you can date girls as well as boys. No yanderes, no push over, nothing cringy or borderline non-con like we usually get, if you want something cute and 100% consensual this is it. I played all the routes, expecting some of them to be downright annoying but even though I have my preferences I enjoyed them all. And third, the setting. You get to work in a cat café which is all kinds of amazing in itself, with the added bonus that all the employees can turn into cats themselves. I mean, sure, it's a bit of a stretch, but we've had people-turned-into-pets before (Dandelion) and stuff even less... likely (Hatoful Boyfriend, My Horse Prince) so really, nothing we haven't seen before.
And it's funny. Like, really funny, with a lot of pop culture references because Avery is a nerd and I often found myself laughing at their lines. Some scenes even got me tearing up a little. The story is surprisingly compelling, the relationship with every character is sweet and cute and never feels forced or cheap, and the dialogues are delightful. I should add that there's a real story besides the romance aspect. And there's even a - very satisfying - secret route. Also, cats. The art is good, although I felt the CGs were a bit rushed sometimes? The gameplay is overall standard but that's really all we ask from a visual novel. I should warn that the game can be a bit buggy though. Took me time to unlock the secret route because my save files kept disappearing and I had to start all over again (thank god there's a skip option), which was really annoying. That's the only negative thing I can say about this game though. ...Did I mention there were cats?
And with it being on sale right now, do yourself a favor, don't hesitate: grab it!
Could I possibly be a furry? God knows I am now.

Let's underline a thing, at the moment of writing this review, the new update and a patch(1.6.1) have just been released.
One of the most negative things about PCE have always been the unbalanced teams when it comes to deathmatch mode: generally speaking people don't like very much playing as human, because most of the time the human team loses. So, before this update was released, people tried to avoid playing human by switching team when they were put in the human team, and this led to unbalanced matches, like 5 humans VS 10 dinos. This also caused players on the dino side to be autobalanced to the human team, even if they already played as humans in the previous round.
This update aimed at "solving" this problem. How did they "solve" the problem? By disabling team switching. This is what now happens: you play your round as human, then a new match starts and you get to play as dino, BUT people who should play as human this round leave the server, so the teams aren't balanced anymore and autobalance moves you to the human team(even if you were already human last round) and you CAN'T SWITCH BACK to the team you were even if you have the RIGHT to play on that side.
So, is the problem solved? No, not at all. I could say it's even worse than before.
The problem CAN'T be solved unless playing humans becomes as enjoyable as playing dinos, this is the real problem: playing human is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If it was enjoyable, people would on purpose choose humans, neither would they leave a server when it's their turn to be human. Do you think forcing them to play on whatever team happens to be in minority is a good choice? What a great idea.
Oh and what about the progression system? This update has implemented the progression system too. Every time you level up you get a random drop, as in CS:GO . Personally I don't like it because leveling up doesn't feel rewarding. You could get a common skin or a rare skin, it's totally random. But this is not such a big problem as the previous ones.
