A hidden gem by Bioware (creators of Mass Effect, Dragon Age, KOTOR)
Set in a fictional, steampunk representation of China, you are a promising student of a quiet training school of Martial Arts. When assassins attack, you are forced into a journey seeking answers, closure or revenge depending on how you handle the moral system.
The game also includes Bioware's trademark romances, which also include the capacity for gay and lesbian relationships (whilst the homosexual romances are censored, mods are available to remedy that)
Story is engaging, controls are simple to master, however the game is very glitchy and the voice talent - with few exceptions - is a bit cringeworthy.
It should be noted however that installing the game via steam will require a bit of tinkering to allow it to work on more recent operating systems, but help is available in the steam forums.
In spite of it's flaws, Jade Empire is grossly underplayed and still holds up to be a very entertaining and rewarding game.
I still hold out hope that a sequel will one day appear on the horizon as it holds ample franchise potential.

It is either a great controller or a useless, funny-looking piece of plastic. There is no in-between.
For games that use mouse and keyboard, or even better, M+K and Gamepad simultaneously, it can work wonders. For games with heavy d-pad usage it can bring out your inner scotsman's vocabulary.
It's functionally useless for fighting games, but amazing for flight sims. There's a fine line to how much mouse is too much mouse for a game to use it. Inventory management is a pain in a lot of CRPGs.
Its strongest ability is its customization. You can map so many things to the haptics and the buttons, add modifiers so holding another button essentially unlocks an alternate mapping on the controller. You can tweak sensitivity until it's perfect (Though trackball mode leaves a bit to be desired on the tweaking front).
You can make this controller your perfect tool for I would say 40% of games. 20% of games it makes a passable handle, but is beat by either controller or M+K. Another 20% of games, it's beat by both, but still a nifty way to control it, and for the last 20% of games, it's just flat out not an option, either for technical, comfort, or speed reasons.
Also it's designed for folks with large hands. It's not quite an original xbox pad, but it's definitely on the large size, so people with small hands, beware.
Also, the haptic on the right has nothing in the way of locational feedback, so you can't tell where your thumb is on the pad until you hit the edge, where there is a small band of no detection.
Battery life and connectivity is PHENOMINAL, but my haptics started to make a worrying sound as my AA batteries got lower in charge, so mind that.
The over/under on this controller is that if you love tweaking control settings, it's for you. If you find it to be a chore, don't buy this. I personally love the dang thing.

The issue here really is the right touchpad trying to replace a traditional joystick. You can monkey with the precision all you want but it's impossible to get just right for camera control in 3rd person games like dead space, batman series, tomb raider, skyrim. I've been trying to play batman arkham city for an hour with it and the xbox 360 controller just feels better. The touchpad on the steam one is either too sensitive or not enough, and you have to go into a ton of settings to get it to work right. I got it to where the game is playable (hint go into advance settings for joystick and adjust the anti deadzone), but my other controller still responds far better. If the xbox 360 controller is a 10 then this one gets a 5 or 6 for me.
There's really no reason to get it unless you are looking for a mouse emulator on a controller. Otherwise, cool concept that doesn't work out in the reality. Plus xbox 360 wireless controller for windows is about 20% cheaper. Just get one of those.
I also prefer the xbox controller layout, but that may just be because it's what I'm used to.

I wish I never bought this.
Even after getting used to using it, it's inferior to both a gamepad and a keyboard+mouse.
This controller attempts to be both, and excels at neither.
It's weak as a replacement for a gamepad because the trackpad lacks the precision, comfort, and ease-of-use that a secondary d-stick offers when playing games that are best suited for gamepads.
It's also weak as a replacement for mouse-and-keyboard games because the trackpad lacks the attributes mentioned above, and its only practical use in my eyes would be for casual point-and-click games.  Using this controller for RTS's, FPS's, and other games that require quick and precise mouse movements puts you at a serious and uncomfortable disadvantage, and you're better off using a wireless mouse and keyboard on a dinner tray if you insist on gaming on your couch.
The hardware is solid, responsive, and for all intents and purposes, a sleek and impressive chunk of technology, but none of that makes up for the fact that no matter what type of game you're playing, there's always going to be a control method better suited for it than the Steam Controller.

This is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. Perfects the art of storytelling in the medium of video games with a plot that only gets deeper, darker, and more engaging after its "first" ending, yanking your emotions from despair to faint hope and back again with characters that are much more than just the eye candy or buckets of bolts that they seem to be at first glance. Even though the main story is reasonably linear for the most part, sidequests still channel that same amount of emotion and add meaningful weight to your actions. Gameplay wise, fighting is very satisfying with flowing combos that change based on your weapons, and throws out a shocking but welcome changeup after your first playthrough. Music is a masterpiece similar to but rivalling that of Final Fantasy, varying, all in the same song, from quiet, haunting melodies to tracks more than suitable for fighting mountain-sized metal colossi. Overall, this is a very compelling argument for video games as an art form.

Adventure Capitalist has come a long way since its May 30th release. I acquired the game a couple months after release and played the death out of it. The game does have a microtransaction element which does not affect the game at all as it is a single player game; I will talk more indepth about this later on in the review.
Being a clicker game graphics aren't the main focus by any stretch of the imagination, but this game goes beyond the pixelated and cheap graphics seen in other clicker games and establishes its own bright and colourful scheme with interesting graphics.
This game genre has it easy, customers don't expect flashy and fancy Unreal Engine graphics or Michael Bay sound effects, however this game delivers both with a good effect. Ofcouse their are an abundence of sound effects as that would be a waste of production time. The key part of this section is the music, the melodic singular tune repeating over and over in an endless loop never bothered me whatsoever (whilst being an individual that normally plays with the ingame music mutes) I particularly enjoyed this games music and it kept me whistling the tune weeks after I'd stopped playing the game!
The basic premise of this game is that you are here to make some serious cash, starting with the basics you aim to dominate the lemon industry whilst branching out to many other industrys in the meantime. The simple yet addictive feeling of watching your bank balance rise like the middle of a Skrillex song is massively fascinating to me and the 27,000 other people with positive review of this game as of now. The game does not require you to be on the game to make money, you will be raking in them $ whilst enjoying a long deserved rest or even in your work hours. Overall the gameplay fails to get boring and stale instead it becomes bigger and better as you progress through the game.
I felt like this needed it's own section as some people will be wondering how the microtransaction system works. Yes the game has microtransactions, but hold your horses. Don't leave yet as the game is single player and in no way competitive, so in reality their is little need to actually purchase the microtransactions at all. There's 4 different types of microtransaction in this game and I am going to go through each one.
1. Getting angels without resetting - if you reset you can get to the same stage at about 10 minutes, maybe a little longer.
2. Skipping 1 day - if you don't play this game for 1 day you will have the same effect.
3. Getting x3 multiplier - you get money 3 times faster, and it stacks with multiple buys (x3, x6, x9, ...).
4. New suit for your character - only visual change.
Now having briefly explaining the types of microtransaction the term P2W can't be used for this game as there is no way to win, you aren't competing against anyone and your purchases won't affect anyone but yourself. A positive for these transactions is that you can use them as a term of tipping the developers for the great game supplied for no cost whatsoever.
To conclude this review, this game is definately worth picking up and giving a try; its not coming to any expense to you or your hard-drive being free and less than 1 GB in storage usage. The graphical art style is fun and creative mixed with funky musical backing track and impecible gameplay mechanics. This game is not affected by the microtransactions at all and if anything should be used to tip the developer.

It's so nearly very good.
The remastered music is cracking, the voices are spot on and the redone graphics are excellent (Although Guybrush's new hair cut is atrocious).
You can also instantly switch between the old version and the new one by pressing F10.
And thank god you can, because the new controls are flat out awful. Changing verb is a chore. Using two items in your inventory together is a nightmare. The old game was playable entirely with the mouse. The new one pretty much requires either the keyboard, or to switch to classic mode for the complex puzzles and play it like that for a while.
You can't skip dialogue. Which you couldn't in the original either, but this is a remaster; we've learnt ways of improving game play since 1990 and this seems to have forgotten the last 26 years. Some of the dialog is long, repetitive and annoying (Especially Stan). You can hit backspace and skip the entire conversation, but then you've missed any important bits. Where's the "Click to skip to next line"?
It's Monkey Island. Monkey Island is marvellous. I keep wavering over recommending this just for the graphics and music. But then I look at how often I play it in classic mode (Which switches off the voice over, thus killing that as a selling point), and wonder why I don't just play the original instead.
And then I notice you can't actually by the original any more so this gets a recommendation by default for being the only version available. But play it in classic mode. It's superior.

A nice multiple choice game with a high replay value due to its actual shortness (5 to 15 minutes per playthrough, depending on certain choices and the amount of text you get to read)
But that's okay, because then you can start all over, make different choices and get completely different results:
• Lecture fellow monsters about the dangers of human tools OR convince them that not everything human-made is THAT bad.
• Comfort a grieving woman OR just eat her.
• Scare away birds from some bread crumbs and eat those OR follow the crumbs to a strange little house made of gingerbread. *hint hint*
• End the feud between monsters and humans OR go to war and either get killed, enslaved or succeed and become the new ruler of the world.
All of this is just "shown" in textual form (nope, no animated cutscenes and no running around, just reading, choosing, clicking, reading, choosing and clicking), but it's still a lot of fun when you get to read the results of your doings:
________________________
[Eat some monkey poop.]
WHY WOULD YOU DO THAT!?
________________________
Sadly, the best choices will get stuck in your head and you'll just click through everything in less than 5 minutes before you start a new game again, but that's only the case if you don't care about the different endings, because getting those is the actual challenge (which adds even more replay value).

Unlimited ammo introduction sequence with fitting drama makes for a great ride to launch the story, though you'll already notice the hugely flawed gunplay in the game, which actually contradicts having guns in the game. You'll get the most rewarding experience if you play  full-out stealth, but the game could have shifted some of its focus to melee combat or refined stealth mechanics. Instead, you get a cluster♥♥♥♥ of wannabe game mechanics that fall short on many levels while trying to appease the many.

Important Note: Your previous saves don't carry over into the Director's Cut due to the integration of the DLC titled Missing Link. Be warned that if you're at a personal point of no return then you may wish to hold off on getting this version.
An amazing redux of the original title it does have its flaws. The first of which being that the implimentation of integrating the DLC mission was rather poorly handled and its entirely possible to accidentally leave your guns and even Praxis (the upgrades to augmentations) points behind without meaning to as I had nearly done this had I not gone actively looking for them. For those curious, they're to the left at the end of the mission before getting onto the boat but positioned as such that it can completely escape the eye when crossing by it.
There is also NO balancing for New Game Plus. You don't get to carry over your weapons (why?) but your augmentations carry over, which is an odd choice since by the end of the game even a casual player can almost peak out the character and almost break the game when launching into a new game, which wouldn't have been the same had inventory carried over as weapons and items don't have quite the same effect on gameplay that some of the augmentations do leading to some awkward moments where you've long since passed an area and the dialog is minutes behind on registering because you're flying through levels faster than anticipated.
The graphics did get a neat little boost, but having come from playing the original version straight to the new one, its hard to really tell unless you know exactly what you're looking for. Lighting effects are perhaps the most noteable and easiest to miss unless you're familiar with specific areas of the game that would have otherwise been completely overlooked.
Boss fights are perhaps the most  changed out of everything since there are now alternate ways to take out a boss rather than resorting to using up your ammo or praying you outdamage them. They're still rather frustrating however as their AI hasn't really been modified to accept these changes in level design leading to a rather awkward moment where the Boss paces in just a small area attempting to find you in a room they are completely unfamiliar with, or have to rely solely on bull rushing to get to you before you're able to hack a panel.
Overall though the game still stands up, but if you're looking for an amazing Cyber Punk experience and don't mind some dated graphics, seek out the original Deus Ex as it has the most in terms of balance, but for the modern era of gaming there really isn't an experience like Human Revolution.

Jade Empire could easily been seen as the first step for Bioware towards more simplistic and action based gameplay however it manages to avoid the scorn many felt towards the Mass Effect and Dragon Age series by providing a beautiful and inspired world, the writing is excellent and the characters are interesting.
You start the game off as a student at a martial arts academy. Things quickly change however as you are charged with saving the world and restoring balance in the world, pretty standard hero stuff really. You won't be on your great all important quest for long before some random peasant will ask you go save a cat from a tree however. Jade Empire is a game that loves procrastinating. Despite what should be a fairly urgent overall plot you will find yourself spending most of your time solving the problems of various little people around the world. Sometimes I'd even forget why I was doing all this in first place.
Jade Empire is gorgeous game. The graphics are stunning, the art style is impressive and the sounds and music work well together.
There is a certain open feeling to many of the quests and although this is only a disguise for the relatively linear progression you have throughout the game it does work well to keep you from feeling like you are completely on rails. The morality system, despite it's flaws, is probably one of the best ones ever concocted by Bioware and it hints at shades of grey quite often, particularly during the later stages of the game.
There is only really one major problem with Jade Empire and it is unfortunately a rather big one. The combat, the basic gameplay mechanic that the entire game is based around, is dreadfully dull.
The controls are fairly standard, light attack to deal damage, heavy attack to break blocks, your own blocking ability and an area effect strike in case you get swarmed. This is all very simple and not very interesting so what Bioware did in an attempt to make the combat more dynamic is provide you with a wide range of combat styles. Everything from familiarly named martial arts styles and weapons styles to magic and support styles and even transformation styles that morph you into various mythical creatures. The idea being that you need to switch between the different styles to maximize your combat potential. Unfortunately the entire execution of this is flawed and while you do need to change styles every blue moon to match enemy immunities there will only rarely be a need to do this in combat even on the highest level of difficulty.
Something that probably deserves a mention here is that Jade Empire is some very nice romance options and is quite possibly the only game to have a three-way romance option that didn't make me feel like puking.
All in all Jade Empire is a great game marred by some unfortunate design flaws. The world is beautiful and well crafted, the characters are interesting and engaging and Bioware's attempt at grey morality pays off surprisingly well. It's a game I'd happily recommend as it is a great play but the horrible combat unfortunately keeps it from getting that all time classic status that some seem to want to bestow upon it.

Coming from traditonal controllers, I was excited about this, and placed a pre-order for one early on. However, there are more negatives then positives in Valve's creation.
For starters, the right touch pad is great, and accurate for precise aiming on games such as PC shooters. However, the left "D-Pad" is awful, for both the touch and movement controls are (at least for me) extremely hard to get used to. For example, I found myself strugging to switch weapons in CS:GO or moving accurately in Half Life 2 which are frustrating to play as a result. As a nitpick, the right and left trigger buttons are harder to press then they should be, and usually lead to my aim changing slightly when trying to press the button while aiming.
Most controller settings for games that support controllers such as the Xbox gamepad choose to use the lower buttons and analog on the controller, without the use of the touch pads. Alone, this isnt an issue, but playing for longer than 10 minutes using solely the bottom analog and button hurts the hands, and kind of defeats the purpose of using the Steam Controller since the touch pads aren't being used. However, when using touch pad configurations for the same games, they just seem to lead to less precise actions, or cause additional movement when not desired.
All in all, the controller still feels like a prototype, and needs a lot more work in its design and functionality for me to recommend it. I really do love the right touch pad, but everything else about the controller makes it hard to use for any other action. If you are using it solely for shooters, then it may be a good choice. However, for any other game, I'd recommend a normal Xbox/Playstation controller to get the job done.

Overall, the Steam Controller is an excellent piece of hardware, but even more importantly, it's an excellent piece of firmware and software, PROVIDED you are willing to A) invest the time to customizing nearly each game's control profile on an individual level, and B) run steam in big picture mode. Seriously, why? I could even accept needing to be running steam, but there's no reason at all that we should HAVE to be playing in Big PIcture mode to access the controller profiles and without those customized profiles, the Steam Controller is nearly useless.
Of course, these problems could easily wind up being fixed in the future; the hardware itself has given me almost no trouble at all. It works well whether it is plugged in with no batteries, or wireless and battery powered. The only thing lacking is rumble, I suppose with the intention of conserving battery life.
As far as hardware goes, it feels pretty much like holding an Xbox One gamepad. I'm sure most people will be happy with this, but I greatly prefer the layout of the PS3/PS4 gamepad. All the buttons and joystick feels solid, the touchpads don't track their ENTIRE area, but most of it, the triggers are comfortable to pull and have a gentle but firm "hard press", the gyroscope tracking is very accurate and responsive. The two grip buttons occasionally feel like they are too easy to accidentally press, but really that might just be a matter of practice.
The firmware is what really makes the difference. The joystick has configure options that include key "fluttering" to allow you to use a keyboard/mouse setup while still simulating analog movement when your stick isnt pointing at 100% in one of the 8 primary directions, but you can also set up a gamepad configuration where the touchpad is treated like a joystick, but simulates the feel of a touchpad or trackball. I use this latter setting for Skyrim, and it seriously feels like I have a trackball spinning under my thumb instead of a joystick for aiming.
There are only a few features I'd like to see before making this my standard gaming interface:
- standalone app that can work even without steam running.
- allow the "dpad" Touchpad to be used as a 3x3 grid of buttons(compass points+diagonals+center), rather than the current limit of only 4 (compass points, diagonals=multiple compass points)
- allow both touchpads to be used as steering wheels (full circular motions turn wheel, letting go recenters wheel)
- allow the customization of your own "joystick" style keyboard, so instead of needing to do 8 direction with 4 options for typing, you could do 6 and 6, and could put the keys in any order you wanted.
- allow a button press to CYCLE through different gamepad configs, instead of only acting as a single modifier.
- allow a button press (or touchpad button press) to individually simulate a combination of keys or buttons on its own.
- allow a general controller setting to make it recognized (or not recognized) to the game as an Xbox controller, for those games that automatically apply certain gamepad settings only when the xbox gamepad is detected.
The best part is the potential for future gaming. Valve has already set up all of their games to fully capitalize on the Steam controller, so you can adjust all aspects that the controller affects. In HL2, you can adjust the controls for driving seperately from the controls for moving around normally, possibly for operating the crane as well (havent checked thoroughly into that)
There are still a few niggly little issues. Sometimes the touchpad just doesn't quite manage to pretend to be a joystick well enough, and so you wind up with just a few recent games that still need a proper dual joystick gamepad. Where the Steam Controller does best is either supporting old legacy games that were never meant for a gamepad at all, or for newer games that are specifically designed to take advantage of the steam controller interface.

If you have the patience to map controls to the buttons and pads on this device, there's almost nothing you can't do.

While I had sprung for the first edition back when it had originally came out it had languished in the queue untouched.  With the Director's Cut recently released I decided to pick it up and finally play the game.  I enjoyed my experience immensely, that's what Deus Ex is really, an experience.
Human Revolution provides a wide, interesting world to discover, a story to unfold, and quite a bit of freedom approach it as you wish.  For instance when confronted with “combat situations” I really thought about how my character would try to handle them.   I took what I knew about Adam Jensen’s and my own moral standards and applied them to the game.  Therefore except for a few instances I tried to avoid casualties.
From a graphical standpoint I found the game very aesthetically pleasing, the art direction especially mitigated any shortcomings it might have had when racked up against current triple A titles.  The sound and music likewise fitted the game perfectly.
Overall Deus Ex Human Revolution was one of the finest single player adventures I’ve had in a while.  It’s the kind of game you get to really savor.

in terms of a good mmorpg this one is very low on the list. First off, it took a few hours to download off the second launcher. i left my computer running for the majority of the afternoon and over night for it to complete. So, after that was finished, i booted up the game, having high hopes that it would be worth the wait. in terms of servers, not many of them are free, there were two or three to choose from that weren't COMPLETELY full.
Then there were the classes to choose from, each class seemed well-balanced unlike some other mmorpgs, wich i was satisfyed with. The grenader wasn't too OP like, say, TERA's gunner.
Next comes the character customisation, theres little to none of it. no races, 10 different hairstyles, an okay amount of colors to choose from. Me being one to love the character diversity from such a high coustomisation opprutunity, I was a little dissapointed.

Once i got passed that, however, the screen became such a buzy clutter. it was unclear what i was supposed to pay attention to and there were too many boxes all over the screen. the general layout wasn't bad, but it just needed to be smaller

After completing the game with every route, I feel comfortable in saying that all of the characters have fulfilling stories to tell, depsite me disliking a few of them when I first began playing --

Overall I'll give it a 9/10 as I enjoyed the experience, but wish there was just a bit more depth and explaination in the story. Perhaps a sequel will float my way someday.

Here's the teal deer:
BUY, BUT ON SALE
+ cute characters
+ nice artwork
+ fun premise
+ very LGBT+ friendly
+ funny & cute dialogue
+ likable protag with an actual personality
+ well-designed interface
+/- very railroaded once you've gotten into somebody's route
- weirdly-paced
- much shorter than you'd expect
- ?difficult to really get to know the characters
- generally left wanting More
Overall, I enjoyed my time with Hustle Cat, although I have a few criticisms.
There wasn't as much player customisation as I usually like, but being able to choose pronouns (including they/them!), hair length, and skin tone were nice touches, and definitely better than being shoved into playing as a character you can't identify with like in some VNs. The game places basically no importance on your chosen gender, too - no homophobia or locked-out romance options here, folks!
The interface in general was really nice and very well-designed - a nice change from the same Ren'py layout every second VN uses! - although I would have appreciated a faster skip button and more than 8 save slots. (I'm a save-scummer, what can I say.)
The characters are generally cute and interesting, with witty dialogue and nice vibes. However, I didn't find myself getting as personally attached to them as I have to other VN characters - I'm not sure whether this is something to do with the writing or because of the short amount of time I got to spend with each of them. (The routes I played only took an hour or two each from start to finish, and less with skipping.) Their sprites (and Avery's!) are all well-done, with a decent variety of poses and facial expressions.
Once you make a few choices about your first few days (who do you follow around? do you try to sneak a donut or not?) you're basically locked into a romance with one character and only have (I think) one more choice to make
. Don't get me wrong, each route is cute in its own way, but I wouldn't have minded more personalization in your interactions with your crush, or even the ability to get a bad or neutral ending.  (Or even the ability to not romance anyone? I would have been really interested in friendship routes as well!) Also, there aren't many choices provided when you ARE given decisions to make, which makes it hard to really personalize Avery. (That being said, the writing is overall very good, they're a cute, funny, relatable protag, and I generally liked and agreed with them, so I wasn't too mad about this.) Depending on your priorities and what you like in a VN, this may or may not be a problem for you.
As for the wider story - you really do have to play multiple routes to get a sense of what's going on, otherwise you're left with more questions than answers at the end. It's also paced a bit weirdly - there's a lot of time spent on introducing the cafe and the characters, some time spent at work slowly getting to know everyone, one or two cute dates
with your crush of choice where it feels like you just start to get to know them and then
I also wanted to be able to spend more time with the characters and get them out of their shells more - even though you're dating and it's cute, you only effectively get a couple of days "together" before the game ends (and much of that is either skipped or just kinda brushed over), and it doesn't always feel like you the player got to know the characters very well.
Overall, though, I enjoyed my time with Hustle Cat, and I'm really only critiquing it so heavily because I see a lot of potential in it. It was a fun, cute time for anyone who likes light urban fantasy and VNs. I definitely wouldn't pay $19.99 for it, though - try to get it on sale if you can. (I grabbed it in a Humble Bundle after having my eye on it for months.)

Bought the 3-pack (Dungeon Siege I, II, and III), and decided to play through them.  Dungeon Siege 1 is old.  It came out in 2002, and the graphics are reflective of its age.  The gameplay itself is amazing however, it's a great RPG from days long past, and the ability to have up to eight party members was actually a breath of fresh air.  There are some definite balance issues, especially with how effective mass melee is.  Still, it provided a great atmosphere and RPG experience, with fun leveling mechanics.  The ability to change characters are you go is actually fun, although it felt like specialization was almost always superior.  The loot system had a few flaws, but overall was great.
It begins rather slow, and the first level farm + forest levels felt rather tedious.  After you begin to immerse yourself, the experience takens on a better form.  It feels almost liek Baldur's Gate, with a bit less character and world building.  For it's time, I think it was an incredible game, and I wish I would have played it back then, I think I would have found it amazing.  Despite that, I think if you are a fan of RPGs, this is a fun Action RTS with minor questing.  Some of the quests are more difficult, but in general it's focused entirely on the action and the character building.  While some later battles do require micromanagement, the game itself it's very long or difficult.
I played on medium difficulty and finished the game in 14 hours, while taking a leisurely pace.  Recommended for fans of RPGs, especially older ones.  Aside from that, DS1 probably  won't be your cup of tea.

In this game you play Adam Jensen, an ex-Swat agent, who now works for an artificial limb company called Sarif Industries. The worst though has to the the performance. After having completed the original with no issues I'm gettin lots of constant stutter and have so far had 9 crashes to desktop, most of them when loading a new area. As far as I've been able to figure out this is a port from the WiiU and that might be the reason it's so bad. And bad it is, from a technical standpoint. Worse lighting, frequent crashes and constant stutter. Not worth it, I find.
If you really want to play Human Resource Management and you should, you ought to do youself a favour and just buy the original. It's the superior game.

I picked up this game randomly while searching through the visual novel category. When I looked up a summary about this, I thought it was quite interesting and decided to buy it during the deal. Since I love reading lots of visual novel, I said why the heck not. I decided to play on multiple of routes and after playing for a while, I saw some good things about it and also the bad ones.
Some pros:
+ I love the art style. It gives the overall game a relaxing theme in the game.
+ The songs are catchy and fits well with the situation.
+ Interesting character personalities. Even the main character her/himself is interesting.
Some cons:
- Music tends to stop here and there. I kind of understand what the creator was trying to do (such as building up tension and such in different situations), but at the same time, the music is suppose to be there to keep the reader from losing their attention from the game. Many games have music playing on repeat (even with environmental sounds in the background), so when there's nothing but soft, environmental sounds, it didn't feel right anymore. It might be different for some people, but for me, I did not enjoy it as much.
- The plot was questionable. Not only did it felt rushed, but there were a lot of things that was left unsaid. It is fine to have some things left in question for the readers to figure out, but when there's nothing around the plot that can be easily theorized, it just left the players questioning what is going on overall.
- The game crashes sometimes even while I'm playing or skimming through the routes. Sometimes, I get to the next scene (when the scene fades to black), and then I'm left there, waiting for more than a few minutes in darkness before it crashes the game.
-Main character is "customizable" but not to an extent. I thought the layout of it was cool and interesting, but the way it was done was not that exciting. When I found out (after trying to click the box) that I could not change the name, I felt disappointed. Seeing a character profile sheet laid out almost made me think I can actually change the name, skills, and other things. I feel that it was better to have a different layout to choose a character instead.
Overall, I did like the game, but not to an extent. It was a relaxing game, but it was almost stressful too when I see flaws here and there. I would recommend this game to you if you are not that picky with visual novel games, but overall, I wouldn't think of this as a part of my top choices.

I LOVE Hustle Cat. It was an absolute joy to play through all of the routes - each one was suprisingly likeable and well-written! Cons?

This is your standard VN/dating sim game. Nothing earthshattering here--in fact, this may be one of the weaker ones I've played as you really don't get to make too many choices in the game. You don't even get to develop a personality for your character; Avery Grey is predetermined. The only thing you can change is your pronouns, and your look to a minor extent.
The story is quick. Like many romance games or novels it's TOO quick really; the plot advances so fast that there are gaping holes left when you've finished the story. But it's a cutesy story with an interesting twist (a twist that you may have gleaned just from reading the game blurbs or store page). It is absolutely nowhere near worth the $20 steam price however--I'd be furious to pay that kind of price for such amateur writing. If you're a completionist who wants to play every romance option in a VN, well, I can't give you any advice there as I can't imagine playing this a second time through. The pacing without options is too slow for me to even consider that. Expect an hour or two out of this game and call it good.
You may also want to stock up on coffee and jelly doughnuts before playing this game. Just trust me on that one.

VNs are, or maybe should be, ultimately about getting to know characters, and Hustle Cat gets this, avoiding the usual otaku-pleasing route of assembling the bunch of bare-bone, trite anime tropes, and presenting instead a likable, for the most part, cast of characters that, while somewhat archetypical, don't look like building blocks out of a set; the anime art-style is nice, but if you switched it out for a different one, the word "anime" would probably and hardly cross your mind.
The premise, in equal parts Faustian of sorts, Human Centipede, and Cats-and-the-Internet, is about a young'un, out of a job, with no money, and trying to find a way in the big city while living at their aunt's flat, who carelessly signs away their soul, or better yet, takes a job at a cat-themed cafe, involving a curse turning employee into cats whenever they leave the premises; it is one that if you had pitched to me, I would have replied "thanks but no thanks".
I found the writing enjoyable overall, if a bit lightweight, and it's definitely a plus that the gender identification of the main character is customizable, and all of the characters can be romanced, regardless. Also, no sex whatsoever.
The ending, however, feels somewhat simplistic, hurried perhaps?, and left me kind of disappointed, not very willing to go back and play a different story-line, as I imagined this would have been, for the most part, replaying the same story with just a different character being romanced. BTW I got in a same-sex relationship with Finley in my first playthrough, without trying: I was fine with it, although it felt a little sugary, lovey-dovey for my tastes.
I cannot remember the last time I was able to finish a VN, without succumbing to continuous attacks of eye-roll-itis, so this gets my thumbs up: while not without flaws, I would say the positives prevail, and Hustle Cat is a relaxing, enjoyable experience that doesn't go anywhere terribly interesting in particular, being content with entertaining the player with a tale of finding friendship and love.

+Fun, challenging platforming with tight controls
+Teleport gun is a cool gimmick
-Extremely short, with very little content and replayability
-Lazy level design that misses the point of the Metroidvania style
-Lazy presentation
-Ham-fisted shmup sections at the beginning and end don't work
-Awkward dialogue
Above all, this game feels lazy. It feels like the dev wanted to make a metroidvania but quit halfway through because it was too much work. It is so short. One hour and I finished my playthrough. No real replayability either; I could probably squeeze another playthrough out of it to try and get to more "secrets" and upgrades, but the game isn't fun enough to make me want to sit through it again just for that. The metroidvania-style screen-to-screen progression is wasted when your game is this linear and small; it just comes off as a level design cop-out. The upgrades are uninspired and the one that actually affects gameplay, the gun, is implemented really awkwardly. It pretends to be a metroidvania, but doesn't actually succeed at anything a metroidvania does, and we're left with a platformer with clunky levels that just feels unfinished. It's like a kid stomping around in dad's big shoes, but with none of the charm. Meanwhile, it has two shmup sections, one at the beginning and one at the end. They're bland and rather slow-paced with wonky hitboxes, and they don't really tell you when you've gotten hurt.
The presentation of the game is mediocre across the board, neither offending nor dazzling. Mediocre "retro-style" pixel art and music only make the game seem even lazier. The levels look like they were made in a level editor for an actual complete game - outside of background setpieces, almost every single part of the environment is blocks with repeating textures. From a visual standpoint, this game is just bigger, uglier Terraria. The sound effects are unremarkable, and while the music isn't inherently bad, it's extremely loud even on the lowest setting and gets grating fast.
I do have to give this game one thing: the platforming is fun. As a puzzle-platformer, this game shines. It's challenging, but not frustrating, and the wide variety of things you can do with the teleport gun really makes movement in the game feel free. The controls are tight and responsive (with the exception of firing your gun feeling a bit clunky at times), and I enjoyed the mix of puzzle solving and technical skill that the game encouraged. Unfortunately, this alone just can't support the weight of the game's flaws.
Out There Somewhere is based on a good core concept with the teleport gun, but it doesn't go anywhere with it. If there was more content and the game encouraged exploration better, it could be a solid metroidvania. If it ditched the metroidvania level style and instead had actual levels more like your average puzzle platformer, it could be a solid platforming game. If this whole game was only the first world, and the game had more worlds like it with more and more challenges, upgrades, and progression broken up with shmup sections, the game could succeed as the weird mix that it is. But as it stands, Out There Somewhere is little more than a proof of concept.  As cheap as $2 is, there are better ways to spend your money. It's a decent experience if you get it on a good sale or in a humble bundle, though.

60 hours later, I own the entire town, have killed all my rivals, murdered thousands of people, destroyed dozens of cars and helicopters, own all the stores, and have created a system of income that basically gives me infinite money since not all that many things require money after awhile.
Destructibility is nice. Buildings are invincible, but street lamps, post office bins, trash cans, water towers and fences can all be destroyed or thrown, while even the train can be taken out if hit long and hard enough. After awhile, it's hilarious to just drive around, plowing through people like bowling pins and firing random shots and explosives for the lulz. "If they ever want to track you, all they'd have to do is track the bodies!" It's fun to grab 3 homies and have them shoot and draw fire, and it's also funny since they will shoot anything moving that you shoot first, so you can get them to blast random civilian cars. NPC behavior is also pretty cool - varied NPC models like old people on walkers, power-walkers, yuppies, random gangs, while they have realistic reactions like running or fighting when you attack or taunt them. Sometimes you can get whole groups of people involved in a general melee.
Cars are plentiful so there's no need to buy one. Not being able to call in vehicles from anywhere at any time is a pain, though you can call up services that have regular cars, as well as the taxi that you can use to warp to any marker. Driving recklessly is encouraged by the respect meter when you do something risky or plain insane, though sometimes homies in your car will randomly make cutting comments about your supposed driving prowess and will offer to drive. Plowing through fences and taking alleys is also encouraged, since this opens up new route for the game's auto-routing GPS to use.
There's little realism. While at first you are vulnerable, eventually you just unlock enough bonuses and weapons and infinite ammo to be a terminator. It doesn't help that the police never seem to really care about the mayhem you're doing, unless you fire a gun or hit a car in the 90 degree cone of vision in front of a police car. At first, they try to apprehend you by just using batons, pepper spray and flashbangs, and if you get below half health you can actually get arrested! When they do respond at higher levels, law enforcement can suddenly drive faster than you and even perform PIT maneuvers! The blockades that police set up are usually pretty ineffectual in that you can plow right through the gap where 2 SWAT vehicles are (but not the APCs) or drive past the blockade. However, when the police start calling in helicopters with air-to-ground missiles, it's time to switch vehicles or shoot down the helicopter.
Another thing that's nice is plastic surgery, where you can change everything about your character, including taunt gestures and even melee style. This is especially handy if you screw up the customization in the create-a-character screen.
The game is very buggy. Sometimes the sound of an ally firing an assault rifle will go on forever. Some map markers are missing, and the game speed is originally useless. I had to fix it by going into the DLL files. There's also a mission where you have to exit a cutscene before it ends or it just freezers. Not to mention everything in the game is grayed out due to horrible graphics. This reduces visibility, most egregiously during missions set in the rain. The addition of a phone is cool because you can call in homies and services, but the interface is slaved to a console, so you have to use CTRL and LSHIFT to navigate instead of simple arrow keys. Also, things tend to completely disappear if you see something and then let it go out of your view.
The game is usually funny, but there are some unexpectedly brutal moments, like the death of Aisha and Carlos and Jessica and the first Ronin guy. Gunshots and explosions are so conventional when you can just drag someone around on your car.
The campaign is slow and boring. Most missions are short and unmemorable. Major landmarks are not marked, though the things you need to advance through the game are, and the overview of the map allows you to filter icons by type.
Multiple activities are simply broken or not fun. Snatch is best played with an APC. Mugging never works. Robbery almost never works. Streaking is hard to do because the clothes are only found in one store. Multiple places that are huge have no maps to guide you, so getting lost becomes tediously routine.
In the end, Saints Row 2 is undeniably fun. But is it very enjoyable or memorable? No. It's good enough to sustain interest until the end, and for me to complete a lot of the missions and activities. A special plus is the level of detail on some of the aspects, like how police will respond with different weapons based on different situations. But it's not good enough for me to recommend, and in the end the vast amount of glitches and bugs and washed-out graphics just made the game unpleasant.
But the music is nice, so I'll probably buy some tracks.

Creds: I have been apart of the Paladins community since CB10 (closed beta 10). We are now looking at Open Beta "OB64" coming up in a week and some change. I have rolled with this game through massive, gameplay altering changes, and my recommendation hasn't waivered. This game is definately worth a try.
_____________________________________________________________________________
Paladins is a f2p fps hero shooter. It approaches the genre from a pretty unique perspective, and continuously challenges competitive titles both in gameplay and business modeling.
Pros:
The heroes are all interesting and fairly well balanced.
The player base has been increasing since the game was promoted in Closed Beta.
The game is COMPLETELY FREE TO PLAY.
Microtransactions apply only toward asthetic changes and level progression (which doesn't have any effect upon gameplay performance).
Dev team is top noch and very responsive to community input
Fun to play with friends or solo
High skill ceiling, but friendly to new players as well
Cons:
Some patches come out with bugs (name a game that doesn't)
Aesthetics purchases are typically rng based
May not appeal to players who do not enjoy hero shooters, or who more strongly resonate with overwatch pacing
***If I had to choose 1 reason why feverently stick to Paladins over some of the game's direct competitors, it's this. The Hi-Rez devs in charge of Paladins development are the finest group of devs that I have ever come across in any game or company. They are extremely supportive and responsive of the Paladins community.
Additionally (can't just have 1 reason only XD), Paladins goes through a fairly large update EVERY 2 WEEKS. This update is broadcasted on Twitch.tv and Facebook, and typically presents players with 3-7 new hero skins, new test maps, new balance changes (which keeps the hardcore game meta in a state of change and evolution), and format updates to currency systems and hub utility.***
Cannot reccomend this game higher for anyone who loves hero shooters!

A quick review:
~ THE GOOD THINGS ~
+The new combo weapons and vehicles are original and fun to use
+Zombies are way more aggressive now so you cant just leisurely walk through a horde
+Building upon the previous point, huge zombie hordes are everywhere in this game so it's hard to get around
+The posse system makes survivors slightly less useless
+Psycho designs are still funny and interesting
+The way it ties into DR1's ending is cool
+Chuck Greene cameo is cool
+No gas zombies
~ THE BAD THINGS ~
-Nick becomes a gigantic ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in cutscenes and has almost no personality
-Also he isn't Frank
-Story is bad
-Los Perdidos is boring and unmemorable
-Los Perdidos' atmosphere is too serious for a Dead Rising game
-Can't build combo weapons before you find the blueprint
-Despite having a huge focus on vehicles there are so many roads that are blocked by debris (A particularly annoying one comes later in the game and you will ALWAYS run across it when trying to get places)
-While the Psycho designs are still good, the fights are easy as hell and boring
-I don't think there was any themes for the psychos? If there was I never heard it or it wasnt good enough to remember. The boss soundtracks are a very vital part of Dead rising
-Game in general is just really easy (Almost unlimited supply of weapons at safehouses, non-combo guns are ♥♥♥♥ing amazing this time around, some combo weapons are too good e.g. Gloves + Battery)
-The new upgrade system has the potential to make Nick incredibly overpowered when compared to a Lvl 50 Frank or Chuck from the other Dead Rising games
-6 days of in-game time is WAAAAY too long
-Story missions can't time out unless you expend all 6 days without doing anything
-Survivor AI still isnt good
-Controls are unresponsive
-At the time of the writing of this review, it has some big performance issues that usually plague console ports. Apparently it also crashes a lot, though I havent experienced a single crash yet
-The new "King" zombies are pushovers and nowhere near as big a threat as DR2's gas zombies were
-The overtime plot is crappy
- No Frank West
Overall I recommend it because it's still fun despite all the flaws, it's just not a good Dead Rising game

I saw this on the recent updates list, and the glowing reviews convinced me to give it a try. "Oh, it's version 3.0!" I said to myself, "It must be in a pretty good state of development!" I was, however, very disappointed.
The first issue is the guncrafting. The way they advertise this game, you'd think there are hundreds of different options. Nope! Unfortunately, as others have said, the balancing is so skewed that you end up with pretty much the same three or four guns over and over again. Any other combinations are so underpowered that they can't compete.
This imbalance is further exacerbated by the fact that levelling any of your gun components requires a steep grind-- the first upgrade for a component costs roughly 4000 blutes, and then the second level is 20000. You earn about 300-400 blutes per game. Let's go with a generous 400 for the sake of this argument-- so 10 games to level 1, then 50 games for level 2.  While this doesn't sound so bad, the upgrades only give you tiny, tiny bonuses (1-2%) to your gun stats. The grind becomes even worse when you realize that each gun component is separated into its own "skill tree" by ammo type (shell, slug, fire, tesla. launcher, etc), and leveling one component in one tree doesn't carry over to another tree, even if they use the same part.
Consider that each game is roughly 20 minutes...20 minutes times 50 games = 1000 minutes, or SEVENTEEN HOURS.
The grind is that bad!  Multiply this grind by 5-7 components per gun, and you are talking an absurd thousands of hours before you can reasonably improve your weapons. You do get a "daily bonus", but this is worth the same as playing one game (250-450 blutes). You also get 2000 blutes when you level, but after gaining your first couple of levels quickly, the grind sets in as your levels take longer and longer (classic IAP bait strategy seen in modern classics such as Farmville). And because changing your weapon to another type would mean starting the grind all over, you are actively discouraged from experimenting with different builds. Once you find something that works, you are pretty much stuck with it forever and ever.
The second issue I have is with the character customization. Let me make this clear--
Period. Everyone pretty much looks the same among the three different avatars.
I admit that the graphics are pretty decent. The cartoony style works, and it's satisfying to see yourself or your enemies die via burning, dismemberment, electrocution, etc., ala Loony Tunes. That is the one good thing this game has going for it. The colors are vibrant and beautiful, and the few avatars you have to choose from are well-animated.
Unfortunately, the developers decided that video games these days don't have enough machismo, so the one female avatar has giant boobs with Antarctic-hard nipples permanently showing through her shirt. The dances/taunts are full of pelvic thrusts, jacking off motions, etc. It's so transparently obvious that the developers don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about women gamers. And even if you don't care about issues of sexism, the masculinity in Loadout is so crass that it detracts from the goofy Loony Tunes style. There is a distracting clash between Clockwork Orange style "ultra-violence" and WIle E. Coyote style explosions. It's not impossible to have the two tones coexist (Conker's Bad Fur Day comes to mind), but they don't work well here.
Lastly-- the gameplay. The controls are decent, and fairly responsive. However, the camera angles on many levels are poorly designed. Every player can quickly roll around or dive out of the way of shots, and you often have duels that look like dogs chasing their tails. This isn't bad, and it's actually quite fun. But when you throw in the bad camera work, you end up getting lost behind a wall or in a corner with no idea what is going on, which is frustrating.  This is doubly annoying when you have parts of levels where you either hit the sweet spot perfectly, or you careen off and die.
The recoil and aim mechanics are challenging but not unreasonable. The game has a "low gravity" sort of feel to the jumping and movement, which is nice when your character leaps and bounds over tall ledges and objects. Being able to climb to the top of a scrap metal wreckage in a few seconds, then surveying the land below you, is very satisfying. I wish more games had this kind of "free" feeling movement.
I want to like this game. I really do! I had a decent amount of fun with it, and it works in small, short gaming sessions. But for version 3.0, I expected something much more complete. Honestly, this game still feels like a half-finished beta. This game has a lot of promise, but there are already much better shooters out there that can at least offer me some sort of long-term character development. This is just Farmville with guns and dismemberment.

First off-I'm typically not a huge fan of dating sim/visual novel type games. Many tend to either pin you with basically no ways to change the plot and just present it like it's an actual novel, or have the protagonist do things to woo potential dates that don't fit with the protagonist's personality/are basically lying to get characters to like you. This game does neither, which is great to see. First off, the protagonist (Avery Grey) has a rather defined personality, and some very amusing dialogue. Secondly, while some of the stuff gets repetitive (they have a fast forward feature probably for that reason) the story is very engaging and how things play out does change with each path--at least in how the end is reached. The only two 'bad' paths are ones that are fairly easy to find and avoid (or do--they've got achievements for both and they're both worth looking at, even if you only do them the one time) and won't force you to totally restart the story or anything like that.
All the characters are fun, interesting, and have more depth to them than many dating sim ones do--no completely shallow stereotypes here! Also, while Avery is set personality and dialogue wise, you can (somewhat) choose their appearance and you can choose their pronouns as well (she/her, he/him, OR they/them). Also you can date whoever you want, no matter what pronouns you went with, and to boot you can change the pronouns at any time from the main menu when you've started a game as well.
Overall, if you like cats (and some other stuff) and dating cute coworkers while working in a... mysterious cat cafe, I'd absolutely recommend this game.

OK, this is a game that I need a meh button again. The game is an above par HOG based on a TV show. You are a police officer who need to solve a series of murders. The story is not bad, audiovisual quality is good, HOG scenes are above average but there is at least one bug which kills the game. Literally. Two times it crashed and both times my save file disappeared. Now I want to see the end of the game but I don't want to see the same HOGs for third time. It's a bit risky but you should give it a try.

Though this game is at least somewhat interesting, I can't recommend it. Compared to other HOGs I've played, this one really leads you by the nose. What I find really bizarre is that the main characters have no problem doing a little breaking-and-entering, burglary, and disturbing of crime scenes. It would have been nice if I could have participated in making deductions based on the clues, but that is all handed to you.
The HOGs themselves are decent. The other puzzles range from easy to mind-numbingly difficult. The infamous arrow puzzle is one example. Even though I was able to figure out there are seven forced moves, I could not find any logical way to solve it. An organized, methodical brute force method would take several hours. Unless you enjoy this sort of thing, you'll want to refer to a walkthrough for this poser, at least for the first few moves.
I hit a bug in the folder sorting puzzle where one folder disappeared and I had to exit and reenter the puzzle to make it show up again. The phone puzzle, which looks different hanging on the wall in the main scene than it does in the close-up, requires the third number to be one not in the clue list in opposition to the puzzle instructions. The game crashed when I was working on the storage lot puzzle at the end when I accidentally dragged a person off the edge of the puzzle. In addition to all the preceding complaints, I found it really irritating that whenever I was trying to read a page of text, the game would decide it had waited long enough and would exit the text close-up before I could finish reading.
There are better HOGs out there. Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden comes to mind.

Ok, only took me a year but I've finally come to a firm conclusion about what this game is.
This game......is not bad. It's not bad. However, it just screams extreme mediocrity. If I had the option to put neither positive or negative on this game I would do it.
Let's start with the only truly positive thing that I praise this game for, it's the content. This game has a ton of content for it's price, as well as many original features that the original game does not have. It has...like 1000 skins or something I didn't keep track, as well as new features such as the subclass system which is very nice.
However, note how I compared the original game to this game for a minute. Now, I wouldn't be so hard on this game if the original game did not exist, because guess what? That game is way better than this one!
The balance in this game is not good at all, infact it's one of the most unbalanced dinosaur games I know of.
The humans in paticular, compared to the original game are dreadful in terms of their abilities.
The commando does less damage than a nerf gun. My own♥♥♥♥♥♥has better range than the grenade launcher.
The scientist is extremely clunky compared to the original game with it actually being extremely difficult to hit stuff as well as the sniper rifle having extremely poor rate of fire.
The pathfinder is probably the best of the classes but despite this the hit detection with his weapons is so terrible.
The pyro also has extreme♥♥♥♥♥♥poor damage.
The trapper relies purely on its nets because hte pistols are dreadful in terms of damage as well.
To add, there's no class on the dino side that's underpowered, infact they're a few that are overpowered.
Raptors are by far the most OP thing in the game. They're stronger than a tyrant, and I'm not kidding you. They're circlejerk ability they pull on humans is nearly impossible to counter, and the pounce is pure skilless beyond beleive.
The carnotaurus is also a tad overpowered (kinda ironic considering the carno in the original game is a tad underpowered), with it moving a lightspeed and being able to pull lightspeed combos on humans to instantly kill them.
I know a freind who had actually kept an eye on this game's balance. He played nothing but TDM for around 100 hours of game time. Guess how many games humans won? 17
Meanwhile, the original game is cheaper and has way better gameplay with much better balance (literally the only big balance issues are the Tyrants being a tad OP while the carno is a tad UP, but even then they were at a tolerable degree).
Don't even get me started on the loot system either. There are alot of people saying the devs focus more on the loot system than the actual game, but I can tell you for certain that is not true. The main problem with the loot system is not that it exists, but because of how it's played out. The loot is sooooooooooooo inconsistant to the point where you can't even bother playing the game for drops, and the craft system is so cashgrabby that it's completely disgraceful. Depth, at the time of this writing, has just released their loot system, and it's already better than this one.
Now, the final main topic:freeroam servers. Now I know alot of people hate the freeroam servers saying that once again people care more about skins than actual gameplay, which, once again, isn't completely true. You want to know why freeroam is so popular? Because you can see all the pretty stuff you're getting without having to go through the dreadful gameplay. Freeroam is a way out for many players to not have to deal with the bad gameplay. I end up doing this myself on occasion honestly.
Final Verdict:This game.....is not the best. It's not on a level of most games of this caliber where it's not even worth playing, it's tolerable....if barely. I can't really say whether this game is bad or good because...it's neither. It's just mediocre. What I can say is.....GET THE ORIGINAL GAME. Whether ur thinking about buying this game or you're already an owner of it, buy it. Worth every penny.

More game, better bosses, and less yellow. It's still amazing that this game somehow escaped being just another classic IP completely ruined by foolish publishers.
One solid look at this game will show it was made by fans for fans who actually meant what they said about loving everything that made the original great, it also manages to marry common console gimmicks like cover and regenerating health into an enjoyable experience. Every obstacle can be over come in so many different ways and the xp/praxis system is an ideal compromise of the original Deus Ex's skill system and Invisible War's over simplification of augmentations.
Callbacks, shout outs, and little details that refer to the original help cement this game's ties to Deus Ex while maintaining its own plotline dealing with transhumanisim and the ethics behind augmentation, this game wasn't just an excuse by Eidos to try to grab cash, it's a worthy prequel to one of the best games ever designed and it's been made that much better by dealing with the problems the original release had while integrating The Missing Link into one large seamless experience.

The game world is crafted masterfully and in great detail: from the essential characters that are interesting and flawed to the futuristic settings for the intriguing tehcno thriller of a story, the player is treated with such quality and class that only a few games do. The game offers an astounding amount of information and small details for the player to consume (should they be so inclined).
The levels and character customization provide the player with a number of options to achieve the goal in any given mission and indeed DX:HRDC is one of the very few first person games that actually offer the player multiple ways to finish the game. Moreover, depending on player choice the mission outcomes may vary significantly and the story unfold in a different manner. If you explore the world and finish side quests it will probably take around 25 - 35 hours to finish the game. The new Director's Cut edition integrates the Missing Link DLC seamlessly into the main game in addition to which it also comes with a "making of" documentary, commentary mode, a new game+ option and a host of other changes and tweaks.
DX:HRDC is the best version of the game yet and a truly epic experience that should not be missed!

Some of my initial thoughts:
physical aspects

+doesn't feel cheap - feels like a regular game controller controller
+haptic feedback on the triggers and joystick are nice
+gyro is useful, haptic feedback on gyros feel nice too
~variable learning curve; if you've ever used a laptop touchpad you should be alright, otherwise it'll take a while
~glossy parts of the controller can pick up fingerprints, but you don't touch them very often
-haptic feedback on touchpads feels somewhat clunky, too discrete. would prefer smoother.
software aspects
+massively customizable controls, with room for future improvements and new features
+can be used with non-steam games now, very easy to setup
~configs are easy to make but annoying to save
~required to use big picture mode, where ingame overlay lacks similar functionalities to regular overlay (setup FPS counter, access deeper settings etc.), but outside works better with the controller
-don't even bother typing lol
it's not a very large investment for what is a very interesting controller. if you don't like how the touchpads/gyro handles then you get a $50 standard gamepad controller which can be deeply customized. considering the investment valve made to develop this hardware, it's almost assured they'll continue to actively iterate on it for at least a year, likely longer. and even if other developers aren't interested, it'll still work for their software so it'll always have some utility.

Rough Plot-
Jade Empire,  is loosely based on the legends of China - although Bioware has been careful to stress that it's not actually ancient China, which allows them to play around with all manner of elements ranging from geography to the inclusion of technology (often magic-powered) such as aircraft. Your character starts out as the star student of a martial arts school in a remote village, and in typical RPG style, you and your companions are quickly caught up in Much Bigger Things - to wit, the aforementioned ghouls, firebombings, and balance of heaven and earth - and sally forth to travel around the Jade Empire putting things right.

This is one of the best early Bioware games. It's reminescent of Knights of the Old Republic, plays in a similar fashion, but the combat is much more engaging and action oriented. Go Ten Thousand Fists. Support, magical, weapon, martial and transformation styles all feel unique and work well, and there are plenty and plenty to choose from. Upgrade them to become more awesome, and use your spirit amulet to enhance your core stats. Followers help by either fighting along side you, or offering support. The only real downside is once you beat the game and learn the styles, it's a breeze and a half, but there's four difficulty settings, so even the most veteren player can have a challenege. If you like old Bioware style games, kung-fu action, a good story, moral choices and all around baddass awesomeness, this game is definitely worth getting.

All in all a pretty good visual novel. Not the best, but solid. The story is fairly strong, though after you've settled into a route it starts to railroad you pretty hard. Some of the options are pretty obviously the wrong one, and the really, absolutely vital relationship decisions are made for you. The choices you do make are more geared towards deciding what route you'll be going down. If you're a fast reader, you can finish a route in an hour.
The art is well done, and this is one of the few visual novels I've played where you have at least a small character creation section. While you can't rename your character, you can pick from six different appearances: 3 with longer hair that are slightly more feminine, and 3 with shorter hair that are slightly more masculine. You can also pick your character's pronouns, and switch them at any point during the game.
However, the differences in character appearance really boil down to hair length and skin colour. I understand it takes a lot of work to allow more customization, but it's important to mention that if you're looking for a visual novel where you have full control over appearance, this game won't be able to do that for you.

So a friend gifted this to me since he got it in a Humble Bumble and has no interest in VNs unlike me.
I went in with pretty much no expectations (saw the trailer, thought it's gonna be your classic run-of-the-mill dating sim) which is probably what really made this game amazing for me.
Just a note, this game crashes. Often. Try to save regularily, if you don't want to have to use the skip button eighteen times a run.
Story:
Unless one has played every route, both the main storyline as well as some of the characters behaviour and motivations is very obscure. Some routes reveal a bit about the others (Reese explains some about the main storyline, Landry about Mason, etc), but for a full picture one has to play all (and even then it leaves a few things open, sadly).
But the story was interesting and quirky and I especially loved the character progression in each route.
So the most important part is: this is NOT a cute, common dating sim!
Don't go in expecting to spend the entire run playing with cats and flirting with your guy/gal.
There are sceletons, dubstep, fire, rust (loads of rust actually, someone should clean that up xD), vampires? and possibly marine butterflies.
The game is weird and has a really obscure feel to it in it's humour. Let's just say I was giving a very, very simplified summary of a scene that got my attention in my friends group chat and they got so confused and intrigued that they now bought it as well (and they haven't regreted it to my knowledge yet).
Characters:
First of all, while the main character suffers from the occasional idiocy (let's run head first into a guy with a baseball bat, what could go wrong?!), they are relateable, cute and amusing to read along with (and I say "they" since you can chose the gender).
The other characters all come together in typical harem style: the cool type, the cute type, the shy one, the tsundere, etc. But nice is that all have a layer underneath (they're sweet or insecure or or or) which makes exploring their route fun, including learning a bit about who they are and how they ended up in the cafe. No one feels unecessary and the endings with everyone helping you is always quite heartwarming.
My personal favorites would be Mason and Hayes, but everyone is absolutely lovely and adorable during their respective route and I couldn't surpress grinning like an idiot whenever the inevitable started.
Art:
The art is solid, pretty much. Both the character and background drawings look a bit rough and smudgy, but it's charming and coherent, so it doesn't disturb in the least. And though the UI is flashy in colours, one soon stops noticing it. Plus, I really love title screens where you can see your progress.
Audio:
The game has a soundtrack of - what - six songs? It's a small game and music usually eats most of it, so people complaining about how repetetive it is obviously never made a small VN. The music at least never is annoying (I actually enjoyed listening to it, it's a bit cheesy but works with the mood most of the time and it could be way more jarring). The use of NO music is also used smartly whenever it happens, making you drop for a second every time.
There aren't any sounds of notice but that might be a good thing since certain games can become annoying with it.
Routes/Endings:
The game has six route endings and two Game Overs.
The first half of the routes is (almost) always identical and defines who you chose to be your darling, the second half then splits to the path of that character up until the end.
Be aware that this game is what I call a 2.5 kinetic novel. It has choices, but those only define who to date. Once you are in a route, you barely get a choice anymore and are only left with reading what happens. If you want to be able to meddle in everything, have a say to stuff and such, then this game will be very underwhelming (big props to the job interview though, I have never been this amused by choices).
It's also fairly easy to figure out when you're gonna get locked into a Game Over, but if you're into VNs as much as me, then you're probably wanna try and see them anyway.
Other:
While it would be a lie to say that this is the best VN I have ever played (there are some small typos and repeating words for example, there's also a bug where two CGs won't appear in the gallery despite having been seen in-game), it is definitely a lot of fun, quite interesting and very intriguing.
And hey, it has cats, dubstep and loads of lemonade (and Dracula), so you could hardly want more ;)

I enjoy the game, it has a way of being playable at least partly single player, but to get past certain hurdles you'll need at least two good team mates. It's the sort of game where you need friends most of the time and while I don't love the game, I don't hate it either.
The game has a PvE MOBA feel over it, there are 4 classes, Tanks, Slayers, Medics and Crowd Controllers, each class has 2 characters each who focuses on one play style often which can be Solo healer, Tanking DPS etc.
This is further done by what I feel is the worst part about any MOBA, items, you can get better by buying items and such and each item often has it's special things it gives you to help in a certain area of fighting, but at the second half of the harder levels you can so easily lose the chance to get money to get items to get better just because you don't land the finishing blow, say, because you're all dead or a bot does the last damage.
The game has a very slow progression and a lot of the progress is just simply "Kill X amount of enemies with Crits and all slayers start with more crit chance" etc, which in the end, makes up for a lot of early game advantage, and makes the difference between struggling in the Pro League and wiping the Master League.
The community is really low as it's a really old game by now, but from time to time you can find a server or two up and maybe get to spend a few hours having fun with someone.
The game does seem to have some issues, such as the typical lazy "Move and stop to attack if you get in range of enemies then move again" command is really off with some characters, like the "mobile turret" character, if you move she will lose her turret mobility, and sometimes she will not autofire. There also appears to be a bug where your progress gets flushed, happened to me just the other day, and it's not even funny how tragic it is.
All in all, a decent game if you got friends who like Mobas but hate PvP and enjoy a grinding but rewarding co-op experience. Sadly Fatshark is suckling on the Warhammer teat so don't even try to ask for updates if you ask me, the game is far too unpopular to get any real attention.
