But once you''ve got it running, it's a well designed, thoughtfully crafted game, and probably the best Game-That-Got-a-Sequel-by-a-Different-Team-After-a-Decade ever.
If you're a fan of stealth gameplay, minor RPG elements, and cyberpunk/futurism, there's not a better modern experience out there. Knowledge of the first game is not a must, but it was the best stealth/RPG hybrid of its time, too (I recommend it if you can handle old school games). There's a second game that's largely ignored; you can ignore it.
For those who already own DXHR and aren't sure if there's justification in making you pay for what is largely a patch, well, I agree with the sentiment. I only got this because I had the money in my Steam wallet and was willing to take a leap, and I'll say that the value is there. Boss fights are somewhat-to-much more fun now, and the Missing Link DLC is integrating almost seamlessly. Coming back to the game after two years to make this many changes makes the cost worthwhile, to me.
Fully recommended.

Though Primal Carnage/Primal Carnage: Extinction is not one of my most heavily-played games, I have been a Primal Carnage player since the game first released, so I've seen how it has evolved for better or worse over the years. I also heavily followed the game's development in the years leading up to its release, so it does mean something to me.
That being said, I am for the most part quite dissatisfied with the direction the game has taken. I should first get out of the way the evident fact that Primal Carnage: Extinction is more like "Primal Carnage: Rebooted" because the *first* game was ruined by shoddy development. The developers didn't seem to know what they were doing with the game, and that led to progressively worse "updates" that ultimately warranted a fresh start.
As it is now, Primal Carnage: Extinction has a lot going for it, but once again it lacks sense of direction or purpose. It seems the game has succumbed to the overhwelming pressure of obnoxious roleplayers who for some inane reason bought an FPS game to play The Land Before Time With Guns. "Free Roam" gamemodes dominate the multyiplayer servers, and at any given time there are only two or three actual deathmatch or any other relevant gamemodes to play. Clearly when it comes to dinosaur games, players want to just ~be a dinosaur~ without necessarily killing and getting killed in a fast-paced FPS environment, and the Primal Carnage developers have adjusted poorly to this audience by simply letting the game drown in a cesspoll of unengaging free roam servers.
As it is right now, I absolutely cannot recommend it to any prospecting players. There are plenty of upcoming new dinosaur games around the corner that have the right idea, like The Isle, Mesozoica, and Saurian, so I would recommend just saving your money for those games.
UPDATE: After a period of a few months I decided to try Primal Carnage: Extinction again to see how it has been coming along since I last played, and see if its situation had improved any. Unfortunately, the multiplayer servers are still dominated by that rediculous Free Roam gamemode, and while I am impressed with some new features that have been implemented, such as a ranking system, it's difficult for me to even take advantage of it because only a fraction of the servers (literally only two or three at any given time) are relevant gamemodes like Team Deathmatch and Get to the Chopper--all of which are usually either completely vacant or completely full, which makes it very difficult to play Primal Carnage: Extinction the way I paid money to play it. Therefore, I am still witholding my reccomendation of this game, but I am hopeful that change will come with time.

As far as hidden object games go, its not the worst I've played. The problem with this one is that it seems kinda lazy.
Music is dull and from what I can recall only 1 track.
Artwork (whilst decent for most of it, and an okay representation of the actors in the show) is very minimal, often having the characters awkwardly staring out of the screen instead of at each other in certain scenes.
But the big flaw was that the final scene/ending of the game had no rewarding feel to it. The music was the same (Ominous for some reason?), the artwork the same, and generally no feedback that you were supposed to feel congratulated for playing though the rest of the game. Not even end credits... which left me thinking that some bug had occured - but I really didn't want to play it again to find out.
Whilst most of the puzzles are okay, some of them lack that realistic logic to them that keeps the world believable. I mean, having to play BubblePop to open a phone? And a few times you get that "Our logic, not your logic!" design flaw. As an example - you're given a jar with a key in, and a hammer. You'd think you could smash the jar with the hammer and retrieve the key... in the real world, and against time, this is what most of us would do - but for some reason here, you need to get the Lid Opener item... If you want me to do that, give me the lid opener and not the hammer then?
Ah well, Im sure if you're a fan of the show, all of this this can be forgiven. But as limiting as the genre normally is, I expect a bit higher quality from them. Its a shame as normally I would put this as a low recommendation rather than give it an outright "NO". I did enjoy what was there, it just needed a bit more to make me actually say YES to recommending it.

You definetly shouldn't judge this as being a bad game because it's based on a TV show. If you do, then you will be missing out on a decent and worthwhile game. Do you like Castle? Do you like murder mysteries? Or maybe hard puzzles, decent art, and a generic but decent plot? Then this game is for you!
I'll admit I was missing a level on this simply by never having watched the TV series, and never intending to. On a 1 to 10 scale, this was a solid 7, slightly brought down by it's steeper than average difficulty curve on its puzzles. Not majorly so, but definitely overall they tended to be on the challenging side.

Having clicked 'No', I will add the proviso that I WOULD recommend 'Castle: Never Judge a Book by its Cover', but ONLY to fans of the 'Castle' TV series! Anyone else should probably avoid.
Whilst I enjoyed the game, that was primarily because, as a fan, I recognised the in-jokes to some of the episodes of the series and the faithfully recreated scenes from the sets of the show.
The gameplay itself is a bit lacklustre. Most of the game is spent playing the missing objects mechanic whereby you pick out a small list of items from a large screen full of stuff. A bit 'Where's Waldo', but fine, although this does get tedious rather fast. Of more promise are the many little logic puzzle games which are many and varied - most are familiar and simple, but some are a bit more challanging. The only downside to these logic puzzles is that the 'Hint' mechanic allows you to completely skip the games, thus rendering them utterly pointless.
And here we get to the big drawback to this game: the 'Hint' mechanic. In most games where hints are given, usually you get actual 'hints' to what to do, but leaving you to continue to work things out. In 'C:NJaNbiC' the 'Hint' machinic leads you around by the hand. Not sure what you should be doing? 'Hint' Go here, do this. Can't solve this puzzle mini-game? 'Hint' Solved. Really, the button should be labelled 'Bored Now' or 'Too Lazy'.
I bought the game with the understanding that there would be no animations, just still scenes, but I was disappointed that there was NO actual voice-acting at all. The entire game takes place in virtual silence, with some barely adequate, low-key synth music to fill the void of all the text boxes as the characters 'talk'. This is a real shame since the game is based on the 'Castle' TV show which has characters with distinct and charming voices, so why not get them doing some voice acting for the game? And the synth music is hardly inkeeping with the music used throughout the TV series, which is chock full of funky current music tracks. I guess the licensing costs too much?
As already mentioned, there were no animations, it was all character portraits and still scene imagery, but the game would certainly have benefited from animated characters and backdrops. But hey, costs, what can you do?
And finally, lets mention length. It's short. I played it through in 4 hours, and that was by doing ALL the puzzles. If I skipped through all the ones I had trouble with, that time would probably have been halved. Considering that the game is made without animation or sound content, could they perhaps not have made futher episodic iterations with new games or mechanics to it? Shame, as that might have made it worth the money, to have further stories to work through, like actually playing a season of 'Castle', with themes continued in subsequent episodes. That would at least have given the game a lift in it's simplistic and obvious storytelling.
Which leads me to what is probably the biggest issue I had with the game: the story. Without spoiling it, I will say that it was obivous from very early on what the situation was and who the killer was - Ok, so that reguarly occurs in episodes of the show where you can guess who-dunnit, but the story doesn't do anything clever with it, and comes to a boring and obvious conclusion. For a game based on a TV series with pretty decent storylines, and featuring a professional Author, it commits the ultimate sin of 'poor story telling', and that's the final nail in the coffin.
To summarise: the game has some fun little puzzles and recognisable scenes/characters from the TV series, but lack of good sound, animation and poor storytelling make it very bland, and the short, limited story is too brief, with no hope of any kind of replayability. For a casual game, it's... Okay. Ish. For a point & click game, it's... Poor.
One to avoid.

A gripping serial murder story featuring characters of a television show in the form of a hidden object game, which strangely has no voice acting in it.
When a television series is adapted to a video game, there is always a chance to get some incredibly shoddy cash-in title, or something with an actual effort in it. Never Judge a Book by Its Cover is somewhere between the two.
As a crime story, it is exceptionally well-written with good pacing, good setup, and it knows when to stop before it gets ridiculously overcomplicated. But why is it sold as a Castle game, I have no idea. It has no voice acting, theme song, or anything really related to the show.
As a game it is a mediocre hidden object puzzle title with gorgeous, yet overcrowded scenes, and long and frustrating puzzles. But it’s the point ‘n’ click part that kills it: adventure game logic takes over every last shred of realism, which stands in stark contrast of what is seen in the original show.
Still, if you like hidden object games, or just want something related to the Castle series and already read all the books, this one may be a nice afternoon pastime.

Castle is this crime drama TV show on ABC that's been running for several seasons. It follows mystery novelist turned investigator Richard Castle and homicide detective Kate Beckett.
Apparently it's pretty popular and has won many awards.
I've never seen it. I can't even remember the last time I watched network television. Nowadays I just netflix everything.
It's kinda weird that I decided to play through this game then. This feeling of weirdness isn't helped by just how bleah the direction of this game is. Licensed games are a crapshoot. Usually they're trash or have little to do with whatever it is they're licensing. NJABBIC is the latter.
Like I said earlier, I've never seen the TV show, but I'm going to assume that it has capable writers that help bring the characters to life. Everyone in this game has cookie-cutter dialogue, most of the jokes are stuff you've read/heard too many times, and there's just no personality. Even the sub-title of this game makes me feel a little ill. Never Judge a Book by its Cover? Oh... Castle is a novelist..so books..covers..There is a mystery and...BARF.
Aesthetically, the game isn't much better. The technology is available, but I think more effort was spent on having the characters only slightly resemble their real-life counterparts. Also no matter the situation, everyone has the same facial expression. People are getting murdered and all of the characters have this perpetual smirk. "Look at me! I'm so smug! I'm solving a murder mystery!" The TV show is apparently really good, but this game gives a really bad impression. To be fair the mystery itself is actually pretty decent. It could be the plot for a solid two-parter.
This is probably my first foray into the hidden-object/puzzle genre. This resulted in even more weird feelings than originally thought possible. In the very beginning of the game, Castle has to collect some stuff from his den. I walk in and it is the biggest mess imaginable. He's got gloves, shoes, watches, belts, horses, cats, dogs, fruit, vegetables, and all sorts of other crap just lying around. I go somewhere else and it's the same damn thing. Apparently that's normal for the genre? Wow. It's pretty entertaining finding all the hidden stuff, but the massive leaps in logic is...normal for the adventure games I grew up with.
This game is a master-class in "adventure game logic". Everything you pick up is used once and then discarded, even if it could be useful in the future (like a screwdriver). Instead Castle will find another object that achieves similar results. Some of these puzzles are laughable in their absurdity, like everyday houses having strange locks that require intricate jewelry or random objects. This is some Resident Evil-level ridiculousness. If you ever stop to think about what you're doing in this game, your head is liable to explode.
SPOILERS
At one point you have to get some tongs that have fallen in a hot grill.
-Don't ask how the tongs got under the grates.
-You have to cool off the grill to get the tongs.
-This grill is located on a porch, but you can't use a water hose.
-You have to buy a soda from a machine located in a storage facility.
-Castle is a successful author who lives in a loft in New York City. His rent must be over $10,000 a month. He doesn't have $2 to buy a soda.
-He has to solve puzzles to find $2.
-WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥?
Thankfully, there aren't any ways to totally screw yourself. In other words, there is nothing you can do that would result in an un-winnable game. If you get truly stuck you can access a handy skip button.
Finally there are the logic puzzles. No hidden objects, no finding things to open other things, it's just you and a puzzle. The puzzles in this game are all pretty good, although a couple of them (wires) it's much faster just to solve via process of elimination.
That's the extent of the game really. If you're a fan of the show, don't expect to enjoy this game more than a non-fan. It's possible you might even enjoy it a little less, just because of how poorly-written the characters are. Still, if you happened to acquire this game via a bundle and have a couple afternoons to kill, it's not bad at all.
Now I'm tempted to go through my Steam library and see if I own any other Hidden Object/Puzzle games.

Finally - A controller I control!
The more I use it, the more I appreciate the improvement over the XBox pad I used before.
It won't replace the keyboard+mouse in all games, but is as close as any controller can get.
I quickly got the hang of the touch pads.  Although a little overwhelming at first, the configurability is fantastic, and improving with each update.  It's easy to reconfigure and fine-tune settings in-game with the overlay - just hit the Steam button.  All settings are saved as multiple per-game profiles that can be shared online.
Only minor downside is that it relies on Steam's Big-Picture Mode to handle the profiles.  I only use steam on my desktop, so hadn't spent much time using BPM before.  I find the steam desktop interface far quicker to use and navigate so am now switching between desktop and BPM (windowed) depending on whether I'm using the controller.

Don't pay to be an alpha tester for another Valve passion project that may or may not be abandoned a year from now. The software is in an alpha state, meaning this device is only suitable for tinkerers and hobbyists. The software is NOT suitable for consumer use. It is also directly tied to Steam's Big Picture Mode, for reasons I can't fathom.
Once again, Valve assumed the community would do all the hard work for them and create profiles for every game, but I don't see any of that happening. The controllers aren't popular, so the community support is almost nonexistant. I'm left with an expensive controller that doesn't do anything, and doesn't even have rechargeable batteries. I feel ripped off.

The game is another well made TellTale adventure. Don't listen to the whiny 10 year olds or the idiotic "critics" that say this game is terrible just because it's not like the original Minecraft, or whatever other bad excuses people use.

Minecraft is an extraordinary building simulator game that allows you to mine blocks and then change them into complex structures. It’s so easy a five year old can do it, but it’s fun for any age because of the imagination you can put into your creations. Not only that, but it includes a survival system that adds a whole new level of enjoyment to it. This makes it so while you are building things you have to try to protect yourself and your buildings from various monsters.
The only thing the game was missing from being perfect is more NPCs and various towns people you could talk to (Note the game has villagers, but they are for trading items to and nothing more.) So believe me when I say I was genuinely interested in a Minecraft “Story Mode”. The idea of it is cool and it sounds like it would be a great addition to the game. Hell, maybe it would've been if done right.
But it was so poorly executed. Instead of a story mode integrated with the game itself, what we got was another telltale excuse for an adventure game. Don’t get me wrong, I like the telltale games. They are kind of a guilty pleasure of mine, but the company really needs to work on putting more adventure into the game and less pointless dialog that is so unoriginal to the point where it starts ripping off of it’s own stories to make a new game.
So to start off, we take control of the character known as Jesse. Jesse can be customized to be male or female, with the three  diffrent skin options for each gender. It’s not an RPG so I can understand why we didn’t get a full character customization option. It is nice how you could choose your gender and would respectively get a male or female voice depending on what you picked. I know something like that is starting to become the norm in gaming, but it still does impress me when the developers put in the extra time and money to get a male and female voice for the protagonist so we don’t have to feel pigeonholed into what gender our playable character can be.
After we make our character we are then introduced to the story. I won’t give too much away as it’s really the only thing that makes this game worthwhile, but our hero (Jesse) finds themselves in a dire situation with only their friends and a couple of fabled heroes to guide them. Along the way you will make choices as in any other telltale game that ultimately affect the outcome of the chapter and among other things, change the story. There is a big fuss that goes around about these so called choices, but I don’t want to get into the whole telltale story formula discussion. You need only have to play two or more telltale games to see what I am referring to.
Here is the massive issue I have with this game. The action sequences or QTEs known to most people is the thing that drags this game down. QTEs (Quick time events) are a lazy way of putting action into a game without having to develop any kind of combat, platforming, or action system of any kind. For instance in a game like Super Mario you have to time your jumps and use the controls to get across obstacles. However, with QTEs instead of having to actually move your character and manually control yourself, you instead just simply press or mash down a key such as Q, W, E, A, S, D, etc. Once in awhile QTEs are okay. There doesn’t always need to be tons of action to make a game fun to play, but telltale has a way of just littering the game with mindless QTEs after more mindless QTEs.
Going back to what I said earlier about Minecraft, it’s not the type of game where you just mash down a button that lights up on the screen to do something. It’s a game where you can take your time to build great structures and craft interesting objects in order to further progress in your world. To be fair, telltale gives an attempt to implement the crafting system into the minecraft story mode, but it’s so seldomly used that it’s almost insulting to anyone who has actually played minecraft.
There is a part early on in the game where your characters actually get to build something made out of blocks. Instead of allowing the player to go around and start stacking away we are treated to mashing down Q so that the game can automatically build what we are trying to make. It would be like if you went out and bought the newest Call of Duty or Battlefield game only to find that you no longer go around aiming your gun to shoot, you instead have to press down the buttons that appear on screen and the game will automatically aim for your opponents head to kill them. Do you know how much that would suck? Well that’s what it’s like playing this game.
Overall, I do not recommend buying this game. I consider myself to be a hardcore minecraft and adventure game fan and even I cannot stand what Telltale did to this game. Telltale really needs to go back to the drawing board and start learning about what made the point and click games in the 90s fun. It was the exploring, the weird quirky ways you had to solve problems, the complex puzzles that stood in your way and so on. Monkey Island would of been a lot less fun if all you had to do is walk down a hallway and just talk to people along the way.

Quick Note: The original Deus Ex: HR entry has now been replaced by the newly released Director's Cut edition, so I will write my recommendation on this.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an action RPG set within a modern cyberpunk world in the year 2027. You enter this world as Adam Jensen, a private security officer working for Sarif Industries. As you initially start the game, you'll see it is a time where humanity is split due to their contrasting views on human augmentations, but of course, that's not all there is to it.
Story-wise, this game is absolutely perfect. The game is set before the original Deus Ex game (25 years earlier to be exact). The script is very thought-provoking and quote-worthy. As you proceed through the game, you'll be able to read scattered e-books lying around, as well as e-mails on specific computer workstations. This will give you more insight into the story. If you approach random NPC's, they will tell you their own personal views. There are 5 main locations that you'll be able to visit, all of which have their own side quests scattered around that'll also give you even more insight within the outstanding plot of this game. There are many organizations, such as the aforementioned "Sarif Industries" that serve their own specific purposes. There are also references to certain mythologies that serve a subtle connection to the original game.
Graphically, the game has a wonderfully intense gold and black theme that is present throughout. There is a somewhat common issue that you may experience where certain glitches such as tearing and stuttering may occur, as well as character models (both face and body) acting quite irregular. However, I am pretty sure this has been corrected within the Director's Cut edition of the game. (Don't quote me on this). Textures have generally been improved also.
In regards to gameplay, you essentially have two approaches: stealth or non-stealth. Hell, you could go for the mixed bag, but I wouldn't recommend it. Both styles have their own advantages and disadvantages, but I'll leave you to decide your play-style for yourself. The game showcases specific weaponry tailored to either style that you'll come across whilst playing. There are boss fights within the game that the new DC edition has reworked completely to allow players to use different play-styles instead of being restricted to a non-stealthy approach. There is also the addition of a new documentary and commentary by Eidos Montreal. Previous DLC expansions and missions have been fully integrated within the game and another new and exciting feature that has been implemented is the 'New Game+' mode. This mode allows you to carry over your augmentations and weaponry from your first play-through. For anyone who likes collecting achievements and trading cards/backgrounds/emoticons, those have also been implemented.
Personally, this game is a firm 10/10. I absolutely adore this game and I could not recommend it enough. It is worth the full price-tag by far. This game is a firm number two on my top-ten list of games. Also, if you happen to own the original version of DE:HR, you'll receive a 50% discount for the Director's Cut edition. Furthermore, if you own the 'Missing Link' DLC expansion, that will add 25% to the discount giving you 75% off the entire game, which should work out as $5 for those of you in the USA and around £3.25 for the British.
I implore you to buy this game. It is outstanding.

This review was written after completing every route and achievement in the game. I'd rate this game a 7.5/10. Although it is a wonderful game, there are some minor flaws that I hope will be improved in the future.
The first thing this game did right was to include three different pronouns, two different hairstyles and three different skin tones for the MC! There were also two female and four male love interests. Each character had different personalities and backstories, while the MC was both snarky and relatable. Art, although sometimes inconsistent, was beautiful.
However, the game was a little buggy and would often crash once in a while. I might be nitpicking here too - but the fast forward button was still pretty slow. Ctrl+Tab to access steam in game + F12 to screenshot do not work. Other than technical / programming errors, I felt that the story was very repetitive (at least for the first five love interests that you would be romancing). The overarching storyline is the same - for each of the five characters, you would experience the same common route and (almost) the same conflict and ending. Furthermore, after the common route ends and your love interest has been chosen, there is no further choices that you make. There is no bad ending.
This visual novel is also pretty short, which might make the drama, conflict and romance seemed a little rushed. Graves' story (I assume it is the true ending since it ties all the loose ends from the other routes together) - was different from the rest and made it a little less boring to read. Overall, I would recommend buying this game on sale - especially if you love light-hearted romance, nothing too serious... and cats! You can never have enough cats. Unfortunately, I don't think this game is worth buying at its full price.

At the risk of sounding like a machine gun spewing forth a volley of cliches, I begin my review...  "this controller puts you in command of your own gaming experience", well...  yes, it does.
Should you find yourself in possession of a steam controller, I can offer some small advisements...
-do not expect it to behave like a typical
Xbox style controller, it isn't.
-take time to learn it's functions and the
capabilities of it's software.
("Big picture" handles the honors)
-experiment, you are best served        finding, your own way to utilize it.
-become familiar with the profile community, then contribute to it.
In my opinion, it does nearly everything well.  The only drawback I have encountered is the requirement of big picture use for advanced functionality... In particular, because some games just won't run with big picture.  (The 2 I encountered  issues with were "wolfenstein - the new order" & "blue estate - the game" , both run fine without the big picture, but are non-starters while running it...  this really sucks as I had wanted to play both with the controller.)
Also, there are some games where a dual stick controller is the better way to go, 3rd person action games, or combo based fighters.
However, if you play First person shooters, this is the best controller on the market.
For example, my borderlands profile allows me to use one of the grip buttons as a toggle/clutch to tighten the precision of the view controller for dead on accurate aim.  The movement stick also is set to sprint when pushed into contact with it's outer ring...  no need to switch
The gyro is also great for aiming and flight control, and can be engaged with a switch so you can use it selectively.
Almost ever parameter can be independently adjusted to exactly what you desire.
I absolutely love the grip buttons.  Every controller should have them..
If you are thinking of acquiring one, do so.
Update 10/2016
I honestly can't imagine playing first-person shooters without the controller, since it was released steam has only improved upon its features and adaptability.  With the newly-implemented edge spinning you can use it very effectively for 3rd person action games, and for twin stick shooters.  I still have a bit of trouble with it on games where the right stick is used to dodge.
The touch menu feature allows easy accessibility for keyboard base games that have dozens of key commands.  ( single button press)  I have a profile for Sacred 2 gold that escience 32 functions to the touch menu on the left pad, I'm able to use the controller to play a game for which it would otherwise be impossible.
Another great feature is an extremely precise setting on the touch enabled gyroscope, without having to hit any buttons the gyroscope is automatically enabled and you can tweak the aim on whatever you're doing with slight tilt of your wrist.
I have attempted to use the gyroscope for steering on both driving and flight games, well I haven't got it perfect for some of them it's usually just a bit of work to tweak my profile.
I can't recommend it enough.
Update 03/2017
Read a review by a curator panning this controller, and talking about a redesign.  GOD, I HOPE HE WAS JUST THE JACKASS HE SOUNDED LIKE.  This controller is astoundingly capable and dependent entirely on user aptitude.  (Or you can use templates.)
I can't picture playing a first-person shooter without it.  If I truly find out they're going to make major changes to this controller, I'll be buying a couple extra ones to put away in case I wear mine out.
I still use an Xbox 360 controller for third person games but this is just habit.   I've tested personalized configurations out on the steam controller for games like Arkham Origins, with proper adjustment of the "edge spin radius" for the right trackpad, it worked very well.  After a half hour so I didn't even notice the difference.
I love the grip buttons they provide an intuitive replacement for Less convenient control configuration, ie: clicking the left stick to Sprint, or the right stick to melee.
Love the touch menu feature, both for shooters and keyboard centered games (like sacred 2), requiring 30 different buttons for commands.
Another vital use for my left grip, is a "clutch" for tracking speed on the right "aim" track pad.  I have it set that when I engage the left grip button it drastically slows down the movement speed for very precise aiming.
This doesn't even begin to scratch the surface of what's capable if you engage the gyroscope.
Valve, got this one right.
After over a year, I still love it.

Final Score:  3/5 Stars.

Overall, a great concept for a game, carried over from similar games on Warcraft III. You control a single hero among a group of heroes defending a missle silo against waves of enemies. Buy items, Kill enemies, Repeat. And that might sound like a casual dismissal of the genre of hero defense, but it's not. Personally, I love the hero defense genre. Bloodsports has an interesting aethetic and a unique setting for the hero defense genre, but ultimately it falls flat and just doesn't have the replayability that a game like this could, and should, have.
Characters - There are 4 classes, and only 8 characters (2 for each class). Which isn't a terrible thing on it's own, but there isn't enough variation and interesting abilities to keep things interesting. In a game focused on controlling your hero and slaughtering waves of enemies, you want your abilities to feel impactful and great using them, but that doesn't really happen playing Bloodsports.tv. Your abilities scale up as you level them, with increased damage and lower cooldowns, but there's nothing added that makes it feel like you're getting stronger, since your enemies are scaling with you. Having level 1 of most abilities feels the same as levels 2, 3, 4 etc.. I don't think the character design is either terrible or great, but in a game so dependent on controlling your hero, having a lackluster hero experience is definitely a big minus. Couple that with the absurd progression system, and games can seem more of a grind and a hassle than a fun experience.
Items - There are a good number of items in the game, but the build path for most characters seem fairly linear. There are a few deviations and customizations you can make, but if you're looking for the optimal build, it's probably the same in nearly all situations. And that takes out a lot of the strategy or planning, and is another factor leading to your character, and game experience, very cookie-cutter and lacking originality.
Enemies - I really like the diversity of enemies. There aren't tons of varieties (maybe like 10?), but they all serve a bit of a niche, and depending on their combination it can really cause you to alter your playstyle. This on the fly decision making to adapt to the spawned enemies is something the rest of the game lacks, a sense of strategy and coordination between players. Some enemies heal, some enemies are very mobile, some are stealthy and go for your back line of characters, almost all have channeled abilities which can be interrupted (and it feels great when you do interrupt them, and when you don't or are unable to, you feel like it's something you could account for in the future. I think the enemy design is probably one of the high points of the game.
Multiplayer - Fortunately, I primarily play this game with friends. I've played it briefly solo, but the maps are pretty clearly designed to be played with multiple people. And the community is essentially dead. If you are interested in playing this game, you'll have a much better time if you can find 2 or  3 or 4 friends to play with, but don't expect to find a single other player in this ghost town of a game.
Overall - I really would love to be able to recommend this game and sink hundreds of hours into it. But the replayability and the overall experience just won't allow me to. If you can rouse up 4 friends, I'm sure you could have fun for a few hours. But ultimately, the game is lacking a lot in terms of depth. I would call this a very promising base for an incredible game, but it's missing too much and has too much that needs to be improved.

There is only one mode in Bloodsports.TV: co-op. You can run through the tutorial or set up a match for just yourself to test things out, but there are no campaign or competitive matches. All that’s left is straight up five-player, drop-in/drop-out, cooperative action. You’ll start each match (assuming you’re hosting) by choosing from one of the game’s six maps, setting the game difficulty, and finally selecting how many waves of enemies you feel like facing.
There is enough variance that players should be able to find a hero that suits their particular play style. Each class (and to a degree each hero) also has their own set of challenges to complete - called the “Path to Glory” - that apply stat bonuses to that class. This gives players a little extra incentive to try out all available classes and characters.
There are some issues with the game - like the look and feel of the UI, crucial stats getting lost amidst a cluster of health bars, and the occasional drag of repetition - that stick out from time to time, but these are quickly forgotten once you clear a difficult wave or kill an especially tough boss.
After all, nothing beats that elation you feel when you win a hard-fought battle with a group of friends!

This is easily the best hack n' slash RPG I have ever played.  I started playing this title when it was first released, and I still find myself coming back to it after over a decade.
The control and combat system is pretty intuitive, and camera only bites you when you have your back to a steep wall (extreme zoom).  That isn't much of a problem, however, since you can turn the camera around with ease.  The party manipulation options are somewhat in-depth, with multiple selections for formations, movement ranges, and aggression.  Probably more than what's needed to play through the game, but workable nonetheless.
Another great feature is the loading screens (or lack therof).  You load once at the beginning, and the game "streams" the entire world without a pause; the entire map from start to finish.  The maps are not huge by any means, but big enough that this is an impressive feature given when this game was released.
Character development is also interesting; your party members develop thier combat effectiveness by how you use them (melee, ranged, caster, etc.).  You can also switch fighting styles at any time, just be mindful that a jack-of-all is a master-of-none (unless you grind all your skills on the multiplayer map).
The single-player campaign has just enough content to keep you focused on why you're stomping your way through hordes of hostile creatures, and doesn't overload you with too much "lore."  The multi-player offers an additional map that you can use, and both the single and multi maps can be used for it.
There is also a massive mod community for this game, which also keep it alive for those who own computers that have left this old title in the dust.
Like I said, it is downright fun (and cheap, too).

The first, "Dungeon Siege I", is the best! That and its expansion, "Legends of Aranna!" The best thing about this first of the series is the ease with which you control your hero and the accumulated party. It's all mouse driven, not a lot of messing around with the keyboard (no - W,S,A,D)! The camera viewpoint, the movement of your characters, the designated attacks are all based on point and click, mouse selections.
As for the RPG elements of the game, it's up there with "Diablo", "War Craft", and the "Dungeons and Dragons" entries to the genre. There are elements on par with "Morrowwind" and "Skyrim", although as may already be obvious, this is not a First Person Shooter! It is all 3rd person, bird's eye view from beside or above your character and their companions. It is Real Time, which is significant too. But with an adequate save facility, and pausing as needed, this is not difficult to manage, even for those who may prefer Turn-Based games.
Also there is an extensive weapon, spell, armor, skill upgrade system which is built-in, almost automatic. Whichever weapons or spells you use the most, you get better and better at. It is broken down into the general categories of; Melee, Ranged, Nature Magic and Combat Magic. With lots of ways to cross train and improve abilities outside of your initial choices.
Plus there's lots of loot and ways to improve your gear as you go along. not to mention lots of great monsters and villians to master. But one thing console players may be looking for is not so fully represented here are the boss battles. You have to beat increasingly difficult and powerful creatures and opponents. But these usually do not culminate in a boss battle. There are several really tough bosses, don't get me wrong. But this is not a level by level occurence. They are only sparingly sprinkled here and there, not through-out as some console, button pusher games have!
And that's another thing I like about the first version. You don't have to sit there and continue to push the attack button, push the attack button, push the attack button, push the attack button, push the attack button, push the attack button! It's a lot like Diablo in that you set your hero on a creature and they will continue to fight it until it is killed, they are killed or you redirect their attention to a different foe or beast. Oh, there's plenty of action! But you don't have to train like you're going on a marathon, to progress fairly decently! Like I said, it's not so much button clicking! There! You like that or not!
Some folks may not be attracted to this sort of gameplay. I understand that DS III may be more compatible for consoles, and more gamepad driven. It's okay. I got my game right here! "Dungeon Siege I" and "Dungeon Siege I, Legends of Aranna" are the best in my book. In fact, it's my favorite dungeon crawler, PC mouse driven, fantasy Role Play game! I rate it = 10 out of 10! Thanks for reading, I hope this helps some folks decide to try this version out!   PEACE!  Awwa - \A/

I just finished the game.  I have to say it was a great journey back in time to a more classic feeling game with a wide array of settings.  The challenge was fairly good and would have been more challenging if I had played on hard mode.  I loved how a lot of the battles consisted of a large number of enemies and that you could have a large group of party members.  Some of the dungeons are very long (Sometimes I felt like I was playing a solo World of Warcraft classic style dungeon because of the roles of the party members, large battles and the length of dungeons.).  It was also nice to see that the items you could buy in the store were actually useful and that you would want to buy them.  There are so many ways to play this game that my playstyle of trying to be everything was hindered.  That isn't really a bad thing.  You could play this multiple times, being different types of characters, though I'm not really one to play through a game again.  I like to move on and try something new.
The music (in the majority, is very nice) reminded me a lot of The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind.  Some are repetative though (very short and then it repeats), making those annoying.  I didn't realize that it was the same composer until today.  Early on, some of the voices were annoying, but a lot were interesting and sometimes funny.  Hearing the click of selecting or opening a persons inventory became annoying, fast (and you did this a lot).
At the beginning of the game, the amount of inventory space is annoying (not enough).  It was a long way to the first town.  Also, with very large areas between two shop areas, you will find your inventory full and have to travel back long distances to sell things.  One other thing deals with organization of inventory.  I would group my health and mana potions together, seperately.  When I would use them, it wouldn't use them in order from top to bottom.  So, I ended up with a scattered mess that I would end up having to organize again.  In a shop with spells to purchase, it would have also been nice to sort and seperate the two types of magic (nature and combat).  It would have also been nice to be able to grab multiple items in your inventory to move around.
When I would have multiple characters's windows open or just a shop along with one character, the inventory windows for the group would appear extra small (with shop window open this actually only occurred with the pack mules).  It made it harder to do what I wanted.
It took me to long to figure out how to clearly get everyone to play their roles in battle (some wouldn't move or attack, even though I had set things to do so).  I eventually figured out I needed to select a character and then hit ctrl-A to select everyone or press ctrl and click on the members you wanted, to get things to work properly.  This was after figuring out what the different battle options did and setting them for each of the party members.  It is also to easy to click on other characters, which then deselects everyone else.
If you want to take any screenshots and not have the adventurer's handbook open, you will need to go into the input options and change your hotkey for the handbook.  The default screenshot button is F12, which is also the adventurer's handbook.
Sometimes it is hard to get all your party on a transport elevator before it moves.  Then you have to wait to get everyone together.
It would have been nice if they had labeled the area you were currently in on the map and when you are entering a new area.
I had a few crash to desktop occurrances and exceptions while playing through the game.  The last crash I had was a memory error where the game apparently didn't deallocate correctly.  This was in Castle Ehb.
I disliked the dropping of a party members complete inventory onto the ground when it dies.  It creates a mess of text on the screen (you could turn the text off), as well as having to keep up with who was carrying what.  I also hit max gold and then when I would sell things, it would drop the gold on the ground.  This eventually created a pile of text.  I'm not sure if it was play style, to much stuff for the amount of gold one can carry or that to much gold can be found in chests or dropped from an enemy.  I also came back to the dropped pile of gold one time, after many, and found it gone.
The pack mules don't follow behind my party in a speedy fashion during battles, which can sometimes cause problems of them getting out of the way from being hit by an enemy.
As far as the ending goes, I had to watch it on YouTube.  I find this a very bad thing.  When you defeat the final boss and it explodes, it drops loot and then the screen goes black.  You are then returned to the start menu.  In the non-steam version, you are sent to a black screen with text and narration to end the story.  Then, you get the credits.  After this, you are returned to the game to be able to pick up the loot and do as you please (play multiplayer or expansions).  I guess since the steam version doesn't come with multiplayer and the expansions, they cut this out.  It still should have gone through the ending credits and then returned you to the game to pick up the loot.
Though it seems I mentioned more of the negative aspects to this game, it is a very good game overall.  It is definately worthy of being played.  Hopefully steam will release a fix for the ending and sparse crashes.

This is a really good remake of the original game. I hadn't ever played it, but I was already familiar with the Monkey Island series :).
The first I actually played was MI 3 (there's at least 4 of them to my knowledge).
I can vaguely remember seeing bits of MI 2, and thought it was really awesome, so I'd most definitely recommend getting the pack (The Secret of Monkey Island + Monkey Island 2 - special edition).
_________________________________________________________________
The best thing about Monkey Island is it's wacky & silly sense of humour. I just love this stuff. It's not meant to be taken seriously!
If it wasn't for the built-in hints system, I most probably would have been stuck (especially near the end). I really was clueless as to how to proceed at one point, due to experiencing issues with pointing & clicking (which was rather frustrating, since this is a P&C game after all!).
So when that's a bit "off"... well, it definitely doesn't want to keep you going (which made me rely on the hints-system, more than I normally would have).
But considering it's old age, it really is a quality game, and well worth the money!
It's beauty lies in it's simplicity and lighthearted nature :). The story is very straightforward & ridiculously basic.
[...young guy wants to be a pirate, ...goes off on a journey to become one, ...meets a girl on the way, ...they instantly fall in love (literally!), ...she gets in trouble, ...he faces the bad guy who got her in trouble & gets rid of him and then the lovebirds sail off together] :)
This is excellent for when you want to play something different for a change, where you're not expected to think too realistically and just have a good laugh.
I needed some time to grow accustomed to the graphics, but after playing a while, I became fond of the style (especially the way Guybrush was portrayed). They definitely captured his spirit visually!
Also, there's a neat option that let's you switch from the "vintage" pixelated style to the remastered style by pressing F10 (it even helped me find something I couldn't see in the remastered version - go figure!).
The voice-acting is very well executed! Apparently the voice-actors each covered more than one character and I couldn't tell! And when you can't tell, guess what? That means they're really acting!
And as for the music, the main theme is very catchy and fits the atmosphere perfectly. Same goes for the in-game soundtracks - very fitting!
Once you hear the OST, it's very hard to get it out of your head :).
Lastly, some of the subcharacters could definitely want you coming back for more :), they're just so much fun.
PS I'm especially fond of Carla & Otis :). If you ever decide on playing the game, you'll soon figure out why ;).

Very good mix of story-driven RPG and hack and slash game.
Visuals are good, animations are top notch. The soundtrack is amazing; sure, you need to like the orchestral vibe, but it's on par with DOOM's OST, on a different style. The combat feels good, it is not difficult, without feeling like a chore despite the little variety of enemies. Regular, "sandbox" fight lean on the hack and slash genre while boss fights are more of a bullet hell.
The story is good as a standalone game, but also as a sequel to other games, and as a philosophical question about existance and the meaning of "life". And yes, I realize how cheesy this sounds.
Decent replayability thanks to the 19 "joke" endings, such as
, and the side-quests, some of them being simple fetch quests and others being whole story arcs tying to the original Nier game.
One of the things that stand out in this game is how the story and the level design affects the game mechanics. You start the game with a top-down section, then it turns into a twin stick shooter, a bullet hell, a hack and slash, a 2D fighting game and a top-view hack and slash, all in the first hour of gameplay depending on what you're doing, and all of this is made in a very controlled, yet fluid manner, so that you, the player, can see all of the creative work that went into this game, and oh boy, the japanese are still excellent at making deep, creative games.

Rising Storm 2: Vietnam
Of a select few games, RS2 was my most anticipated release of 2017.  After falling in love with RO2 and RS1's gritty cinematism with engaging gameplay, I could not wait for Tripwire to release their next title set in the most underappreciated and hardest to represent theater of war: Vietnam.
Needless to say, when word came around regarding the beta, I enthusiastically filled out my application and waited ever patiently for my invitation, confident that I would recieve a masterpiece, however unpolished.
What I DID recieve, however, was far bellow my expectations.  The gameplay was not only buggy, but it was uninspired and overall unbalanced, and it did not mesh well at all with the two maps in play, Song Be and Hue city.  RS2 had thoroughly dissapointed me, despite how much I wanted to love it.
I never bought the game until months later.  Just a week or so after the Bushranger update, I picked it up while it was on sale for 10-something dollars.  Oh boy, I'm glad I did.
I'm not quite sure how to quantify it exactly, but Tripwire did a 180 with this game.  If you were to play through RO2 and RS1 and then pick up RS2, it stands amongst them as a proud game worthy of its franchise title.  The balance is good, save for a few underpowered weapons (mosin, cough cough), and the gameplay flows naturally from the theater in hand and meshes nicely with the beautifully made maps; it plays and feels like a Vietnam war movie-- albeit more like Platoon as opposed to Apocalypse Now or Full Metal Jacket-- and the addition of position VOIP is priceless.  It's a mixture of horror and hilarity when you're being beseiged at all angles by VC yelling, "GO HOME GI.  WE PROTECT RICE" in crude Asian accents while a comrade to your right affixes a kabar to his Aussie rifle and boldly proclares over VOIP, "You ever seen a knife, Charlie?  Now THIS is a knife," before storming into their ranks.
Overall:
8.5/10 would yell "protect rice" in voice chat again

TL;DR: You'd like to play a DOTA-like game without the stress and rage of PVP gaming with some friends? This game is for you. (Not worth for solo though).
=============
Meet Bloodsports, a futuristic take on ancient Roma's gladiators. You play a character among 8, each with a set of class skills geared towards one of the classic MMO roles (tanker, striker, healer, crowd-controller) to take on hoards of enemies and defend a nuclear missile (your core).
Game is classic in mechanics but very good in implementing them. Each class has its own feeling and variety of tactics, combining skills and items to bring out powerful abilities.
Obviously the game is made to be played with friends. It's nice to play a few hours in solo but gets repetitive quickly. With friends, it's basically up to your own love for the genre.
As for realization, nothing to criticize: the art is nice and develops an identity to the universe, music and off-voice contribute weel to the cynical atmosphere, and I have no memory of any bug.
Although it's no more updated, unfortunately, game is still worth its full price. You'll net between 10 and 40 hours of fun depending on your taste for the genre and how many friends you play with.
When on sales, it's a premium pick if you have at least 2 other friends interested.

The Steam controller is really a controller made to be as versatile as possible. This thing has so many options and settings for its insane amount of buttons that you can play literally anything with it. It really is a controller with the PC mindset, you get all the freedom in the world with your piece of hardware. No restrictions. I wouldn't say it's the holy grail of gaming, because it's actually not as good as a mouse and keyboard in a large amount of cases, but it can simulate it (and more importantly: both this and a controller simultaniously) very decently. Some people have noted that it's worse than a 360 controller for things like racing games, but I didn't have a single problem with this in that respect. It wasn't notably worse than my 360 controller since steering is still done with the anolog stick, looking around is at the trackpad and it works fine. As for simulating a mouse, well it's certainly not as precise as an actual mouse. Playing multiplayer shooters with this won't work, I don't think it can replace the mouse in multiplayer fps games. It is, however, a lot better than an analog stick. For a story-fps like Wolfenstein it does its job fine. Plus when twitch reflexes don't matter as much (say in management games) I found it to be just as good as a mouse. It only lacks some of the shortcuts, but I'm sure you could bind those to some or other button on this thing if you have the time.
As for the feel, it takes some getting used to. Certainly different from my ol' 360 controller, you'll have to relearn the whole lay-out of controllers. It feels about as sturdy as my 360 controller but with way better haptic feedback, and after a while the buttons become more familiar. Also it has a ♥♥♥♥ing gyroscope because options. No expense spared here.
In total, yeah I'd go as far as to say that this is a straight upgrade from a 360 controller. Maybe some people are upset that it won't actually win you CS:GO matches, but hell that wasn't really realistic from a controller now was it? This thing can play anything ever from your couch, and works as good as if not better than your 360 controller. I'm very satisfied with it, Valve did a fine job.

Beautiful and stylish state-of-the-art gadget.
Pros:
+ two touchpads fully programmable, many functions can act like analog-joysticks, mouse-touchpad, a 4 button pad, etc.
+ one analog-pad
+ two trigger buttons that can act like right-analog-axis-X.
+ two shoulder buttons
+ two paddles on the back, to be used for shifting gears.
+ usb cable, extender and a wireless dongle.
+ rumble (configurable)
+ gyro (yes that's right, a gyro sensor)
+ additionally you can buy a hard, stylish box to carry it with you on trips.
+ constant software updates, bug fixes (although some bugs I've noticed have never been addressed)
cons:
- not working properly without steam, meaning it works, but if your game has a launcher you cannot add it as a Non-steam game, you in fact add the launcher. (FIFA)
- no official Windows/Linux/iOS drivers, hence the controller cannot be detected by the system as a controller. (kinda the reason of the previous point)
- NOT A SINGLE GAME THAT MAKES SENSE TO BE PLAYED WITH IT! Besides 2d platformers, some (yes some) racing games. F1 2015 is so ♥♥♥♥ed up that the only way to steer smoothly is with the gyro, but it's no steering wheel, you move the controller away from its X axis (tilting its upper side forward or backwards) will ruin the smoothness of the gyro, it virtually creates a 90% deadzone. I haven't tried it with PROEVO, since I don't have it, but if I try FIFA in order to play I add FIFA inside steam, use a custom controller configuration having a lot of keyboard buttons. But get this, you have to set this controller configuration to be your DESKTOP configuration. That's because FIFA.exe starts a launcher, and your FIFA controller setup is in fact in effect on the launcher, but as soon as the actual FIFA starts it turns on the Desktop configuration. I tried CSGO with it, :D 30 minute deathmatch ended up killing a few. It's definitely challenging. If they make matchmaking to make games only with steam controller that will be a lot of fun :). If you're PC gamer like me, my experience with controllers is mainly with Nintendo/Amiga and SEGA MegaDrive 2, You won't get use to using the controller with games like Rocket League. You can try but you'll stick with the safety of mouse and  keyboard.

This is a strange game to recommend as I personally don't believe that the PC port for this game is the best version. This is NOT a very well optomized game and if you're running it on lower end systems you're going to have some trouble keeping this at a smooth 60 fps. However, this is this games biggest issue and honestly doesn't undermine what may be my favorite game of all time.
-An extremely engaging story that keeps you around for multiple playthroughs. Think Evangelion with more boobs and about just as many giant robots.
-An awesome spectacle fighter combat system. A little more calm than a game like DMC or Bayonetta but still just as fun and fluent keeping the game moving fast.
-Plenty of secrets and reason to come back to play. The grind is real but only for the completionists in the crowd, and that's not usually me but this time I got drawn in for the long haul. It's one of the few games I've ever gotten 100% in and for the most part it's worth the haul. Go for the achievements, it's worth the haul and not too time consuming.
-Finally, this game has, hands down, the best soundtrack of the year. Composed by Keiichi Okabe, you're going to get one of the most beautiful and atmospheric soundtracks I've been engrossed in since TES IV back in 2006. Seriously, even if you don't buy the game, check out the soundtrack and just let each track play. It's beautiful and I'd buy a hard copy if I could find one.
This game has some problems, namely the resource hog that it is and a lack of post launch content but the core game itself, with it's heart wrenching story, beautiful visuals, amazing soundtrack and fluent gameplay, is one of my favorite games of the year. I've seen nearly all it had to offer and I couldn't be happier with what it had.

Well, I thought GTA was a lot of fun... but Saints Row 2 easily took over once I started playing and got a place in my heart with its loveable criminals, heartwarmingly stupid jokes, nice storytelling and cut scenes, great silly side missions, a detailed well-designed city to explore and a fine selection of music to blast from your stolen car's radio.

I first played the sequels from SR3 onwards. Some years after its release I thought I'd give what I've heard is the best in the series a try. I wasn't disappointed.
This is an infamously bad port suffering stability and framerate issues (specifically when the game starts to lag intensely, it always seems to end in a crash once you tab out, but you can still save your game in this situation). The bugs can largely be fixed and the game made playable, along with the addition of new content, by the essential Gentlemen of Stilwater mod.
With many of the issues cleaned up the game is a fun open world shooter. Its narrative is superior to the increasingly ridiculous games down the line, telling a gritty tale of gang warfare between the Saints, and the three gangs that have taken Stilwater in their absence. This story achieves a perfect balance in contrast of the grim and the absurd, as it is more serious than later sequels, frequently deploying both dark humour and tense, emotional moments that are stronger in the context of the previous game's events, yet your character pulls off ludicrous stunts throughout. The main character is back, and out for blood; I found the character of the boss entertaining throughout, ever bold and fierce in the face of insurmountable odds, especially with the default cockney voice from Charles Shaughnessy. More games need a default cockney voice. "♥♥♥♥ you say?"
Combat is often satisfying with a decent variety in weapons, some of which have to be picked up or bought and others unlocked. You have all your bases covered in the firearms, there being some iterations of the same weapon type with each different enough to suit a given playstyle, but also a wide assortment of altogether disparate death dealers. There are myriad ways to dispatch the police and gangsters that stand in your way; you have your fists to start with (the melee system is made more dynamic and responsive with light and heavy attacks, the ability to block, and 3-hit combo moves), brutal melee weapons such as katanas or the chainsaw, a swift shot to the head or hail of bullets, and naturally explosives. I found the accuracy of the police pistol to be particularly satisfying. Also a great feature is the ability to dual-wield pistols, submachine guns and sawed-offs, but also to go back to a single weapon when you want. The enemies do feel somewhat fragile when using heavy firepower, but the risk of a quick death if you stand in the open or handle a group carelessly maintains their challenge. I think the camera angle in SR2 (behind the player and over the shoulder when you zoom) gives you a better view of your character and your surroundings than that of SR3.
Driving is actually a bit lackluster compared to that of SR3. It will get you from one point to another, but it's simply not as much fun moving about without better vehicle physics. (Do note that the handling can be made softer with an optional mod in GoS.) Some vehicles are still a blast however and incredibly practical, such as the heavily armed helicopter and swat truck. You can upgrade and customise your cars to get around in style, and gain the upper hand in chases and combat. Fortunately, you can also call a taxi and use it as a fast travel system if you are near a road, so you don't have to constantly trudge back and forth to get to things.
Customisation is much better than in later sequels, with a choice of different wear options and designs for some of the clothing, three different layers for the torso, and tattoos which can be exchanged and unequipped in the wardrobe, accompanied by a robust character creator. (Also note that GoS has a handy optional mod which allows you to recolour everything from the wardrobe.) You can finely tune your look and create a unique appearance, as opposed to the less personalised costume-ish clothing system from SR3. I found a certain style that I was very happy with and stuck with it; sleek black and purple business attire complete with a swat vest nicely befitted my leader of the saints, and this was easily modifiable according to my whim. You may find you start to play in different ways depending on the kind of character you've created. (Be warned, the outfit saving system can sometimes break.)
Unlike in SR3 onwards, you don't upgrade your abilities by buying them from a menu. You have to complete activities, diversions and missions to unlock things, the completionist's delight. For example, successfully landing on the vehicle that appears during a base jump will rid you of all fall damage (beware, the low gravity cheat will remove this effect). Each activity has multiple stages and some can get repetitive, but the upgrades and unlocks are generally worth the effort for introducing new elements to the game. Most importantly you can choose whatever you want to do.
The visuals are somewhat dated, and while Stilwater's textures do little to immerse, the gameplay is spot on. More important than its graphics is the sheer variety of the map, you can explore the very green suburbs, graveyard, trailer park, underground cavern, industrial grounds, vast shopping mall, university, richly refurbished Saints Row district and more. Idle nodes produce interesting NPC behaviour, giving each of the already distinct areas a more unique feel as people dance in clubs, fish at piers, sell hotdogs, sit in the park, perform cheerleading routines or do yoga. There are many little things to appreciate in SR2, like the simple joy of picking up a dustbin and throwing it at someone's head. It is a charmingly destructive, fairly replayable journey at a pretty good price.

Overall: 70/100
Overall I would still recommend the game as the gameplay is very good, but the quality of the port really brings the game down from what it could have been on PC. Review broken down below.
-------------
-------------
Gameplay/Mechanics: 100/100
It's as good as you can expect a single player and co-op hack and slash zombie game to be. Solid controls, difficulty settings are perfect, all deaths will feel like your fault rather than some cheap shot or a glitch, and multiplayer is seamless with even a halfway decent connection. I can't find a single thing to complain about as far as the core gameplay goes.
-------------
Story: 75/100
The story is perhaps a bit whacky. I was often reminded of the newer Saints Row games, where some of the story lines and the characters in them were quite a bit over-the-top. It seems the story in Dead Rising 3 is equal parts gritty survivor looking for a way out of the city (main story) and stopping insane madmen who want to set people on fire with a flamethrower shaped like a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(side quests). Not necesaarily bad, in fact it was quite enjoyable, but jumping back and forth between the two extremes comes across as a bit odd, especially as side quests don't really tie into the main quests at all.
-------------
Graphics/Technical: 35/100
Now this game has the potential to look nice. If you have an insanely strong computer, it will look nice. The thing is, anything short of a Titan will not be able to max this game out because this port is so poorly optimised for anything besides 720p/30fps. There are settings in the options menu for 1080p@59 hz and whatever else you'd expect, but you will still achieve a maximum quality of 720p at 30fps without changing the game files directly, Luckily the graphics are still halfway decent at 720p (which I would recommend leaving them at due to the terrible, terrible optimization) and it's pretty easy to remove the fps cap for smoother gameplay (although some people have issues with stability when they do this, I would strongly recommend doing this as even cutscenes look choppy at 30fps).
This game does not play well with some graphical drivers and will crash until you roll-back to drivers from 2012 if you do experience crashing.
This game also has very long loading times that you'd expect only to see on consoles (just shy of a minute) that appears every time you connect/disconnect from a game, but there are no loading screens that will inturrupt actual gameplay. So it's not necessarily a dealbreaker, but having to wait a minute for the game to launch and then another minute to load a save can seem like an eternity when you want to just play a game, especially when you are setting up your graphics options the first time because most of the settings require you to go back to the main menu and back before they are applied (which essentially adds two minutes each time you change settings).
-------------
Replay Value: 70/100
While the game doesn't necessarily offer any new content or challenges after you have beaten the game, you get to keep all of your levels and unlocks from the first time around which will allow you to more easily complete all of the side-quests in time and eventually max-out your character (which will take several playthroughs).

Dead Rising 3 is an open world Zombie Game in the city of Los Perdidos, but its real short 5-6 hours.  The city is broken up into four small areas.  The game starts getting boring when the city can be open world but all of the four areas look the same.  Usually when a game has different areas they change them up, one being a suburb, instead everything looks the same.  That makes the game feel small like an old 2d shooter where the background loops making the level seem longer but in modern gaming its just lazy.  There are vehicles but their pointless, its impossible to go more than 20-25 secs before hitting some kind of roadblock that is impossible to get over.  The entire vehicle mechanic is a waste of time.
This is NOT a traditional Dead Rising game, as the devs stated they hated the past DR games and their mechanics.  While past games relied on saving survivors to advance the story or unlock the truth.  This game is designed as the devs intended to remove any need to do anything but just rush through the core story parts and finish the game giving you an S rank ending even if you ignore every side quest.  Past DR games the game revolved around saving people whereas in DR3 the side quests are useless offering nothing but a survivor affecting the progression of the story or ending in no way at all.
This title is made by Capcom Vancouver the same team who stated in interviews like at SDCC in the same breath that they were remaking Dead Rising but also that they hated all the past dead rising games.  What a terrible start and the outcome isnt any better.  They got rid of Frank West, Chuck Green makes an appearance at the end and crafting is taken to insanity levels, there are around 150 blueprints.  That is 100 more than people need or will care about.  There is a difference between crafting in a game and just going bonkers with stupid ideas most of which are useless.  For example you can make boxing gloves with knives.  That sounds cool but noone would make that when early in the game you can make a melee scythe that is on fire and with every hit flings grenades at zombies.  Out of 150 blueprints there is NO WAY to make a molotov cocktail, the most basic of things, epic fail.  Capcom Vancouver didnt care about the franchise or the game, makes it mind boggling how anyone could let them make a dead rising game if they hated the series but here we are.
Zombie spawns have no AI or thought behind their design process.  Thinning the herd of zombies does nothing if you walk away and go back its full of zombies again.  In older games this was ok, but in 2014 they coulda put some thought into making it so if the zombies are taken out or thinned t reduces their numbers in an area for a given time.  State of Decay pulls this off nicely.
There is no replayability, since saving survivors dont carry over, and nothing affects the outcome or story of the game there is no incentive to replay the game except to collect some items which isnt very rewarding at all.  This team who hated the DR series offer no branching stories, no reason to do things different, in other words why bother playing at all?
Ignoring all the bugs the game was not made for PC.  The game is locked to 30fps requiring a config tweak to make the game run at 60 fps.  Its terrible that a big company brings a game to PC and cant make it PC ready.  Double Fine studios was able to port Brutal legend from 30fps and make it run creamy smooth 60 fps with no problems.  Playing the game through at 1080p at 30 fps without adding any tweak it looked fine, normally this gives motion sickness but somehow it works in this game which just begs the question why not just make it 60?
To unlock 60 FPS do the following:
> Open notepad
>Type in: gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate=True
>Save the notepad file and rename it User.ini
>Move the notepad file you just created to your Dead Rising 3 folder, which is located in Steam/SteamApps/Common/Dead Rising 3.
>That's it
State of decay offers a far more satisfying experience than DR3 for open world, for good ol zombie fun DR OTC is better suited for PC gamers.

Hustle Cat is a game unique to the dating genre as you can date both human and cat, a feat attempted by not many developers.
I picked this game up recently during the Summer Sale and fell in love with it to the point where a friend and I basically finished the game in a day because we couldn't stop playing.
The game revolves around you, Avery Grey, and your new job at a cat café. Within your first few days, things get stranger and stranger, involving magic, cats, and all sorts of mayhem inbetween. The story, although not complex, is one that is best experienced by the player rather than read in a review, mostly due to its sweet and fun nature.
Pros:
- (limited but at least its still an option) character customization
- ability to pick your own pronouns
- can date any gender regardless of pronoun choices
- characters are unique
- writing is captivating and fun with very few grammatical errors
- the routes are well written when it comes to developing the main charcters/your dating choice
- art is very well done, bountiful cgs per route
Cons:
- game occassionally crashes, though the autosave feature will always have your back (in my 11 hours of playing the game crashed a total of 4 times)
- some of the story is kind of vague. even in the final route you don't get too much of a how or why things happen
- i lowkey wanted to date the bad guy but that wasnt an option
You wont really need too much of a guide for this one as the choices you can make have it be pretty obvious as to who you'll romance with what you'll say. I highly recommend this game for dating sim beginners, those who want to relax with a casual playstyle, or just want a generally cute but not extremely deep story (though it does have its moments).
Hustle Cat receives a 9.5/10 from me.

A worthy successor in the Red Orchestra lineage.
It's difficult to make a dissimilar FPS, but they've pulled it off quite well here, the Americans/Australians have firepower and helicopters but the VC/NVA have tunnels and traps, so it's a well balanced game. That said, it's still teamwork that wins the game, like all realistic FPS's.
Graphically it's not as good as other FPS's around, although it's a good improvement over the previous titles in the series, but some quirks are still around like getting stuck on stuff.
The gunplay is as good and realistic as ever and there's quite a variety of weapons to go around as well as classes. In this title you can also customize your fighter, unlike the previous games.
The environment and sounds are terrific, they bring back memories of movies like Platoon and Apocalypse Now. The whole game has a Vietnam vibe about it, when you play as VC you feel like waves of ghosts in the jungle, only the sound of the foliage when running towards an objective. Napalm is a awesome sight, you see that F-4 Phantom swooping in and the earth turns into hell.
Maps are also great and varied, you have urban, jungle (off-course), hills and open areas, I believe most replicate actual battles like Hamburger Hill, but all in all very well thought out. In the beginning there weren't enough maps but the game keeps receiving updates from the developers and the community so it's getting a lot of content added (no paid DLC! no loot boxes!).

Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is a great game.
It's a first person shooter set during the Vietnam War (when you die you can watch your squad in third person view).
I love that it has Aussie soldiers as well as US troops.
You choose your character from a range of several classes, and there are a variety of weaons to use - as well as anti-personnel traps.
There are also several different maps, as well as different game types.
The game is mostly foot soldiers, although there are some helicopters as well (you can't drive, or fly, any other type of vehicle).
There are various nuances to playing the game, which might not be apparent at first.
I would suggest that new players get used to the game by playing a few rounds as an ordinary foot soldier.
The gameplay is sort of a cross between Vietcong: Fist Alpha and Call of Duty.
The artwork is great; overall, the game's ambience is very good.
If you like Vietnam War era games, then I highly recommend that you give this one a try.

the Steam Controller is a bit strange at first. I bought this immediately worried about the track pads, being as i hate the track pad on my laptop, but that fear was quickly laid to rest when i loaded up Fallout 4 for the first time with it and simply chose one of the default layouts. Aside from button position, and a quick tweak to the right track pads sensitivity, I almost couldn't tell it wasn't my xbox 360 controller. However this in no way shape or form replaces my mouse and keyboard for RTS games, but its great for older games that don't have gamepad support.

There's some kinks that need to be worked out with this and a few awkward things that keep happening with FPSes where the uh, pad basically flings the mouse to the other side of the screen, but it works well enough, feels nice to hold, and is very responsive, so I can't completely fault the thing. I think it's worth a purchase if you're looking for a controller solution that's definitely going to work with your steam library, but I wouldn't be surprised if Valve releases a better version of this some time later.
