So, I bought Hustle Cat on the sale because it seemed like kind of a cute/casual visual novel about cats, but honestly I wasn't crazy about the trailer and didn't think I'd be THAT interested in the visual novel itself. I was wrong. Albeit a nice little intro to the characters and art style, in my opinion the trailer doesn't do the game justice. That's not necessarily a bad thing, since I was very pleasantly surprised by how good the game actually is. I'm gonna talk about the characters and what I thought worked well about them.
Avery Gray is the character that you play as. You can choose your pronouns (he/she/they) as well as whether you look more masculine/feminine, and there are three skin tone choices. Avery is a preset character with his/her/their own behavioural traits, but the fact that the player can choose certain details about Avery grants a decent amount of immersion without taking away from the quirks of the character. In all cases, Avery has grey/silver hair with pink-red eyes. They are quite mischievous and dorky, and just a fun character to play as. Their interactions with the other characters range from tear jerking to hilarious. Avery is a fantastic protagonist.
Mason is the archetypical "too cool to care but warms up to you" character. She's a woman of few words and says only what she feels necessary. She's serious looking and quite androgynous in style, much like the main character. Mason is the chef at A Cat's Paw and is an extremely talented cook.
Landry is your typical "nice guy" character, full of smiles and fun to be around. He's a tall guy who's good at woodwork, and he puts this to use for the cats by building toys and towers for them in the cafe.
Hayes is a quiet cutie who isn't very good at social interaction. Much like Mason (but for different reasons), it takes a while for him to warm up to Avery. He is the cafe's barista and is an expert at making coffee. He can often be found working in the kitchen alongside Mason. Hayes' character design lends itself well to his shy personality.
Reese is a typical wannabe cool guy who acts tough on Avery. He swans about like he's in charge which works surprisingly well with the workplace dynamic between the characters. But, he's a sweetheart underneath his overconfident demeanor. Reese is the assistant manager of A Cat's Paw and is always up to date with fashion.
FINLEY. Wow. Okay. So, I played Finley's route last out of Avery's five work mates. Why? Because I didn't like her. In a lot of cases she's nosy, over the top and obnoxious. But when I played her route, she became my favourite character. She's fantastic.
So, as you can see from the very start of the game, Finley is quite the meme queen. She's the fashionable girl in charge of social media for A Cat's Paw. She's bubbly and fun to be around, even if she does meddle in other people's business.
The boss himself. An old-style-gothic gentleman who looks a little bit like a vampire. He's quite estranged and seems like a hard person to figure out. He's quite full of bravado and the fact that he quotes people like Poe just makes him a great character. His own cat, Dracula, is a nice addition to the story too.
All in all, I highly recommend Hustle Cat to fans of visual novels. All I'd say it's missing is an unanswered, "food for thought" question that a lot of high quality visual novels have, but honestly the story is so good that it doesn't really need it. There are a few mysteries to work out, though.

I purchased this game after I had already watched some of the routes on Dodger's and Octopimp's playthrough of the game, so I already kinda knew what this game was about. And while normally that would ruin the gmae for some or make it far less enjoyable, this game was still super fun to play.
Now I have a played a lot of otome games (serriously like those companies have way too much of my money), so I'm not going to say that this game is particulary revolutionary in the visual novel genre. However, I does have some diffenreces that I thought made the whole experience much more enjoyable to the player. The first major distinction that I noticed was that there are no "good", "normal", or "bad" ends for each path. After you achive reaching your love interests route in the beginning, you no longer have to make any choices on what you should say or do in a certain situtation. The game simply plays out just like you were reading a book. Thus it leaves the player with only one ending to the path, which is always a good one. Some may agrue that this aspect delibertyly removes player interaction and thus makes the whole experience much more boring. And while I agree that it does infact place the player in more of an observiotory role, it is actually an improvement. One of the things that stresses me out the most when playing a route is whether or not I am going to get that "good" ending. "Should I say this?" "Is this the right thing to do?" "Does this read as sarcastic or is this going to screw me over in the long run?" Eventually I just have to break down and look at a walkthrough to make sure I don't royally screw up. Then there is extra added effort of having to play through the exact same story line again with only a few small changes to the dialouge because you chose to wear red to the party instead of blue or some other bull crap like that. And for what? A few extra CGs? By eliminating that option it gets rid of all that stress and allows the palyer to stay fully emersed in the game and just enjoy watching what happens.
The second distinction that I saw in the game is that some of characters weren't so tropey. I say SOME because of certain characters (looking at you Landry and Finnely). As many experience dating sim players would know, there are six, maybe seven personality types that get reused over and over and over agian in games to point to where you can resonably preict how a certain characters path is going to end before ever playing the route. But with characters like Reese and Mason, the player is left intrested and guessing. Reese is a little brat and remains that way until the end, but there are unexpected sad moments and embarassments and other things that would normally seem outside of his character troupe (at least from what games I have played). And as for Mason, she isn't the normal strong woman type. She ofcourse remains completely stoic while also remaining completely femine. Sure she isn't the standard definiton of girly girly, but there are some sweet moments with Mason in where her feminie charm really does shine. These vartions are really enjoyable and keeps the characters fresh for players who frenquetly purchase titles in this genre.
Finally I would say that MC is not annoying! Like serriously so many games these days make MC's that are either stupid or annoying or both. But Avery Gray is super intresting with a personality of his/her/their own. Avery is nerdy. Avery is lazy. Avery has no understanding of what the word clean is. And best of all, Avery is a huge dork. All of these qualities make Avery Gray feel like an actual person and somebody that you could relate to. Even if Avery's personality isn't your own, you can probably think of somebody you know who behaves like this. He/she/they aren't some bland, boring, cardboard like personality meant to be be so generic that any player can relate to but not really because nobody actually acts like this. So having Avery being a real person is highly refreshing and much more entertaing.
Overall, I would highly recomend a play through of this game. you won't regret it.

"Hustle Cat" is a true gem among visual novels, that are currently available on Steam. I absolutely adore this game. That being said, if you are interested in buying it, there are two things you need to consider. First of all, it's short. When you look at my playtime (add 1 or 2 hours for offline), you should know, that it took me that little to finish the WHOLE game (all six routes). Another thing is that decisions have very slight impact on the game, they are pretty much limited to choosing the character you will end up with. And while each route presents new scenes with your "chosen one", the overall storyline remains the same, no matter who will you pick. I write about it here, because even though, usually, I considered things like that a flaw, that didn't bother me at all with this game.
It's light-hearted for the most part, but besides humor and warm atmosphere, it has intrigue, danger, it has stakes, it has tension and mystery, so everything you could expect from a game like this. Plus, writing is great.
Avery (name, for same reason, isn't changeable) is very relatable protagonist. They are adorably awkward at times, sweet, caring and smart. Also, I like how you can chose your pronounces (He/She/They). I think more visual novels should implement system like this, to give their players flexibility when it comes to romance options.
They look different from each other and they behave in a different way. They are not cliche and each of them has an interesting story. I liked every single one pursuable character. Graves and Mason are definietely my favorite. If I would have to pick my least favorite, that would be Finley - I like her as a character, but her route felt waaaay over the top and I didn't enjoy her ending. Still, all routes are worth exploring.
I'm not very sentimental person. I don't cry on "Titanic" and I don't really care about "The Notebook" and other tear-squezers, so when game is able to make me tear up a bit, that game does something right.
I love the fact, that this game doesn't take itself completely seriously and, with full awareness, often reminds players that "magic is weird, huh!". At the same time, I really appreciate those little details, that are thrown on various routes and explain more about how magic work in this game-world.
Dear God. Scrolling? Seriously? It still takes way too long and you can skip over seen text, which is annoying. There is also a skip button. That skips everything so slowly, that you can literally step away from your computer and make yourself something to drink. Oh, but when you come back, you may also realize, it skipped over not-seen text. This is a basic function for visual novel these days, so it's almost baffling to see how bad it was implemented.
Option menu has like four functions. No speed regulation, no skipping options, nothing of importance to someone, who doesn't want to regulate music.
First of all, there are moments, when you need to click several times before the dialogue moves on (and I'm not talking about those moments, where dialogue is still added to the same box). Then, saving either goes smoothly and takes a second or the game will freeze for a good few minutes. At one of those time, I needed to Ctrl+F4 my way out of it and restart my laptop soon after, because game was still running at the background and slowed everything so much, that I was unable to close it even via Process Monitor. Then, if that wasn't enough, there are issues with achievements. I needed to go through one scene like four times before Steam registered that I actually did what I suppose to do.
It may seem unreasonable to complain about optional feature, but I feel like there is a reason to do it in that case. When you start the game, you can chose between two very similar avatars. Both are rather boy-ish looking, both have white hair and the same eye color. The only variations comes from skin colors. Picking between how my character looks did absolutely nothing to make the game more enjoyable or immersive. I would much rather have an option to change my character's name (it's very strange that this wasn't implemented), than having this slight, barely noticeable difference between protagonist's look. I'm bringing this up, because I feel like this had an impact on price. And that lead me to the next point.
When I truly enjoy something, I usually try to avoid judging price as "too high", but in this case, it would be hard to avoid and dishonest. I like this game a lot, but my playtime, technical difficulties, similarities between the routes and general lack of content (especially when I compare this game to other visual novels in the same price-range), makes it hard to justify selling "Hustle Cat" for 20€. I've picked it up for half the price and I recommend you to do the same, if you don't want to feel disappointed.

This is the story of a young man who though he could fool evryone and ended up the fool himself. It's a fairly short game, broken up into four distinct acts. There's narration to the static cutscenes and music which doesn't get too monotonous.
Beyond that, there isn't much to say about The Fool. It's pretty standard fare, with simple puzzles and occasional hidden object scenes that have just enough difficulty to make them interesting. This is a really difficult review as there are a lot of ups and downs in this game.
The main plot is not original but the little sub-areas are extremely varied; there was not, however, a lot of fleshing out done in each area and it left me wanting to know a little more about each place.
Voice acting is limited to the narrator and that was well done.  Music and sounds were decent.
Graphically not stellar but certainly passable; hidden object scenes were clear and there was no pixel-hunting or looking for badly-labeled items ("is that blob a football, or is THAT blob a football?" isn't an issue in this game),
Some of the puzzle solutions were downright silly, but I think that's actually what the game was going for.  I'm not thinking that they're taking themselves too seriously here so it's pretty important that players suspend disbelief too.  The solutions do make sense, they're just sometimes... well, silly.  Like I said.
As the tags clearly state, this is a hidden-object/casual puzzle game, not a full-fledged adventure game.  Make sure you read what you're buying before you buy it and are disappointed.
The worst thing the game has going for it, honestly, is length.  Since most of the puzzles aren't grossly difficult, I pretty much plowed right through in about two and a half hours.  This makes the $9.99 cost WAY too expensive for what you're getting.  I would not get this if not on sale.
So in the end, I am going to recommend this as a short, silly HO/puzzler AS LONG AS IT'S ON SALE - there are plenty of better games out there if you're going to pay full price.  But it's by no means godawfully bad, and worth wasting a couple bored hours with.

Let me start by saying it sucks that people have been having so much trouble with the stability of this game. Personally, I haven't had any problems with it crashing (knock on wood), but I have experienced some of the graphical hiccups with low frame rates and screen tearing.
Those problems aside, it is a blast to play. I've always liked the Dead Rising series and zombie games in general, but the constant time limit in the other games took away some of the enjoyment for me. I'm a completionist, and I felt like I couldn't see everything and save everyone in the other games. I know the point was probably to teach you that you can't save everybody, but I'm stubborn. I want to explore everything and take in the sights. I feel like I can do that in this game. You're still on the clock, but it's less pressing. I can seek out collectibles and screw around in Los Perdidos and still find time to do the story and side missions. Call me a filthy casual if you must, but when I come home after a stressful day at work, I play games like this for catharsis. I don't need more stressful deadlines to meet.
The gameplay is familiar to anyone who has played the other Dead Rising games. Both leveling up and the menu interface are a little different, but it's easy to get used to them. It recommends using a controller, but I did fine with a mouse and keyboard.
As I mentioned earlier, it has a few visual bugs. Hopefully, those will get patched in future updates. It's definitely an improvement over Dead Rising 1 and 2. The amount of zombies they can cram on screen is staggering. There's nothing more satisfying than plowing through hordes of the undead with your crazy weapon or vehicle of choice.
I won't say much about the story because I'm not that far into it yet (I've restarted a few times to keep leveling up). From what I've experienced, the tone switches from dark and depressing (it is a zombie apocalypse after all) to quirky weirdness. I personally like its style, though it could be oddly jarring to a newcomer. The plot seems pretty standard, though I'll see if that changes if I can break away from just slaughtering everything that shambles.
If you're fortunate enough to get through it without crashing and the few visual bugs don't bother you too much, Dead Rising 3 is a fun addition to anyone's zombie game library.

TL;DR This game is gold. Cheap gold, at that.
It’s a delightfully simple platformer that is much more of a “puzzle platformer,” if such a thing exists. The game mechanics are very simple and the controls are nicely tight.
The game mechanics involve avoiding various obstacles (the usual, lava, monsters, projectiles, although there are very little and it’s more trying to get around the level than dodge), and using your Teleport Gun which may or may not have been stolen directly out of Portal or something – I don’t know, as I haven’t played Portal. Whatever its origins, it’s quite an interesting mechanic as it conserves speed, meaning that if you have enough space (and are required to do this twice) you can climb up an entire screen.
The game has nicely low quantities of threats, focusing far more on actually getting to the next stage – especially as you only get something that can actually kill mobs mid-game (and if you head back to that screen, they respawn) You can afford to misjudge a jump or a teleport and nothing bad will happen, really – there’s checkpoints on most levels, and when there isn’t it’s usually because there was a checkpoint at the end of the previous one (“level” is an odd word to use, “screens” is much better).
Surprisingly, the game does not through absurdly large quantities of obscure once-use-only bricks at you that you see in two levels and then never again. The only example is the “Mirror” block, which reflects your teleport bullet horizontally; this appears in three levels and then is completely forgotten about; rather amusingly it’s possible to complete those three levels without using the mirrors anyway.
There’s two other unwritten rules of platformers this game breaks:
- The final boss has only two, not three phases (three is a magical number in video games)
- There is no screen whereby “Jump over the lava pits” / “Jump repeatedly onto platforms”
Speaking of bonus sections, despite being a rather memorable platformer whereby the main challenge is routing, meaning it’s much easier the second time, the game has surprisingly large replay value (for a simple platformer). It took me an hour and a bit to beat the game the first time, but I continued to complete it about five more times (and a good deal of that was in Offline Mode, so that’s why the playtime is so low). The game has this high replay value thanks to a large quantity of bonus sections (on your first playthrough you probably won’t go through about 1/3 of all the screens), which are accessible from the get-go but you haven’t learned the ins and outs of the teleport gun yet. And because the game knows that it’s going to be easy and a bit of a slog, it makes the game easier for you – these bonus sections contain three types of useful stuff. It’s also got interesting, not grinding, achievements which is always something worth noting – and also ones that you probably won’t unlock by accident whilst merely idling through. Most achievements are either “Grind grind grind” (e.g. AOE2’s “Win as Civ X 1000 times for EVERY SINGLE CIVILIZATION (about twenty of them) or “Play the game” (e.g. Terraria’s “Chop a tree! Make an anvil! Find a chest!), and it’s nice to see some achievements that you not so much have to actively think about getting – it’s more they don’t happen by accident. If you explore lots you’re bound to get a good deal of them.
This is also the only game whereby I have been able to stunlock the boss thanks to some exploits in the boss AI, as well as fire more bullets than the final boss does – however, this requires intensive exploration. When you fight the first phase of the boss, despite only having one life his attacks are easy to dodge when you know how (although I spent a solid seven minutes dying repeatedly until learning how to dodge) – when you have four and a machine gun it does become a bit of a joke. Still, it is a lighthearted final boss in line with the light difficulty of the rest of the platformer. It’s more puzzle than run ‘n’ gun, although not much “running” happens anyway.
The difficulty curve is very nice, probably slightly too slow – but the game is very lighthearted and not meant to be insanely difficult. The game gives you a decently large quantity of hints in the game on tips of your teleport gun, but not enough to be an insta-win and also low enough to keep me occupied on a single screen for about ten minutes before finally working out what to do.
Progression is extremely linear with the exception of about three cases, which is a bit odd as this game would have lent itself to a multi-route system extremely well.

Oh, and the game has precious little plot, enough to give you information on what’s going on but nothing particularly huge – but unlike some platformers, it doesn’t throw you into wacko things that should never have existed (why are there so many homing rockets and landmines in some icy mountains? To start this off, I need to say that I would have gone with a neutral option if it existed. That being said, the game is what it appears to be, a free to play game with some freemium elements added. I use this description because I think the developers meant the game to be played like a freemium game, but the game play does not require the pay to play aspects to get “enjoyment” out of the game play. And there is the key about this game, it provides “enjoyment” in the same way that, as a kid if an adult was give you a speech while you were sitting in a grassy area you would start pulling up the grass because it’s more enjoyable than doing nothing at all.
Gameplay:  The game play consists of clicking the screen in a given location to move bars, you can then spend the in-game currency generated by these repeated clicks to gain “managers” which do the game play element of clicking for you. The managers allow you to click other areas that increase the rate at which the managers provide you with the in-game currency, which you then use to open up more areas of the screen to click and then purchase more managers… rinse and repeat. That’s the gameplay. There is a bit more as you advance, where you actually start from scratch with a multiplier that makes the process go faster on successive play-throughs, but that’s it.
So then, if you enjoy this style of non-game game, then this will eventually provide you with steam achievements, and by eventually I mean many of the achievements are locked so that it requires multiple weeks of play-through to gain the achievements. The reason I’m recommending (remember I’d prefer to choose neither) is because the game progresses without you even needing to have your PC on, so you can turn this game off and go play a real game as you slowly earn steam achievements. And that is the appeal of this game… “free” (depends on if you consider your time valuable) steam achievements.
Final Thoughts: I don’t really have anything else to add on this game, it’s pretty straight forward, if you have some free time and you need something to kill it with, this is a free option, although there are probably better free options out there for you.

I downright LOVE this controller. I began my foray into next gen gaming with my pc, so naturally I got used to playing games with my mouse and keyboard / key profiler. While this is all well and good, I began to long for the familiarity of a handheld controller so I could give my back a break from being hunched over a keyboard for hours at a time. I wanted a quality piece of hardware, so, natuarally, I then purchased a wired XBox 360 controller for use on my pc.
As soon as I began playing games, especially FPS, I noticed how much less precise my control of the games was. While the gamepad was fine for platformers and RPGs, chasing targets in games like Far Cry 3 and Titanfall became a chore. Even with aim assist, the gamepad just can't compete with the mouse and keyboard for straight-up precision.
Then I heard about this little beauty, and, like any pc user with has a brain, I was skeptical. The thought of combining trackpads with a good, old-fashioned gamepad intrigued me, but innovations like this usually don't work out well on the first try. After reading early reviews I broke down and purchased the Steam Controller. This had been hands down the best decision I have made as far purchasing a gamepad. There are still some bugs to work out, but all-in-all this controller lives up to the hype.
Pros:
- FULLY customizable like a key-profiler (Works well for games that aren't designed for contollers)
- Super sensitive trackpads respond extremely well to touch, and are MUCH more precise than using a joystick.
- Haptic feedback for every button can be adjusted for intensity or turned off completely.
- Community profiles are available from other gamers for nearly every game.
- Multiple profiles can be saved for each game.
- Support is being added for non steam games (Way to not be selfish guys!)
Cons:
- Contruction initially feels a little on the cheap side (no actual issues yet though)
- Positioning of the buttons can feel awkward at first, as they are farther away from the thumb than on most other pads.
- Trackpads aren't quite as precise as a mouse.
There are tons of other features that I haven't even mentioned, and it's still being updated frequently. Steam is really taking the time to listen to the gamers as well. Bottom line, this controller won't replace your mouse for competitive games like CS:GO or other shooters, but for co-op and single player gaming, not to mention couch gaming, You just can't beat this thing. You couldn't pay me to switch back.

Splinter cell: Double agent. Oh boy, talk about missed potential. I heard some bad things about the PC port before, which is why i never bought it, i got the game when it was included in a bundle with the older Splinter Cell titles + Conviction, which i wanted to replay and i thought why not play them all. After all, how bad can it be. Oh was i wrong, theres plenty of wrong with it. The game itself would be good, but its ruined mostly by the god awful PC port, if that wasnt enough, there is several things wrong with developement decissions about the overall gameplay too.
Lets start with whats done well with Double agent:
- To this day, Double agent would be the only Splinter Cell game with somekind of replayability (other then playing on harder difficoulty), there are multiple endings and a bunch of big choices in the story.
- The missions here are diverse, actually well done, with enough variety in locations, objectives and most of all, they dont repeat themselves. Only downside here is that the number of missions is pretty small.
- Characters are way better, more memorable, better voice acted.
- The consept of double agent is pretty good, you have trust meters for both the terrorist agency you have infiltrated and the NSA, each mission, and the "sub area" between main missions has objectives, some of them non mandatory ones, which will raise the trust with one organization if completed, or lower the trust with another one. Also stuff like killing civilians factors into play here.
And then, the long list of negative...
First the obvious quality of the PC port, its not totally unplayable like some ports but it has A LOT wrong with it.
- First thing that caught my eye was that the game is limited into 1440x900 resolution, thats the maximum from ingame settings, which makes the game awful to look at, almost like looking it through a small fish eye lense, luckily the game can be forced into 1920x1080 with few minutes of config game files editing.
- And then the Bugs, i encountered a lot of them, smaller and the more frequent ones like object and graphics glitching, audio bugs like guns not making any sound when fired, doors not working correctly, getting stuck on objects multiple times, safe cracking system only working when it bloody wants to. The list is endless and i had some bigger issues like few crashes and objectives not completing even if during the mission i get a notification saying it is completed.
- I think graphically, Double agent is a downgrade from its predecessor Chaos theory.
- luckily they didnt absolutely ♥♥♥♥ up the controls, they are mostly how Splinter Cell controls always were, but few things suffer with the port, the maps screen while beign more usefull then ever, is absolutely horrendous to navigate with mouse and keyboard, the same goes for equipment switching.
So, thats all the problems with the actual port, now, even if the port was working perfectly, theres still great many things wrong here:
- The gameplay mechanics are painfully simplified, some techniques are completelly gone, like how you could jump agains a wall and bounce into another direction mid-jump is just gone, visibility and noise meters are gone, so you are just guessing how well you are hidden or how much sound you make. They removed the HP bar completelly, so you basically have 3 stages: alive, wounded or dead, and you regain health from that wounded state, in a matter of few seconds, which means you can survive an infinite ammount of near fatal falls without having to use a medpack in between, it also means that you wont have to think about how much health you have left if you need to get into a firefight.
- Even tho the actual controlls are almost 100% like they were in earlier titles, the game lacks that "tight" feeling with controlling the character, many a times was i doing actions i didnt mean to, slipping away from covers etc. Its a bit hard to explain this.
- Less humour. Theres some of it still there, but less.
so all in all. its pretty bad.
And i did give it a fair shot of proving me wrong, i enjoyed the xbox 360 version i had years ago, when i started this one, i felt that it was not so bad, but as the hours went by, the more i played the more i grew to dislike many things about it. It would be a decent game if the port was done right, but even if that was the case, theres a bunch of stuff wrong here.
PS: Steam stores schreenshots are from the original version of the game, not the "next gen" remaster.

Since the release of the third part of Splinter Cell, which is highly praised by Chaos Theory players, it has been almost 20 months. That's a lot, especially considering the fact that previous releases of this series appeared at annual intervals. You may wonder how these extra months have been decided, and whether the changes you have made can actually be described as revolutionary (for the whole series, not for the "stealth" genre). The Double Agent has been announced as a product from the beginning of its existence, which should significantly differentiate itself from its predecessors. This was due, among other things, to the choices we made, often difficult. After several hours spent with the final version of the game I can say that some changes actually make quite radical impression. But the question arises - are the enthusiastic supporters of previous parts of the game these modifications will come to the taste? An unambiguous answer could not be given without proper preparation. You have to look at all the most important elements of this game.The story of the Double Agent was much talked about before the official release. So I think it would be best if I recall only a few of the most important facts. The two initial levels of the game being reviewed have been constructed in a very typical way for such skill. In the first mission we are dealing with a relatively well-developed prologue, thanks to which we can "remind" ourselves which types of behaviors this series was mostly associated with. So we have a suit for our hero (with mandatory goggles), clearly set goals, and a whole bunch of gadgets, which would be worth the right time to use. All this changes very quickly. Fisher learns about the tragic death of his daughter, and the story itself skips a few months ahead.The main character of the series lands in an urgent guarded prison. Fisher is trying to contact the members of the John Brown's terrorist organization, becoming the title double agent. I will discuss this in a few moments. Now I would rather stay on issues related to the storyline. In my opinion this element of the game has been treated a bit after the man. After a great initial stages, the plot is clearly pushed to the background. The lack of a proper briefing can be annoying, so you can learn more about your tasks, or the negligible contact with the NSA and the well-known lovers of the Lambert series. We also made interstitial scenes very rarely, something we rarely find interesting. The presence of members of the terrorist organization mentioned earlier, which we have the opportunity to get to know more clearly, is a plus. This is especially noticeable when playing levels at the John Brown's Army base.As I mentioned, one of the main strengths of the peer review should be the election. These were due to the role of a double agent trying to reconcile the interests of the government agency he continues to work with and the terrorist group, very suspicious of the new members. Admittedly, in this regard Double Agent definitely did not disappoint, although some things could be given in more interesting form. It would have been right at the outset to point out that the objectives of the mission were divided into five different groups. Recognizing the specifics of most orders we should not have any problems. So there are mandatory tasks that need to be done to complete the mission, as well as secondary goals that can be completely ignored. There are also challenges that focus on the need to find specific documents or to get samples of the voice of selected people.
However, the goals that require us to make a choice are most interesting. It is a pity that they are relatively small during the game. It is worth adding that most of the choices can be reflected in our relations with each of the factions. This also affects the appearance of subsequent levels of the campaign or the end of the campaign itself. It may be that the rescued agent will have to liberate and then safely lead to the evacuation site. Returning to the remaining jobs for a while, each task presented is assigned to one of the two major factions (NSA or JBA). You can also see the satisfaction level bars in both organizations. All this was solved in a very simple, yet well thought out way. While performing the task, we can increase the satisfaction of one of the fractions. It is also sometimes possible that we lose trust among members of the other organization. This can also be the case when the order is being drawn out too much. As a result, you have to be very careful. Satisfaction straps are one hundred percent effective only on the highest difficulty level. On Easy and Normal levels, you do not have to worry about it, assuming, of course, that we will try to do most of the tasks assigned to us.It's probably time to say a little more about the proper gameplay. I want to calm down those fans of the series who feared that the Double Agent could turn into a full-fledged action game. We are still dealing with a sneak peek. Actually, while playing some stages (especially the final ones) you can (or even need) to afford more, but this kind of action does not usually take too long. The only exceptions are the levels played in the headquarters of the JBA. We must count on the time limit in which we should fit. You can not afford to look very closely at the environment, often risking your position. The main character moves in a well-known way by performing very similar sets of activities. With such obvious issues as choosing the speed of movement I do not even have to mention. Suffice it to say that the vast majority of the shares of the previous series, moved in unchanged or slightly modified (improved) form.There are a few other things that I would like to mention. Completely abandoned the detailed interface, which some fans of the series may not come to your liking. In particular, I mean here an option to determine the degree of discovery of a controlled character. The Double Agent employs a poorly designed mechanism that operates on three different colors. The green color means that we are in an unlit place, and as a result we are practically invisible to our opponents (they would have fallen on us). Yellow color appears most often when we are walking through brighter corridors and rooms. Enemies can notice us, so we need to use different curtains and watch their moves. The red color is, of course, tantamount to an alarm. The health bar was also removed, using a similar mechanism for the second part of Call of Duty. There is nothing to complain about, since the completion of the game without triggering the alarm does not cause any problems.It would be worth saying a bit more about the opponents. Their SI presents unfortunately unequal performance level. In most situations enemies are quite clever, noting that leaving the door open or turning off or destroying the light source. But it also happens that they let themselves go without any problems, and at the sight of our characters or bodies of their colleagues in no way react. It is easy to use two different maps, including three-dimensional. They allow you to easily locate more enemies or places to go to.
During play we can use the whole mass of more or less useful gadgets. It is worth pointing out that when playing on the highest level of difficulty we have to count on many limitations in terms of allocated equipment. This is a nod to the more advanced players. For new items, you should pay special attention to Ultrasonic Emitter. This device produces the specified sound, in addition to the selected location (the same as the classic giver). I do not have to say more about the applications. To say that this is a very useful device, especially if you plan to go through the next board without having to eliminate or stunning the opponents. Short version: It is good, but doesn't replace mouse and keyboard, or the contoller.  It is a great third option to play games with.  It is my go to for some games, but not all.  Also, not plug and play.  It takes a lot of tinkering to get used to and get the best performance.
TL:DR
Well, the first 3 hours of using this controller, the only thought in my head was "I'm sending this back".  However, something happened after that 3rd hour, I got used to it.  All of a sudden it just clicked.  I've been using it since.  I will say that I feel that the marketing is completely off.  It is nowhere near a plug and play.  Every game I play, I go into the settings and change the controls and sensitivity to play that game.  You can save your controller set ups which is great, along with looking at the communities, and the developers recommendations (if they made any, probably not).
Does it replace my Xbox 360 controller I've been using for years?  For some games yes.  For others no.
Does it replace my mouse and keyboard?  For some games yes. For others no.
It does provide a great third option.
I also game on a surface pro 3.  The biggest issue I had with it is using that keyboard and mouse to play games.  I would only download and play games that either supported a gamepad, or mouse only (like 4X games).  Now with this controller, I've been playing some FPS that had no native gamepad support on my surface pro.  Is it as good as KBM, no.  But for gaming on the go playing some classic FPSs with a gamepad, it is great.
The feedback you get on the touchpads is great.  The track ball feeling really comes through.  It has got me thinking I might even want to try and trackball one day...maybe...anyways, its a feeling you need to try to fully understand.  Its nothing like touch screen phones/tablets.  You actually get physical feedback from the touchpads.
The greatest feature I have been using is the Gyroscope.  I usually assign it to the right touch pad, that way if I want to go from touchpad to the more accurate Gyro, all I do is click.  The gyro is really good, but takes some getting used to.  But again, it is fully adjustable with its sensitivity.
The last thing I wanted to touch on was the buttons on the handles.  Before the controller, I didn't know if I'd like them.  Well I do.  Assign reload to the left one, and reloading just comes natural without having to take your finger off the touch pad.  They are in a great position and feel natural.  One thing I noticed, one of them stopped clicking and felt soft.  What happened is the battery got loose and was pushing against the button.  I pushed it back into place, and it clicked like normal.  FYI.
Overall, great controller.  I've really enjoyed it, but it does take alot of getting used to.  It took me about 3-4 hours to get used to the controller.  Even now I am still getting my muscle memory down with the new setup.  I like what they did with it, but please give it a good honest chance before you make your decision.  I was dead set on sending it back, but I stuck with it and have really enjoyed it since.
Thanks for reading my rant.

As a fan of the franchise it is with some sadness that I give this title a thumbs down. I played the game in reverse order (4, 3 and now 2), so I was expecting a solid Linux port. 3 and 4 run smooth, 3 rarely crashed and I think 4 only crashed once or twice. SR2 was a bit of a dissapointment. (Like always, my reviews are about the Linux port for other Linux users to consider)
Gameplay looks like it's fun! Just like the later titles in the franchise, this game has a wonderful narrative and fun open world feel to it. The activities (side quests) are more fun (and challenging) than in SR3 and SR4 and they are related to the actual game you're playing. Street racing, hijackings, etc. Good times, right? Nope.
All of it's favourable points are ruined by low frame rate (between 15 and 40 on the lowest settings, compared to SR4 that ran 40-60 on the highest) and there is a 200-500ms lag spike occurring every 5-10s that makes controlling vehicles really difficult. If you're on Linux (may be a problem on Windows too, dunno) and you're new to the Saints Row franchise, skip this one and just get 3 and 4.

The Secret Of Monkey Island holds a dear place in mine and many gamers hearts. My first play through of the game happened in 1998, when I picked up a copy of the "Monkey Island Madness" CD as part of a lucasarts anthology at a local cd and movie shop. I spent countless hours playing and enjoying the unique story and challenging puzzles. I have to admit I fall into the "hardcore fan" category for this series and take it quite seriously. As such it took me a very long time to come around and actually finish playing this special edition.
My first play through had me cursing the controls, hating the new shiny graphics (I know, I know you can switch to the old style), and being unsure of many of the voiceover choices. Dominic Armato returns to voice Guybrush as he has done for every Monkey Island since Curse, which is great because he fits the character amazingly. That is about where my praise stops for the voice actors however. Many of the characters made me cringe because of their bad interpretations of the dialogue. One of the things about 'SOMI' that made it so great was the amazing humour and fantastic character writing. Much of that charm and emotion did not translate well to voice actors (again, I praise Dominic for doing an amazing job despite the other actors). I found myself playing without voices for any cutscenes heavy on the dialogue.
Next I must address the art. Which perhaps I have the most to gripe about (until we reach controls). The original SOMI is a GORGEOUS game, and the included "classic" gameplay showcases just how well the game has held up despite limiting tech when it was created. The carefully utilized colors and pixelated characters retain a charm that is hard to find in most modern games. The characters look terrible in the new art style, though none took as harsh of a beating as guybrush himself. Guybrush was given the neck of an irritated girrafe and the hair of a bad anime character that literally defies gravity. Much of the cutscene conversation interactions are more cartoony looking, and lack a gritty reach for realism that it felt like the original game tried to achieve. The characters lost much of their appeal and had it replaced with cartoon imitations in this new art style. Now before you accuse me of rampant fanboyism, I DO think that the special editon artwork has some charm despite it's faults.
So what's positive about the new art? Many of the backgrounds are fantastic! Melee Island in particular benefitted greatly from this update and if not for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ character design, I would have found the ambience damn near flawless. I was excited to go places I knew very well and see how they now looked. If there is one thing I LOVED about this special edition it was most certainly those gorgeous painted enviroments. Kudos to the art team for that.
All of this was nitpicking however, and the true reason that despite my love for the series I had to not reccomend this game is that it's controls are simply not well suited for many of the puzzles. There is one puzzle in particular
that was literally impossible to do quick enough in the new control scheme. It felt like they wanted to simplify the system to leave the original action menu hidden, but it just ended up being confusing and hard to use, severely detracting from the experience. I was often switching back to the classic gameplay just to finish things quickly and easily without fumbling through the controls.
Am I glad this was released? Hell yes, this series deserves more fans, and more people getting to enjoy it. And I acknowledge that my review will likely not be the typical experience as the special edition of this game is highly recieved by many many critics. If nothing else, I am happy to have a fully updated version of the classic game packaged with this so I do not have to bother with scumm or dosbox whenever I am feeling nostalgic. I promise my review (coming soon) of Lechuck's Revenge SE, is much more positive than this one (because its a much better update than this was).

My one issue is that they don't offer the expansion pack which includes a whole other campain and some extra functions that help make the gameplay a little easier. I would love it if steam added the expansion. I do admit the gameplay is a bit linear, but overall the environments that they create and the ways they manage to blend them together with no loading screens is amazing.
No multiplayer?!?!?!?!?! WHAAAAAAAAT!!!!    Big let down....

Do I recommend this game? To most people, yes. To some people who only favor the new generation of video games... Not so much.
Dungeon Siege is mainly a game you would play for nostalgia; or if you're just a fan of mysterious, old school RPGs that don't hold your hand or if you're just a RPG collector in the first place, and seek a new game to add to your collection.
Since Dungeon Siege was the first game I ever played, my review may bare some bias: but hopefully, that shall not be the case.
Dungeon Siege MIGHT not have the most advanced combat system, but with the amount of interesting characters you can control (8 at maximum, if I'm correct) such as a dwarf, an archer, a alcoholic yet skilled warrior and even a half giant (in the expansion pack!) you can create a team of adventurers with all kinds of strategy and you can find and loot all kinds of accoutrement to independantly equip each party member you are controlling.
The game may seem very linear at first but if you're willing to playthrough the game over one time you'll discover many secret locations and party members which you may not have discovered from the first playthrough, something special Dungeon Siege always captured me with was the mystery. SPOILER ALERT: In one area, you find extremely large (seemingly dragon) bones... Who knows what that was before it died? I suppose we'll never know.
You have three classes: Melee, Ranged or Magic. There are many spells, swords (or even clubs or hammers or axes) and bows (or crossbows in the expansion pack) to collect, and a large amount of armor to follow.
Not to mention the brilliant voice acting and enchanting sound effects which if you played Dungeon Siege awhile ago shall capture your heart with nostalgia.
Dungeon Siege is overall an AMAZING game. The first playthrough you will find incredible since you won't know what to expect, then there's always the expansion. The only complaints I have is that the multiplayer is disabled, I wish there were more party members and it wasn't as linear (The secret locations and party members does get slightly limited, there are many side quests though too!)
The final verdict for Dungeon Siege is... A 8 out of 10. The game is incredible (a 10/10 for the first playthrough) but there are a few flaws that could keep someone from playing.
Until the next review, seeya!

Hustle cat is such a great well written game!  The story is better than I expect from most Otomes, the characters were varied and believable.  Each romancable option have their own plot, while there is an overlying plot that is there through all the characters.  Once you've completed all of them, it unlocks a final character whose story ties up the larger overlying plot.  I haven't finished yet but so far I'm very happy with it!  I've had otome games where I just push myself to complete characters I don't care for just for completionism's sake, but with this I'm excited to read and experience every character's story.
The main character, Avery, is slightly customizable with their appearance (Skin color can change, and you can choose between short or long hair) and you can designate pronouns.  It's nice, and I appreciate having a gender neutral character. Due to this design decision, Avery is going to feel pretty gender neutral regardless of your appearance or pronoun decisions.  I don't know if I'm phrasing this right, but you don't get to choose between playing as a guy or a girl or a gender neutral character, you just play as Avery, and get to choose their pronouns.  I bring this up because personally I like playing as a girl, but I don't really view Avery as a girl, or as a guy, regardless of what pronouns I give them.  That being said, I really did enjoy Avery's character, and they're one of my favorite main characters from a dating sim!
What I really REALLY appreciate SO MUCH from this game is honestly just being able to date guys or girls! I just! Don't get that from many games and I really enjoyed it!
My only downside for this game is that the actual  mechanics could be improved. I'd appreciate a skip button that actually skipped faster, and that didn't turn into "auto" when it got to parts you haven't seen yet.  This is just a little annoying when you have to play the first main part of the game with different choices for each character.  But as far as the actual game goes, I have no complaints!

To start this off, I need to say that I would have gone with a neutral option if it existed. That being said, the game is what it appears to be, a free to play game with some freemium elements added. I use this description because I think the developers meant the game to be played like a freemium game, but the game play does not require the pay to play aspects to get “enjoyment” out of the game play. And there is the key about this game, it provides “enjoyment” in the same way that, as a kid if an adult was give you a speech while you were sitting in a grassy area you would start pulling up the grass because it’s more enjoyable than doing nothing at all.
Gameplay:  The game play consists of clicking the screen in a given location to move bars, you can then spend the in-game currency generated by these repeated clicks to gain “managers” which do the game play element of clicking for you. The managers allow you to click other areas that increase the rate at which the managers provide you with the in-game currency, which you then use to open up more areas of the screen to click and then purchase more managers… rinse and repeat. That’s the gameplay. There is a bit more as you advance, where you actually start from scratch with a multiplier that makes the process go faster on successive play-throughs, but that’s it.
So then, if you enjoy this style of non-game game, then this will eventually provide you with steam achievements, and by eventually I mean many of the achievements are locked so that it requires multiple weeks of play-through to gain the achievements. The reason I’m recommending (remember I’d prefer to choose neither) is because the game progresses without you even needing to have your PC on, so you can turn this game off and go play a real game as you slowly earn steam achievements. And that is the appeal of this game… “free” (depends on if you consider your time valuable) steam achievements.
Final Thoughts: I don’t really have anything else to add on this game, it’s pretty straight forward, if you have some free time and you need something to kill it with, this is a free option, although there are probably better free options out there for you.

I originally did not recommend this game. However, after revisiting it months later, while the game has its problems it can be an enjoyable experience.
The game is a first person platformer with small puzzle elements. Progression is very linear, so your exploration is not "open world", but exploring the world.
The platforming is at times very unforgiving, where I would have wished for a more forgiving placement of platforms. Especially with the long death animation (/fall). Respawn points are ok, although in combination with unforgiving jumps a little frustrating (because of backtracking).
The unobtrusive music appearing at times is good, providing a nice atmosphere. The visual style is unique.
The game sometimes feels "slow", and aerial control is not very high. The glasses do obstruct the field of view quiet a bit, although this is probably a deliberate artistic choice.
So, this first person platformer lets you explore an interesting world in a linear manner with small puzzle elements. It can be enjoyable.

Just finished 100%ing Hustle Cat, and its pretty excellent. Its not like the next greatest VN of all time or anything, but♥♥♥♥♥♥at least its better than Katawa Shoujo.
The visual novel starts off by asking your gender and skintone, and you can choose from three pronouns, He She and They. Youre Avery Grey, a ♥♥♥♥in nerd who lives in their aunt’s house. You find a cat cafe with a HELP WANTED sign in the window and decide to stop in, immediately getting the job. Throwing caution to the wind, you spiral down into an adorable little adventure with 6 routes and 2 bad ends.
Not spoiling much here since you find this out in the first act, but there’s a curse over A Cat’s Paw, where anyone that works there eventually turns into a cat outside of it’s walls. Its up to you as Avery to find out why, and to break this curse over you and your co-workers. My favorite route was Mason’s, as she is waifu stronk and bae. and all those other dank maymay words for saying you really like someone’s character. Im a sucker for stories where you help someone break out of a shell, and her’s is really good considering she throws fridges at people.
The game does have some flaws, with the third act being incredibly predictable (big bad shows up, Avery cant do it, waifu/husbando shows up and scrungises him), and some very wooden characters (lookin right in your direction Landry), but the positives in the game outweigh the negatives. The cast is lovable and sweet (yes, even you Landry), the soundtrack is catchy, and the artwork is lovingly drawn.
It took me 9.3 hours to 100% complete Hustle Cat, but of course play times will vary when it comes to visual novels. As far as visual novels go, Id rate it at a solid 7/10, easily worth checking out.

Here's my bias upfront: I've been into Hustle Cat since I backed it on kickstarter ages ago. I'm still into it. I've replayed my favorite routes, watched Dodger and Octo's LP, and blatantly harassed friends to get the game too. I just love this game.
Avery is hilariously relatable to any person remotely in the same age range, and has a remarkably clear character voice that consistently makes the entire story more fun. And it's already fun to start! Your coworkers who Are Also Cats are all unique personalities that are highly romancable and generally endearing even as supporting characters in other routes. And of course, the option to choose your pronouns and character appearance is absolutely fantastic and incredibly conscientious of the developers, as is the opportunity to romance whomever you like without being restricted by your gender choices or theirs.
I don't think I can overstate how much I love this game.
My biggest complaint is only another point in its favor: I want more! The various character endings do feel a bit rushed after the length of buildup in the shared storyline, but really I'm just desperate for DLC. Please. I'm so attached to this world, I want to stay in it longer!
tl;dr this game is the good stuff and everyone should buy it.

Super, super cute game. I thought I'd only care about dating the boys, but the girls won me over too, haha! It's rather simple, not a deep or convoluted story to the extent that, say, a Japanese visual novel would be, but I got many hours of entertaining reading out of it. The art is mostly pretty, though sometimes proportions go wonky or the image is inconsistent with the text if you're picky about details and notice that kind of thing. Some CGs feel like they were drawn with a lot more care than others, too.
My only real complaint is that after you make it through the choices at the beginning to lock in a character's route, there are almost no more choices for the rest of the game (at least as far as your relationship with said character). You can't "bad end" by failing to properly support your choice in romance or anything like that. Once you have your partner, it's all just reading material until the story finale. I like the sense of accomplishment that comes from successfully navigating a VN to its good ends so this was a disappointment for me, but it's just a small blemish on an otherwise pleasant experience.
Wish Avery was a bit older, or didn't have a canon age, but that's only because of Graves' route.
I played in the order of Finley > Mason > Reese > Hayes > Landry > Graves and found this to be surprisingly ideal in terms of revealing deeper layers to the story and worldbuilding. This appears to match up with how easy each character was to 'lock in', as they are not equal opportunity in giving you chances to appeal to one character over the others. There's a definite dance of "only be nice to this character to lock them", which sucks when you want to be nice to everybody, but such are the trials of a VN~
There's holes in the story and a lot of questions left unanswered, but it's kind of nice to go away wondering and wanting to keep thinking about what I've played.

Considering how insignificant an impact buying this game will make on your wallet, and considering how much fun it is to play, there really isn't a reason not to buy it.
The game is fast-paced, challenging, and well-designed: all the makings of a great classic platformer. There isn't much of a story of course, but then with platformers, especially at this length (the game only takes about an hour to finish) there never really is. To make up for it however, the game elements are fantastically put together: everything feels so cleverly thought out, from the enemies, to the teleport gun, to the 80s space battle homage.

For a game I paid about $0.20 USD for, I got 75 minutes or so of fairly straightforward puzzle-platformer-with-teleport-gun gameplay.
Nothing stood out as exceptional but nothing was lackluster either, which is a plus really considering the price and what someone might expect from the saturated indie platformed genre.  I didnt feel like my time was wasted and I had some fun with it.  I dont particularly like chiptune / bit-aesthetic music. but it was pretty catchy and pleasant to listen to.  The NPC character sprites were also pretty well animated which is a good touch as well.
Some players I see complaining about the control scheme.  I could see it as a problem for some, but I'm used to a few similar games so I handled it pretty well.  I didn't test a controller but with the Steam Controller API I don't think it should be much of a problem if you want a custom mapping.
All in all, it was good!

Absolutely worst Splinter Cell game ever made. Don't waste your time or money on this one.
- No shadows. In a stealth game. Most of the time you have no way of knowing if which patch on the room is hidden and which is not. There's some fixes suggested for this but the one's I tried didn't seem to work. Or maybe they did and didn't make any difference, who knows.
- UI is too heavily simplified: Visibility meter is gone and is replaced with idiotic LED/Dot/whatever which simply shows that you're either hidden/not hidden/under attack. ALSO, no sound meter so no idea how much sound you're making.
- Grabbing enemies into the chockehold randomly doesn't seem to work.
- All of the Night Vision Goggles view modes, especially the basic night vision mode, are so unclear and almost painful to look at that they're completely useless. Because there's no shadows and everything is evenly lit, it's actually easier to see around without any of the goggles.
- Autosaves don't actually seem to save the game.
- Can't name manual saves and even though they're timestamped, they're in completely random order. Makes jumping back to a much earlier point in the game annoying guesswork.
- Loading saves has about 1/3 chance to crash the game.
- If it doesn't crash on save load, then it just randomly crashes whenever it feels like it.
- Sam gets constantly stuck on every corner in the game. Especially on furniture. Makes moving around pretty difficult when you need to constantly avoid touching any walls or furniture.
- The computer access UI is infuriatingly annoying. Once you Esc out from an email, you have to wait forever for the needlessly animated menu to properly load before you can press Esc again (twice) to exit the computer screen thing. If you're too quick and don't let the UI load, pressing Esc opens pause menu for some reason.
- Bunch of other annoying stuff I can't remember now.
It's a shame that this is such a horrible game. They really had some cool ideas on this one. The JBA Base missions are pretty cool: You have time limit in which you can choose to do a bunch of tasks for both, the JBA (terrorists) and NSA in whatever order you like. You can move around pretty freely, but some areas are restricted and you don't want to be caught snooping around there. These missions brought up very nice feeling of pressure and uncertainty and can really make the player feel like they're undercover. But that's pretty much the only positive thing in this game.
Final verdict: Avoid.

1) Controls: the movement is a bit weaird starting off, instead of your standerd WASD keys to move and the QE keys to strafe its QWE to move and AD to stafe I found it it a bit weird at first but got used to it quite fast, im not sure if you can change the key bindings but it wasnt too much of a bother, your attacks are quite basic as most mmo's, use the 1-8 keys to use diffrerent skills and there is an auto attack but its weak and doest do much, there are 2 more sets of hotbar keys by combinding the 1-8 keys with ALT or CTRL but i perfer right-clicking them, also you can fly (or glide I shoud say)
2) Quests: quests are as basic as they get, usually quite dry and straight forward, theres even the option to click your quests and your character will automaticly go towards it for you witch kinda takes away from the intensity (but thats just me), there are a few quests that let you take control of another character in the main story, witch is kinda cool, but its not too much and  you probley wont remember it too much as it is very basic, run towards here or like kill 2 guys or whatever, now there is a surplus of side quests, most are basic and casual.
3) Playerbase: very quiet and as most said theres a bot problem, as far as size goes, its ok I guess, you will run into people daily (at least I did), but i'll let you be the judge
4) Graphics and gameplay: I did add the 2 to the same category because I feel the 2 go hand-in-hand and heres why, the graphics are pretty good, a cutsy anime style and thats ok, It gets the job done but if the graphics are good and the gameplay sucks its a waste of effort, to me its gameplay over graphics, fortunately the gameplay is good, fast and rewarding, theres is a total of 12 playable classes and at level 40 you get to choose a secondary weapon giving the game high replayablity.
5) Overall: and finally we reach a overall, I did give this game a hard time but I fell you guys reading this need to know the whole truth, now is this game bad? no! its quite good actually and as angry joe said mmo's are about gamplay over everything else, now the devlopers are very quiet and there hasnt been an update since lord knows when I also wanna touch up on armor and weapons, armor isnt visable you need a costume to change the way you look, theres also other things like fishing that is like a minigame in of itself but it gets boring and you will probely resort to leaving him there for a few hours and let him do it himself, now is this PTW? no! and thank god too!
6) Endgame: theres quite a bit but mainly saidequests and a few doungons but at level 65 you get to do the sky temple, witch as rare loot but is quite hard and can only do it at key times of the day.
7) Verdict: and now we reach the end of my review, now i'm gonna give it a thumbs up because I feel this game is worth a try at least and its free, so what are you losing, I recomend this game to people who want to try an mmo, to me this is a great starting point for newcomers to the world of mmo's.

TO THOSE THAT ARE CONSIDERING BUYING THE STEAM CONTROLLER:
The Steam controller is by far potentially the best gamepad you will ever use on PC.  Not THE best but POTENTIALLY the best.  There's a difference.  Depending on your coordination as well as the controller configurations you use your experience will vary.  I suggest you take everything every reviewer has ever said about the controller with a grain of salt as configuration (more so) and coordination (less so) will make or break your interest in this controller.  Let me go over some of the basics of the controller here.
The look of the controller is a bit bulky, at a glance it's about the size of an Xbox One pad.  Track pads on both sides of the controller feel good, give rumble feedback and are extremely precise if configured correctly.  At first it took me some time to get used to the joystick/button layout but I'm slowly getting used to the placement though I occusionally hit the wrong button.  There are also two extra buttons on the back that you can use as shortcuts so you don't have to take your fingers off of the track pads as often.  This is VERY useful especially for shooters.
The controller is EASY as hell to setup for each game.  When you start a game you have the choice to use the default Developer configuration, a list of custom Community configurations or make your own.  Choosing either still gives you the option to tweak the options so don't be afraid to experiment.  This also applies to non-steam games as long as you put them in your library and browsing the internet.  Cool, right?
Furthermore, you can set your controller to emulate an Xbox pad, keyboard and mouse or a combination of the two if your game allows both forms of input.  So you can play games using Xbox button prompts AND games that only use mouse/keyboard.  ABSOLUTE FREEDOM.  You can even set your multiple fuctions to the same buttons.  Example: In my configuration holding left trigger aims but holding left trigger also makes your aiming sensitivity lower as well as changes all of my face buttons to different functions.  Can you say "20+ buttons for casting spells in RPGs!"?  Now you can play WoW or Guild Wars 2 with a pad.
It is an easy recommendation but be warned.  Many (not all) youtube reviewers suck at this pad as they only use mouse/keyboard as they can't get used to it.  If you game often with a game pad then you should have very little trouble adjusting just don't expect to master it right away.  For fighting game fans, think about that time you switched from a controller or fight pad to a fight stick.  It's kinda similar to that just with much less derp moments of not knowing how to do basic stuff.

I never write reviews on steam but for this controller it's worth the time.  I've been looking for something to replace my keyboard and mouse to reduce the strain on my hands and wrists (I write code all day) but nothing quite did it well enough until I got this controller.  I've tried the XBox controller but it just doesn't quite do the trick for FPS aiming and, beyond that, it isn't always supported.
I hesitated to buy this controller based on reviews that said it felt too cheap and that the track pad wasn't good enough.  My impression is that the controller does feel a bit lighter and not as solid as an XBox controller but it sure doesn't feel cheap.  The track pad isn't as precise as a mouse but it's close and is a minor trade off that I'm willing to make.
I really like that there are community profiles for individual games.  I picked one up for 7 Days To Die and then made a few customizations.  The depth of customization is amazing.  I can now recline and play the game without fumbling with a keyboard and mouse.  It's a thing of beauty.
I'm excited for future updates that allow the controller to work with non-steam games.  I have a feeling this peripheral will be in my hands for many years to come.
Overall, the product is refined and gets the job done.  My only con is that I didn't realize that I could have bought it on Amazon and saved $9 on shipping and received it a few days quicker.

The Steam Controller (and to a lesser extend the Link) has reignited my love for playing games and has single handedly saved my interest in video games, and this is not even hyperbole in the least. Over the past few of years due to me spending more and more time sat at my desk working, and a lot of that in my home office, the amount of time I have been spending playing games has declined from an hour or two a day to an hour or two a week. It got to the point where I spent far more time reading about games than playing them. The reason for this is that after spending 8/9 hours in front of a computer screen in my office, the last thing in the world I want to do is sit there even longer at night (even if that time is playing games and not working).
I was on the verge of giving up playing games all together, which would have been a crying shame considering what a huge part of my life games have been ever since I got my first Master System in 1989. I considered getting a console, or even just running a HDMI cable to my lounge and using an Xbox controller to play stuff, but at the end of the day I'm not really interested in games that can be controlled with an Xbox controller, just like there is hardly anything that interests me on the consoles.
Then along comes the Steam Controller to save the day. Thanks to it, I can now happily sit on my sofa playing the types of games I like (turn based stuff, RPG's etc), while at the same time♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of the girlfriend because she can't watch the Kardashians (win win). It may not be perfect but the mere fact I can sit there in front of the TV with a controller in my hand playing Legend of Grimrock 2 is ♥♥♥♥ing epic.
So yeah, the Steam Controller has literally changed my life and saved my favourite hobby.

Death Goat is a twin-stick arcade shooter that is full of blood, guts, gore, and metal. The title spent a bit of time in Early Access before eventually being fully released on June 7, 2016. At the time of writing, it is the only game that the developer/publisher Terminal Press have released on Steam.
Being an avid, enthusiastic fan of metal, it's obvious that I was excited to play Death Goat. What could be better than slaughtering hoards of enemies to epic battle hymns and deathly doom ballads? Unfortunately, due to lack of overall content, the game falls incredibly short of anything spectacular. There are three "levels", which are just really different backgrounds, and five total characters to play as. The characters are simply different skins, and none of them have any deviation whatsoever.
Your goal is to stay alive as long as possible, which is actually pretty hard. The maps are small, and your overhead field of view isn't very wide, so it's very easy to get overrun by foes quickly. There are only three or four power-ups that you can pick up from fallen enemies; a laser shot, a melee-ranged ice sword, and a couple different burst shots. You start each game off with three lives, and three pentagram bombs; the bad guys will drop a bomb pick-up for you every now and then, but as far as I could tell you cannot regain a life once it is lost.
If your metal tastes are like mine, then you will find the soundtrack on-par at best. It's filled mostly with metalcore, deathcore, and melodic metal bands, while some blackened death, groove, and progressive metal is scattered sparsely. I won't deny that this is a good opportunity for these bands to gain some new fans, and to spread the word about themselves, but for those who enjoy heavy doses of death, black, and doom metal, you will find yourself disappointed. I was personally better off hitting the mute button and throwing on my own mix of tunes. As well, you can only pick one song per time you play... so if you survive the duration of the song, it will just repeat.
Overall, is Death Goat good? It's a mediocre twin-stick arcade shooter at best. You try to survive, to get the highscore, you die, you rinse and repeat. Once you get a certain amount of kills, you unlock the Death Tank which I suppose completely ravages your enemies, but by the time you reach that point you'll be completely sick of the game itself. The metal soundtrack is a good aspect, but it's really only an attraction gimmick at this point. There aren't exactly a wide variety of enemies or "levels", either, so the aesthetics really become boring over time as well.

Fun game from 2002.  I started as a huge Diablo 2 fan.  I'm catching up and enjoying the era of now-cheap RPG/action games before upgrading my system to run more modern games.   Just so I don't spend before I really need to.  (currently a Radeon X-600)  This includes the Dungeon Siege series + Fallout, Torment, Torchlight 1/2, Baldur's Gate, Titan Quest, Morrowind, Oblivion ...before hitting Skyrim, D3, etc.  Bottom line: In many ways, this fits in the older era.  -- So, those are your ganeral Action/RPG + hack/slash comparisons.
** Graphics:  It's 3-D.  Steam graphics are representative.  Sure, it's dated, but that doesn't ruin the game for me.
** Team: You can manage 8 characters drawn from three general classes from which you can customize: Melee, ranged, mage.   Two kids of mages: Combat, Nature.  Former is mostly offensive; the latter mainly includes healing spells, etc.   Buffs and spell selection are typical.
** Multiplayer: No multiplayer anymore.
** Loot: Regular items for purchase and souped up loot (some have tradeoffs).  One of your 8 chars can be a moving mule: non fighting with 3 times inventory.  ... One /very/ cool minor feature is casting a "transmute" spell that turns items into gold on the spot at a fraction of the value.  Thus, there's no need to leave loot unless you want to leave mapping markers or don't want to bother with the super-cheap stuff.
** Overview of Attributes with examples: 3 areas: Strength (perks: melee combat damage, eventually wear better armor), Dex (ranged damage), Intel (mana pool, spell damage, mage armor).  -- Dex provides minimal advantages.
** Character development is actually more complex than usual.  Use a melee weapon, you build strength.  -- but you also gain a slight boost in dex and a very slight intel boost.  Reverse is true.  This enables your ranged character to VERY gradually build strength for slightly better armor.  Although you delay advanced specializion perks, I like a little flexibility.
[EDIT: Recommendation: Specialization for fighters.  Don't broaden their attributes/abilities beyond strength.  ...Be very cautious about mage/fighters.]
** Replayability?  The only replayability factors would be different party composition, which IMO is little to none.  No randomness at all.  I think it's a great one and done.
** Monsters: Once you clear an area, the monsters don't respawn.  I expect that next game, they'll be in the same place.
** Other: You can remap keys like a bandit.  You can raise/lower difficulty.  Quick save capability.
Note one can purchase overview maps (which includes secret area locations), but it does NOT show caves since they're underground.  Sometimes unlit areas aren't obvious, both of which are authentic and nice touches.  I haven't investigated mods.
EDIT: Just completed the game (12/12/14).  This game has a let-down for an ending.  Still worth the purchase, but oh my goodness, Steam version has removed all sense of closure!  Does this matter?  Think of it as a 98% great game, and subsequently see a therapist for any emotional damage.  I'm going to install DS2 now. :)
** Advice: If you like the standard old ARPG like the above, get this game.  Cheap Steam bundles are occasionally available at humblebundle, gamersgate, bundlestar, etc.  Probably will hit gog soon if you want no DRM. Thanks for reading.
