Paladins has been released on Steam. And within 5 days, the game reached the top 3 F2P Games on Steam Store. Even 8 days after release, it is still top 3. However I doubt there is a chance it will top TF2, Paladins will just stay at the 3rd spot. With so many downloads, I was a little curious if the game got better. I made a post a few days ago wondering if it was worth downloading from Steam, and the answer went along the lines of, "with the growth of players, it's worth checking out again." I was curious, and decided to test that curiosity. As soon as it was downloaded and updated, I loaded the game. The UI was very impressive and dynamic. It was a little confusing at first having not played so long, but it was fairly easy to understand. I found a game relatively quick, something I didn't notice back when I played so long ago. The champion screen was also innovative, something I was fond of. I noticed competitive mode was locked until 12 or more champions were master 4, and despite me having so much experience in the game, I only focused on a few characters, which I was a little glad about considering so many have changed. Note I have tried every champion so I knew how they played and what they were good at. Wanting to try competitive mode, I immediately hopped on champions I never played much. I started with Grohk, and since the last time I played him, he changed completely. He is definitely not as big of a damage dealer than what he once was, but more of a support character and healer. I definitely dig the change. More characters worth noting that I now like in which I didn't like before:
Barik - Didn't like the feel to him, seemed to be a character that lacked compared to others. However, he is particularly fun now and with the TF2 skin you can get for him, a lot more new players are trying him out.
Ruckus - By far one of the worst champions I've ever seen. When I used to play, no one played Ruckus as, like Barik IMO, lacked so much. Let me start by saying it sucks that people have been having so much trouble with the stability of this game. Personally, I haven't had any problems with it crashing (knock on wood), but I have experienced some of the graphical hiccups with low frame rates and screen tearing.
Those problems aside, it is a blast to play. I've always liked the Dead Rising series and zombie games in general, but the constant time limit in the other games took away some of the enjoyment for me. I'm a completionist, and I felt like I couldn't see everything and save everyone in the other games. I know the point was probably to teach you that you can't save everybody, but I'm stubborn. I want to explore everything and take in the sights. I feel like I can do that in this game. You're still on the clock, but it's less pressing. I can seek out collectibles and screw around in Los Perdidos and still find time to do the story and side missions. Call me a filthy casual if you must, but when I come home after a stressful day at work, I play games like this for catharsis. I don't need more stressful deadlines to meet.
The gameplay is familiar to anyone who has played the other Dead Rising games. Both leveling up and the menu interface are a little different, but it's easy to get used to them. It recommends using a controller, but I did fine with a mouse and keyboard.
As I mentioned earlier, it has a few visual bugs. Hopefully, those will get patched in future updates. It's definitely an improvement over Dead Rising 1 and 2. The amount of zombies they can cram on screen is staggering. There's nothing more satisfying than plowing through hordes of the undead with your crazy weapon or vehicle of choice.
I won't say much about the story because I'm not that far into it yet (I've restarted a few times to keep leveling up). From what I've experienced, the tone switches from dark and depressing (it is a zombie apocalypse after all) to quirky weirdness. I personally like its style, though it could be oddly jarring to a newcomer. The plot seems pretty standard, though I'll see if that changes if I can break away from just slaughtering everything that shambles.
If you're fortunate enough to get through it without crashing and the few visual bugs don't bother you too much, Dead Rising 3 is a fun addition to anyone's zombie game library.

Way better than GalCiv III.....not that that's saying much. Stellaris looks great, comparable to Sins, but unlike Sins this has much more diversity in every aspect with lots more individualised species, government forms as well as map,tech and development options etc. Modding community is very active and inventive which is always a huge plus for any game (although game patches seem to break many mods).
Stellaris does have quite a number of problems though and two of them in particular I must confess♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. It's a slow burn game - I mean it takes hours and hours and hours of gameplay to get anywhere - thats fine, as long as you don't end up in an RNG blackhole for your effort. I recently had a 10 hour game, 135 years into my galactic exploration - 4th generation hyperdrive, massive starbases, advanced labs and.....level 1 lasers because tech access iuses an RNG - I randomly missed out for 135 years on ANY space weapon upgrades - RNG blackhole. Simultaneously I had 7 starving worlds...why i hear you ask....because while I had level 4 hyperdrive, my farms were the same 'till the ground with a hoe and bring me a bucket of water' farms that I started with - no farm upgrades were randomly generated for 135 years, it seems travelling at 500 times the speed of light is more important that optional stuff like food. Apparently issues such as this are known and plans are afoot to address them in a coming patch, but that doesn't help the game now though.
The other issue driving me nuts is scaling - you know. You start out with 1 crappy ship, run across a big scary amoeba with three times your firepower so you run away, build two more ships, come back and low and behold now there are 3 amoebas with three times your firepower, so you go away and rinse repeat. This scenario repeats endlessly for all the early game hostile random encounters you have - so what's the point, let 1 ship get its face kicked in by an amoeba now, or let three ships get their faces kicked in by 3 amoebas later....your choice.
A couple of other issues I have had include being told I just picked up bonus research point from an anomoly but the points never get credited to any research project and non-combat ships path into hostile systems on long journeys even though the system is marked as occupied by hostiles with any damaged non-combatant respawning months later at the nearest starbase half a galaxy away.
This game has great potential, but like so many other 4X and strategy games the mechanics to keep the game 'interesting' seem to rely on the AI and environment just automatically compensating for whatever the player does which seems to make whatever you do largely pointless - I had hoped for a game where the AI is actually playing the same game as me rather than this mirroring effect. Couple this with random starts that can be pretty crappy and RNG tech options it means you may need to invest 3-4 hours before you realize that you are screwed and have been from the very start. That may be reflective of the real world...but as games go not really a fun way to spend my gaming time. I give it a hesitant thumbs down out of protest as much as anything else, but I really hope it improves so I can give it a positive review.

Fantastic, but short, puzzle-platforming game. The primary mechanic is your telegun, whose bullets don't hurt enemies but do instantly teleport you to whatever surface they hit. The devs manage to stretch this mechanic quite a bit and create a few very tricky rooms. Art is just pixel art, but it's very good pixel art, and the music is stellar; overall, the alien atmosphere feels very well-fleshed-out. My main complaint is that this is not a Metroidvania game, as the inspirations it lists on the store page would imply; there are a couple heart containers and ship upgrades, but the latter are pretty useless and the game itself is basically linear. Rather than drawing in fans of Super Metroid or Cave Story, I think people who enjoyed VVVVVV would be the most likely to have fun with Out There Somewhere. Again, it's short: my first run through the game took about 50 minutes. Though, it's a good bit longer if you're a completionist, since getting all the achievements was about 3 hours total without a guide. Plus, if you're of the speedrunning type, then the telejump mechanic offers a lot of potential there. The game's only $2 at full price and gets even cheaper in sales and with various bundles, so if you happen to see it it's definitely worth picking up.

Splinter Cell Double Agent is like getting shanked in an alley after a nice dinner.
You play as Sam Fisher, the worlds sneakiest man. Sam Fisher was once a likable comedic character with a lot of personality and likability, but one day the writers said “Lets not do that.”
And then they ruined everything.
The first thing I noticed about this game is that It has nowhere near as many resolution options as Chaos Theory. Oh boy oh baby we're off to a good start.
So after I dicked around in the .ini files for a bit to get a decent resolution I embarked on another journey with my favorite NSA super agent.
After completing a mission in Iceland, Sam Fisher is informed that his daughter was killed in a car accident. Distraught, Sam leaves Third Echelon and bums around for a total of two minutes or so before joining back in on some mission where he pretends to be a terrorist for a bit. Instead of, you know, letting Sam do his thing and just getting the info out of people with just his delicious gravely voice.
Double Bigmac has the unfortunate problem of having to come out a year after the masterpiece that is Chaos Theory, and it absolutely pales in comparison.
“But Dirk, you stupid stinky idiot who doesn't know what he's talking about.” You inquire. “How do you expect Double Agent to compare to Chaos Theory if it only came out a year after?”
Please don't hurt my feelings.
The thing is, Chaos Theory felt like a natural evolution to the series, like they tested and practiced their game design in 2002, improved it in 2004, and then perfected it in 2005. Double Agent feels like they threw it all away. Don't get me wrong, it still kind of controls like a Splinter Cell game, you still control movement speed with your mouse wheel,  you pick locks the same, you hide around corners the same, and you do actions...Kind of the same. It's all still there, it just had a lot of questionable design decisions.
For instance, in the last game when you hacked a computer it would happen in real time, Sam would bring down his goggles and the computer stuff would overlay your normal vision. In this game for some reason you get a FMV of Sam looking at his wrist watch and being taken to a computer screen not in real time. It's really jarring and takes you out of the action and atmosphere.
The lighting and environments are also nowhere near as good or well done as the last game. Everything is way too bright and the shading is off so sometimes you're invisible, but standing in the same kind of lighting will make you completely visible to the enemy.
They also completely changed the UI. Instead of having every option neatly presented to you in the top right like the last three games, they instead tried to go for some streamlining of a already streamlined system and making it very...I don't know, consolidated, I guess. Even picking weapons is kind of a pain.
Before you would just hold CTRL and you could just click on what weapon and attachment or item you wanted to use. Now when you press CTRL you have to flick your mouse in the direction of the item on a D-pad lay out and then scroll through the attachments like that. It's janky as all hell and barely works when you need it to.
The sound detector is also gone and you can no longer properly measure how much sound Sam is making when he moves around. It's not that hard to tell how fast you can move before you make too much sound, but it was still a nice edition to Chaos Theory, it doesn't really make sense to it being gone.
There's also this trust system they slapped in for some reason, it doesn't really add anything to the game. If it hits 0, it's game over anyway, and it doesn't really ever come into play during the actual game.
Everything about Double Agent is just kind of worse in every way, the stealth isn't as good, the UI is a pain to get around, the comedy and charm from the character interaction of the last three games is gone in favor of this dark and gritty junk that they actually thought was an improvement to the original formula considering they kept it up for the next two games as well.
What else can I complain about? Okay hold on.
The graphics are glitchy as all hell. For some reason, at least in my game, light sources wouldn't actually start making light until I got close enough, otherwise they were just completely dark until I got in a certain range. These weren't motion sensing lights either, since my status would go from invisible to visible if I moved quickly enough to where the light should be shining before the game decided that the light should be on. There was also a lot of flickering going on on character models, assets disappearing for a quick second before reappearing, and just really bad looking environments even on the highest setting.
This one is clearly a console port with no effort put into it at al- WAIT HOLD ON! THE MULTIPLAYER!
So in the last game there was Spies vs Mercs, which was this really tense game of cat and mouse where spies had to secure an objective while the mercs guarded the objected and hunted down the spies. In the last game, unless you could visibly see the spy, the only way you would know if that he was around you is if he set off a trap or your sound detector gave them away.
So in Spies vs Mercs they gave the Mercenaries a proximity sensor of sorts. As in if you're in the same room as a spy it just starts beeping, and beeps faster and faster the closer you are to the spy. That means if you, as a spy, actually want to lose the merc you have to leave the room and get distance from the Merc and hope that he leaves to go looking for you. It leaves very little room for strategy and you have no chance of maybe juking the Mercenary and making him believe you ran off because he'll always know if you're nearby. It's just not fun.
I feel like that Ubisoft panicked when they saw the TGS 2005 trailer for MGS4 and that's why Double Agent feels so bland and rushed. MGS was going to have a War torn level in the middle east/ Africa so Double Agent had to have the war ton middle eastern/ African level. MGS4 looked like it was going to have a lot of daylight missions so Double Agent had to have day light missions everywhere. Mind you back in the day, people saw Splinter Cell and Metal Gear as competing franchises. It's even funnier when you realize that MGS4 came out in 2008, while Double Agent launched in 06.

While this is good entry into the Splinter Cell series this game feels less like the weakest. Somehow they managed to make this game not feel like splinter cell. The overall story was ok, but the missions were rather short. After you beet the game the first time around it might take a while (especially the JBA HQ missions) but say you want to go back and play it again the whole thing will take you...I don't know at the most 5-6 hours at the longest? When I finished Chaos Theory I would go back to see if I missed anything: Other ways to get from point A to point B, new ways to pass enemies, & new ways to do certain things, and it was still fun. In Double Agent I felt like it was not hard on you as another Splinter Cell.  You even get a mini-map! It showed you where the bad-guys were and if one saw you. Just let that sink in for a bit. You were not allowed you chose how you played a mission either. In Splinter Cell Chaos theory you could chose what and how many thing you could take in a mission by clicking on Assault, Stealth, and Recommended. You do not get those liberties in DA. While Double Agent does introduce new things like: When you ADS with the F2000 there is a red-dot sight (like in CoD) if you are hugging a wall you can now attack enemies walking towards you, and you get more gagets to help Fisher with seeking around (Did those gadgets unlock for anyone else or are they 'unlockable'?). SPOILERS Fisher's daughter dieing felt really tacked on and out of place. The only reason for it was to build up to Conviction which does not even work on steam. And does anyone know why fisher is the only one who can move his lips when he talks? Overall, I would recommend this game if you have played and like the other games, bu if you want it for it being a stealth game...I would not really get it...I don't know....Get Blacklist or older splinter cell games. this one was the odd child in school who never seemed to fit in.

So you're a nice person,  quiet, minding your own business, not making any waves. But one day you get fed up, you blow your steam, let loose. And you really start to wonder, what would it be like to...
play Saints Row 2?
You wake up in prison, you've done something bad, something bad's been done to you. Following this theme, the next obvious choice is to bust out of prison. Of course there's people blocking your path to freedom, and in this game, where there's a will there's a way.
Back on the streets you find the people rather lacking in patience and understanding. The meek seem to have become extinct. The one who's got your back is the one that's got the most to gain from your death. Fee will is rampant, freedom abundant. Playing Mister Nice Guy is not an option, anything else is fair game.
Nobody respects compassion, respect is earned through surviving the impossible, and there's plenty of opportunity for that, just use your imagination. Respect is the key, here. Not respect for laws or leaders, respect for breaking them.
The hassles of the bugs that prevent this from ever working well don't alter the fact that this will be your only opportunity to have some real fun.

As a metal fan I found the presentation to be fantastic, it has black metal cheese all over it, the characters look metal as ♥♥♥♥ and the soundtrack is kickass. But what makes this game just fall apart is the gameplay and some technical issues.
First off the gameplay is so bland and cookie cutter standard, the power ups are nice but only last for a short time and don't drop fast enough, there are not enough power ups, you move way to fast and keep knocking into enemies, some enemies are hard to see since they  are so small and you die so quickly since your shields hitbox is absolutely huge and after it runs out it's just a matter of time before you accidentally run into an enemy because of the crazy movement speed. And excluding the issues I had with the power ups the game also lacks a lot of content, there's just a handful of bland boring maps and the fun cool characters all play the same but I've heard that the tank that you unlock at 1.000.000 score plays differently but I'm not gonna sit and play this game for that long. So you just choose your boring map, choose your cool but boring character and then top it off with an awesome metal track, every game plays like the one before and they last so shortly because of the issues listed above.
And now to the technical issues I had with this game, first off the game don't start on my main monitor and it took some time before I figured out how to move it over to my main screen since there is no option to change what monitor the game is played in. And the other problem I had is that you can't switch off controller support without plugging out your controller, and having a huge desk with a huge setup with a lot of wires that's pretty annoying just to play a simple cheap game.
Now I could live with the technical issues but because of the lack of content and bad gameplay design this game is just a no for me, if the gameplay was improved on with a bunch more power ups that don't run out instantly, the ridiculous speed gets fixed and more content then I might consider picking up this game again since I just love the theme and the presentation.

-Not compatible with EU keyboards AND no key rebinding ! I should not have to switch between two different keyboards configurations each time I open a different game. That's just stupid.

-Power ups are temporary, and there are very few of them = No form of progression during the playthrough.

Also, from my experience in shoot'em up and bullet hell games, I'm pretty sure that there is some thought that should go into how large the player hit box should be with respect to the avatar model to allow for proper difficulty balancing. <PROS>

The game has a terrible loot system, which you get items way to rarely, and they are way to commonly duplicate loot. The game is already $20 which it isn't even worth that much, it would barely be able to earn a $10 price tag and yet they still shove micro transactions in your face.

- Game Isn't Complete
There is way too much missing from this game to call it a full game, it should still be in alpha, maybe even pre-alpha.
IN CONCLUSION
If you want the classic Primal Carnage experience with Deathmatch's, Get to the Chopper, and Capture the Egg then go and get the original. If you want customization, and alot of horny 5 year olds hosting Tyrannosaurus Sex (See what I did there) servers then go with this alpha game falsely titled a non-alpha game. When it comes to PC gaming, I prefer a trackball and keyboard about 85% of the time. The rest of the time I use an Xbox 360 controller. I have to admit that I'm really starting to like the Steam controller. Using the right stick sensor as a trackball controller feels very natural on most of my games after only a little adapting. It feels pretty natural and is highly configurable. I have a feeling I'll be using the Steam controller most of the time now.

Was really looking forward to trying this concept for a new way of gaming... only to find does not  fully work with the new Star Wars Battlefront ... or so it would seem any game that sits outside of Steam!! - DOES NOT replace a trustworthy 'older' controller.

50 Euros for it is pretty bad deal.
Its nowhere near quality of DS3/4 or even Xbox controllers (ie. Upper part seems to be slightly bigger than lower - they're not perfectly fit).
For tpp action games - Trackpad is way worse than regular analog sticks - it lacks either speed or precision. It has great customisation possibilities, but the trackpad is just not a good tool for action games.
FPS games are just slightly better than on regular controllers, but still nowhere near the precision and speed offered by kb+m.
In both instances it fits in between the standard controller and kb+m.
Having said that, I must admit I quite like the desktop mode. Its almost perfect for navigating around windows from the couch or playing mouse-based games (ie. total war series) Its good enough for games with simple controls (ie. not requiring second analog, like binding of isaac or platformers)
It also has software problems - having hard time detecting transition between controller and desktop modes. Switching between steam window, big picture and launching game may require numerous resets - either of the game or controller , before the game launches in correct controller mode.
tl;dr:
It wont replace regular pad for pad-designed games, but if you want to play mouse-based games or games with simple controls from the comfy couch - it's a decent piece of plastic. But still you should wait for Price drops. Definitely not worth the 50 Euros for the quality it has been made with - both hardware and software quality.

I thought I'd put in my imput on this game. First off, when looking for an MMO with Anime Graphics and free-roam style... this is so far the only game that has hit the spot. I fell in love and I now have been playing it non-stop for three days, just short of 40 hours now.
TRUE - Players are not overly friendly and do not go out of their way to say Hello or RolePlay (I come from World of Warcraft) so players NOT roleplaying was a little different.
FALSE - Players only seek to use you. I've met some very nice people and have joined a guild that is actually reasonably social. Good players are out there, they are just hidden. Hah.
TRUE - The Quests are mostly gathering and killing - basic MMO stuff. Still, I love them because if you listen to the story behind them, they actually make sense. In WoW - they say go get some candles. No explanation for why... just go get me some freaking candles. So you do. In this game, your goal is clear and everyone's quests are to help them help you. It makes sense why you go gather mushrooms or kill beetles.
TRUE - The AI and BOT models are VERRRRRY overused, but I don't mind it much. As for player models, I haven't seen any close look-alikes and the character creation gives just enough imput.
Other Things I Love?
I love classifying in two specializations. So i can use guns and swords, etc. It's very cool and something I was sad they started taking away from World of Warcraft (its basically nonexistant).
I love the dungeon system. Dungeons are completely solo-able or you can join up and do a party-version. This makes it easy for SOLO players (like myself) to get everything in the game accomplished without searching for people I don't even want to talk too.
The game is easy. Not in the sense that it offers no thrill or excitement, but its not overly complicated. Everything is explained in words first and then (for visual people like myself), most everything has a little video to also explain how each element works. Using Gems is explained, creating armor and gear, and even fishing.
Fishing is FUN. Its also one of the easiest places to get Gold (WInk WINk).
I Love the Companions - they are fun and sooo helpful. I especially Love Merilee!!
Costumes are great - no mismatched ugly gear while you're leveling. The best ones must be bought however (SIGH)
What I Don't Like?
No open world RolePlay - but thats ok. Hey, if you want to Look Me Up. I love Roleplay
Not a whole lot of servers.
Can only create 9 characters, but there are 12 classes [This isn't overly important since they have duel-classification at level 40, so you can make up for lost classes then.]
Gold Farming is Slow. And I do mean SLOOOW. I've farmed gold for weeks in several games but I've never had so much difficulty as in this one.
In-Game Real Money:: I've always had a problem with this in games. It bothers me that I can't buy nice things with Gold. They have implemented another Currency to get most of these Real Money items, but its a lot of work (almost too much). Still - despite adding this it is in no way PAY to WIN. You don't have to spend any money to be freaking amazing in this game.
I don't if my review helped. But these are some things that I looked at, disliked, loved, and enjoyed.
Overall. Get this Game. If you like RPGs with a GOOD Storyline (who doesnt?), Anime Graphics, and MMO, get this game. People say a lot of crap. But this game has been completely worth it for me. :)

At first, I really liked Aura Kingdom. It's bright, colorful, has very engaging combat, and is, just in general, fun.... but only for the first two levels (Or 'locations.') Later in the game, you start to wonder "What the hell am I doing and what does any of this have to do with the story?" This will happen A LOT.
Here's an example from one of the earlier quests where such an instance first appears. You need to make medicen for your character because he/she passed out. Well, you need antilope blood. Okay, fine. But you need to kill six of the giant creatures for their blood. WHAT THE HELL? HOW MUCH BLOOD DOES THIS DOCTOR NEED FOR LITTLE OL' ME?!
This is fine in those quests where the particular creature you're killing needs to be driven out of the area, but when you need to collect items from them? It's VERY monotonous. Another reason this sucks is that, when you're collecting items from creatures, there is a 20% chance that you will actually get the item you need. As a rough estimate, if you have to kill 4 fish to get scales, you'll probably have to kill 8 fish to get the four sets of scales. This becomes even worse when, in higher level areas, you have to kill 7 and 14 creatures to gather the specified number of itmes you need to complete a "Main Quest" that doesn't seem to have anything to do with the story. This makes playing the game the way your suppose to a chore.
Another problem this game has is its dungeons. These are usually big cave-like areas where you fight large waves of monsters. Most Dungeons require the player to be in a party of three to actually activate it. This would be fine if players in this game were actually considerate. No one wants anything to do with you unless you wear expensive costumes and hats, or have the best mounts and weapons. It's like, if Team Fortress 2 met World of Warcraft in a very ill-considerate and rude way. This is most evident, unfortunatly, for players who speak english. My first language is english and my spanish is a little rusty (But little to no spanish speaking players play this game anyway) meaning I am stuck dealing with the ruder end of the player pool, which is the dominant end. The worst part is these dungeons are REQUIRED to finish the story. Which means you could be stuck for a LONG time on the same main quest, not because you cannot defeat the enemies because they, themselves, are quite easy, but because no one wants to join you. Making friends in this game is hard for the same reason, even if the player is a noob at the same time you are and has the first constume as well.
This game is so pay to win it hurts.
In all, Aura Kingdom is a game with lovely visuals, fun combat, a promising story, rude and selfish majority players, monotonus quests and pointless quests. Have fun.

"Game of 2017" for me
Nier: Automata is a great ARPG developed by Platinum Games and Published by Square Enix. By the visionary Creator Yoko Taro (I never heard of before).
It has the full package. Great Story. Nice Atmosphere. Awesome Combat Mechanics. Likeable Characters and a Stunning Soundtrack.
It is still a hit or miss experience.
You may find the story boring or too complex (given that there are 3 Playthroughs/Game+ to get the full picture and multiple "fun" alternate endings) or just the fact that the Prologue of the Game has no means of SAVING which didnt amuse a lot of people (but is intended). Or just dont like the Genre-mix.
Some Sections of the Game wil be Straight 3rd Person ARPG - then it will become a Top Down Arcade Shooter, and revert to a Sidescroller etc. Sometimes the game tries too hard, but its a very creative and nice approach to mix different Genres that way.
The Combat overall is very well made (as expected from Platinum). The Chip System (Character Customization) is a nice idea and fun to use. The Story is a fun ride, but if you do every Sidequest and Explore every bit of the open world you may become "over"leveled and every encounter will be way too easy. Difficulty is adjustable at any point though Choosable From "Game holds your hand Easy" to "You have to be a god with superpowers to beat it difficult".
For completionists: After you finish the game every Achievement becomes "buyable" at a Vendor for little amount of Ingame Currency.
Story: 9.5/10
Style & Aesthetic: 10/10
Music: 10/10
Sound Effects: 8.5/10
Gameplay & Combat: 8.5/10
World Design: 8.5/10
UI: 9/10
Leveling and Weapon / Chip System: 8/10
Time to complete 100% - 25-35 Hours.
Overall: A solid 9/10
BUT (HUGE BUT) the port is mediocre at best.
With release there were a bunch (a lot) of people with graphic problems, freezes, crashes, stuttering.
Those issues haven´t been addressed properly by Square Enix at all. Which is very poor.
So before you get this, you should check if there are any issues reported by other users running similar or identical setups, or just refund if you happen to be one of the unfortunate people who are unable running this game properly.
Despite this huge mess related to the port its a GREAT game. Recommended.

There is a very real sense of exploration in the early game, as you branch out into the galaxy and discover planets and anomalies.  This hooked me in quickly and enjoyed reading of each discovery, I especially loved the ones that lead to interest quests.
However by the mid to late game, these are largely skipped over as some of them become repetitive and matter less and less as the universe becomes less of a great unknown, and more of a mass graveyard as you slug it out with awakened empires, alien species and battle the end game crisis.
This is the kind of game that is difficult to "win", and is similar in many ways to Civ, where games can span many, many hours. This can lead to a degree of burnout, since there will come a point where you are just churning out ships as quickly as your economy can support them.
There are a few odd design choices, for instance, the fact that you have to pay influence to attain resources from a sector YOU created. Gratefully there is the workshop and plenty of QOL mods to improve the overall experience.
If you enjoy civilization, grand strategy games, and have a interest in the vast universe, you'll enjoy this.

Let me start off by saying I really like old school rpg games,  but this game is the epitome of boring.  The dungeons feel overly long, as if they extended gameplay through the sheer length they make your characters walk.  The combat is pretty bland.  I went almost all archers with my squad since, at the hardest difficulty, 1: Melee gets decimated and 2: It costs no resources unlike spells.  It does fairly well but the gameplay is just blah.
99% of the item drops fall into 2 categories:  Items you can't wear and Items you can't use.  Either all of the drops have stat requirements that are way beyond what my characters can use or they aren't even close to being an upgrade.  It's almost exclusively vendor trash.
Leveling:  It's pretty much a use a skill get some auto xp gains system.  There is no decision making other than what to use.  I chose to focus on a single discipline rather than jack-of-all-trades.  That said, since I am ranged, my armor selection is pretty♥♥♥♥♥since it's based on str and int for useage requirements.  The choices are poor even if I DID have the appropriate attributes to wear said equipment.
Quests:  I'm sorry, there are quests?  Basically it's talk to the 3 npcs you'll encounter per chapter then walk linearly through a massive dungeon crawl, completing the quests.  Hardly what I'd call quests.  There's not really even a reward for doing them that I can see.
It comes down to this: I am playing this through JUST to beat it and play it, but it's not very fun.  I was hoping for a NWN-type game and it comes off as an overly long poor diablo clone with a bigger party and crappier combat.  My playthrough on the hardest difficulty is basically, set my party to hold/engage freely/strongest target, have them all ranged, then pull with a single guy into range and have the mobs explode.  I move the party about 3 feet then repeat.  Ranged is kind of necessary since even melee die in 3-4 hits and you can get swarmed by 5+ if you aren't careful.  It's a slow slog through dungeons that seem to never end.  Since I bought Dungeon Siege 1, 2, and 3 I am hoping the sequels will be much better.
Do I regret buying this?  No, I paid like $2.99 or whatever the super Steam sale was, can't regret that.
Do I enjoy this game?  Nope.

Simple and short but extremely fun and creative little platform/puzzle game. This game was made by a very small team, and it's a really impressive achivement! You've got an extremely limited move set - you can jump around, you can fire a teleport beam, and you eventually get a blaster - but you'll use that limited move set in a wide variety of funny, clever, unexpected ways. There were so many times where I thought, "Oh, this trick move won't work", and then it did! So then what if I jump off here and then shoot my beam there, but before I land, I jump and then...oh, that worked too! The game is just full of surprises like that and all these puzzles that test your creativity, logic, and ability to exploit the mechanics. I also really like the pixel graphics - the art style is charming and memorable. I don't actually have any real critiques here! It's a short game, but it never outstays its welcome. There are even a decent amount of secrets and it'll take you a while to really collect everything. On top of all of these strengths, Out There Somewhere is really cheap - it even often goes on sale for something like 25 cents. You can't beat that! You can wait for one of those super cheap sales if you like, but this is an awesome little game at any price. In fact, this is probably one of the best deals on Steam, bar none.

Sadly, this game's faults outweigh the few positives. On the plus side, the soundtrack is pretty neat, and they are continuing trying to expand it. The game runs smoothly, which is nice.
Then we go to all of the negatives. The combat feels weak. The sound design is poor, and lackluster. The enemy design tries to look cool, but it just lacks that special "oomph" when you're splattering them. This game tries to copy Crimsonland and manages to be worse in every way except for the soundtrack.

First and foremost, since music is main selling point of this game, I must say that, although I do sometimes listen to metal music (though, rock and punk are my favourite), I generally don't like death metal... Because of that, I won't be commenting music, but will talk about gameplay (or the lack of one) in the game...
Anyway, Death Goat is a simple twin stick shooter in the style of Crimsonland (that I played and loved, long time ago); So you play as a Death Goat (or as Death Granny, or Kitty, or...) and while running around relatively small area kill everything that tries to hurt you...
The controls are responsive and feel nice, graphics are ok, but screen tends to become cluttered after some time, interface is generally ok, not too pretty, but in style and readable enough...
What I did find frustrating is that hitbox for "shield" is very large (as large as shield xD), and you cannot just squeeze through enemies and run away. I usually like that last second squeezing about this type of games. Not a special problem, but it did get on my nerves... :)
So, why I don't recommend this game... In its current state it has no content... I know that it is in early access, and that devs say that they plan on adding content when (if) more people buy the game, but currently it is more like a demo than a game (and they also say that 'Death Goat is a finished game in its current state', which it ISN'T!)... You can choose between 3 locations, that are completely the same as far as I can see, and between 5 characters, of which 4 are completely the same (gameplay wise), as far as I can tell... Other than that, you start the game, and kill the same hordes with same weapons (stronger weapons show up from time to time as power ups, but you lose them after some time). When you lose all 3 lives, you are back at the starting point without any progress (except overall point count).
Since pretty much whole description of this game is the list of bands that contributed to it's soundtrack, and that Music is the second on the list of planned features (though I have no idea why is that), this game feels more like 'Let's do something while I listen to this music', which is pretty much the same as playing snake on YouTube videos (if that is still possible xD)... Or playing actually finished games (like Crimsonland), while listening to audio of any band you like...
Pros:
Music (if you like it)
It has potential to be good twin-stick shooter once it becomes the game, and not just the demo
Cons:
It generally has no content
Music (if you don't like it)
Since I like twin-stick shooters, and it has potential, I will check this game again in a year (or so), to see if they added anything... I really hope they will... But at this time, it is, just, not a game; even for this price... Unless you buy it for the music... If you like music, buy it for it...

Well to start off with my review of the steam controller.
I will state I am not a big key board and mouse person to begin with. I've never been great or really accurate with them.
I have been into PC's since about mid way through high school but before mainly just played consoles.
So now that you know where I am coming from you can understand my views a bit better.
When I first saw the controller I had mixxed feelings on how it could work as a hybrid KBM/Gamepad.
But recently I have changed my PC setup no longer having room for both a desk and a home theater, and choosing to keep the home theater this intrested me alot.
Like most gamers thou I thought laptop trackpads??? thats not gonna work.
And hey wouldn't ya know they do work.. And dont at the same time.
(RTS)
Well its great for games like Civ 5 and RTS games they play just as well as on pc if played casually.
(Racing games)
Are fine to with or without the gyro it feel its on par with a xbox one controller minus the amazing trigger rumlbe feature. Even sim like games like Project Cars and Dirt Rally play great and just so you know I am huge racing game fan I love the forza series and I own a Logitech G27 racing wheel and the gyros fun and the analog sticks good too.
(2D scrollers)
And games of the nature most comfortable on a D-pad really dont work too well. But it feels ok with the analog stick. That being said I have yet to fine tune and get into the D-pad settings so it might work or maybe in the future someone might find a way to get it feeling right.
(Third person)
Games like GTA5 are great I have fine tuned the setting to a nice blend of mouse and gamepad. My ownly complaint is with the game it self. If i use the right pad and then hold A to run to quickly it starts recording. Its really annoying but not a fault of the controller, Rockstar please just let us turn off recording all together. but other then that I like playing third person games with the steam controller.
(Moba's)
Well I should say DOTA2 because thats the only one I like playing. Its... ok for on the couch but your not gonna be doing super great unless your some sort of master and or you really spend alot of time tuning the controller to what works for you. I not the best at these games but I do feel that new hotkey function coming out son might help a bit but i am not sure at the moment if it will feel 100% right for people.
(MMORPG's)
Same story as Moba's and again hotkeys might change things. But still playing rift from the couch with a steam controller its dam comfortable but still I feel its 80% there hopefully that changes in the future.
(FPS GAMES)
And Finally what is going to be the most hit or miss genre is FPS games. I have played Counter Strike, Half life 2, Portal 1 and 2, Left For Dead, Borderlands 2, And Fallout 4, and in Fallout 4 I only play in first person. All of the more single player games I played feel good but if you fine tune the right pad and if you have the option to get it to act as a mouse and not emulatea  joystick or analog stick (some game dont allow this). It feels amazing great especially if you get the edge spin setting and sensitivity just right it you feel in way more control then any other controller I've used. Fallout 4 took the longest to setup right mainly because I could not get the game to use the right pad as a 1:1 mouse and that could be changed in a update hopefully but either way the setting i have now are great.
Ok now the big question....How is it with heavy online titles like counter strike...Well believe me or not but I love it. But to be frank like I said before I am not super used to or good with a normal mouse and keyboard. I am more comfortable with a gamepad. But its not all sunshine and rainbows here. Button layouts, right pad setting being fine tuned to your liking and in some cases the gyro all need to work together and you need to give It time to get used to and learn (That should be said about the whole steam controller in general).

This is probably the buggiest game I've ever played. I generally don't write reviews, but I wanted to compile a list of the issues I've faced, along with some advice.
Before anything you should get the 1.02a patch from here :
This patch is not included in the steam version and already fixes some issues.
1) It will crash. There's no real way around it. It WILL crash. However, 99% of all crashes happen during loading, so once a loading is done you shouldn't get too many crashes (I've had one or two in my entire playthrough). The crashes are extremely random, and to get past them you need to try loading a save multiple times, until it finally succeeds. If you look up how to resolve this problem, you might find people saying that you need to launch the game with a '-ll' option. This is useless and only made the game crash a bit faster for me. Sometimes adding '/safemode' to the game's launch command seemed to get around some persistant crashes (although it could be a simple coincidence). To do this, simply right-click on the game in your steam game list, select 'properties', and click 'set launch options'. There you can add or remove '/safemode'.
At the very begining of the game I had a crash a few seconds after loading a game, which was solved when I tried using a third party patch to fix widescreen support
. Again, this might be a coincidence.
2) I strongly advise against trying Windows' compatibility mode. I tried it and it only made the game start dropping some FPS' every few seconds.
3) In some areas in the game you can get stuck (especially when you are crouching). To avoid trouble you should save often.
4) In some areas in the game you can instantly die if you save there and load the save. Again, to avoid trouble you should save often.
5) At some places you will have to pick some locks. Probably due to porting the game to PC, there is a glitch during lockpicking : you need Sam to be at maximum speed to be able to pick locks (scroll mouse wheel up).
6) At some point, when selecting 'continue' in the main menu, the game said that no valid save files were found, but all I had to do was going to the 'load' section and saves were still here.
All in all, you should avoid this game if you're not too patient, as it can be irritating to launch it 3 times in a row for it to randomly succeed and load correctly.

Treeker is a relatively short but fun puzzle game. It took me 2 to 2.5 hours to beat it, and I'm not particularly good at this genre. The cell-shaded graphic style works well and looks phenomenal, but there are certain sections that are particularly dark and somewhat hard to see. The mechanic of flipping between the glasses is neat, but it would be better in my opinion if there were advantages to NOT wearing the glasses aside from it being easier to see (the glasses add a fog around the periphery). As a result, you will end up wearing the glasses the vast majority of time, especially toward the end.
There are some quite frustrating platforming sections. I'm a fan of Portal and other 3D puzzle platformers, but some of these platform sections seem unnecessarily difficult. I think the issue is due to a somewhat-low field-of-view. If you're looking straight ahead, it can be hard to see the platform you have to land on. As a result, you have to jump forward then look down to make sure you land correctly. The controls work fine, and I rarely felt like I had been "cheated" by them. I will say that jumping off moving platforms is a bit odd, as you continue to maintain the momentum of the platform more than you would expect. Also, your jump changes a LOT when you're sprinting, so if you run out of stamina during a platforming section, your jumps will suddenly be significantly shorter. This could be addressed by adding a stamina bar.
The puzzle clues are typically enough to get you in the right direction without being too obvious, but story is unfortunately kind of light. There's not a lot of explanation about the world or why you're in it. Hopefully, this will be explained a bit more in the next section of the game that's released (which will be free to current owners).
Overall, I had fun with this game. It came in a bundle I purchased, so the cost was quite low. I would say that $8 seems a little bit high for the current content, but I think it's worth picking up for 50% off. As I mentioned previously, the game states that the next part will be free to owners of the current game. If that part is released and is of similar quality, I think Treeker is well worth the asking price.
Overall rating: 7/10

The game shifts from stark bright colours to neon tinged night, and presents itself in a rather pretty and minimalist low poly aesthetic. Its quite a stark and beautiful contrast, the developer is clearly a visually orientated artist. The music plays the same snippets on repeat, but they're nice soothing classical tunes, and thus do not cause any irritation.
Granted the price may be a tad steep for some, considering its length, but no more expensive than say seeing a movie, or having a couple cups of coffee/pints of beer out, so value is what you make of it. Indeed, the developer is apparently working on further content/episodes that are free for owners of Treeker.

It's more fun to play this game via co-op (it supports up to five players at a time), but is fairly enjoyable as a single player experience.  Essentially, it's a cross between a MOBA and tower defense game.  It's like the former in the sense that you'll choose a character (there are four characters for each of the four classes, each with different skills) and start at level 1 at the beginning of each match.  As you level up, you can put points into your four skills and buy new items to place into your inventory.  Instead of fighting other heroes, you'll be fending off waves of enemies (where the tower defense bit comes into play) who are trying to get to your missile silo.  As you play a particular class, you'll level them up in a "path of glory" tech-tree/xp tree-esque system which unlocks different buffs and the like.  Not as hardcore or complicated as say, "League of Legends", but it scratches that MOBA itch in a pinch.

Why do I not recommend this game to others, especially new paradox players? I started my Paradox gaming on Hearts of Iron 4, not the easiest start, but that game there it has a very linear line of functionality. Two factions, and neutral. If you're in America continents, stay neutral or join the allies. If you're anywhere else, you're going to be a major power. Stellaris is different.
Stellaris will offer a lot more diplomatically than most games I have seen. A chance to play a game of back door deals, subterfuge, or straight up annihilation. The ability to creat a faction- Federation as it is named, is a very powerful tool, or is it. One thing that sticks out the most as I play this is that the why diplomacy is very open ended, and free to choose, the AI is not, The AI as in most games is programmed to see you fail. Not just the enemies, which would make sense. Even the allies, I am finding that they often go out of their way to find little bits and pieces. Conveniently placed political changes withing moments of my success that throws all sense of victory out the window. And with no way to convince other nations to say. un-rival others, the federation system is broken even further by making territory gain, by federation, impossible after a certain point. This leaves federation victory a no go.
Aggressive playing, what I noticed is if you take an aggresive trait set, you get curb stomped. If you are not outright destroyed, you are automatically vassalized to avoid this. I am not quite sure if that means an instant loss in the long run, because I am usually wiped out trying to free myself later on. In addition to that, it usually happens by powerful neighbors, even with advanced neighbors off.
One last bone to pick, this applies to both aggressive and federation players. When a crisis comes into play, or your federation goes to war, the AI take al their fleets, and majority of the time hide in the back of the territory. My first game I ever played, I fought the Unbidden. I spent the next week trying to figure out what those guys were, but what I learned in game, was defenders of the galaxy, lots of armour, and kinetic weapons destroyed them. I managed to roll a solid 50k fleet and push them back to their main gate, and then watch 150k pop out. Took a bit longer to figure the anchors out. That aside, I had two different factions engaging me in war, so I was juggling the unbidden, recolonizing during the lull of their spawn time, and the two enemy nations attacking me. In the case of my federation going to war, this situation is most prominently done by the actualy nation starting the war. Every ten seconds, they would vote to engage in the war. War halts all diplomacy, pretty much but after about 20 revotes, I finally caved. They take all fleets under federation command, hide in back and do not enter the combat AO. My little 20k, 30k, 40k, and eventually 50k fleet kept having to engage the war mostly by myself. Mind you, I was on the opposite side of the galactic center.
Because of these issues, even the easiest difficulties are nigh impossible to achieve a vitory, if that is even an option in the coding. I highly suggest a thorough rework of the AI in this game to make it much more enjoyable than it is. No game is fun to play, if there is next to no chance at winning.

Out There Somewhere is a platformer game with a unique mechanic in the form of the teleport gun. Using this gun you fire a shot that when it hits a wall, will teleport you there, as is its name. Sounds simple, yes? But not so, no. The things that you can do with it are many, which you will find as you figure it out to get past levels. Never did it feel like the game was impossible, though frustrating certainly (lot of it self inflicted). The experience was quite good.
Pros: Unique mechanic, good art style, acceptable level of difficulty.
Cons: Lack of any real story beyond good guy chasing bad guy (see those guys on the cover art? you'll only ever see each one once except the main character and throwaway alien NPC's), my own gripe on the short delay on firing your teleport gun after using the gauss gun (your basic pew pew, nothing fancy), and that you're given a health bar of sorts despite it being redundant as you'll always die in one hit (exclusion being the bullet hell shooters, but those are literally a game apart from each other)
Verdict, play it. I'd say get it on sale, but if you're a fan of platformers than it's not a bad purchase full price.

A pleasure mixture of teamwork and artwork. This game follows the competitive format with a precise edge and balances between casual players and competitive players alike. While some people insist this game is a copy or clone of an existing, not to be mentioned, game, I can assure you, it is not. It has similarities, such as an ability system and a class limitation system per game, but other than that, this game is unique in its own manner. The characters each bring a different aspect to the table, and with a limited team of five players, you really need to make the decision to either play your style and the champion that you've grown to master, or play a different champion to fill in the holes no one else wants to. I've seen entire teams of Flanks and I've been apart of an a entire Support team, both of which have been successful. Why, you may ask? Because we were working together, in a team-based game. Most team-based games nowadays are split between people who want all the glory, and leave everyone in the dust; or people who don't know how to even aim a gun correctly and expect the rest of the team to defend them. These games exist, these people exist, but we need to work with them eventually. This game is about teamwork, and while a good composition is excellent, it is rare. I've had to give up my wants to play my favorite classes, in an attempt to fill in the holes of a team many times. And each time, I enjoy it because I'm learning something new. I am also enjoying the world the developers have built. Each map is masterly crafted, each character and artwork brilliantly sculpted. As an audio engineer, I shiver over the beautiful sounds this game produces, crisp and clean, clever and complicated. The world this game offers, is a sight to behold in and of itself. Sure, this game needs work. It needs balances, reworks, fixes. All games do... but at least this game is fun to play while those bugs exist. Some games are unplayable, but this one manages to push past that. If you manage to play this game, getting past the sour communities that exist, getting past the obvious issues, it is a worth while game that can be very rewarding. This game has a lot of potential, and I've enjoy each second of each hour playing it, especially with friends. (And did I mention, its free? That should be benefit enough. Just try it out, with damages, and determine for yourself, if this game has potential. You can read all these reviews you want, but in the end, it is your choice. Make it good, enjoy the game, see you in the Realm!)

How to run Dungeon Siege on Windows 7/8/8.1 that will fix flickering and tearing
STAGE 1: Configure your graphic card setting via graphic card control panel
1. Open your graphic card control panel
2. Go to 3D setting
3. Add "dungeonsiege.exe"
4. Disable or turn off any 3D enhancement
5. Click "Apply"
STAGE 2: Edit Steam Game Launcher
1. Open Steam
2. Right Click on Dungeon Siege
3. Select Properties
4. Uncheck "Enable Steam Overlay while in game"
5. Click "Set Launch Option..."
6. Enter this string
bltonly=true width=1366 height=768
Note: You change the width and height base on your system resolution
7. Click "Ok"
8. Create desktop shortcut"
STAGE 3: Edit ini file
1. Right click on Dungeon Siege shortcut on desktop
2. Open File Location
3. Run DSVideoConfig.exe
4. Select any graphic card that dont have TnL
5. Click OK
6. Double click on DungeonSiege.ini
7. Select the first line and copy
8. Go to your Document folder
9. Open Dungeon Siege folder
10. Double click on DungeonSiege.ini
11. Select the first line and paste
12. Save
Stage 4: Edit Video Option ingame
1. Run Dungeon Siege
2. Select Options
3. Change Shadow setting to "None"
4. Select OK

Stage 1 & 4 = Razali Rambli
Stage 2 & 3 = Various source from internet

The classic dungeon crawler lives!  Dungeon Siege remains one of the most dynamic, engaging and complex games in its genre and it plays smoother than ever on Steam.  Do not hesitate on this.  The price is great, even when it isn't on sale, and stands high among modern Dungeon Crawlers like Torchlight 2 and Diablo III.  If you are a fan of the genre, this is a must-play.
Leveling is smooth and effortless, requiring little maintanence, as skills and stats level through use.  You start as a blank slate, and as you use weapons and spells, your stats and your proficiency in those attack types increases automatically, similar to something like modern Elder Scrolls games.  It's a fluid and fun style.  Add to that the strategy element of having AI-controlled companions fighting alongside you, who can take commands or be set up in formations with proiorities and focuses that you choose based on their stats, with a number of optional playable units to hire from towns and dungeons.
This is a fast game, too.  It has all the challenge you would expect from an entry in the genre and encourages exploration and experimentation as you progress through the game.  Do not hesitate to invest in this title.  It is one of the greatest PC games of all time and remains one of my all-time favorite Dungeon Crawlers of all time!

I'm very happy with this game. I got it based on the visulas alone, and it turned out to be exactly what I wanted. It's fun, magical, and enjoyable to explore. Treeker does plenty of things right  but at the same time I felt the game was underwhelming. The game itself is gorgeous, using vibrant colors and visual effects perfectly. Combining these with the reality shifting glasses adds a whole new layer of visuals. Where things begin to fall apart are the puzzles themselves. The puzzles are rather easy and most of your time is spent traveling through the large areas in the first part of the game, more then actually puzzle solving. The difficulty does kick up but it does in the wrong areas, specifically the platforming aspects to the game, which doesn't really work. Why? Cause the first person view of the game is very limiting when it comes to platforming so all those breath taking visuals go away when your staring at your feet, trying to make the right jump. On the other hand some of the puzzles do work very well, the Morse code puzzle was cleverly done.
Other areas like music, game bugs,  narrative/story telling take a hit as well. The story is almost instantly abandoned as you start the game up. Music seems to cut off and repeat itself quite frequently. Despite the troubles though, I had fun with Treeker. I was entertained by the unique sights and some puzzles were fun. The game has many good ideas and plenty of potential, it just needs more content. The glasses/shifting visuals are not enough to carry the game and it ends up being a one trick pony. Thankfully more content for the game is on the way sometime soon and I am excited to see what the developer has cooked up. In all its a impressive display for a (I believe) one person development team.

First impression:

instead: it has no precision jumps, but it does have inhabitants you can relate to, and it was actually fun exploring.

There is a mundane irony in how Treeker: The Lost Glasses manages to be so unfocused while being designed around an object whose function is to create clarity.
I can’t decide if Treeker’s messy collection of badly implemented concepts is the result of the developer lacking a proper vision for their game, or simply thinking it was far more clever than it actually is. As best I can tell its biggest aim was to transport you into its highly saturated low-poly world, but it abandons exploration and environmental storytelling almost immediately in order to draw your attention toward a basic puzzle or tedious platforming section. The way Treeker is designed – with little pockets of interactivity stretched out across a wide landscape – causes it to feel very small and disconnected from itself. There’s no continuity to its environments, no history or life of any kind to be found among the odd floating structures and technology that’s only ever there when it’s needed for some mechanic.
I spent almost all my time with Treeker jumping around random platforms to unlock the portal needed to take me to the next set of suspended blocks, occasionally being fed a line regarding time, the universe, and how I could somehow cross boundaries with my new pair of spectacles. Any attempt at exposition however was drenched in so much self-obsessed philosophical nonsense that it was hard for me to care about why anything was ostensibly happening as my eyes had already glazed over before Treeker could finish a sentence.
There’s just way too much and too little going on here and Treeker has no better idea how to make sense of it than I do, resulting in it all getting tossed into a blender and spat back out into blobby slabs of content held together by their shared insubstantial meaning. Once the end begins to come around (at about an hour or so for me) Treeker was practically begging me not to leave, forcing me through abhorrently designed platforming levels for no purpose but to kill me a couple dozen more times before I could finally brute force my way through and be rid of the game. With that in mind I couldn’t help but laugh when I returned to the main menu to be told more content was on the way, a final effort from a game that was already trying too hard.

Treeker: The Lost Glasses.
First of all, I'd like to say this is quite a pretty game, and I enjoyed to some extent the sort of game this is. But, it's definitely not to everyone's taste. Yes, it's short (just over 2 hrs for me), it's graphically clean (reminds me of some of the Legend of Zelda games, but some areas are a bit too dark to enjoy properly), and the music isn't too bad (although maybe not varied enough), the game had bigger problems.
My single gripe could stem from the fact that it doesn't fall into a single category or genre. While that may not be a bad thing, what I mean to convey is that it is trying to have everything (except shooting) - it has the first person, casual, exploration, zen, platform, puzzle, platform, [hard-core rage quit], calm down and retry platform, hidden object, collect and return quest (rpg?), platform, platform, did I say platform?
If you didn't like games such as the 3D Rayman games, or Jak & Daxter, you may be put off by the abundance of platforming. Personally, I think the first person view in this game makes that even harder. You will die. Lots in my case. As someone else mentioned - don't jump down onto that moving platform, you will die! You will also miss platforms, because distances appear hard to judge sometimes. Then again, if you do like platforms, there is honestly not enough to enjoy about the other elements of this game - it's just not fulfilling enough.
To sum up - this starts out really peaceful, but things get crazy with the platforms. And it's too short. The pretty world in the beginning doesn't make up for the lack of stuff to do, and the excess platforming.
I don't want to flat out say No to this game, but given it's problems, I can't recommend it to most people either, due to there being so many games out there that are either more fun with either puzzle-platforming or zen/exploration.

Like any good "B" movie, headless bodies will geyser gallons of blood, burning people flail about and scream, people will stare stupidly at their bloody stumps and just fall over, and so on. Just like gory cartoons, if you shoot someone in the face, their eyes and brain will just . . . hover in place and still function.
Best part? THE GUNS! So many different parts to customize with, and level up by spending the in-game money! You want a five-rocket shooter that fires sticky fire bombs? Done. A gatling gun that fires sub-sonic rounds? Done. A pulse rifle that shoots laser-guided plasma balls that bounce around corners? Done. A laser cannon that shoots a pillar of scalding light that HEALS your people? Done.

Too simple, too little.
You'll find better hero defense style games elsewhere.
The premise has always been simple: Each player grabs a hero, and starts killing the incoming waves, defending one or more central structures, while managing time, inventory and a few skills.
And Bloodsports brings nothing new to the table.
And that's just it. There's nothing new. This is nothing that hasn't been achived in various other games as mods. It's simply a standalone version with it's own price tag.
The heroes in this game (10 of them) each have 4 buttons to press, each rather simple in implementation: self-buffs, power attacks, teleports and so on. Again, nothing new.
And so goes the list of each feature: Quite nice, but nothing new and exciting.
Final verdict: Grab another game with a Hero Defense mod/map. That will bring you the same game + whatever the basis game brings.

A spin on the old classic Hero Defence popularised in Warcraft 3. The game truly plays best in a group as unlike previous Hero Defence games you can’t just stack all agility and solo the whole game. There’s a good variety in items and heroes to use, with a decent number of maps to keep things from getting to stale. You also have to do combat with elite and boss minions who actually reward skill through dodging abilities and using your abilities and classes effectively. In saying that the bosses are quite bland and poor AI and pathing leads some silly situations.
Outside of the core gameplay there is some humour and some callouts to the original game “Krater”. There is some external progression that is a little questionable but it being a PVE game is can get away with it. There is an endless mode and a leaderboard so there really is never ending content if that’s your kind of thing. I highly advise to get your friends into this game or make some, it can be hard at times to find people.
I can recommend it, especially at this price (yo that 5 pack :O). It’s a nice PVE multiplayer experience that is really lacking today in the gaming scene.

This is a great little game! Very short (I beat it in under 1 hour), but it was very enjoyable, while it lasted.
The visuals are nice, and so is the music. Nothing new in these 2 aspects, but they're faithful to the games that inspired this game and they're well done!
The game has one main mechanic, and then some variations that support it. The mechanic is simply a teleport gun. You shoot a pellet that teleports you to it when it hits a wall. That's it.
Despite its simplicity, though, it changes movement just enough to be "surprising", in some way, reaching escape velocity from "generic platformer".
The level design is pretty good, always pushing you to use what you've learned about the teleport movement, instead of presenting normal platforms. There are also details spread throughout the game for speedrunners, which gives it another layer for those interested.
The one complaint I have is that it is too easy, for the most part. There are hidden health-ups and armor for your ship, but these are mostly inconsequential to the game, so they're there for the extra challenge. Which is ok! The problem is that the game locks you out very often.
You cross a certain section, and then you can't go back. This is a bit annoying, since the upgrades seen in one screen may require you to go around from another screen to get. So you may keep pushing forward, looking for the path, and then realize you can't go back... oops.
Since the game is 1 hour long, this is not really a problem? But it's not optimal either, I would have prefered the other way.
Anyway. Not much more to be said. It's not groundbreaking, but it's a very enjoyable title if you're looking for something quick, but still good!

It's about time I gave this a review, considering how strongly I feel abou it. Just finished another playthrough of it, and I have to say that this game had me on a leash for my entire playtime. It could practically toy with my emotions at will, and has. And ninety percent of that comes from the writing, which is humorous, but still touching.
While I can't give too much away (you might be tired of hearing that, sorry), I can say the characters are memorable and well-rounded, the world building is fantastic, and the twists always had me. That's probably the number one thing that will stand out about this game; the major twists (which you certainly won't find within one playthrough).
There are flaws, and I should be outright about them. While the character design is, as I said, memorable, and the color scheme really pops, the pixel art itself is not the best. It's not always easy to interpret what you are looking at. And while the writing is still great, sometimes it gets into weirder territory, which annoyed me a little. It also does go a little too far with what it's trying to do sometimes.
The gameplay also has a unique twist on the RPG formula as well. Rather than leaving things to chance, Undertale judges your hits on a simple quick time event, and allows you to simply avoid enemy attacks. On top of that, you also have the option to spare an enemy, if you can figure out how to calm them down. This means that every enemy encounter is a moral choice, and while that's usually a bad thing, here it completely works, due to, again, the writing. I found myself not wanting to kill these monsters after a short while, even though it raises your LV thus giving you more health. Still, sparing monsters becomes more and more difficult as time goes on, as does avoiding taking damage. It does get tiring sometimes, but the formula is shaken up from time to time.
Overall, it had me absorbed from beginning to end, and I highly recommend it for the story alone, on top of the gameplay that manages to mesh with the plot so well.

What is the SECRET of Monkey Island? Well your going to have to figure that out yourself. But one thing that is not a secret, is how amazing this game is. Quite possibly the first adventure game I ever played and the game that got me hooked to the genre. I love the music, the humor, the storyline, and almost everything about the game. Now looking back 25 years later I do see that the game is not completely without flaw. First, the game was made in 1990 so the graphics aren't all that great and there are no voices. Second, the game is relatively short by today's standards. This is not something that bothers me and shouldn't for most people, but might to the more recent fans of adventure gaming. Luckily the Special Edition gives the best of both worlds graphically (sorry but the story is still just as short), as old fans and new fans can enjoy the game they would want to play. Because trust me, there are some old fans that would cringe at the new look. The classic version and new version can be switched seemlessly by hitting F10. The old version staying true to its ancient (voodoo?) roots of a verb menu and an inventory box. The new version many good additions added to its gameplay as the new version intoduces 3D art, voices, and a much larger screen of play (due to the fact that the verb menu and an inventory box have been removed). Although I do enjoy a much larger screen, this is the one thing about the new version I am not fond of. They do have a drop down menu for the verb menu by hitting Ctrl or V as well as one for the inventory by hitting Alt or I, but this feels like more of a hassle than the old game used to be. At the end of the day, this game is a keeper. So don the adventurer's cap and become "Guybrush Threepwood, mighty pirate!"
Check out my other point and click adventure reviews on my page!

Welcome back, Guybrush Threepwood! You're the stupidest/best pirate around!
Quite literally a dream come true for me, and I'm sure many others.
Secret of Monkey Island, and LeChuck's Revenge, were a couple of the games that defined my childhood.
Many hours as a kid were spent playing, and watching my sister play, as we tried to figure out the silly and sometimes ridiculous puzzles, to progress without the aid of guides, because the internet wasn't quite as available as it is these days.
So words can't express my happiness when these remakes kinda came out of nowhere!
The characters are all memorable, and the humour never gets old, and while the Special Edition remade graphics are great, sometimes you just can't beat the good old pixely memories of Lucas Arts adventures, so it's awesome that this version of the game(s) actually lets you switch between the two graphical styles at the simple press of a button!
The voice acting may seem a little jarring for those very familiar with the original games, but it's well done and not as out-of-place feeling as I thought it might be. But even that can be turned off if you're more of a reader, and/or don't like the voices!
Overall, a VERY worthwhile investment for those looking for some nostalgia, but not just wanting to buy the same game again. This is not just a simple cash grab, it's very clear that time and effort went into this Special Edition (and the one for LeChuck's Revenge), and it kept me smiling from start to finish, just like it always used to.

Come on, it's a classic. It's one of the most famous staples of the peak of the adventure game genre, and one of the reasons why Tim Schaefer is considered a deity in the games industry. Of course it's good, and of course you should play it.
That said, this particular update has its flaws. Most of the new art is great, but there are a couple of instances where it isn't, and it sticks out. Most prominent of these is how stupid Guybrush's head looks. The UI is kind of a step backwards. The simplified point and click works fine in newer games that really only have 2-3 verbs, but since they preserved all 9 verbs from the original game (a good decision, IMO, for faithfulness alone), scrolling through them with the mouse wheel or using keyboard shortcuts isn't as nice as having them all on screen in the original game.
But you can switch between the new mode and the completely untouched original version (technically it's the CD version as opposed to the Floppy Disc version, but if you care about that distinction, you probably already own this version), so honestly, what's there to complain about?
It's fun, it's funny, just play it already.
