i played through in one sitting, and i absolutely intend to play through it again to see the other character paths. i literally could not turn it off until i found out what was going to happen next. Over and over again....  The plot turns super serious kind of abruptly, which made it feel all sudden and scary (in a good, immersive way) and made it even harder to turn off.
The writing is great, very engaging and often laugh-out-loud funny. Important, since Hustle Cat is more like reading a book than playing a game. Which is also great as far as i'm concerned. The art is nice, and has just the right mix of stylized and realistic aspects for the tone of the game.  The characters are interesting, well rounded, and distinctly individual. The game does a great job of immersing you in the community of A Cat's Paw.  And the cats are cute. Since presumably you like cute cats if you want to play this game... A thoroughly enjoyable game. i can't say much more about what i liked without massive spoilers.
i don't think i would really describe this as a dating sim however, since you don't get a ton of choices that affect your relationship. The relationship path you are on dictates most of that and there doesn't seem to be a way to change paths after you start down one. i didn't mind too much.
In the interest of balance, things that were less great:
i wish the game lasted longer. Granted i am a very fast reader, but it took me less than 3 hours to complete. There were some "and then time passed" parts that i feel like could have been fleshed out with more interactions and dialogue, even if it was just mundane working-at-a-cat-cafe and getting-to-know-your-coworkers stuff. Replay value seems high, though.
There is a bit of railroading, and the way you answer a couple questions very early in the game (before you even know what's going on) have a profound effect on the plot that you get to follow, and there does not seem to be a way to change your path once you are on it. This is sort of a mixed thing... a bit frusterating, but i think it will improve the replay value.
Most (like 95%) of the music is great, but there were some auto-tuney parts that made my ears sad. i don't like high pitched music though, so it might be fine for most people.
MINOR SPOILER!
Breaking the curse happens too suddenly, and without enough explination of what is happening, at least in the first path i followed (Landry). It felt a little anti-climactic, though it isn't the end of the game.
SPOILER OVER!
In summary: This game is not perfect (few are), but i really enjoyed it and would reccommend it without hesitation to anyone interested in visual novel type games. And cats. It definitely lived up to my hopes/expectations for it.

Hustle Cat is one of the best dating sims I've ever played, and I have played quite a bit in my time. What makes this one stand out especially is the main character (The character you play as), Avery Grey. Although you can't choose a name for them, you can have the choice of being called he, her, or them. That type of thing is always a breath of fresh air for someone like myself who constantly goes between female or other. Another positive thing about Avery is that he/her/they are not and idiot! Most dating sims have characters who always seem to lack common sense or are pushovers, not Avery. There were very few times where you were left thinking that the main character was an oblivious dumbass.
Next, the dating characters. There are no genderless dating options, but you can pick between either boys or girls. There is some speculations on at least one of them being trans, but that's not at all mentioned in the game, so don't get your hopes up. There is a wide variety of personalities and physical features, so no one looking for a hot computer date will feel left out. They are all also super cute.
Overall, this game kept me guessing. The thing I thought going into this game instantly changed once the first playground was over (in a good way). I would highly recommend this game for any dating sim/otome lovers out there.
Also, Reese is the best. <3 <3 <3

RS2 felt unfinished at release, like either Antimatter got rushed or got lazy, and to add to that it took them 6 months to add any new maps.
Something TWI has always been good about is releasing free content, and I appreciate that. But again, with the Australian update, it feels like Antimatter got lazy or they just have a small budget. Someone playing as a machine gunner or sniper who just sits back isnt going to actively provide artillery marks or act as a mobile spawn point. Plus they no longer have smoke which is key to advancing on objectives as attackers. The smoke has been passed to radiomen and scouts which is ok but not ideal IMO.  Lastly the radio man class is handy but not tactically paramount like in Day of Infamy nor is radioman really that fun to play due to the class' limited loadout. This game could really shine but it still needs some polish, which I doubt it will ever receive.

Loadout is a hilarious game with a deep weapon customisation system. It's flawed yes. Some combinations are overpowered. But its still mad and stupid fun. I still remember the first time I died and my character lifted up his middle finger right before he died. Then there's the microtransactions. You can buy cosmetic stuff or gun parts. So its not unfair. Most of the time.
THE GOOD
1. Deep weapon customisation. You'll always see a variety of weapons being used in a match.
2. Taunts! Yeah you can dance over someone's body after he dies.
3. Matchmaking is quite fast. Players are always there. Ping is low too. They have Asian, North American and European servers.
4. Constant updates. The developers respond to any bugs you find. They're nice people.
5. You can run around naked. Enough said.
6. Not pay to win. You can earn blutes (in game currency) real fast.
7. Hilarious at times. Mindless fun.
THE BAD
1. There's hackers in the game. I saw only one. But it was enough to make me angry.
2. Cosmetic options can ONLY be purchased with money. So no hipster glasses for you, stingy dude.
3. Some players who paid for the game are hilariously overpowered. Thankfully there's not a lot of them (or is that bad for the devs?)
4. Maps are few.
5. Most of the times, the guys with the best guns win. The game doesn't depend on skill that much.

I am not too familiar with other Telltale titles, nor was I hyping for this game, but I liked the idea and went ahead with it.
The game surely ISN'T impressive and life-changing, but it certainly isn't bad enough to receive THIS much hate. It's the moderate/good experience it is either because Telltale tried to add a few good elements but didn't bother to refine them, or because they limitted it with the intent of not overwhelming younger players.
Honestly, you know how Minecraft is about making up your own stories, (almost) failing, and trying to get better at it? That's what this feels like, and so the unimpressiveness is nice because of its familiarity. However, with all the potential Minecraft itself has, it deserves an actually mindblowing, highly interactive, rich and deep experience (which you definitely don't find in this story mode). Hopefully, that too will come along one day.
Pros
+ Lots of Minecraft lore and some humerous critiquing of it
+ Some interesting builds to explore
+ Branching story to make your decisions as the player count
+ You get to choose how to respond to the more unusual of developments
+ Feels like the Minecraft adventures you might go on with your friends (without the unnecessary delays obviously)
+ Adequate/good voice acting
+ Explores various emotional situations although without much depth
Cons
- No open-world stuff; just Interactive cutscenes or small maps to roam around in. Big disappointment.
- Characters aren't that deep.
- The lip-syncing - or whatever you might call it - gets annoying.
- The plot, although not so predictable and free of many loose ends, doesn't get quite thick.
Verdict: Give this game a chance, especially if you like Minecraft, but don't expect too much from it.

Anybody who gamed in the 90's will remember LucasArts' SCUMM engine which was a scripting lanuage and engine built originally for Maniac Mansion and spawned a range of highly successful "click adventure" games which never required any talent or hand-eye co-ordination to complete but the games always tested memory muscle and made you think about what you're doing and how to proceed. These games gave away very little of how you can proceed without prior consideration.
It's the tale of want-to-be pirate Guybrush Threepwood travels to Melee Island to seek his fortunes and become a pirate by completing the Three Trials. Unfortunately his timing is terrible and the pirates of the area are hiding out in the Scumm Bar to hide from the famed specter pirate Le Chuck. Guybrush proceeds to complete the Three Trials before the towns Governor is abducted and taken to a desolate location nobody wants to go to in fear of their lives. Guybrush assembles a team and travels to discover the Secret of Monkey Island and defeat Le Chuck.
Monkey Island has spawned a culture in video games, with many people contributing to the game's world and adding elements and stories. While many of these stories are officially unofficial, the user base has been growing for a very long time now.
LucasArts click adventures reminisce of my childhood. The Day of the Tentacle for example I have fond memories playing with my father in all black and white, colour, and with voices. Another game which is much longer has been re-released for Steam is Monkey Island. I remember fondly of receiving the original Monkey Island from my grandfather. Even though I never played this game with my grandfather, and he wasn't a gamer himself, I still remember the moment I received this game in its oversized box.
Like DOTT, MI is a LucasArts click adventure built using SCUMM. It's a fun and exciting classic which has been remastered with modern graphics which you can switch to classic mode to play using the original game. The ability to switch to classic mode is an exceptional feature which not only makes the game easier to play but it plays exactly like the original.
I highly recommend this game in classic mode, for those of us who have any appreciation for how games used to be, and for those of us who have watched games evolve to where they've come to. If you fall into this category, you'll truly love this game.

Now a classic and despite the series and fanfare it spawned remains undeservingly without a true spiritual successor. The reviews I've read from my peers thus far are spot on. This little Tactical-RPG was way ahead of its time. Touted as a "Diablo killer", clearly inspired by Baldur's Gate the expectations were high (to say the least) upon release.
Admitedly though and to no surprise the fledgling developer (at the time) Gaspowered Games may have bitten off more than it could chew (as the title falls short in many aspects of its predecessors). Still this shouldn't deter you from giving it a go as it is a solid piece of work from start to finish.
Unfortunately however Steam has failed to acquire the Exanpsions which contain necessary patching and multiplayer is relegated to LAN, TCP/IP, Hamachi or GameRanger. All of these options require time and effort to coordinate play with others rather than being able to just jump right in. Still if you like ARPGs give this one a chance.
It should also be noted there were many mods of varying qualities great and small including a couple of conversions such Ultima V & 6 all thanks to the dedicated Dungeon Siege Community -- should you be interested extending the experience.

This game is one of those games that might have been a technological wonder at its time but it has not aged well at all. I can only recommend it to die hard fans of hhaack & slash .
Where to start?
First of all the textures are watered down and are not pleasent to watch at all. I found myself using the overhead map just to avoid looking at those low res textures all the time.
Yes it does add that oh so fascinating idea of progressing your character by using either a weapon or a spell. The idea is very interesting at start but when you actually get to play the game over a few hours you realize that only melee chars are viable in this game. Magic and ranged are practically useless or at least utterly inferior to melee chars.
The first few maps have a really slow progression curve,which is both satisfying at first but gets absolutelly frustrating way too fast. You get too many pointless drops and too little gold to actually progres the first quarter of the game and right after the game literally starts throwing thousands of gold at you and the sense of progression is really out of the question.
All monster drops dont really mean anything because you get tons of gold to buy all the best gear from the next shop. And by gear i mean just get the weapon with most damage for your melee chars and you are good to go. All the other items are absolutely pointless.
Oh and speaking of chars,its all fun  when you have one char,and get 2-3 more..but soon enough you get a total of 8, leaving inventory management a burden. Everything you pickup is esentially worthless anyway. You only need the weapon with most damage in the next shop for each of your chars and to fill your inventory with health potions.
Yes only health potions ,because the mana potions are redundent since most of the wortwhile spells in the game cost your entire mana pool in 2-3 casts. There are several spell options but all of them are completely pointless as most of them try out a tactical point of view to a game that literally throws hundreds of mobs at you for no particular purpose.
There is no feeling of progress nor of getting the next best item.
The story is almost non-existent,battle the generic utter evil that plagues the land.
The environments are very detailed though and vary a lot,unfortunatelly both the environments and the enemies fall in the generic hack & slash creatures and zones and neither stand out.
The music is probably the best part of this game.The main theme is one of the most memorable music display in my game experience, which is both a good and a bad thing. Why a bad thing? Because there is only one god damn piece of music that  gets recycled all over the game.It is sad to see a game stand out only through its music.
Speaking of sound, the sound effects just do their job but they are utterly forgetable and lackluster as well. The voiceovers ? They almost dont exist at all which is not helping with the immersion at all.
The story is poor to say the least,itt is another generic farmer that starts out to help a friend and ends up saving the kingdom, so unique .
Getting back to gameplay. The progressing system is pretty cool as an idea as it does not limit you to a specific class.
The stats progression is insanely slow and limits the item usability tremendously. A huge amount of mage/ranger items require a high amount of strength for example,which esentially limits their use.
All this can be overlooked if it werent for the almost complete automatization of the game. You just need to run in and click in the middle of a group of mobs and the game will take care of the rest. You just need to have a potion handy from time to time,which does not make it challenging at all.
The game is overall all too tedious and it throws too many enemies at once making certain areas feel like they need an eternity to finish off
Conclusion? Dungeon Siege is awfully slow paced,non immersive and tedious to a point where you just stop caring about the quests,story and gameplay overall. We have way too many better games than this now for me to be able to reccomend this

Pros
+ Crafting on the go
+ Safehouses & garages-- lockers, wardrobe, survivor & vehicle boards
+ One big map (no areas to load between)
+ Varied enemies
+ Improved Survivors
Cons
- Easiest boss fights yet
- Occasional texture glitches
- Picking up items
There seems to be a reoccurring theme with negative reviews of this game: crashing and long load times. I have not experienced crashing outside of quitting the game so for me this hasn’t been an issue, and while the load times seem pretty standard I am really happy with them as unlike previous games DR3 takes place on one giant map instead of being split between areas. This means that after starting the game the only time you’ll see load screens are when you load a cinematic, which means you can roam the world to your heart’s content and the only pause you’ll ever take will be when you pop the pause menu, a huge plus to immersion for me!
Crafting
DR3 improves on its predecessors by improving what it does best: crafting crazy items. Nick can anywhere providing he has the parts and blueprints required, and as you level up you can make it easier still by spending points on item categories. For example, the sledge saw requires a sledgehammer and cement saw to craft, but if you’ve purchased the blunt item category you’ll be able to substitute the sledgehammer for any blunt weapon.
Safe Houses
In addition to this there are now various safe houses that you can clear to gain access to their lockers, wardrobes and survivor boards. Here you can access any item, combo weapon, clothing or survivor you have picked up or rescued which eliminates tedious backtracking and keeps the focus on exploration and fun!
The combination of the above changes were significant for me as they changed the way I play Dead Rising titles as my inventory no longer felt cluttered – I didn’t need to hang on to 2-3 items to craft when I found a bench, I’d simply combine them on the go and free up two slots, and I never felt the need to have 2-3 powerful items on hand in case one broke as it was a cinch to create something new at a moment’s notice, and this simplicity means your much more likely to use new, fun but perhaps less functional weapons more often.
Enemies
I’m really enjoying the variety of enemies in DR3. Without deviating from the standard zombie they’ve added some subtle ‘types’ that behave differently. Certain zombies are now capable of using items, some are much tougher and others have abilities that allow them to tackle you. These zombies are well hidden in the horde and have occasionally knocked me out of a rampage by tackling me to the ground. Other than this you have a few human types which you will be familiar with if you’ve played any previous games.
Survivors
Survivors were often a bit of a headache in previous games, and while they definitely still do some stupid things—blowing up cars, blocking doorways etc—they’ve been much less suicidal this time around. I personally arm them with firearms (ZAR’s) because otherwise they get too close to my reaper scythe which seems to be the only time they take significant damage, and they make quick work of hordes and bosses. Furthermore, if I’m running through one of the many massive hordes they actually keep up! Not once have I lost a survivor this way, and THANK GOD we have waved goodbye to transition areas because one of the biggest pains was losing survivors that didn’t stand close enough to the door and was left behind in the previous titles! So survivors are much better in this game, however I’d still like to have seen a mini command menu, less crowding around me in tight spaces and annoyance number 1: how easily it is to trade items when trying to pick something up!
Which brings me to…
Picking Things Up
A bit of nit-pick here but 3 games in really wish they’d address this, which is probably my main frustration: picking things up. In certain areas you’ll find yourself picking on a coat hanger instead of putting on that tuxedo shirt, or aiming at the wrong item while you try to juggle the camera in such a way that you highlight the item you actually want, and then just as you have it a damn survivor walks in front of you and you end up trading instead of picking said item up. I can only imagine this is why the jumping kick exists, and even then you get snubbed by said survivor. A better aiming system for items doesn’t seem like too much to ask!
Bosses
It could be me, but I’ve found the bosses in DR3 to be the easiest yet. I’ve not died once this time around, barely lost health and have never lost a survivor. And when I later brought survivors armed with ZAR’s the bosses literally dropped in seconds. Perhaps it will be tougher in new game+. FYI I’m playing normal mode because I enjoy the freedom that comes with the timer, I’m not sure whether nightmare provides greater difficulty or just less time, but the time’s a deal-breaker for me. I play these games for the sandbox and I feel the timer works against that, so your experience here may vary.
All in all this game has been a huge improvement over previous titles. I felt more immersed, I had more time and a never ending supply of zombies to slaughter. I would mention that I have definitely seen some texture issues here and there—disappearing shadows and road markings—but that has been a bump in my overall enjoyment of the game. The story also isn’t all that, but then that’s just Dead Rising right? Lastly, while I’ve been playing on Co-Op Completionist I’ve yet to team up with anyone in 25 hours of gameplay during opening weekend. This seems odd.
Overall this is a great game and provided plenty of enjoyment.

What I liked:
- Super glad this was put on PC to begin with -- let's not forget it was announced and advertised as a XBOXONE exclusive for the longest time.
- Definitely an improvement over Dead Rising 2 in a lot of ways. If you even liked the last game a little bit, this game will likely be a lot of fun for you as well. The game keeps that odd mix of sillyness and seriousness that the other games had.
- Playtime of about 21 hours (Did most side missions and beat the game with [S] rating within 3-4 days of the 7 day limit), with a lot of reasons to keep playing for additional fun (Bonus DLC missions, game reruns, Nightmare mode, etc). EDIT: An additional speed run-ish on nightmare mode (only did story and one or two psycho missions) granted an 8 hour playthrough. So, if you ignore everything, you can beat the game in about eight hours.
- Despite complaints from others it ran relatively fine on my system, albeit not always at 60.
What I didn't like:
- About half as many psychopaths as the last game (ish).
- Terrible issues with texture popping.
- Half the time NPCs (especially the co-op character) are invisible.
- Crashed several times in the middle of doing co-op for seemingly -no- reason. One particularly annoying crash pushed a friend of mine out of the game right as we were about to fight the final boss. I was not able to reinvite him.
- 60 FPS came and went, which kinda isn't justified for a supposedly next-gen experience. Also, shadows would often mess up completely, but that could be anything.
- A lot of people are having issues with optimization.
- Anyone who plays this game is going to learn this: Blockades are ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. Someone tell the Dead Rising team to STOP DOING THEM.
Overall, I'd recommend it, but you might want to wait to see if your computer can run it, or even just wait until it goes on sale. To me, 20h is a fine amount of first playthrough gameplay.

Overall, I found this game quite enjoyable for the most part. For an MMO, it's fast paced and enjoyable and removes grindfests for most of the game, minus a few areas. If you enjoy grinding you can still do that.
PROS:
- Fun and addictive gameplay
- Very little grinding if you don't want to
- Easy for the most part
- You can play it on your own. Solo it if you want and it will still be an enjoyable experience
- Great graphics
- A greatflexable upgrade system
- Dungeons have several different modes: solo, hard solo, group, hard group.
- Dungeons are incorporated into the quest lines
- If you're trying for a certain drop but you never get it, there's an auction house which can be used to purchase it from another player.
- The sky tower: this is what makes this MMO the SAO MMO, a 100 floor tower for raiding.
CONS:
- There have been a fair few glitches that I've come across, only one of them was game breaking but that was fixed after waiting a few days.
- When you have to grind, it will take you forever and a half to get to the appropriate level to continue the questline
- The smithing system is pretty expensive. You will find it hard to smith unless you invest money into the game for in-game currency. You can also grind to get the money but I never did because it wasn't my cup of tea.
- The sky towers opening times. With the game situated in another country, the times for the tower opening aren't the best if you're in the UK. It's only open a couple of hours a day around 12pm making it rather hard to get into during the week.
- Eidolons (the pet system) is pay to win. In the game, you can have an eidolon which servers as a 2nd party member. You have the choice of 3 different ones at the start (or more if you pay for them) and then you get more over time... Or you can just buy them. Unless you're in a guild, they can be rather hard to get in-game.
Overall, the game is good if you just wanna enjoy the storyline. I wouldn't play it for anything more than that due to it being pay to win. If you wanna invest money into an MMO, buy something like Guild Wars 2.

Summery Review: Splinter Cell Double Agent is a Third Person Action Stealth Shooter Released in 2006 as part of the Splinter Cell Series by Ubisoft and Tom Clancy. Splinter Cell Double Agent has alot of improvements from the previous title Splinter Cell Chaos Theory. The first really big Noticable Change from the previous title Chaos Theory is the graphic's. Splinter Cell Double Agents Graphics when it first released were updated from Chaos Theory but games grow old and with age comes with updates. Several of said updates added significant improvements to graphic's and added more options than before. Some other changes include new animations being added, more stability for modern system as well as compability for out-of-date systems (If your computer really is that old). Next thing players are gonna notice right off the bat when first playing Double agent is the length and difficulty of the missions. Double Agent Contains many things that no other splinter cell has one of them being the extreme length of the mission. These missions can be very comparable to the missions we seen in the original splinter cell and may take 40+ minutes to finish. The AI has gotten Tougher in this title and I found it hard to complete missions and playing on the hardest difficulty seemed nearly impossilbe due to the AI's ability to seemlessly shoot you through the wall but that is made but for by it's "Call of duty Style" 1-3 Shots results in the player dying. The game will get you through about 11 hours of total gameplay before beating the story I have owned this game for years and always find myself going back and restarting the game just to find that one area I never discovered or could never get into because it always seemed near impossible to get into without getting killed or detected. Replayability is also fun to find those computers that you may have missed or forgotten about with some splinter cell lore contained. One thing Splinter Cell Double Agent Introduced to the splinter cell Series in Unlockables. Unlockables in splinter cell double agent is obtained by completing "Star Objectives" which are usually optional objective but completeing them unlocks equipment that give the player an advantage in there undercover black operations within john brown's Army" Splinter Cell double Agent did include a CO-OP Mode with a Seperate story portrayed by the two characters from the previous splinter cell co-op Story mode but the servers were shutdown and the mode is no longer available. There is a feature in this game exclusive to double agent allowing the player to make story effecting decision's. Such Decisions will effect the Trust Meter between the NSA and the JBA. If the player allows one of these meters to expire the mission fails immediately until the player increases the expired meter. During the Beginning of the Story another Double Agent Exclusive Feature is found in the game which is Snowy enviroments. During the Beginning of the game Sam is given his "First Real Test" mission by the JBA and is taked with hijacking a supertanker Somewhere within Northern Russia and the Entire Mission is a Snow Enviroment where the player has to navigate through a blizzard and a white out which can be very difficult even when using the Goggles. Continuing on with the double agent exclusive feature, Underwater enviroments and combat. In Splinter Cell Double Agent we find a feature that is not in any other splinter cell that allows the player to swim around in water and submerge under. During the Mission to Hijack the Supertanker and the Very First mission in Island the player has the ability to surface but will be blocked by frozen water and has to cut through it to reach the surface. If there is an enemy on the ice above the player, the player has the ability to grab through the ice and pull there victim under and stab them to death. If the Victim is on an ajacent Shore by the frozen water or unfrozen even, the player also has the ability to take care of them this by pulling them off the shore and under the water.
Conclusion: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell is a pretty dated game from the Early 2000's but The game introduced alot of feature we see in Splinter Cell Conviction and Blacklist. Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell Contains many things only seen in Double Agent that I would like to see in future splinter cell titles. The Game has excellent graphics for its age. The difficulty for this game is a bit much when going into the hardest difficulty settings due to the AI being able to shoot through the walls at the player. I recommend this game I think its an excellent title and I think it brought us some great features that we see in modern titles and future titles. Some Exclusive Features such as the ability to use water as cover and a means of killing your enemy id like to see in future titles. I had alot of fun beating it years ago and still do today.

I love Primal Carnage. I played the original since release when I was 12, and I have loved it ever since. The concept is amazing, who doesn't like being a tyrannosaurus eating humans, and who doesn't like being a commando blowing raptors to bits. Extinction (now having been released for over a year now) has made a slight improvement over the old one. Better graphics, more content, bug fixes etc.
But, it has a long way to go.
The original has imo much better gameplay and actually more balanced teams, as I still play it and often win as humans. (Surprised?) The deathmatch system in the first one is much better, and is overall I'd say funner than the DM in the second one. I also like the fact (even though I am a skin collector) that no-one really cares for skins in the first one. You just load it, select a server and play. No faffing about skins, market or whining that you haven't got a feathered raptor.
That brings me on to the cons of the game. The community is lovely at most, I met some wonderful people on this game who genuinely play for the fun. However, there is that dark corner of the community that beg for skins, riddled with trollers and hackers. I do enjoy the addition of the loot system, though. The skins are remarkable, and do add that creative side to the game, with moddable features on its way. The multiple skins of the game bring pros and cons to the game.
Moving on to another con, the gameplay and the unbalance. The humans have a massive disadvantage to the dinosaurs. The shotgun for the pathfinder is way too weak, the dinosaurs don't take fall damage and the numerous amounts of tyrants each round make it hard to play as the humans. However, when you are winning as the humans, it beats the dinosaurs by a long way.

Minecraft: Story Mode. This is a spoiler-free review.
First and formost, lets speak about if it's necessary to play Minecraft to play this game. The short answer is no, you do not require any experience whatsoever with Minecraft to play this game. In the few crafting parts, there is an option to the bottom right that shows you the recipe you must use to aquire the item you're attempting to obtain. Although it does feel as if we are playing in the Minecraft universe, this is something I thought was very important to point out.
The Story follows a character named Jesse. At the beginning of the game, it offers you six options, in which you get to pick from three skins for each gender. Although I cannot say much about the story itself without spoiling how the plot unravels, the game follows Jesse (you) and a couple of side characters, each joining you according to your decisions. The game centers around these decisions. What made the story fascinating to me was mostly the characters, for they were the ones who made this game truly enjoyable. Often I'd find myself thinking I was watching a movie, and laughing or chuckling at these characters as they have a funny script, and amazing personalities.
For the characters, and how the story is unraveled to us slowly, I'll give this a fine 9/10. The story could've been better, but the characters are the ones who truly made rise to this.

Minecraft: Story Mode's gameplay is very similar to The Walking Dead season 1 and season 2 from Telltale games aswell. You have very simple controls, the typical W, A, S, D. to move, L-SHIFT to sprint, Q, and E on some occasions and in the fighting scenes you must use the Left Mouse click and Right Mouse click.
The most important factor of this whole gameplay is the decision making. If you are here for fighting scenes or even COD graphics, this is most certainly not the game for you. The game is what I could easily say 93% of the game is you in a cutscene, making choices as other characters speak to you. What I found very handy is that while making these choices, you are allowed to press Space Bar, to pause the game and think in case you are a slow reader.
There are some rare occasions in which you will be forced to fight mobs. In which you use W and S to move forward and back. Left-Mouse click to swing/shoot and Right-Mouse click to switch weapons. The A and D only play part in changing targets. This at first seemed pretty hard for me, but I got the hang of it quickly.
Each episode from the game is pretty long, but the game itself will save automatically in between cutscenes or when you're changed to free movement. There is an in the main menu in which you can search for, which is the "rewind".. This will allow you to jump back in time to one of the 6 most important points of the chapter in case you feel you did something wrong. Feel free to leave the game whenever you want, for the save system happens rather frequently.
The gameplay deserves a 10/10, for this is an easy system to learn and really enjoyable too for the right public.
At first I was gonna say the graphics on this game are not impressive, as it is already expected the game will give you blocky characters, blocky landscapes. I soon changed my mind once I saw how proper the animations were on every character, and the moment I had forgotten I was playing Minecraft: Story Mode but instead felt like I was playing the original Minecraft because the mobs look identical. I thought this was something I should highlight, considering it has great animation on their faces, since they make expressions and movements. I wouldn't have expected any more, but I sure expected a lot less. I found myself wondering if I could build these places, and also looking at the game as if it were a movie, because its animations surpassed all my expectations.
Graphics deserve a 10/10 for surpassing my expectations.
Music on this game is rather repetitive. During cutscenes I'd find myself humming to the song because it was the same one. Although I never minded the music, I found that some people would find this annoying. It does not use any music by Mojang as far as I'm concerned.
I never was a fan of music, but I liked this particular theme so I'll give it an 8/10.

For a game that's only about 3gb, it's managed to make all 3gb of repetitive grinding, expanding, exploiting, and inevitable demise work towards being an engrossing experience that’ll have you exhausted and exuberant all at once. The basic premise is that this is an rts version of the Civilization series in that you and all other empires are making their decisions simultaneously. You’ll have to make decisions on the ground level of the planets you own, tech you research, ships you build, traditions you adopt, planets you’ll soon own, and empires you’ll fight against in real time rather than in reactionary turns.
At first, it feels daunting given the spreadsheets of data they throw at you at once and the constant assault of pop-ups reinforcing your disdain towards your science ships. Rest assured, the fact that you can set the speed freely so that you can either pause to evaluate the situation, take it slow, or bull-rush through means that you’ll have every opportunity to plan out you moves and get an overview on what’s going on around you. After you master the art of pausing and seeing what the actual hell is going on, the game boils down to a simple game of balancing resources and trying to get all the numbers you see on the screen to be bigger than that of your enemy empires in order to destroy, enslave, or peacefully form a federation with.
If any issues needs to be addressed with this game it’s that the game requires a better way of teaching all the game mechanics, but this can be resolved by watching a video on it, playing with a more knowledgeable friend, or banging your head against the wall with multiple attempts at seeing whether or not you can merge one fleet of ships with another. Along with that, the game can do with reevaluating how they work the rng elements research. This can lead to some games being a slog to get through as you wait for the tech you need to be available or a stomp through all opponents because you unlocked the big bang blasters before they even found out how to put thick bits of metal to their ships. It could do with a system of early, mid, and late game research that scales to the amount of research points you have at a time.
In the end, if you utilize your empire in an efficient and wise manner, you may achieve victory in a timely manner. Either that, or run the timer until the end game crisis spawns a theoretically invincible swarm of reapers and wipes out all life in the galaxy. 9/10, would gladly spend 10hrs in a losing game again.

Ah, Stellaris. Grand space strategy at probably its finest. As opposed to the turn-based, more relaxed pace of games such as Master of Orion or Galactic Civilizations, Stellaris proceeds as a real-time game. This means that while you're instructing your ships to explore uncharted space and build mining stations, while you're figuring out which nearby planets to colonise and which to leave until later, and while you're deciding which of the various technology options would benefit you best, all the AI empires are doing exactly the same thing at the same time. AI empires - and other players, potentially. While turn-based 4x games have often had a single-player emphasis, Stellaris integrates multiplayer at the core of its experience: players can co-operate against the AIs, or turn on each other in all-out brawls to the death. Expansion at the start is deceptively calm, but once your borders are running up against those of other empires, beware! You may well be able to keep many of them sweet via diplomacy especially if their political and ethical leanings are similar to yours, but the random nature of the galaxy generation means that your pacifist democratic explorers may find themselves sandwiched between a pair of militarist xenophobes with very little way of appeasing them! Stellaris is deceptively easy to start out but turns fiendishly difficult very quickly after you start meeting other empires. And this is before you throw Fallen Empires, endgame Crises and other unpredictable events into the mix. Don't be caught on the losing side of a War in Heaven, for example: you may find things getting very uncomfortable, very fast, as the Vorlons and the Shadows - oops, sorry, I mean, two Awakened Empires - stampede across the map, allies in tow, intent on slaughtering each other to the last man/lizard/bird/tentacled monstrosity.
Stellaris is a magnificent achievement of grand strategy only made better by its various DLCs.

It may take a while to make it to the best part of the game, but once I got past that damn troll, seeing Stan brought back to life from my childhood absolutely made every moment of play worthwhile. They even got the solid checkerboard pattern right.
Naturally, even if it won't outright murder you at every turn, it's still an early 90's adventure game, full of tricky and at times non-sensical puzzles. Sometimes you have to think non-logically before something makes sense, but it all does, eventually! Power through, and you'll keep being rewarded with absurdity and dry humor that's still fresh more than 20 years later.
It's too bad the Special Edition interface was never updated to match the much superior sequel's, nor were the speech samples tightened up (they're full of long pauses and seem stilted), but it's still a good buy. They hit the comic cluelessness vibe perfectly, and really did a good job breathing new life into an old game.

And when I heard that there wasn't a damn kid needing to be fed zombrex every 2 hours, I was simply delighted.
Crafting new weapons, especially quirky, interesting weapons like these, has always had an appeal to me.
Do you like this axe? Yes. Like it better with fire? No. How about a voice that says quirky videogame one-liners? Sure!
Teddybear with a machinegun that you can put on a wheelchair to act as a mobile turret, lightning / ice / fire staff, blow up zombies with your voice...
All in all, I think the game is fun, but not that engaging. I log in, kill my fill of zombies and quit the game. I think it would've been a lot better without the constant threat of time running out, but I guess otherwise, people would never play the boring storyline.

I think if I had played this game when it first came out I'd have been more into the game, so as a fair warning, this review is from a gamer here and now only recently playing this game.
So what are it's problems?  Bloated loot system with no town portal to sell said items, a difficulty step missing between normal and easy (easy is too easy and normal is punishing even at higher levels), scant story and an enviromnment that obscures almost every monster to come your way.  The game almost plays better being constantly on the map rather than the normal top down game mode, the party member's battle AI is atrocious, the pathing is specious at best.  Traps are either very deadly or inconsequential with no in-between.  The textures of everything blend into a hodge podge.  The battles do better than constant pausing (a la Baldur's Gate), which can be done at any time, but is really only suitable for corner cases.
Basically, any advancement that had happened since this game was released casts a pall over the game which I think would have been much more revolutionary at the time than it is now.  It's old school and not in a fun, engaging way, but more of an, "I'm only hanging out watching my guys fight just in case I need to press the 'heal' or 'mana' keys" or "I said kill the freaking wizard/cleric that keeps ressurecting the monsters, you dolts!" kind of experience.
Loved it, wish there was more to it though.

Dungeon Siege is a pretty solid Action RPG in the vein of Diablo. Although it requires some coaxing to get functional on a modern OS it has aged remarkably well and mainly only suffers from somewhat wonky controls (which get worse when you've more party members to manage), a rather awkward camera, and some exception crashes; though in my case that last one plagued the bandit cave area so horribly that it effectively ended my campaign, so your mileage may vary.
The graphics are still pretty passable and in some cases still quite beautiful, no complaints aside from character display UI issues in the inventory screen probably caused by playing on a higher resolution than the game was designed for. Throughout the game, a fairly dark, earthy theme is most-often employed.
The game features an excellent, genre-appropriate, soundtrack composed by Jeremy Soule (
,
,
...) but has some weird sound effects issues wherein an item drop sound may play when no items are dropped. Some basic, often unconvincing, voice acting is employed for important characters.
A pretty standard fantasy storyline that doesn't really stand out in any way, although it's not unbearable, it is very linear and can get boring pretty quickly, making it hard to play for extended periods of time. Characters are very basic, as seems very common amongst Action RPGs.

*WARNING*
If you want to get this this game you will need to download the Gentlemen of the Row mod. This has a patch that fixes the PC port and adds a few extra mods that makes the game even more insane than it already is.
Now the review:
STORY
This game has the best story in a Saints Row game in the entire franchise. Reason being is that it keeps a level balance between the serious and the wacky which makes the crazy moments even more special because they aren't being shoved is you're face constantly.
Don't get me wrong, I still like Saints Row 3&4 but they don't take themselves as seriously as this one dose.
PRESENTATION
Since this game came out in 2009
the graphics have dated a fare bit (Jony Gat's face looks like it has been smacked in the face with a shovel with a angry face drawn on it) but there are far worse looking games on the market these days. There are also quite a few problems with the cutscenes as well. Some of the items don't connect to some of the characters hands so you get some situations where the protagonist is threatening someone with a gun that's floating inside the person he/she is threatening.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is very fun but can get a bit too easy later on in the game when you do enuf challenges to get infant ammo with the OP machine pistols. Speaking of the challenges they are just as fun as the main game itself. These challenges can range from escorting hookers to pretending to be a cop shooting down attack helicopters with a minigun and it makes you want to compliant al the levels on these mini games so you can get the perks that come with complicating them (except the fire quad bike challenge. That can go swim in a pool filled with battery acid). The character customisation is insanely deeper than any other in the series. Not only is there multiple layers of upper body options, but you can even customise the angle that you have your hat on your head. I did my first play through as a fat, big bearded lumberjack with a cowboy hat and tutu that duel welds katanas and tells people to F#%K OFF.
CONCLUSION
Even though the game can get easy at time and is a bit dated it is still one of the best open world games out there. Just remember to install the mod I mentioned at the start otherwise you will want to gouge your eyes out with a ice cream scooper in rage.

5/10 (or possibly 6/10)
While I do appreciate the work that went into
, its flaws make me regret paying £15. Perhaps I will feel differently after I complete all the routes but I am not so sure. This is due to two issues: there is a great amount of overlap during the first half of the game and during the second half your ability to make choices dramatically decreases. I think that on Finley's I only had one chance to engage with the story once I had her attention. I think that some voice acting would have inclined me towards more of an acceptance of the asking price.
The plot is definitely fun. Again, I won't know all of it until I do the final unlockable path. However, I think it's fair to assume that it will not be built on much further. This is disappointing as while there is a fair story duration for your first jaunt, much of it will be taken up by that repeated text I mentioned. The skip function isn't as fast as I would have hoped for and there's not an option to only skip what you've already read. I'd love to see a second title involving the same background, only with a less lengthy "introduction" phase.
A part of
I really despise is the music. It's repetitive and, for me, highly distracting. I can't read with it on. Without the BGM, the game is mostly quiet. It would have been nice to enjoy ambient noises and perhaps increased sound effects.
I found the art to be both amusing and cute. Special full-screen moments diverging from the usual backgrounds were a treat.
Being able to chose your preferred pronouns is refreshing. You have the choice of three feminine avatars with varying skin tones and three masculine ones. They're still fairly androgynous. Your customisation may be quite limited aesthetically but it is still a welcome touch.
It's possible that I might have more to add later, I'm not sure. I
enjoy the game but I'm not sure I'm particularly drawn to replay it any time soon, having attempted to do so after completing my first route.
Either way, I laughed and I smiled. That's got to count for something.
[Conclusion:] A great deal of potential which may not have been completely realised and perhaps a little overpriced in comparison to other titles of the same quality here on Steam. If you're a visual novel or dating sim addict like myself you will probably enjoy the experience. I imagine you'll enjoy it best if you catch it on discount/in a bundle, or you receive it as a gift.

The Secret of Monkey Island is a very classic and revolutionary game. Although it was made in the 90s, it will always be a brilliant game, and this special edition shows that it can even stay up to date with modern video games (Although you can never beat the classic graphics).
The Secret of Monkey Island series is one of the most funny games series that I have ever played, with the brilliantly weakened forth wall, and the cute child-like innocence of Guybrush Threepwood, every time I replay a Monkey Island game I cannot help but to laugh at the jokes and the little references, and every time I replay it, I always find new brilliantly absurd commands and interactions.
The special edition of this game is in some aspects an improvement, but in most, quite a disappointment. The inventory is different, there's voice acting, the Stump Joke is missing and a few more differences. The special edition shouldn't be thing to deter you from buying, or from not buying this game. If you don't like the notion of a special edition, and would rather the classic, floppy disk version, you shouldn't let that stop you from buying this version, quite a lot of the special edition factors can be turned off and, apart from the missing Stump Joke, not much else was changed. If you love modern, newer games, and feel that old games are in the past, you should still not let that stop you from buying this game, for the special edition has updated the game to look sleek and new, and if you cannot stand having to read dialogue, just turn on the voice acting.
The Special vs Classic edition aside, the dialogue in Money Island is very funny, Guybrush Threepwood constantly breaks the forth wall, so much so, that by the time of the second game, you would have forgotten that it was ever there. There are lines of dialogue that are just so perfect in the game, that you simply cannot help but to pick, sometimes it is Guybrush Threepwood saying he wants to be a fire-fighter (instead of a pirate) or him asking if two brothers are his mother. The plot of the game is not that thick and at some times it barely even makes any sense. But the love story in the whole series of Monkey Island games is the cutest love story you could ever see, with the stupid, innocent Guybrush, and the strong, independent Elaine, why they are even together boggles the best of the fans.
There are many good things about The Secret of Monkey Island, but one big factor that cannot be turned off or on is the difficulty. This game is very, VERY hard, because it is an old fashioned point and click game, it has absurd logic, Guybrush Threepwood cannot reach something a few metres off the ground and thinks that if he mixes red flowers with meat it will poison it, also somehow he is able to use a kitchen pot as a helmet....  The game thus feels as if it goes on forever when you play it, whether you spend ages pondering over a specific puzzle, executing trial and error, or you have a walkthrough up in a tab, trying to not overuse the hints, you will spend quite a bit of time on the game. Sometimes it is merely a simple puzzle that with stitch you up, or maybe it will be the whole game, either way, I heavily recommend having some sort of hint system or walkthrough handy, just in case.
I would heavily recomend this game to you, even if you are a very serious person, the humor is not all there is to this game, it has a brilliant soundtrack and very difficult puzzles, and on a whole is quite an enoyable game.

No idea who would read this because of how reviews are posted on Steam, but here I go.
It's a good controller and I recommend it, but, you will need to get used to it slowly. Not because of the touch controls. That part feels rather well and easy to get used to, but if you have been using other pads, this one has it's buttons on slightly different places and you may press buttons you don't want at first until you get your bearings.
As for what you can do with this pad, well, you can configure it for anything. Now your mileage may vary and you may have a better experience in some types of software than in others. The controller configurator is robust and can set your buttons , stick and track pads in a lot of ways. You can set all trackpads, sticks and triggers to pretty much anything and configure their sensitivity and behavior with a multitude of tools. As you browse the configurator, you will learn from easy to read instructions and descriptions of each function. Then you can save your edited config. Now, it's highly recommended to learn to use the config maker because not everything you use will have a config out there for you to download and that you may like, though the community has already released amazing configs for pretty much every big and not so big game out there.
One thing I liked was that you could set your track pad to mouse while at the same time pressing a button of your choice for as long as you are touching the pad. I used this for MMOs where you are forced to hold a mouse button to move the camera.
Another thing that bought me was that you can make your trackpad keep moving, for example, turning a camera around, as you hold the edge of it after you run out of space as you slide your thumb around it. So you won't have to lift your thumb, get it back to center, and slide again.
Last thing I want to talk about is the fact that also on the track pad, you can set an imaginary ring to have an extra button press around the edge. So you can make it press a set of buttons towards the center, and another button at the edges. For now it only allows for one button. Maybe the future will bring more functions to that.
Anyway, in the end, this controller has pretty much replaced my old ones almost completely. So while it's not a perfect thing, it has a strong configurator and with some practice the pad shape will become second nature. Good job, Steam.

Games tested:
Skyrim
Borderlands 2
Guild Wars 2 (yes, I use an Xbox controller mapped with Xpadder to play this regularly)
First problem is the size. I'm a 5' 4" female and I can't comfortably reach all the buttons without some serious wrist rotations. Using the controller very quickly caused fatigue and pain in my right wrist especially. It seemed like I had to rotate my wrist a full 45 degrees to reach the A and X buttons. After pressing one of these buttons (if I hit the correct one without looking down) returning my thumb to the track pad would usually lose my place or would reposition my camera to a place that I did not want/expect. It made for an overall frustrating experience.
The second problem was mapping out the keys. I've used programs like Xpadder to map my Xbox controller with great success, but the Steam options felt unnecessarily complicated and unintuitive. This was further exacerbated by the fact that anything I ran from the Big Picture would crash my computer.
The quality of the product is nice though. I think they could have made the touch pads smaller and swapped the positions so that they lined up with the positions on an Xbox or PlayStation controller it would have been better. Using a touchpad versus a joystick was weird, but I could definitely see myself getting used to it if I were able to use it for longer periods of time.
Unfortunately, aside from the touchpads, there was nothing about the controller that isn't already available and done better with other controllers and software already on the market.

I have been playing with the Steam Controller for the past 3 days and here are some of my thoughts about it, hopefully that will give you some more information to consider if you are looking into buying one.
Its strongest suit is its customizability. It has a few more buttons (the back grips) than your average X360 controller and its touchpads are really powerful in certain games. You can basically mix and match different control schemes to fit your gaming purposes, the level of details you can go down is very deep. For example, I have tried playing Rocket League with it and have to say it is really great compared to playing with M+KB, the back grips were really useful. Not to mention the gyroscope, I switched to motion based mouse control while out on desktop and it was a pretty neat idea.
On the other hand, I tried playing the Witcher 3 with different schemes and they are a pain in the butt. I feel the ABXY are too far away for my right thumb (I have small hands). It has to move too much which really cause a lot of strain on the hand when gaming for long hours. After some time I decided to experiment with using the Left Touchpad to replace the Right Analog Stick for navigating around. I have to say it does feel more sensitive. But because there is no actual force feedback like on the analog sticks to hold my thumb in place and my thumbs feel restless which also tend to tire my hands quickly. I probably will need time to relearn how to finely control it.
I also tried a to emulate the Right Touchpad as ABXY and in my opinion they are quite good. Took me a while to lose the habit of smashing the button but it is going to be a none issue in the long run I think. However because the controller has no right analog stick to control the camera I had to experience around a bit and came up with combining the Right Grip to activate and use the touchpad. It worked kinda but will probably need more time to get used to. Also there was a bug/glitch causing the camera to spin if I held the Left Grip - the reason why I ended up with the Right Grip. Here I have to admit the controller's ability to customize down to different levels sensitivity or area of touch recognition is really powerful. Still I would prefer a dedicated stick.
Final thoughts:

Some games do not age well. And Splinter Cell: Double agent is a great example of that. There is a lot of things wrong with the game and not many that were done right. I finished the game but there were times I thought about not trying to.
Lets start with bad then shall we.
The game crashes. And it crashes a lot. And there is no pattern just when will it crash. Sometimes in the middle of the mission, sometimes on mission load, sometimes on intro or outro of the mission. And sometimes it works just fine for an hour or longer. But on other times crashes after ten or fifteen minutes. Quite annoying. And once you decide to exit game, it can freeze itself forcing you to restart the windows in order to regain control.
The graphics are aged and it shows. Fact that highest resolution is 1600x900 does not help either. To top that the first mission is really ugly which makes matters even worse at first. You get used to it later on and it's not that bad as the first impression.
Audio seems fine most of times. Though lack of subtitles is extremely annoying. This was almost a reason not to play the game.
The game does not introduce itself very well. It lacks that modern tutorial/guide style so present everywhere. This is somewhat refreshing but leaves a lot for player to figure out. Some things I've learned on almost ending missions. But the lack of waypoints saying exactly where to go was a bit of back to the roots trip. When you actually had to figure stuff out instead of going after the flashing blip.
The story is rather bland. The start of it a disaster I would say. It gets a bit better later on but it is not to original or interesting at that.
Mechanically it's not too good as well. The three vision mode, night, head and electronics are pretty much useless. I don't think I used them even once in a meaningful way. Shooting and combat are bad. Most annoying thing being - why the hell is a pistol more accurate than a rifle? I mean really. Grenades are useless as well.
As a stealth game it fares much better. Sneaking is satisfying as much as stabbing the guys in the back. Most of the missions can be completed by remaining stealthy which is nice. Safe cracking is a nightmare though. The controls for it are terrible.
That should be about time to tell something good about the game. So what it does going for it are pretty well designed levels and missions. They're interesting and challenging. Some of them are approachable by different ways I guess though it's not the same amount of freedom as Hitman games for example.
Also the JMB headquarter levels are very nice - especially with the trust mechanic. This is the only part that makes the game worth playing. Time you are given to complete some additional objectives really adds to the double agent atmosphere.
Overall I'd say 6/10 if you disregard the crashes. Not really something I can wholeheartedly recommend though I've played worse games.

Even though I have a "mere" 1200+ games in my Steam library, oft-times I wonder when and how I purchased most of them. The other day I was doing a little spring-cleaning, and stumbled over Death Goat. I don't remember getting this game, but whatever. Maybe my Steam account has become sentient, and it's just adding games on its own.
It's more likely that I recieved this game as part of an indie bundle, but why should I bore you with facts?
I'd rather bore you with opinions instead.
Death Goat is a pretty cool little game. You're trapped in the 19th circle of Hell, and there's no chance of survival. All you do is slaughter demons until you run out of lives. Over time, you learn the ins and outs of how this game works, and slowly but surely you learn to stretch your limited resources further. All you're really playing for is the high-score, but there is enough depth to keep you entertained.
Like the arcade classic Smash TV, your primary means of survival are the weapons. Your default gun/stave/??? is pathetic and wimpy, relying on it will get you killed. So as soon as a monster drops a weapon orb, you grab it and start kicking some butts. There are four weapons, and you're going to want the purple orb. Why? Because it's a spreadshot that clears the area quite nicely. The catch is that all of the weapons are temporary, and the orbs are only on-screen for so many seconds. Still, in a game like this, every second matters. If you have a purple weapon, and a purple orb drops, don't just rush over and grab it. Let that orb sit there for a little while, so you can make the most of your current weapon.
It's fair to say that luck plays a slight factor in your survival. If you're not getting good weapon drops, or you just can't seem to get your shields and bombs replenished, then you'll probably have a bad time. It's important to learn the ins and outs of enemy behaviors/spawns and your movement. Basically, it's all about preparing for the dry spells. If you can handle bad situations with no weapons, then you're sure to improve your score.
It's also nice that games of Death Goat are extremely short. Some twin-stick shooters take awhile to get challenging, and that gets old quick. Business starts to pick up after the first or second minute of every game, so you're never relaxing for long.
Overall this is a simplistic game, and will only retain your attention for as long as you're trying to top the online leaderboards. It is pretty solid though, so give it a look.

Having only played the first game, the addition of the other two titles in the Dungeon Seige complete pack was very welcome, even more so thanks to the expansions included, but the cost of the pack is justified easily by virtue of the quality game that the Original is.
Bursting with atmosphere, Dungeon Seige is a 3D take on the Diablo 2 model, though with fixed level layouts.
Dungeon Seige is a long game - you progress across the world map seamlessly and you easily notice the distances that you are chewing up, as key towns are few and far between. The experience of this game is probably more akin to the idea of a Lord of the Rings type quest than anything more computer-game/zone-based, because as I have mentioned before you really get the feeling that you are blazing your own path, one that only occasionally intersects with civilization. Echoing ice caverns full of crystal avatars fill you with apprehension as the prospect of questing for hours without seeing the light of day is very real and a gameplay element in itself, and once you escape a gruelling forest zone midway through the game you are confronted with a seemingly impassable swamp, rather than the stereotypical sunny metropolis populated with traders.
Dungeon Seige is also a difficult game - an example being the afore-mentioned swamp which pits your squad - albiet experienced and doughty - against hordes of difficult creatures marshalled by witches and targetting your most vulnerable members.
The difficulty of the game, and the sheer distances of travel involved, is counterbalanced by the joys of a steadily improving squad. You have the choice to ally yourself with various squad members - more than you can ever hold in your total squad, in a feature that reminds one of the Baldur's Gate series and adds to the sense of blazing one's own path - and you can't wait for your hitherto skinny and ragged heroes and squad members to stumble across great shields, shiny helmets or keen longswords. Improving your skills relies simply on using related items - keep using a one handed longsword and a mini experience bar built in to your 'melee item' combat slot will reflect your character's steady improvement in it's use, ditto for ranged, nature and fire spells.
In summary of this ragged and ill-formatted review (for which I beg your forgivness - I am partially distracted) I assure you that this game is a worthy investment of time and emotion - love your squad, covet your packmule, listen to every word of pre-recorded dialogue and seek out all encounters, because you are living through a bonafide high fantasy advanture, and it does, eventually, end.

Looking for a LGBTQIA+-friendly dating sim? Do you like cats? Well then, you're in luck!
"Hustle Cat", by the studio Date Nighto (AKA "They made 'We Know The Devil'") is a fluffy, adorable game for those who love cats, lovable characters, fun humor, and some pure, innocent romance. The player takes control of Avery Gray (pronouns, gender presentation and skin tone choosable by the player), a twenty-something who finds out that a nearby cat cafe needs employees. They love cats. They also need a job. Seems like a match made in heaven, right?
Well, let's just say that Avery, along with the other characters, get a bit more than they bargained for.
This is the kind of game where it's good to go in with a fresh slate, so I won't go into too much detail, but it's a delight. Honestly, even if the story can seem contrived at points (it's explained in the special route, don't worry, though I wish they explained a VERY IMPORTANT PLOT POINT a bit more overall), that's a small complaint, since it's so goshdang adorable. That, and the characters really carry the game. Hayes', Landry's, and Mason's routes ended up being my favorites.
Avery, the protagonist, is phenomenal. They're a believable young adult/late teen (they're 19) and most of their internal monologue matched what I was thinking as I played. On that note, everyone's dialog is wonderful. Whether it's being self-referential, humorous, or poignant at points, it's a joy to read. It's clearly a labor of love on the part of Date Nighto, and this love shows in every moment.
The CGs are also wonderful! I love the art style, which is somewhere between anime and American cartoons. The skin-color changing option for Avery, along with the alternate gender presentations and pronouns, are also a nice touch, and alternate forms of Avery in each cut scene can be accessed via the CG gallery. It's fun to tinker around and see what the scenes look like for other players!
Also, unlike some other dating sims on Steam, this one is entirely family-friendly, save for some language. There are a few "mature" themes underlying some of the routes, but they are presented in a way that is suitable for any player, no matter of age. I, as someone who lives for fluffy cuteness, was pleasantly surprised, especially after playing darker dating sims like "Nameless: The One Thing You Must Recall" and "Hatoful Boyfriend".
My few complaints are that sometimes, the game wouldn't save CGs, so I had to play routes a few times to get them. The game would sometimes crash on me randomly. That, and the storyline can get a bit repetitive within each route, since there's a general story point you have to reach in each for the sake of concluding the plot overall.

I absolutely adore this game. Yes, it has flaws. Yes, not everyone is pleased with the changes the devs are bringing in. But this game has so many positives that it's worth picking up at any price.
Stellaris melds successfully 4X and grand strategy. It's simple and highly addictive. You create your species, explore, conquer and colonize. Want to be space cats who love everyone? That's doable. Want to be evil, slaving arachnids hell bent on galactic hegemony? That's doable. Robots akin to the borg? Check.
Stellaris gives you freedom to play however you want. Be who you want. And that is why it's the best game of it's blend of genres. It's also beautiful, with great 3D ship models, burning stars and lasers that put star wars to shame.
It's flaws are generally around combat and diplomacy, which both feel a bit empty at the moment. Wars are often won or lost in a single battle, and trade is limited to research or basic resources.
But the devs are great, understand the flaws, listen to the community and work tirelessly to improve the game. Changes coming in the next update should help in these areas, too.
TL;DR: an excellent game that, despite some flaws, has brought me back time and time again to wage war on the galaxy. Buy it!

I love this game.
Monkey Island is my old favourite game and I 90% recommend it, the remaining 10% leaning towards the fact that if you don't enjoy point and click puzzle/adventure games this is NOT for you.
This game has incredible characters, amazing smart puzzles, incredible adventures and an eerie feeling throughout the whole game (I better not forget the monkey's! They're awesome!)
So the story of this game (Which is very well written) is that you are Guybrush Threepwood, a wannabe pirate. You must go on three trials to become a true pirate, once LeChuck, the evil ghost captain, hear's that Guybrush is in town and up to no good (Well, no good for him) he attempts to capture him, torture him and kill him. He also want's to marry SPOILERS Guybrush's girlfriend, Elaine.
It's very difficult to find a flaw with this game, it seems almost perfect. The only problem is that sometimes there's no music which can be just eerie and just doesn't feel nice, it's a very scary game in that sense.
The other thing is some puzzles are too hard and keep you trapped on them for sometimes weeks, but you could use the hint system to help you which is a helpful add on.
The voice acting is pretty good in my opinion and so is the music (If it's even there) and the sound effects, although scary they're superbly atmospheric and you won't get tired of them.
Another thing you won't get tired of is the adventure: It seemingly never becomes boring, it always feels interesting and enjoyable.
And there are a HUGE amount of locations and now for my favourite part of the whole game... The sword fighting. But let me keep that a surprise. Let me just say, it's not sword fighting like how you'd imagine it.
The graphics are good too, especially with the special edition's effect.
And the final verdict for The Secret Of Monkey Island: Special Edition is the highest verdict so far... A 9.5/10. The few flaws JUST deprive it of that beautiful and unachieved 10/10 but it's still an amazing game and it will forever hold a piece in my heart.
Until the next review! :)

Secret of Monkey Island: Special Edition is a 2009 remake of old classic DOS point'n'click adventure title, that came out back in 1990. This version actually allows switching between original and remake on-the-fly. If you just want to play original, you can do it pretty much from beggining to the end, with almost no changes!
Monkey Island itself is a classic LucasArts adventure game. It's well remembered for it's pirate (including voodoo) setting and humor, having world to expore and having puzzles to break head against, guessing what they want player to do. By that point, adventures games already had point'n'click setting in place, just clicking on needed verb and using it on object. Just clicking on object itself always uses the most logical verb (and often the only one possible), so you may just forget of this aspect.
The game is divided into three chapters, the first one being the biggest and most open one, travelling on Melee Island, talking around and trying to complete three main objectives in order to become pirate, while starting to figure out what Le Chuck has to do in this game. Second chapter has you on another island, bigger in space, but less in NPCs, just having this funnily annoying slightly crazed inhabitant of island dropping in and out. Final chapter, "Kicks Butt", kicks some serious butts. Linear, short, but bumps you up and is very worthy compared to Adventure games.
Now, being classic adventure game, it's more concentrated on non-stop solving of 'puzzles' and interaction, with the only action sequences being sword fighting. Well, not exactly what you think. INSULT sword fighting, used only in chapter 1 anyway. Worth noting, you have to beat such "battles" by choosing correct reply to insults, while later throwing your own. Heck, most of them is spend on "farming" new insult and replies, by losing, to collect them all and beat the Swordmaster.
Otherwise, standart classic LucasArts. Which means few things. First, there is no way to die or get stuck in dead end in this game, so you can do stupid things all the way you want, unlike classic Sierra. Second, you can choose few options in conversation, but none changes the plot or progression - it's either a puzzle by itself or "choose your own joke to make". (You can even choose "what we have learned" reply in the end of the game!). Third, the puzzles are either easy and logical or they are hard and make no common sense. Quite a common thing in classic adventure games, doing something unexpect for goals that plotwise aren't the ones you would want to do, Like, suddenly finding out that you have and actually can 'combine' items in your inventory, for single puzzle, to rescue some shady figure who probably wouldn't be much of good if freed.
Special Edition keeps all of those and provides an upgrade to both graphics and sound, while messing around controls. Hands down, music is superior to soundblaster and art has more resolution than what original offered. But the gap is too big and those who grew with original may be put off. Difference between pixels-art that leaves something for imagination and defined art, you see. Where main character, Guybrush, was a normal guy in black and white in original, with who most people could reliate, becomes character in it's own with that hair. And sure thing, close-ups aren't drawn in same realistical way. But otherwise, it's fancy in it's own!
It also added voice acting to it, but because of limitation of original engine, it has awkward pause between each line, putting some players off. And once again, "it's not the way we imagined it when we played original".
And you can switch between original and remake on the fly, with press of single button, no loading required! Nice! Though, you can notice that animation in remake somehow feels to follow animation of original closely, having same amount of animation frames, not always having art to make same sense in these cases.
Actually, it switches not only visual and audio, but interface too. And it's another reason to stay on original, being made with in way to allow it to be controlled by gamepads on consoles as well. It tries to be as good as in modern point'n'clicks, but clumpsier. Much. Main fault comes from technical aspect, actually, where for some reason sometimes it playes like the actual cursor is placed lower/higher than it's actually shown.
And sure thing, to keep modern players sane, it incorporated hints system, when on the magical press of button, you get a hint hint hint. Good joy, much needed. Not always as straight as you would want it to be though, but anything helps.
Thus, nice remake of classic adventure game, which most recommend to play at least once, having humor, story and some puzzles that make no sense, this fault of adventure games eased up with hints. Not too long either and with charm.

Since it is so different from the traditional twinstick layout, it is not plug and play, games have to make use of the Steamworks SDK to take full advantage of it, input configuration is bound to Big Picture Mode, you need to create game action vdf files and still feed steamworks the actions you allow manually, ... there are more than just a few irritating things in there. -ARPG (Torchlight 2)

-Strategy (Cities skyline)
Pros
