Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is a perfect example of the kind of hard work and dedication paying off from the guys at Trip Wire being a certain kind of beast not to every FPS lovers taste.
This is Red Orchestra 3 by any other name, but being that this is the 1960's, The jungle, and completely Ostfront free... the name is more akin to the RO2 DLC "Rising Storm" which featured the American Pacific campaign of World War 2. It shows through though what kind of game this is, directly rooted in the ideals of gameplay from previous entries made by the lads and lasses at Trip Wire. Not for the faint hearted, twitchy, or casual, Rising Storm 2: CHARLIE IN THE TREES! is a FPS with a lot more in common with the likes of hardcore military simulators such as ArmA 2 rather than its openly arcade Battlefield Bad Company gloss and sheen.
Graphically this game is a gem. The time and effort that the team spent on assets and effects is truly worth their time. More than once I found myself dangerously still and motionless as I watched a napalm strike on some sector full of targets a few hundred meters away. Taking in the beauty of this game even on lower graphics settings (although on ultra it is eye wateringly good) rewards players with a finished and polished appearance that actually beats out the heavyweights that should really know better but don't.
A note on audio; Directional sound is very important in a game like this and I find myself struggling sometimes with the doppler. Maybe one of the key let downs here is that there's not a whole lot to be done in terms of training for it. Eventually you'll hear noises and pick up the nuances of direction with training, but I would have preferred better directional emulation as standard. The doppler effect is heavily multiplied also; meaning that although you can hear most noises in a game, you can hear them thinking that some dirty G.I. is unloaded next to your head, when in fact he's nearly a hundred meters away.
The maps are beautiful, nothing short of excellent in most cases. There are some absolutely enraging choke points, funnels, and killing fields of course... but that is very much in keeping with what the Vietnam war was.
Interestingly I would love to hear opinions from Vietnam War survivors on how this game either trivialises or encapsulates the look, feel, and tensity of a situation when simulated. I suspect not nearly as full on, but in some small measure I hope that when a player finishes a round or a match of RS2:V that they think to themselves about how horrifying and cloying this war must have been for everybody involved.
In summation this game is something else entirely from the usual gun laden romps of multiplayer focused FPS. It does indeed have both tactical, thought out approaches as well as fast paced panicked action but not in the flavour that the demographic has become used to. Play this for a few hours and then pick up any other commercially successful FPS such as Battlefield or Call of Duty and you'll realise that this thing, this monster of an experience will make you in to a death merchant.

The Secret of Monkey Island - a game reverently enshrined in a hallowed place of honor from the golden age of adventure games.  The Secret of Monkey Island is indeed a definitive masterpiece of adventure gaming and one of the most important games in its genre.  It's also incredible fun to play, even today.  While the Special Edition is a mixed bag, the underlying game is as funny and charming as it has always been.  Every gamer deserves to treat themselves to this timeless masterpiece.
The Secret of Monkey Island was a watershed game for Lucas Arts.  While their earlier efforts were also excellent (especially Zak McKracken, which is so unfairly forgotten), The Secret of Monkey Island is where everything comes together and the stage is set for a truly incredible run of masterpiece adventure games that would culminate with 1998's Grim Fandango - the greatest adventure game of all time.  The Secret of Monkey Island takes the brilliant ideas in Loom and for the first time, fully realizes them.  The Secret of Monkey Island is a game that refuses to allow the player to reach a dead end - one of the most maddening aspects of earlier adventure games where the player could reach a point in the game where further progress was impossible due to the lack of an item missed earlier in the game.  This required reloading an older save game, or even restarting the game entirely.  Not fun.  The Secret of Monkey Island also refuses to kill the player.  Unlike so many other early adventure games where death was a frequent and often unforeseeable occurrence, Monkey Island recognizes that dying is unnecessary and detracts from the fun.  The heart of adventure games is the exploration, story, and puzzles - and these are exactly the elements that The Secret of Monkey Island embodies.   The Secret of Monkey Island thus laid the foundation upon which the future of adventure gaming would be built.  No longer were adventure gamers going to be satisfied with unforeseeable deaths or maddening dead ends.
Not only is the game a hallmark of the genre, but it is also a joy to play.  The characters are simply drawn, but charming.  Mighty pirate wannabe Guybrush Threepwood is a hilarious lead character and he is impossible to dislike.  His one liners will have you rolling.  Even some of the dialog choices you don't choose will have you snickering.  The story of Guybrush's quest to become a pirate is a wonderful mash-up of pulp piracy cliches.  There's buried treasure, thrilling sword fights, voodoo magic, mysterious islands, and even cannibals.  It's an inherently lighthearted and silly game, and every one of those elements (and much more) are inverted or lampooned in very funny ways.
The Special Edition update, however, is a mixed bag.  The game's graphics have been updated for significantly higher resolutions than the game's original 640x480 resolution and now supports widescreen resolutions.  I have mixed feelings about the update.  There is a certain flatness to the graphics work that I don't find attractive.  I do give the artists credit, however, for their attempt to remain very faithful to the original artwork as well as subsequent games in the series.  The animations are also rather rough.  Characters moonwalk around the screen in a decidedly unnatural way and there are some clipping issues.  All of these faults are almost certainly due to Lucas Arts not investing enough resources and trying to get by on the cheap.  It's a shame, because there is indeed potential for a wonderful remake.  The game also now supports full voice acting for all characters using the familiar voices from the later Monkey Island games.  The main cast is wonderful, but some of the supporting voices are a bit rough.  Also, some of the jokes are ruined with the poor timing of the audio - for instance, try asking the Men of Low Moral Fiber in town about what's in the keg.  It doesn't work like it does in text.  The other poor aspect of the Special Edition is the changes to the inventory and verb (interaction) system.  The game no longer has the classic SCUMM verbs in the lower portion of the screen along with inventory items.  The inventory must now be accessed via keyboard hotkey, and verbs must be selected via mouse scroll wheel or hot key.  This is a significant downgrade, in my opinion.  The original system was more streamlined and allowed for faster interactions.  There was one puzzle in the game that I couldn't manage in the Special Edition due to the cumbersome inventory system, but can easily accomplish in the original.  I won't spoil it for you, but will say that it involves grog.
The truly brilliant aspect of the Special Edition, however, is that the original, unaltered game is included and can be seamlessly switched between.  Essentially, you get two games and you can try them out and see which you like better, or complete the game both ways.  I still prefer the older version, but I'm an old grey beard gamer.  As I see it, there's just no improving on perfection, and The Secret of Monkey Island is a very near perfect adventure.

Great game, D-grade port.
Let's start with the positive. This game is a LOT of fun. If you enjoyed Dead Rising 2, you'll enjoy this game. If you haven't played it, imagine that you're stuck within quarantine with thousands of thousands of zombies, plenty of tools at your reach (ranging from rakes to car batteries to assault rifles), and a lot of ingenuity. The draw of this game is your ability to combine even the most mundane things into an amazing weapon. Got an animatronic bear and an assault rifle? Boom - Rambo Bear sentry gun! Got a katana and a rake? Now you have a rake made out of katanas. I won't spoil any more of those, because part of the appeal is really seeing what crazy combinations exist.
Something else that's new is the addition of vehicles - because the map is so much bigger, you'll find it most convenient to just drive from point A to B. The creative weapon combination system exists with vehicles, as well - and though I haven't discovered too many of them yet, they add another whole layer of fun to the game. Some of them are adept at trimming whole zombie hordes down, and it feels satisfying.
The story is just kind of "there." I haven't finished it, but it occupies this kind of middle ground between "a well-written story" and "a chore to endure." Honestly, it just kind of exists. It's not BAD, and the acting and voiceovers are actually pretty good. This isn't a game that you play for the story, and it's not a game you play in spite of the story. It's just kind of standard fare, but that's okay, because it wasn't really the selling point anyway.
The game also functions as an RPG, with you gaining experience for zombie kills, quest completions, and event completions. Improvised weapons gain more EXP with how unique they are, and level-ups let you dump skill points into various trees. All of the benefits seem pretty helpful. It's brought the game a long way from Dead Rising 2's "everything breaks almost immediately and weapons have no ammo." That's a slight annoyance, by the way - the protagonist still doesn't know how to reload weapons. If you're out of ammo, the gun seemingly explodes in your hand, with even your character taken aback by it (and that opens you to attacks during the "whoa" frame, which is pretty annoying). If you have a pistol with 3 ammo, if you run over the same pistol out in the open, you won't replenish ammo. You can actually have, say, three pistols in your inventory, all with seperate ammo pools. It's really kind of annoying. There's no way to refresh ammo other than running across the weapon again - but since you can regain all of any weapons you've picked up for free at safe houses, it's a minor annoyance.
Now, let's get to the bad...
If you save someone, they may choose to follow you. You have no choice. You can't tell them to go away until you reach a safe house. The problem is, your followers CAN die, and they're also hit by friendly fire. Some of the weapons in the game aren't exactly easy to control, and I've found myself chipping away at follower HP and sending them across the room on more than one occasion. The first follower I recruited seemed like a good recruit...until their terrible AI meant they wandered into a zombie horde without a weapon and just died. That was it. Permadeath. They won't even pick up weapons on their own, meaning you need to hand them everything (and they can be picky, too!), and you will need to hand them food so that they may recover. The "posse" or "group" or however they named it feature really kind of sucks. At its best, they just serve as a target other than you for bosses.
Next is the port itself. It just isn't very good. For example, it's currently not possible to change the FoV - and the FoV, combined with the terrible camera if you use a gamepad (as recommended by the devs to fully enjoy the game) leads to a frustrating control experience. Also, the game is 30 FPS by default. During normal gameplay there were a few moments I noticed this, but I really noticed it when going through my screenshots - plain and simple, most of my screenshots came out blurry. It's so bad that I'm not sure if the game actually looks like crap and I haven't noticed or if the low FPS has just smudged all of the textures in the game in screenshots. You need a decent GPU to even run the game, but if you want a 60 FPS experience (like EVERY OTHER PC GAME) you need a higher-end GPU. Still, because I've barely noticed the difference in-game, it's not that much of an issue. FoV is a major problem and even .ini hacking to fix it should be regarded as a REQUIREMENT to launch on PC.
What surprises me, though, is the day 1 problems. My game was crashing every ten to fifteen minutes. It turns out that I'm supposed to use NVidia drivers from March 2014. Okay. The misleading thing is that the game's devs have been streaming PC footage for months, now, and people seem to be experiencing problems that the devs never have. They were actually surprised to hear about NVidia desktops crashing the game, and the devs are currently "looking into it." Also, the game interestingly has a myriad of problems on laptops, which is kind of surprising. I fully expect all of this to be patched out, but having to re-do the intro five times with a bug that the devs have conveniently never seen has left a little bit of a bad mark.
Also, the game has launched with four of DR3's minor DLC packs (for free!) which is kind of nice. There was a neat-looking expansion, but Capcom may pull the "We doubt you PC players will appreciate this, so it's an Xbox exclusive" card again (and then release it years later). Who knows. They've said there are no current plans for it to land on PC.
All in all, this is a GREAT game, but you will have to enjoy it in spite of its flaws.

Incredibly poorly optimized.  Borderline unplayable without a modern desktop.  Gameplay is somewhat fun, but there's many issues.  First of all, there is absolutely too much need for vehicles.  I get that we've increased the number of zombies and increased the map size so it seems like it must be done, but there has to be a way to balance this out.  It almost seems like zombie density is TOO thick at some points simply because it's incredibly thick at almost any given moment.  Zombies also respawn over time so really there's no point in trying to defend an area, especially since some areas are unreachable for zombies no matter what.  While the game has always had inflated humor, it was much lighter in the original game, and it could still be taken seriously even with those funny moments.  It feels like the series is trying to hard at this point, slowly falling prey to the fate the Saints Row series has had where the funniest thing about the game is just how hard the developers tried to be funny and failed.  The franchise is losing its identity because of gimmicky features like weapon combinations.  This really wasn't the direction I had hoped for this franchise.
When I played the original Dead Rising I saw so much promise in the ideas for the series.  The time frame for completing objectives.  You also had the ability to stack objects together and have a somewhat makeshift base.  Zombies did respawn, but only a small percentage of what was in the room would respawn making you feel like when you killed the zombies, it actually made a difference.  If you did the right strategies you could complete difficult tasks in short time frames that you otherwise couldn't complete at all.  It had tons of replayability.  I really was hopeful.  Now Capcom is just digging in the gutter for ideas.

Saints row 2 is the second installment in the saints row series and is in my opinion one of the more challenging game. The story begins with the leader of the third street saints breaking out of prison after waking up from years in coma and learns the gang he once lead has been disbanded and the areas they used to control has been taken over by the other major gangs of steelport, he quickly sets out to break his friend Johnny Gat out of the hands of the law and begins working on rebuilding his gang and take back what belongs to him.
The game has alot of features I would have loved to see in SR 3 and 4 such as the free costumization of your overall crib style and some sub categories without being locked to the later purchases.
As far as the story it has some fairly solid writing, while it could be improved here and there it is not to shabby at all
Diversions are unfortunately where the game begins to show its flaws, they honestly doesn't feel rewarding enough to be bothered with, and may feel pointless every now and then
The PC version also have some major problems with random frame drops which can be especially annoying during races. The game also seem to crash randomly when Steam Overlay is enabled.
The menus also have no mouse support which should be mandatory in all gamed ported to PC
Graphically the game looks fine considering it's not exactly a new game
If you're on a dual monitor you might have to do some tinkering with the options to not have the game window extend over to your second monitor thereby pushing what you already have on it half way off screen. This can be a bit annoying as some resolutions require you to restart the game before it takes effect
So is the game worth its current price tag? Considering the above mentioned problems on the PC port I would hesitate to buy it at full price, while it is a lot of fun to play it's not something I in good conscience can recommend. If you're thinking about buying it here on steam I would urge you to perhaps wait for it to go on sale. Alternatively you could buy it for xbox where I suspect the some of the major problems mentioned above will be less of an issue or nonexistent

I posted on the discussion forums, I e-mailed the game's support - I got NO response. This game's lack of support, on top of its inability to do basic dating sim functions, on top of its price leads me highly disappointed. Do not buy this game, buy Hatoful Boyfriend or look online for one of the many free, more polished, less buggy, VN's/Dating Sims.

Simply put, Loadout is awesome. As stated by the trailer, the diversity of weapons is incredible, however not all of them are applicable to playing well, but regardless it's very easy to create a weapon unique to you.
First off, how it looks. Many people have stated Loadout looks like TF2, and they do share a cartoony style, but Loadout is much edgier, being quite gory and excplicit, it's nothing too bad though, as it's all extremely over the top. The world of Loadout hasn't really been explained, despite the fact that the game is in 3.0, but regardless it's one of the more unique you'll ever find. Most of the maps are either enclosed or floating in midair and all of them have unique quirks, whether it be a giant drill in the center or multiple alleys and corridors the maps are all diverse and colorful, unlike some other FPS games.
Though there isn't a ton of music in Loadout, the music that's there is great, suiting the edgy, macho style of the game.
Lastly, the gameplay, Loadout is a hell of a fun time, to say the least. There are tons of different ways to play, maximized by your nearly infinite arsenal of guns. Not only can you choose from four chassis and 5 payloads, but you can also change the scope, stock, barrel, and trigger, with certain chassis having even more options to choose from. There is also another set of items you can use called equipment, which range from deploable sheilds, to grenades, to disguises ( but of course ). The way Loadout plays is focused largely on mobility, with there being many different "techniques" to move around. My one complaint however, is how easy it is to make a high fire rate weapon, jump around holding down the fire button and win. It can get frustrating, making weapons designed for situations, and then running into an overpowered weapon great at almost any situation, despite the fact that it takes next to no skill. I would reccomend the developers reduce the fire rate or range of these rapid fire guns in order to balace it out. Aside from that however, it's all good.
I would reccomend Loadout to anybody looking for edgy, hectic fun, but if you prefer something with a bit more... elegance, this may not be for you, welcome to the gun show.

Hello darkness, my old friend
I've come to talk with you again
Because a vision softly creeping
Left its seeds while I was sleeping
And the vision that was planted in my brain
Still remains
Within the sound of silence
In restless dreams I walked alone
Narrow streets of cobblestone
‘Neath the halo of a streetlamp
I turned my collar to the cold and damp
When my eyes were stabbed by the flash of a neon light
That split the night
And touched the sound of silence
And in the naked light I saw
Ten thousand people, maybe more
People talking without speaking
People hearing without listening
People writing songs that voices never share
No one dare
Disturb the sound of silence
“Fools” said I, “You do not know
Silence like a cancer grows
Hear my words that I might teach you
Take my arms that I might reach you”
But my words like silent raindrops fell
And echoed in the wells of silence
And the people bowed and prayed
To the neon god they made

In the words that it was forming

Are written on subway walls
And tenement halls
And whispered in the sounds of silence”

Inverted crosses, burning pentagrams, walking skulls with spider legs, sexy half-naked demoness, and most of all - tons of great music to accompany the senseless, yet glorious mayhem, "Death Goat" has it all in spades. If you love extreme music and appreciate the imagery, this one is no-brainer and deserves its place in your Steam collection.
"Death Goat" is a bare bones twin-stick shooter where you are put against the endless waves of enemies. Using controller is recommended, but not mandatory. There is little variation to it, but you wouldn't notice, as your life expectancy oscilates around 2 minutes. This is clearly a type of game to be enjoyed in short bursts.
On a technical side: graphics are beautifully drawn. Game stability could be improved a bit - it can crash on occasion. Fortunately, it happens during startup or in the menus, not during the actual gameplay (at least in my experience). This is a minor problem and easily forgiven considering it's in Early Access. Music is one of the game main assets, obviously, and it doesn't disappoint (note for purists: majority of the music is not necessarily Death Metal, but it gets the job done). There are several tracks to choose from and - another good news - developers are willing to expand the catalog in the future.
OK, I did my job as a reviewer, now's your turn - go grab your weapon and KILL THEM ALL!!!

So where do I start? This game is really fun, especially more so if you have friends. I will divide the review into three divisions; gameplay, aesthetics and player interaction.
Gameplay
This is one solid game with a variety of choices of champions to choose from. I find the grind system fair as you can unlock champions at a good rate. Unlike OW you can't swap champions mid match, and I like that system. There's plenty of customization available to decide how you want to play a certain champion. This is achieved by way of Decks, which are made of cards which give different power-ups to different skills. Mix and match cards to make your own play style.
Aethetics
Almost all champions are distinct in looks. You can easily identify champions purely by visual indicators. The game's graphics are passable for the art style it depicts. It's natural for people to make comparisons when many characters boast similar aesthetics. But Paladins does hold it's ground.
Player Interaction/Multiplayer
I mostly play on the SEA server, as such I will comment about players there. In every 5 games, you will have at least 1 game where you stomp the enemy and 1 game where you will be stomped, that's how I've felt with this matchmaking. Matchmaking in this game is decent, but not top notch. A lot of games have that "unfairness" to them. That being said most games people don't chat a lot and toxicity is rather minimal in casual. I mainly play casual.
Issues
Being Early Access, this game has a ♥♥♥♥♥ON of bugs. I am not joking. A patch or two ago I would have at least one bug in each game. Some bugs are just visual, while some will be borderline annoying. For example: If you are logged in while the game server goes to the next day and pops daily reward, you cannot claim it even after clicking the button. And the message keep popping every time you go to the main menu.
I would recommend you play this game if you are looking for similar shooter-moba esque games.

I'm an old-school, WASD and mouse gamer.  As much as I love console gaming, I can never play any first person or shooter games on a gamepad.  It feels like you are driving a tank instead of controlling a player!
This controller helps bridge that gap.  It is still not as good as keyboard + mouse, but it suffices to make mouse + keyboard games more acceptable and faster spins/manuevers than a dual-stick analog gamepad.
Setup was super easy.  Simply plug in, press the button... done.   I already run Steam in big-picture mode in my living room so I also opted for the beta client and recommend you do the same to get the latest firmware and big-picture updates.
Community support is amazing!  Just about every game already has several community made controller mappings so you don't have to spend hours configuring games by yourself.  If you like that sort of thing, this controller is SUPER configurable.  Pages upon pages of insane configuration and tuning, feedback, haptics, etc. etc.    You have every possible configuration you can imagine and you can fine-tune just about any "feel" you are looking for.
The "gyro" control is pretty neat- you can twist and tilt the controller for added precision or to replace steering controls if you wish.  Also, the under-controller paddles are perfect for things like jump, reload, melee swipe, etc. etc.  There is also next to ZERO controller latency so controls feel crisp and fast.
I recommend this to anyone using Steam in big-picture mode and wants to couch-play mouse-style games.  It works with every Steam game I have thrown at it and it makes first person and shooter games MUCH better than my XBox wireless game controller.

As someone who despises gamepads, my expectations were fairly low - I find it hard to play games with a gamepad, the camera control always seems to inaccurate, slow and frustrating, and the gamepad is horribly inefficient in more complex user interfaces when compared to a mouse.
Valve are pretty good at doing amazing things, and as it turns out this is no exception - The touchpads just seem so much better than sticks - They also have several modes, so you can pretend they're sticks, touchpads, scroll wheels, trackballs... whatever. You can rebind the crap out of every game with ease, even if the game doesn't do rebinding. There's also great community controller setups so you can simply pick one and get right into the game. The amount of rebinding options is staggering.
The controller also works both wired and wireless - YES! The best of both worlds, you can pick if you want no wires or no batteries! Its great.
It takes some getting used to (especially for a non-gamepad user like me, who isn't even familiar with the basic controller binding setups) but its actually really good, especially with a Steam Link. Using the Steam Controller doesn't feel like a huge downgrade from a mouse and keyboard, its just a new control system that I need to get better at (which actually doesn't seem that hard, especially when I can rebind ALL THE THINGS)
Valve have taken the PC philosophy of choice and customisation and applied it to controller design, then mixed in their community driven secret sauce. Great stuff.

Best controller I have owned. Works great with all games, even non-steam games. I've never been a large controller user but now I use it for every single game I play. It may not beat the accuracy of a mouse for an fps game, but it really isn't far off and if you're a casual gamer like myself then the Steam Controller is perfect. The game has been a blast so far. If you've played the other games in the dead rising series and were looking for a larger game world this will be right up your alley. The world is densely populated with things to do, collectables to snag if that's your thing and tons and tons of unique weapons. While it is unfortunate that capcom has decided that you have to collect blueprints before making a combo weapon it does drive players to get into the world and explore.
The story isn't the greatest unfortunately. Nick seems more of a go with the flow bystander than someone who's active trying to acomplish what he sets out to do. His voice actor seems subdued compared to some of the other characters, which isn't a good thing as he's the most prominent character. The voice acting on the various bosses is pretty good however, with each of the optional ones beig patterened after one of the seven deadly sins. The story related bosses have some interesting gimics to their fights to accounts for any level of character that s fighting them.
The drops in drop out mutliplayer is a ton of fun. Thankfully any collectables picked up by either player in the game are given to both, saving a lot of map hunting. Unfurtunately the same doesn't apply to safehouses at the time of writing, which means if you're helping a buddy clear a map from a fresh game you'll have to empty them back out before you get to use them in your own game.
The only real complaint about the game I have is that it's very very hard on your computer. I'd recomend taking a good look at the minimum system requirements and the forums before buing, as the game has some signifigant hardware related issues right now. Notable it functions extremely poorly on a couple of specific latpot configs and titan boxes.
tldr; Fun game, good mutliplayer. Check your system specs before purchasing.

I don't write reviews often, but with this game getting so many negative reviews due to crashing and bugs, I thought I'd weigh in.

No complaints about the graphics.  It is clearly only minimally optomized for performance, but it is decently optomized to give extra graphical quality tweaks.  If they are not going to spend much time on the game, I'd rather they did what they did here and make it look good and run so-so.  I have fast systems, so not that big a deal.

Westerners are obsessed with being politically correct, and the developers clearly never got the memo to be so freaking PC and boring.  Nice.  I like it.  Shallow characters?  Sure, stereotypes are similar to archetypes which are an easy storytelling device with little depth.  They are cute/funny though.
8/10 so far, I expect it to get more fun the farther we get.  $100 well spent for me and my wife to have some good co-op gaming fun.

Pros and cons.  The short version is I like the game, and like any game, there's stuff that bothers me.
The Good: Empire building is great, and the 'explore' part of 4X is decently represented, though I'm starting to think they need to have anomolies randomly spawn in sectors you've explored just so you can keep gaining experience for your science officers.  I'll talk more about officer xp in The Bad because it's kinda' dumb.
The game has a lot of micro going on, but not so much where it's overwhelming.  I particularly like that the development of the game is active and continuing, so definitely reccomend if you're looking for a game that's got some legs to it.
The Bad:  You'll see this one a lot, the AI -blatantly- cheats.  I know why the AI 'has to' cheat, but that doesn't make it any less '...wut' when the AI rebuilds their entire fleet in half the time with only one functional spaceport and a completely decimated empire.
This is bad enough before you consider how they balanced all the economics-it will cost the vast majority of your resources to have one fully capable fleet.  If you're operating your fleet at capacity, you will likely go into debt.  Fine, expected, etc.  The computer operates its fleet at capacity all the time and suffers no penalties for it.  It reminds me of playing Armored Core and discovering that yes, the AC's in the arena actually ARE cheating like all hell.
So...generally in 4X, more planets/settlements/whatever is good.  Stellaris however punishes you for expanding your empire beyond simply the maintenance costs of having more stuff that costs resources to maintain.  It also increases the literal cost of your research.  So you colonize five or six worlds to get ahead in the research game, well, not so fast sparky.  Apparently there is a Conservation of Science principle at play where the fewer scientists you have, the better they are at their job.  I'm sure conceptually this was to mitigate the advantages of a colonizing-heavy player, but it feels really gamey and artificial.
Also, that limited micromanagement thing I mentioned.  You can tell the game how to play itself, to an extent, with your governors, and in fact, you will have to rather than micro'ing everything yourself because the game places a penalty on you when you try to do "too much" of the micro yourself.  However, grouping everything up into a semi-autonomous sector ALSO grants you a penalty as it costs you influence per month.  Get started in a crappy corner of the universe, and you will find yourself basically unable to expand because you will be influence starved.
Speaking of influence, expect to be starved for that the moment that factions start breaking out in your government.  This also seems like one of the systems that the AI -blatantly- doesn't have to deal with, especially since so many things you do to expand have an upfront cost in this resource and a maintenance cost as well.  Now I'm guessing there's a way to game the factions that break out in your government for more influence, but it generally works out one of those factions will like you and the others stop giving you the time of day.    Influence also bothers me from the stand point that it's literally your 'Expand' resource, placed on top of all the other economic resources you need to be able to expand.
Artificially limiting your diplomatic options based on the sort of government you are seems a bit questionable.  Oh, and having your ally that you made a DEFENSIVE PACT WITH *START A WAR* that drags YOU into it is a VERY questionable design choice.  I agreed to defend them, not act as their vanguard.
The Ugly:  ...what the heck is up with those ship designs?  Like is it a limitation of how the game can process things or what?  And not even a color picker?  A LITTLE bit of customization woulda' been nice.
Conclusion:  So yeah, decent game, interesting.  A few things feel a little half baked, but that's every game.

I want to like Stellaris. I really do. I've been a hardcore Paradox fan for a while, and the idea of CK2- IN- SPAAAAACE really excited me.
The game does have its charms; there's a lot of customization that you can do, and Paradox being Paradox, you can go full on xenocidal mind-munching mutant race, happy space slug species in space, and everything in between. My beef is that there doesn't seem to be the same sort of depth in Stellaris as there is in CK2 or EU4. You always start from a single planet, always have to steer your research ships to explore planets, always have to colonize quickly, a beginning that can get sameish after a while. It's just another 4X game. Alliances and federations don't really have that much depth to them, without the intrigue, economics or diplomatic manuevering that make EU4 or CK2 compelling. Warfare is flat, and I question why armies are even in the game since they're so pointless.
So if you buy Stellaris, word of warning: the earlygame, while there is still a galaxy to explore and anamolies to discover and special projects to do, is going to be great. The midgame will suck. The endgame crises and fallen empires will spice things up again. But the replay value is low, and it'll get lower as fewer and fewer event chains or endgame crises will be novel to you.
Rating: 7/10, could use an expansion that offers alternate starts, and makes polity-polity interactions actually worth a damn.

Hustle Cat is a great visual novel which implements some excellent basic lgtbq positive charcteristics. Playable character gender options are available as well as some simple skin shade and body type models to choose from.
The story is short, whimsical, fun and easily playable with a diverse cast of characters that are well written and nicely illustrated. I would deffs reccomend this game to anyone who's a fan of dating sims. You can really tell this story is just dripping with love from the creators.
A few suggestions for future games or patches:
-I would love to see more choice based options. There are more in the beginning of the game, but once a route is locked in the choice based elements sort of stop, it would be really cool to see more.
-The artist(s?) who worked on this game did a great job, especially with character models and expressions. My only reccomendation would be to keep practicing composition - especially critical for visual storytelling - and some anatomy. There are a couple wonky bits, but so much passion and potential in the entire game, I can't wait to see more games from these guys in the future!

I loved this game; the writing was stellar, the characters are fantastic, and it felt a lot different than a lot of other visual novels to me. As you go through each route, you learn more and more about the story, from different perspectives. A really great bonus (in my opinion, at least) is the ability to choose your character's appearance (between six different portraits) AND pronouns (she/her, he/him, they/them). It was a really pleasant surprise, honestly!
(not plot spoilers, but super duper minor spoilers, sort of)
There's a route guide if you're not a fan of exploring around, and it's pretty spoiler-free. It was released by one of the co-writers of the game!
The only thing that is tedious about this game is that there's a lot of repetitive text in the game, but there is a skip-button if you don't want to reread it when you go through all of the other routes. Once you're past a certain point in each route, pretty much everything from there on out is different, though.

Metal, bombs, power-ups and always on the brink of death! That is what Death Goat is all about.
:
- Good selection of metal
- Teaches you how to kite (walk backwards while shooting at the enemy while also avoiding damage)
- Micromanage your character to his/her fullest potential
:
- Bombs. Sometimes bombs will go off twice, thus using them up (you start with three). I think there should be a one second delay each time you hit the right mouse button (bomb button)
- On the ice stage it's hard to sometimes see the power-ups due to it blending in if it's in a certain spot
- Power-ups feel too random. What I mean by that is you're going to always be looking for the shield and purple (spray gun) power-ups. The others: blue, green and orange seem to be lacking and not up to snuff with the purple power-up
- Too luck-based. If you're planning on getting a high score you're going to need luck. Now, I know a lot of people don't mind this, I just thought I'd let you know that power-ups could make or break your game. If you don't get the one(s) you need you're good as dead.
- No spawn armor. You get three lives, and if you happen to die you'll start back in the middle where you initially began. Sometimes an enemy will hit you before you even have a chance to move, thus causing you to take damage on your shield. I think there should be a 1-2 second spawn armor where you take no damage until either: a) those 1-2 seconds are up, or b) you shoot and/or use a bomb
Overall, it's a fun game worth playing. Metal + slaughter = fun, in my book. Just needs a few tweaks.

This game is a twin-stick shooter, with an awesome heavy metal theme. (The art style, music and enemies are definitely metal!) The game is pretty simple from what I have seen so far; pick a location, pick a character, and pick a heavy metal track, then start shooting demonic creatures before they can reach you. With awesome gore and blood splatter, fantastic creature designs, upside-down crosses for lives, and pentagrams for bombs, this is by far the most metal twin-stick shooter I have ever played. As a metalhead, this game appeals to me a lot, and I'd probably be willing to pay twice the asking price.
The only real negative at this point (note: it is still in early access at this point) is the lack of variety. Each location and each character affects nothing except what the location and character looks like. The locations have no unique enemies, traps, obstacles, powerups or anything else, and characters don't have different stats or abilities. (I haven't unlocked the tank, so that might be a little different.) So, it probably won't take long to get bored of. Also, if you're not a fan of blood and gore, or metal music, you should probably keep away, but then you probably should have looked at the videos and pictures and deduced that before making your way to the user reviews.
But for its price, it's definitely an easy game to recommend. Like twin-stick shooters? Like metal-themed games? If you answered yes to both, get this game. It's great for what it costs.

I've played through Double Agent on DVD shortly after it was released on PC. Somewhere near the end of the game (in one of the Kinsasha-missons), I got stuck. Everytime I tried to load a safe, I would spawn under the map, resulting in Game Over.
When I recently discovered Double Agent on Steam, I picked it up. I was hoping that they fixed at least some of the bugs and I would finally be able to play through the story. Unfortunately, I was wrong.
The engine is very buggy. Sometimes there's no sound, sometimes you get stuck. Many times, the game will crash when saving or loading. Saves are very unreliable: they either disappear or just don't work.
The stealth isn't great. The levels are rarely dark. The sound- and lightmeter of the previous game(s) are replaced by a big light on Sam's back. That light indicates if you're hidden, not hidden, or spotted. It doesn't always work: often you're supposedly hidden, but a guy at the other side of the map can still spot you. Sometimes you're not hidden, but there's a huge snowstorm going on and a guy on the other side of the level still raises the alarm. Especially on "Hard"-difficulty, not getting spotted is VERY strict.
The interface is ported almost straight from the console-version. The inventory and interactions are kinda slow to use, as you have to cycle through them. There is no way to bind different weapons or gadgets to keys on your keyboard. You can't just plug in a controller to play this game. One positive note: you can use the Steam Controller set to KB/M-bindings. That works pretty well.
The options in the menu are very limited. You can select "Normal" or "Next-Gen" graphics, and resolutions up to 1600x1200 pixels. Not all keybindings can be changed. The list of saves is very short, so you have to scroll a lot (and as mentioned before, the saves often don't work).
There are some good things about this game, too. The story is arguably the best part of this game. The undercover-aspect is a fresh approach which works well enough. There are some very interesting locations, and they often look well (for their age). And finally, it is more Splinter Cell.
If you are a die-hard Splinter Cell-fan, you might be interested to pick this up. But be warned that the experience might be troubled by technical difficulties or can be plain frustrating. If you're new to series or only a casual fan, check out the other games like Chaos Theory of Blacklist.
=====TL;DR=====
+ Story
+ Locations
+ Undercover
+ Splinter Cell
- Interface for controllers
- No support for controllers
- Unreliable saving / loading
- Very limited menus
- Many crashes
- Many bugs
- Average stealth:
* It's barely dark
* Enemies are super sensitive
Conclusion: Double Agent is a very bad port which suffers from many bugs and is often frustrating. Only get if you're a very big Splinter Cell-fan.

Though there are a few jokes that have become dated, overwhelmingly the humor and wit holds true.  Because I've purchased this game despite already owning a still-working copy from way-back-when, I'm making myself play the "Special" part of the Special Edition.  The graphics are fun and stylized enough to keep in the spirit of the quirkiness, but something about the airbrush quality doesn't sit well with me.  That and some of the voiceover work seems to displace a bit of the charm of this game.  Reading the text, you put your own emphasis and voice on the dialogue, making it fit your idea of the game's voice--something that gets extinguished when a voice is actually provided (and it doesn't match your own).  In a way, it's like reading a book and then watching the movie.
What's a guy to do?  Ditch the movie and reread the book!
Press F10.  Wannabe pirate life becomes wonderful again.
In short, just as good as I remembered and now I can play it on my Windows 7 laptop, not my decades old desktop.

"My name is Guybrush Threepwood and I want to be a pirate!" These words will stick with you long after you've completed the game. It's one of the most creative games in terms of plot, dialogue, art direction and characters. You won't get a chance to get bored. Oh, and the general overhaul of the game(without changing any of the gameplay) is a nice and welcome adaptation for the 2010s. You still get the option to play retro style, if you want to, with all the magic of 8-bit music and state-of-the-art 1990 graphics. So it's all extra, no downsides. The Special Edition is hands-down the best version of the game.

Having played the original Amiga release, there is a high nostalgia factor in this game for me. One of my favourite games of the era.
So the Special Edition has been updated for the 21st century and the graphics are a lot easier on the eye, but what set this game apart back in '90 is still at its core - the humour.
Play with the original graphics and it still has the entertainment factor.
The puzzles aren't too difficult to figure out, but at the same time they're not overly obvious either. At worst you may need to back-track to get something you didn't know you needed.
TSOMI is a delightful trip through silliness and fun. Not a long or deep game at all by today's standards but it never needed to be. Just buy it at the ridiculous price is usually is, then install, relax and have fun.

This game is a classic. Probably the number 1 reason why I work in the videogames industry. If you are a complete stranger to point&click games, buy it ASAP. It's a must have, and probably the first step you should take in this genre (along with pretty much any point&click from the Lucas Arts golden era). The Special Edition doesn't bring anything new but graphics and voices, yet it's still worth every penny because it's an insane amount of funny quotes and silly situations to solve. The OST is pure gold, and even better in the Special Edition.
I honestly don't know what to say against this game, except maybe it's a bit short for nowadays standards (keep in mind I've finished this game at least a dozen times already, I'm still not bored of it but I kind of know every puzzle by heart now). I guess some people could complain about the new graphics but if they do, they can switch to the original style anyway... I'll end my review with this quote, taken directly from the game itself:
"Never pay more than 20 bucks for a videogame."
...Oh, and look behind you! A three-headed monkey!

At the time I was blown away with the graphics and was furious that I could never get off melee island.  The puzzels were just to hard for a 7 year old me.  This updated version of the game is fantastic.  The updated visuals and sound along with voice acting really put the old game to shame.  The fact that at any time you can turn on the 1990 version to switch visuals and sound is just a cool addition.  I found myself doing it every screen just to see what the old game looked like.  Now, this is a very short game, so I wouldn't spend more then $2.50 on it, but the humor still holds up and the story is still a fun pirate romp.  You can easily tell why Pirates of the Carribean copied off of this game. #Worth $5

Sadly doesn't seem to work for me at all.
It starts from the enormous size of the controller. I used an XBOX 360 controller before (and now again) and can easily reach all of the buttons there. On the steam controller, when I try to press the A button, I often happen to press the B button because it's where I expect it to be. I don't have big hands so I always have to decide wether I want to reach the top and back side of the controller or if I want to reach X, A and Y key.  Obviously, only being able to reach the B buttom comfortable doesn't really add to my gaming experience.
The touchpads... I don't know if mine are defect, to be honest. I imagined them to be kind of like the displays of a smart phone: you touch and it reacts to the touch... but it doesn't do that. The sides of the touchpad don't have any kind of sensitivity, so I can only use like 50% (the inner dircle) of the touchpad... which is not really much. Also, when trying to to make fast movements that are not straight lines, it only goes in one direction and then "skips frames" or something, which leads to unplayable movements.
Big picture doesn't add to the experience either, because it takes up ridiculous amounts of graphics power for me. Like, I don't need that stupid bubble background when I'm ingame, just make it black for god's sake. Sadly, configuration of the controller as well as updating firmware requires big picture mode... yea... I play on a PC because I want to be versatile. If I want big picture stuff, I buy a PS4, thank you very much Steam.
The design of the controller itself is kind of nice I guess. Having it a little bit more adapted to normal sized hands would be great as I can't reach the buttons but it's not exhausting to hold in hands.
Overall, I imagine my controller might very well be broken when I think about the problems with the touchpad - but even if so, the rest of the controller doesn't really add up to what I expected. I guess spending the money on a X-ONE controller would've been a smarter choice and I'd recommend anyone to first try that one first. They're longer in the market of controllers and experience seems to be key here.

Ok, so after weeks of addiction, its about time I posted my thoughts on Aura Kingdom! :D
Ok so Aura Kingdom is an awesome Free 2 Play Fantasy/Anime MMO. Set in the semi-linear world of Azuria, you are an Envoy of Gaia, a human with special abilities and the power to summon powerful & mysterious partners called Eidolons to your aid, as you travel the world, defeating monsters, helping the towns, and defending against the ShadowKnights, a strange and powerful foe!
Discover your Eidolons true potential by fighting alongside with them and leveling them up, into more powerful forms (somewhat like Pokemon :P ) and use their skills to aid you in battle with the upper-hand!
12 awesome classes to choose from, including Ravager (High DMG), Scythe (Necromancer) & Grenadier (2-Handed Cannon Wielder), and blast, slice & shoot through the games many challenging dungeons and Main Quest line. Become a dual-class at Lvl40 with the ability to adopt a 2nd classes skills (for example a Tachi + Katar), and gain many more kickass skills and abilities!
- Very balanced classes (PvP can be won by any mix-up of classes)
- Amazing soundtrack (very fitting for areas, a little repetitive, but fitting)
- Great Group Events (including Battlefields, enhanced Dungeons, and special Party Quests)
- Smooth Graphics (easy on the eyes, simple, but aestheticly pleasing)
- Lots of backstory / lore (Simply read what people have to say, it will make sense)
- Not Pay2Win (Can easily get to Max Lvl with High Quality gear, without spending a cent! (although you can get some cool looking apparel and mounts, etc for some cash if you wanna spend)
- Main Quests can be pretty repetitive (lots of Fetch Quests, Kill X Amount of Monsters, etc)
- Hit Boxes is slightly Buggy (sometimes cannot target opponent until they hurt you first)
- Sudden jump in EXP needed to Lvl after 45 (1-45 quick leveling, 45+ is grindy)
Overall, I love Aura Kingdom, its an amazing MMO that I would highly recommend trying, especially with friends (plus Bonus EXP in parties so Win-Win! XD)
Give it a go, and if you don't enjoy it, no money was lost since F2P! :D
Overall Score - 8.5/10

-People with weak cpu´s will not feel it has good optimization!
Even with instanced rendering the game on the largest maps  f  u  c  k  s   low core/lowsinglethread cpu´s and amd gpu users, due to custom UE3 in DX11 in use which generates a great amount of drawcalls.
Ryzen and Sandy Bridge will be what you should have for higher graphics settings. Even though a bloomfield (i7 900) cpu will get you through the day too, phenom II´s and quad 2 core series users will have a bad day. Bulldozer, well look at what i wrote at phenom. Overclocking will be required. Playable but the game is best experienced with high framerates for that smooth pwning. So I recommend playing it with lower graphics settings and always leaving instanced rendering on, if you notice graphics bugs with instanced on and low graphics settings, either bump up graphics a bit or disable instanced rendering.
Instanced rendering helps a   s  h  i  t   ton for people who are cpu bound so make sure to enable it first and run benchmarks ingame on some 64 servers. Even on my Xeon E3 and 1080ti it makes a huge difference.
Instanced rendering basically "outsources" drawcall work to the gpu so that the cpu gets some breathing room and doesn´t bottleneck as quickly, resulting in higher framerate pushed by said cpu if your gpu is capable of that while increasing gpu usage if too low. Do not enable if you have a gpu usage of 99%+ and are hitting a gpu bound bottleneck.

Somewhere between Baldur's Gate and Diablo lies the awesomeness of Dungeon Siege.
This is one of those sadly under-rated classics which should be much better known, Give it a good shot and you'll see why.
I'll be the first to admit that it's pretty ugly, even by standards of the time, but that's OK. The story isn't as well executed as BG, but better Than most Dungeon bashers. Voice acting is minimal, but competent, just enough to give a little flavour and highlight major plot points.
What you get, though, is A HELL of a dungeon basher, Amazing atmosphere and tension a load of options for selecting your squad and what skills and equipment they take with them, and a horde of enemies more than capable of taking you down if you get sloppy. Watch every step, keep an ear out for ambient sounds which may be clues of a coming ambush, and don't rush in to grab loot unless you're sure your exit is clear!
RPG aspects are a bit like the Elder Scrolls series, you get better at what you do most, and the skills that go with that. Eventually your squad will be moulded to your play-style, although some party members for hire have clear advantages in one field or another.
If you like dungeon bashing RPGs and haven't tried this one, why not?

A Western visual novel with good art, solid music, and a great story. Features a fresh and interesting writing style, with a blend of American and Japanese tropes turned on their head.
The world-building is very immersive; it's easy to step into the main character's shoes, and fun to do so. When reviewers for Hustle Cat say the game is LGBTQ+ friendly, they absolutely mean it.
Love it or hate it, Hustle Cat will always feel 5 hours too short. After 2 or 3 routes, the writing can feel formulaic. Some characters' routes (
) feel shallow compared to others' (
).
Features good, subtle writing, but sometimes leaves the player feeling lost. The game tends to crash (saving grace: frequent autosaving). Fast-forwarding is
slow, which can be frustrating when replaying the common route.
Hustle Cat is one of the best Western VNs available on Steam. Its primary flaw is that you will always want more; you'll be thinking about this game for weeks, despite its 10-hour playtime. I can't recommend this game enough.

What can I say about Hustle Cat that hasn't already been said in some format?
This is an amazing game, a wonderful storyline that keeps the audience engaged throughout the entire game, no matter what route you play you get more and more backstory to the main plot, while also enjoying the sideplots for each route.
The music really helps set the mood for each scene, and it kept pulling me in, having me wonder what was going to be the next theme, the next suspenseful moment! Not repetitive or annoying like some games, it was actually refreshing and I've found myself taking small breaks with the game open just to listen to the music play.
The characters are really well fleshed-out, and their routes only help to do more. Each one has a very distinct personality, and through their routes, you get an insight on what's shaped them to be how they are now at the cafe. I love every single one of the characters, I do have my favourites overall but there is no character that I dislike how they were created in this game. Their visual designs are also absolutely adorable.
Overall, this is honestly the best visual novel / dating sim that I've played in a long time. I definitely recommend it!

The Good, The Bad and the Ugly.
The Good.
Good design. The track pads are in a comfortable spot for your thumbs to play games.
The pads act like a Stylus/Mouse which opens up endless possibilities on customization.
Controller feels solid and well built.
Comes with multiple plugs for just about anywhere in the world.
If you love customization. You will love this controller. There are hundreds of ways to customize it. You will spend many hours playing with the settings figuring out the best for each game you love to play.
The Bad.
You can use rechargeable batteries, but the controller will not recharge them.
To my knowledge, there are no rechargeable battery packs for this controller. Only AA's can be used for wireless.
You will need to keep a supply of Duracell AA's on hand unless you plan on playing wired all the time.
A,B,X,Y buttons take some getting use to. Especially if you play a lot with PS or Xbox controllers.
Track pads take time getting use to.
Controller is designed for hard core gamers. While they try to make it simple for everyone. In order to get the most out of it you will spend a lot of time playing with the options. So this controller may not be for the casual gamer.
The Ugly
When you first turn on the controller and connect it to your Steam Link. It will tell you that you need to do a Firmware update in order to use the controller. It also tells you that you can not update it VIA the steam link, but have to hard wire it to your PC.
The problem with this is... there are no instructions on how to update the controller and steam gives very undetailed information on how to do this.
What they tell you to do is to start your steam client on your PC.. open Big Picture Mode (controller picture on upper right hand side of screen) plug in controller and turn on. Then it will automatically start updating.
Problem is... this didn't happen for me and many other people.. but this is how I fixed it.
I use Windows 10 OS.
Open up your steam client. Go to your Settings.
STEAM > Settings > Account > Sign up for Steam Beta.
Restart Steam
It will download more files.
Restart computer.
Open up steam Client
Start Big Picture Mode
Plug in controller (be sure that your steam Link is unplugged or controller may try to connect even being wired.)
You should then get a message that pops up asking for update the firmware.
Click yes
Wait for it to finish.
Now your ready.

An excellent remake of an absolute classic.  The Secret of Monkey Island is the quintessential point and click adventure game that is full of puzzles, witty humour and memorable characters.  The game is obviously at its best when you are playing it for the first time as it will be difficult and all the jokes will be fresh.  This hasn't stopped many players, including myself, playing the game dozens of times.
This remake allows you to play the game in its original form or with updated graphics, voice acting and controls.  This is where I found there to be a few problems.  The updated special edition gives you a fantastic way to play the game, but I found myself switching back to the old version during a few puzzles that require specific timing.  The updated mode forces you to scroll throw actions such as "Look at" or "Use" instead of having them all on the screen at once.  This can be frustrating and I think this is the wrong sort of game to force a controller like interface on players.  Having to switch between versions due to a frustrating control scheme isn't really good enough.
The game itself is challenging and it has more than one puzzle that will stump new players.  I would also go as far as to say that one specific part of the game has a ridiculous amount of back and forth between a few locations.  This has always bothered me, but it's a minor issue.  I simply recommend that you avoid a guide and give this a try, it's difficult, but you have all the time in the world and it's certainly rewarding when you make your way towards the end of the game.
This special edition is well worth the purchase as it offers new players the chance to experience a fantastic adventure game while offering the old fans a chance to play it with a bit of a makeover.

To summarize our full review:
"Gameplay wise; it’s your fairly typical top-down shooter with a nice pallet swap. It follows the more arcade style top-down shooter road with a score system rather than a level system with 3 lives and a lot of power ups along with a speed boost and what we can only describe as a nuclear pentagram. There’s plenty of enemy variety to keep the player coming back, and (upon death) enemies explode into a pile of gore, guts, and an otherwise unruly corpse that looked amazing. We managed to stay alive (at best) for 8 waves, but I’m sure there are other players out there who are far better than us. During the game, you can also find temporary shields, weapons boosts, and other power ups to aid the player. The gameplay is simple, but fun and we enjoyed our time with the game. It’s a different flavor of top-shooter, and it’s more enjoyable then one might initially suspect. Coupled with its $3.00 asking price, even if someone is on the fence about purchasing the game due to it being in Early Access; the low price of the game combined with it’s fairly professional look and interesting pallet of color choices and the ‘death metal’ ascetic would make those who are on the fence most likely jump on the purchase. It doesn’t have a story, but it doesn’t claim to. Unlike when we harped on Gone Home for it having a weak story, Death Goat doesn’t try to put one in at all. While I think a story along the line of Serious Sam layered on may have brought some added humor, it’s fine as-is and doesn’t really need to be there.
Overall, if you’re looking for a cheap top down shooter that may see improvement over time, enjoy heavy metal music, and you can risk not having that Starbucks coffee for a one whole morning, this game is probably for you. It’s cheap, it has a cool look resembling a heavy metal album cover, plays great, and got hooked trying to beat a friend’s score."

A top-down perspective shooter flavored with metal music.
Select a map, a character and a song.
Start the rampage!
A Wave after wave hordes of monsters pouring in from every direction.
Within three lives slaughter as many enemies as you can.
Repeat!

Death Goat:
~~~~~~~~~~
Whether you are a goat, a witch or a granny, you have to survive as long as you can in this epic arcade action game!
Death Goat is a top down arcade action/survival type of game where you have to push back waves of enemies until you die! Basically you need to last as long as you can and score as many points as possible!!
At  the start of the game, you will have to choose between 3 different battle arena (map), then you will be presented with several characters: Death goat (of course), a witch, a kitty, a tank (when you reach 1,000,000 points) and my favourite, the granny (I always used to see my grandmothers as nasty witches, I loved them!!)! The aim of the game is to survive as long as you can by pushing back the incoming enemies waves!
You will be equipped with a shield (protection orb) and a wand at the start to eliminate all incoming foe, but be assured you will have other great weapons to help you to survive to the next wave! But will it be your last?
What I like about this game its setup as an arcade game and it is unforgiving…fun…fun! And if you like heavy metal music, you will be well served with 14 available tracks which fit this game perfectly! It is absolutely hectic stuff!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Fun and challenging top down arcade game
-	Several characters to choose from
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	A bit repetitive
Death Goat is a fun and hectic top down arcade game…. Hard and truly addictive!

Don't be fooled by the title, folks. A review of the steam controller from my experience with it. I own/used for multiple hours a Logitech g710+ keyboard and g502 mouse, Xbone controller, 360 Controller, Dualshock 3 and 4, and Wii nunchuck(oh yes, it counts).
Pros:
-Very ergonmic feeling, fits into palms perfectly.
-The back buttons are quite nice and very functional.
-Touchpad haptic feedback and accuracy are great.
-Dual stage triggers work amazingly for any shooter.
-Analog stick feels and works well.
-Extremely customizable, able to find just the right layout and function.
-Very long battery life, 80+ hours of use.
-Feels reasonable sturdy, doesn't feel too flimsy and feels higher quality (in my opinion) than a standard 360 controller.
-Packaging is good, controller and accessories are packed well and the box is of reasonable quality.
Neutral:
-Weight is not bad, a bit more would make it feel more quality.
-Non rechargable batteries, this makes the need to buy batteries/rechargable batteries as well but has really long battery life.
-Light up steam logo, a bit bright for night playthroughs but looks pretty cool.
-Triggers have not enough resistance, but they work fine as the dualstage would not work as well with too much resistance.
-Face buttons are a bit small, not bad buttons just a bit more size would work well.
Cons:
-Glossy plastic, ♥♥♥♥ing hate it. It makes it look cheap and gets fingerprints just by looking at it.
-Bumpers have too much resistance, a bit annoying to use.
-Kinda feels cheap in general. It doesn't feel awful but you can tell the price cuts in order to add all the features internally and drop the price to 50$.
Verdict:
One of the best controllers I have ever used. It does its job of a controller mouse hybrid quite well. While it has noticable flaws, has a sharp learning curve and is not the most "premium" controller experience, what it packs is something that many wont like, but I have grown to love.

2: This controller was clearly built with FPS and simulator games in mind, the kind of games that you would normally play with a mouse like Cities Skylines or The Sims etc. It excels in that area...but only that area. It was designed for these game genres and nothing else.
3: The controller is borderline niche market, if this pad was sold at gaming retail stores it would sell poorly, and that's a fact. In a nutshell this controller barely does anything better than the 360 pad, and the 360 pad remains my No.1 controller. Sorry Valve, I generally like what you produce be it games or hardware, but this one fell flatter than a pancake

So I had about 250hrs of gameplay with my steam controller before deciding it wasn't worth it, so don't say I didn't give it a try.
The touchpad is no where near as accurate as it stated it was going to be, even adjusting the sensitivity and using gyro for aiming in FPS I still didn't find this controller anywhere near as comfortable as my preferred dualshock 4 controller (most people prefer xbox). With certain games that don't allow gamepad/kb+m compatiability, using the touchpad as a mouselike joystick only disoriented the accuracy, and putting mouselike joystick on gyro completely disoriented the controller even after calibration and messing with sensivities (controls won't fully work using mouse bindings in games without gamepad/kb compatiablity like black ops 3).
The D pad is honestly a joke. It's a flat touchpad with slight grooves for each direcection. If you're expecting to be able to quickly navigate the dpad controls in game (for example a scorestreak in cod or a gadget in battlefield) you'll only be causing stress on yourself from having to stop moving completely to activate the d pad or just completely clicking the wrong direction. I've tried various techniques to avoid this problem only to be wasting my time.
The back pads are a great feature, even being the aggresive controller user I am, I honestly found the backpads very useful in games like rocket league and fps for quick access to reloads or crouch without having to leave your aim, and not being in the way when not in use. This new feature is probably the only decent feature on this controller.
In conclusion the only useful thing about this controller is the back buttons. The right touchpad isn't as accurate as you want it to be (a normal controller having no problem keeping up with it) and the dpad being a flat touchpad itself makes it very difficult to navigate and click certain directions in game effectivily just makes this controller IMO a waste of money. I wanted and tried making this controller better than the rest out there, but ended up spending hours of my time in the configuration menu, and guess and checking a bunch of bindings. Using reddit forums to get help from other users, it was all just a waste of time. Just stick with what you're comfortable with.
In the future get rid of the touchpads, find out a more accurate way to use analog sticks to compete with actual controller companies, and use the back buttons for an advantage in the market. This review would be completely different using two analog sticks with the added back buttons.

You know that feeling? When you get a game you saw in a LP and which seemed good, a game even your friends and relatives told you was good, and when you finally get your hands on it, you realise it's absolutely terrible?
Well that's my Double Agent experience for you.
Let's start from the top. The game has an unskippable super long intro, one you must endure every time you boot the game, but also every time you come back to the main menu for some reason. Loading times are attrociously long for a game that old, especially seeing how good and new my computer is.
Controls are bad, especially the "new" water controls. You also no longer can grab an opponent on stairs, despite the fact you could do it in Chaos Theory, and that game was a lot older. Somehow the elevation slight difference mess up with the prompt.
The game is crash heavy. First I had a bug where the game automatically loaded my last save without giving me the main menu, which always crashed said game until it stopped to do that for some weird reason. Then the game crashes every single mission change. In multiple parts missions, it crashes at zone change.
The HUD that was so convenient in Chaos Theory is completly gone. The new system is too simplistic and vague and seldom helps.
The PC version smells like a terrible port. It's choke full of bugs. If your remap your keys then try to rename your profile, instead of using your normal keyboard, it will change every key you remapped to its new equivalent. For exemple if you put couch on ctrl, you will need to press ctrl to write a C, because the original key for crouch was C... The safe cracking game is horrible because it was obviously designed with a controller in mind. Not only that, but there is a crippling bug which prevents you from moving the gears if you don't raise your speed to max. On some missions, bodies will get detected even if they are hidden and there is no one to detect them. On others, you will get your stats messed up, like one mission dependant kill which will somehow count as two kills... Ennemies see you with their butts. The particuliarly huge offenders being snipers, who are similar to the ones in the very first splinter cell in terms of complete bull. It's especially obvious on some missions where you can watch a video of someone playing on hard and doing something on console, and not get seen, while you do the same thing on easy on PC and will get noticed(Shangai mission, the guard opening the vent when you're hanging from the ledge).
Controls are klunky and overall unresponsive. Jumping is particularly awkward, but any kind of "platforming" is terrible. You can't rename your saves, so identifying which one is which is a nightmare. Besides the system is so bad if you select a save with your mouse to overwrite, you may overwrite an other save. Only the one in the middle of the list is the one affected, even if you selected the top or bottom one. And yes, this can cause you to delete a very important save. You can no longer use the mouse to press the key on a keypad to enter the code...
The list goes on. It's like a HUGE step backward from Chaos Theory. It's just so bad I can't focus on the story... I just can't because every enjoyment I could have is ruined by thoses crippling problems. And like I said, they all seem to share the same origin: Being a terrible console port. It's just a wonderful exemple of "When Ubisoft started to really decline".
This game is pure pain, and I recommend to anyone to stay clear from it.

First off this game is very fun, but it is also not optimized well if at all.
Now, I said the game is fun...and it is....If You Can Get Past The Load Screen.
The game is extremely unstable, and thus far Capcom's support has been of almost no help. Updates - SINCE LAUNCH - have come only three times. That may not sound that bad, but the number of issues experienced by players are HUGE. For instance, many users are experiencing random crashes in game at random times. They are also experiencing massive framerate lag unrelated to the on screen action - i.e only a few zombies on the screen and indoors. The Official fix for this is to roll back your Nvidia drivers from the current 340.52's to the 335.23 package. Results of this step vary person to person. They recommend that you verify your game cache as well because people have encountered missing files. Again, mixed success is reported with this for any kind of fix. They addressed this further in their first (and only) actual patch. It was only available to users who had purchased the game outside of Steam, and not all users recieved it (I bought from GmG and didn't recieve it - more on that in a minute). I am guessing it was one or two specific retailers.
This leads me to my final issue: Nvidia Optimus Based Laptops
It became clear as the support threads developed that virtually no one with an Nvidia Optimus setup could get past the loading screen. Many of us in the threads addressed Capom repeatedly asking them to speak to the issue. Yesterday afternoon they finally did, and boy was that response a doozie. I am actually pasting this in directly from the thread to do it justice:
"While laptop graphics fall outside of the minimum spec requirements and aren’t officially supported, we understand many users still choose to play DR3 on laptop systems"
Yes. That is Capcom boldly stating that NO LAPTOP meets DR3's minimum system requirements. Let that sink in for a moment. Here are my specs:
MSI GT7020C
Core i7 4700MQ 2.4 Ghz Base ALWAYS runs @ 3.2 Ghz Turbo (CPU Z Monitored Before and During Gameplay)
12 GB DDR3
1TB 7200 RPM Sata III
Integrated Intel HD 4600 (Don't freak out yet)
Nvidia GTX 770M 3 Gb GDDR5
.........You get the idea
Capcom is foolishly stating that machines like mine (and I have seen more powerful machines than it cited in the support thread) are not at minimum system specs.  For those not geek minded let me clear this up:
Minimum required video Unit (using Nvidia to keep it in the family): Nvidia GTX 570
VS.
My Video card: Nvidia GTX 770M
FIGHT!
Result of this showdown: GTX 570 hopelessly outclassed by GTX 770M
In the end, the "While laptop graphics fall outside of the minimum spec requirements" statement could not be more boldly untrue. This is a clear cop out for Capcom. Nowhere on their store page does it even suggest that Laptops are unsupported. Now, on to the final volley-
You might notice that earlier in this review I mentioned that I monitored with CPU-Z before and During gameplay. That was not a typo. The user population came up with a workaround. I am now able to play the game, but this is a workaround, not a fix. Again allow me to stress this point: WORKAROUND WAS USER DEVELOPED.
Some Optimus users can workaround the freeze on loading issue by running an external monitor via HDMI. It seems to bypass the Integrated Intel HD chip and goes straight through the Nvidia chip. Success with this method is inconsistent, but it did work for me. I am running the game maxed out in 1080p with the 720p LOD at a fairly solid 30 Fps. I have not run a frame check on it since I created he user.ini file to unlock the framerate yet, but it does appear to have smoothed up further, I would guess around 40 Fps. On a machine that "Falls outside the minimum specs".
Conclusion:
This is a fun game if you are one of the 12 people that can actually get it to run. Even if you are able to get past the Loading Screen Boss, you may still experience graphical issues such as objects not appearing properly, flicker, and other issues - see the support thread for further detail. It doesn't take very long to finish this game, but I personally don't mind, because I'll continue to replay it. The art is lovely, the characters aren't one-dimensional (in personality), and the writing and plotting is deceptively simple. In fact, it's the writing and plot that caught my attention; at the beginning, with the quickness of the first playthrough, it seems as if the formulaic style will drag the game down as you continue to play and find other endings. However, that was definitely not the case, as each playthrough, while keeping to the "formula", was very clever and not heavy-handed in its dialogue and scenes. The lore, if you will, was a quiet background interest that slowly unfolded as you finished each playthrough. This is an excellent game, one that will make you feel what my friends would call the "warm fuzzies."
