Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell Double Agent is a game that i want to like, but I just can't. The bugs and glitches in this game are abundant and are a glaring problem. Add this with where autosaves and hard saves don't actually save, and you got yourself a piece of crap. I have given this game 7 chances (meaning I have restarted the game because of the issue with saves being deleted) and each time have recieved the same bugs and glitches.
Splinter Cell Double Agent is like every other Splinter Cell game. You stealth your way through each level and complete the set of objectives given to you without raising to much alarm or getting killed. Not to hard right? Well it is when game breaking bugs come into the picture. For example, in one level you are prompted to make mines, but before you start making the mines, you are supposed to listen to 2 people talk. I listened to the people talk, and when I went to make the mines, the mini game to make the mines didn't work properly. However, as little as I played, the game itself was an average stealth game.
The games graphics are average in my opinion. They aren't anything spectacular, but I can forgive it for how long ago it came out.
The story is rather mediocre. It's a story that countless spy movies and game have copied and pasted for years now and it's not very creative. In my reviews I don't tell plot summary, so if you want to read the story, look it up or read the description for the game.

Chaos Theory really was the pinnacle in terms of stealth for this series. Instead of keeping the perfect light and sound meters, they decided to just completely remove the sound meter, and attach a traffic light onto Sam's back, to let you know if you're hidden or not. There are plenty of instances in this game where you should be 100% hidden, but because of the terrible lighting system they opted to use for this game, you're not. There is no absolute darkness in this game and for that reason I never found myself having to use the trademark goggles. The Stealth in Double Agent is a joke.
Lastly, you can look forward to suffering through a nonsensical barebones story that will leave you with a bitter taste in your mouth after it's over. In some alternate reality Ubisoft didn't hire a b-team to crap out this game and instead allowed the Chaos Theory team to port over their version of Double Agent once the 6th gen one was out. This version (the 7th gen) of Double Agent is where Splinter Cell died. Rest in peace.

A twin stick arcade shooter called Death Goat, what's not to love?
BRUTAL

RELEASE THE CRACKHEADS!!!
Death Goat is a hard-core wave based twin-stick shooter where you play as a Satanic goat (or maybe someone else if you prefer, like a death metal granny in a wheel chair) shooting down hordes of demons in a wasteland of your choice. It doesn't really matter who you choose though because all the characters seem to function the same - although the tank does seem pretty difficult to monitor the protection aura level.
Death Goat also has a lot going for it music wise. If you like metal, you're going to like this. You can select what you want to listen to, or just go for shuffle track on death which is the best way to go really until you've heard it all and picked your favourite tracks in the game.
In terms of actual game play you move about on a fairly empty wasteland - there aren't any environmental obstacles like mountains; it's just you and tonnes of demons (though being in early access maybe some environmentals will be added later). The worst of all the demons you will encounter is the tiny skull spider, and although they are the easiest thing to kill, there's lots of them, and they move fast. Your character is surrounded by an aura and each time a demon touches it (regardless of its size) the aura degrades a level and that demon dies. Once the aura is gone you're ready to be eaten by the next demon you come into contact with unless you find an aura refill. If you're eaten you lose one of your three lives, and explode killing everything before respawning. I found it not uncommon to run into a couple of small spider skulls at the same time and suddenly lose all my aura. The aura could probably do with having a brief moment of invulnerability when you get touched to make the game a little fairer, but then Death Goat isn't really about being fair. As well as the aura pick-up there's also nuke style pentagrams (of which you can hold three) and various power-ups for your weapon. Weapon power-ups are timer based and do not stack which made me a bit sad when I realised I couldn't combine effects. My favourite power-up so far is what I would describe as a psychic chainsaw, though most attacks are variants on your base projectile style weapon.
Death Goat is made in Unity, and it works pretty well. It automatically detected my ideal resolution, and I haven't found any bugs or anything that makes it difficult to play. My Xbox 360 controller worked really well with Death Goat - you use the analogue sticks and the triggers only, so you never have to shift the position of your fingers. One stick to move, the other stick to shoot in a given direction, one trigger to run, and the other to pentagram (nuke). Death Goat is just pure twitch: dodge and shoot twin stick badassery.
Being in early access Death Goat shows a lot of promise, and the dev seems to be very active in the community, and the current price of $2.99USD is pretty fair. The fact that the game appears to be bug free at this point means that development is going to focus on adding new features as asked for by the community, which is pretty exciting. I'm particularly looking forward to the possibility of multiplayer modes being added.

I'm on the fence about recommending this to everyone. While being locked at 30 FPS doesn't really bother me much it still stresses the hell out of my rig, and while it's not the best it's not that bad. But beyond that it's a good game.
Pros:
Weapon customization is up there for me I mean who doesn't like combining a katana with a sickle and cut zombies in half? Lighter fluid and a super soaker? Count me in.
Enemy variety: Yes I know they are all zombies but it's actually hard to find 2 zombies exactly alike, which sort of shocked me after playing games like Dynasty Warriors where all the enemies besides the bosses were the same same with games like State of Decay all the zombies were just bland but not here. While it's a small thing it's just nice not looking at the same zombie pallete.
Fun factor: Let's not lie games like Saints Row work because of the fun factor, and you can find that as well here. Dialogue costumes ect bring more of the light side of the zombie apocolpse. Because who wouldn't want to have a lego head while smashing zombies with a robot toy?
Co-op: One of my favorite Zombie type games was State of Decay and the thing that was lacking the most was co-op and that's to be found in the game and it's pretty damn good. While I may change this section of the review later because I don't have much time in co-op as of yet but so far what I have tasted isn't bad at all.
Gameplay: It's just your usual button masher with combos thrown in there after you've chain killed a certain amount of zombies. It's at least fluid but it has it's downfalls read on in the cons section.
Cons:
Gunplay: I'm not sure what is up with the gun play in the game. Aim for the head hit an arm aim for an arm and hit the head. The targeting seems sketchy at beast at least for guns. Some of the design choices I don't understand you can break through glass but the hit/miss while shooting through windows seems a little sketchy. Plus there's the usual if you're within a few inches of a car while trying to hit a zombie on the other side  is a no go there's a small deadzone around each item in the environment.
30 FPS Lock: While it's not a big deal to me I know a lot of people believe this is unacceptable to me it's fine I have photosensitive epilepsy if I start going too fast I end up having to take more frequent breaks. I put it in cons because even if I can't play it at 60FPS it's unacceptable in this age.
Soundtrack: Eh I could have went with a little better selection, usually blahsay affair.
Overall I'd get this game however if you have a lower end system I wouldn't even bother until you upgrade unless you want to turn everything down to low and if that's the case if you have an Xbox One just pick it up on there. If performance issues are a problem with you then I'd wait for a bit longer until maybe there is a patch or 2 to deal with some of the issues I listed above. I've seen a lot worse ports but I've also seen a lot better ones. If you're a fan of the Dead Rising series it's of course a must buy.

Dead Rising 3 generally has been working fine for me.
The only issue that I've been facing are ♥♥♥♥♥♥ framerates and the lack of resolution options.
(I use 1680x1050 which isn't provided under options.)
^ But for the resolution, my way of getting around that is using Alt+Enter to turn the game into Windowed mode and then resize the window to fit my screen.
The game does indeed need patches to optimize the game for PC, but aside from that:
Dead Rising 3 follows its regular tradition of allowing players to pick up the most randomest objects scattered across the map and use them against zombies. The crafting system is similar to that of Dead Rising 2 but now instead of having to find a workbench to craft weapons, you can do it on the spot. In addition to that, you can create "Combo Vehicles" which turn the regular vehicles you see into some weird things that you can murder zombies with.
Other similar things include:
The Queen Bees that you can smash to kill a group of zombies at once.
The usual time-constraints that ruin the game for me. ;_;
Hilarious apparel including female clothing and large♥♥♥♥♥masks.
Ridiculous weapon combinations that prove to be effective.
The disturbing psychos with their lovely and "touching" stories/motives.
The leveling system. (Acquire PP to gain levels and attribute points to make your person stronger.)
Co-op.  (Which has been working without a problem for me as well.)
New things include:
Survivors aren't as much as a hassle as they are from the past Dead Risings because you can easily dispense them into the multiple safe houses located around the map by interacting with a bulletin board and they teleport to you when they fall behind.
Of course, new characters with a new larger environment.
And although this is my own personal opinion, I felt that the increase in the number of present zombies active at once makes up for the decent graphics in Dead Rising 3.
Combat is much more fluid in my opinion as well featuring an "Over-the-shoulder" aiming when using a projectile or throwing an object.
A combo system that allows the player to perform a gruesome special attack to gain more PP.
Book benefits are now permanent and can be selected through the menu.
Mostly everything is fed to you in the sense that you don't have to search for psychos or events, they'll just mark everything for you.
Overall Dead Rising 3 is okay for me and co-op with my friend makes the game a lot more fun.
Yes there are bugs here and there that need to be fixed but at least in my experience, none of them are game-breaking.
^ Aside from a car being possessed and blowing up randomly in my face.
Would recommend in general, but with all the optimization and bugs that other people are facing, I would say to wait a while.

If the idea of strapping an LMG to a giant teddy bear and setting it loose on the masses in a wave of bloody destruction is enough to get your blood running south of the border, then this is a title that you'll more than likely enjoy.
If, on the other hand, you like the idea of being able to play a game for more than 30 minutes without fear of it locking up and crashing out to your desktop, then you might want to wait a while before grabbing this one.
As far as performance goes, I don't think that this is nearly as bad as most people depict it to be. My modest PC, running an i7 950 (practically ancient) and a GTX 660SC (also getting on in years) is able to pull a consistent 40FPS, sometimes dipping down as low as 30. It's definitely playable, but if you're a framerate junky, or value overall stability (which I think most of us actually do), it might behoove you to wait a while and see if the developer or the modding community is able to tighten things up and optimize performance a bit better.
The gameplay, though, oh boy is the gameplay fun.

Dead Rising 3 is a blast! As other reviewers have said, there are indeed truckloads of zombies, and there are some pretty exotic ways to mow them like grass. Because I didn't play the earlier games carefully, I faced a bit of a learning curve here, most especially with things like the map and getting a feel for the distinct flow of this game, which rewards you for running all over town. As I have finished chapter 3, I'm already feeling like I want to go back to the beginning and play it better.
There are other elements that are just crazy fun. DR3 has the paper doll thing going maybe wilder even than Saints 3 and 4. And because items don't show up in your warddrobe till you've selected them when you find them -- which then puts them on -- the game rewards you for willy-nilly putting on goofball ensembles. Check my screenshots: welding mask plus sci-fi princess exotic outfit turn you on? White fedora on your swat uniform, and wrong color boots that are too short? How about a sombrero to go with that kung-fu gi and skater jeans? It is a riot.
One meaningful critique is that the control model of this series has always been weird for me. Your hero will swing religiously in the wrong direction till you turn him around, and the controls are different for that -- and feel loosey -- compared to some other FPS's (e.g., Dishornored and DE:HR). Another feel/ambiance critique is that your character, Nick, on the streets is an absolute bada**!!! He is slaughtering like a demi-god -- by end of Day 4 I was at 10,000 zombies killed (!!!), but when you get to the cut scenes, he is so mousy!!!! The scenes would fit better with Mad Max or The Man Without A Name, or someone who could do what this guy does with SUCH power!
This game is an instant favorite. Even though it's got a linear story line, I will play this one more than once.  And for all you completionists, getting all the recipes, etc., will keep you exploring! Excellent!

UPDATE:  A year later, this is the only controller I use. I bought a second one and got rid of the xbox controllers.  I love how I can set it to make classic video game noises.

The touch controller is a game-changer, but it does not replace the xbox controller.  Each excels at its own games.
This controller is amazing in games intended for mice. It displays unexpected precision and smooth flow.  Its great in first person games, as sight it a little more organic than button control would allow.
There are, however, some controller games that just feel inferior with this.  A good example is Mortal Kombat, which originated on a controller and really doesn't have a good way to utilize the touchpads.
It also works great with Windows 10. I am able to use the controller for my picture password, the start menu, etc. Weirdly, the Microsoft controller does not do this.  The controller keyboard is GREAT- it is not difficult to type with 2 thumbs. Really the only thing I am forced to use a mouse for are annoying user account control confirmations.
Overall, a great product - just don't throw away the old controllers yet.

Because, no playthrough, is ever the same. Even if you play the same "faction" 10 times in a row, in different  or same sized maps, will it ever be the same.

Dungeon Siege is a classic RPG and I always get nostalgic playing it. When I first played Dungeon Siege I was really taken by the simplicity of the skills mechanic and the fact that once you are in the world there are no loading screens - you just constantly walk through one giant map. There's not much story to the game, just some serious grindy RPG action with some side quests thrown in for the completionists like myself.
One thing I originally liked about the game was that there aren't any confusing skill trees, just specialisations and attributes in which you can level up simply by doing things - hitting things with a stick gives you melee skill and mostly strength, while casting spells gives you magic skill and mostly intelligence, etc. This is now the very thing I dislike about the game. While it's nice and simple it does kind of make combat slightly boring as you don't have an array of special abilities to manage (well, none unless you have a mage). Sure, mages have spells which they can switch between, but only being able to actively switch between two spells without some complicated process and having no autocasts just gets tiresome. I still really love this game, but I think if it weren't for the nostalgia I probably wouldn't be enjoying as much as I am today.
If you played Dungeon Siege on its initial release and enjoyed it back then, then it might be worthwhile getting for another play through, but if you're new to the series I would recommend skipping over this one and starting with Dungeon Siege II, which has much better gameplay. Now, back to the grindstone.

I've seen "ports" as they're called before and as much as my fellow PC gamers complain about them I usually don't mind. Sometimes I'm just grateful a game is available on PC. This time however I feel I must join the complainers since it's actually justified this time.
The game itself is pretty great in my opinion, but it's ruined by many bugs/glitches like game saves frequently getting corrupted for no apparent reason, invisible obstacles, and sounds not playing like the audio files are messed up or something. On top of that; you can only select resolutions below 1080p. The resolution actually didn't bother me much, but it's just one more mark against the PC version and I know it will bother some gamers.

I really wanted to like this game.  The level designs and concepts were great.  But the huge number of bugs/glitches/annoyances managed to suck all the fun out of this game.  I regularly I had to do internet searches on how to get around various problems so that I could progress in the game.
The game crashes frequently.  And the saves sometimes get into some sort of corrupted state so that you have no choice but find a previous save (if you have one) and replay parts of the game.
And if the save system wasn't so bad, this could be tolerable.  But quick saves don't work at all (apparently related to what drive you have the game installed on).  So you have to do manual saves and the saves don't get any sort of name and just appear in an unnecessarily small window (can see 4 at a time) in a random order (not even by save date) -- a total pain if you need to find the 2nd or 3rd last save so that you can replay to work around a problem.
And the final level was just a travesty.  The game crashed in so many places and saves got corrupted.  You work around all of that and then you finally difuse the bomb and then the game just freezes -- nothing.  You have to use task manager to shut down the game and restart yet again.  Then finally found out that you had to change screen resolution to 800x600 just before you completed the final task so that could see the final cutscene and progess to the bonus mission.
I can't believe that a product ever got released like this and obviously received such little support from the developers.  I don't really care whether this was Steam's fault, the publisher's fault or the developer's fault.  But the result is that a potentially very engaging game has become an epic fail.

This is so bizarre.  I remember having this game on Playstation 2 back in the day and having fond memories of it and yet people keep saying this is not nearly as good as Chaos Theory.  While Chaos Theory is amazing I recall Double Agent having most of the same mechanics and an interesting undercover element.  So I install it to give it one more playthrough only to see what everyone was fussing about.  This is NOT the game I played on PS2.  Not by a long shot.  The missions are all different.  The story, the gameplay... Everything dumbed down.  As a long time fan of this series I was always confused by how so many people said this wasn't a good game.  Now I see why.
PC Double Agent is a very different animal to the console Double Agent in every way.  All the things I liked about the PS2 version is not here.  I enjoyed this game but despite its flaws and unlike all the other Splinter Cell games I have no desire to ever touch this one again.  The biggest problem was just how hard it was to avoid being spotted.  Like when you thought you were well hiddent and it turns out you weren't and there's no chance seeing it coming.  Enemies can spot you miles away and will shoot you instantly with pinpoint accuracy.  Sometimes through walls.  The undercover aspect between missions where you sneak around the terrorists base to do things during a time limit has been significantly dumbed down as well.  Oh get spotted in a restricted area "Fisher you're not supposed to be here" with a little bump in trust.  I rememebr the stakes being much higher on PS2 with them shooting you on sight and better level design as well.  There just doesn't seem to be any tension in the stealth.   You either succesffully sneak through or you dont.  Half the time I would just go around a corner after being spotted and wait for the alert to go away after a second and its like nothing happened.  Oh noes my stealth score goes down?  I can't unlock gear that I'll never need?  pFFFFt say what you will about Conviction and Blacklist being more action oriented but at least those game's mechanics work well.
Edit: I didn't even talk about the crappy interface and other issues that plague this game.  When spacebar is your action button for everything from opening doors to turning light switches to grabbing guards from behind it makes sense to have a prompt on screen to let you know exactly what you're about to do.  All the games before this had it simply say it at the bottom of the screen.  Here its shoved in your face in the middle of the screen as if to say "YOU'RE ABOUT TO DO A THING JUST TO MAKE SURE YOU HAVE ADD AND CAN'T TELL"  As if thats not bad enough you can't use your mouse while hacking computers or reading emails.  You can't even type in the numbers when using a keypad lock!  Sometimes while opening safes it doesn't register the keys until you play with the mouse wheel for some reason.  Top it all off with glitches such as bodies flying away after you drop them completely destroying your efforts of hiding them.  On a couple occasions they just flopped around for minutes until enemies nearby noticed and i was screwed.  This doesn't even touch on the save issues when it doesn't read its own auto saves or in one mission reoloading a save causes the game to crash.  Its all these little problems littered throughought the game that just made it more of a hassle.  I mean Chaos Theory (the game before this) had gamepad support!  It didn't work very well.  It didn't register R2 and L2 on a PS3 controller but it was there.  This one has none.  Doesn't read the controller at all... How do you have so many downgrades?  Its so counter-intuitive to PC gaming when even the first Splinter Cell was more intuitive than this!!!!
This is the only game in the series where I will say skip it.  If you can get an old copy of a console version in a bargain bin somewhere go for that.  That version is far superior to this extreme change for no reason.  Makes no sense why they made two completely different games for different platforms.  For all I know the Xbox version is even more different so I would play it safe and just find a PS2 if you must play every game in the series.

Firstly, I uncapped the frame rate of DR3 so my frame rate was about 40-50 fps on high settings in 1080p
Secondly, I won't be really mentioning the story or characters (except the main protagonist)
The game itself is an improvement to DR2 in a couple of ways, the most noticeable thing being that in DR3 you only have to go through one loading screen before going into the actual game, which is a plus compared to DR2 which was a nightmare to travel through due to the frequent 1-2 minute loading screens (I played it on Xbox 360)
The graphics look great!, the faces of the humans, the zombies themselves and the scenery look fantastic!
The addition of vehicles (for me) is good, it makes travel easier but all vehicles break and blow up quickly
There are also combo vehicles which are just badass (a motorbike with the front of a steamroller that has flamethrowers anyone?)
Theres a wide variety of weapons, melee and ranged, and there is also the combos which now can be made on the go (as long as you are away from the zombies) which is nice.
The main character is a mechanic called Nick Ramos, who comes across as whimpy and generic to me and thats all I'll say about him.
The psychos (mini bosses) are.... well mad and funny (in a WTF way)
Overall, if you can get over the Performace issues and crashes or use the fix, Dead Rising 3 is a good game with hours of fun, oh and did I mention that you can play it in co-op mode? 8/10

Here are the instructions from jbneoh on how to remove the FPS cap:
Guide to remove 30fps cap
>Go to your deadrising3 folder. Default should be (C: Program Files (x86) \ Steam \ Steam Apps \ Common \ deadrising3)
>create new text file in the folder
>name it "user.ini" (make sure you change the file type from txt to ini)
>open the new text file and type in “gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate = True”
>save the document
>start the game
>enjoy!!

Best controller out there right now, capable of comfortably playing the widest variety of games of any controller currently out.
But don't buy it for fighting games.
I'm honestly not quite sure what the left touch pad is even for. The right pad works perfectly well for controlling cameras and such, but I have no clue what the left pad was intended for. It certainly doesn't work very well for controlling movement. Not even in sidescrollers. It just doesn't feel right to press it in, and drag your thumb around like it was a d-pad. It just feels like so much more effort than with other controllers. I honestly think I'd prefer that the left pad was replaced entirely by a really good d-pad, opening the controller up to being usable with fighting games, without really losing anything, in my eyes.
Other misc. problems: the bumpers feel a little more uncomfortable to reach and press than they should. I tend to avoid them if I can, mapping whatever the bumpers do to the grips instead (and btw, the grips are lovely; they work really well for jumping and sprinting/ducking in FPS games). Another thing is that I feel like the stick and face buttons are maybe set a little too far into the controller's face. Sometimes it can feel like I'm really reaching for them. And an annoyance that can sometimes happen is if you're holding the stick to the right and trying to hit the x button at the same time, you can end up bumping your thumbs together, which isn't a good feeling. It makes the whole thing feel cramped.
Other than these minor complaints, I love the steam controller. Never thought I'd comfortably play an FPS with a controller before. As a games developer, this will be a lot of fun to play around with, and was well worth the money. However, to the general public, I wouldn't recommend spending 50$ on this, unless you just cannot contain your curiosity. Wait til it's cheaper if you're not already sold on the concept. It is quite nice though.
I'd give it an 8/10. Replace the left pad with a d-pad and its a 9/10. Better spaced out controls and easier to press bumpers, and its a solid 10/10 from me. I hope Valve does explore further revisions of this controller.
oh, and btw, the battery life is quite good as well.

I really wasn't sold on this idea when I first heard it. At first it seemed like there would be too much going on, but after playing it I find at times there isn't enough. While I wished there was more depth, there is enough depth here that allows for some very interesting playstyles and if you are willing to leave your comfort zone you could find that there is a way of playing that better suits you.
The greatest thing that this game offers is it always makes you feel like you are excelling, that you are clearly doing better than everyone else, but that is never the case. The moment you become complacent the game will show you how far you can fall. Past failures are a constant reminder that some new danger always lurks just around the corner, no matter how well your empire appears to be doing.
The political side of things is very interesting and each government feels unique. You can really get a sense that you are trying to stay in command of something much greater than the sum of it's parts. Small factions vying for power, that you can easily ignore but can gain the powerful influence resource from befriending.
Unlike other titles however, I don't think I would enjoy playing this solo. It is much better with a friend or two. It's not a title I would recommend to just anyone, but I enjoy it enough that I would hate to see someone not try it and miss out.

I saw this game first on a youtube Let's Play. After watching a couple of their episodes, I had to try this game for myself. As a cat lover and dating sim fan, how could I pass it up?
Pros:
My first impression was that the music was really good. I like the art style and the fact you can romance any of the characters regards of your choices on the character select screen.
I thought each of the story arcs was interesting. Each person has their own backstory and their own personality that affects how they interact with Avery. It didn't feel cookie-cutter to me like other dating sims. I found the dialogue really funny at times; so much so I laughed out loud! While I did go through to play every route (romanced every character), I enjoyed Finley's the most. She's really friendly and exhuberant and I found her the most enjoyable to interact with.
Cons:
It is a bit short. I kinda wish I had more time with each love interest. You have a couple of moments and then it time skips the story a bit. I have 8 hours logged cuz I went through each route but it took me about 3 hours to do one.
I kinda wish there were other outfit options, but meh, not a deal breaker. That's more of a personal thing.
It could just be me, but I felt like unless you played all the routes, you didn't get the "full" story of how everything goes down in the end. That is, if you choose character A, none of the other stuff that happens to the others (if you choose them) could happen. I want all the good stuff to happen no matter what! :D

This game is wonderful. Released back in 2002, I learned about this game through a cousin of mine, and I fell in love with the game. Spending well over 500 hours into its singleplayer and online multiplayer (now defunct -- LAN works great though), I never realized how much I would come to miss this game.
A classic dungeon crawler where you're not limited by classes or levels. You can be whatever you want, a pure melee character, an archer, a mage, a combination of two, or all of the above. You have the ability to choose how you level up your skills. Instead of levels, there's strength, dexterity, and intelligence. These act as your levels towards what you want to use in combat, and progressively increase through combat. This is different from the timeless classic of Diablo 2, however has a great leveling system that's sure to let you play however you'd like. The storyline is wonderful, and with co-op multiplayer, it adds on more difficulty so your not running around finding too easy.
Unfortunately, this doesn't come included with Dungeon Siege: Legends of Aranna, but if you happen to have a copy, you can install it over Steam's installation (plus with a little renaming of game executables) and be able to play it through Steam.
One of the downsides is that since its been over 11 years that Dungeon Siege has been released, multiplayer is now defunct. In Dungeon Siege, you'll find that the Multiplayer button gives you the message "Disabled". Is all hope lost? Of course not. By adding the launch parameter "zonematch=true" to your game, you can access multiplayer LAN and direct connection games without the use of warez, cracks, or patches. Its a shame that you need to bypass that message just for direct and LAN capabilities, but it gets the job done, and it still works perfectly.
I would definitely recommend this game for anyone who's a fan of dungeon crawlers, especially playing them with friends, and for those who are looking to try something new. It's not hard to get the hang of, but it won't get too easy on you either.
Even though the Multiplayer has been disabled, I still now have the chance to enjoy this game.

The skill system in which your party members' powers grow according to how you play was innovative for its time. It was also notable for its real-time combat that could be paused for considering options and giving orders. It's a fun game, but it suffers from several padded levels that don't offer a lot of variety over their long play time. The graphics have aged, but the gameplay is still solid.

A nice little game that's easily worth the price of admission. Short and sweet, but doesn't fail to dissapoint you in the aspects of the game.
The game itself is a fun game to play. The story isn't anything to rave about, but it really isn't meant to be a story driven game. After completion of the game, you won't really feel like you have been cheated out of a story because the value lies in the gameplay.
The formula of the gameplay is well done. Combine the likes of Portal and Cave Story into a unique game, and you have yourself a couple hours of shooting portals trying to go from Point A to Point B while trying to reach the goal.
The enemies themselves aren't really challenge, and felt more like something to be aware of than enemies that you need to mindlessly kill. Killing an enemy was essentially removing the obstacle needed to advance because in all cases where the enemy wasn't blocking the way, the enemies could simply be portalled past. The bats got a tad annoying at times, liking to slowly home in on your character, but were a mere annoyance more than an actual threat due to you not being able to tank any hits.
The game was happy to provide you with lots of save points, mostly at the start of a room so that you didn't have to redo a previously completed puzzle in the case of death. On top of that, the save points themselves act as a respawn point, and with infinite lives, you were free to try to work out a solution for the puzzle without fear of getting a game over screen.
The beginning and end of the game consisted of pilotting your ship through space. I didn't truly enjoy it that much, as it's been done a million times over in countless games, but at least the beginning of the game immediately sent you to the platforming phase when you died. The end of the game had the final boss in two phases, one of which was in space. Neither of them were that hard, but the space phase, whilst a mere annoyance of having to reenter space after the fun platforming, felt needed due to the fact that the entire game revolves around you trying to fix your ship.
Overall though, the game is short, perhaps a little too short. As soon as the game really started going, and you were doing some intricate puzzles, the game immediately has you enter the final bosses tower and the game simply ends there. In my own personal opinion, the game ended almost a little bit too soon after reaching it's potential.
Verdict:
Pro's:
+ Fun gameplay with a good scaling difficulty
+ Good fitting soundtrack to accompany the game
+ Puzzles that were fun, and with the nonexistant penalty of death, you felt no pressure to rush yourself.
+ Graphics are nice for a game that uses pixel sprites.
Con's:
- Game is a little short, and feels like the game could have gone on a little bit longer once it has shown you its full potential.
- Slightly tedious and annoying space sequences at the beginning and end of the game.
Overall:
Highly reccomended. The downsides are easily overweighed by the upsides when also taking into account the price of admission. Would easily buy a fleshed out sequel, possibly even shell out more than the nickles and dimes spent on this one if it was longer and improved upon the successful formula of the first.

I've seen many reviews about the Steam Controller that treat it for something it clearly isn't. It is neither supposed to be a better XBox gamepad, nor a keyboard and mouse replacement. It is something completely new. A prototype that luckily doesn't have the hardware quality of one.
This means that, even though the Steam Controller is well designed and crafted, games haven't been designed for it yet. The games you can buy on Steam are either optimized for gamepads or for keyboard and mouse. The Steam Controller doesn't perfectly replace either of them, but you
play all the games with it. And this is the one and only strength of this hardware as of yet: Sit on your couch, start Big Picture and play. Pretty much any game. Even strategy games, which have been mostly unplayable for controller users before. It will just get some time getting used to, since it's a new concept. But it works.
While I think that there will be titles that have input also designed and tested for the Steam Controller, the current configuration of the hardware gives you enough power to play anything that's here already. You can not only map all of the buttons to whatever you want, you can set up the control stick, the trackpads, the gyroscope, accelerometer and the triggers to do anything you want. If you're not in the mood to setup the controller yourself, browse existing setups that the community shared. You will find something well playable within seconds, and you can improve it for yourself later on.
My Conclusion:
Many people have a feeling that this hardware feels unfinished. That playing with it doesn't feel as right as it does with one of the alternatives. The reason for that is simply that the Steam Controller doesn't try to be something else, but better. It is something new. Something that no game is optimized for yet. It allows you to play any game you want with it, like no other input device will. You just need to be ready to get used to it, since it doesn't feel like anything you used before, either.

There were a lot of things upon release, and still now, that suck about this game. Suck in the way that I'm surprised Paradox, given the good work that they've done and continue to do, actually let come to market. But as of this writing I've played 94 hours of the game, so that's all the complaining I'm legally and ethically allowed to do. This is a good game, possibly the best of the space 4x's. It has yet to reach "Europa Universalis In Space" status, but patches and DLC are rolled out fairly regularly, so maybe one day it'll get there.

No other game combines the ambition and scale of a grand strategy title with the approachability of a 4X quite as successfully as Stellaris.  To boot, it is a love letter to science fiction and space opera, brimming with experiences that harken to film and literature embedded within emergent gameplay.  Mods were supported from release, and the game is now a platform for deep strategy gameplay set in your choice of classic sci-fi settings as much as it remains a RNG-powered sci-fi simulator in its own right.  Long term support from Paradox has meant a continuous stream of free updates, including major revisions to game mechanics, and fun DLC content for purchase.  The 2.0 update in early 2018 should once more revitalize the Stellaris universe and carry on the hopefully very long life of this genre-bending work of art.

When I started to play Primal Carnage: Extinction I wasn't sure what to expect. Let's be honest - it's hard to make a multiplayer game nowadays, when most of people play free to play games or some rather popular online titles and totally ignore the lest known out. So, is this game worth anything? I guess it is. It's probably the best multiplayer game with dinosaurs. I mean, it's fun to play team deathmatch where one team is full of people and other one is made of dinos. It's rather active, not like more popular online games, but still have some playerbase so you can be sure there is always someone to play it together. Maps are fun, game is rather balanced. What's also important, it does have drop system like in CS:GO - which means, you can earn yourself a few cents while playing, or finding yourself a nice skin for your dinos or humans. Items don't make you any more powerful, those are just cosmetic stuff which is good thing. Also, there are new patches still coming out, so you don't get an abandoned game.
If you want to play something other than MOBA games or online shooters with "good" vs "bad" guys you should at least try Primal Carnage: Extinction. You can't miss it if you are fan of dinosaurs!

Although Hustle Cat is short, it's charming and definitely worth the price. I can tell there were multiple CG artists and possibly sprite artists as the art style is inconsistent at times, but I don't mind much. It's obvious a tremendous amount of work was put into this – props to everyone who worked on this game! 6 versions of each CG including the MC, even if they're only minorly different, and 6 sets of sprites for the MC, alongside the quality music and equal attention paid to each route among many other things. There are a few spelling and grammatical errors, but nothing too extreme, and they're not frequent enough to distract from the story. The pronoun choices and the MC customization options were a nice touch and helped make this game unique. There are a few issues, like lack of interactivity throughout a lot of the game, but the pros easily outweigh the cons.
Pros:
Quality music and writing.
Inclusive of different genders, sexualities, and races.
Diverse personalities of the characters.
Refreshingly entertaining and non-bland MC.
Healthy relationships!
You get to date cute kitties.
Cons:
Short. 8-9 hours to be expected.
Very limited amount of saves.
The game will likely feel somewhat unsatisfying unless all routes are done.
Not a lot of options on the options screen.
Mostly linear once on a route.
Only one ending for each character.
As long as you don't mind the length and the mostly linear nature, this game will be very enjoyable to the majority of otome and dating sim gamers, assuming you're the kind of person to play through all the routes.

From the getgo, Dungeon Siege has been my very favorite game, standing the test of time for over ten years.  It is a gem in the rough, lackluster hack 'n' slash genre.  Some of it is nostalgia, sure, but most of all it is a quality that whispers softly to those that will listen.
The most accurate and common description praises Dungeon Siege as being atmospheric.  The music from the now esteemed Jeremy Soule is top notch, fitting the game's open scenery, environments, dungeons, and caves very well.  The often peaceful music of the open outside landscape fits well in the different environments (wood, snow, desert, swamp, etc.) and contrasts with the sudden tense quiet of many caves and dungeons.
The other thing about Dungeon Siege, which I mentioned, is that it rises above the rest of the genre, simply.  Other games feel like an endless cycle to get a quest to go in this cave where you kill an unremarkable boss and destroy the crates only to find yourself looking at a bunch of junk.  So much junk.  And then the only thing you ever equip are the occassional super items that the boss happened to drop for your class.
Ok, so Dungeon Siege is also an endless cycle of wading through the countless monsters, minions, and grunts of the local denizens.  But what Dungeon Siege does is a journey on a highly linear path that winds through the wilderness of those monsters.  It's the same in the sense that it's another screen full of those enemies and you gotta punch through them.  But it really makes you feel relieved as you emerge from that dungeon and think, "wow, that was a long dungeon, I'm really glad I got outta there."  The crate and barrel smashing is not as dull when they may explode, breaking others in the radius, and arrow traps.  Seriously, when is the last time a crate fired an arrow at you?
Enemies will spawn from bushes on the side of the path.  Tiny swarms of little spiders skitter from passages on the ceiling to rush you.  They ambush you from grating in the floor and in the wall.  Small mage creatures appear on the edges of the snowy hills.  Ice creatures will shatter their frosty pillars and surge toward you.  Goblins go at you with...oops no spoilers.
Although it may get tedious (if you let it) at times, you lead a party of up to eight(!) adventurers.  The story is the same cliche but I think executes it well.  It is however, sparse and far between.  Most of the game is in the journeying bit.  My favorite dialog from this game from a cranky mountain shopkeeper (maybe it's just me):
"Who are you then?!  Another of that short goblin's cussin' errand runners?  You tell that little green snotball..."
The graphics are quite dated, and if you aren't someone who played games from the 90's period, you may not think they look good.  However, the environment still has a lot of detail that you might not realize at the first impression.
I recommend playing this game for between two and five hours in a session, although I have been guilty of spending ten hours for several days.  If you enjoy the genre, I believe Dungeon Siege is a great pick.  Although the age of the game is apparent (there are no abilities), the sequel, Dungeon Siege 2, is also very good and has includes those more modern ideas in the gameplay.

NieR:Automata is a brilliant masterpiece. The gameplay, story and looks are great, really not too profound or detailed, but entertaining and fun. The crown jewels, however, are the incredible music and the many moments of surprise and astonishment that ultimately elevate this game to an outstanding experience. Despite the fact that the poor port is a deficiency, it, thankfully, can be easily fixed by installing the community made FAR mod. And with this out of the way, there's nothing that can disparage the achievements of this game.
Yes, it's sexy but not embarrassing. No, the writing and characters aren't cringy or facile despite their Japanese authors. 2B's dry pragmatism, 9S's sincerity and A2's vexation are candid and reasonable character traits. Surely enjoying the game takes some affinity for East Asian culture, but NieR:Automata lacks the exaggerations, both written and visual, that bear no rationale and depreciate other East Asian titles.
The combat is designed to enjoy. There's no sophisticated combo or blocking system, instead there are different weapons with their own movesets and interactions. Including the Shmup and hacking interludes, the combat gameplay is mechanically shallow even with regards to the constraints of the genre. Overall though, the importance of depth in the combat system is neglectable because its focus clearly lies within the refinement of what little there's to it. Spot-on controls and fluid animations evoke a sheer delight, especially while trying out different weapon combos. Even though the game doesn't have high fidelity graphics and uses rather muted colours, the character models and particularly the combat animations are simply beautiful.
Although the story doesn't shy away from big philosophical thoughts and concepts and, in that regard, even bigger names, its complexity is based on a mix of caprice and circumstance. During the majority of the time, the player is presented with an elusive fait accompli that leaves just enough space for own thought experiments. It's not a light story but not a heavy one either. Beyond dispute, the true ending puts everything in perspective and absolutely needs to be played. NieR:Automata doesn't repeat after the credits, it's not a new playthrough, despite its initial appearance. Until the very last proper credits, there's new content, story, areas and gameplay and not only a different point of view.
The metalevel aspects of NieR:Automata are so ingeniously implemented that they regularly generate overwhelming feelings of wonder and excitement. Paired with the comprehensive story, the sense that everything is in the realm of the possible emerges. But even when the player is ready for any twist, the game still manages to surprise. Ranging from small things such as an unexpected camera perspective to significant story and game related turns, all of it's profound, thought out and well executed.
Across the board the music is fantastic but really shines and takes on an important role during boss battles. Since the majority of the songs with vocals are sung in a completely made up language, the music never interferes or distracts from the gameplay. Instead, selectively appointed vocals generate a hype while the driving beats lead the combat perceptibly. The quality and intensity of these integral music tracks effectuate a gameplay rush unmatched since Hotline Miami.
I can say that NieR:Automata is my favourite single player game to date. Even though it's certainly not perfect in detail, it's the whole package that's so convincing to me. Experiencing the final credits caused a feeling of euphoria mixed with frustration and at last a poignant sense of bliss. If there were a game that I could forget and play all over again, it'd be this one.

The Secret of Monkey Island's Special Edition revisits the classic Point&Click adventure "everybody" played when they were young (and some not so young).
It's one of the best games ever and groundbreaking for its genre (besides the fact that some games like "Maniac Mansion", "Zak McKracken", "Indiana Jones  and the Last Crusade" and "Loom" were there first).
SoMI:SE has updated graphics, sounds, music and -for the first time- voice work. All of them are great but the detailed graphics take away a bit of the flair of the old 8-bit, at least for me: I've played the original game for years and the "new" Guybrush doesn't look at all how I imagined him back then.
I liked the old SCUMM interface (using action verbs and written inventory names) and couldn't quite warm up to the new and easier interface of the SE.
Fortunately one can switch between the classic look-and-feel and the remake at any time - so you can choose which experience you'd like right now.
SoMI:SE is a great addition to everybody's library of games and I can absolutely recommend it - especially if you've never played it before!

My experience from this game goes as such: Community basis, is very accepting, and kind. You can join a raidcall and within a minutes make friends. In the actual game you do busy work until level 60 where you can finally start to do something entertaining. However, after 65, the leveling gap really becomes apparent. at level 70, an entire run of dungeons gets you roughly 1 percent of your current level and less so the higher the level. Also with the rarity of the drops. You either have luck, or stop playing you are waisting time. This game is based on luck on time. If you don't have both of those, don't play. 124.3 hours in game in the past two weeks got me nothing of use from dungeons, high level monsters, high level anything.
Now that my rant is over, in all seriousness:
Pros:
Very friendly community
Weekly updates
Teamwork oriented
Cons:
Very time consuming
Very luck based (you need to be very lucky)
Progessively large xp and level gaps (One size fits all)
Foot in the door type currency systems (difficult to make money, items are usually very expensive, unless you have a sugar momma/daddy, refer to Cons 1 & 2)
Very difficult to get level up armour and weapons (Cons 1, 2 & 3)
"OP" Idolizing (You are either over powered, or weak and if so, be useless, refer to cons 1, 2, 3 &4)

I'd like to start off by saying, I LOVE this game. Have spent an absolutely unholy amount of time on it compared to any other game I have, and I'm unashamed to admit it.
it is not without its flaws.
1.
It's gameplay is very simple as of right now, even after a year it's still not much more than thinking and clicking. That's not necessarily a bad thing, and certainly detract from the game itself.
2.
I wouldn't necessarily say that's a bad thing, because I know plenty of people don't see this as a problem, it'd just be nice if mid-game wasn't a lot of "When's my next tech coming in?"
3.
If you have any experience with Paradox games, this should be a no-brainer. By itself, the base game is pretty fun, and held me off for a long time, but I eventually caved and bought the current DLC. Which, in my opinion was a good investment, but I'd recommend saving that for a sale like I did. But again, I personally feel a game shouldn't require DLC to feel complete, and it certainly feels that way.
4.
This is more opinion than anything, but despite this game being very diversified in empire construction, the game simply boils down to "how well can you destroy and/or conquer everyone else". Which, yeah, it's a 4X game, but for Federation playthroughs that simplifies something that could be much stronger. Federation gameplay is just a bigger version of what was stated earlier. However, you'd think they'd add something that could allow for better relationships between empires, such as more indepth trading and the like, and I'd
for them to add something like that in later titles.
Some pros I feel this game offer would be:
1.
this is a good game for you. Sure, you're not some hero or anything, but it's still got this decision-like things you'd find, but on a grander scale. For example, I personally prefer to play a Megacorporation empire, whose purpose is mostly just to be a buyer/seller among empires and avoid getting any real enemies. This also extends to using primitives to be integrated and later adapted into it.
2.
This ranges from just renaming leaders all the way to designing your empire from backstory to name to name
3.
If you don't mind putting a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of time into a game, and/or looking for a game like that, this is a good one. A game could go up into the double digits of hours, and beyond.
4.
As previously stated, there's a lot of downtime, but in all reality that's mostly just midgame. Early game is a lot of exploring, building, diplomacy, and pre-planning. Midgame is mostly just strengthening your empire and continuing diplomatic relationships. As well, wars start to pop up more frequently here. Late-to-endgame gets a little more finicky, lots of things depend here being the continued exist of major powers, the creation of any that hadn't gotten strong midgame, and a good bit of diplomatic ♥♥♥♥ery.
Personally, I recommend this game, however, I do see this as mostly a hit-or-miss, it's simplistic gameplay and mechanics kind of make it a "baby's first 4X", but that's mostly just from the surface.

Having played Stellaris for over 200 hours I can say it is definitively a fun if flawed game, however because of recent actions by Paradox I can not in good conscience recommend this game.
Stellaris not only suffers from the classic “tons of DLC” problem common for Paradox games but the developer team has announced that it will remove a core feature in the next update; more specifically as version 1.9.1 Stellaris has three possible systems FTL, hyperlanes, wormeholes and warp, a recent developer diary has announced that as of version 2.0 wormholes and warp will be removed from the game.
Not only removing the asymmetric FTL system completely changes the way the game plays and greatly limits customization and play style options but the removal of a core feature in a non-open beta game sets a disturbing precedent.
Worse case scenario we will see the removed FTL systems again in the future as paid DLC.

Game starts off as a shoot'em up side-scroller, which really took me by surprise. I mean, judging by the screens you'd rather expect a puzzle platformer and you get that not so long after the game starts, too. And then it just hit me, the brilliance of the idea: you fly, fighting your way to a new planet. Then you land, 'meet the locals' and proceed with the featured mission, which involves solving puzzles, fighting your way forward and doing some cool oldschool platformer type trickjumps. It's just all there. Again, really awesome mix.
The puzzle part is rather fun, the puzzles are not terribly easy, but also not too complicated. Can't imagine spending 8 minutes trying to beat one though (one of the achievements). As the game progresses, different beams are implemented, which change the behaviour of your teleport gun. The variety of enemies is rather limited - 4 kinds, erasing them is a bit of a chore, spam your gun until they drop dead. The game could feature no enemies and no one would probably miss them. The NPCs remind me the ones in old NES games, like Duck Tales, sometimes you have to sweat a little to get to them, but they might have some useful information or will say some funny things.
The shoot'em up part is just there I guess. It covers approx. 5% of a game that lasts for an hour, so you don't really spend too much time in it, shame.
It's mostly just your basic 'oldschool-nes-like-game-graphics'. Anyway, the art style is pleasant to watch. The only thing that somehow buggered me was that some maps looked a bit mundane and dull, with only same bricks of terrain laid over another same bricks of terrain. Adding more background details and decorations would probably make the game look a bit nicer, but then again, it's not really about the graphics this time, is it?

I've had my fair share of bad ports on PC, however this one is... well, I can't even describe how bad it is. Let's start at the beginning.
While the previous game of the franchise - Chaos Theory (yes, yes, one of the BEST stealth game of all time, however I won't go into further detail now) - got an update (1.05) to run in widescreen resolution (up to 1920*1200), this game did not, so you have to do some .ini tweaking to get the desired one.
Since we're at tweaking, there are couple of options in the .ini which aren't even present in game (for tweaking and issue resolving I recommend this page:
).
Even after you've done everything in your power to make the game a bit better, the shadows frequently flicker or just outright don't appear.
Then comes the sound: sometimes after loading the game, the game won't display a huge number of sounds (but you can still hear Sam's breathing, steps and muffled/glitched gun shots).
Then comes the loading issue: the save system is abysmal, you have 3 spaces to choose which one you'd like to load from / save to, you can't rename your save files (maybe you can, but I got so frustrated with the menu that I'd rather used the quicksave/load option) and sometimes quicksaves just outright disappeared. This usually happened when the game crashed, I reloaded my game using the "Continue" option which did load the quicksave file, however after wanting the quickload said file, I couldn't. What?!
I've written about the menu and how bad it is, but why you ask? Sometimes you can't navigate it with the keyboard (moreover it defaults to WASD rather then the arrow keys, but whatever), the mouse is janky and you can't use your mousewheel while browsing your save game files.
The OPSAT (Sam's ~infobar on his wrist during the game) is also equally bad, has all the problems just mentioned.
"Okay okay, but how's the game play?" You might ask. Well I could have gotten over all of the above, if only it was good or at least not as bad as I've come to know it. One word: awful. The controls are sometimes unresponsive, Sam just doesn't want to grab that ledge or crawl into a ventilation system no matter hard you try (like he's also fed up with the whole game "Nope, not gonna do it"). More often than not you get stuck on some random object which can also lead you being discovered or just missing your chance.
I might have missed some issues because there's plenty and I didn't write any of it down, all of this is just off the top of my head. A real shame though because it was a great idea executed so poorly...
So the question is: would I *recommend* the game? NO. If you like Splinter Cell, just skip it, if you're a "hardcore" SC fan, then you might, only might, want to give it a shot.

This is an original tale from Telltale games, after all, Minecraft itself is a storyless game. It's a blank slate to work with.
But Minecraft certainly does have it's tropes, it's communities and it's staples. And it's with those ingredients that Telltale was able to build an epic tale that is akin to saturday morning cartoons.
If you want a story that is both entertaining and leisurely without too much sophistication, this is can fulfill that need. It's like having a simple burger instead of a filet mignon. It's great, you'll like it and it can stand out on it's own, but it won't change your life.
Point is, it's fun and it really gets better as you keep going. If you LOVE Minecraft and have ever gone beyond just messing around in singleplayer survival, and you've attended Minecon, watched the youtubers, built amazing things, participated in communities online, then this game will hit all the right buttons for you.
If you're not a fan of Minecraft, then... I'm not sure what you'll get outta this. But you might enjoy the story? I don't know what it's like to not be a fan of Minecraft.

SEASON 1
Episode 1. 8/10
----------------
One was definitely my favourite episode. With the introducement to the main characters Jesse, Axel Olivia and Lucas. This sets off as the three friends attempting to build a fireworks stand at a builders tournament and a introduction to the 'Order Of The Stone' in which the victor gets to meet Gabriel the warrior one of the members of the Order. After all of this crap happens you lose your pig and gotta find him meeting Petra the female feminist empowering character. You and her out to sell a wither skull she has found to the main antagonist Ivory or as I call him 'The Shady Guy'. After the interview with Gabriel, Ivory builds a Wither in which the flask inorder to control is stolen from your good buddy Axel and the witherstorm gones ape S**t and starts consuming endercon completey. After a chain of events in which you can save Petra or Galbriel you enter the nether after this you find yourself at the Order's temple you have to finish puzzles in order to use the amulet Galbriel gave you, oh ye he gives you this magical amulet to track the order. You have to choose to go with Olivia to find Ellegard or with Axel to find Magnus. A great fun episode.
Episode 2 6/10
-----------
In this episode you have to choices I went with Olivia so I will tell the story of Ellegard you find her in her city redstonia in which you have to do some redstone crap and get into her thinking block there you must help her build a command block before the witherstorm comes and flips s**t up yet again. After you return you find Galbriel just chillin in the temple with Lucas. Also Axel went to find the other dude. After this you find the tracker to my boy Soren and attempt to track his footsteps at his temple, The two Order members you picked up get hella mad at each other and leave after you run into Ivory in which you find out he was a former Order member, you engage him in battle until he uses some elixir and runs away trapping you and your buddies in a library. This was an ok episode probs oh though I still reckon it was the worst out of the four.
Episode 3 7.5/10
-----------
In this episode you attempt to find Soren yet again losing the amulet while diging out of the temple finding a mob grinder leads you to the End. In there you find a whole wool world Sorens built and a bunch of enderman he is attempting to make them build. After putting the enderman suit on you try to find him, after finding him he punches you and takes you inside his house. There the enderman siege it and you and your buddies must escape. After coming back to surface you make the Super TNT Crap and Magnus and Ellegard are back together fighting the Witherstorm. There you build the bomb and blow the thing up leading to the death of either Ellegard or Magnus. Getting surviors you see that the command block is not damaged and it starts sucking everything up again yet this time there is 3 of them. Finding either Petra or Galbriel you run away into the next episode. This was a good episode exploring some unique themes of the power of being alone for a long period of time.
Episode 4 8/10
-----------
In this episode you run away from the Witherstorm once again and retreat to a crib in the mountains there you find out that Petra has forgotten everything and doesn't remember you. In which you try to figure out stuff about the Witherstorm. Ivory comes along and Soren gets hell mad that the bomb didn't work but Ivory figures out to destroy it using a Enchanted sword in which you and some of your buddies have to use the horses to go the 'Far Lands.' when finally getting there you complete this maze in which it leads you to Ivorys lab there you find out the truth of the Order of the stone and craft the weapon strong enough to destroy the command block in the Witherstorm. After leaving you finally engage the Witherstorm in combat and destroy the command block but not without pay your poor pig Reuben dies. After Galbriel reveals you and your friends are the new 'Order of the stone.' In the end you can tell to reveal the truth about the order or "Let the people dream." This episode was sick finally ending the Witherstorm and knowing that nobodies can truly become Legendary.
Overall Minecraft story-mode is really fun game with unique character creation semi-predicatable and for a so called 'kids game' actually pretty dark with touching moments and moments of sorrow and lack of salvation, though the game was pretty quick only took me 7 hours to finish it's still a really funny sick game defiantly  worth buying.

I thoroughly enjoyed playing this remake of Lucasarts’ classic adventure ‘The Secret of Monkey Island’. A wonderfully nostalgic experience. Playing it now as a more analytical adult, I was able to appreciate just how well designed & written this game really is. Very few modern adventure games come close to this kind of quality. So it’s good that in the remake Lucasarts kept all the puzzles, screens and dialogue unchanged. But they’ve enhanced the experience with perfectly cast recorded voices, fully re-recorded live music, gorgeous HD painted backgrounds, a fantastically updated interface and a useful hint system. The best feature though is the ability to “hotswap” at any time to and from the original version of the game!!
If I was to do a little nitpicking tho, they did cut a few corners: character close-ups had no mouth movement when they spoke; the walk animation cycle for all characters was too “floaty”; 3D character designs fall just short of blending nicely with the painted backgrounds; visual effects for water, lava and ghost movement are admittedly pretty, but look more like an iTunes visualiser than something fitting into the visual style of the game. It also would’ve been nice if there’d been an option to hotswap to the classic version but still hear the new voices and music.
None of these shortcomings seriously affected my enjoyment of the game tho.  All the awesomeness is still firmly there!

Easily the best controller I have ever used.
The trackpads seem unusual at first, and take a bit of getting used to, but once you're adapted at even a basic level (a month or so), the capabilities of the pad are evident. Mixing it with the excellent gyroscopic motion control in the controller, and you have the recipe for a FPS experience that is comparable to a mouse, though arguably more fun thanks to the gyro motion.
The amount of customization available on the controller software side is wonderful. For some it may be overwhelming, in which case you can simply use the top community profile for that game. This is indistinguishable from using a regular controller, as with a normal controller, you don't generally get a choice of keybindings anyway.
If you do want to tweak controls though, the customization is impressive. A lot of people had problems with the D-Pad at first, but by turning haptics on to High, a high dead-zone on the D-Pad, and making click not required, it replicates the feeling of a true D-Pad. I have been playing Axiom Verge a good bit lately using the controller in this way.
Perhaps the best advantage of this is in games with driving and shooting. Games like FarCry or GTA. There's always been this trade off with games, whether you want the aiming precision of a mouse, but get the 8-axis motion of WSAD... Or get the high precision of motion of a joystick, with the shoddy aiming of a joystick. With the Steam Controller, this is no longer a choice you need to make. The trackpad can input joystick controls into a game, but make it feel like a trackpad. This allows a game to read everything on the controller as a gamepad, so you can blend Analog motion with Mousepad precision. Adding gyro just steps it up another notch.
There has been no game I have played so far that I felt it would be better to be using a dual analog controller. Not a single game. There are some games where I still prefer a mouse and keyboard (CSGO for example), but this controller has replaced a number of other games that I used to play on M/KB, such as The Witcher 3.

So, first impressions of the controller. Once I picked it up I first noticed how natural it felt to hold. It felt “tight” and “hard” on the sides when holding it. Compared to the Xbox 360 controller where the weight and feeling seems to feel centered and the handles feeling like there just there to make sure you dont drop it. I want to say this feels like a mix of holding the sides of an N64 Controller with a PS3 controller (maybe even more so like a gamecube controller). It feels like the sides/handles are like a steering wheel and the handles makes up the whole controller. I know that might sound terrible but it just felt so..... right. Difficult to explain.
Using it however is a different story. This controller didn’t give me the feeling to just jump in and start playing games and get used to it instantly. It felt like it wanted you to be careful. Carefully press the buttons and get a feeling for the controller and understand it. Step by step. To keep it simple, holding it felt natural, but playing it did not.
The longer you use it, the more you notice that you have quite a bit to learn with using it as well as the flaws that start to come into play. The two circular pads that you see are trackpads. This is to emulate the keyboard and mouse feel. I tend to have an issue with the aiming trackpad with running out of room. As well as my thumbs tensing up and fatiguing from time to time.
The face buttons (ABXY) feel far too low but this is definitely because of the fancy trackpad that is above it. To the bottom left is an analogue stick, which most games seem to use. Currently the left trackpad is not to useful and seems to just be used to change weapons and/or as a D-pad. I hope soon it will be common to see them used for weapon wheels or something.
The triggers are actually really cool. They are a two level kind of triggers. They have a travel, then at the end they click. They work fine for shooters and you dont even need to make them click to shoot. I’d like to see stealth games use this feature to maybe put down weapon that is aimed or maybe when you’re playing a driving game and you click it down all the way for boost. I could see some games working well with this controller. Below the triggers are these clamp like click pads where the rest of your fingers are behind the controller. These usually just emulate X/B but for some custom profiles for games with leaning, its actually incredibly helpful and feels very natural.
You can download custom profiles that the community has made or you can make your own. The controller options are insane and there is so much you can do with it. I really love the option for the trackpad to emulate a trackball so you can have momentum in your aiming. You can make actions have actions. You can make those actions change sensitivity, do keyboard commands, etc. It’s really cool.
Does this replace a keyboard/mouse? Certainly not. Is this better than a Xbox360 controller? I can’t say for sure yet. Once I get better at aiming, then I will be able to tell. This is a cool purchase and I will definitely see myself using this a LOT in the future. There are some kinks and I am positive that they will be ironed out in the months to come. So far its functional. I’m not exactly impressed but I am very interested. Hopefully this poorly written post has been some sort of help or made some amount of sense.

Short Version:
This game is truly a masterpiece in gameplay, music, story and storytelling and should be blindly picked up by anyone who likes Japanese games. Trust me, you'll love it.
Long Version:
First the only negative point:
The PC port does suffer from poor optimization and narrow draw distances most likely to be blamed on the fact that is was developed with the PlayStation 4 in mind. Sadly, the developers have not issued any significant patches whatsoever. Something I have to point out.
So you probably need a mod that fixes these issues, which I myself have used as it was pretty easy to install.
On to the rest:
I won't go into specifics to avoid even slight spoilers, so bear that in mind while reading. The gameplay has huge variety and it therefore never gets boring. I have been blown away by the love the game developers have put into designing the game and its core mechanics. It was so addicting to play that I even neglected real life obligations.
The characters you will meet and grow to love all have a distinct appeal to them and this is where NieR:Automata can truly shine. I will forget and have forgotten a lot of characters in a lot of games, but I will not forget a single character from this game. That is how dear they have grown on me.
Music is a 10/10. It PERFECTLY captures every emotion in every scene and amplifies those emotions to make you feel even more immersed. You have to experience the music in-game to fully understand how great it is.
Japanese voice acting is - as usual - superb. Nothing to add there.
Story is unique, exciting, interesting and told in a manner which I have yet to come across anywhere else. It always had me on my toes and I could never predict the outcome.
This game is what I call innovation and I applaud the developers for creating such a masterpiece which will have a place in my heart forever.

Dungeon Siege is the most playable Diablo clone out there. It was made before the consolization frenzy, but it's not so old that the graphics make it hard to play.

Dungeon Siege is an RPG masquerading as an ARPG, blending the best features of each genre:
1) It offers a party composition system that is reminiscent of Baldur's Gate. You can hire key NPCs into your party as you meet them. You share weapons and loot among 6 characters at a time.
2) Similar to The Elder Scrolls, you gain skill ability by actually using skills, not as a pickable reward for gaining levels. Love this.
3) Lots of side quests.
4) Lots of hacky-slashy gameplay, and a breezy lightness to the whole thing.
Today, you will need to look past the dated graphics, but this is a solid game.
Be warned that Dungeon Siege requires a little effort to get running on a modern computer. As delivered from Steam, you'll get crashes and black screens. I was able to find what I needed in the Steam Forums, though, to get it running on Windows 7 at 1920x1080 resolution.

I will preface this review by saying that I put the most importance on gameplay when judging a game and that items such as graphics and general interfaces are secondary critiques. If a game is good, I will enjoy it no matter how it may look.
This game has a free demo on the internet, but it was so good that I decided to buy the full game. Simply put, this game has some of the most innovative and fun gameplay mechanics in a third-person shooter that I've seen in a long time. The controls are easy to pick up, and the movement capabilities of the in-game avatar seem limitless. The ability to toggle the gravity boots on and off allow for grounded gameplay or zero gravity mayhem. This, coupled with the beam that allows the player to grapple around the map, allows for immensely satisfying and exciting gameplay. I've only played for a short while in the full game, but it is so incredibly amazing how much fun I've gotten out of the gameplay.
Now of course this title is still in Early Access, and as such there are a few issues. The problem that sticks out the most is the lack of a stable player base at the moment. If you have friends or are on during peak hours, finding a game is simple, but the lack of AI in the current build of the game means that you're out of luck playing solo unless you're content practicing your movement, which I must say is still a ton of fun to do even by yourself.
The graphics are pretty decent, but the graphical interface needs some work. I fully expect the graphical interface to be ironed out, and the game definitely looks good for what it is. The particle effects are nice and the lighting is definitely good-looking. Just look at the screenshots and videos above for an idea of what to expect. Overall, the game has a distinct lack of visual polish, but that is to be expected of a game in the early stages of development.
I have not experienced any major glitches or hang-ups at this point in time with this game, so that should not be a major issue. However, I have not experienced the full depth of this game at this point so that remains to be seen in its entirety.
As a last note, I must say that I consider this game to be amazing. The developer has definitely hit on a great idea for the basic gameplay, and with a little bit of polish and further development to add more features, this game will be at the top of my favorite games list in no time.

Now, the playthrough I have going now, nothing breaks down. Not because of a building, not because I have traits. I have an emerald hammer, had it since gen 2. 800 years repaired....
