I'm not impressed, I don't hate it, I have the worst emotion you want a gamer to have.
Boredom.
I get how it's a roguelike. You have one lineage you try your best with. Fail to generate an heir and you're done for.
But why can't I keep on questing while my mate raises my child? Every time you get any sort of stats, you can either retire early and thus lose them again, or keep being useful with a chance of your run failing. How do people even still exist if every couple can only procreate once?
Everything seems so inconsequential. I apparently made my home town into a kingdom because I had 12k Fame. I couldn't make it back to my Kingdom, as my time was almost up. When I went to the Kingdom, it was already a Slum. What use is there in generating something fancy if you can't even see it once?
But fine, that was because I didn't plan well. I trained far too hard, had about 100 str when I died. I should have gone for 60 str, then go after the 60 str boss. But you have to beat the boss three times! He can easily knock 30 years off of my life! Or 60! Or zero. Like every roguelike, playing high-risk is rewarded, as that is the only way to break highscores after some time. But it's also boring to fail runs in a row.
So just plan ahead. Instead of beating the boss, buy high level gear, get a kid at the Fort, inherit good gear, and beat the boss early. Maybe. And if you DO lose too much time, that's it for that run. You won't see a Kingdom.
RNG aside, as that is quite inherent to roguelikes, the music is meh and repetitive, and the animations just take so goddamn long. See 10 numbers fly by on the red star dice before saying what our strength rolls are. Show me my damage given/taken, which you already know way ahead, for 2 seconds more. Deal damage for 2 seconds more.
It got worse when I got a +0-1 damage bone. Most of the times it didn't even matter, as targets have 5- hp anyway. But you lose 4 seconds more every combat, to see it roll a 0, and to then add 0 to a different number to not change it.
SOBORED
At least you have "meaningful" choices when mating. You flip 6 out of 25ish cards to determine your character. But the cards are face down. You see the type(but not strength) of 3ish cards. You don't have 25 choices. You have 4. Which of the 22 random cards you flip is not an option. It's waiting for the numbers to show. This is made worse at the aging Milestones, where you always see 4 blind cards and 1 typed card, flip one of them. This isn't a choice out of 5. It's out of 2.
In this way, I'm bored just as with (unpopular opinion ahead) FTL. Sure, you can do stuff, but you don't have real control. If I find a derelict spaceship, the "don't investigate" option isn't really an option, I will have just wasted my time on nothing. This is quite the same: you have 20 life left, explore? Well yeah, sitting around is even worse. But if you get back after losing a battle, your mate might suddenly not want to be with you anymore. Ending your run.
Such fun.

This game is more a space empire simulator than a 4X game.  There are a lot more options in what kind of government you create and it's policies, and those civics have much more detailed effects on the game beyond "you get +x to something".  If you have a democratic system, elections are held, political parties develop with varied priorities and can change your society, and it tracks which populations and which planets are part of which party.  How much political influence you have is tracked and is used by various actions.
Slavery isn't just a civic that gives you some bonuses and penalties, it has large socio-economic implications and effects diplomacy with other civilizations.  Inter-species migration can happen among civilizations, and you have to make decisions about what you will allow, will you take refugees, what rights will they be granted, how will you deal with populations on conquered worlds, or will you play a civilization that does not conquer planets, but only uses force in self defense or to liberate oppressed worlds into their own independent states.  This is the only 4X game I've played where you can start a war not over territory, but to demand the other side stop barbaric practices, or you can be the civilization that takes over planets and rounds up racial minorities into death camps, or turns them into Soylant Green.
There's even more detail than this and they pull it off without the game being particularly complicated at all.  You probably know if you will like a game like this or not.
If you buy it, probably also buy the Utopia DLC.
There are a couple problems with the game.  They're not deal breakers.  If the above sounds appealing to you, I'd definitely try it out, but there are some issues that keep it from being an amazing game, and put it more in the category of pretty good game.  Probably the biggest downside is just the raw amount of time this game takes.  They try to put in some things to mitigate this, but it either doesn't mitigate it enough or absolutely backfires, and it just still takes ages to accomplish anything.  It plays in real time, which grows on you as a mechanic and helps alleviate some of the aforementioned slowness.
They have a system where you have a max number of "core worlds" and planets beyond this max have to be put in a "sector", and sectors are controlled by the AI.  On the surface this might be a good method of avoiding the problem many 4X games have where things slow to a snail's crawl when you get too many cities/planets, and might help offset the classic "there is only one strategy, and that's colonize everything as fast as possible", but the A.I is dumb as bricks, like dumber even than normal dumb A.I.s and having them wreck your systems is frustrating.  It also fails in its attempts to slow down "fast as possible colony expansion" strategy because your fleet size cap is entirely dependent on the number of planets you have.   So you end up having to grab as many planets as you can, like in most 4X games you get certain penalties for each planet you have, yet they are being run terribly by the AI, and they end up controlling so many of your planets it starts to become a bit like the AI playing against itself.  It also doesn't help speed up the game at all, because for a variety of reasons you have to babysit the sectors more so then you would if you just had direct control over them.
There are a bunch of things like this.  I had fun playing it, but I was definitely banging my head against the keyboard by the end of my first playthrough.  Again, if my initial description of the game sounds interesting, it's a different experience and I'd buy it just to check it out, but otherwise pass.

The community presets are a great idea, but many games still lack satisfactory presets.

So if you are a casual gamer who wants to spend more time playing and less time fiddling, I would not recommend getting it. Or waiting until more games come with official steam controller configs (a la Portal 2).

*** 3 MONTH UPDATE ***
I'll preface my update by saying: age-wise, I'm probably an artifact compared to most of the people on Steam. Let's put it this way... I'm old enough to remember the original "Pong" console. I've played games on EVERY major console and PC since then. That said, I had NO trouble adjusting to this controller. Yes it was awkward for the first day or so because it was a new experience, but now, with very little time... I'm a master. I almost hate playing without it. The gyroscope (when turned on) gives you the feeling that it's an extension of your hands, because it picks up subtle, natural, hand movements. Will it kill my love for a keyboard and mouse? HELL NO! I'm O.G. K&M forever baby! But, it is REALLY fun and almost as accurate in confident hands. It's certainly better than my XBox controllers. Yeah I said it!
To me, all of those whining haters out there are just plain lazy. Man-up, woman-up... do somethin'... just quit yer cryin' already! If you loved your other controllers so much why did you bother buying this one? I'm sorry but it had to be asked.
To those who are unafraid, buy this controller. t's worth every penny.
P.S. - The batteries last an extrememly long time in this thing. In 3 months of gaming almost everyday, and a couple game-heavy weekends, I've replaced the batteries only ONCE. That kind of longevity trumps an over-priced battery pack every day, all day.

Polarity has simple yet interesting concept with the puzzles. However it feels kinda lackluster; made me wished there's more to this game.
First, the game is really short: I beat the main campaign and its bonus levels in about 2 hours. I beat the coop campaign in another 1,5 hours. The rest is completing all achievements perfectly. So in total I completed the game in about 4,5 hours.
Second, the level design doesn't feel consistent. At times it can be incredibly hard, at another it can be incredibly easy. Some levels utilize very clever design. Sometimes the same cleverness is brought over to the next levels, but more often it isn't. Each time the puzzles get challenging in 2-3 levels or so, in the 4th level it seems to throw away the challenges and introduce something new. I'm yearning for a level that mix every challenges that the game can offer, unfortunately such level never comes even to the end. This game is screaming for mod support to fill that gaping hole, but again unfortunately there is no mod support.
Putting those two things aside, this game actually can be interesting. The puzzle, when it's good, is really good. Co-op support makes the game more fun. The futuristic atmosphere, even with its simplicity, is kinda charming.
However, if we consider the downsides, buying the game at $10 doesn't feel like really worth it. I got this with only $1 myself. So I recommend this game ONLY if it's on discount or packaged in a bundle.

It masterfully tells you only that what needed at the exact time when it needs to be told. At first you are a solder, fighting for good of humanity, then, that it looks like, you are destroying machine network, then you've being told, that *spoiler*, then turns out that androids *spoiler*, *spoiler*, and the end like everyone will say "WHAT THE F-K!!?" because even I wasn't able to predict this anyhow, this is some incredible clusterf-k of event that only master of such clusterf-ks can create.
Whole game looks seamless. From the very main menu, loading screens, and to the FX. I haven't felt interrupted, you can just play and play, nonstop, just like you are exist in this point of time. This keeps atmosphere whole. Every trick game uses fits perfectly: unusual text in loading screen (have anyone noticed "MP: 100%"?), sound distortions, image glitch effects, novel text screens, paper theater, UI glitching etc. When you walk on this wooden bridge as poor infected 2B, you can't see anything from static, there is digital noise flowing into your ears, than something explodes, screen and sound freezes for a moment, then returns back, but your screen black-and-white, your sound degrated to 2 bits per sample, you UI started some shenanigans - you really feel like you really f-d up. Like REALLY f-d up. It was just fine before, but became disaster pretty quick and unexpected and in a perfect way. Platinum Games loves to do these tricks and I LOVE them, both Platinum Games and these tricks.
Remember I told "although they are an androids", this means I didn't thought about androids as human-alike lifeforms. I thought of them as they are only robots. This game presented them as humans, or their perfect replication. There is absolutely nothing that at first glance can tell you whether this is an android or a human. They act as humans. And you know what, as some who knows what AI is, I should say, that it's POSSIBLE. The one thing that can break any sense of bulls-ttery is something, that you didn't know was possible and it's absolutely something new and worth discuss. This game did exactly this with me.
There is not much combos, not much hits, but for me it's only better - it's not overcomplicated. It's still though rocks, I often ended battles without a single hit, just because I wisely chose targets. There is not much to say about battle system: it's Platinum Games, someone will like, someone will not like. I liked MGR: Revengeance exatly for battle system, so I like NieR:Automata as well, since it looks very familiar. But there is something about the battle itself there. See, I'am a male, grown... man... I would like to say big 20yr old boy. So, girls becoming for me more and more prescious (in a good way) and if something bad will happen to them on my watch I will feel like I did a huge mistake. Especially when they looks like these androids - it's just "must be as accurate as possible". "My buttchecks was clunched for 50% of time" is exactly about this. I died only twice, both times from my own stupidity: as 2B when I did not expect that press one shots, I walked happily under heavy hammers until one sratched my hip... Was hoping for perfect first run, but not this game it seems. Second time when I triggerend giant robot bunny as 2B, and it was 30 levels higher than me. Tried to attack (I don't know what I was thinking about) dodged into one sphere and had been one shotted. A2 run was clean, ONCE I was like 5% of health left and that was EXTREME! To be honest I was thinking about "not letting the girl die", but at most "not letting the girl hurt". It was hard to attack A2 when I was told to do it... Very...
The thing is not impressed me: graphics. I will not protect the graphics since it's obvious, that it does look akward. The reason is strange though: they didn't use baked lightmaps, I have no idea why, but this game tried to look like as AAa (2.5 A) by using dynamic secondary and trinary bounce light volumes. This technique is powerful, but costs a lot of performance, so everything else is turned down. Yes, simple and strange. Notice how object being lighten from below with green light reflected from green grass, or yellowish from yellow sand, or simple white from building ceiling - dynamic light volume in action. On PS4 maximum amount of objects to be affected with this volume is 32, for PS4 Pro - 64 and for PC - 128. 128 is overkill, it will not be visually any different to 64, but will cost twice as much. But try to disable it - light looks flat. I played with around 25-40 FPS in 1080p on GTX 750Ti (below minimum specs) and 35-60 FPS in 720p, and it was pretty comfortable. Interesting, that Wolfenstein II also assumes minimum GPU to be greater than GTX 770, but I had there below 25 FPS all the time in 360p and it was unplayable. So optimization in NieR:Automata defenitely not bad.
Music is something. Music is perfectly fits. Music is geniously composed. Music brings all the mood. Disable music - game will be halved. I'am into making music for more than 10 years, I have compositions of hard genre, classics, ambient, electronics, almost everything. I have experience of probably around 3000 hours. But for god's sake how can you be such god to make something like they did in this game!? This is... Insane! Every time I hear this music I'm being triggered!
So conclusion: best plot, best girls, nice and familiar gameplay, insane decorations, perfect atmosphere, music - masterpiece, though not so impressive graphics, but you know what, I will close my eyes on graphics. Best game.

Summed Up: A really awful port to an otherwise pretty fun game. Buy this game on any other platform and you'll have a fun time, but avoid the PC version like the devil.
In-Depth: I'll start with the game itself. It's not going to be anyones favourite Splinter Cell as, quite frankly, it's one of the more linear and demanding of the series. Gone is the option to play the game your way and still get the best score if you complete the objectives; now the game ranks you on stealth. It provides penalties to how many guards you knock out/kill, locks you break etc. Meaning you have to basically be a shadow to get the best score. This is a fair idea, but the problem is, the level often throws enemies at you you HAVE to move out the way, or you have to do something ridiculously convoluted to get them to move; which just takes up way too much time.
Also introduced is the trust system; a fine line you have to take between both the terrorists and your employers. Alot of people were kind of iffy on this, but I honestly liked the idea. The main issue stems from the fact it's completely pointless. There are enough side objectives and such that you'll honestly always have full trusts 99.9% of the time; even on hard mode where you lose trust more and gain less. If they had made it much more imperitive to the game and maybe had it so you gained rewards from having certain levels, or even something as simple as dialogue change, it might have been  a worthy addition. As it stands, it's just kind of there; a nice idea that dosen't realise it's full potential.
As for the core game, it's pretty much Chaos Theoy's mechanics again. This is fine as, in my opion, Chaos Theory really got it right when it came to the stealth aspect and design; n both games have a nice, easy to navigate ingame inventory, the layouts easy to see etc. One major gripe thought is that they changed the stealth meters; as in, they no longer exist. In Chaos Theory, they had two bars which showed your visibility and sound. This was useful as it indicated how alert enemies where sound wise and indicated clearly how sneaky you were being. In this game, you have a light, that's it. It's green when your safe, yellow when not, and red when spotted. The problem is, while it takes into account shadows and does change when enemies are more alert, it never shows how much noise your making; which can be a HUGE problem if your next to an alerted enemy and want to sneak past him QUIETLY. But, that aside, it is for all intents and purposes just more of Chaos Theory sanded down. Back handed as that is, I'm not complaining at  a few more levels.
Now for the crux of the problem; the PC Port. The best summary would be 'A glitched up mess that everytime I play I find another'. The most common one is random crashes and lost autosaves, but there are weirder ones. Lost sound, not gaining your bonus equipment, a door not supposed to be there stuck in another door (Yes, that actually happened), do I need to go on? Not to mention graphically, the game just looks off. There is a guide to tweak this on steam, but the fact you HAVE to do this is pretty appaling; without the tweaks, the game looks... well, off, it's hard to explain, kinda like the world is slowly falling away pixel by pixel in the background. There are alot of things in this port that just make it dissapointing, and I really tried to look past them. But the bugs really were the final straw. Avoid the port like the devil, patches have been known to exist, but wether they work is apparently 50/50. Go buy another version of the game elsewhere; you'll be glad you did

I'm just going to give my honest review on the game. No witty, sarcastic comments.
(there's a tl;dr version at the bottom of the review.)
First off.
I love this game.
Albeit I suck at it, I love it.
Here's my pros and cons list.
Pros:
*Very fun, fast-paced, competitive gameplay.
*Tutorial tells you everything you need to know. Everything.
*It runs on the Unreal Engine (the same game engine Goat Simulator uses). Happy derpyass ragdolling time!
*Great with friends over LAN.
*7 maps to choose from.
*4 different gamemodes.
*5 different weapons that spawn in each map.
*The guy who made this is one of the most friendly devs I've ever seen. He responds to alot (if not all) of his comments and suggestions.
*This game updates SOOOOOOO frequently. Seriously. Just wow. I absolutely hope that this dev doesn't stop updating.
*This game truly has some potential in the long run.
*The dev is currently working on a Steam Workshop feature, which would allow people to make and upload new maps. Amazing. Absolutely amazing.
Cons:
*The biggest con is that it's hard to find open servers sometimes. This makes sense, as it's a relatively unknown early-access game. This can (and definitely will) be a real buzzkill though.
*All of the weapons spawn in the same place in each map. For instance, on the Pipe map, the rocket launcher always spawns in one room. This might sound nice to some people, but when you have some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥puppyguarding the sniper rifle, it's really annoying. This also gives more experienced players an advantage, as they probably know from the get-go where all of the weapons are in one map. You get swarmed by a guy with a rocket launcher before you even know how half of the map is laid out. I don't think they can fix this, but if you COULD randomize weapons spawn points, it would make the game just a tiny bit better.
*No singleplayer bots yet. (it's only multiplayer)
Did I mention the game is only 3 bucks?
That is one of the best deals I've ever seen. (other than like when gmod is on sale and it's only like $2)
tl;dr version:
Terrific game at a reasonable price. The game itself has so much potential. A couple problems here and there, but amazing in the grand scheme of things. I absolutely can't wait to see how it progresses. The final version will be amazing.

text:
I'm going to start this review by telling you guys how happy I am that this game was SO much better than what I expected.
Lot of people gave this game sh*t because it was way different from what we've gotten used to seeing from Telltale Games, and simply because it was based on Minecraft.
For whatever reason, people assume Minecraft is a game for young audiences who have very little understanding about videogames. But I beg to differ, I personally think Minecraft is suitable for all ages. For anyone who wants to have a game where they can explore a world full of mysteries, where they can put their creativity to work.
You guys have no idea how many messages I got from people saying like "ehhrmageerrdd you're playing Minecraft what are you, 10 years old???" as I was playing this game..
The point I'm trying to make is that, people tend to have misconceptions about Minecraft itself just because it's known for having somewhat cancerous fanbase filled with immature kids. It's kind of sad that this is why people aren't interested in it because Minecraft: Story Mode is a fantastic and fresh experience from Telltale Games.
So many people were sh*tting on this game before the first episode had even launched just for the sake of it being a Minecraft game. And you know what? I thank those people for giving me the wrong idea of this game, because of that my expections were low and oh man was I blown away with what I got.
I'm very biased when it comes to Telltale Games but don't worry, I'm not going to try and say this game was flawless.
I think I've been rambling long enough now, time to actually review the bloody game.
- Voice-acting
- Action sequences
- Atmospheric Soundtrack
- Choices do actually MATTER
- It stays true to the Minecraft world
- Characters are all very likeable in my opinion
- Animations have improved and look lot smoother than in previous Telltale titles
- Opening credit scenes are very well done and highly entertaining for each episode
- Emotionally very touching even if it is lot more toned down from the previous Telltale titles like "The Walking Dead"
- Not as many puzzles as you might expect
- Ambiance constantly switching from funny to depressing
- The game's filled with clichés and so are the characters. But you know what, it actually isn't that bad.
( The characters are all unique compared to each other and likeable in their own ways. )
- Quite a lot of bugs ( especially in Episode 2 which was honestly borderline unplayable. )
- Some actions of the main / side characters feel very off and it feels like they've become completely different characters
- Episode 2 was extremely short and honestly a total mess when it came to the dialogue and overall script
- Dialogue is bit awkward and cringey at some points
- Certain scenes felt very rushed but this is honestly with every narrative Telltale game I've played
- Many people have lost their save files including myself but this is not necessarily to blame the game itself for it

You know, I got this game on a give-away. I had played it already on Xbox 360 but I’m an old fan from the series, and I was considering picking it up for PC since I no longer have that console. What I didn’t know however, is how bad the PC port was. As usual I will talk first about what the game does poorly and then move up to the good stuff:
First and foremost, what mostly ruins any fun you might have with Saints Row 2 on PC is that, as I just said, it’s a port. A really bad, horrible anal evacuation of a port. Now for what I know the port was NOT done by the original devs and instead made by a different company (the Windows version was made by CD Projekt or something like that), but f#cking hell on a pogo stick made of hats, there’s no way they could’ve looked at this and think it was properly finished. Let’s do something different here, I’ll list out some examples of what problems you can expect on this port, if you think you can deal with them, then go ahead and consider picking it up, if you don’t, then just try to play it on Xbox instead:
First, the frame-rate. It never drops below single digits but it sure as hell tries. It’s extremely inconsistent and will most of the time stay low enough to make shooting a pain in your #ss but never low enough to be game-breaking.
Driving controls are as bad as an abortion done with chainsaws. A lot of activities and missions task you to drive AND shot at the same time, however the slightest turn on your vehicle will also move the camera, which makes aiming to a single moving target harder than beating Dark Souls with a Guitar Controller. It also doesn’t help that the driving controls are EXTREMELY sensitive, and just tapping a direction will make the vehicle pretty well take a 45º turn to that direction.
Screen resolution is also something so f#cking basic and yet so stupidly gone to hell. You’ll have most likely to mod the game to have the game run in a screen resolution that runs well on your screen.
The keyboard control layout is pretty damn vomit inducing by default. Aiming at people feels more like a struggle, thank Morgan Freeman that the enemies are mostly incompetent and won’t kill you so easily. It can easily be seen when trying to spray walls, as it feels insanely difficult to move the mouse arround because it still seems to think your mouse is an Xbox joystick.
Lastly there are bugs running rampant on the game. There are a few that are quite hilarious, such as hostile NPC’s killing each other for apparently no reason whatsoever, but then come the “not so funny glitches”. Things like touching the water with a car and suddenly be sent a thousand meters into the sky to then take half a minute to die by the fall. Things like some of the bosses pinning you down to a wall and constantly doing the same attack which you can’t block before you can even run away from him OR EVEN GET UP FROM THE GROUND, killing you eventually.
The game is a broken mess of a port. But does it have good stuff on it? Yeah! Most people consider it the best Saints Row game, and I do believe it deserves such a title.
To begin with, the story and characters are well written, voiced and feel alive, a problem that the previous game had. They’re not as one dimensional, and some of them are actually quite f#cking entertaining.
Second, the music. The first game had an okay list of radio music, and next games tried to have less variety but better music; however I like it more as it’s done here, there’s a bit of everything and you can just pick whatever you like the most. I mean for f#ck sake, this game had FUNK MUSIC. Most of the time I end up hearing The Mix anyway, but the Funk one is my second pick.
Guns are also pretty okay, nothing too spectacular but works pretty well. Sure as hell better than how broken they were in Saints Row The Third, that’s for sure.
There's also a better variety on distractions and side-activities. Stellaris immerses the player in a great setting and brings about a genuine sense of wonder as you explore the galaxy while building your space empire, contending with a variety of different species, galactic events and challenges to your empire both internal and external. However it is prone to dredging the player through monotonous stretches of gameplay where nothing happens, a questionable combat system and some unsatisfying game mechanism. There is much potential that is not realized and that might be the lasting impression you might get from this game. However, if you are a fan of the 4X space genre this is a game you should try. This review is primarily based on the 1.9.1 patch + All DLC’s; having been a long time Stellaris player (300+ hours on non steam account) I will also touch on the base game.
Much like any empire building game, Stellaris allows you to pick a civilization/species and guide them from humble beginnings to a superpower. Along the way you will chose the technology, ethics that your empire will follow, explore long lost technology and interact with a variety of other galactic entities and this is where the game’s greatest strength is. There are a host of empires to interact; from powerful fallen empires that you want to avoid provoking until you are strong enough all the way to primitive Stone Age empires that you assimilate when the time comes. There are a host of planets to colonize with diverse species having their own preference as well as mining and research station to builds. This part of the game is extremely fun as your race the neighboring empires to colonize a planet or lay claim to a resource rich frontier system. The purchasable DLC content adds all manners of “Objects” to interact with on the galactic stage which really serves to flesh out the experience and make the galaxy feel more alive. Additionally, the DLC content also adds powerful ascension perks which opens up the ability to construct powerful artifacts or modify your populace to more closely align with your gameplay. This will be glaring omission in the base game as the DLC’s add tangible goals to work to during the mid to late game stage. In addition, the ascension perks add much needed buffs to a small size empire by allowing them to fill out tradition trees faster which open up these ascension perks. The DLC’s also add new end game “Crisis” events as well as allow different types of machine empires.
War is a guarantee in Stellaris; whether you play as a peaceful empire, an aggressive devouring swarm bent on enslaving the galaxy or somewhere in the middle. This however is one of the biggest problems with Stellaris as of this review. There is no espionage system, the interactions with the AI empires are limited, the federation route can be intrusive but that is not the most glaring problem; combat simply put is not good. Space combat consists of putting together the biggest fleet you can muster; a “doomstack” and smashing it against your opponent’s stack. Fleets take a while to build up and the higher tonnage ships cost quite a bit of resources so war’s come down to one decisive battle. Further compounding this is that none of the defensive space structures hold any value in late game war.  This makes combat feel very unfulfilling; the war score system does not differentiate a border skirmish from a full scale war.  Every war ends with the utter destruction on one side and a slow and dull grind for the victor as you jump system to system. Ground combat is even worse as you load your troops and drop them onto the battlefield with no strategy to speak of.  Unlike Space combat you do not get to choose loadouts for your soldiers and the whole affair feels very shallow.
The game implements a sector system; you can only assume direct control over a certain amount of planets before you have to turn it over to the AI. This too holds room for improvement as there is no big internal political considerations to worry about. The latest version of the game introduces the concept of factions but this pales in comparison to some established strategy games where you have to deal with internal politicking. Paradox has a rich history of delivering intriguing in-empire politics and I cannot help but be disappointed with this aspect in this game. It is also disappointing that sectors cannot be directed to raises ships or armies and there is not a deeper mechanism that affects how a sector interacts in an empire.
Happily, the future looks bright for Stellaris as Paradox has been very receptive of its user community’s comments and are activity working on changing some core mechanisms to make the game more complete. Regardless, this game is hugely fun in spite of all the features that are missing. If you are a fan of the 4X game genre I would highly recommend that you try this game and spend the wee hours of the morning glued to the monitor looking for what else is around the corner.

Hello Steam Community!
Well, I finally have enough hours to write a complete and truthful list of concerns for Primal Carnage: Extinction. While I like this game, it has some major issues that should be understood before anyone buys it. I will, then, endeavor to point out some of these issues. Please remember, I am no expert on games or media. I am an aspiring engineering student with a good vocabulary. These are only opinions, and are in no shape or form certain undeniable truths. We are not talking about “a priori” knowledge here. Please allow me to share my opinions, if I may be so bold. :)
Economy:
I feel that this is a major issue for Primal Carnage: Extinction. As of now, there are skins and textures that sell for ridiculous prices upwards of 300 US dollars. While it can be certain that “legendary” economy items are exceedingly rare, they are simply not worth that sum of money. This is even more truthful when one considers the fact that the game itself has very few players online. In a few years, these high-priced visual items will be almost worthless. I assume that many people will wonder why they went to such an extent to obtain them when they could have spent their precious time and capital elsewhere.
Furthermore, these skins do nothing to improve the game. Many individuals on this game associate high-priced skins with experience, status, or skill. The logical flaws in this sort of assumption are too great to even bother covering. I am an extremely good player myself, and not one of my skins exceeds $30 in value. Still, I have been literally ridiculed by other players for my lack of quote, “skinz”.
Despite these various issues, the developers seem all too poised to continue their economy efforts. It can be certain that while they did issue many fixes, they maintained a major focus on skins and economy. In my view, the excessive and illogical pursuit of the economy system has dealt the game a serious blow.
Community:
Let it be known that Primal Carnage: Extinction has a very polarized player base.
There are incredible people on this game. Many are extremely helpful, logical, coherent, understanding, and friendly. There are some truly good administrators on this community that genuinely care about providing a quality experience for their players. (I like to think that I am one of these, but I cannot commend myself for that would be biased.) When a question is raised, they rush to answer and help. When a troublesome person is spotted, they enforce the rules as necessary.
However, some individuals are absolute rubbish. They are rude, arrogant, disrespectful, conniving, and deceitful. I cannot even begin to list all of the scams and devious ploys I have witnessed. The nature of the “economy” -which I have previously talked about- brings out the worst in some people. It is not uncommon to see individuals begging, scamming, and deceiving in order to obtain items. In addition to this, the game seems to be infested with trolls. As an administrator of a server group, I have watched individuals purposefully attack and disrupt a server’s functionality. It appears as if these trolls literally want to be kicked. In their mind, they can effectively destroy a server by injecting themselves into the session and deliberately inciting a virtual riot against officials. The entire process is sad to watch, and really speaks towards the community’s immature and delinquent views.
I have observed many players who are dissatisfied with the fact that there are very few “deathmatch” servers. Their complaints are valid, as there are rarely any competitive community servers. As an administrator, I can verify one reason why this is so. It is nearly impossible to control the rage, frustration, trolling, and delinquency that such game modes attract. It is likely –although I do not claim to hold tangible evidence for this- that administrators find it easier to host manageable games.
To be forthright, this community both inspires and repulses me at the same time.
Gameplay:
The final and most important issue regarding Primal Carnage: Extinction has to do with gameplay.
There are rampant glitches and issues in this game. From dinosaurs to humans, many weapons and classes can become bugged to the point that they can no longer be effectively used. One good example of this is the raptor pounce attack. When a player changes class to anything besides a raptor, they run the risk of losing their pounce attack’s functionality. This is a horrible issue for competitive players who want to attack the enemy using a diverse strategy, because it limits their ability to change into a more suitable class during different situations.
The team balancing in the game is inferior. On any competitive “deathmatch” game, most players monopolize the dinosaur team resulting in unequal matches. This is dreadful for anyone who cares to master both human and dinosaur gameplay, because it makes the human team a bad choice for anyone. When a match does start out with teams that are in the correct proportions, players often switch to whichever team is currently doing well. In most cases, players will abandon the losing team and join the team that seems to be more secure. In truth, the option to “switch team” during a "deathmatch" round should be abolished.
Conclusion:
While I like this game and some of its community, I feel that individuals should be aware of certain things. I do not profess to know exactly what is wrong with the game. I have simply provided a list of things that, in my experience, trouble the game. I keep an open mind, and I never attempt to imply that I understand everything about the community. I am only giving you my experiences. On a more positive note, I think that game is quite good aside from these flaws. The lighting is spectacular, and the graphics are very pleasing. I would give it a 6.8/10.

The reason is strange though: they didn't use baked lightmaps, I have no idea why, but this game tried to look like as AAa (2.5 A) by using dynamic secondary and trinary bounce light volumes. This technique is powerful, but costs a lot of performance, so everything else is turned down. Yes, simple and strange. Notice how object being lighten from below with green light reflected from green grass, or yellowish from yellow sand, or simple white from building ceiling - dynamic light volume in action. On PS4 maximum amount of objects to be affected with this volume is 32, for PS4 Pro - 64 and for PC - 128. 128 is overkill, it will not be visually any different to 64, but will cost twice as much. But try to disable it - light looks flat. I played with around 25-40 FPS in 1080p on GTX 750Ti (below minimum specs) and 35-60 FPS in 720p, and it was pretty comfortable. Interesting, that Wolfenstein II also assumes minimum GPU to be greater than GTX 770, but I had there below 25 FPS all the time in 360p and it was unplayable. So optimization in NieR:Automata defenitely not bad.
Music is something. Music is perfectly fits. Music is geniously composed. Music brings all the mood. Disable music - game will be halved. I'am into making music for more than 10 years, I have compositions of hard genre, classics, ambient, electronics, almost everything. I have experience of probably around 3000 hours. But for god's sake how can you be such god to make something like they did in this game!? This is... Insane! Every time I hear this music I'm being triggered!
So conclusion: best plot, best girls, nice and familiar gameplay, insane decorations, perfect atmosphere, music - masterpiece, though not so impressive graphics, but you know what, I will close my eyes on graphics. Best game.

I purchased Hustle Cat on a whim after watching Dodger and Octopimp play some of Finley's route on PressHeartToContinue. I was skeptical at first (some mix of "I don't want to spend money" and "Why do I want to play a game about cats, I'm allergic and don't know the first thing about them"), but BOY was that $20 well spent. Hustle Cat has to be my favorite commercially-released dating sim in recent memory. Heck, my favorite ever.
The world of Hustle Cat (as well as how magic works in it) is really engrossing. The writing, art, and music are all wonderfully done and always fitting. The story was touching at times and laugh-at-loud funny at others. The main character Avery was an absolute delight (not gonna lie, I related to the trash witch bit), and each romance route was unique and interesting. I'm fairly certain this is the first time I truly enjoyed playing through *every* route in a dating sim.
The game is a little on the short side, especially considering the price, but what it lacks in length it makes up for in everything else. Hustle Cat is a gem of a game, and I couldn't recommend it enough. If you’re looking for a dating sim or visual novel, especially one with a refreshingly interesting and diverse cast, this game is very likely right up your alley (even if you're not all that fond of cats)!

Out There Somewhere is a 2d puzzle platformer with a hint of old arcade-space-shooting at the start and end, making the nice sandwich, which is "Out There Somewhere", developed by MiniBoss and released Mar 14, 2016.
You play as the Protagonist: Small-pixel-man-with-goldfish-bowl-on-head. Goldfish bowl head starts out by flying a ship trying to shoot down space-captain-who's-his-face.
While the story and plot are pretty forgettable the game controls aren't in the slightest.
The basic controls are straight forward, you move right and left, jump and fire a portal gun, later you unlock a regular gun you can use to kill the various hostile NPC's. The controls work, I have been guilty of mixing up my two fire keybindings, which has resulted in death-by-NPC-face-hugging, or teleportation-into-pits-of-death
, the controls weren't so bad for me, but the game really seems like it was designed more so with a controller in mind.
But I'm getting ahead of myself, you start with just a Teleportation Gun, you fire a shot and when it connects with the wall, you teleport to the location of the laser/bullet. You actually have a few tricks you can pull off with the Teleportation gun early on, but don't learn about later in the game, so there is some skill that is developed with the Teleportation gun, rather then fire and teleport.
So once you finish playing the game, and if you start a new game you realize there are many hidden spots in the game that you originally had no idea where there. So that hints at the amount of time it takes to finish the game: it's a pretty short game, think an hour or two on average
.
While I personally didn't find any of the puzzles too overwhelming, there's definitely plenty of difficulty to keep you mumbling obscenities under your breath as you get murdered again and again. While there's definitely more to the game, and plenty of content to keep you coming back, that's about all there is to say for the gameplay.
As a whole, I enjoyed playing this game. This was one of the games I downloaded and played on my laptop while I was on a short little vacation away from my normal habitat. For using on lower powered computers I highly recommend this game, but when it comes to powered up computers that are normally playing MMORPG's or triple A titles... Out There Somewhere is still a pretty good diversion of a game. Pick it up on sale, play for a couple hours, go back to playing something else.

Hello Steam Community!
Well, I finally have enough hours to write a complete and truthful list of concerns for Primal Carnage: Extinction. While I like this game, it has some major issues that should be understood before anyone buys it. I will, then, endeavor to point out some of these issues. Please remember, I am no expert on games or media. I am an aspiring engineering student with a good vocabulary. These are only opinions, and are in no shape or form certain undeniable truths. We are not talking about “a priori” knowledge here. Please allow me to share my opinions, if I may be so bold. :)
Economy:
I feel that this is a major issue for Primal Carnage: Extinction. As of now, there are skins and textures that sell for ridiculous prices upwards of 300 US dollars. While it can be certain that “legendary” economy items are exceedingly rare, they are simply not worth that sum of money. This is even more truthful when one considers the fact that the game itself has very few players online. In a few years, these high-priced visual items will be almost worthless. I assume that many people will wonder why they went to such an extent to obtain them when they could have spent their precious time and capital elsewhere.
Furthermore, these skins do nothing to improve the game. Many individuals on this game associate high-priced skins with experience, status, or skill. The logical flaws in this sort of assumption are too great to even bother covering. I am an extremely good player myself, and not one of my skins exceeds $30 in value. Still, I have been literally ridiculed by other players for my lack of quote, “skinz”.
Despite these various issues, the developers seem all too poised to continue their economy efforts. It can be certain that while they did issue many fixes, they maintained a major focus on skins and economy. In my view, the excessive and illogical pursuit of the economy system has dealt the game a serious blow.
Community:
Let it be known that Primal Carnage: Extinction has a very polarized player base.
There are incredible people on this game. Many are extremely helpful, logical, coherent, understanding, and friendly. There are some truly good administrators on this community that genuinely care about providing a quality experience for their players. (I like to think that I am one of these, but I cannot commend myself for that would be biased.) When a question is raised, they rush to answer and help. When a troublesome person is spotted, they enforce the rules as necessary.
However, some individuals are absolute rubbish. They are rude, arrogant, disrespectful, conniving, and deceitful. I cannot even begin to list all of the scams and devious ploys I have witnessed. The nature of the “economy” -which I have previously talked about- brings out the worst in some people. It is not uncommon to see individuals begging, scamming, and deceiving in order to obtain items. In addition to this, the game seems to be infested with trolls. As an administrator of a server group, I have watched individuals purposefully attack and disrupt a server’s functionality. It appears as if these trolls literally want to be kicked. In their mind, they can effectively destroy a server by injecting themselves into the session and deliberately inciting a virtual riot against officials. The entire process is sad to watch, and really speaks towards the community’s immature and delinquent views.
I have observed many players who are dissatisfied with the fact that there are very few “deathmatch” servers. Their complaints are valid, as there are rarely any competitive community servers. As an administrator, I can verify one reason why this is so. It is nearly impossible to control the rage, frustration, trolling, and delinquency that such game modes attract. It is likely –although I do not claim to hold tangible evidence for this- that administrators find it easier to host manageable games.
To be forthright, this community both inspires and repulses me at the same time.
Gameplay:
The final and most important issue regarding Primal Carnage: Extinction has to do with gameplay.
There are rampant glitches and issues in this game. From dinosaurs to humans, many weapons and classes can become bugged to the point that they can no longer be effectively used. One good example of this is the raptor pounce attack. When a player changes class to anything besides a raptor, they run the risk of losing their pounce attack’s functionality. This is a horrible issue for competitive players who want to attack the enemy using a diverse strategy, because it limits their ability to change into a more suitable class during different situations.
The team balancing in the game is inferior. On any competitive “deathmatch” game, most players monopolize the dinosaur team resulting in unequal matches. This is dreadful for anyone who cares to master both human and dinosaur gameplay, because it makes the human team a bad choice for anyone. When a match does start out with teams that are in the correct proportions, players often switch to whichever team is currently doing well. In most cases, players will abandon the losing team and join the team that seems to be more secure. In truth, the option to “switch team” during a "deathmatch" round should be abolished.
Conclusion:
While I like this game and some of its community, I feel that individuals should be aware of certain things. I do not profess to know exactly what is wrong with the game. I have simply provided a list of things that, in my experience, trouble the game. I keep an open mind, and I never attempt to imply that I understand everything about the community. I am only giving you my experiences. On a more positive note, I think that game is quite good aside from these flaws. The lighting is spectacular, and the graphics are very pleasing. I would give it a 6.8/10.

This game would probably be worth $5 if the game were polished a little more. I spent $0.69 on this game, and even that is worth more than the game to me in its current state. I was only able to play through the first few levels before having to quit due to not being able to jump consistently.
Pros
-Game runs well, which comes from how simple it looks.
-The levels I played seemed designed decently, however the data (collectibles, there's 3 in each level) locations were boring and uninspired.
-Boost pads felt perfect.
-You chuck cubes like you're 5 olympic shotput medalists put together.
Cons
-Lack of meaningful options in the options menu. The only useful ones are toggle on music/sfx (separate) and sensitivity.
-View bobbing.
-JUMPING IS INCONSISTENT. This is the thing that really killed the game for me, there is a focus on jumping and when you miss 1 in 3 jumps and you have to jump 7 platforms in a row, you just want to quit the game. I have found that if you attempt to jump at the wrong point of your bob while walking/running, you will hear the jump sound, but not jump, in fact, this happens while standing still too, making me think view bobbing is on a global timer or something.
-Forced Vsync. This is honestly pretty minor because the game runs so well.
-Mouse movement is bad. I can't tell whether or not it's the vsync or if there's built in acceleration, but I have input lag (probably vsync) and my mouse doesn't go where I want it to on fast movements.
-If there is a ledge that's 1 inch high, you have to jump over it, you don't automatically step up.
-If you tab out and tab back in your mouse will be on the screen, this is minor because opening the menu then closing it will fix this.
If the developer fixed the jumping issue I would probably change this to a recommendation with the caveat that you should only buy it while on sale.

Overall I had quite a lot of fun with Hero Generations. It's what it says on the label: A fun strategy roguelike. It has a solid tutorial and the core gameplay is easy to learn hard to master. Traits randomly passing down from both parents is an interesting mechanic and forces you to try and woo the best mate each generation. Also, buildings are named after their builder and age which gives the feeling that time is actually passing.
Unfortunately though once you do master it you will quickly find that it isnt balanced particularly well. By the 3 hour mark I had found a way to cheese the game and become a 1000s of years old vampire living off the drained lifeforce of other adventurers. Kinda arguable who the real villian is in the game at that point. There are also a few glitches that still remain in the game that at this point I'm assuming are there to stay, they are not game breaking though so not a huge deal. Despite these negatives it was still quite a bit of fun for around 5 hours, but once you've killed and done everything there really doesn't feel like any reason to start again.
TLDR: A simple but deep strategy roguelike that despite a few balance issues and glitches still managed to keep me entertained for around 5 hours, definitely recommend it to anyone who likes strategy games and roguelikes.

This game is, in my opinion, the best game of 2017 and my personal favorite game of all time. It's amazing in so many aspects.
Combat is fluid, fun, and has little quirks that arent made readily known to the player that takes some toying around with to fully grasp, and 2B just feels perfect to control. Her movements in and out of combat feel like they were perfected, and for me it's fun just to run around the map. With the upgrades system, you can really customize the way you play. Like when im playing as the final character you unlock, I love playing super high risk, high reward by adding character upgrades that make it so when you taunt, you can do 3 or 4 times as much dfamage while an enemy is enraged, but they'll do the same. Add this on top of the character's berserk mode that ups damage recieved and taken already, and it's a fun game of being able to kill even the toughest enemies lighting fast, but also having to have your wits really about you. (On a side note, it's also one of the only games with an upgrade system that makes actual sense within the logic of the story). The music is easily one of the best OSTs for any peice of media ever, The world and characters are beautiful looking, and the story has one of the few narratives in gaming that actually takes advantage of the fact that it's interactive entertainment in genuinely emotionally impactful ways.
And yet, while it is my favorite game, I have to confess there are a few things about it that annoy me.
Starting off, this PC port is not amazing. I had to go get a fan mod to get it to run above 30 fps despite the fact that my computer mostly surpasses the recommended system requirments, and even then I swear it does nopt run as smooth as my copy on the PS4. Not the PS4 pro, the regular PS4. So there's that.
There's also the nitpick with the overall game that I have that once you get max level, going back through 2B's story is just way too easy since the enemies do not scale in level with you. Which would be fine, if new game plus at least scaled enemies to your level.
Which it does not. That makes going through the first two campaigns again just way too easy since by that time you'll be more likely than not just one or two shotting every enemy that gets in your way, and they'll be doing basically no damage to you at all, even if you somehow were to completely forget about the generous dodging you can do.
So aside from a bit of a lackluster port (which I guess square enix has totally forgetten about at this point despite the fact that this game tops steams sales charts every time it goes on sale), and a bit of annoyance with the leveling system, i'd wholly recommend this game. It's an unforgettable experience. Unfortunatley in it's current state and with it being clear that square enix has basically forgetten about this port, I can't recommend this at full price, despite how much I want this game to succeed evenm more than it already has for yoko taro and platinum games.
I can, however, reccomend this game when it goes on sale for $40 or less, especially if you're willing to take 5 minutes to install the fan mod that greatly improves performance.
Should be a mobile game and even then not really worth $15.

The glitch is that sometimes these buildings will deteriorate away whether the turn timer is over or not, which makes planning your buildings for future generations a dicey proposition as you never know if the buildings will last as long as they are supposed to or not. This is not a new glitch judging from the forums, Unless and until the glitch is taken care of, as the planning of buildings for future generations is a MAJOR part of the game, I can only recommend picking this one up if there is a really good sale going on.

This is not your father's roguelike. It's your grandfather's roguelike.  And his father's before his. And his father's before his.
Such a clever concept, so refreshingly different from the usual dungeon crawls.  It reminds me of a line from Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead: "For all the points on the compass, there is only one direction.  And time is its only measure."

Game is not what I expected. But perhaps my expectations were wrong, because I was unfamiliar with the roguelike genre. I had hoped that this game would be more like a sandbox in which you can play out your own stories. However, there is no way to create interesting stories in it at all.
You can marry to have children (in fact: you always only have one child and after that you die, and play on with the child). Besides the marriage itself, there is never any interaction between your character and the one you marry. There is never an interesting interaction between parent and child and friendship is non-existent.
In fact it's just some simple economics: building, harvesting, killing, gaining loot. Marrying is also entirely an economical decision. I think if that is what you play it for, it's fine.
In general I tend to dislike it, when games that pretend to be about adventure, are in fact only about economics and statistics. Wastes the theme for me.

I was so surprised by this. Honestly, it looked a little amature and I went into it expecting near crap- like most lesser-known visual novels/otome games on Steam tend to be. What I got was the exact opposite. The main character, Avery, and all of the cast are unique and likable. Avery's narration is relatable and I chuckled quite a lot at some lines. The magic mythos touched upon is interesting and left me wanting to know more. Doing all routes clocked out at around 17 hours for me, which is fanatastic considering this was an independently developed game. The art, while not the best (which can be an issue for some considereing visual novels, are, well, VISUAL) is charming and colorful. The backgrounds are very nice, more so than the character portraits. The abilities to choose your perfered pronouns and have some variety in apperence are also a big plus.
My only complaints about Hustle Cat come down to a lack of variety- which I know is strange, considering what I just said. The music got annoyingly repetative (two songs in perticular were played way too much during upbeat and relaxing moments that made them anything but). All the routes boiled down to the exact same big conflict at the end, with the exact same antagonist. The only thing different about each route is how he is taken down, but all of them end up being  essencially the same conflict. Worse yet, said main antagonist is given no development in any of the main routes- he is only given any sort of meaningful explaination for his actions AT ALL in the unlockable route, a trend in otome games that really bothers me. He was the driving overarching threat in EVERY ROUTE! It cheapens the impact of the original routes if all important story and weight is placed in the extra route. It would have been better if the antagonist of every route was more tailored to the chosen LI somehow. It made playing routes get very samey very fast when I knew what was coming.
Overall however, this is still worth checking out, if only to support the developer in hopes they build upon what they did right in this game and make more. If you're more of a casual otome fan, this is just for you. If you want something with  more meat, I'd reccomend Ozmafia!! (a newly released game not without its own issues, but has a bit more bite) or Nameless, the one thing you must recall.
Do it.

Well, what is there to say about Hustle Cat? I hope my grammar in this review is better than the game writers' in their game (pardon my English, it's not my first language). I guess we can start off by saying "It was a rusty relationship."
I think it's easier to put down the pros first.
Pros:
I laughed a lot because it was so terrible. At least my friends and I had fun?
and that's it.
As for the cons, I don't know where to start.
Cons:
The game was very inconsistent throughout, no matter what route you played. The character dialogues were really off. It takes them a while to notice something completely obvious. Repetition is usually key when memorizing things, but it doesn't do well in a visual novel. it makes the audience feel stupid...like Avery. The artwork was inconsistent, and very sloppy. The perspective was off in just about every background. The anatomy is really strange. The necks were too long; in particular, their collarbones were too low. The arms and hands were oddly positioned. It works for CLAMP, if that's what the creators were going for (however, this can't be compared to CLAMP because at least they're consistent with their artwork). There were so many grammatical errors (my friend who is an English major even cried), it was clear that the game did not have an editor. There were a lot of spelling errors too, and they should really check all of these things before publicizing the game. The fast forward option is nice, but it would have been nicer if they had varying levels of speed. The game was pretty laggy on more than a dozen occasions. The user interface was simple, which was okay, but it feels like the creators tried to make it too simple. The "menu" button looked more like a replay/loop button, and I didn't know it until I clicked on it.  No real effort seemed to go into it. Not only that, the color scheme of the interface was atrocious. I'm not an art major, but I know that the colors chosen for the game did not go well together. Speaking of colors, they felt too flat in the game. The shading was really sloppy and so was the line art. Plot wise...well there seemed to be too many things missing from the plot; this confuses the audience. A lot of the information wasn't really given in game. I had to look on tumblr in order to make sense of the game. Not only that, the ending was anticlimactic because the main antagonist simply disappears with his tail between his legs. There was no real struggle between the protagonist and antagonist. Character development in each route seemed too fast paced. It didn't really feel like you got to know the characters before you went into their routes. Too many internet tropes were used. I understood some, but honestly, not everyone will understand them, and it will only leave them confused...like Avery in most of the game. Honestly though, nothing was a surprise in the game because the final climactic CG was part of the opening. Also, the opening was very heavy on auto tune, unless you enjoy that sort of thing. The background music was okay, though I had it muted most of the time. The slider for the music wasn't as smooth. Just one click and the music was pretty loud.
Dating cats was such an interesting concept and had so much potential. Choosing your pronouns and skin colors was pretty cool. However, that doesn't make up for my long list of cons. In all, this game wasn't worth the $20 I spent. The routes were pretty short and not well written. It was a good attempt at an indie game, but it just didn't live up to my expectations. I don't recommend this game to anyone. My advice is to just save your money and fund Ono Kensho instead. if you're still interested in the game though, just watch Let's Play videos. My biggest regret is that I should've done that instead.

So, the game has a lot of technical issues that needs to be worked out. So far I haven't had any crashing others seem to get, but I often get huge FPS sinks and I can run pretty much anything on here with max quality without a hiccup.
This is a thumbs up for the game as a whole because I feel these technical issues shouldn't change my judgment on the game itself. If you have an XBO, buy it. Obviously if you're getting it for PC, wait or find a way to be sure it will work for you, otherwise I say wait. I thought at first it might have been due to too many zombies on screen at once, but even though that seems to drop it a tad, the game sinks for seemingly no reason even in empty areas.
Anyway, besides that and a few personal issues with the game (like trying to open the weapon locker only to keep picking up♥♥♥♥♥♥that piled up around it) it's a great zombie game and the best in the series imo.
The graphics are alright, not spectacular but it does set the atmosphere in some of the buildings quite nicely. It's definitely a step up from the previous games in every way, especially with the amount of zombies on screen now. The gameplay is fun especially with all the things you get to beat the zombies (and others) with. If you've played previous DR games, you'll know how it plays. The ragdoll is pretty amusing, uppercutting a zombie with a sledgehammer and sending them flying is pretty hilarious. The costumes this time around are your usual mixture of WTF and coolness. The combo weapons are great as usual and some of the additions are fun to toy with (Super Messager anyone?). I even love the combo vehicles; they bring a nice addition to the zombie slaughter. The story is interesting, nothing to write home about but it does make you want to get to the end when you're not mindlessly killing everything.  The characters are great; some you will love, while others not so much. Hell, I even liked most of the psychos I came across...except for one but due to possible spoilers (some people may not want the psychos to be spoiled) I won't say who/why.
All in all it's a great game; definitely a nice addition to the series. Though, I do hope these technical issues get worked out. It's sad to see such a good game become tainted with such tedious issues. The worst part for me is I need to beat the game again on nightmare mode, but the last chapter and onward seems to have caused the game to run even worse. I'll give it time and play some more, but I got a good 20+ hours out of it so I'm satisfied overall. But still, I hope in the near future I can play with little to no performance issues caused by poor optimization. Good luck to anyone willing to give the game a go.

Felt I should add my input since a bunch of people are negatively reviewing DR3 for the wrong reasons. When a game comes out, it'll have bugs; You have no right to negatively review it Day 1 just because it had some minor and a couple game-breaking bugs that were clearly all fixed the exact same night, which is when I started playing and I'm having zero problems so far. Will update as I go:
Graphics - 8/10 - May not be Ultra maxed out Crysis 3 settings, but they're as good as I expect from the Dead Rising Franchise.
Sound - 7/10 - I only put 7 until I find out if the character voice echoing is coming from the game itself or just from my headset; Otherwise everything else sounds fine.
Gameplay - 9/10 (So far) - Same basic fighting mechanics of Dead Rising, but upgraded with a few minor welcomed tweaks (Magazines no longer taking up inventory space, performing awesome-looking kill streak combo moves, survivors don't need to be babysat constantly and are actually more useful in combat ((Thank you, Capcom!)))
Co-op - No comment so far as I'm doing my first playthrough Singleplayer only.
Complaints - My only real complaint so far is the changed saving mechanic. You can now save anytime [in Normal Story Mode], and to me it feels like the game is much easier than it needs to be since I can save, quit, and feel like I don't have any pressure of surviving like I did from the previous games.
In conclusion, I recommend Dead Rising 3 with credibility as a Day 1 participant and I hope other people will enjoy it as much as I am so far.

The controls worked just fine with keyboard and mouse in previous installments but they don't work well in this one. The game itself is a mixed bag. I wish Steam would have a "maybe" option for recommendations. There were quite a few frustrations. Instant failures are common and it is not always clear where can you go and were you can't. The levels are still pretty linear with a few exceptions.
The theme though. While it is still a Splinter cell game and you will sneak a lot this time you are a double-agent breaking the terrorist cells from inside. The biggest addition is the trust meter of both Terrorists and Echelon. You need to keep both factions satisfied otherwise you loose. It makes the missions more tense as you get multiple objective from both factions (often conflicting with each other) and you have to choose on fly which ones you can afford to skip. This system also rewards skilled players. For instance killing innocents will couse the Echelon to be displeased with you, therefore players ability to stay hidden and avoid contact with the enemy is rewarded.
My favourite part of the game ere the semi-sandbox levels which take place in terrorist hideout. In these the player is given a main and sideobjectives from both terrorists and echelon and has around 30 minutes to complete as many of them as possible. It is a great idea which works really well and uses Sam's stealth ability in a very organic way.
So yeah, I think it is an interesting game and it is a worth a shot when caught on sale. It does have a lot of issues though.

While the third Princess Isabella game is still the weakest in the series, at least this Steam re-release finally has the bonus chapter, plus trading cards and achievements.
Artifex Mundi tried to spice up their re-release of Princess Isabella 3: Rise of an Heir with their usual achievements and trading cards, but even these additions cannot hide the original issues of the game, like the bland hidden object scenes, lack of puzzles, or the repetitive item gathering.
New players have the luxury of not knowing how worse the gameplay and the helper system got since the previous games, but they also won’t really know what is going on, since the short plot dump at the start is hardly enough to catch up. (This is why it is baffling why they re-released only the third part of the trilogy.) Returning players may also feel alienated by a new protagonist, the daughter of Isabella, even if her task is to save her mother from the witch’s curse. (20 years after it was cast. She was apparently busy until now.)
This release also includes the previously missing bonus chapter to give a proper ending to the trilogy, but even with it, I can only recommend this game for those who want a full Artifex Mundi collection.

Princess Isabella: The Rise of An Heir [CE*], is a HOPA* game, developed by Gogii Games; World-Loom and published by Artifex Mundi.
*CE - Collector's Edition
*HOPA - Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure.
Princess Isabella: The Rise of An Heir is the second installment of the Princess Isabella game series. Other games from this series: Princess Isabella and Princess Isabella - Return of the Curse.
Since this is an collector's edition game, it comes with some extra features, that aren't available in the regular edition game.
I want to mentioned that the visuals for this game is nicely done even though it's a bit dated. The visuals can be adjusted in the option menu.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only three difficulty game modes to choose from: Casual, Advanced and Expert.
Diary Notebook it keeps track off all game's objectives and notes.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations.
Magic Wand tools - There are two kinds of wands: Fairy and Dark Magic Wands. Both needs to be built before they can be used. They can be used in certain situation. Both have different functions.
Dragon Helper can be summoned by using its pan flute. The Dragon Helper can do certain things that the individual player can't. Like removing large objects that are in the way.
Fairy Godmother Helpers. They can do certain things that the individual player can't. Each of the fairy godmothers has different abilities.
Most of the hidden object scenes consists of find "x" amount and traditional word lists with little or no interaction. Some of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the game's extra content section.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them. Some of the puzzles can be replayed in the game's extra content section.
There's a bonus chapter, but it can be access, only after the main portion of the game is fully completed. The bonus chapter is the direct sequel to the main story.
There are nine different achievements that can be unlocked from playing the game. Each of these achievements do has some requirement before they can be unlocked.
There are total of five different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

Okay... so I am not quite sure on how to best describe this here game... Primal Carnage: Extinction.
Overall, it's quite an interesting game. The graphics, which actually reminds me quite a bit about the 2007 Crysis game from CryTek (bless the heart of Cevat Yerli for creating such an awesome game!), are fairly decent and so is the gameplay. The game isn't sluggish and it performs well -- both on solo gameplay and on multiplayer online based gaming. There is no stuttering and there is no glitching or flunking graphics when your fast-speed running, or when there is a lot of action taking place. On that front, I'm inclined to give this game an 8/10 score.
In this game you can play, either, as human character, a dinosaur of various kinds (T-rex, Velociraptor, etc), or you can simply be a spectator (online gaming only) to others playing. Regardless of your character, dinosaur or human, you make your way around in a rich and well-made landscape, not unlike what you may have seen in dinosaur movies such as Jurassic Park/World, where you have to survive or roam around freely but cautiously. On that front, I'm inclined to give this game a 6/10 score.
But something just seems... missing. At this point in time I cannot put a finer point to what I feel it is, but something just seems to be, as I said, missing. It's not in any way meant as a negative critique or anything as such. Perhaps it's just me who might have had a little bit too high level of expectations for this game, but I feel like this game and the graphics has so much more to offer rather than just a gameplay where you're running around killing obscure and outrageously weird dinosaurs that comes at you in waves upon waves, some of which are entirely stealth-cloaked not unlike the Brotherhood of NOD's stealth-tanks, in the also 2007 released game, Command and Conquer: Tiberium Wars -- for those of you who may have played this game back in the day.  I'm not even kidding here guys, there are STEALTH dinosaurs in this game!
So what is it that is lacking about this game? Well, if I were to say something straight-out-of-the-bag, I would say "Story line". There is simply no story line to this game at all! The entirety of the game concists of you running around and killing dinosaurs or hunting humans to feast on them, either in solo or in multiplayer game mode, perhaps together with your friends, which is absolutely fine (and possibly even more fun than playing solo gameplay).
So if you're looking for a game where there is a lot of no-brainer action taking place, meaning that you just have to survive and shoot (or eat!), then this is definitely a good game for it. But if you're like me, and like a game with a good solid story and such, I'd definitely look for something else to play because such you simply will not find it within this game. On this front, I am inclined to give this game a 2/10 score.

"Polarity is made exclusively for experienced gamers."
Agreed. This is a science fiction themed game, that for some reason decided it was too good for video game physics.
It seems to want to have advanced momentum, but it is very poorly implemented. This makes segments of jumping between moving platforms difficult at best, and near-impossible at worst.
As for the puzzle element: You're going to get VERY familiar with the restart button. It's very easy to get yourself stuck, often because you'll have to THROW a key into the right spot, without the ability to retrieve it if you happen to miss. In fact, throwing the key-cubes is a HUGE risk on it's own, as I've seen them glitch into the ground and walls on multiple occasions.
This game has something very interesting built in: An apoloy. It seems the game's creators were aware of the flaws, but since they were working with a very small team, they could not fix the issues before moving on from the project. I tend to have a lot of respect for game creators who decide to at least share their work with the world, and in this case, it's no different. What I do not respect however, is the fact that they hype it up on the store page, ask money for a game they know is unfinished/buggy, and then issue an unsuiting apology in the game itself.
With how tedius the game can get, I'll say: Don't buy it just for the achievements. I recommend this game when it's on sale, to completionists and masochists. If you don't tick 2 of these 3 boxes, you probably won't have the patience for this game.
