"The Secret of Monkey Island: Special Edition" is an OK game.  That might sound like faint praise, but considering that I first played the original edition around 24 years ago and it was distributed on floppy disks, it's actually a testament to how good the game was.
For the positives, the updated graphics, story, and humor are pretty nice.  It's also nice that you can't really mess things up so bad that you need to load a saved game.  Saves, for the most part, are there just because you might want to stop playing for a while and come back later.
Unfortunately, there are negatives.  The biggest is that a lot of the game is hunt-the-pixel.  Many of the items that you need to find/work with are fairly obvious in the environment.  But, many others are essentially indistinguishable from the background (a couple of planks especially spring to mind as well as the maps):  if you don't happen to mouse over the correct pixel, you'd never know you can do something there.  The "verb" and inventory system, though ground-breaking back in 1990 is a bit awkward today (I'm playing Monkey Island 2 right now, and they fixed this there).  Also, because the cut-scenes and dialogs are not skippable, the pacing drags.  Similarly to the hunt-the-pixel issue, in many cases you don't know that you can walk off the screen and get to another area.  And, finally, the introductory and ending credits are non-skippable.  There's nothing you can do about the introductory credits, and the only way I was able to quit the game during the ending credits was to Alt-Tab out and close the window from the desktop.
So, yes.  Pluses and minuses.  It's a shame I can't say the game is better than OK (it was tremendous in its day).  But, if you can buy it cheap enough, its current rendition is a good way to spend about 10 hours.

Dead Rising 3 is a mixed-bag. It's a bag filled with delicious chocolates and overly salted pretzel. You can pull out something sweet and succlent, and other times nothing but♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dead Rising 3 is one of those games where it had a lot of great ideas and fun elements but get weighed down by plenty of pretzels.
Dead Rising 3 is the next installment in the Dead Rising franchise, a franchise of which I love. Seeing Frank West plow to hordes of zombie in a shopping mall was one of the greatest things I had seen for the Xbox 360 at the time, and my love for the series pushed forward by the new combo weapons, B-movie style, wacky game that Dead Rising 2 was. It seemed Dead Rising 3 might of been a spark for another entry in a series that I had always found enjoyable, despite it flaws. Yet, Dead Rising 3 had proved me wrong.
Let's talk about the good things first though, Dead Rising 3 features plenty new elements to franchise. The game feels more fluid and less clunky, Nick is able to create combo weapons on the fly, and the city of Los Perdidos is much more massive than Willimette and Fortune City. The game features two modes, Nightmare and Normal. Nightmare is more in the style of the previous Dead Rising games, with a tight time limit and a saves only available in safe houses and bathrooms, for those who like a challenge. While normal mode has a very long time limit, and lets you freely explore the undead-infected city at your leisure. Some very minor changes include being able to eat/drink while moving, improved psychopath health bars, less escort missions, and the abillity to access clothing and weapons from the safe house you've previously unlocked or picked up. The zombie-slaughering is a blast, with a wide variety of effective and silly weapons at your disposal. Combine a katana and a scythe to make the all-mighty Reaper, and you can combine that together with a gasoline can to having a Fire Reaper. Put rubber ducks on boxing gloves, or put a shotgun and an assault rifle togheter and face hordes of thousands of undead obstacles with your powerful weapons. Slicing and dicing zombies feels satisfying, and finding new blueprints to a new combo weapon is always a blast. Unlike most open-world games, Dead Rising 3 has a lot of interiors. It's choke full of hardware, clothing, and yes, even porn stores. The absurdity is the finest part of Dead Rising 3, even if it feels a bit juvenile or silly at times, it feels wonderful to plow through the hordes.
Now here's the bad news, let's just get this out of the way, very few will deny it. Dead Rising 3 runs poorly. It's playable, but don't be expecting to run on 60 FPS on the highest quality of machines. Is it a crappy port? Depends on how you look at it. The Xbox One version of Dead Rising 3 (a launch title for the console) was known to run terribly at times, with many technical issues. One could say the PC port of Dead Rising is actually much better compared to the Xbox One version, the thing is, it still runs like crap at times. The weirdest thing is that during cutscenes, the game's FPS tends to drop even less. One very frustrating annoyance, is the game tends to crash every so often. It's almost impossible to do Nightmare mode as the game crashes so frequently that you might end up losing your save, because you couldn't make it to a safehouse or bathroom before the invisible "crash timer" rings its bell. It's a very big problem, unless you don't care all too much about running Dead Rising 3 on the highest settings, or don't mind getting under 50 FPS at times, then the performance issues shouldn't really affect you. Even then, there are still some weird texture pop-ins, objects appearing out of nowhere, and some low quality textures even on the highest settings. Plenty of games look much better than Dead Rising 3, and play much more smoother.
As for negative gameplay aspects, it may very from person to person. Los Perdidos is big compared to the last two locations of Dead Rising. It's also very maze-like, unmemorable, and twisted. In the previous two Dead Risings, the landmarks were very clear. The giant slide in Pallisades Mall in Dead Rising 2, the courtyard of convicts in 1, but Dead Rising 3 doesn't have those types of memorable landmarks. There's no way to tell where the gun store once was, or the knife shop, or the pizza place. The streets, more often than not, look the same. Most locations have to be travelled to by car along a confusing routes of highways, and frequent roadblocks that require you to find a new automobile. It all felt tedious getting around. The side missions, are just your generic open-world ones, such as find 5 guns and bring it to Tommy, or take Sarah to a certain store. A lot of the psychopaths in Dead Rising 3 felt underwhelming, they weren't as interesting or challenging as the previous two and lacked any real great rewards. In Dead Rising 2, deafeating Randy gave you the massive pink chainsaw or defeating Seymour gave you the powerful 60 bullet Six Shooter, and in Dead Rising 1, defeating Adam gave you the mini-chainsaw. However, defeating psychos in 3 only give you PP, a key, sometimes survivors, and only three the six optional psychopaths give you some sort of weapon, none of which are very good. All these features can really tone down some of the great potential the game could have, there's so many minor irritations that just turn into one big itch you can't scratch.
Despite the hordes of zombie killing, the incredibly fun combo weapons, and the bizzareness of the entire game. As hard as it is for me to say this as a really big fan of the series, I can't reccommend Dead Rising 3. It's performance and crashing issues are much too big to ignore, the twisted and unmemorable map of Los Perididos are frustraiting, and it's lack of any real sort of accomplishment from rescuing survivors or doing side missions makes you hesitant every time you get a call. The game could of been so much more, what sounds better than a open-world sandbox co-op zombie killing game? Instead, you're left with a technical mess, and a bland game. With all the things it does right, there's just too many damn pretzels in this bag.

Out There Somewhere is a simple as well as simply priced game on Steam with a lots of detail added in such a short little space adventure.  While it is short in stature, it makes up for it with the quality put into the the low price, sprite-work, and the gameplay.
The game itself costs two dollars on Steam, so it is very unlikely you will regret your purchase with all of the fibers of your wallet if you dislike it, unless of course those two dollars were needed to save you from dying of hunger. Of course, there is a chance one might receive a coupon for it upon crafting a badge or something, further decreasing the affordable price.
The sprites give off a very solid Metroid reminiscence, which is fair because the game was reportedly inspired by Super Metroid.  Each of the environments are tailored almost exclusively with each screen that your character passes through.  They may have an underlying theme to it all, be it uncharted wasteland to menacing metal, but they all have something unique in level design incorporated within the game.
The game is built around a teleportation mechanic.   A specially designed gun fires a blue bullet that, upon impact with any solid platform, teleports you to that specific location.  The gameplay revolves around you, and how you determine when to fire, not to mention time how long the bullet takes to reach your designated location.
Of course, with all of those pluses, the game itself is rather short.  If you do not go out of your way to find any collectables, (and even if you do) the game boils down to a solid hour or two of total playtime.  Which is a shame, because the teleport gun mechanic is rather fun to play around with.  Another issue I have with the game is the way the levels are organized.  I feel as though game is very linear, each level designed to be a simple obstacle that prevents you from proceeding, so any unique level concepts are used once and left behind.  If one wanted to find the collectables aforementioned, they would have to backtrack through each of the levels that appeared to be designed in mind for separate challenges meant simply for providing something to hop through once and be done with, compared to games like the original Metroid or its remake, Zero Mission where there are several tunnels connected in a sense where you can be familiar with the layout and return without it feeling like you have to return through a single linear stretch.
However, the game is a solid buy through and through.  If you feel like adventuring on an alien planet with a trusty teleportation machine, feel free to buy for a short yet sweet playthrough.

With only four of the five episodes released, this game could be finished and I'd be completely content with the ending. When I started with episode one, I knew that i would enjoy the time I spent playing this game. From the well written script and nicely spoken lines by each of the characters, to even the gameplay. The simplistic TellTalle formula has yet again shown that it works and works well. Some may complain that you can't control what happens in the game, but that's the point, it's a story. It's not all about the gameplay, it's about engaging in the narrative that TellTale time and time again has shown what amazing things can come out of a story.
Now let's take a more in-depth analysis of the game. At the beginning, I was a little unsure of how I would feel about the characters, but i did my best to pay attention and take the time to listen to each person that was in my group. I would also select the options that I thought I would be most likely to preform in that situation. By doing that, it made me care about what was going on between the different characters that I interacted with.
Another upside to the game is the combat and quick-time events. Through most of these instances, I was on edge. I wanted to succed in the task at hand because I wanted to continue my epic quest in the world of Minecraft with these friends that I have gained (I know they're basically just pieces of dialogue strung together but I tried to be in perspective of the main character).
The next thing up is the original Minecraft game. For Story Mode, it would be beneficial to you if you have played the original game and possibly have been part of the ever-expanding community to understand fully what you are doing. There are also references to famous "events" in the original that I would chuckle at because I fully understood what was going on. BUT even if you didn't play the original, then the game still made sure you were able to progress. Crafting, for instance, i blew past the crafting bits because I knew the recipies, but for those who didn't know, they added a recipie list to help you out.
Downsides. Okay, i know that some parts of the dialouge, like in every TellTale game, gets messed up and is strung together wrong and I found myself asking "what? that didn't make sense?" but there were only two or three instances of this. Some audio errors occured where characters were silent, and drop in framerate from time to time. Though, I find this completely forgiveable. Many people do say that the story is boring and they don't care what happens to the characters, but this is completely subjective. The only way to know fully is to play for yourself.
Final thoughts. A game that is priced at the same as the other episodic TellTale games, but is not as long timewise. It only took me a little less than 7 hours to beat the first four episodes and i've logged more than 10 on both Walking Dead games. This didn't bother me in the slightest, it's just something good to know going into this game. I had a very enjoyable time playing this and am looking forward to episode five.
Also, I don't usually cry at video games but for some reason, the final scene with Reuben really got to me. Who knew a pig could bring out so many emotions.
I give Minecraft: Story Mode a 8.5/10

I love this thing from the perspective of laying in my Sumo Lounge Bean Bag chair playing games; that I could previously only play with a Keyboard and Mouse, on my big screen tv.  Don't expect this thing to be a replacement for a keyboard and mouse YET.
You are going to sacrifice some of that accuracy you have spent the last 2 decades honing with a keyboard and mouse, but you know what...I'm okay with that.  And further more, I feel like with practice...this could easily become as accurate as a keyboard and mouse.  There is really nothing preventing it from doing so.  I really feel like the limitation is just us as gamers adjusting to such a controller.
This aside, never have I had something that just "works" in Steam like this.  And it works for everything from Starcraft to Left 4 Dead.  From retro to next-gen.  The way they allow you to customize the controls too (and share your configurations with the world), makes this thing a gamer's wet dream.  What are you waiting for?  Get this thing now!

Princess Isabella: The Rise of an Heir is one of the most recent game of Princess Isabella series and is the only one with the Artifex Mundi stamp!
Despite its graphics (some people doesn’t like the old style), its length (about 3 hours if you’re really good) and some pixelated cut scenes: the game has many unique features that make it a very great game.
As Bella you’ll embark on a scary and thrilling adventure in order to free the kingdom from the clutches of the evil witch and set free the god-mothers (little fairies) as well as your queen mother. And of course face and destroy the evil witch once and for all. She will also have the help of some magical friends.
The bonus story let you play after the events of the main one, when the kingdom come back to what it was before. Well almost because several rooms or the castle are still cursed and several souls are trapped between the living world and the afterlife. So Bella need to lift the last curses to restore the castle and send the souls to the afterlife.
As every Artifex Mundi game you can move freely in different area (of the kingdom and the castle) and need to solve some puzzles and find all objects in hidden objects scenes. The game has (different difficulties? and) a guest feature: every one of the family can play an independent save and resume the game where they left it. When you first play the game you’ll have a notebook where you have all your objectives as well as all your notes. You also have a map to not get lost and you may be able to fast travel. Adding to that you’ll have a hint button (thanks to two of your magical friends) that will help you in many ways but be warned that you may not use it in any puzzle or hidden object scene (HOS)or investigation scene (IS). Hints can be used to know where you need to go, where is the next interaction or to show an object or clue in an HOS or IS or to skip a puzzle. To conclude this part, you’ll also have an inventory to store useful items through your journey.
Puzzles are good, different and perhaps short. There are 2 kind of Hidden objects scenes. (HOS) The one where you need to find objects hidden with the help of their name. Colored or white names (one of the two) mean that you have to interact directly with the scene or use an item in the scene. And the other one is a special one which I’ll talk in the unique feature of this game.
One of the very good thing of this game is that there are 5 unique features you won’t find in any other Artifex Mundi game:
•	You’ll have a pan flute which will be really helpful through your journey.
•	You’ll have a magical wand which will be really helpful through your journey.
•	You’ll have up to three spells which will be really helpful through your journey.
•	You’ll have some special hidden objects scenes.
•	Finally you’ll have 2 different fighting game.
The pan flute will allow you to play a song that the dragon of the kingdom will hear and then help you. When you’ll see golden music notes flying through an object that will mean that the dragon can lift it or set it on fire in order to help you.
The wand will be able to be upgraded up to two times. When you first get it you’ll be able to use its first power. When you’ll see some sparkling blue bubbles that will mean that you can use the first power of your wand. You can then ask (an) animal(s) or insects to do a task for you. The second power let you
Finally the last power

I have been using this controller for the past two weeks and I have been very impressed. It took me about 15 minutes to get used to the controller, but I quickly began to appreciate the sheer customizability of the controller. Not only is every button and pad on this controller fully rebindable, but the ability to pick community voted control templates is also great. If anything, they can give you a great starting point for your own control scheme. Along with the vast array of custom control options, the controller is also one of the most comfortable controller I have every used. Big Picture Mode also become worth using with this controller. One use I did not expect, was as a computer remote. I often have pulled up netflix and used the controller's right track pad as a mouse, right trigger as Left-Click and the left pad as a scroll wheel and navigated sites with ease.
Some might be put off by the fact that this controller uses two AA batteries, however I have had no issue with battery life so far. That, and one could use rechargeable batteries with this controller and be just fine. I have also experienced very rare instances of glitches with the controller, where the controls do not work properly, but this is usually fixed by exiting Steam and relaunching the game.
Overall, I am extremely happy with this controller and it has become my favorite. It works very well with games that are made with controllers in mind, and with those that aren't. I would heartily recommend this controller to anyone with an interest in it.

Okay, so this is kinda typical VN fare, but Hustle Cat not only does it really well, but does it in a special way that's super unique to Hustle Cat.
Of course it mixes things I personally am super fond of (hot dates and witchcraft), but the characters are very well-designed and unique, and their stories tend to really let them grow on you.
For instance, I watched a couple of LPers play the Finley route just to see what the game was about, and while at first I was kinda "meh" about her, she's started to grow on me. I also played the Landry route for myself, and was pleasantly surprised to find the same thing happened. The game really does take the time to allow the characters to open up to Avery, and you get to learn a lot about them. You get to see them face their "demons" so to speak, and it kind of endears them to me to get to see them trust Avery with their stories and problems. It makes them awesome and relatable.

I am seeing a lot of reviews stating that this game is poorly optimized and crashes a lot.
I am here to tell you that they may have experienced that, but I have not. I am running on windows 7 Pro 64-bit, quad core i7 intel processor, a Nvidia Geforce 660ti - 2 gb, and 32 gb of ram, and I have experienced no crashes, nor any optimization problems OTHER THAN CUTSCENES. By god, the majority of cutscenes are literally unwatchable. I don't understand. The cutscenes look relatively the same as when in-game. Why they run like sh*t is beyond me. Other than the cutscenes, the game is running beautifully. I don't know why, but it is. Maybe I'm lucky or something, who knows. But, overall, I am happy with my purchase. This game is extremely fun, and, looking past the poor optimization of the cutscenes, is a good buy. There are many, MANY weapons to choose from, the use of vehicles to move around Los Perdidos is a very nice feature (I hated walking everywhere in the other entries), the map of DR3 is at least 3 or 4 times bigger than DR1 & 2 combined (meaning many more places to explore), MUCH larger amounts of zombies (crazy amounts, as in to the point where driving a car through the hordes is extremely difficult, like driving through Louisiana muck), and, my favorite, the time is extended from the original 3 days, to 5 days (or was it 7?)...Hm...Whatever, it's more than 3 days, and that's what I wanted - More time to explore, finish quests, savor the story, and, of coarse, slaughter the undead hordes with beautiful weapons of blood-spraying destruction.
Now for the juicy part:
Graphics: 8/10
Optimization: 4/10 ( Needs a lot of work - Those cutscenes are stress-inducing)
Fun Factor: 10/10
Replayability: Very High
Overall Rating: 9/10 in my book.
(P.S - Make sure you fix the 30 FPS lock. This can be easily found via youtube and/or Google. It is relatively simple, you find
C: Program Files (x86) \ Steam \ Steam Apps \ Common \ deadrising3 on your computer (thats normally where it is unless you have it saved on another drive), create a new text document and name it "user.ini". Once you've done that, open it (being the file that you've just created), and type in "gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate = True". Save, and you're good to go.)
(P.S.S - I believe there is a Review somewhere below saying pretty much the same thing about the FPS lock, but with a little more detail, and providing a link.)

Okay, this isn't just an OverWatch clone; it's trying to be Blizzard in an almost stalkerish way.  A lot of their character designs borrows heavily on the sylization of not just Overwatch but Warcraft, Diablo, and even Starcraft if I'm being honest.
The biggest difference is how hard Paladins pushes for your cash ....and they are so utterly shameless in how blatent they are.  Constant reminders.  Notifications.  In game reminders in between rounds that you can absolutely give them money right now.  It made me feel like I was playing a commercial.  Yeah, they need to make their money some how....but the cynicism on display was revolting.  Game is already out of my library; if I feel like you are nagging me to spend money (LOTS of money) when you advertised you game an F2P in early access?  I want nothing to do with what you're selling.
OverWatch has issues; the LootBox model is greed incarnate.  Somehow, Paladins feels greedier and sleezier without making you pay a nickle up front.  The cynical copy/pasted art style, the cynical copy/pasted design ideas, and the constant nagging for pennies for a product that the designers are advertising as unfinished...everything about this game feels off.

Primal Carnage: Extinction was supposedly an "upgrade" from the original Primal Carnage however it wasn't, and still is not, the step up we were hoping for. Now, this review has been witten since the latest november patch and I am not going to be biased about any of the game's aspects there are still some good and bad features about this game and I believe that the developers can easily fix these issues and make this game as good, if not better than the original (although I doubt it).
Pros:
- Dinosaurs
- Fairly balanced gameplay (except for a few features I will get onto later)
- More variety within the dinosaurs (dilo/cryo, etc having individual abilities) and some enhancements to some dinosaurs since the original.
- A large variety of skins and/or cosmetics for both dinosaurs and humans.
- Humans have more in depth features (new weapons, equip items, etc)
- A large variety of in-depth, detailed maps
- Fun easter eggs for you to search for (The egg is a lie.)
Cons:
- Many bugs and glitches (although some have been fixed since this patch)
- Tyrants have been seriously nerfed since Primal Carnage. Honestly, a pathfinder could go one-on-one with a T. rex. In the original, tyrants were mean't to be feared and required teamwork and skill to take down. Nower days, they represent little threat to even the average PC:E players. Why not add some sort of damage resistance to larger dinosaurs?
- Pathfinders are insanely powerful, carnos are practically useless against them and tyrants even more so. Just nerf the damn shotgun to 300 damage tops.
- Tranq rifles. Why were they necessary?
- Roleplaying servers. In a fighting game, roughly 50% of them are diehard roleplayers. Pathetic. I don't mind freeroam as it allows the player to explore the various maps and apreciate the work gone into the game but we need more people on TDM and GTTC (although I do understand that the devs have no control over that but it is still a massive issue).
- Which brings me to my next con: Get to the Chopper is dead! Why is no one playing get to the chopper anymore?
- Terrible community full on players which lack any sort of skill in combat. Most result to spamming explosives, tranquilizers darts and pouncing. Those who do manage to get kills then go on to tea-bagging their victims. The rest of the community avoid combat altogether and become diehard roleplayers or spam skin/trade requests in the chat.
In short, it would not be entirely honest calling Primal Carnage: Extinction an "upgrade". If you want to mess around on freeroam or become a 24/7 roleplayer and create some sort of dino/humans-fire-breathing-hybrid-that-looks-like-it-cane-out-some-sort-of-cliche-anime then go ahead and buy this game. However, if it's co-operative fps action you're looking for then buy the original (surprisingly there still is a thriving community of players on Primal Carnage). Sadly, the visuals and skins were enough to keep me here...for now... However, I still have some faith in this game. If the developers actually took the time to read what the players want instead of cramming in more skins then maybe we could restore the franchise back to it's former glory. If only they knew...

This is one of the cutest visual novel dating games I've played so far! Its overall vibe is very sweet.
In
, you play as 19-year-old high school graduate Avery Grey, currently crashing at their aunt's while looking for a job to help pay the bills. After scouring the internet for job openings and cat videos, Avery comes across a cute cat café in the neighbourhood, and they're hiring! That immediately ricochets Avery into the world of coffee, cats, latte art, ridiculously cute co-workers, and their mysterious new goth boss. But some of the cats Avery encounters near the café look an awful lot like their new friends...
+ You get to pick pronouns, skin tones & body type looks for Avery
+ The cute pastel meme/internet aesthetic
+ You can initially romance 4 guys & 2 gals
+ Everybody has various, distinct & interesting personalities
+ Avery is no passive pushover protagonist
+ The overall story is quite interesting
- The romance-specific endings are a bit short
- The game is a
buggy; sometimes it crashes randomly or the skip button doesn't work
- Some of the proportions on the CG art are a little off
- Not all the story elements surrounding the supernatural angle are well-explained
I had such a good time playing this, mainly because its tone is so friendly and cute! The witchy/supernatural story elements were a nice addition as well, and it was great to see how magic affected all the co-workers differently. All characters have a deeper issue that they're trying to deal with during the game, which gets fully developed during their romance route. I also very much enjoyed Avery's character! Realistic, relatable, and not just another blank slate.
After playing through everybody's romance, you unlock the "secret" romance with Graves, your mysterious boss. This one is probably one of the best and also explains more about magic and witchery. Only downside for me was that it could have been longer, especially the romance-specific endings, also when taking the game's price into account.
Overall, an extremely nice addition to the romance-themed visual novels here on Steam! I will definitely revisit some of its lovely characters again :D

Hero Generations takes an interesting concept and turns it into a game that you can pick up for a few minutes or spend hours with. --Original review posted Jun 19, 2015--
Just doesn't deliver.
I wanted to like this game so much, I really did.  I liked the concept and I was hooked by the write up.  But it just doesn't deliver a fun and engaging experience.  The real and true fault to the game is that it doesn't do what the main hook of the game is delivered as.  The legacy system is really no different than a game reset in the long run.  In most roguelikes, you get a game over and maybe you've made some progress towards your next game.  In this one you have a limited number of turns, usually around 40 or so, and then the game forces you into and end scenario.  Often times you spend the last quarter of your life just trying to FIND a mate so that you can continue your legacy of mediocrity.
So, it's billed as a "roguelike/4X strategy game about life, legacy & love"
4X ?  Maybe only in the very loosest of definitions.
Do you 'explore' yes, you explore a bland and ultimately uninteresting proceedurarly generated world.  But once you explore the area, it doesn't change in future legacy characters.  HOWEVER the fog of war DOES reset.  So either hope you have a really good memory or ask yourself why the fog of war reset.
Do you 'expand' ?  I would say no.  You don't really have any classic base or sphere of influence that you expand.  Oh you can upgrade other towns, but since they 'rot' over a generation or two, there's no sense of actual building or accomplishment.
Do you 'exploit' resources?  Yes, ok, this is one of the 4 "x"es that you actually do.  You kill monsters, loot mines, find artifacts, etc.
Do you exterminate?  Kinda.  You fight monsters and other 'heroes' like yourself, but there's no sense of accomplishment because they are constantly respawning every generation.  So it's more like whack a mole, not exterminating any enemy.
Have you found the common thread in everything that I've written yet?  It's that the legacy system is basically broken in my opinion.  There's really no sense of accomplishment or forward progression.  You spend 20-25% of your turns looking for a mate to try to continue your legacy instead of trying to do quests or explore, and then you start all over with a new hero.  After playing for 90 minutes, I felt like I'd accomplished absolutely nothing upon my new hero.
I might give this game another go if they do a signifigant update to the legacy system, but otherwise it's getting banished to the 'never to be played again' list of steam games.  On the off chance that Heart Shaped Games LLC reads this:
Get rid of building decay, have coins automatically carry over on each legacy, and maybe a percentage of the previous hero's strength and / or fame.  Otherwise the whole legacy system in it's current incarnation is nothing more than a soft reset.
--updated review Oct 13, 2015--
Sometimes it's a shame that you can only 'reccomend' or 'not recomend' a game when you write a review.  Because with the recent update, I really don't know if I feel like a  "YES" or "NO" is exactly how I feel any longer.
Scott a dev from heartshapedgames was kind enough to take the time and write a feedback response to my original review.  Let me say first of all any dev who takes the time to listen to feedback and reviews and then try to make their game better is already leaps and bounds ahead of others in the industry.  That point alone scores major points in my book.
But lets get to the game and the changes.  I will try not to rehash my original review too much and focus on the changes that I noticed in my play time.
Pro:
-Building decay, this is a NOTICIBLE difference from when I played last time and a very much needed change.  The buildings still decay, but picking up a hammer or the right trait, and you can really make your buildings last forever.  Ignore them and they will rot away in a little while.  That's fine.  It's not like you have to rebuild every year.
-Items: I don't know if this is just my memory, but it seems like there was a slew of new items dropping from the last time I played it many months before.  Training swords, hammers, rafts... these items were in the game but I only ever saw them in shops before.  It's entirely possible that I just missed them somehow during the first few hours of my play, I don't know.  But it does have a positive effect.
Con:
-I was really hoping the legacy system would be boosted just a little.  Everything I said in my original review still holds true.  Gold doesn't carry over, nor does strength.  Fame does to an extent, in that your legacy once built up starts to build, but it's very small.  It's a bit disheartening to have someone with an epic legacy and their child is a no body.  Really the son of Grokthak isn't even at ALL famous?
- Fog of war.  I really don't understand why this exists at all on each new playthrough.  I could almost understand if there was a 'semi' fog of war, a see through fog of war on each generation that obscured the monsters, but let you see terrain previous generations had explored.  But since the world doesn't change between generations, resetting the fog of war just makes the game feel tedious when I'm thinking "now which town had the strength forts, and which had the farms?"
- Age, I've actually changed my mind on the whole 'looking for a mate' at the end of your life.  Since your strength goes down in old age, that's when you should be retiring from adventuring and settling down to find a mate.  So my gripe about that has been removed.... unfortunately it's been replaced by something else.  The 'age' that you become an adult and gain a strength boost is fine.  But middle age, and old age, shouldn't be 'set in stone' they should be a portion of your maximum life.  Far too often I found myself effectively being forced into 'late game' by age for a hero because he hit a magical wall of age and lost a chunk of strength.  Now I understand that any game has to have a 'game over' situation, and in this it's not finding a mate before you die.  But I feel like pushing that old age penalty back a bit would be a bit better.  Let me have the choice for one last epic battle with the dragon thing before seeking out a mate if I want to risk the loss.  By making me lose 10 or more strength, I know I'm going to have next to no shot.
ANYWAYS, wrapping up, I DIDN't change my review from a 'no' I would not recommend this game.  However, it comes with a caveat.
--THE CAVEAT--
Now, for the average player, based just on the description in the store page, NO, I would not recommend this game.  However, that being said, I WOULD RECOMMEND this game, BUT with a caveat;
I would recommend this game as long as people know what they are getting into first.
Despite what it says on the store page, this game ISN'T a 4x strategy game.
This game ISN'T really a roguelike.
This game ISN'T really about life, legacy and love.
This game ISN'T really anything like Civilization or legend of zelda.
But what this game is, is a unique and interesting twist on tactical rpg-lite gaming.  It's more akin to a board game than anything else in my opinion.  But it can be very engaging and quite fun at times.  Especially for the price, it's not a bad way to while away a few hours.
I feel like this is a pretty solid game, though it could be better, and hope that heartshapedgames continues to improve upon it.

There is
pay-to-win aspect that usually comes from F2P MMOs - cash-shop items all have an equivalent which can be purchased with 'loyalty' points - points you get from earning achievements, grouping with friends or greeting players. It's a game I'd recommend to

The dungeons are fun, and can get very difficult. Make sure your first run is in normal or party mode. Do not pick Hell mode unles you know you're ready. Going in unprepared can lead to death and frustration.

But honestly, I don't see why people complain about a voluntary option to pay for better stuff. It's there as an option, not to force you to pay.

Aura Kingdom is a wolf in sheeps clothing,  don't let anybody fool you into believing AK isn't a pay to win MMo, because it really is.   Fans will say you can earn everything payers have in-game,  which is a lie -  I'd like to see non-paying players get highly fortified gear and the best costumes/mounts, after all - this is why most people play and this is where the wolf appears -
AK is a free to play game, yes you can 'earn' some stuff if you play it enough, but don't expect rare eidolons, don't expect orange costumes, shiny weapons or epic mounts without either paying some serious cash, we're talking hundreds of dollars for the teired spenders PER MONTH, and lets not talk about the gambling boxes which have an extremely low chance for nice items,  so new players joining AK will have an even tougher time with the heavily bloated economy, it was bad back at launch and now its just stupid with some items costing 20,000g+ and gold isn't that easy to acquire unless you....buy the teired spenders and sell them for gold....and this is what Aura Kingdom is mostly about here, don't let anyone tell you otherwise because they are either lying, or naive.
The problem is that with the P2W elements, or pay to 'show off' with the best looking gear/mounts - if you put all that aside, the actual game itself isn't bad, the anime styled graphics and characters look good, the combat flow is slick and there are some interesting storylines and locations,  the game has improved since Aeria was sold to ProSieben but the old dirty tricks and sheer excessive spender promotions is an abomination on MMo gaming.   Unfortunately, the real culprit is the developer X-Legend who are well known for creating these predatory anime styled MMos which lure many players in with ultra cute graphics and then fleece the customers for every penny they own.
The other problem Aura Kingdom has had since launch, and that is bots and gold farmers,  Its near impossible to go 5 minutes without recieving automated gold spam.  And certain areas are filled with bots, this has been going on since launch - and unfortunately is a major problem.
Overall.  Aura Kingdom is a fun game, nobody can really deny that.   But you  have to ask yourself, what do *you* want to get out of the experience,  playing with friends, raiding and creating cute or cool characters and don't care that'll you never get the best gear, the coolest looking pets or mounts then Aura Kingdom will keep you interested -  however, if your the type who is competitive, then be prepared to either be very disappointed, or open your wallet wide open.

This is one of the better more complex 4x games available to you, though it does have noteable differences from its competitors. To be fair I have not played much of Endless Space 2 so I cannot compare it to that game, as I only played what I could of ES2 on the free weekend it had available on steam.
I have to mention the space battles...
It does not have the same level of ship customization and battles as Sword of the Stars 2 but has some level of customization for its ships.  Ships can have AI behaviors that are complex where needed (EG launch fighters from afar while your main assault ships get in close) though.  The combat is based on a 2d map and not of the complexity I would have liked.  For reference the Combat in Sword of the Stars 2 is much more dynamic and interesting, but the rest of SoTS2 does not have Stellaris's complexity in its many other areas.   Endless space 2 has great looking ships, but pale in comparison to the complexity of the Sword of the Stars 2 heavily customizatble ships (and its very dynamic combat).
Now onto the rest of the Review...
Where Endless Space ships look pretty and SoTS2 dynamic custimizable ships, Stellaris has everything else in much greater detail.  Some of the glaring examples include.
-Migration between Empires that can help each empire colonize new planets for the migrating pops.
-Migrating Population can start their own political factions, like your start species population
-Federations can be formed and allowed building of ships across techs between federation empires
-You can set species rights and let them live on welfare or not at all (some of this was done in Sword of the stars 2)
-Diplomacy is has many options, like setting defensive pacts, non-agression treaties, Guarantee Independence, Vasselization,
The basic gameplay on the galaxy map is easy to navigate and commands to fleets to be set in a Que.  Planet surfaces are easy to manage and when needed the AI can run them for you inside a sector of systems.  The AI is intelligent and will make good diplomacy decsions so that they are protected.  Pacifist empires can survive in this game using defensive pack teatys and with federations.
War is also different in this game, as it reminds of moderm convention war.  In most games your goal with war is to eliminate your enemy,  Instead of always killing the population you can subdue it until the war is over.  In this one you end up turning the defeated empire into a vassel and slowly incorporate them into your empire.  Those pops in the defeated empire have their own factions and will then to be added to your current factions.
There is a lot to this game and with its mod support it has a long life ahead of it.

From what I understand this game was made by two guys at home with some help from a handful of other people. Being that it's from such a small crew I really hate to put up a negative review because it's not a bad game, but it's also not worth the $7 asking price. Considering during a sale you can get Sleeping Dogs for $5 or Just Cause 2 for $2.50, both AAA games that will each last you 50+ hours, this one for more money that is only 1-2 hours long is a tough sell. Even Portal is only a 2 hour game and goes on sale for 99 cents.
First, the graphics are good, everything is clear as to what it is, and controls are fine. The problem is it's a puzzle game with no real puzzles. The concept of the game is you can change between having red and blue polarities to pass through red and blue energy fields or lasers. There are red and blue cubes you grab to place in the corresponding colored ports, which usually activate a platform or a bounce button. But beyond that the mechanic doesn't really go anywhere. It's very straightfoward: when you come to a blue barrier you turn blue to pass through it. Red cubes can't pass through, so you have to find a way to get it around, but usually that just involves standing off to the side and throwing it around the barrier to the platform, then walking through yourself. Two rooms in the game involve rotating the room to get to new areas, but that's the extent of that, ONLY those two levels have that mechanic. I would have liked to have seen it used more and for more complicated puzzles.
Each level has 3 "data points" to collect, but most of the time they are sitting right out in the open or in the corner of a room with nothing stopping you from walking right up to it to grab it. There are only 11 levels in the game and then you win. You get 10 more bonus levels, but they're not any harder and still only take an average of 4 minutes to complete. There are about 10 or so more co-op levels but you either need a second person or another controller to do them.
I'd hate to say it comes off more as a tech demo than a full game, but the fact is most of the mechanics were not utilized to their full potential. It's a good start but the game just needs more meat and challenge to be a satisfying puzzle game. It's well made, just lacking content. Considering what 7 bucks can get you, it's better spent elsewhere. On sale for a buck or less then why not, it's still alright for those two hours.

I loved Chaos Theory like a brother, but this might be the worst game I've ever played.
It's not just the glitches and the crashes. Alpha Protocol was buggy (though not as buggy as this), but I still love that game. I can get past a few bugs, but this game was broken from its inception. It's muddled in terrible, dumbed-down, counter-intuitive design. It's an insult to the brilliant design in the previous three. The horrible PC port was just the icing on the cake.
The first three games were reasonably paced, and emphasized a reliance on light and sound. If you were going to complete your mission, you needed to be a master of the shadows. In Double Agent, they dial it back to the lowest common denominator, and just make you hide behind conveniently placed objects. They try to pretend that light still plays a factor with a little yellow light on the back of your suit, but even when the light says you're concealed, enemies can still spot you from miles away. Direct concealment, and exploitation of predictable patrol patterns, is your only option out in the field.
But it's out of the field where it really hits the fan. In the JBA headquarters, Sam is tasked with skulking around the base and completing tasks for both the NSA and JBA, but doing so requires mastery of one of the worst level layouts in history. If you remember that 3D map that you never used in Chaos Theory, just because it worked so poorly that the game was easier to navigate without it, you'd be happy to know that it makes a triumphant return in Double Agent. Prepare to squint like your life depended on it, as you try to make heads or tails of all the different branching paths that lead to dead ends, and plot a precise route to your objective, only to be sent back to the drawing board when you come across a secuity door, and need to plot a new route to whatever grand McGuffin will unlock it. None of this is even challenging at all, it's just unbelievably tedious.
And that's my biggest problem with this game. It's so lazy, so insecure in its ability to give you a single, satisfying experience, that it just piles on busywork and hopes that'll keep you satiated. I do not play Splinter Cell to navigate through a cartoonish series of security doors, I play it for a challenging, satisfying stealth game. Double Agent is the complete opposite of everything the original three games stood for, and as a result, has none of what made them fun or interesting.
It's a horrible game even if you forgive the bugs, but they're still well worth mentioning. The game crashes during every mission, mandatory safe-cracking minigames don't function in any capacity, the frame rate dips and the graphics glitch out even on systems well above the system requirements, one snow mission near the beginning will run for maybe five seconds before giving you a BSOD, and some events will flat-out fail to trigger.
The first three Splinter Cell games had none of these problems (with the exception of a buggy shadow engine in Pandora Tomorrow, and one scripting bug in that same game that made me restart a level), and Chaos Theory somehow even had better graphics. Double Agent has no excuse. It's just a terrible game on every level.
The only thing this game has that's even remotely interesting is its morality system, and it's bare-bones at best. It's not a moral dilemma if the numbers on your screen clearely dictate what's the right choice. You aren't making hard decisions, you're just balancing stat bars, and like all the other busywork in this game, that isn't any fun. I know I already mentioned this game, but Alpha Protocol had a far better idea of what espionage morality entailed, on top of just being better, more inspired, more fun, and more functional than this game on every count.
Even for the more hardcore Splinter Cell fans, I wouldn't recommend this game. It's just horrible.

After owning the first Splinter Cell for years but never finished it. I then bought the first 3 Splinter Cells on PC and finished all three of them a couple of years ago. Each one was fantastic though I felt that the shadows in Pandora Tomorrow were a little off but otherwise good. The game that stood out of the three however was Chaos Theory with hardly anything to critise about it. It had brilliant stealth mechanics, a great soundtrack, great level design, good story, supposedly good co-op (haven't played it) and of course the legendary spies vs mercs mode.
After three amazing titles, you would expect the 4th installment of the series to be able to live up to its predecessors right? Wrong!
This game makes me rage in so many ways! The game feels rushed and unfished, the first game had good stealth mechanics, it beats this in terms of stealth mechanics by far which means that this isn't just a step back, this is a few jumps backwards. There are rarely any proper shadows in this which means that the only way you can tell if you're invisible is by looking at the indicator either on your back or in the bottom left hand corner of your screen; if it is green you're invisible, if it's yellow, you are visible and are at risk of being detected and if you are red then you better run mofo because you're about to get your backside handed to you.
This sounds like an okay system and may have been more acceptable had the light metres in the previous games never existed, but the problem with it is that the shadows aren't dark enough most of the time like they were in the previous titles which makes running into the shadows game of chance as either it will hide you or it won't, it's not obvious when you're about to enter an invisible area and because of this, I was constantly being detected in absolutely rediculous ways which was not fun at all and because of this I was constantly autosaving way more than I would of needed to in the earlier splinter cells, I think on average I autosaved about 55 times per level.
The story however is actually good and I did enjoy it, what this game does offer that the previous titles did not were the ability to make choices in the game and making those choices would result in different outcomes which would give the game more replay value if the gameplay wasn't so bad.
But one of the biggest problems I have with the game is it's incredibly bad PC port, it is so sloppy despite it being the same version of the game as the xbox 360 and the PS3. Why is it so bad? it crashes constantly for no reason and I have quite a high spec 3 month old pc and this is 2014, the game is so badly optimised and it is absolutely outrageous that ubisoft haven't fixed it, I'd hate to think what would happen if I were to run this on my old computer with 10 year old hardware.
The menu system in the game is annoying and every time you want to hack into a computer or look under a door, you have to watch this stupid animation on your opsat which lasts 3 seconds, that might not sound that bad but when you have to watch it so regularly and it's the same animation over and over again it really gets frustrating.
I've also heard that Spies Vs Mercs was completely ruined in double agent which is just another reason not to like the game so just throwing that out there.
Oh, and every time you either want to hack a safe or the mine assembly (both of which are annoying events that you have to do), make sure that you are in running mode as the game was so badly ported from console that when you try and do this whilst in walking mode, your controls to crack the safe or assemble the mines will simply not work.
The only thing I can praise about the game are it's graphics and it's story oh and about that! I finished the last level last night and it loaded a cutscene in game, but the AI kept getting stuck on one of the textures which means that the cutscene was just stuck and my camera was stuck on the guy who was stuck and kept clipping through the catwalk so basically, I couldn't actually finish the game properly and so I had to look up the endings on youtube, absolutely redicolous given how old this game is now!
One other thing I forgot to mention is that for the JBA which is the organisation you're working for but are actually a double agent, you have to visit and carry out objectives within their safehouse 4 times! 4 times! That's just repetitive and it's confusing trying to get to know your way around it especially for the final level seeing as the map on your opsat is just plain awful.
So all in all, this game is worth playing I believe, but not on PC. Get Double Agent Version 1 on Xbox 360 or PS3 but not PC, it is just too buggy and it will annoy the hell out of you otherwise!
One final note, there are actually two versions of Double agent, version 1 is on Xbox 360, PS3 and PC and version 2 is on Xbox, PS2, gamecube and wii. Version two was done by Ubisoft Montreal and as a result, I've been told that version 2 is much much better than version 1 and it is a completely different game with a completely different level layout even though they share the same name, apparently it feels more like Chaos Theory so I can't wait to check that out at some point.
The bugs in this game make it unacceptable and it is a dissapointment given how great the last splinter cell was, only thing that holds it up are the graphics, the story, voice acting and I guess the level design.
All in all, this game gets a 4/10 for me on PC as even though the story was very good, the gameplay was littered with bugs, bad stealth mechanics and felt nothing like its predecessors.

In short, this is one of the buggiest, glitchies worst games I've ever played. Usually the splinter cell games are awesome, but not this one. The past games have all been great, and the games after this one were great aswell, but this one had truley awful gameplay. Other than the gameplay, it was a good game, but why play  a game with awful gameplay? the shaders are broken, making it impossible to know if you'll still be in the shadow when you're in a dark hallway with enemies, expect sound to randomly cut out too, making it impossible to know if you make alot of noise where you're walking, or if enemies are shooting at you. and the ending... oh wait, I never got to the ending because one of the characters glitched making the game impossible to beat, as in, he wouldn't walk up the stairs during a scripted event to trigger the credits, I had to look up how it ended to have context during conviction! I bought this in a steam sale with the other Splinter Cell games. After really enjoying Chaos Theory, I had very high hopes for Double Agent.
The first sign of trouble was the game did not support 1080p.  Chaos Theory from two years prior did, but Double Agent did not.  Instead, I was stuck with 720p.
Double Agent suffers from bugs and graphical issues throughout the game.  The lighting engine went from being very powerful and realistic to downright terrible.  The designers also removed fun features such as the sound meter and degrees of light.
Everything has been dumbed down in this game.  To make the UI more minimal, the light meter is now green for hidden, yellow for visible, and red for spotted.  Half the time you'll be standing in total darkness and have it still be yellow.
The PC port of Double Agent also crashes horribly.  Expect it to freeze up when loading requiring you to restart your computer.  Like previous Splinter Cell games, it lets you save wherever you are in the level.  Unlike previous Splinter Cell games though, there is no way of sorting your saved games.  So expect to have to dig through all your saves when you are trying to find the one you are looking for; there is no way to sort them.
Lastly, the gameplay is horrendous.  Half the missions take place during the day and are better played like a first person shooter than a stealth game.  Just shoot everything, don't bother with stealth.
I had high hopes for Double Agent and was sorely disappointed.  Don't buy this game!  Just read the synopsis and move on.

The steam contoller is a very handy piece of kit for sitting back on the sofa and play on the pc.

It takes time and practice to get used to using it. It's not perfect in every situation. But it's way way better than a traditional gamepad in my opinion.
The lack of native support in most games is annoying, but not as much as you might think. The customization options allow for an amazing amount of customization and will get you up and running fairly quickly in almost any game once you figure out how you like to have it setup. The community profiles are nice, but they're not perfect. Quite often top voted profile is just the first one that doesn't suck, not necessairly actually the best one, and for big games if you make an awesome profile it better be within like the first day of release or it'll never be seen amont the multitudes of random profiles (many of which are just re-uploading the defaults which is kind of annoying).
I've had mine since the early October 2015 release and I've been using it almost exclusively since I got it. The software and firmware updates that Valve have put out for it have improved it's usability A LOT since then and it's just been getting better and better.
The battery life is amazing. I played quite a bit and only just changed the batteries (about 1.5-2 months after I started using the controller). You can also get rechargable batteries and charge it with a micro USB cable or just use it plugged in if you don't feel like dealing with batteries.
I'd love to see more games start to natively support the controller. There are only a handful as of now (December 2015), and while it's not necessary for a game to support the controller for it to be great with the game, it would always be a welcome thing to have cleaner integration (with proper button prompts and stuff)
I instantly got the hang of it when I first picked it up. The amount of customization you could do with it is great.

Aura Kingdom is a wolf in sheeps clothing,  don't let anybody fool you into believing AK isn't a pay to win MMo, because it really is. AK is a free to play game, yes you can 'earn' some stuff if you play it enough, but don't expect rare eidolons, don't expect orange costumes, shiny weapons or epic mounts without either paying some serious cash, we're talking hundreds of dollars for the teired spenders PER MONTH, and lets not talk about the gambling boxes which have an extremely low chance for nice items,  so new players joining AK will have an even tougher time with the heavily bloated economy, it was bad back at launch and now its just stupid with some items costing 20,000g+ and gold isn't that easy to acquire unless you....buy the teired spenders and sell them for gold....and this is what Aura Kingdom is mostly about here, don't let anyone tell you otherwise because they are either lying, or naive.
The problem is that with the P2W elements, or pay to 'show off' with the best looking gear/mounts - if you put all that aside, the actual game itself isn't bad, the anime styled graphics and characters look good, the combat flow is slick and there are some interesting storylines and locations,  the game has improved since Aeria was sold to ProSieben but the old dirty tricks and sheer excessive spender promotions is an abomination on MMo gaming.   Unfortunately, the real culprit is the developer X-Legend who are well known for creating these predatory anime styled MMos which lure many players in with ultra cute graphics and then fleece the customers for every penny they own.

This is a fun little roguelike/lite that lives up to its name as "10-minute civilization". It's a fairly simple game but the difficulty ramps up fairly quickly and the different terrain generated on each playthrough can really vary how you approach things.
I did a quick-look video of the Beta of this game where I go through the different game mechanics and explain the basics if you'd like to learn more about it:

A fun, unique 4X. A lot of the poor reviews are from tech issues of old; just today fullscreen was added. The game is actively being developed even after release.
You start as a nobody Hero, building farms and strongholds, trying to impress a good mate or two. Soon you're exploring new biomes, slaying bosses for Honor, and uncovering secrets. The biomes feel distinct. You will genuinely care about your cute little heroes and their legacies. You will find the perfect mate and make demigods with them. You'll delve into the heart of a volcano and ride airships.
The game's fairly fast-paced. A generation could go by in five minutes, ten minutes if you're really going for something special. (30k honor) Even with a poor mate, it's hard to get a useless offspring. If you do get lackluster child, you can use that generation to build your towns up. You're always progressing because of this, there's always a way to improve yourself somehow.
The game offers a fair challenge: it took me about 5.5 hours to beat over three separate game files, and I didn't truly "beat" it. You will certainly need to employ strategy and forward-thinking.
Some weaknesses.
- Two items can be stressful to manage. You want to maintain your buildings with a hammer while also building your hero's legacy. At least because of this, the game has you making hard decisions between two traits and two item slots.
- Combat needs some kind of minimum damage formula. It is possible to have 120 strength and lose to someone with 20 strength if they roll a 20 and you roll a 19, as improbable as that is. While it thereby offers lucky shots to the player, you will only take lucky shots in the most dire of moments.
- Needs just a bit more polish. The screens will transition to a mostly-white combat screen, where the combat really should just pop up in a separate view.

I really love this game; it's a relatively simple/easy to learn 4X grand strategy game. The only "problem", which is understandable (and somewhat unique/cool) due to the scale and nature of the game, is that it takes so long to play through a single save. I've spent probably 25+ hours on a single save and I'm nearing the "end" but I still have at least 10-15 hours to go until I can achieve a victory.
There are huge stretches of time where nothing is happening since it takes so long to do certain tasks or you're waiting for an AI to act, however it's not in vain; The scale of the game as in the size of the galaxy and the flow of time are both massive. I can't keep track of my measly 1/6 chunk of the galaxy because there are so many systems, and I've been ruling this area for about 350 in-game years. It's all really amazing how well it works, but it takes SO LONG to do things. I'll play for 4 hours, then come back a week later and spend 30-45 minutes trying to situate myself because there's so much going on. I've had to resort to naming my planets "DROID PLANET PLZ TERRAFORM" or "SHIP AND ARMY PROD PLANET" because I can't keep track of 11 planets any better than I could 11 fully grown cities in Civ 5. I have resorted to writing a diary/log of what is happening in-game because the politics and power struggles are too complex to keep in my head for more than a few days.
This game is great, I love it. But I probably won't be able to play it more than once or twice due to this. If you are a NEET or have 5+ hours a day to urinate away, then I highly recommend this game. If you are a busy-body and gaming hours are precious, expect to only play through it once or twice.

Now that being said the game does have drawbacks. I own a rather highend computer but it's hard to maintain a stable 60fps framerate (which is capped by default). The graphics isn't stunning compared to other AAA games. And of course, keyboard controls were horrible, I would say if you're not familiar with playing with just the keyboard it would be a nightmare and it would really ruin your experience.
BUT, there are so many redeeming quality of NieR:Automata. As for the storyline and characters, it's up to you to play and give your thoughts on them. A rich story and those who has been fans of the NieR franchise (yes, this is a sequel to the PS3-exclusive game NieR), would feel even more excited to finish this game as it brings in so much meaning. And you don't have to play the first game, NieR:Automata doesn't have much ties to the first one, so you needn't worry about enjoying the story. Of course, it's still much better if you played the first one haha. Sountrack's amazing, tear enducing even, once you really get to understand the songs.
Combat's rather smooth, though there aren't any obvious tutorials on all combat mechanics, but once you got everything down, playing on Normal is a breeze, as a matter of fact I find it rather easy, especially with a controller.
So here are some recommendations for those picking this game up on PC.
1. Get a controller, playing with a keyboard would be gruesome.
2. Make sure you have a rather powerful computer as the game is a bit badly optimized. You can look up the FAR mod, and install it (it's free) to somewhat enhance your fps.
3. Try figuring out the combat mechanics or just go online look for videos explaining it, should make the game more enjoyable.
All in all, I love NieR:Automata, there's so much meaning to the story, so many things underlying that you can't see, you gotta play the game. Music and soundtrack is just perfect. The characters are just loveable.

is a re-release of a game of the same title previously available on Steam. Now in the hands of a different publisher, the game has been given a bit of modernization while still retaining its charm. This title is the third in a series of hidden object games centered around a woman named Princess Isabella, however this time you take the role of her daughter Bella. I’ve played the game before and played it again for this review, as well as played this release twice so I’ll do a little bit of comparing as I go along.
The story remains unchanged, Bella’s mother, Isabella, previously fought against an evil witch to protect the kingdom but was turned to stone when Bella was a baby. The witch has finally found the child, despite the protection of her fairy godmothers and now Bella must follow in the steps of her mother to save the kingdom. The story in the game is very basic- it wasn’t good before, and it’s still not very good. The characters all have uninspired names; Bella, Owl, Dragon, Fairy, and have personalities to match. Bella never says anything, not to other characters and even to herself so we have no idea what kind of a person she actually is. This updated version brings collector edition bonus not previously available on Steam, including a bonus chapter. You learn more about what happened to the people in the kingdom after the witch’s curse and tie things up a little bit but this still doesn’t add much of anything to the story.
This is a mouse-controlled hidden item game, you point and click on items and people to interact with them as well as to move around. You collect useful items to progress through the game while solving puzzles and playing hidden item scenes. The scenes are good and offer some fun and sometimes a challenge but none are too difficult at all. The mini games on the other hand have been insanely dumbed down from the previous release with some being omitted all together. The game has been made entirely too easy in my opinion. One of the omitted puzzles I didn’t like anyway, but the mini games have become boring. While some of the changes aren’t too bad, most might just make hidden object game veterans feel a little insulted.
I found that the audio wasn’t changed much, if at all, from the previous release. The music is all the same, the voice acting is all the same as well. This is a bit of a shame because the voice acting isn’t that great. It’s not bad but there could have been some better direction and actors. One note, a certain old man in the story has not the best sounding mic quality. It doesn’t say much so it’s not critical but I did notice this. The art was also unchanged except for making things look crisper. Certain items in the game were moved but it effects nothing. The artwork is nice, very magical and fitting but dated. The user interface had a huge graphical update, everything is smoother looker and more up to date with current hidden item game standards. The menu, your inventory, speech bubbles and such look pretty good.
In all honesty I didn’t like this title when it was released before, I found it to be the weakest in the trilogy so I was excited for this remake...however it’s not a remake at all, just a re-release. It does improve on some areas, like giving you a map, but if you’ve played the game before you don’t need this unless for the achievements and trading cards. If you’ve never played this title before, maybe grab it on sale. This game would be good for younger fans, especially with the level of difficulty being so low but more avid fans of this genre should probably find another title to play.

I got this Game for free from Dev. to review it for our Site "Die Gamer". Thanks Artifex Mundi for that.
I try to review this Game without telling too much about the game, also I review this game how I liked it, no matter if I got it free or had to pay for it. I may do a few mistakes, english is not my native language and for our site I always write reviews in german.
You play as Princess Isabella "called Bella", a young blonde princess, you have to save your mother, she was kidnaped from an evil witch, who can look beautiful and ugly in the same second. On your side is a Dragon, the three Elfes and an Owl who help you beat the witch.
On an extra Level, after finished the Base Game you need to do some work and help peoples who died and still live in the castle as ghosts.
Its a typical Hidden Object Game. (similar with Point and Click games). With a lot of different puzzels. You can always skip a puzzle if its to hard for you to solve it. Also there are hints when you dont know what to do next. Most puzzles are repetitive, like the one where you have to search obejcts. (mostly the same objects on this puzzels too) Also story lets the end with your father open, if you like to hear more about him, you need to finish the bonus game as well. All achivements are easy to get, there is no achivement for finishing the bonus mission.
You can choose how to play, you have 3 options like easy, normal, hard.
Well, its a bit hard to say because its not an AAA Titel or a game where you realy need a big graphic. You see mostly only moving Pictures not an 3D animation. Drawings are nice, but there are a few pictures who doesnt look good, at least not on full screen. They are to pixelated, what is realy sad because the game is good. There is no graphic setting but you can choose how load youz want the music and SFX and if you like to play on fullscreen or window mode.
Everyone playes different and need more or less time solving the puzzles, for me on the hardest gameplay, it took me ~4 hours with the base game and the extra missions. I didnt skipped the puzzles or used hints.  I have to say that I played a lot of Point and Click games before, they are much harder to beat then hidden object games, and this one was made realy easy compair to other games from AM.
:
If you like hidden object games or like games where you can relax, just buy it, you will enjoy it, even if its to easy for you. Some puzzles are realy nice and clever done, graphic is mostly okay and the story is good. Gameplay time was for me a bit short but I think 4-6 hours is not bad at all. If you don`t like to pay 7,99€ because its not enough gameplay time for you then waite for a 50% sale, I think its worth to play.
You can also buy it and try it max. 2 hours, if its not your game you can refunde it on steam.
I would give this Game for a Hidden Object Game a 7 from 10 points. If you care about graphic then a 6 of 10 points. I enjoyed the game and can recommend it to play but only if you like relax games and hidden object games.

is the last game in the titular series, and probably the weakest game in means of gameplay dynamic, puzzle choices and story elaboration to begin with. It was in the Steam Store for ages alongside other two games before Artifex Mundi got the rights from Gogii Games to remaster. The old original game - a cheesy, yet okay conclusion to otherwise beautiful series - is sadly not acquirable through the Steam Store anymore. This is the remaster arranged by Artifex Mundi, and even though that I'm a fan of the publisher, I'll go out on a limb and declare that they didn't even try to make a decent job here.
Spoiler Alert! Isabella's last battle with the witch didn't end happily. Yes, she managed to rescue Bella with the aid of her companions, yet her momentary distraction costed her everything. The witch turned her into a stone statue, Prince Adam completely lost his mind and the kingdom has fallen under the tyrannical rule of the witch... Yet, in a silent and peaceful corner of the realm, three fairy godmothers and the dragon raised little Bella to be a capable wizardess just like her mother, for her to return and complete the deed that her mother failed to do so. Upon finally discovering Bella's location, the witch sends her hounds after Bella, and her hurry to clean this mess begins... Will there be a happily ever after, after all?
Let's start with the display options. The old original - just like previous games - was weaved out of pastel colors, dusty environments and all pictures carried an elegant shimmer. With new rendering of the images, filter and tone choices for colors got bolder and shinier. As a personal choice, I found that a bit of an unnecessary contrast with the original setting, lessening the atmosphere. Quoting from a friend's comment: "Pictures look like Walt Disney threw up all over the place." Well, that is kinda appropriate of a definition here. I usually adore Artifex Mundi's color choices, yet playing prior games it felt unfitting for Isabella series' elegance and naivety. Resolutions compared to the old game are marvelously better though, I won't lie. Art works and HOG scenes are much clearer, and it got a lot much easier to go through item fetching.
Some great annoyance on my part was that some voice acting got changed - to a lesser quality, surprisingly - and others are completely missing. Some character introduction scenes and other cutscenes are cut out, leaving small holes in the original plotline. The setting was overwhelmed with the concept of catholic evil to begin with - cleansing the evil out of all places that we run through, wickedly laughing villain, Eye of Sauron-ish watching eye of the witch, a curse so sticky that it takes 3 games to clean thoroughly - and not very original about it. Cutting out content leaves it fatally wounded. Sure, we are lucky that this is a collector’s edition which offers some bonus gameplay and references to older games, but I'd appreciate if I'd be able to see mandrake's introduction scene or hear the voice of the whale that resides on the beach.
HOG scenes got a heck lot of easier with lesser items to find on cleaner picture renderings. They are mostly redone with the same items. Puzzles are altered too; some getting ridiculously easier, others unnecessarily complicated. Item interface has also been changed with your wand being in dangerous proximity to hint button; just be warned. I do not recall whether there was a map or not, but I certainly hadn't any need for it. The environment itself is somewhat limited anyhow with a backtracking being mandatory.
Overall, this is most certainly not one of Artifex Mundi's better games, neither the best game in Isabella series anyhow. I could recommend the game only if you've played previous games and curious about what will happen to Isabella in the end. Even then, I recommend finding and playing the original through Big Fish Games.
