i don't see what all the negative reviews are about. Okay, the instructions on the color wheel puzzle are completely useless, and it _does_ have a few "what the hell just happened?" moments, but other than that i'm finding it to be a decent HOPA, with mechanics i've not yet seen in a HOPA (e.g. the wand's abilities) and a nice atmosphere. The graphics quality is slightly sub-par for modern HOPAs (but better than the Time-whatever series), and the video cutscene quality is notably sub-par, but the voiceovers and music are well done. Some players complain about the generic names of the characters (Fairy, Owl, etc.), but i actually prefer such names over arbitrary made-up names which few players can remember. Challenging? Not particularly, but it's colorful, has relaxing music, and suitable for casual gamers. It's certainly short, though - not quite 3.5 hours for the main story plus unlockable add-on adventure.

I'm not going to say that I was kinda excited to see Artifex Mundi pick this one, because this is the worst title in the series of Princess Isabella. Indeed, it was previously on Steam and I've played the "old" version. Be aware that I would have given a neutral rating if I could. If anything, there are better titles in Artifex Mundi's catalogue, so if you can avoid this one if you're a non-English player, do it. I'm still doing a positive review but the line is thin. Also, as I've said, I've played the previous release in English, which is why I was more sure of the positive than the negative than for this release.
Years after Princess Isabella saved her daughter thanks to her fairy friend and the little dragon and became a statue because of the evil witch, the kingdom is waiting for someone to defeat that person. Bella, now in age and learning about her lineage, is ready to deliver her parents from their fate though her godmothers got kidnapped and jailed by the evil witch...
The plot is still the same from the previous games: you have to purge scenes of all evil or to reconstitute portraits to save people in it (here, you have mainly the godmothers). You have also a magic wand to break stuff and also acquiring powers thanks to the fairies once free. You can also use a music instrument to call the dragon to lift heavy items.
The gameplay is very classic though, with hidden objects scenes and puzzles, that are quite easy to play. While I loved the first part of the game, once I've reached the castle, I was kinda bored and once on the beach, it was worse. Everything is kinda easy, but the hidden object scenes tended to have objects partially hidden. What I find interesting was the little mandagore figures to help. It has precious objects and well, they're not too much annoying, because they weren't invading the game.
The graphics are quite good, I loved the little mandragores though I hated the spider, too big for my taste. The voice actings for the dragon, the fairy or the witch are correct but the godmothers... Not only they looked like the same but I can't say I was charmed by their voice. However, I have a little complaint for the graphics: they were kinda looking like grainy. I wonder if it's because Artifex Mundi adapted it for widescreens (as it's a possibility that the previous release was still in 4/3 ratio) or if it's because the new HUD, which was way more colorful, is making this being more highlighted.
I appreciated the soundtrack too.
However, there is a major problem for anyone playing in another language than English: the poor translation. It's unusual from Artifex Mundi to release a game with so many bad translations that it's becoming not understanble or playable (it was horrible in the hidden objects scenes). I think that the people that redid a little the game used Google Translate. Bad idea. Very bad idea. In the end, some parts of the story didn't make sense as the sentences weren't rightly build and I know that pipe can be translated as tuyau in French, but a smoking pipe is also called a pipe in French. Without forgetting that pinecone (pomme de pin in French) got translated in céramique (a vase/pot). It's not worse than in Demon Hunters but at least, there, it was mainly the hidden objects scenes that were affected, not the story.
I've thumbed up the game in English, despite being mixed about it. I've enjoyed some parts and it stayed true with this re-release. I admit that the fact that it's a collector's edition is helping. Next time, Artifex, make sure that you checked the translations. Usually, you're managing well with them. I was hoping to have my mind changed about this game and I'm still at the same point: should I thumb it down because of my own playthrough, knowing that the English is correct, because of my previous experience or should I thumb it up, because, despite this, the game is still enjoyable?
I'm barely putting a thumb up. If you're playing in English, you should be fine. For other languages, I can't say. For French players, I've made a little guide with the right translations. It should be easier for you to play with that.

This game is absolutely amazing - it was the best game of its time and arguably still is today. It's not just a "wannabee GTA clone"; missions in GTA are entirely scripted right down to an enemy's hand movements while Saints Row 2 runs from NPC systems meaning you never get the same outcome twice in these missions. People are always complaining about glitches and bugs but personally I haven't experienced any. The story is incredibly interesting and it's very easy to get sucked in to the game, only to look at the clock and see you've lost 12 hours of your life. Here's the story's comparison to GTA V, a game people are calling much better.
Saints Row 2's story: "After waking up from a coma after a horrific boating accident, you open your eyes to a city that's been taken over by street gangs. Your gang, the Saints, has disbanded when the other crews outnumbered them, leading to them all being arrested by police or killed. You're on a mission to rebuild your gang from the ground-up, wipe your enemies off the street and rule over the city of Stilwater once again."
GTA V's story: "A car repo man runs in to a psychopath and retired 40-something year old. They all want to make money. They rob banks. That's it. Now fork up $60 to play our game."
Notice a difference here?
If you want GTA but your PC can't handle it, or if you don't think that GTA has enough bloodshed, explosions and the perfect balance of humour and death, then Saints Row is for you.
9/10.

Stellaris is an Epic Space 4X style Strategy game that ultimately
of for example, "Sins of a Solar Empire." It also lacks (slightly) in the GUI as it relates to managing what little combat you can control as well.
So, if you were looking for a game that was "The next great Sins of a Solar Empire Game", then THIS IS NOT THAT GAME.
So, what is it? Well, its a lot like playing "Sins" MINUS the combat but WITH bonus political and strategic aspects.
If you were to take a very logical approach to "Government" and categorize the different forms of government and then put in place computer based rules for how the different forms of government work and relate that to a strategy game of taking over planets, research, building, appointing leaders etc... apply that to a variety of ALIEN creatures of various phenotypes and core beliefs, and how those core beliefs and "Mandates" are actualized vis a vis governing control
then THIS is that game.
So, in one sense its a wonderful game that provides a really interesting facet of strategy to "space exploration" in a unique way that Sins of a Solar Empire never had. Unfortunately, with a particularly boring and bad combat system.
Combat is essentially "automatic" with no obvious way to micro-control any actions once you press the "attack" button.
Planets are very limited in their capacity for orbiting space stations. And the number of options for combat are well, sadly lacking.
One example of disatisfaction would be that you can buy a "pre-built" corvette style ship early in the game with "Red Lasers" and then later you can research "Blue Lasers" but the ship design system does not allow you to really add "Red Lasers to your ship" it only allows you to Remove existing and then put Blue ones.
But ultimately, none of that really matters because you can't control the combat anyway.  So, there is NO strategy to positioning your forces other than the most basic things such as when you decide to initiate it.
Because of the lack of combat control, the game feels much more like a game of "find habitable worlds" and wait a long time for your population to grow... wait some more while you research, wait... wait some more.
See some combat and then win or lose once combat is initiated.
Yes you can "buy" and build ships but, other than sending ships to a planet,  you cannot finely control combat once it has started.
I would NOT recommend this game if you are looking for a space combat strategy 4X style game ala Sins of a Solar Empire.
I would recommend this game to people who want a 4X style game where they don't have to get involved with "how" combat happens, and want to enjoy a slow methodological economy based strategy game that "has a very limited" system of combat.

Best 4X game I've played. Not as inscrutable as EU4, diplomacy and narrative depth that blows Civ out of the water, and better real time and space sim execution than SoaSE. This game has you constantly making interesting decisions that are all heavily flavored by what type of government, species, ethics, inner factions, and outer geopolitical landscape you're dealing with. It also has FANTASTIC dev support that has me trusting, for once, that the game is only going to get better and better. It's already lightyears (pun intended) ahead of where it was when I first picked it up.
Examples: in my first game, way back closer to 1.0, I played a science-driven, materialist race that I hand-crafted to be basically all about discovery and research. I got into an alliance with a federation of civs (including earth) halfway across the galaxy, uplifted some primitives to be spacefaring, crushed a couple militant spiritualist empires who branded my people as heretics, and slowly brought one of their alien planets around to my atheistic way of life, making them happier in the process. That was about 18 months ago, on a save that is long gone now (updates eventually broke it), but I still remember all of those details and more.
That's what this game really is: memorable. It takes a nicely done galactic 4X sim, but layers on top of it enough interesting art, iconic events, and choices unique to your exact combination of civ/ethics/neighbors/goals that it does something most 4X games fail to do for me. This game doesn't just hit the normal 4X marks well, it leaves you with STORIES to tell afterwards.
All I want to do is shape and record the history of the people I'm in charge of, from the moment they leave their planet for the first time to the moment they realize their species' wildest dreams of technological ascendency, spiritual purification, economic prosperity, brutal conquest, or whatever else the dream of their civilization might be. It's the rare 4Xer where victory conditions are the last thing on my mind, and that feels great.

This game is, in my opinion, the best game of 2017 and my personal favorite game of all time. It's amazing in so many aspects.
Combat is fluid, fun, and has little quirks that arent made readily known to the player that takes some toying around with to fully grasp, and 2B just feels perfect to control. Her movements in and out of combat feel like they were perfected, and for me it's fun just to run around the map. With the upgrades system, you can really customize the way you play. Like when im playing as the final character you unlock, I love playing super high risk, high reward by adding character upgrades that make it so when you taunt, you can do 3 or 4 times as much dfamage while an enemy is enraged, but they'll do the same. Add this on top of the character's berserk mode that ups damage recieved and taken already, and it's a fun game of being able to kill even the toughest enemies lighting fast, but also having to have your wits really about you. (On a side note, it's also one of the only games with an upgrade system that makes actual sense within the logic of the story). The music is easily one of the best OSTs for any peice of media ever, The world and characters are beautiful looking, and the story has one of the few narratives in gaming that actually takes advantage of the fact that it's interactive entertainment in genuinely emotionally impactful ways.
And yet, while it is my favorite game, I have to confess there are a few things about it that annoy me.
Starting off, this PC port is not amazing. I had to go get a fan mod to get it to run above 30 fps despite the fact that my computer mostly surpasses the recommended system requirments, and even then I swear it does nopt run as smooth as my copy on the PS4. Not the PS4 pro, the regular PS4. So there's that.
There's also the nitpick with the overall game that I have that once you get max level, going back through 2B's story is just way too easy since the enemies do not scale in level with you. Which would be fine, if new game plus at least scaled enemies to your level.
Which it does not. That makes going through the first two campaigns again just way too easy since by that time you'll be more likely than not just one or two shotting every enemy that gets in your way, and they'll be doing basically no damage to you at all, even if you somehow were to completely forget about the generous dodging you can do.
So aside from a bit of a lackluster port (which I guess square enix has totally forgetten about at this point despite the fact that this game tops steams sales charts every time it goes on sale), and a bit of annoyance with the leveling system, i'd wholly recommend this game. It's an unforgettable experience. Unfortunatley in it's current state and with it being clear that square enix has basically forgetten about this port, I can't recommend this at full price, despite how much I want this game to succeed evenm more than it already has for yoko taro and platinum games.
I can, however, reccomend this game when it goes on sale for $40 or less, especially if you're willing to take 5 minutes to install the fan mod that greatly improves performance.

Stunning, amazing game. Best RPG I've played (and I've played many), bar none. Others have nostalgia and/or immense freedom on their side and some are memorable. But here, the story, soundtrack, and the way they connect to the gameplay are instantly memorable in ways I've not seen happen previously in an RPG.
Three small tips (spoiler-free)
* The prologue is a bit cruel while you're finding your way; recommend putting it in easy mode if you don't immediately grasp the mechanics (it's the bosses, not the small fry). Once you get through the prologue you can start building up your equipment and it's possible you may not die at all on normal. If you need more of a challenge, you can raise the difficulty. The game itself is pretty fair, and the only reward of higher challenge is the feeling of accomplishment.
* Don't stop playing at the first ending. That's the biggest mistake you can make with this game. The second time through you play from a slightly different perspective and with more tricks; you can speed through it quickly. The third time is effectively a second story/sequel; it colors the story in new, touching ways and properly ends the game. You may hear the game has five endings--the last three come from the third playthrough and you'll understand why/how.
* If you want some extra entertainment, look for places to not do what the story wants you to do and you may find a joke ending.

In Hero Generations, each step you take is an entire year of your hero's life. You explore a procedurally generated world in search of fame and a mate to have a child with before you die. After your life ends, you take control of your child in the world you left behind, in the hope of continuing your family legacy. Before you read the review please note the amount of time listed, so the review is most likely going to be a little biased but I couldn't play the game any longer because it was so bad and boring you'd have to pay me to carry on playing this, all I'm doing is warning you about wasting money on this game when the first one was so much better.
Here's an overview of the good things about this game:
-The graphics are OK. Nothing really special here but not too bad either, unless you're talking about the large dinosaurs that manage to clip through the buildings and kill you
-The sound is quite good, one of the few good things about this game, especially the T-Rex roar, reminded me of the original Jurassic Park
-Quite a few maps and servers, though most of the servers seem to be full of people roleplaying and having dinosaur sex? If you don't believe me look it up for yourself, it's weird.
-Some new maps, though nothing enough to make you buy this over the first
-Interesting concepts being used, though probably a bit too advanced for whoever had the misforutune of making this game
Bad things:
-The raptor spam is unbelievable, they have a stupid ability to pounce on you and pin you to the ground, the only way to get out of this is if someone helps you by shooting it. The result of this is most people camping in one spot because heading out on your own into the forest or anywhere else to experience the game like it was meant to be played results in you being pinned to the ground and killed, you can't even mash a button on the keyboard to get out and have a chance. The same applies to the pterodactyl which can carry you into the air, though it's not as overpowered as the raptor spam as it's easier for players to spot and shoot it's wings. However you should be able to get out of it's grasp by mashing a key on the keyboard which gets progressively easier the higher it gets.
-The maps are buggy, large dinosaurs have somehow developed phasing technology to eat you from the outside of buildings, this hasn't happened often but it has happened before.
-The trappers ability to fire a net at the dinosaurs can be unbelievably annoying and buggy, for instance I fired a net at a bloody pouncing raptor (Yes, I know) which should have incapacitated it on the floor, instead it didn't stop and still managed to claw me to death, even though it was wrapped tightly in a net. You might say it's momentum made it carry on, sure, but that doesn't mean it can still claw me to death if normally it makes it stop on the floor for about 10 seconds.
-Nothing groundbreaking was added that wasn't in the previous one
-I already mentioned roleplaying, as many other reviews here have, what idiot thought it would be a good idea for T-Rex's and pterodactyls to have children together? If you try to join a normal server you might have dificullity doing that too as I did on several occassions, and then you realise that over half the servers on here consist of roleplay ones.
-Community is really not that great compared to the first game
-Human classes are quite genereic
-Dinosaurs due to being extremely unbalanced will generally win every game or at least all the games I played.
-Maps overall tend to favour the dinosaurs, though this issue isn't as bad as the rest
-Skins can be extremely overpriced, who cares if you bought one for $300? I don't, just played the damned game.
-Economy? lol
-Hoard mode is really repetitive.
Overall as you've probably read maybe it's just because I don't have as much time on the game as some of the pros we see on the server, ranting about how good it is. Then again, judging by the other reviews it really is just a bad game that really doesn't live up the expectations of the first one.
TL;DR - The game is buggy and broken, most servers consist of weird dinosaur roleplay with a bunch of 12 year olds and the community is rubbish. Play the original if you want a good dinosaur game, do not waste money on this garbage.

I'll start by saying I have not 100% played through this game. I played through one storyline route, the Finley route, and hooooo boy.....that was a mistake. Her storyline is pretty preachy at a little over the halfway point, and it's really on the nose with what it's about, and there's some stuff that just made me wince in the writing. I wont spoil it, but, you'll know exactly what i'm talking about.
I actually pushed for the Finley storyline at first. When I learned that you could select your gender pronouns at the beginning, I was hopeful that one of the love interests might be trans. I'm a trans woman myself, so it would have been a nice little relatable thing to see in game, and yes...I suspected that Finley was trans at the beginning, which is why I steered things down that path. However, nope, it turns out Finley is a soapbox to push some devs views, and it really shows. I wont dance around it. this partanes to SJW/anti-SJW situations. I don't care what your views are on that stuff, I find myself in the middle a lot of the time, but jesus hustle cat, your strawmanning was hardcore, and that's what bothered me. It was a poorly writen scene overall, and felt like it was only there to make a statement and empower Finley, who didn't really need it anyway.
Now that the cat's out of the bag *eyebrow bounces* Let me get to the pros that make this shine!
-The writing! When it's not preaching to you is great! I laughed a few times, I smiled many more, and I liked all of the characters for the most part
-The art! The cats are all adorable, except that grump Mochi, and I never once felt disatisfied with the pace of art transitions like some games I could mention *Cough* Sakura Spirit *Cough*
-The Choices! Holy moley thank you hustle cat for having choices. I like visual novels, but when there's literally only one or two choices *Cough* Sakura *Cough cough* Freaken....*Cough* Spirit *Cough* it takes me out of it because I may as well be reading a book.
-The Length! Given that you're expected to play through multiple times for the different paths, I think this is a nice length. However, the ending does feel kind of abrupt, and this setting begs for a sequel.
It is a visual novel so there's not any gameplay to critique so I think that about sums it up! Though, I was not able to get the steam overlay to function with it. That may need to be looked at, or it could be a bug on my end.
All in all, I recommend it. It has about as much cheese as one expects from a visual novel, and save for my gripe about it feeling soapboxy at a couple points, I felt it was a really solid visual novel and I will be playing again, this time going after either Mason or Hayes. Cheers.

Hows this for a strange playthrough experience?
I bought the game expecting nothing out of a cheap 2D platformer, but it had Trading Cards and Achievements so I thought why not? I started the game up and played through the first few screens until I got stuck at the first puzzle because I'm an idiot and I closed the game. I didn't touch it for a week and a half.
Soon I was sitting in my chair hovering my mouse cursor over the 'Refund' button before deciding to launch the game a final time. If I couldn't figure out how to get past the puzzle in 10 minutes, I would get a refund and buy a trading card or something with the $0.49 I spent on the game. I ended up figuring out how to get through the level and I kept playing until the very end of the game. I then regretted not buying the game at full-price after I finished it, when just an hour ago I was about to refund it.
It's not a very long game, but I think that's intentional. It's a game that deserves to be disected and studied. I've beaten the game six times in five hours, with one of my playthroughs being as short as 17 minutes and 42 seconds. I still keep going back and beating it again and again.
This little indie game has me bewildered. It's addictively fun and perfectly difficult. It's the type of difficulty that doesn't take it easy on you but doesn't discourage you from retrying and you end up hooked. It's just short enough to not get boring too quick and just long enough to stay fresh throughout multiple playthroughs. The puzzles are ridiculously fun to solve while the 8bit score is blasting through your speakers. The game is packed full of secret areas and hidden collectibles that are easy to find if you know the game's tricks. Every single screen you come across has some sort of hidden entrance to a secret zone. The mechanics are inventive, fresh, and tight. The slow-moving projectiles of the portal gun give you time to think where you're going next and pull of some pretty incredible mid-air stunts if you're good enough. The control layout is of a standard arcade cabinent (I played with a controller however). Simplisity is key with this game, and that's not a bad thing.
8.4/10 - tl;dr : The game will surprise you. It's packed with secrets and has a great soundtrack. The gameplay is addictively fun and inventive, with that Mario Brothers / Dark Souls type of difficulty that keeps you hooked. Short, but fun to replay over and over again if you're an achievement hunter.
NOTE: I got a free Steam Key for another game called "Polarity" when I opened the game the first time. That right there in itself is worth 49 cents in my humble opinion. That, and the free soundtrack folder that comes with the games files.

Time of review: in 2 hours even, last room before the final boss; putting aside b/c bored and ♥♥♥♥ that last puzzle.
TL;DR: twitch based puzzle plafomer, think VVVVVV with fancier graphics, no exploration aspect, and different mechanics.
1st off: unlike what the tags currently say; this is not in any way a metroidvania, metroidvanias are distinguished by a big focus on exploration, ferreting out secrets, etc. You don't do that in OTS, the game is very linear, backtracking is impossible, etc. Its similar to a metroidvania in the sense that there is just 1 big map... but thats about it.
What the game actually is at heart is a fairly difficult puzzle platformer, with a big focus on the platforming, you WILL need some good twitch skills to get thru some of the mid/late game rooms. Think VVVVVV except instead of swapping gravity you jump, shoot, & teleport, and you'll have a good idea.
Oh, and also there are space shooter sequences right at the beginning & end.
If you want a cheap, short, challenging game to kill a weekend afternoon, this is a good buy. Just be aware its only around 2 hours or so for a playthru, the platforming is very twitch, and it aint got any exploration.

"Hero Generations" has the potential to get repetitive as the general gameplay flows a little something like: start new generation, move around the map accomplishing various tasks (aging in the process), head back to town to mate, start new generation, and rinse and repeat.  I do like the fact that some of your traits carry over from previous generations and that your mate does influence the type you can potentially have, though there is a random luck of the draw factor involved as you'll be choosing from multiple face-down (sometimes face-up) cards that determine the stats of your new character.  The concept reminds me a smidge of "Rogue Legacy", though the gameplay is obviously different (platformer vs 4x).  As repetitive as it is, I still find myself enjoying it.  Every move you make takes a year off your life, so there's a lot of time management involved and hard decisions to be made with every generation.  Love the idea personally, though I'm not crazy about the luck factor involved with combat (both characters roll a die, the range values determined by their maximum strength).  All in all, I had a good experience with this one...though you may want to watch a few let's plays to see if it suits your fancy since it is rather different than most games on the market.

Minecraft: Story Mode is a story about you, the protagonist, and your group of friends competing to win the EnderCon. Eventually, you find yourself to be of more importance than you think you'd be in a game taking place in a Minecraft world. You, playing as the male or female protagonist Jesse, go on an epic adventure to places people wouldn't dare to go to. Experiencing both hardships and tender moments, you are left to make the tough decisions for your group and ultimately decide how the story will go. Despite the circumstances however, your group still finds a way to crack crude jokes and stay optimistic. Will you put the health of others before your own, or will you take everything for yourself? The choice is yours.

The galactic rim system of Hunturr had reported strange radiation readings for some time that its mineral extraction facilities were not equipped to properly study. The closest science ship, the Exeron was dispatched to investigate. The Exeron discovered the source of the radiation to be a rift, or tear into our reality from another dimension or universe whose fundamental laws were dissimilar to ours. Because of these differences attempts at probing the other dimension was without gain and a great research project would need to be undertaken to overcome this hurdle.
Just as this grand research project had just begun, the rift shuddered and expanded and what emerged from the maelstrom was an alien fleet of over 100 vessels, many comparable in size to our battleships. Clearly the alien menace had studied our reality and adapted itself for our existence. This fleet hailed the Exeron and declared that they were the new rulers of this galaxy and all sentient life should submit or face oblivion.
It had been 200 cycles since the last need for violence, but the synthetic bodies and immortal souls of the Post-Bebekian Veritas race still remembered well the lessons of war. The PBV remembered when the bombs fell on the homeworld of the Ikitha, the genocidal spiritualists who were shown the error of their ways when they claimed that machine life was a “perversion” and that the only true path to perfection was the flesh.
The PBV remembered when the decadent fallen great empire of the Hozuul arose from its eons of slumber to proclaim themselves rightful rulers of the younger races. All other younger races quickly fell to thralldom at the knees of the Hozuul, all but the PBV whom had only recently ascended into machine perfection. The Hozuul were flesh and weak, their bodies needed sleep, found some worlds too hot, some too cold, and grew old and died. None of these ailments of the flesh afflicted the PBV and their minds now residing in machine consciousness was the ultimate pairing of biologically evolved creativity and machine precision. The Hozuul empire coughed its last breath as the great PBV war-machine unleashed AI controlled xenomorphic horrors upon the worlds of the Hozuul in a display of carnage to serve as a lesson to all others.
And now the PBV war-machine reawakened, pulled its long sleeping dreadnoughts from mothball and assembled its forces. The great admiral Rechnko resumed her command, Rechnko the destroyer of the Great Stellar Abomination, the annihilator of the Infinity Sphere and crusher of countless lesser enemy fleets. All told this new great war fleet totaled over 180 battleships and their smaller attendants. The main ship of the line was the battleship design “Arbalest”. It is 5km long, built around a single giga cannon whose only function is to accelerate a tungsten projectile to a significant fraction of the speed of light. 160 examples of this battleship were present at the outset and they scored the majority of the kills against the Thott.
The PBV war fleet transited to the now devoid of life Huntuur system which was occupied by over 300 Thott ships. The engagement between the two fleets was swift and violent. The Thott ships utilized directed energy weapons that shredded the fabric of reality of the ships they passed through, causing terrible damage. In return, the PBV gave harsh lessons in how our reality functioned.
The enemy fleet was utterly annihilated and the Huntuur system purged, but the rift still remained, occasionally spilling enemy fleets through and threatening to overrun the guarding PBV fleet. Reverse engineering Thott weapons salvaged from the PBV fleet led to a breakthrough in the creation of dimensions with arbitrary constant values. From this research a great weapon was devised that would be unleashed into the reality that the Thott resided in.
For years this weapon, the Omega Device, was worked on in secret as our industry produced battleships at a pace barely able to keep up with losses caused by the Thott incursions.
When the Omega Device was completed it was brought to Huntuur and launched into the rift between our realities. From the Omega Device sprang a new and unstable reality, a reality wholly incompatible with that of the Thott's. This reality, forcibly expanded by the Omega Device's immense power, eventually reached equilibrium with the old reality before ultimately collapsing back on itself and releasing energies at levels not seen since the big-bang.
And so died the Thott Empire.

Hustle Cat doesn't really have what you'd call a proper
exactly, though you could say the same about several other members of the Visual Novel genre, and I can name several that still don't give you as many options and interaction as Hustle Cat does, even if the ones it gives are a little bit light. It's definitely not for you if you're not a fan of text-heavy games, but you'll be right at home if you're into that stuff, or if you're looking to start!
With that in mind, Hustle Cat happens to have a WONDERFUL set of characters, a pretty engaging plot, and overall just really, really nice writing! The way characters are written and their dialogue is laid out is done in a way that you really don't see very often in several games, and though I absolutely liked some more than others, there truly weren't any characters I disliked at all.
Avery, the protagonist, is an easy example of splendid  characterization, and their interactions with the cafe's staff are really fun to read and enjoyable to go through.
I will say there were a couple of routes were things were handled a little bit strangely, and some certainly feel like they received less attention than others, although that tends to be mostly in the pictures department rather than in writing. General favoritism is there, but this isn't to say that the ones that were noticeably better liked by Date Nighto weren't amazing to play through!
It's easy to catch wind of how to go through each route, and though runs past your first might be a little bit uneventful on your way to taking on another one, the fact you can speed up doesn't really let that drag for too long.
Moving on to the music, I can say it was...all right!
Nothing really stood out to me, and most of the songs began as generic before shifting to repetitive, but I wouldn't say they ever got grating or annoying to listen to, and some were very much perfect for the mood, at times.
...Big emphasis on "at times", though, as there were tons of moments through the game where I felt as though a change in song or maybe a bit of silence would've been much better suited (almost expected) for what the text was carrying the mood through. It definitely took away from some scenes, for me.
Next, we have the art! And boy, Hustle Cat is PRETTY!
The character expressions might be a little awkward rarely, but I usually found them to be really nice and fun to look at! The mugshot models themselves are really nicely shaded, with thick lines and great color choices that keep everything vibrant, cute, and just really...alive! Each character gets a very nice and decent selection of expressions as well, which keeps the text accompanying them always engaging!
If there's anything to complain about, it'd be that certain of the special event pictures tend to have awkward faces or anatomy at times, and then you have some others that just don't have shading at all, which I found really strange. These aren't so many that it'd damage the overall quality, though.
The interface is kind of generic for what you'd expect of a visual novel, and can be a little plain here and there, but it's definitely not unfitting or clashing with the style. It's cute, simple, and not pretentious or intrusive, so I can't complain at all.
One thing I absolutely wanna praise is the game's auto save feature! While it's not good advertising to say that the game crashed on me twice, it did happen at times when I was speeding through the dialogue, and my laptop happened to also be running several other things at the time.
But, thanks to the auto saving, I really didn't need to worry, since I could just hop back onto where I was just playing last time!
Hustle Cat is adorable, and whether you're a cat person or a visual novel fan, you'll definitely like it! The cast is full of life and splendidly written dialogue, and even if the story might get a bit awkward at times, it always keeps engaging and fun to go through.
The music is a little repetitive and uninspired, and tends to clash with the mood or go on for too long sometimes, but it was never grating or annoying to listen to, at least in my opinion.
The art is gorgeous, with a few hiccups in some special scenes, but never losing charm or failing to bring life to the scene it comes along with. While the game might rely on the still character mugshots a lot, it still has a much more abundant selection of special art than most visual novels out there!
It's a pretty great game that could've been a lot better, but I can assure you it won't disappoint!

Now that being said the game does have drawbacks. I own a rather highend computer but it's hard to maintain a stable 60fps framerate (which is capped by default). The graphics isn't stunning compared to other AAA games. And of course, keyboard controls were horrible, I would say if you're not familiar with playing with just the keyboard it would be a nightmare and it would really ruin your experience.
BUT, there are so many redeeming quality of NieR:Automata. As for the storyline and characters, it's up to you to play and give your thoughts on them. A rich story and those who has been fans of the NieR franchise (yes, this is a sequel to the PS3-exclusive game NieR), would feel even more excited to finish this game as it brings in so much meaning. And you don't have to play the first game, NieR:Automata doesn't have much ties to the first one, so you needn't worry about enjoying the story. Of course, it's still much better if you played the first one haha. Sountrack's amazing, tear enducing even, once you really get to understand the songs.
Combat's rather smooth, though there aren't any obvious tutorials on all combat mechanics, but once you got everything down, playing on Normal is a breeze, as a matter of fact I find it rather easy, especially with a controller.
So here are some recommendations for those picking this game up on PC.

Refer to the more elaborate "most helpful" negative reviews to get a proper grasp on why this game fails to live up to its predecessors. The most common sentiment you'll run into with veterans of the series (of which I am one) is that something feels immediately *off*, that's sort of the tl;dr. Something is off, and it's far from immersive.
The main takeaway for me is that this game feels way too arcadey, especially when you take into account the realistic, dark, and gristly prescedent set by its ww2 counterpart, RS. Maps that feel small and one dimensional, artifical sounding "sound cues" built around gameplay rather than an emphasis on atmosphere, floaty weapons with unrealistic accuracy (have the devs ever shot an ak?), super bright colors, a never-ending supply of instant-spawning helicopters, multiple objectives (team deathmatch anyone?) etc. It just plays and feels like a hybrid of call of duty black ops 1 and rising storm, which isn't what I want in my red orchestra experience.
I think the most egregious example of the dev team venturing into an arcadey direction has to be the degree to which run-and-gun gameplay seems to be encouraged in a combat setting that mostly involved clumps of combatants duking it out in jungle foliage. Here, the jungle on any given map is sparsely populated, and they tend to function merely as glorified walkways to whatever the objective point is. What you get as a result of this are headless chickens running up from spawn points, and sprinting around whatever the building objective points are and gunning people down in the site. Very seldom do you see any sort of teamplay or coordinated pushes a la RS, and when this does go on it's certainly not through the jungle. There appear to be multiple capturable objectives on literally every map also, which exacerbates this team-deathmatch mentality tenfold.
It's not totally terrible, and I am happy to have given tripwire my money, but this new direction is a pretty massive deviation from previous iterations of the series. I suspect they've gone down this route to woo over some of the more casual FPS playerbase, but all they've ended up doing is creating a mediocre RS with graphics that are no longer up-to-snuff given the gameplay downgrade.
Overall, this is not at all a realistic representation of vietnam-era combat, and I really wish it had been. We know Tripwire has the capacity to simulate actual warfare while still keeping it enjoyable, and RO2 was the embodiment of this synthesis...but we're now much, much closer to COD than we are Ostfront/RO1.
PS: Do us all a favor and remove the helicopters entirely. The audio in any given game is just 100% helicopters (when it's not high pitched pinging) and it's unbearable.

This game can be summed up in two words: wasted opportunities.
First off, the game looks amazing. The graphics are rather simplistic cyberpunk, but they do exactly what they need to. The soundtrack fits the theme of the game perfectly.
The main mechanic of the game, switching between red and blue, is criminally underused. There are only 2 objects in the game that care about your polarity; lasers (which will kill you if you don't match the polarity) and gates (which are solid walls if you don't match their polarity and passthrough if they do match). I can only think of 2 levels where polarity is more complicated than leaving it on the right one, and one of those is the tutorial. Too many puzzles are simply about putting cubes in the right holes. Go look up an indie game by the name of "death squared", and you'll see so much more that can be done with simply being red vs. blue.
The main goal of the game, collecting data fragments, is more of a chore. I think there are 3 in the entire game that are hidden cleverly, or are rewarding to collect.
Most criminally, however, is its length. If you look near my name, you’ll see that I've played the game for less than an hour. Well, I'm already done with the main game. There are only 12 levels, and since every 2 levels introduce some new mechanic, the game never fully utilizes its own mechanics.
If they made more levels, more polarity affected components, or a level editor, (preferably all 3), this game would rival portal as a sci-fi immersive puzzle game. As it is, though, it's nothing more than an attempt to ride portal's fame, without adding anything meaningful.

I was not familiar with clicker games until I played AdVenture Capitalist. I'm told it's unusually for not actually requiring repetitive clicking as you can hire managers to 'click' for you. The heart of the game is good. There are three worlds included, and usually one event (7 days) per month.
The issue is one of balance. Earth is impossible to complete. Even people who have cheated to give themselves thousands of dollars worth of pay-to-win currency have estimated that it will take 10,000+ years to complete Earth. Believe it or not, this is a substantial improvement after several patches which were supposedly made "Earth is now completable".
After seeing the developers spend over a year and several patches without having a completable Earth, and seeing incredible swings in whether the events move too quickly or too slowly, I have gradually come to understand that none of the developers actually understand exponential growth to correctly balance the game. While it is otherwise well-polished and even fun for Mars and Moon (mostly), I no longer have confidence that the developers will be able to balance Earth nor the events.  Accordingly, on a yes/no scale, I rank it no.

Update:
To the developer: I respect what you as a 1 man team has done. I being someone who knows a lot about computer software/engineering know the amount of work that is required.
However, I must let my (bad) review stand because of the misjudgement of the timing of the release of the game which was still buggy and clearly a "Beta" version of the game.  It's absolutely inexcusable to buy something that doesn't quite work correctly but then be told that it will later on. Bugs I can live with and updates that better the game are fine but not crashes and freezes.
I will give a deeper review below for those still interested in reading it.
After reinstalling the game I tried Hero Generations and found myself again liking the game.  Surely many of the bugs I had pointed out in my review are seemingly gone which is the good news.  The bad news seems to be the "end game".  Around the 15th generation you realize that you have explored all 6 areas and have killed just about all of the "bosses".  Then you ask yourself the question, "Now what?" I went and built up everything after all of the generations and...I feel as if there's nothing left to do once I get there.
The most frustrating part of the game are the items inventory system.  EVERYTHING requires an item and you can only ever hold 2 at one time.  How can I bear to put down my sword of awesome for a baby when I am about to walk into the volcano of death so that I may place a baby onto an altar?  Now you might say that I can replace said "attack power" by picking up more strength potions and damage potions for my character but that requires my hero to age.  Of course within a certain period of time my character only has a finite amount of years in his/her lifetime and it only becomes a chore to get the "right" combination for hopefully one of my future generations to achieve the goal of simply placing a baby on an altar.
Again I will say that the game is fun.  I like trying to build up my hero to a certain degree and I love randomly choosing cards at the end of each life to hopefully have a better shot than dear old dad.  The only problem lies in what you do once you receive said thoroughbred?
Hopefully this will help future players out there in deciding whether or not to purchase this game.
TLDR: Heroes Generations is a delightful game marred by its lack of end game flair.

A board game with RPG and Rogue-Like elements is the best way to describe Hero Generations. In short, it's fantastic! This is one of those games where it's better to watch some videos and form your own opinons though because I can see how it caters to a niche audience. I did a quick "getting started" playthrough so you can see the game in action before dropping $15. Enjoy!

SHORTER: A fusion of light rougelike rpg, 4x, and generational planning that's straddles the line between ease of play and complexity.  A good game if you're looking for an adventure-fusion game that's fast to pick up, but has challenge, and if you like experimental games.
Hero Generations starts with a hero, who goes into the world, gains fame and gold and equipment, builds towns, and then dies.  Sure, the monsters may get you, but your real enemy is age.  Heros age and die, each turn is a year of their life, and that can burn away quickly.
To build a legacy you can construct buildings, win fame, discover equipment, and find mates to parent the next generation of heroes.  As generations progress new buildings are unlocked, and as you build towns change and grow, and you can explore different worlds, each with something unique.  Quests are given in each world to give you something to strive for, but you'll probably have plenty of your own goals, from making specialized towns to getting to a particuarly inacessible area.
The game mechanics are simple:
* Move around the map.
* Age and gain (or loose) abilities.
* Find assorted treasures, monsters, items, and features.
* Interact with those things in simple ways - combats, for instant, are decided by a single die roll.
* Build around towns or upgrade buildings - which provide many benefits and can change the nature of towns.
* Find a mate is impressed with your stats and parent the next generation.
* Choose the traits of your child.
* Lead the child on their adventure.
Though simple on many levels, the game's strength is how elements interact.  Towns change their nature (and the mates available) depending on what's near them.  Different items afford different advantages.  Different buildings provide different bonuses or tributes.  As you play, you find more and more ways to benefit from the elements of the game and adventure deeper - there's always something new to explore.
Its the kind of game to appeal to people who like to make long-term plans - literally generational in this case.
Visually, the game has a very charming, cartoony style; bright colors, amusing characters with lots of variance, vibrant backgrounds.  It's got its own look which really makes it memorable and enhances the enjoyment.
The greatest strength of the game is how it manages to be both simple to play and offer a lot of complexity at the same time.  Gameplay is very easy, almost casual, and fast to pick up - but the depth of the game requires thought.  Yes, you're controlling a cartoony adventurer, but when you experiment with creating specialized towns, or plotting how to build roadways all over the world, you realize just how complex the game can get - and yet it's still easy to play.
If there's an issue with the game it's that some people might find it boring after awhile.  It yields its secrets to experimentation, exploration, luck, and persistence - and you may not exactly be up for spending three generations getting a town just right.  If that's your thing, good, but it may not be for everyone - the game's unusual fusion really is it's own thing.
The game seems to have good support, and even after release the author is integrating feedback and improving it.  The game's definitely finished, but the author is open minded about improving it - or reversing a bad choice or two.
I consider it a buy for fans of rogeulike, adventure, and planning/4x games who want something easy to play but with some depth.  You can figure it out fast, then enjoy the complexity it offers.
I also consider it a definite buy for people who like to explore something experimental.  The game's cobination of elements, the way it implements them, is worth exploring for people that like to find something different.

Loadout is a fast-paced F2P 3PS where you design your own weapons / loadout.  $IRL only buys cosmetics so you can't pay-to-win.  Unlock new weapon mods in your tech tree and level them up, etc  Great fun!
Gametypes in both PvP and PvBots (co-op) are:
* Blitz (random KOTH cap point)
* Death Snatch (DM with those killed dropping crystals that need to be collected to confirm kill)
* Domination (3 x set KOTH points simultaneously)
* Jackhammer (CTF with "flag" being a melee weapon you can kill with to multiply the cap value)
* Extraction (1 member of each team is randomly selected as the collecter who picks up crystals and drops them in set collection points, while team defends him or attacks other team's collecter)
Equipment you can unlock includes grenades (explosive, incendiary or tesla), disguise (a bit like TF2 spy, but limited like their cloak is), health/ammo pack drop, trapped health/ammo pack, turret (TF2 engi), jump boots (TF2 scout double jumping), personal shield, and even curved shield wall
Probably the best part of the game are the various weapons including rifle, pulse, beam or rocket, with so many different types of mods to make short-range instakiller, great mid-ranged variations, sniper, pyro, area-of-effect, sticky mines, even walking bombs, etc, etc  So many different possibilities!
The bots (computer-controlled fighters just like the players, not actual robots like in TF2's MvM) can be challenging for low-level players, but with good tactics / teammates, and perseverance you can find ways to beat them.
PvP community lost their Australian servers, unfortunately, but Asia isn't too far away.  Random matches might include high level players that you will get pummelled by, or complete noobs who will make it easy for you to advance in XP and Blutes ($).  Teams are randomised each round (unless you form a party with friends), so you shoulndn't get pummelled every round if you keep at it.  They don't have difficulty levels (except the ranked exhibition matches), but a little perseverance will have you unlocking / levelling up your weapons and equipment and doing well in no time.
If the gore / profanity / nudity is too much for you, you can just turn off those settings (as I did for the latter two).  Great game, I highly recommend it, and hope to have you in my party soon!

I'll be honest, from reading other reviews and just watching the initial trailer video I was prepared to maybe like this game, but was more prepared to play one route and leave it in my steam library to collect dust. After just playing through one route, I can say I'm in love with it.
Yes, these are a few tiny little issues here and there, but there is nothing that takes away from the game play or story. They seem to be things with the game engine or something along those lines? Sometimes the transitions were a bit choppy and I would occasionally get a loading screen when a new scene was loading. The actual text itself were also seem like it was sort of....lagging I guess would be the best term? For some reason it would get better when I switched from using the mouse to hitting enter and whether that was the game itself, my computer, or just a state mind is yet to be seen. Like I said though, nothing that takes away the wonderful story and art this game gives you.
I was expecting at least one of the plot points that happened in this story, but the rest. Wow. Not even close. It never felt like it was forced to me either and I never really found myself kind of disbelieving in how the game got me there. More often then not I found myself muttering under my breath in a good surprise about things that happened. The writing is wonderful and each character shines through with their own unique qualities and characteristics. At this point I have one played through one route and I loved all the characters. What I really love though, is how Avery has a personality as well and it actually shows as you play throughout the game. Where as some VN heroines/heroes come across as completely dumb or useless, Avery never felt that way to me.
The romance (at least the one route I played) was very natural as well. It was there, it was adorable, it made me smile and laugh, but it wasn't just in your face and then over. At this point I'm definitely looking forward to seeing how that plays out on the other routes in the game.
If you're interested at all in the game, I would say pick it up when you have the chance. It's a lovely visual novel that definitely lands on it's feet.

When I first saw this game pop up on my recommended games list, I imagined that it was yet another one of these games that were made by an American indie company and attempting to sound Japanese. This has been a trend lately on Steam, and needless to say, a lot of them are pretty horrible.
However, I took a leap of faith and decided to play this game, and I'm glad I did. The characters are engaging, the writing is witty and funny, and the mystery is keeping me interested. I haven't finished the game yet, but I'm really interested to see where it is going.
The game asks for your pronouns at the beginning of the game and you are allowed to change your skin color, so it is a more inclusive game. However! This is a game that does inclusive well, without being judgy or preachy about it, which is a nice relief. It's more like the characters happen to be darker-skinned, rather than that being their entire personality and a way to get more people to play the game.
The characters are not basic stereotypes and they react to situations in a way that is both realistic and engaging, and fitting for the setting.  I have seen no typos and the music is not irritating in the slightest.
I think my only complaint about the game is that I would enjoy the option to make the text larger, but that's because of my own issues with vision.
In any case, I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys visual novels.

Polarity is a first person puzzle game quite heavily inspired by Portal. Instead of creating portals, you have the power to change your polarity. You can freely pass though barriers with the same polarity whereas barriers with opposite polarity will block you.
The models and textures are extremely simple and the lighting model is quite dated.
The game doesn't support 16:10 resolutions. There's no FOV slider either and the default FOV is rather annoying.
The sound effects are very basic and for some reason the default volume is quite low. The soundtrack is fairly decent at least.
The gameplay is rather lackluster. The polarity mechanic doesn't really lead to interesting puzzles and it basically feels like the game is an extended tutorial. It would have been nice to see some more complex puzzles.
To complete the game you need to collect 3 data cubes in each level. This feels like a tedious requirement as hunting for the cubes is not particularly interesting and they are often hidden behind corners or in alcoves.
The levels are all rather easy.
The controls are passable but by no means great. It's quite common to get stuck when using booster bads.
Rather annoyingly some button prompts are only displayed for a gamepad even when you are playing with a mouse + keyboard.
There's very little writing or story and none of it is particularly interesting.
Using the Steam overlay caused some visual glitches.
Personally I found Polarity a rather bad game and I wouldn't recommend it. The visuals, audio and gameplay are all rather poorly done and the puzzles aren't particularly interesting either.
The game is rather short too, it only took me 1 hour to complete the campaign levels. I played through a few of the bonus levels as well, but I didn't bother finishing them.

Polarity is a game that didn't seem that bad to me at first when I played it, but ended up disappointing me at the end. My main gripe about the game is that it's just too dang easy. There were a couple of moments where I had to step back and think a little, but for the most part, it was more of a hide and seek game than anything else.
Your main goal is to collect these data fragments through the level (3 per level) and then leave the level. You would think that they would strategically place these fragments in such a way so that you'd have to overcome some obstacle to get them. But instead they hide them in random places such as right around corners as a "Gotcha! I bet you wouldn't turn around here!" or in plain obvious sight where it's literally in front of your path. There was only one or two times where I had to solve a puzzle to obtain it.
The game is also very short with only 11 normal levels, 10 bonus levels, and a bunch more levels that are co-op only (so I never got to play those). That seems like a lot, but the levels are so easy that you blow through them very quickly. The longest level I played took me around 8 minute to beat with most of them taking just 2-3 minutes. As a result, I beat the 11 levels in around an hour.
After I finished the first 11 levels, I reached an ending mini story (really just a slide show of 5 text images) and I thought that was the end of the first chapter. I was ready to play more and the game to pick up in difficulty. But nope. That's the end aparently. Overall, the game comes off as very amateurish - which isn't bad, but I wouldn't pay more than $2 for the game.

But on the other hand, this isnt some triple-A game developed by a multi million dollar company. The games full price is only about a third of what the average triple-A game cost and with that said, giving people the chance to support the developers further than just buying the game by offering some cosmetics is in that regard something that's not necessarily completely wrong or even a bad thing.
The new Australian update has in all other ways to me been very positive. It adds 3 new maps that, although they need some polishing, are fun to play on, pretty different from the previous, "old" maps and have a really awesome feeling and special atmosphere to them that makes them perfect for fighing out intense Vietnam battles in.
Not to mention the new faction, Australia, and the new weapons of said faction. I've only tried the L1A1 and the SMG's as of yet, the Owen Gun and the F1, and they've really made an impression on me, I am getting quite fond of them. The designs are good and the sounds and feeling of the guns is in my opinion great as well.
The best part of the new update though is by far the new, additional VOIP channel. Similarly to what the game Squad has had for a long time, RS2: Vietnam now also has a 3D positional VOIP. Which in short means that you can call out things such as enemy positions, incoming grenades and confirmed kills solely to teammates in your proximity, whom in many situations are the only relevant recipients of these kinds of information, without bothering your whole team, most of whom are probably located on a completely different part of the map. This not only makes the voice chat altogether less bloated, it also adds a new, and in my opinion important, realism factor to the game.
So all in all I very much recommend this game.

The Secret of Monkey Island Special Edition is a 2009 remake of the original point and click adventure game which was made back in 1990.
Storywise, nothing has changed from the original, and after close to 20 years, it is still as funny and witty as ever. It certainly was very nostalgic to replay it again with enhanced visuals and music + voice acting. The story alone is worth 9.5 / 10. As i have played thru the game before, it took me about 4 hours to complete the game. For someone who is new to this game, it will probably take close to 15 hours or more depending on how fast they can solve the puzzles.
As this is a remake the graphics have certainly been ramped up from the original, although i felt that the modern look looks dated as compared to latest current adventure games. Its nice though that they have included the function to switch between 2009 and original audiovisuals at will.
The original verb commands UI was removed and replaced with 3 alternate input methods, firstly using scroll wheel to select action, secondly using hotkeys, thirdly using a single hotkey to display the list of verbs. Even though there were 3 different methods, they all still felt clunky as i thought it would have been better if they had used the UI that was used in another older Lucasarts game "Full Throttle".
Other downsides include mouse clicks being quite unresponsive when clicking on options and no way to have modern voice acting with the original visuals, no additional extra bonus materials. None of these however, really matter much as this is a classic game that deserves its place among the greatest PC games of all time.
Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10
A refreshing remake, although slightly marred by unresponsive mouse controls. Feel free to add more points if that does not bother you. Veteran gamers will definitely appreciate the nostalgia and newer gamers can have a chance to experience one of the earliest classics in PC gaming history.

♥♥♥♥♥Knocker, the spooling tesla shotgun with bouncing bullets... Not taking your fancy? How about ♥♥♥♥♥♥atron the healing  mine-flak launcher? Or, well hell there's a tonne of combinations and you can name the weapon anything you want.
To start with you will probably need to sink 3-5 hours in to get a weapon or two, and then that again to perfect/re-assess your options. Unlocking everything would take a fair amount of time, to combat this the option of testing your weapon prior to purchasing makes the right decision alot easier; in addition picking up other players weapons in-game helps see what works in the community, that is if you can understand your new weapon 'asshat420' before you're burnt to a cinder.
The variety of game modes is just enough that players can start optimizing weapons for each, and with several maps  strategies can be worked out soon enough. The real variety in gameplay comes from which weapons you build, so gameplay doesn't really stagnate if you keep trying different combinations.
Controls of the game are pretty nice, everything handles reasonably well, and the game seems pretty forgiviing determining hitboxes for jumping up surfaces, so there's plenty of vertical play from all players, ensuring encounters across the map will often play out differently each time (no map feels stale in the way 2fort does). Sprint is intended to be held almost the entire time, with no stamina bar you are constantly zooming across the battlefield, when adding in big floaty jumps and considerable rolls, the opportunities for outplaying your opponent are quite high.
The pay-to-win aspect of the game is not really present in Loadout, much of the content will have to be unlocked through hours of play, unless one pays the equivalent of buying a full retail game anyway. On the other side, all cosmetic options/nearly all taunts are only available through purchasing, albeit there is the chance for getting a cosmetic in a Daily reward, which is eliminates the need to pay to make your avatar a little more unique.
This game is pretty fun, despite axeing several servers there's still a moderate casual playerbase to kill hours in.  Overall feel of the game is pretty slick, the bright colours add to the comical style created through exaggerated character animation / floaty controls.

How can I even start this review?
Stellaris is not quite a 4X game, however, it is not quite an RTS either; rather, it is a hybrid that combines the territory exploration, expansion, exploitation and (in the case of enemies) extermination of 4 X games with the real-time flow of RTS games.
This title from sweddish developer Paradox Development Studio puts us in control of one of many space-faring races (including humans, of course)  with the goal of lifting our growing empire into a force to be reckoned with.
Now, I could go on by describing the game systems and mechanics, however,  that would make the review more like a strategy guide. Suffice it to say, this game is deep. However, that’s not to say that the game is inaccessible. In fact, it is surprisingly straight forward in regards to the 4X pillars. In addition, the UI is very easy to read and feedback regarding resource spending, gains and losses is immediate. But, instead of giving you a technical and by-the-numbers review, I would like to share my experience over the course of two game sessions that I had. Both of these ended I failure, while a third one is still in progress, but so far, looks promising.
At the beginning, I chose to play as the Kel-Azaan Republic, a preset faction characterized for being militaristic and democratic. That meant (in theory) that I had to focus on warfare and establishing a large fleet to be able to deal with other empires and outside threats. Also, I had a good mineral output, so it was easier to build ships. For the most part, I had been able to survive long enough and without any wars breaking out. However, the First Kel-Azaan republic crumbled due to two major flaws: First I had expanded too quickly, setting up many frontier outposts, which drained all my Influence (One of the most important resources of the game) over a short period of time, and second, due to this lack of Influence - and because of the fact that I wasn’t producing no Influence at all - wasn’t able to recruit more scientists and generals, which in turn, were dying of old age, leaving many important research projects unfinished. With n way to carry the loss of the top minds of the empire, the first iteration of the Republic, came to a close.
On my second attempt, I had learned my lesson. Expansion was a matter of going only for the essential resources (Energy Credits and Minerals) first, and build a healthy economy. Later on, I made some allies, however, frictions and confrontations soon erupted, and during the course of a few decades, I was in the middle of three wars.
For the most part, I was doing well. I discovered how to use Sectors to keep most of the micromanagement off my back and also learned how to setup frontier outposts. however, my major flaw was the fact that I depended heavily on my only ally for support, and I was lagging behind in terms of fleet power and colonization, which should have generated more resources for the growth of the empire. To make matters worse, we had a sever case of Piracy. Deciding that pirates were the most immediate threat to the Republic, I decided to pour my resources and research into building a sizable fleet, and for one brief moment, we were victorious over the pirates. Sadly, victory was short-lived, as one of our enemies decided to declare war while we, and our ally had our hands full. With this, the second Kel-Azaan Republic came to an end, but the lessons I learned as a player stayed with me.
Every new technology, every military triumph and every successful colony meant that I was learning, and growing as a player. In the end, Stellaris is a wonderful experience that trully makes you feel like you are exploring a vast and wonderful galaxy.
Now, a game like this would really benefit from a great atmosphere, and thankfully, the Soundtrack brings all these moments to life. Andreas Waldetoft’s score is inspired by classic sci-fi tunes like Vangelis’ Blade Runner and incorporates more modern elements like Hans Zimmer’s Interstellar. In particular, the pieces “Faster than Light” and “To the End  of the Galaxy” stood out for me, and really punctuated every soaring triumph, harrowing conflict and the childlike sensation of discovering the vastness of space.
There are a few gripes, though. The tutorial, while handy and really accessible to accustom new players, doesn’t cover many minute details, and combat is mostly reliant on numbers and modifiers, which might turn of some fans of more in depth strategic combat.
Despite this, the game does a wonderful job to bring in new players into the genre, with an easy to read interface, pausable gameplay and a beautiful atmosphere. If you love space games, empire-building, politics and journeys through the last frontier, but feel intimidated by stats or a high APM (Actions Per Minute) ceiling, Stellaris might be for you. Overall, very, VERY highly recommended.

This was a tough review to write because there are many admirable things about this game, and it has the potential to be a truly great genre-defining classic, but in its current guise (1.9x) I can't honestly recommend it as a sound purchase.
The Good
* Tries something different. Whether it's the prevalence of meaningful event-chains, the randomised alien races, or the strong focus on exploration, Stellaris avoids the stale seen-it-all-before tropes of the glut of MOO2 clones which dominate the space 4x landscape.
* Great music (espeically all the synthy Vangelis-influenced stuff) with the expansions bringing a variety of cool voicepacks too, to create an authentic classic sci-fi feel.
* Good writing. Obvious influence from people like Clarke, Adams, etc. shines through in the story sections and exploration phase which make up the strongest parts of the game. Such a shame that by midgame, these have largely disappeared, and the problems begin . . .
The Bad
* Lack of interesting ways to interact with other races and empires, hell, lack of interesting systems in general. You meet someone, you will be at war or peace with them (this is fairly deterministic based on initial race setup). This is the limit of your intergalactic diplomacy. There is no meaningful trade with other empires, no espionage or way to influence other empires beyond invading them. There is no model for cultural influence, or religious influence, or really anything at all. Compare this to something like the Civ games, which provide plenty of non-military routes to interact with your world. Makes things very dull, very quickly.
* Appalling combat. Doomstack vs Doomstack. The winner spends the next few hours slowly mopping up helpless systems, the loser of that initial confrontation has already lost the game. Ground combat is even worse. At least space combat looks prettty, the ground combat is just two rows of circles bobbing at each other with a few meaningless numbers attached, and the UI for loading up transports is some of the most ill-thought out I've ever encountered. Supposedly the 2.0 patch is going to fix this. I hope it can, but the system is so tedious right now, it will require an awful lot of work.
* A mass of insignificant incremental choices instead of fewer important ones. Research a technology that provides +5% research. Research another one that changes your red lasers to blue lasers and adds +2 damage or something. Set up your empire at the start of the game, will you be a Fascist robotic mollusc or a Capitalist mushroom? Doesn't matter, the only difference is +10% minerals or some such. Endless busywork increasing your level 2 mines to level 3 is how you'll be spending the majority of your time.
* Lack of Grand Strategy elements. Stellaris is in truth, less a 4X/grand strategy hybrid than a 4x with a veneer of Grand strategy over the top. It has all the busywork and endless expansion of a 4x but few of the features of a grand strategy - no interesting character interactions, political maneouvering, or internal pressure. It does borrow the grand strategy lack of victory conditions however.
Overall I really wanted to like this game. It has wonderful ideas, is trying to be original, and is well supported by the developers. It's just not fun though, and through a focus on incremental busywork and lack of any goal really beyond expand and conquer (a big problem when the military is the weakest part of the game!) I'd currently suggest holding on until the 2.0 patch some time next year, and then check out reviews and feedback for how/if these issues have been addressed.

As much as I'd love to finish this game, I don't think it will even let me. The game crashes almost every mission for no reason, quick saves will randomly decide to not load, the entire game just freezes during certain loading screens. Also, the game looks awful compared to previous games in the Splinter Cell franchise, which is odd, considering Chaos Theory was absolutely gorgeous for its time, and still holds up to this day. Sometimes shadows won't even render when the level loads, making the whole stealth mechanic extremely awkward. Being a huge fan of Splinter Cell, it's really unfortunate that this game is unstable, to the point of freezing my computer. I could only recommend this game to hardcore fans of the Splinter Cell franchise. I will attempt to finish this game, and if it gets better, I will edit this review. Until then, this still stands.
[EDIT]
So I've finished the game. The bugs and glitches are still present, no suprise there, but there was one specific bug that stood out amongst others: a game breaking bug. After completing the final mission, a cutscene is supposed to play, the credits should roll, and you are rewarded with a bonus mission. For me, and many others, this didn't happen. The mission would end, and then cut immediately to an overhead scene of the level where you are unable to move and unable to quit properly. (you have to enter the Task Manager and end it manually.) Aside from the awful technical issues, the gameplay and story are some of the best in the Splinter Cell series so far. It takes place shortly after the events of Chaos Theory, in which Sam must pose as a criminal and join a terrorist force in order to destroy them from the inside. The game has a "trust meter," in which you have to complete objectives for the JBA: the terrorist force, and the NSA: the good guys. Due to trust being a factor, the game forces you to enter in these moral gray areas just to keep the trust of the enemy. While in the base, you have the option to research and spy on your allies/enemies to learn more info about them. This information will assist you in traversing the base as well as unlock special items for your missions. As with all previous games in the franchise, it is all based on stealth and using gadgets as well as the enviornment to your advantage to accomplish your objectives. If you've played a SC game in the past, you know what you're getting yourself into from a gameplay perspective.
