This game was given to me as a gift from my boyfriend. He just had the key and didn't really like puzzle games, so he gave it to me. Even though this was totally free on my end, I cannot say I enjoyed this game.
In this game, the first screen you see is a brief introduction. You are a hacker who has been hired to do some serious hacking. It's not going to be easy, but you'll be handsomely rewarded. For a game that looks like it takes place in Code Lyoko's Sector 5, I really did not feel at all like a hacker at all. If the game did not have any sort of storyline involved, Polarity would have not felt any different to me at all.
In Polarity, your main gimmick is that you have a polar charge, red or blue, and you can change your polarity by pressing one of your keys. Basically, if you are one color, walls of the other color will not affect you. If you're standing on a platform of the other color, you will simply fall through it. It's pretty neat as a concept, but this is basically what all the puzzles devolve to: You're on a blue platform in front of a blue wall, and on the other side is a red platform. You are blue. What you need to do is jump at the wall, change your color, and land on the red platform. Sometimes you need to do this fast so that you can meet up with a moving platform. I would not consider something so simple as moving fast while changing your color when necessary to be substantial as a primary puzzle element. This is what the puzzles felt like to me, and it got old very quickly.
Sometimes, the puzzles involve the addition of cubes that you need to put on a pedestal in order to acheive a result. This is a fantastic puzzle element that would have made the game rally fun, but there is one huge flaw with the game that ruins the experience, which is your throwing range. When you pick up a cube, you can throw it, but you have the throwing arm of Hercules. If you see where the cube needs to go, just simply aim and toss. The pedestals are basically magnetic, so the cubes will stick wherever you want as long as you throw it correctly. You don't really need to traverse the area to actually set the cube there. I decided to try bringing them manually to the pedestals without throwing the cubes an insanely long distance, but when I set one of the cubes on a moving platform, the cube did not stay at all. I tried multiple times during the puzzle to get the cube to move on a moving platform, but instead the platform moved under the cube and the cube just simply fell. Throwing it seems to be the way you are supposed to transport the cube, but throwing is just too easy.
The cubes also have polarities to them, as well. They will not be able to be taken through walls that share polarity, and they will fall through platforms with differing polarities. This is a fantastic feature to the game, but I found that this feature was not executed very well. I only remember a couple times where I had to do something other than throw a cube around a wall to get it through, but these puzzles were as easy to solve as finding the polarity changing unit nearby. These units were usually placed close to the areas you needed them or hidden behind a wall somewhere. They were not hard to find and they were all too easy to just change the cube's polarity whenever I wanted, defeating the purpose of the puzzle.
One of the game's best features was its use of stars to gather. You can only get to future levels with enough stars, so you have to collect all 3 in each level. Some of these are protected by puzzles, but these puzzles didn't seem to add much to the game. These puzzles seemed as easy as making a detour. A lot of these stars were hidden in nooks around the level, too, which was frustrating. Instead of having to solve puzzles to find these stars, I instead had to investigate every nook and cranny in each level until I found them all, which felt more like wasting time than playing a game.
While I did not enjoy a lot of this game, I will give credit where it is due. There was one bonus level where the puzzle was satisfying. There were two chambers that you could rotate by pressing nearby buttons. They were right beside each other, so you would have to go back and forth to do things. There is a little hole in each one, and if the room is spun one way you can reveal things that would otherwise be blocked by a wall, in addition to needing to change the orientation of the room to complete specific platforming sections. In the end of the puzzle, you have to get past one of these areas in the left room, but there's no way to get to where you need to be, no matter how I set up the left room. Turns out you needed to spin each room so its revealing holes faced each other, creating a door from the more easily navigatable right room to the more restrictive left room. It was surprisingly fleshed-out for a puzzle in this game and it was the only level I felt like I actually accomplished something in. It was enjoyable.
The soundtrack is also enjoyable. I like the feel the music gives me. The graphics were decent, although the shading was too dark on my end, to the point where I could sometimes have trouble seeing when I should not have trouble seeing.
At the end of the game, your employer sends you another message, which says something along the lines of "well done, your payment will be coming shortly". Again, the plot just felt as if it did not connect to the game at all.
I tried Co-op mode as well, but I barely enjoyed it. The co-op has barely any player interaction, and it more or less seemed like a race to perform better than your opponent.
All in all, this game just did not feel satisfying to me. There is a brief story that has barely any correlation to the game, the main gimmick is initially interesting but lacks substantial depth in gameplay, and the puzzles presented are easily solved, if not avoided, by the player's ability to change polarity whenever you want and supernatural throwing arm. I feel that the game could have gone in other directions, maybe if changing polarity was more restrictive and you could only change at specific times, like going to a small pad on the ground somewhere, for example, and having to worry about only being one color until you could locate the changing pads. I understand that this was a project by a programmer who made this in his spare time and that this project is not supposed to be professional, but even so, the experience I had was not very satisfying as far as puzzle games go.

It’s never fair to judge something by a single aspect, but nor is it unreasonable for a flaw to be bad enough to make the whole package unbearable to some. People are quick to jump on the bandwagon when a glaring fault is revealed, especially when it’s from a prominent source that shouldn’t have let it slip through. Some of this bias I think comes when people compare a game to another, completely different game. If it’s a sequel from the same publisher, then sure, there’s an expectation to live up to, but I hate seeing games compare to others that have been made by different minds.
The name Portal gets gets thrown around a lot when Polarity is mentioned. Why? I’m not sure. Aside from a few aesthetics and a reference in the name of an achievement, there’s not a lot between the games that they share. This is the other side of what I was dribbling on about in my opening paragraph. Attempting to piggyback on the success of one title only really works if you’re a copy-cat or a cheap clone. To me, Polarity is neither and is a title that should be considered to, and does, stand on its own.
The story is a hacking… blah blah… collect data… it’s irrelevant. It’s just a pointless layer to the rest of the game. The real meat is in the multiple levels where you solve puzzles and navigate obstacles. Each level has three glowing ‘data chunks’ that you have to find if you want to get that 100% completion. The puzzles vary in difficulty and were mostly quite entertaining, right through to the end. I have to grumble about the level design near the end. Some levels had glaring faults such has misaligned walls and floors as well as gaping holes though to the ‘void’ outside the world. It felt like designer got tired and started to get sloppy.
I played the co-op mode split-screen with a friend and we had some good fun, but we were glad when it ended as it does get a bit tiring. Didn’t try the VS mode, as we were tired of it by that point. It’s a good game even if it’s a bit plain and a little rough around the edges.

This game is amazing. period.
Pros:
- the loading is extremely fluid. no longer are the days where in the old deadrisings you had to load the map when entering a new part. No lag or nothing
- The combat is SO smooth. The only thing i didn't like about the past DR's was the combat felt clunky. NOT HERE!
- The weapons are insane, out of this world, brutal, destructive, and everywhere across the map.
- The exploration is FANTASTIC in this game. I typically don't like exploring in games, just never feels too worth it too me. But here you will find yourself exploring for hours on end
- Graphics are beautiful (if you have the video card to run this game of course)
- CRAZY AMOUNTS OF ZOMBIES. SEAS OF ZOMBIES. THE APOCALYPSE IS HERE
- The city of Los Pedidos is beautiful, and just the right size; not CRAZY big but by no means small
- Side missions are surprisingly not repetitive, even though most times you're helping survivors retrieve stuff, it's never the same and it's not time consuming enough to take you away from the story
- LONG AMOUNTS OF TIME FOR EXPLORING. THIS IS CRUCIAL FOR ALL DR GAMES
- A F*CKING BULLDOZER MOTERCYCLE. WHAT?! All of the vehicles in this game are ♥♥♥♥ing great
- Zombie AI is brilliant
- Voice acting is pretty f*cking good. I love it
CONS:
- The system requirements for this game are disgusting. I should mention i'm running a Radeon 6990 graphics card and i still need to turn on gamebooster and can only run on semi medium graphics. I get a steady 30 fps, nothing to complain about, smooth, but i can imagine a vast majority of people won't be able to run this beast of a game.
- the file size is pretty big. not a big complaint but 25-30 GB is a pretty large file
- Not many psychopathic bosses in the game. I've been playing for 8 hours and i've only come across two . And i've been doing about 80-90% of all the side missions. I'm sure there's plenty more, since i've seen youtube videos of them, but in past DR's i feel like you'd encounter one every 1-2 hours.
BOTTOMLINE:
The game is FANTASTIC. Easily the best DR. It is EVERYTHING a zombie game should be. The cons are few and more so related to hardware issues. If you have a powerful computer then you should have no problem.
I'd highly recommend this game though. Probably my favorite steam game ever.

To be honest, I would give this free-to-play game a recommendation if it isn't for important factor that basically unhinges the whole experience.
I do think this game is a good idea to have, especially as something to play when you don't really feel like playing a game that requires more investment on your part. Checking into this one and discovering what witty messages you get and seeing your representation go from rags to riches over real time is something that's really worth it. Yes, it's a clicker game, but one that shows some very tight design. For the majority of the 100+ hours that I've been in the game, it never grew tiring on me, and having both the Moon and Mars as places to further capitalize on helped to add a little variety.
But once you finish those places, you've basically finished the game. For me, Earth became a trickle around the sexseptuagintillion mark, where there's not enough cash flowing in for days... even weeks that would allow you to buy to reach more unlock milestones, and even the flow of profit-boosting angel investors becomes a trickle. Now... I could go into the in-game microtransactions and straight up buy more, but then again... I already did, to support the people who made this game. Now that I have to in order to get those last few achievements that require a kitted out Earth, it no longer feels worth it to pool more money into the game. Sure, there are events every month that allow for stuff that would profit boost Earth, but that stuff comes as a trickle as well.
Though the game has stood up for quite a while, it eventually ran straight into a paywall that makes total competitions frown. I consider the game finished, and I have to say... I really do get why this otherwise great game has the recent negative attention nowadays.
Good luck with your future games, Hyper Hippo. I hope you learn what you've done really well and recognize where you've screwed up.

Saints Row 2 is much more serious than later games of the saga (e.g. no dubstep guns, zombie islands and other hilarious things). However, it doesn't mean it's less fun to play. Furthermore, I enjoyed playing the main campagin much more. So, here are my favourite things about Sants Row 2:
1. The city is constantly living - every person on the streets feels unique, with his own reactions to your actions, you can find people talking about the latest events happened in the game, there are skateboarders, street musicians, homeless people and much more. The town itself is not just a bunch of buldings put up together - every district is unique, a lot of places are playable (you can even visit the office of Volition, the developer of SR :) ).
2. The story makes sense. If you played SR: The Third/ SR 4, you know what I'm talking about ^_^
3. Humor - unlike in the later games, SR 2 doesn't need a crazy situation to occur in order to be funny.
4. Customization. It just works, it's fun to play with, and it gives your character some sort of unique style and, well, character :)
As for the conclution I should say that the game is very atmospheric, yet doesn't have any strict and "correct" playtrough, and altogether feels free and unobtrusive.

Where to start, the art is really really great. You can pick between six different character designs. Granted, all that changes between them is the hair length and skin color, but it's still really great.

If you want a fun and beautiful game that has cat curses, trash magic, and mysterious co-workers; this is the game for you.

The art is cute, the characters are likeable, and act III has some good intensity to it.
If you like the story and characters, it has replay value.
My only criticisms are I wish it had been a little longer to dedicate to the relationship building. As it is, it is fine, but it is not the longest game. I also wish there was some voice acting, as I feel it gives more life to the characters, but I also understand that means more time, more employees, and more money involved. My last is the antagonists’ motivation (which I will not spoil here). I feel it could have been something more substantial.
Either way, it is a fun cute story with good characters. As I said, if you like PG otomes with a bit of a weird flair to them, you will like this.

(I've since finished all routes)
It is a VERY, VERY short game, and the price it's at as of my writing this review (17.99 USD) is just totally unreasonable.
I've played all six routes now. Total play time 8.1 hours on record (I did kinda blitz through the mens' routes; like I said, I'm gay and biased towards the women). They were all very well written and engaging, with good art and interesting characters. I stand by everything else I've said in this review - including, unfortunately, my non-recommendation.
I can see why it's priced high; it clearly has very high quality art and text and music (particularly considering that there are six versions of Avery's face). But from a consumer standpoint it's really hard to justify.
So, on to the good.
The art is excellent, and the writing is great. Mason's route actually had me in tears. Finley is absolutely adorable. The beginning, and some short parts near the end, got a bit repetitive, but overall I liked all the different routes, how you learn different things about the characters etc.
I like the ability to choose the pronouns for Avery, your character, and also independently select your appearance (there's a more 'masculine' and a more 'feminine' face available, and you can choose between three skin tones as well). This is reflected pretty well in the gameplay as well, though there were a couple awkward moments in Finley's route where a side character's dialogue seemed to be making the assumption that Avery was male, and noone corrected him? (The pronouns still fit, it was a broader text issue. Maybe just me.)
And some small complaints, other than the length of the game. These don't affect my (non)-recommendation.
There's no text speed option that I saw, so you kind of have to click your way through each sentence of dialogue at a pretty rapid pace if you read pretty quickly. This can also lead to accidentally clicking past a certain portion of dialogue too early because you were trying to get all the sentences displayed, which leads to another quibble...
Most other VN's I've read/played, you can scroll back at least a bit to see something you might've just missed. Hustle Cat, for some reason, does not. There IS a log, so if you just missed something you can open that and see the recent text, but it's odd that you can't just scroll back a little bit. I assume this is in Ren'Py, which I KNOW can do that.
Also, this isn't something I'm actually concerned with at all, but I know some people prefer much more interactive VN's. This isn't; in all of the routes, the first third of the game is making some basic decisions about who you get close to, which determines which route you're on; the middle third is non-interactive; and the last third may have one player choice which either immediately leads to a bad end or continues the story to the end. Again, I don't mind this at all, personally; just putting it out there for people who would.

Hero Generations is a fun light strategy game, all about raising successive generations of heroes. It shows it's Flash roots, but the graphics are crisp and clear and I like the art style. I like how you can build buildings to develop the world slowly over time and the pass genetic traits and items down to the next generation. The forest world you start in is pretty easy but the game gets challenging fast, the volcano world almost killed me and the desert world had lots of challenges (I haven't explored the swamp and island worlds yet). The game has a simple concept, but it executes it well.

EDIT: There is now a newer version of this game, Hero Generations: ReGen. Get that instead.
Hero Generations is a casual, fairly quick playing, turn-based, semi-roguelike game.
(Note that problems many early players experienced with the save system, resulting in a number of negative reviews, should now be fixed.)
The game is pleasant and relaxed, not requiring a huge amount of in-depth thought or strategizing, which suits me just fine. It’s easy to pick up and put back down on whim - sometimes one just wants to vege-out and click, explore a world, and have battles resolved by a quick random number generator (RNG).
Early in the game you are intentionally exposed to a little fear and anxiety, and a part of that is avoiding battles until you're stronger. Later you get the satisfying feeling of stomping creatures that you earlier feared.
The game achieves all this in a quick and streamlined way that is dead-easy to pick up and play without an extensive tutorial, and without having to memorise 16 thousand different spells and item combinations.
RNG is only a small part of the game, as a lot of the decision making is based around deciding how much risk to take in combat - do you push your luck and take on a 50/50 chance of success with an evenly matched opponent, or do you avoid those battles until you are powerful enough to ensure that the odds of an unlucky RNG roll are minimal.
If you're fighting units two thirds your strength you can fairly expect to lose, on average, one in three battles. If you don't like those odds you will need to level your strength up further before taking on those battles.
Consequently, the bulk of gameplay is about boosting your hero's base strength, which is primarily achieved by collecting gold through light questing, and by constructing buildings to generate either more gold, or that provide strength and damage boosts. The buildings you construct mostly accumulate over generations, so eventually you will have put together a small strength and gold generating machine around your core villages.
Loss in combat is a minor annoyance (slightly reducing your lifespan by around 5 'years' (turns) until you need to retire), and the law of averages evens out the occasional unlucky die roll over time.
It is possible for your lineage to end if you push your luck too far and get caught out in the wilds with only a few years left to get back to a town and find a potential mate. Your lineage can also end in the rare instance that you haven't built up enough fame or wealth to impress a potential suitor before needing to retire.
The generations system is neatly done, in that you have a choice about whether to do a big rush of exploration and combat with the current hero, or do you retire early and aim to do better next time. The incentive to retire early is that, the earlier you retire the more boosts your son or daughter start with next time. (For what it's worth, the game is pleasantly gender neutral.)
Like many rogue-lites, there is no formal save system as such. Progress is autosaved at the end of each turn and you return to where you left off next time you start the game (select "load game" in the main menu).
In terms of pacing, the game can hit a dead spot mid-game, where you’ve beefed as much as you’re going to and there is little to do other than random exploring and monster clearing while you wait for building upgrades to unlock (upgrades unlock after a fixed number of generations have passed).
I have had a lot of fun with the game so far, and can see myself dipping in and out off and on in the future. Maps re only semi-random, however, so there might not be quite enough variety here to justify repeated play throughs after the game has been ‘beaten’.
edit: updated review to reflect improvements from recent patches.

Where a traditional roguelike is typically about learning the enemies and their abilities so you can decide how to deal with them, Hero Generations introduces more random elements to combat and uses the lifespan and generational mechanics to make the player focus more on the long term. Every decision must take the hero's remaining years and potential legacy into account. Is it worth fighting anything as a teenager, when the hero's strength is low? Should I repair that building so it will be there for the next hero at the expense of losing a card flip to get them another bonus?
Even though I don't really buy into Hero Generations being a roguelike/4X hybrid, the 4X elements that have been woven into the game make it play differently from other roguelikes. It's turn- and grid-based in traditional roguelike fashion, but deviates far enough from the traditional mold that I'm tempted to call it a roguelite instead. I'm not sure how well die-hard fans of old-school roguelikes will like it. As a fan of both roguelikes and roguelites, I like it quite a bit.

This is based only on a couple of hours in. Oh! My english is not that good, so it's possible you see some mistakes.
That said, let's get into the subject. The game has an interesting concept. The mix of "5 Minutes Civilization" as the dev said and the "Rogue-Like" genre, with the mechanic of mating so you can build a legacy make the whole idea interesting. The devs wanted the game to be accessible to everyone, so the game may be a bit simplistic.
What is the result?
Well... they managed to do something good, but i'll be honest, it's not the indie game of the month. You start in your village, and go fight monsters, build improvements to nearby towns so when you move on these tiles you get bonus (like more Strength, more Lifespan, Gold, etc.)
You get quests as you go to other worlds, and you have a main quest too. So, you have your objectives, now it is up to you to find how you are going to accomplish them.
The fact that they made the game accessible to everyone makes the game way too easy for harcore gamers, or some devoted gamers in general. The casual gamer type will find some fun, or even our kids or just new gamers.
I don't want to spoil anything because there isn't much to discover in the game and it will destroy "the magic" if I tell you everything right now. Let me do a quick Pros/Cons list, so you'll have a better idea about the game.
Pros
___
-Beautifull art-style. Simplistic, but still nice.
-Nice music. Yeah... it's good.
Now the real stuff
-Good mix of genres (Simplistic 4x + Rogue-Like)
-Friendly game that anyone can play
-Interesting RPG system with the gear limit (2) , the traits you pass down, etc
Neutral
---
-Simplistic (i think i said that word a couple times now)
-Easy
-The art style, depends on your tastes
Cons
---
-Too easy for the more dedicated gamers (way too easy for hardcores)
-Doesn't have much content (not enough gear, traits, worlds, monster types)
-Feel sometimes like a pocket game you would play on a phone or tablet
-A girl named Bob, a boy named Josephine... -.- Seriously Heart Shaped Games LLC please fix your name generator (sorry for all Female Bob and Male Josephine out there)
-Only 1 save slot
-A "Main Menu" button would be nice by the way
-More screen resolutions needed
-Fullscreen and Borderless FullScreen is missing
-What is this volume setting? It's like my phone. Make a slider or something please.
-Fights are ful RNG based (My hero have 40 Str, my oponent 10, I roll a 6 he roll 8, he wins the fight and hit me with 5 damage, so i lose 5 years of my life)
-Somehow overpriced (here it's 16,99 CAD$ full price, so i think $14,99 USD. Maybe if it was $9,99 USD (around 11 or 12 CAD), it would be more worth the money.
And there is more i'm pretty sure, but i'll stop here because the rest is my personnal opinion, and it doesn't count right now.
I heard this somewhere and I can't find who said that, but it's a very good way to think about games. Each dollar spent on a game should be worth one hour of fun. Out there somewhere is one of the hidden gems I have found while searching through Steam’s sales, and personally, I enjoyed playing through it.
At first, OTS looks like one of the dime-a-thousand pixel-art 2-d platformers that make up quite a few of the indie games for sale on steam. When investigated further, it is revealed that the game is a bit above the rest.
The main story of the game, is very simple, and is only there because it has to be in order for the game to make sense.
Captain Yuri and crew fight off the evil alien, Grigori, and Yuri goes in alone to stop him, gets shot down, and lands on an alien planet. From there he must repair his ship, and find Grigori to defeat him.
Bland and stereotypical as the story may be, the music is anything but, and ranges from chiptunes to electronic to orchestral. From the moment you launch the game, you are greeted by a dark track that gets you in the mood to play. While it may not be as memorable as Level one of Mario, or the Legend of Zelda theme, the music is still catchy, and because the soundtrack is $0.99 DLC, I listen to it in my spare time, in fact while writing this review I have actually been listening to the music to get in the spirit.
The actual meat of this game centers around teleportation and momentum to solve puzzles. There are two side-scrolling shooter portions, but I’ll get to those later. You are given two guns at the start of the game, the teleportation gun, and the regular gun, with one heart, and one direction to go, right.  The main focus is of course the teleportation gun, which has momentum mechanics, basically, if you jump right before your shot hits a wall, you jump when you teleport there. There are also three beams and various blocks/mirrors that affect how your shot will land. Overall, the puzzle section is definitely solid. There are various power-ups, ship upgrades, and heart/health containers that you can find in capsules by exploring, but they are not necessary to beat the game.
The first time I played through, it took me 2 ½ hours, without picking up any capsules. The game contains plenty for a short amount of time though; there are two ship battles with Grigori, where the parts you collected come into play, and one boss fight that uses the mechanics you’ve learned throughout the game, to go along with the puzzles and side-scrolling.
For the price I bought it, I believe that the game is very good, with a few flaws here and there, and deserves a solid:
8/10

In my journey to explore half a decade of missed gaming advancement, I have come across some games that absolutely captivate me for their brilliance, their artistic direction and writing, the things they accomplish through the unique medium of games. I have fallen in love with many games. But when I need a break from playing games, I find myself playing Saints Row 2.
I skipped Saints Row 1, because I'm not an idiot. But this sandbox is a brilliant mix of challenge (on the hardest difficulty, of course) and sheer hilarity, proving the perfect palette cleanser for 40-50hrs a week of gaming and games troubleshooting. In comparison to the Grand Theft Auto series, the ideal of gritty realism is thrown aside for comic entertainment; rag-dolls fly and flip with disturbing velocity, missions give you unlimited ammo when you need to create mayhem, and as you progress through the story, truly well-written comedy shines through the madcap Saints as compared to the straight-men of the rival gang bosses.
The graphics are absolutely dated, but endless replayability and desire to dive back in and retry that racing or mayhem mission absolutely gives this game its little green thumbs-up.

EDIT: Valve is amazing. They're adding updates weekly. This review won't go over all the features, as some are new. Also bugs are constantly being fixed. Thanks for understanding.
Long story short, the Steam Controller is the best, most configurable, and feature packed gamepad on the market.
And with a price tag of $49.99, it easily beats the PS4 and Xbox One gamepads, which can go up to $70.
The Steam Controller is an Xbox One remote, Wireless Trackpad, and Wii Remote all in one. (As well as some other neat features.) The controls are completely configurable, and with a possible 21 buttons, (Including the dual stage triggers and D-Pad.) as well as motion controls, the possiblities are completely endless.
It sends a signal to your PC/Mac/Steam Machine/Steam Link that could simulate a keyboard or gamepad button, depending on what the game supports.
Explaining the features isn't easy, as there are so many of them. The best way to figure them out is to buy one to experience it yourself.
To make it easy on you, I'll just make a list with some quick descriptions.
- The trackpads could be used to simulate a D-Pad, Joystick, Button Pad, Mouse, or it could just be one big button. It has haptic feedback (See below) and can be used for some many things.
- The trackpads, as well as in some cases the joystick, have haptic feedback, making it feel like you're actually touching something. Let's face it, actual trackpads aren't very good, (With some exceptions.) valve really made it feel more comfortable with the feedback.
- You can change any button to do any action. This is what it has over other gamepads. This is the reason it's for PC gamers. You can make it simulate a gamepad or keyboard.
- You can browse the community to save their configurations.
- If you watched valve's official video they referenced them, but didn't really explain them that much. The idea is that if you do a soft pull on the trigger it will do one action, and if you do a full pull it will do another. For example, in TF2 when I play as Sniper I set it so that when I do a soft pull it aims, and when I do a full pull it shoots. This is pretty efficent, but it is outranked by some of the other great features.
- These are the real things that drew me to the gamepad. On the back of the controller, you have two grips. Each of them have buttons that make a little "click" sound that feels like bumpers. This are great, so instead of taking your thumb off the right trackpad to press a button you can use them to jump and reload.
- Valve barely advertises this at all. Heck, I never realized it existed until 3 days of playing around with the thing. This is what I meant about it being a "Wii Remote." The idea is fantastic. You can make it act like a mouse, or have a learn binding. (Pssst! If you configure it right, you can make it behave like a wheel in racing games just like Mario Kart for the Wii!)
- No one seems to touch upon the fact that the joystick is fantastic. You can feel the quality in it. Probably one of the best I've felt.
- Yes, the ABXY button placement is strange. And yes, the buttons are a little bit to small. But, the buttons are close together, so you can move your thumb quicker, so you can create combos smoother in some fighting games.
- Don't feel like playing games? The steam controller works like a wireless trackpad, so you can navigate through your desktop from your couch.
- Does a Game you like to not support gamepads? The steam controller fixes that. With it, you can even play AdVenture Capitalist from your couch. You'll have to configure it, of course.
- This is amazing, you can configure and play games with full gamepad support. No need to make a configuration, you can just jump right in.
- Barely anyone uses this, but it's still a neat touch. (Heh heh, get it?
?) If I touch my right or left trackpad, depending on my configuration, it will display a small menu in the bottom left corner of the screen. I can choose an item on the menu just like a touchscreen. The items on the menu can be "Pause" or "Weapon 2" or "Inventory". Actually, it could be whatever you want. Although I barely use it, the touch menu is a neat
. No? Fine.
You can set it so if you hold down the button it will repeat the action. The feature doesn't work that well and has bugs but still is worth mentioning.
- I can make it so that if I press RT, it will do RT+Y on the gamepad. This is great for combo games that require you to press multiple buttons.
- These things run on voodoo magic. I've had the controller for 2 weeks or so and they're still on 100%. Glitch? Magic? I don't know. Either way the controller still runs perfectly.
If you actually read what I said above, you should already know the answer; yes.
This thing is a must buy for any PC gamer. It's comfortable, configurable, and replaces all of your gamepads. With the exception of platformers. For that, you might want to stick with a 360 controller. Not that it does bad in them, Xbox 360 Controllers just perform better. It's amazing. GET IT!
I give the Steam Controller a solid 91/100. A must-buy for any PC gamer.

I found Hero Generations to be an interesting little rogue-like game.  Unlike other rogue-likes I've played, this one seems to have much more on an adventuring aspect to it.  There are six world areas to explore with various quests to complete in each world.  You start with a character, and each step you take reduces your life.  Before you die, you must find a partner, so that your child can continue your legacy.
Your children inherit some of the traits / abilities of your character, so as time goes along, your lineage will generally grow more and more powerful.
During each lifetime, it takes time for your character to get into decent fighting shape.  There is always a push-pull tension in wanting to complete more in this lifetime, and making sure you have time to find a mate and spend time with your child.
There were a number of design decisions that will make or break this game based on personal preference.
1)  The battle system is simplistic.
2)  The character can only carry two items.
3)  There is a limited lifetime on a per character basis.
4)  Buildings degenerate over time.
None of them were game breakers for me and they made for some interesting decisions that needed to be made throughout the game.
I have put together an example playthrough for those who are interested:
Gameplay aside, there do seem to be a few technical issues that need to be resolved.  Like other reviewers have noted, I would have liked to have a full-screen mode.  I have also experienced some of the save game issues.  While not a big deal with shorter games, a late game character being lost to a save bug is a sure recipe for moving on.  There is also some lag after some battles that you hope the game will recover from.  I fully expect these to be resolved, but they need to be noted here.

Alright, so I just got this game.. And I like it, I think it's a lot of fun, it's sort of like a lite Roguelike and a Civilization game rolled up into a bite sized game.
There are issues that kind of make you feel like you aren't making progress. For starters, there's a "world disaster" event in the game and the count down to it is far too short, you've barely just started playing when it makes itself known.
Further, any upgrades you make around other towns degrade slowly over time, even with the black smith utility. What makes this frustrating is, there's not really a point to upgrading each "world" unless you intend to spend any extended amount of time there. It feels like wasted resources and can be aggravating.
The random element of the combat can be frustrating; it's all based on simple dice rolls. And even if you have a ability of 200 and are fighting a enemy with an ability of 30, there's still a chance they'll beat you. There's gear and buffs you can get later on, that add on bonuses to your ability and strength, which helps a lot, but early on, it's a problem.
The game isn't really polished all that much either. There's been a few glitches I've run into that is really frustrating. The first is that the game is supposed to save after every move, but several times now my save files decided to just delete themselves or become something entirely different. Another issue I've been running into is, suddenly the game just won't let me move or skip any turns. The game is still running, I can open the quest menu, I just can't move.
The game needs a little more polishing, there's some mechanics that could really stand to be changed and there's a few bugs to squash, but besides that, the game is fairly fun and the price tag isn't bad. Even with the issues I have had, I still can recommend it to like minded players.

Hero Generations is an enjoyable, unique take on rougelikes with mechanics I'd love to see pop up in other games.
Just spent most of my afternoon playing this game. Like the namesake you are guiding your character through multiple generations of questing, monster slaying and loot gathering.
There's a lot to understand so I'd suggest playing the tutorial. It's a good primer for what you need to do to get started.
Here's a video of the tutorial - (It's probably still loading)
The way Hero Generations works is you start as a young adult. Each step you take in the world is 1 year and you have a number of years you are expected to live (shown on the right side of the screen). During that time you must build around towns to earn wealth, go fight monsters to gain fame, and ultimately woo some potential mates that have good genetics you can carry over to your children.
As you age you'll hit a few milestones in your life (Adult, Middle Age, Elder, Sage) ideally you want to mate earlier to get more picks at the gene pool so to speak.
The mechanics of starting a new generation are one of the unique features of this game that I find enjoyable. Depending on what traits you acquire along the way and those of your mate you'll be presented with a grid of cards, imo these cards represent genes. You pick a certain number of them to design your successor. It's a random mix that is influenced by yourself and the mate you choose and the number of picks are decided by certain traits, what town you're in and the age you are when you settle down.
Once picked you start over again and continue the legacy to to stop some evil. I didn't find the evil so I don't know what it is exactly. Your goal is to continue building up cities and earning power and wealth over time to eventually make your way to the end game (My first game I needed to get 30k fame in one life and go talk to some guy in the volcano world, I didn't make it =(
I found this game incredibly enjoyable. Trying to min/max the steps I was taking to figure out the best way to collect items. Figuring out that building 3 of the same building around a town changes the town into a special building. There's so much to find (I found a cave the appeared once I had a certain amount of fame).
Here's a video of my first playthrough from start to my untimely demise. (It's Still Loading It's about 90 minutes)

A couple things did bug me though.
The ability to only carry 2 items hinders the experience of actual exploration considering each step is precious life. It forces you to move to an empty space to drop the item then go back and pick up the other one.
This also creates a problem where you'll have multiple items on the ground in the same tile space with no real control over which item to pick up.
A simple mouse over menu on the right hand side to allow you to select what you want to interact with would be perfect.
The RNG with attacking is frustrating as well, when you reach a certain point you will find your self with 100+ strength, so when attacking you roll your strength  against your enemies and it does this from 0. So rolling super low against a monster you should easily beat becomes a bit aggravating.
Overall Hero Generations delivers a different kind of rougelike open world experience. One that I find charming, unique and overall enjoyable.
-Angelo @EAP

***Anti-recommendation.***
This is an incredibly bad port of the XBox360/PS3/Wii (Current-Gen) version and is riddled with unpatched bugs. Between this and the XBox/PS2/GameCube (Last-Gen) version with the same name, the Last-Gen version is better than the Current-Gen version by leaps and bounds.
Stealth, once a delicate management of light and sound, has been dumbed down to a traffic light indicator of "he probably can or can't see you."
The iconic night/thermal vision goggles which once defined this series have been rendered useless. The thermal mode has an effective radius of about 5 feet and can no longer see though thin doors or curtains. Night vision is little more than a pointless green filter which hardly gets any use due to the large number of daytime missions. For the most part, you'll just rely on your Soliton radar, anyway.
Cutscenes used in both versions of this game are completely devoid of the context provided by the Last-Gen story and feel more or less shoehorned into the Current-Gen version. Subsequently, the entire set-up for the sequel, SC:Conviction, is barely even hinted at. The Last-Gen version, by contrast, made the character motivations for the sequel hook abundantly clear.
If you want the stealth-based gameplay of the classic Splinter Cell, pick up the original or Chaos Theory. For the modern, Uncharted-style cover-based action shooter, just skip straight to Conviction.
Avoid the Current-Gen version of Double Agent at all costs. Save yourself the trouble and just watch the Let's Play of both versions of this game on YouTube.

To be honest, I would give this free-to-play game a recommendation if it isn't for important factor that basically unhinges the whole experience.
I do think this game is a good idea to have, especially as something to play when you don't really feel like playing a game that requires more investment on your part. Checking into this one and discovering what witty messages you get and seeing your representation go from rags to riches over real time is something that's really worth it. Yes, it's a clicker game, but one that shows some very tight design. For the majority of the 100+ hours that I've been in the game, it never grew tiring on me, and having both the Moon and Mars as places to further capitalize on helped to add a little variety.
But once you finish those places, you've basically finished the game. For me, Earth became a trickle around the sexseptuagintillion mark, where there's not enough cash flowing in for days... even weeks that would allow you to buy to reach more unlock milestones, and even the flow of profit-boosting angel investors becomes a trickle. Now... I could go into the in-game microtransactions and straight up buy more, but then again... I already did, to support the people who made this game. Now that I have to in order to get those last few achievements that require a kitted out Earth, it no longer feels worth it to pool more money into the game. Sure, there are events every month that allow for stuff that would profit boost Earth, but that stuff comes as a trickle as well.
Though the game has stood up for quite a while, it eventually ran straight into a paywall that makes total competitions frown. I consider the game finished, and I have to say... I really do get why this otherwise great game has the recent negative attention nowadays.
Good luck with your future games, Hyper Hippo. I hope you learn what you've done really well and recognize where you've screwed up.

Early review from release:
All I can say is:
CONSOLITIS
AVOID THIS UNTIL THEY UPDATE IT AND FIX IT.
With that in mind, I updated my drivers, fiddled with the settings for a bit and discovered that as long as I unlocked the frame rate from 30, and stayed off of 1080p and played on full, I got a whopping 60fps, with occasional dips down to 56ish.
On 1080p I get around 30-50 fps depending on how many zombies are on screen.
If you're still having issues after updating your drivers, then tweak the settings and see if a lower resolution works for you. After updating my drivers for AMD, I now have the ability to pick 16:10 resolutions, or maybe they snuck an update in and I didn't notice.
With that being said, I have run it with a titan 780 and an AMD 6900 series, and it now runs flawlessly.
The story is obviously♥♥♥♥♥♥ but the action is the same old DR1/2 action, refined slightly and multiplied by more zombies on screen at a time.
The Psycho fights seem interesting at first, but later on become muddled and boring with lots of potential squandered. But we aren't here for psychos, we are here to slay zombies.
The combo system appears to be full of substance early on, and so far so good.
Coop works like a charm, though occasionally joining a game you spectate fine, followed by sitting at a black screen indefinitely; reboot the game and pray, it works eventually. Once in, however, expect car lag if you aren't the driver and expect more popins, but it's a good sacrifice to be able to do everything in coop.
Apart from the few hiccups for the game running on Forge instead of framework, everything now runs smoothly, and I do recommend this game, as long as you aren't in it for the story and have blown through better zombie games.
And of course, you have a friend to play it with.
But bear in mind:
Compare this game with Dark Souls 1 PC release day.
At least until they fix a lot of the glaring issues.

While not necessary by any means for living room gaming, it is a welcome addition that I am starting to prefer over a standard 360/DS4 controller.
Pros:
***The ability remap buttons is a big win.  It allows one to find a mapping that fits their preference and style of play.
***The build quality is fantastic.  Everything from the package it arrives in, to the design for the backlight/battery slot is top notch.
***Back panel triggers are a great addition that every controller should have.  I typically remap jump and crouch to these buttons which frees up 2 face buttons for whatever I feel is a necessity.
***Valve is doing an excellent job with iterations and patches.  Any time I've had an issue or gripe, they seem to be reading my mind and addressing it in their newest patch.
***I know it's awkward looking but it's much comfier than you might expect.
Cons:
***It's a pretty hefty controller.  I have bigger hands and actually enjoy that, but my fiance cannot use this controller comfortably because it's so large.
***Still not sure how I feel about it when playing FPS games.  I can get by just fine, but I am certainly less accurate than with a controller.  Yes, you can get better twitch motion with this controller, but it's the finetuning (sniping, small adjustments, etc) that are throwing me off.  I will continue to tweak the settings though and update the review if I find something I am comfortable with.
***The number of customization options is probably overwhelming to most people.  Once you find a setting you like, it's wonderful, but getting there can be a pain.  Best route is to start with a popular community profile, and then tweak it from there.
***I was disappointed to get connection issues only 6-8 feet away from my computer with little to nothing in the way.  Using the extended dongle they provide and putting that centrally under my TV solved that issue though, so not really a big deal.
***Still too slow and clunky to work for fast paced RTS games, but it works GREAT for 4X strategy games where reaction time isn't as demanding.
Final Score:
***A solid 8/10 experience with the potential to be a 9/10 if Valve corrects one or two things.

Got this mostly because of the rocket league/portal 2 bonuses, but feeling it in my hand, it feels a lot more durable and hefty than a dualshock 3 or 4, just about equal to an Xbox 360 controller. The dual touch pads are really nice to have, not only is it easy to move around and see around you with them, but even simple Web browsing is better with it.
Overall here are the key details.
Pros:
-nice TouchPads with great feedback
-buttons feel really good when pressing down on them, not at all cheap feeling.
-extra grip buttons on the back are amazing for intense games like racing or shooting in order to have control while you shift gears or reload.
-really easy to personalize your controls, and foundations for them are easy to find thanks to the shared configurations.
-has an analog stick that definitely helps if you can't get used to using both TouchPads.
-gyro sensor opens up tons of possibilities in games/can also help with things that require precision.
-comes in a fancy looking box
Cons:
-non rechargeable batteries, and rechargeable batteries are not recommended for it according to the manual.
-takes a little getting used to in order to use the touch pads.
-it can be used to play games that weren't made with the controller in mind, which means that the in game prompts don't actually coincide with the buttons you configured.
-the shoulder buttons are a little stiff, but I imagine they'll loosen up with time.
-needs steam to be running if it's going to be used, otherwise it can be hard to configure and even then it's mostly for steam games.
It's a great controller and I highly recommend it for pc gaming. Definitely better than anything else you can get for pc.

Hero Generations is a light rouge-like game. The tension between adventuring with your powerful hero versus settling down before you are too old to properly train the next generation is quite nice. After 5 hours of play, I can say this is certainly a fun game, but I'm unsure of how long that fun will last.
In comparison to my favourite rouge-like -FTL- Hero Generations seems to offer more freedom and strategic choice, while still being relatively simple and accessible. Where FTL wins out is on theme and artwork. I like the multi-generation mechanic in Hero Generations, I just wish your potential mates didn't all look like ugly trolls with gender miss-matched names. This may have been meant as light humour or a statement on gender issues, but for me is a weak piece of world immersion. It would be easier to get excited about finding potential mates(male or female) if they looked a little nicer.
Hero Generations is a small game of exploration, adventure, and strategic choice with some weaknesses in presentation. I'd recommend this game if you can pick it up on sale.

Let me start out by saying that I've been a big fan of the series since day one.  The intensity and excitement of navigating through overwhelming zombie hordes and narrowly escaping is unmatched by any game.  All three installments of the series succeed in making me feel like I'm in a movie.  Each game has improved upon it's predecessor, changing or removing features that were annoying or slowed the game down.  One example of this is escort missions. It used to be that every survivor had to be brought back to the safe house, which is fun to an extent, but could be terribly frustrating at times.  They made the game more stream-lined by having some of the survivors require only that you save them or help them in some way.  This means you can rescue them without having to go all the way back to a safe zone, then you can be on your way.  I also like how they made the survivors better able to defend themselves, and there are even talent points that can further improve their fighting skills.  Yes, now you can spend talent points as you level up, which allows you to customize your character to your play style.  Vehicles in DR3 are alot more usefull than in the first two Dead Rising games, as you are outside (instead of trapped in a mall) and have to travel long distances.  You can modify vehicles into killing machines too.  Lose your vehicle?  Well I had fun just jumping from car to car on their roofs.  Climbing and jumping have been drastically improved and the movement in general is a lot less stiff.  Finally, the boss fights I've done so far have been challenging, dynamic, and kick♥♥♥♥♥  All aspects of the game are substantially better.  Where the first two games were pretty similar to each other, this one stands out as the pinnacle...dare I say, the best zombie game ever?  So far, the answer is yes, prompting me to write my first review ever.
Now, I will briefly address the elephant in the room.  People have been raging out that the game won't run on their computers.  Well, this is a truly next-gen game.  I built my rig to be competitive with consoles so that I can play games like this.  People that are trying to play on laptops and under-geared desktops shouldn't write bad reviews just because the game crashed at the title screen.  If you didn't get past the capcom logo when starting up the game, how can you say the game sucks?  Sounds to me like you didn't even play the game.  I played the game for hours non-stop on the day I got it, interupted only because the sun came up and indicated that I had lost track of reality.  Here's a list of my specs so you know what's required to play next-gen console games on pc:
gpu: GeForce GTX 780 Ti
RAM: 16 gigs
CPU: AMD FX-8350 Vishera 8-core (4.0 GHz)
Motherboard: Asus Crosshair V

Very little of the problems with this game involve the gameplay, bugs, or anything related to the intended aspects of this game. Nearly all of the problems come from the community. (Except balancing. Dinosaurs win every round. Period.)
1: Roleplay Servers
You might be lucky to find one highly populated server that is Team Deathmatch. I rarely see anyone in the Get To the Chopper gamemodes (both of which are very fun). Survival was just added, but definently needs some work.
9/10 servers are ♥♥♥♥ing Freeroam/Roleplay servers. Littered with 10 year olds pretending to have their "territories" and anyone who doesn't want to sound like a ♥♥♥♥ing idiot just crouches around the Tyrants. I don't know WHY they prefer that♥♥♥♥♥♥over the base game.
2: Overpriced Market
Look at the Market. Now look at maybe, I don't know, page 5. Or search "Raptor" or something. Chances are you will see two skins of the same "rarity" (Uncommon, Legendary, Rare, etc) having a price difference of over 40 USD. Don't get me wrong, the cosmetics are a fun little addition, but the tiny community that this game has gets to choose their prices.  Let's get an example (for the sake of the argument) that there are two skins for the Novaraptor. Blue skin, and Red skin. Blue skin could be a measily 4 cents. Awesome right? Look over at Red skin. 56 dollars. That's what happens when you let your tiny community choose the prices, because then you get this♥♥♥♥♥♥ The idiots who think they can cash in on that are a dime a dozen.
So why am I recommending this game?
The only way to fix these problems is to get more people playing. The larger the community, the more people will play with the action. The roleplayers can have their servers, and we will still have tons of servers playing GTTC and TDM. the prices will eventually lower themselves out. This will also allow more feedback to the developers to help with balancing.

All I did to fix some of the FPS and screen tear issues was this...
1. Go to the Dead Rising 3 folder, where game installed
2. Make a text file called ini
3. Add the line gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate = True
4. Save your changes and close the file
5. Place it in the same folder as exe before running the game
(Note: After apply this file, if you are facing crashes, slow performance or low FPS then you should delete this file.)

TL;DR - I know my play time looks insane. You will assuredly not get 190 hours of this game, but you will get 2 of the most fun hours you've had gaming in a while. Buy now!
As my first foray into speedrunning, this game has given me several dozen hours of entertainment beyond what would be expected by reasonable gamers. But I am trying to be unbiased, and think of this game from a casual standpoint.
I still recommend it glowingly.
A quirky 2D platformer with a laser-sharp, utilitarian design approach, Out There Somewhere gives you a light dash of shooting combat, a gentle hint of exploration, and a core game built around puzzle-platforming with a 2D teleport gun. It is bookended by space shooter segments that some reviewers have taken issue with - I won't argue with them for finding these segments disjunct, but I still enjoy them anyway.
It is worth noting that the pace at which new mechanics are introduced is absolutely stellar - far better than many A-list titles. You get a sense for what each button does, a scenario or two that changes your approach, and then a wholly new element just as you are getting comfortable.
It seems like the biggest complaint from most reviewers is the game's short length. Most people should have an easy time earning the "Swift Success" achievement on their first play, it's true, but the collectibles should keep completionists occupied for another hour or so after - they even require a little meta-gaming! At a two dollar price point, this is plenty of game for your buck, and it's not often that this caliber of level design, soundtrack, and art style find their way into a two-dollar title.
I really like it, but I also like this whole genre of platformer, so purchase accordingly.

This puzzler is a limited form of Bejewelled with a weak clicktext plot to "motivate" you to play their version of Bejewelled.  Click the orbs to put the same colours together, with the mild added goal of collecting different colours to progress the story along (which you will probably click through).
Graphics: Simple but workable enough.  They didn't go retro and they hired an artist of some kind, although the assets are fairly low quality.
Gameplay: Bejewelled.  Ripping off someone else's idea for a game doesn't get thumbs up.
Technical: The game works and is stable but there's no graphics support for 4K.  The game is simple enough that it can run on a tablet or in a web browser.
There's no justification for this being on Steam and no justification for asking to be paid for porting a tablet game to PC.  There's no justification for just ripping off Bejewelled.   If you like Bejewelled, play it.  Or Candy Crush.  But if that appeals to you, you're probably not on Steam at all.

Pros:
+Style points.
+Amount of customization is through the roof, is being added to with every update, and can be adjusted mid-game at any time.
+The two under-handle buttons are a welcome addition.
+Triggers click if you press far enough.
+Trackpad feedback is great for thumb spatial awareness and gives the illusion of scrolling a mouse wheel.
+Latest update allows for mapping customization for none-steam games as well..
+A good middle ground between the precision of a mouse and a controller. But...
Cons:
-...learning curve is as strong as you'd expect.
-Requires batteries to use wireless.
-Feels like it weighs slightly lighter than most other 1st party controllers without battries inside.
-Bumpers are uncomfortable in comparison to 360 bumpers.
-Not great for games which need precision D-pad movement, like 2D platformers.
-Not great for NBA2K right stick manual shooting.
-My (and from what I've read online, many) Steam Controller often gets one of the batteries jamed inside. Be sure to look up one of the many articles that already talk about work arounds to this issue.
Summary:
The first week of having the controller it was just okay for me. Much more enjoyable for a handfull of shooters, but not much different from a normal controller for most games.
Now after a month, I adore this thing. While still not as presise as a mouse and keboard, now that I've overcome the learning curve, the Steam Controller makes couch pc gaming so much more enjoyable. It has been nearly impossible to go back to a 360 controller. This is now my go to controller for 99 of the 100+ games in my library.
While the Steam Controller isn't worth throwing out all your previous controllers for, I highely reccomend you still make one an addition to your controller collection.

This game looks cute and beautiful, and seems to be a nice match-3 game mingled with RPG element.
However, if you are looking for a game like the Puzzle Quest series, you won't find anything that can even see the dust at the tail of PQ; you should get 10,000,000/you must build a boat instead, which are much better than the Legened of Fae.

I had been looking forward to playing this game since I first made this steam account. The artstyle is appealing, you might even call it cute, and a match 3 game with combat sounds like it might be a fun time.
As it turns out, Legend of Fae is pretty good!
It is a match 3 game with combat, as I mentioned earlier, where you match gems(orbs?) of an element (Fire, Water, Wind and Earth) to defeat enemies. The enemies can also have elemental affinities so you can't just cast whatever at an enemy and get by. There's also an upgrade system where you can choose from better elemental attacks, combo spells and summons. You can also respec your skill tree if you want to try something different. There's a surprising amount of depth and different ways to play, which is nice.
I played the game on Hard and it's worth noting that near the end of the game it gets HARD. If you aren't in total control of what's going on in the combat in the later levels you will drop so quickly that it's kind of frustrating. I also ran into a couple of points where I had to respec several times because it felt like the skills I had just weren't enough. It is a puzzle game (kind of) so you can "figure it out" in a sense.
The story is also pretty interesting, it definitely goes some places over the course of the game that I didn't really expect it to. If there were somehow a sequel that was a continuation of the events of this game (as unlikely as that may be) I'd be on it from day one.
So yeah, if you want a little lite-RPG in your gem matching escapades then you should probably pick this up. Maybe stick to casual mode if you don't want to have too hard of a time in the combat.

"Endless Fluff" may be an apt description of this game, but not in a bad way. The story is cute, the characters are cute -- even the monsters are cute! But cuteness does not detract from the plot and gameplay. This game actually has an engaging storyline, which one may not expect from what appears to be a basic "match three" puzzle game. While the puzzle aspects of the game can occasionally become tedious, the story and RPG elements keep you coming back after you die. And I actually do like the RPG elements and the ability to upgrade your various elements in order to perform special attacks when you do "match" the correct jems together. In all, I do highly recommend this game.

The combination of RPG mechanics and puzzle game is an oddly rare thing, even though RPGs have classically designed their combat systems in the vein of puzzles.  Only a game like 10,000,000 really tries to do the same thing.
Still, compared to a game like 10,000,000, it's a little more forgiving, colorful, and generally fun.
The game plays on a split screen.  You need to fill up your little power jars by matching blocks in a match-three game similar to Bejewelled. (However, you can make swaps that are not matches.  You just get a power bonus if you keep chains of consecutive matches going.)  When you need to launch an attack, you tap the top half of the screen, and can start tapping your elemental buddies to have them throw down attacks and heals and shields.  Otherwise, you keep your head down in the gems you need to match as rapidly as possible.  At least for me, I'm often so focused on making a big chain I totally forget to look up and realize the heroine has stopped walking, and there's a monster about to eat her face...
It sometimes gets a little hectic, especially against the optional bosses, where you're setting up some big chain you think will help you and in the last two seconds, you took half a dozen attacks that just quartered your health bar, but if things go that fast, you're probably fighting something out of your league, anyway...
The RPG mechanics are quite interesting, as well.  Special piece rewards for good times in a mission (go back to a difficult one with more powerups if you need more power to score a perfect run) are spent instead of gaining XP.  You get offered a path of specializing in elements or going for a broad generalist path with a few special bonuses.
All-in-all, it's a fun game for someone who enjoys the occasional puzzle game, RPGs, and has the ability to multitask a bit, and I'd recommend it to anyone who lies upon the intersecction of those three pools.

First impression: If you liked Puzzle Quest, but thought it was too slow, Legend of Fae is for you.
EDIT:
Second impression: First impression still holds. However, unlike Puzzle Quest, Legend of Fae is...well, easy. I seem to be done with the tutorial parts and have entered the actual meat of the game. You're given an option between two difficulties, easy and hard. I picked hard. Thus far, everything has been an absolute pushover. Each level has an "expert" bonus target for completing it in a certain time and with a certain score, and I've been able to amply reach both goals on every level, often doubling the score and halving the time.
Not to say it hasn't been fun. It has. I'm just also waiting for my HP bar to dip below 90%, so that I actually need to heal myself.
EDIT:
Third impression: First impression still holds.
The game's difficulty has started noticably ramping up. It's still nowhere near "too hard", though I have begun to miss score and/or time goals by smallish margins. Perhaps I spoke too soon on the too easy part.
There's also a bonus boss I unlocked a while back. I've tried it a few times, but it utterly destroys me every time.

At first this game might just seem like a remake of primal carnage with a subtitle and some new skins, but dig deeper and you will find it has many new features and improvements over the original. One of the biggest changes is that humans now have a secondary gun option and have items which they can throw, which can help teamates or hurt dinos. The introduction of the acrocanthosaurus is something great that the original never had or is going to (probably), and is not just a different looking tyrant that does the exact same thing, all three tyrants have ups and downs. The spino has the most health but is the slowest, the t-rex is slightly faster than spino but has a bit less health, and the acro is the fastest but has the least health. There is also a new mode similar to call of dutys zombie mode, but with dinosaurs! It is called survival, and like its name suggests, you have to survive against many waves of dinosaurs, 20 to be exact. Wave 5 and 15 are specials waves, so far being a compy wave and hunter raptor waves. Wave 10 and 20 are boss waves, so far being a alpha novaraptor and acrocanthosaurus. There is only one map so far but more will be added in future, as well as more bosses. There are also a few new maps, and while I still think the original maps are best, they are nice additions to the game. The only problem i have with this game is that a lot of servers are roleplay servers, but there are still a good amount of team deathmatch and survival servers, but hardly any get to the chopper servers, which is a shame. Another problem i have with this game is that it has slightly worse optimization than the original, which is odd considering this had more time to improve its optimization, so people who could not run the original primal carnage very well will have even more trouble running this game, but im sure the devs will sort it out. So in conclusion if you were a fan of the original or just a dino fan in general, I would definitely reccomend this game :)
Edit: Since the November 15th update optimization of this game has been improved dramatically, so even if you dont have a great pc or laptop, it should run just fine now. They have also added many new and interesting features to the game, which you can view on the community page

I have played this game a lot, and I'll explain why I'm not recommending it.
I was a big RO2 player, and when I heard there was a Vietnam game coming I couldn't wait.
The game has been out a while, and the recent update has done nothing to fix three glaring errors.
First: If an enemy appears in front of you, expect your game to freeze up and lag.
I have a decent laptop and fibre connection, so I usually have low ping. Nearly every time an enemy appears, the game will 'jolt' and result in missing shots, the weapon not firing even though you are clicking the mouse, the weapon not firing after 4 or 5 shots in sucession and even teamkilling due to the lag. The amount of times this has happened to me is absolutely ridiculous.
Second: Hitreg.
HITREG HITREG HITREG. If you are right in front of an enemy and fire into their center mass, expect them to take no damage whatsoever and be killed by them. Regardless of lag. I've seen enemies have multiple people firing on them and take absolutely no damage.
Third: Connection to host lost.
If this appears, you'll lose all progress you've made in game. I've reached rank 25 four times now.
When the game plays well, it's great. But until the issues above are adressed, it's near unplayable.
It really saddens me to give this a not recommended rating, but with the recent update not fixing any of these issues, it's needed.

I try to be unbiased when writing reviews for games around here in STEAM especially because this is where I can tell people if the game is great or not. Well, in my opinion this game is worth the check. The game has a lot of places to explore and a fairly large player base of RPGMMO players who love the game. When I started out I had no clue what to do or what to expect. So I kindly asked around for help and guidance and man did I get the best community treatment Ive had yet. The players welcomed me with open arms and attended to my needs. When I had problems with quests or overall the game itself the people were kind enough to join my party and help out in my quest even though they had better things to do. The player base in this game is really amazing and kind from my experience and Ive got to give them credit for that, because if a game like this has a kind player base that tends to help other players who just started out then sign me up! It sure beats the Xbox Live community of 8 year olds screaming "360 NO SCOPE!!!" at the top of their lungs whenever I hit a trickshot and then calls me a hacker -_-
So you might be wondering about the overall gameplay mechanics and core gameplay right? Well here is my initial reaction to it. For the gameplay I found the settings to be "Tweakable" this means that you can basically move things like the move counters, character health bar, Quest Box, Item Box, ETC in a way so that it wont hinder you or stop you from seeing the amazing scenery that this anime-ish MMORPG successfully shows you. Moving on to the core gameplay I found that the experience is what you would find in any MMORPGs nowadays. I admit its pretty generic due to the fact that you are called a "Hero" and you must find your true purpose is kind of already played out since about a million other people have been told the same, but lets move on with our lives and forget the fact that you arent special in this game. The maps are well designed and the monster AI is intuitive at most. In fact I can say that the monsters or enemies in this game are pretty well balanced and are reactive to the players attacks. Therefore this game brings out what it promised at most which is a anime-ish MMORPG aimed at people like me who want to play something that resembles a JRPG but without all the complicated add ons that World Of Warcraft has. Plus, this game is literally FREE so yeah...I gave my wallet some relief there.
BUT! we all know there is a flaw for every game ever made. For Aura Kingdom I think its pretty clear that the pros of this game is pretty visible. It has the fancy graphics, textures, and plot to draw any anime fan or a RPG fan in the mix while maintaining a simple and easy to use interface that almost everyone can use. However, the flaws in my opinion is the latency issues that occur when you havent logged on for a while or if you have a weak connection. When having a weak connection you get a lot of un-rendered textures and areas in the map that doesnt even show up. Also, I should point out that even if this game has a large player base that is supportive and tending to others there is also a majority of people who are not too kind and are almost annoying to deal with. Not only that sometimes quests can be a hassle because sometimes there is no one willing to join your party due to the fact that they have problems of their own, this being due to the fact that there are literally a ton of people who are above the level of a beginner so the beginners have to seek other beginners in order to form parties and complete quests. And finally, the social interface. I think it should be approved upon due to it being a hassle to add people you meet, be it they joined your party or they want you to join theirs. The fact that you have to type in someone's name in order to even send them a request is but an annoyance and a waste of game time. Would you really want to type out "xXMLGquickscoper420blazeXx" to your search bar and then click "Send Friend Request" everytime you want to add a new player to your ever growing list of companions and pals online! HELL NO! That is the thing that annoys me the most in this game....the overly complicated social interface...They got everything right on simple gameplay mechanics and amazing design of the game overall but the social comms are all way to messed up and complicated.
Anyways I hope you guys enjoyed this review and if you wouldnt mind please check out my profile for a youtube link for my channel where I do game reviews but with the use of my voice, I also do cosplay(occasionallty), and overall gaming content. Hope you guys have a fun time in Aura Kingdom and I wish you all good luck and happy fortune!

Leveling up starts out extremely fast and i like that. i wanted to get to the end game content fast. I wanted to reach level cap asap and start PvPing. As you quest, you learn new abilities at a good pace, you can easily auto-path from one place to another so it flows really well. quest path is linear so it's pretty much going along for a ride, slaying mobs and gathering items like nobody's business. there is a ton of dialog, i skipped as much as i could, seeing as it's not exactly a riveting story in my opinion.
The UI could stand a lot of improvement. it's somewhat customizable but not nearly as much as i'd like. The graphics are ok, the anti aliasing sucks and i can't configure it with the Nvidia control panel but i used sweetFX and it looks better. you can tell the game is optimized for japaneze localization as a lot of the english text is awkward, not fitting into its box, missing spaces, etc. it was translated pretty well but the ui is just not quite optimal for english it seems.
The class system is neat, you pick a main class and then when you hit level 40 you pick a secondary class and start learning those abilities. those abilities have longer cooldowns, however, and don't benefit from your masteries or talent specs.
Anyway, the reason i am losing interest is because as i hit level 60, the game became extremely grind-y. the pace of leveling drastically slows down, and until level 62 you're basically just doing dailies. your Eidolon, basically a combat pet that everyone has, doesn't level with you, you ahve to feed it XP crystals, and having fed one that was almost my same level since around 30, with every xp crystal i had got my hands on until then, it still fell behind. There are a lot of things you have to grind items for in this game, that's one of them. you can buy or farm for these XP crystals, "secret stones," scrolls and shards, crafting ingredients, etc... a lot like WoW, but it's just not clear at all on the best way to farm or grind for this stuff, and when you do figure it out it's disappointing how long it will take.
the game makes money with an in-game shop where you can pay real money to get stuff, not that it's p2w but you can save a lot of farming and grinding from there.
So at level 60 i decided to see if i could stop leveling and just start PvPing. then i discovered that pvp is split into only two tiers: 60 and below and above 60. and battlegrounds are scheduled, with 3-4 occurring per day. so to farm honor points for pvp gear you can't just queue into BGs over and over, you have to log in at the right time. and before you get this gear, you're going to get eaten alive in the arena events and such.
as PvP is my favorite thing to do in these games, i was really hoping to be able to jump in and get decent pvp gear before too long, but there's just not a good way to farm "war coins" and "valor coins" at all, to get the gear. Not to mention the game's content is pretty much capped out at 60 even though the level cap is 80, so i have no clue how people get to level 80 seeing as it's taking forever to get just 10% of the way to level 61.
the game went from super fast-paced and easy to ridiculously slow and confusing. and the pvp system sucks. so i think i'll just hop in once in a while to do daily quests and large battlegrounds when i can until i finally have decent pvp gear and can actually have some fun.
