Hero Generations is a beautifully simple but extremely addictive game. It's combination of Rogue-like elements, with a 4X twist make the game easy to learn, but difficult to master. This really is one of those games where only through playing do you actually get a sense of how much it sucks you in.
If you'd like to see some gameplay, I covered a beta version a week or two before release.
You take control of a Hero, with a limited life-span. Every move is one year of your life (and lost battles cost you more). How do you use this time? Do you explore, looking for treasures, wealth and fame? Do you go off in search of monsters to slay? Do you build and improve on the towns to make life a little easier for the next generation? Whatever you decide, you need to find a mate before it's too late, settle down and have a child; a new Hero to continue the adventure.
Pre-Release comments:
Despite my Steam playtime, I've have put many hours into the various prototype, alpha and beta versions of this game outside of the Steam client.
Upon release, the game did not include a full-screen option. However, full-screen has now been added to the options to allow for a HD full screen experience!
All I can say is; it's fun, it's simple, it's addictive. Give it a try!

My Quick Look on Hero Generations:
The game bills itself as a 4x Strategy Roguelike RPG, with the enticing McGuffin being that each turn is one (1) year of time that has passed. It's an interesting mechanic when applied against average human life expectancy.  There is always an urgency regarding your movement and what you set out to accomplish before going to the nearest town to have your next offspring.
The end goal of the game centers around how much fame (any particular generation) you've attained during their particular life-cycle.  More or less, fame is your score and you're trying to get a high score, which are reflected against a leaderboard on the main menu.
These are the basics to the game, which fosters a very tight play-cycle on any particular generation lasting around three (3) minutes on average.  There are methods to increase your life expectancy (which requires either time or luck) but the steady beat of time and unlucky battles widdles away what little life you have.
The game is very easy to pick up and learn with only a (optional) five minute tutorial to get you up to speed.  Animations are crude but get the job done.  Scaling up the game window to accommodate your display actually works against the game, especially during the battle sequences which can make the game (visually) seem not fully baked.
All told, Hero Generations is like witnessing a machine in action.  All of the cogs and pieces have a purpose and fit together perfectly.  But, at least for me, it never went further than a cold, calculated strategy machine and never really addressed the powerful metaphor of how our short our lives can be.
Having said that, it's still a fun game and I enjoyed it.

This First Impressions was Done with a key obtained from the developer.
Hero Generations is a solid game and is a bunch of fun, and the mechanics that are within are interesting. The idea of building up a generation to try to build towards fame and gold is cool, and there's a lot of complexity to it, but at times, there's too much complexity. However, if you want a game that will reward you from learning mechanics and the world within it, Hero Generations is up your alley, because that's what it does best. But if you get frustrated with RNG elements, or want a high skill ceiling that's not based on strategy....you're probably not going to enjoy it.
+:
-Lots of options. Lots and lots of options. From buildings to items to traits.
-Rewards planning and taking advantage of the RNG elements to your advantage.
-Changes in your characters over time are pretty cool and a level of immersion to it.
-Upgrades feel substanial. Like you need them.
-Mechanics work well with each and there's obvious thought put into them working with each other. Feels woven together.
-Difficult, to a good extent. Doesn't hand you everything.
-Lots of replayability.
- Art style is nice.
-:
-Goes one step too far at times. Building degradation is a fine example of it.  Simplicity might have been better in some cases.
-RNG elements can get frustrating, especially when you lose a couple of bad rolls in a row.
-Doesn't use screen space efficiently.
-Tooltips would have added a lot to the experience.
-Doesn't have a knockout punch: something that blows your mind. The thing is, it feels like it was just a  tiny bit off from doing that.

The story is interesting so far, with a very likable and unique protagonist. Welcome to the beautiful city of Los Perdidos! Now strip down to your underpants and smack some zombies in the face with a traffic cone.
Survival may not be always be pretty in Dead Rising 3, but it's fun to roam around in this LA-inspired setting for Capcom's latest take on a zombie apocalypse. You'll be able to hop in a car and traverse from one end of this city to the other in about five minutes, but the thrill is in the journey rather than the destination. And if you happen to be making the trek on a RollerHawg, a combination of a steamroller and motorcycle, that journey will cheerily mulch a couple of hundred zombies into paste.
The original Dead Rising took place in a shopping mall and contrasted its zombie outbreak with the everyday sights of clothes shops, food courts, and pharmacies. Its sequel ratcheted its lens of consumerism up to Fortune City, its gaudy casino complex freshly built upon the smouldering wreckage of Las Vegas. Dead Rising 3 now takes aim at an entire city, but the themes are the same as before, even though its colour palette is certainly duller. Everything in Los Perdidos is a shop, and you are here to consume.
Dead Rising 3 takes to the the west coast in an environment large enough to need splitting across the districts of Ingleton, Sunset Hills, South Almuda, and Central City. But Los Perdidos is built to be a playground rather than a world, and its shop windows are tantalisingly stuffed with countless opportunities to bludgeon, slice, and splatter the undead hordes roaming the streets in their thousands. Few games offer such breadth in their potential weaponry or number of potential targets, and dismembering the undead with hub caps, pogo sticks, and coat hangers still feels both novel and hugely entertaining.
It's all well and good attempting to take out a zombie with a handbag while wearing a summery dress and medieval helmet, but at Dead Rising 3's core the game takes the idea of combo weapons, introduced in its predecessor, and runs amok. New hero Nick Ramos is no longer constrained to stitching together his weapons of mass distraction at a wayward workbench, with the recipes for these 100-odd combinations found in blueprints scattered around the city.
This is the first of Dead Rising 3's many efforts to smooth some of the series' harsh edges, and is ultimately a positive change that further highlights Dead Rising 3's huge focus on crafting, giving players the freedom to build new weapons as soon as they become available. The game justifies this contextually by making Nick a mechanic, one who is ultimately looking to escape the Los Perdidos by cobbling together a plane, but his character arc and mysterious tattoo are largely ignored until the latter chapters of the game, with Capcom instead focusing on the arsenal and body count.
The opportunities for raucous carnage are immense, though many of the combo weapons return from Dead Rising 2, and there's a giddy pleasure obtained from running around in a comedy costume (vintage tennis get-up, anyone?) and playing around with your new toys. Grab the corresponding blueprint and then mix some chemicals with a lead pipe to get the Pukes O' Hazard, a vomit-inducing club. The chest beam, made by combining microwave and a motorcycle engine, shoots out thick, meaty blasts of energy that can atomise a nearby crowd, and Street Fighter fans will eagerly unite an engine with some boxing gloves and shoryuken into the nearest zombie with the rocket gloves. Or, if you fancy introducing an element of randomised chaos, there's always the sentry cat.
New to Dead Rising 3 are super combo weapons, themselves made from taping together two or more constructed weapons. The results are usually devastating. The Fire Reaper, for instance, first requires you to make a Grim Reaper (scythe and katana, very good at clearing at groups) and then further combine that with a gasoline tank. Vehicles, now central to navigating the bridges and tunnels which connect Los Perdidos' districts, can also be fused together. These homebrew constructions, such as the forklift-meets-fireworks display Forkwork, are able to withstand and deal more damage, and quickly prove to be as invaluable as a good electric crusher, defiler, boomer axe, or freedom bear.
The outlandish outfits and versatile weapons clash with Dead Rising 3's ceaselessly dangerous environment, with more and more undead pumped into the streets of Los Perdidos as the game's five-day narrative progresses. Nick's swings are sluggish and imprecise, his movement heavy, and his mix of light and heavy attacks is designed for hacking away at a pack of enemies rather than individuals, which is fine until you need to take on a straggler or boss. Fighting is more about crowd control than outright aggression, and evasion is usually the best option despite having an inventory stuffed with kooky items.
Weapons and vehicles degrade and eventually break, and the game is all too happy to dish out a fatal punishment to players who venture unprepared into the middle of a horde. Zombies line every corner, constantly swarm out of vents, and Dead Rising 3 is also very much the kind of game where the walking dead will also quite happily fall from the skies, or at least off the top of a nearby building.
While everything in Dead Rising ticks along to its own in-game clock, the game layers together its plot-advancing story missions with dozens of other tasks in which you have to save survivors scattered around Los Perdidos, or dispatch its seven psychotic humans, each based loosely around the seven sins. These include a crazed physician, someone aggressively tending to a Japanese garden, and a man so lazy he'd rather attempt to kill you with automated drones than lift a finger.
Survivors, meanwhile, set Nick another task that needs to be accomplished, which usually involves either fetching something, such as a pack of scattered tarot cards, or ferrying someone to a destination. One surprisingly affecting mission has you guide an elderly woman around the city while she tells of her bygone years, offering a rare glimpse of life in a dead city. The game also randomly encourages you to smash through swathes of zombies in order to clear paths for stranded survivors. While many of these missions lack the eccentricity and charm of previous games--there's nothing in Dead Rising 3 quite like carrying a hungover showgirl who was sleeping off a zombie outbreak--the main incentive behind these acts of benevolence remains the same: rack up huge amounts of Prestige Points, which levels up Nick and expands his abilities and moveset.
Some survivors eventually join your party, where they can be armed with the game's less flamboyant weapons to fight alongside you, or can be led back to one of the game's safe areas and stored for later deployment. Keeping survivors alive was a key part of the first two games, as leading them to safety was how objectives were completed, but Dead Rising 3 considers it more of an optional afterthought. Safe rooms, scattered around each of Los Perdidos' four districts, also contains recharging lockers that can spawn in any item or combo weapon you've previously used. This is a game far more focused on having you slaughtering the undead than continually scavenging for items, though it's not always a change for the better. Dead Rising 3's accessibility makes it easier to rack up the kills, but infinitely spawning weaponry ultimately robs the game of the deeper connection I forged with Willamette mall or Fortune City. I can still remember the route to Colombian Roastmasters in the first Dead Rising, and jumping off the edge of the coffee shop to land on the balcony with the katana. I couldn't tell you much at all about Los Perdidos.

This is by far the most cleverly designed, most flexible and feature-rich controller available on the market today!

control your desktop with it when Steam is running in the background so it might be possible, too.

I just got the Steam Controller today.  The USB cord it came with was cut and doesn't work.  I used wireless, obviously, to try out a few things and still didn't seem satisfied.  The touch pad thing on the right doesn't do justice for the kind of games I'd like to play with the controller, but it works decent with some I don't usually play with.  I would much rather prefer 2 joysticks like any PS/XBOX controller, and for the left and right trigger not to have to click to register.  Also, wouldn't mind the Y, X, B, A buttons being in a more unawkward place.

BLUF: It's 'different' than an Xbox or PS controller; expect a multi-day re-training period.  That said it's got a lot going for it and I think Steam hit their desired mark.
Long Story: So I've been working with this for about 10 days now.  Was initially disappointed but figured that Steam doesn’t do much half-hearted, and this was delayed / recycled a couple times so I needed to give it a fair shot.
- Out of the box - it's nicely packaged and comes with all necessary components.  It's larger than an Xbox remote and the angle you hold it at is a little tighter (so your elbows would be closer to your side instead of further out).  Initially felt much lighter then Xbox, but on side-by-side it's about the same.  I think the 'light' feeling comes because weight is roughly the same for a larger object.  The force feedback is also about the same, but i can actually feel it through the touchpad to my thumb, which is nice.  Also noticed it has some paddles under the controller adding a couple more button options.
- Customization - This was my first, biggest frustration.  I knew there was a way to download others custom configs for the controller, but couldn’t find anything in the manual.  You must load up steam in big picture mode, then look at the options.  Absolute must for each of your games.
- Web browsing - I spent my first 3 days just doing this, and it rocks.  Steam definitely found a way to make the web work from your couch.  Took a day or two to get used to it (over a wireless mouse), but now my preferred method unless at a desk.  R/L clicks are your triggers, scroll up/down is a clock-wise motion on L-dpad, paddles do page F/B, R-dpad is minute mouse movements.  Damn nicely done.
- 2-D Games - I tried this with a couple 2-d games (Sword of the Stars: The pit & Revolution Ace) not noticeably different than any other controller; a wash.
- FPS - Then came the challenge of some fallout4.  Was REALLY angering to start with until I figured out the controller customized downloads.  After that it was...alright.  The minute control took a bit of getting used to, but as I said at the start it's designed to be different and you have to give yourself time to learn it.  After a few days I found I preferred it to my previous Xbox setup.  I then switched to a standard keyboard & mouse setup which was a vastly superior setup.  In the end boils down to: FPS is always best done with KB&M, but if you want to use a controller this has been my best experience.
- Final thoughts: It's definitely different.  You MUST give yourself a few days to learn how it works and teach new muscle movements. Given that it's got a LOT of potential, mine will be well used, and I recommend to any others.

SPOILERS AHEAD! In a sense this is actually 2 games, so I will talk about them separately.
The shmup section was short but sweet, I am terrible at these kinds of games but I enjoyed it. My only issue is that your gun won't fire at full speed if you hold down the button, requiring you to mash for the most damage potential. I died as soon as the boss shot his laser, and though I'd need to restart until...
The puzzle-platforming section, which is the meat of the game. Crashing on the planet and needing to find ship parts (conveniently the same model as the shmup upgrades) reminded me of Knytt (in a good way), and so did the slower pace and early lack of combat. Puzzle progress felt steady and fun, though the "double shot" puzzle I managed to solve without learning the proper trick, stunting my progress in the next few rooms. I really enjoyed having a "teleport" gun instead of a "portal" gun, which felt very fresh as a mechanic. Combat was passable, with notable frustration trying to hit the flying bats, and not knowing how long the boss would take to defeat. The biggest issue I had was with NPC conversations, ending the conversation would not close the text box right away and another press would start it again; extremely frustrating.
Going back to shmup at the end was unexpected and exciting, and I didn't die to the laser! I was a bit sad that it ended, but that title call-out was a great wrap up to the story. The art and sound were excellent throughout, with a special mention to alien NPC designs.

Fun, however, after beating the boss, I was like aw yeah now I get to explore more of the galaxy. Nope, that's all folks. Game finished. It probably took less than two hours to complete and it was only slightly difficult. I was notified that this game was 90% off, which is why I bought it. But either steam lied and it wasn't on sale, or the full price is $20, because I spent $2 on it. I would probably recommend this game for two dollars, about a dollar an hour is not bad.
What I liked the most was the learning curve and the difficulty - it's set just right.

Charming visuals, surprisingly fast paced battle, all under the guise of a match-three puzzle game.  Making it through each stage gives points to level up the special things that happen when you destroy gems, and there is actually a story to follow along with as well.  Considering the dearth of reviews this has is sad, because there is a sweet and interesting game to be played here, and anyone who enjoys a good story and some fast thinking puzzle game action should grab this up.

What do you do when the latest puzzle quest is a stupid Pay to win scam? You find an alternative.
Legend of Fae is one alternative, though this actually was released well befored Marvel Puzzel Quest, but I have just learned of this thanks to an Indie Royale Bundle. While I'm not generally into match three games, match three hybrids always catch my attention (self Note, need to play more Gyromancer)
Despite Valve's tendency to improperly label games, this is also an RPG of sorts, due the battle system and skill tree.
The game is about a girl named Claudia, with a disease that caused her to loose her leg, and now due to a replacement leg she gained, caused her to walk with a limp. Since she isn't able to farm like her parents, she ends up staying with her Uncle who is an engineer and has a magical latern that we later learn that only Claudia is able to figure out. This latern, for some reason allows her to match color gems and gain mana "Puzzle Quest style" for spells (this may have been explained somehow and I may have just missed it). Though, gems are switched with a horizontal cursor like Tetris Attack, which unfortunately can put you in a position where you can't match the gems you needs for half a minute or longer, which is awful admist battle. While the story isn't going to win any awards, it's certainly a much more interesting start than "The world is under attack from the Big Bad" (which isn't to say that won't happen later in the game).
The game overworld is a linear path that does appear to have some forks/deviations later in the road. Each level involves moving Claudia to the other end of the level, encountering battles along the way. Movement is performed by matching a total of 4 purple gems to move her to the next section, which could be another walk point or battle. Battles are fought by clicking the enemy you want to target and ordering an elemental Fae friend to attack it, provided you have enough mana from matching corresponding gems. You eventually encounter varying enemy types, such as defensive lizard type enemies that cast barrier spells to protect the enemy party and flying enemies that can only be attacked once they are knocked down by your wind elemental. This adds a interesting layer of strategy, requiring you attack certain enemies before others and do so quicky, but this also means they are pratically invincible if you don't have wind gems in the proper place to line up. The flying enemies are rather annoying since you are sometimes in scenarios of matching random gems for lengthy segments, causing you to potentially lose at the target time and be attacked in the process. (This is a decent challenge actually, but iritating when all your enemies are flying). The fact that attacking is so dependent on elements (and there's no alternative means of attack) means that you will often run into situations where you don't have the gems you need to attack, dodge, or heal yourself in time, and the best strategy is to constantly spam gem switches just to get new gems. This goes against the games spellpower mechanic, which rewards you with extra damage for only swapping gems that cause chains.
You can also succumb to status effects such as poison (which causes damage and corrupts certain gems) or blindness, which makes all but the grey focus gems black, requring you to use any mind gems you already have on the field (From previously matched focus gems), constantly match random gems until you can match focus gems, or wait until the blindness fades. Another reviewer mentioned that the difficulty of the later game essentially forces you down a specific skill path, which, if true, essentially defeats the purpose for a custom skill tree. I have somewhat witnessed the fact that you are so often bombared with status effects, that it can be impossible to match the gems you need to survive, or at least you may be able to survive, but you certainly won't beat the expert time limit. Thankfully, you can easily respec at the cost of one spare part (which unfortunately, is costly since you only get one per completed level).
The art style is pretty, and evokes memories of well animated 2D adventure games. Unfortunately, that art only looks so good at it's native windowed resolution, as fullscreen stretches the game to pixelization, and there are NO resolution options. Other bad design choices including the annoying poison effect, which makes affected gems partially purple (as shown in the first Steam screenshot), which is very confusing in combat and makes it harder than needed to remove the effect and the total lack of colorblind mode or different gem shapes to make the game more accessible (thankfully, this isn't a direct problem for me, and at least different gems have different colors). The soundtrack, while fitting for this game and servicable for a budget title like this, is largely forgettable right down to the battle music, which sounds like they were going for something exciting, but doesn't get there. It's not remotely bad, just meh.
I played the game on hard, which may have been a mistake, as when I got to level 18, I reached a point where my speed wasn't able to keep up with the constant bombardment of status effects and attacks - no amount of healing spells could save me, especially when the cannons from the gremlin cave took 3/4ths of my health, and the only way to mitigate this is through matching purple gems to dodge their attacks, which of course, the game was stingy to provide them to me when I need them most. Considering I can only swap gems left and right, and can't do so in every direction like other similar games, this is cruel when your survival depends on it. This makes me wonder if the dev playtested the viability of all the skill tree setups - as it seemed impossible to complete, and I was matching gems very quickly. This is the part where I'm unsure to give this game a Yes or a No, as it is pretty good, but this major drawback makes it too hard. Normal difficulty is likely more bearable and you may need to find a guide on the best built (I'm thinking it's going to be the earth tree) .
I think I have to lean towards no based on my experience with the hard difficulty - playing it made me feel that the developer didn't properly make sure that any skill path is viable to complete the game.

It can be easy to lose yourself in this game because it's basically a bunch of mini-games. On the other hand, it's easy to get just a little gameplay in if you don't have a lot of time for the same reasons.

The good news is that the light RPG elements are actually pretty entertaining and kept me playing for a few hours. There isn't a ton of depth to them, but they're thought out well enough to give some focus and direction to what you're doing on the puzzle side of the game and break it up a bit. The story is nothing to write home about, but it moves the game along.
I might've kept playing it on and off despite some annoyances (e.g. fighting multiple enemies at once that spam status effects effectively forcing you down an upgrade path that gives you an easy way to clear things like blind/poison), but my inability to see what was going on really started to get in the way after a while. This is one of the few games where my partial color blindness has been a significant problem (especially with the blue/purple gems), and it could've been avoided without even adding a color blind mode. Just making the different gems different shapes would've made an enormous difference. It also really, really doesn't help that things like the poison symbol cover up most of the colored area of the gems, which makes it a lot harder at a glance to tell what you need to match them with to clear them.

Stellaris is a space symphony. It is beautiful, vibrant, haunting, and full.
I highly recommend this game. In spite of the many complaints I have, I keep coming back to this game over and over. Why? Because it does something other games of this type often stuggle with. It tells a story. And it does so from every angle. There's history of the universe to discover, there's not only your future but that of potential allies and soon to be need spacefaring civilizations. Even when I lose, I'll still walk away feeling somewhat satisfied, as if I'd read a book that was wonderful, but ended tragically for the main character.
I have built empires upon the backs of vassals and slaves. I have forged alliances and federations. I have nurtured pre-spaceflight worlds into full fledged partners and allies. I have led my people to discover the fate of civilizations of millennia past, to discover hidden secrets in the void, to build monumental structures, to ascend beyond their frail bodies and so much more.
Every time I play this game, I feel immersed. I'll find new treasures or events. Don't play this game on easy or less aggressive settings. It limits the AI behavior and that's exactly what makes this game feel great. The first game I played I was shocked to realize that none of the AI were "racing" me to a win state. They were all roleplaying their type of empire. The one closest to me not only befriended me, but invited me to war against a more powerful foe, an empire of religious zealots who wished to purge non-believers from existence. We overcame and won that war and three following, only to watch the entire galaxy burn to the ground under the oppression of the scourge, a vile species from another galaxy entirely.
Buy this game, buy the dlc, and settle in for a good story.
Controls - Fairly standard for RTS games. Some small QoL issues, like not being able to see/manage all spaceports easily, or quickly que up armies and fleets across the empire without lots and lots of button clicking.
Graphics - Good. More than a penny has been put into the look and feel of the various "people" and their craft. The stars and planets have some great artwork and the space battles are quite entertaining to watch. The ship "aura" somewhat detracts from an otherwise realistic look, but there's mods to fix that.
Gameplay - Story. So much reading to do! You can skip it if you must and each option given shows you clearly what the direct, mesurable impact on your empire will be, but the story lines and various other details of the universe you can discover really breathe life into the void of space.

This is the best game I have played since The Witcher 3.  The story is excellent, one actually cares about the characters and the events happening to and around them.  It has a great structure where it raises questions, some of which seem like outright plot holes, and then as you play more and more of the game, more and more stuff begins to make sense.  There was more than one point where I'd find myself thinking, "God, THAT"S why some previous stuff was the way it was!"  The only con is that, while the major story arcs established in the game are resolved in this game, the game still ends, at least in what appears to be the most complete and canonical ending, with it unclear how the main characters are doing and where they go from there.  Though I would gleefully pay for a sequel to continue from this game if it's as good on the whole as this game is.
The gameplay is largely very good.  Once and a while the camera will turn as you turn a corner or go from 3D to 2D sidescroller or top-down section (players of the first NieR will know exactly what I'm talking about) and ends up steering you directly into an attack.  It's bloody annoying when playing on Hard and things can easily kill you (stuff on Normal is largely harmless if you bring the rather plentiful healing items).  The sections where you play as 9S are less good than the ones where you play as 2B.  9S only carries one weapon, not two, which he swings like a drunk in slo-mo.  His secondary attack button is for hacking, the hacking minigame being a bit shallow and gets repetitive.  The brawling combat of 2B is just more fun to play through.  There are also a couple sections that force a gameplay shift for some narrative purpose, and it's usually REALLY annoying, but those are very few and far between.
The sidequests are VASTLY improved over the previous NieR, where they were legendarily awful.  It's less completely pointless fetch quests for what may as well be cardboard cutouts with a list of chores glued to their face, and more doign stuff to help out something resembling an actual character, most of which are some variant of fetch or kill quest (it's an RPG, it can't really be avoided).
The soundtrack might be the best thing about this game.  The combat is fun on its own, but when some epic track starts playing when you engage a boss or a horde of little enemies, it rises to a new level.  The ambient music in a lot of areas when you're not in combat is also very good.
This is a game where the developers had a clear idea on how to make a great game, tell a great story, have an identity, and generally reward their customers for paying $60 for it, and it worked out as well as I can imagine them ever hoping for.  It puts the vast majority of uninspired, samey Triple A tripe to shame.

It's very difficult to recommend this game in 2012. 15 years ago, these Adventure games from LucasArts were great fun. Puzzles, story, and humor.
But today, they are so frustrating to play. I can recognize the artificial difficulty elements for what they are -- time wasters. A way to make a short game feel longer. Having to walk back and forth across Melee Island will make you tear your hair out in boredom. In this game, at least, the puzzles do make sense and can be solved with just a little trial and error.
But the control system in this new edition is poor. It's easier to switch to the classic view (F10) and select actions off the menu than it is to spin the mouse wheel and try to figure out what all the icons mean.
I can't recommend Monkey Island for anyone except the most die-hard nostalgia seeker.

Primal Carnage brings an interesting concept of playing as both humans and dinosaurs.
The humans have 5 classes to play as: Pathfinder, Scientist, Commando, Pyro, and Trapper. Each of them having their own kind of weapons and equipment.
Pathfinder uses a shotgun and a pistol, along with the choice of flares to blind the dinosaurs or hatchets to throw. I find him most effective against big dinosaurs like Spino and Carno.
Scientist is basically a sniper. Uses a sniper rifle and also can use tranqulizer guns to slow down dinosaurs. You are given a choice to run with a first aid kit to heal you and your teamates or with sensor mines, to spot any dinosaurs near them.
Commando uses an assault rifle that has a grenade launcher. He fires a hail of bullets to deal some massive damage to both small and big dinosaurs. Supplied with the choice of ammo boxes to supply teamates with ammo or frag grenades.
Pyro has a flamethrower that is also a chainsaw. He deals tremendous amounts of damage up close. He also has a flare gun to ignite a dinosaur at a longer range. You are given a choice of a molotovs or impact grenades to run with.
Last but not least for the humans is the Trapper. He runs with a net gun and two revolvers. He traps smaller dinosaurs and kills them. You can shoot big dinosaurs with nets but it will only disable their attacks for an amount of time. His equipment is only limited to a land mine.
Then there is the other team you are able to play as, dinosaurs! This is again class based but with more variety. There is the Tyrant classes, Predator classes, Flying classes, Spitter classes, and the Bruiser class. Each dinosaur also has it's own roar to buff itself or teamates.
The Tyrants have the T-Rex, Spinosaurus, and the Acrocanthosaurus. All of them have the ability to eat a human whole and regain a little health from it. But each has a second attack and roar that is different from each other. The T-Rex can swing it's tail to hit any human behind it, and it's roar increases attack damage of your teamates. The Spinosaurus can use it's huge arms to swing in front of it, and it's roar increases teamates defense. The Acrocanthosaurus uses a stomp that sends a large shockwave injuring and killing any humans to close, it's roar regens health of teamates.
The predators use stealth or cunning techniques to hunt down the humans. These predators are Novaraptors and Oviraptors.They both can pounce on a human to kill. The Novaraptor's roar gets rid of all it's stamina, but makes you able to attack much faster. Making this useful to take out groups of humans camping in a building. The Oviraptor roar outlines humans through walls.
Next is the Flying classes. There is the Pteranodon and Tupandactylus. They both roar to spot humans. The Pteranodon can pick up humans and rop them from a lethal height. The Tupandactylus though travels at a high speed to ram a human, possibly off a high cliff or building to injure or kill.
Spitter classes are dinosaurs that spit and poison to kill. They consist of a Dilophsaurus and a Cryolophsaurus. The Dilo can spit to blind and damage humans. They can also bite to poison and damage the human over time. The Cryo though uses his spit as a main weapon. SInce the puddles it leaves over time will damage humans and it's bite will only damage, but not poison. Both their roars regains their stamina.
Last is the Bruiser class. The Carnotaurus is a hit and run class. He runs very fast to headbutt humans. He can also bite to do damage. The Carno roar allows you to regain health from damaging a human while charging. Sadly the Carno is alone in the Bruiser class.
Now that the very long intro to all the classes is done, what about the gameplay? I must say each class is pretty well balanced and shows it's strengths and weaknesses a lot. ( I am a little unsure about Pathfinder, he deals so much damage.) My experience with it was fair. They made gameplay a little smoother and easier to understand. I have played on TDM and GTTC and they both are pretty fun. Dino vs Dino mode is also pretty fun. They did add a Co-op mode, but I have yet to play this because every server there is, is always full, empty, or everyone just leaves after I join. Which leads to one problem this game suffers from.
This game and it's server's are very whacky. Almost every populated server is TDM or Roleplay. After playing TDM for so long, it gets boring. Playing an objective based game mode like GTTC is near impossible in a populated server. Which is unfortunate, I find GTTC very fun with a lot of players. I'm not to big on being friendly in servers. Also since there isn't many players for PC:E, making even TDM games with only maybe 6 players. TDM with low population isn't very fun, all the dino's have to do is play has a Tyrant and the game is pretty much won for them.
This game also introduces a loot system. (Pretty much the same thing TF2 has.) You can customize both your humans and dinosaurs with hats, skins, and camo's. Though you can find pretty much every hat and skin in the game. You can even find vey rare things like Legendary quality items. I even found a key once!
Is this community better or worse than other games? I think this community is better than most. Most people tend to get along and congratulate people on a lucky find or skill shot. Many offer trades for skins and hats. And I rarely see people insult others. I have yet to see any cheaters or hackers.
Improvements I think the developers can do: Slightly increase the reload time for the shotgun. Hit detection is pretty weird, espacially with the net gun. Small bug fixes like the ragdolls or minor animation glitches.
Do I think this game is worth your 19.99? Honestly, no. At least not right now. Wait till the game is discounted or more players and updates appear. I think this game deserves a fair 6.5/10 I hope to see you all in game soon!

If you're a fan of the realistic shooters like Arma, Operation Flashpoint, Insurgency, or, bless you if you know this game, INFiltration, you'll love Rising Storm 2: Vietnam.  It's got all the immersive "fun realism" parts like adjusting your sights range, resting your weapon on a sandbag to increase accuracy, lying on a slope at an angle makes the crosshairs in your scope at an angle, without any of the "tedious boring realism" parts.
The game seems to be somehow designed to encourage teamwork, I was getting non-stop information in my ears from my teammates with mics, and even people furiously typing in chat to alert me to the location of enemies, or how we should flank, or what routes are safe.
The maps are very complex and open, with a HUGE amount of spots for creativity - there's no way you're going to learn all the "good spots" in under a week because there's so many of them, there's so much dense foliage, the maps are so complicated, you could find a good spot that even a seasoned player might not be expecting to look out for.
When I check the 3 usual filter boxes for multiplayer - "not empty", "not full", and "not password protected", I get between 10-30 servers available, with maybe half of those with around 60 other players.  Most servers are 64 players, yet it doesn't get too frustrating when there's too many players like Insurgency does, it gets more fun.
I can't comment on performance because my PC is too good, but it runs buttery smooth on Ultra on this PC.
Despite this being a "realistic shooter", the learning curve was extremely quick.  The main menu has a "shooting range" where you can just hop in and experiment with the controls and get a feel for how shooting works.  I spent about 5 minutes in there, 2 more minutes in the key bindings menu, and before I knew it I was in a multiplayer game, spotting enemies and calling for backup and getting headshots.
As for downsides?  As far as I can tell, there are two:
- Spawnkilling is very possible.  I can't tell exactly how spawning works in this game, it seems to be "fuzzy" based on where the rest of your team mates are, but I have definitely had occasions where within 2 seconds of spawning I was getting shot at, and either dying, or having to instantly go prone.  Be aware of this.
- Net performance isn't as great as what I'm used to - whereas on Insurgency I could expect to see pings of 5-20ms, with this game I'm seeing an average of 80-100ms.  Maybe that's because there's double the amount of players per server, I don't know.  Also whatever ping you get from a server in the server browser?  It will be almost exactly double that in-game, guaranteed.
Despite those two minor flaws, I have no regrets about buying this game, it's actually the one I've played the most out of all the games I bought on the steam sale.  Buy it.

Do you like simple puzzles? If you do you'll probably enjoy playing Polarity. On the other hand, if you prefer more complex puzzles, or don't like puzzles much at all, you might not.
Polarity is a first person puzzle game similar to Portal (the objective is to exit the room by activating switches and the like), with the main difference being in the titular mechanic. Basically, some objects interact with other objects depending on their polarity. For example, red cubes will only activate red switches. You can also change your polarity at will for various effects. This mechanic is used in some way in every puzzle. The puzzles themselves have data (the game's collectibles) hidden throughout, and the main challenge comes from collecting all of the data. Data will also unlock new puzzles on the level select, as well as bonus puzzles (Note: data is not required to play most levels, but you will only be able to select most levels after meeting a data quota. For example, if you play through a level without meeting its data quota, you will be able  to proceed to the next level if you don't return to the menu; but if you do, you will only be able to select levels with completed quotas to begin from.).
If I had to complain about one thing it would be that the game is pretty short. There are only about 20 single player levels. To be fair, the game does have a coop mode as well as a player vs player mode, but both of these are only local, and require a pad and a pal to play. As such, I've yet to try either (I'll place and edit here if I do-Edit: the multiplayer content was easily the most enjoyable part of the game for me. the puzzels are similar to those in single player, but playing them with a friend [or in my case a brother] makes the experience much more fun. the pvp mode is also enjoyable even if it is very simple[both players throw cubes to hit switches and score points. the player with the most points wins]. That said, even with the multiplayer content the game is only a couple hours long [I finished single player twice, we finished multiplayer once, and we played pvp more than I thought we would]). The game also doesn't have any story or characters to speak of; and while the graphics and sound work well enough, they don't really add that much to the game.
But in the end it all comes down to one question. Do you like puzzles?

This game is not amazingly well written. The plot isn't ambitious and combat is boring as hell.
But if you're a Minecraft fan, you'll find yourself an experience crafted with surprising amount of care and love put into it.
It is very obvious that the creators of the game spend a lot of time playing it and put effort into understanding it's culture.
It's not just obvious jokes like punching wood with your fists. The game will very often nod to less recognizable but still strong and influential concepts you may know from playing survival for a long time.
On a Minecon 2015 panel, Telltale writes claimed while playing you'll meet various types of Minecraft players. It might seem like they're talking about the very obvious stereotypes of Griefer, Builder, Redstoner, Fighter who are the important characters to the story, but if you spend some time exploring the world, you actually find much more diverse
people whose interests you might even identify with!
-GAMEPLAY-
While the choices in the game don't matter to the main plot at all like in all Telltale games,  this game makes them feel more like actual gameplay.
You will find yourself juggling friendships, saving the world and trying not to offend your little piglet.  The game is aware you know exactly how the story is going to end, but lets you choose who you'll take to that happy end. It will test your trust in your friends, the feeling of responsibility vs how much you care about showing someone you appreciate them.
This is where the game exels at and as long as you are able to enjoy the characters it throws at you, you'll be in for a fun ride.
All in all, this game is a pure fan service story about adventuring with your friends. It does well what it sets out to do, but seems to be fit for a niche demographic.  If you never played Minecraft, don't touch it. If you've been in the community for at least a year, you'll have plenty of fun with it.

Aura Kingdom level 1-30 (A review of the first ten hours,considering most  players  will not go beyond that)
Pros
-Charm: Charm is often the deciding factor between a good and bad game, as it is charm is what causes you to adore the characters and the world and want to come back for more, something i feel Aura kingdom posseses.
-Stunning graphics/art style- the game looks bright and beautiful on my lowish- end pc, and the charming cartoony art style is one thing that makes the game. (better than the average mmo and vastly better than most of theese next gen titles with there 'realistic' graphics/style - an art style i feel is incredibly overused and am getting very sick of)
-Nice Soundtrack (slightly cheap instrument presets but it is well composed)
-Charming Story with resonable variety. Sure, most of the time its not exactly a emotional rollercoaster, but i enjoy its diversity and charm. Theres supply missions, Combat missions, instances,sneak missions and missions to play as other characters. Hidden quests and board quests are actually rewarding unlike many mmos as you can get cool costume items and rare misc items that cost quite a bit from the loyalty shop.
-A resonable Free 2 Play Model, everything can be bought through in game currency and there seems to be few restrictions on area and quest access, unlike most f2p mmos. Of course paying real money gets you the cool stuff quick but they gotta make money somehow.
-lots of cool little features unique to this mmo  such as being able to glide and jump really high from the start, custom guild logos, cinematic finisher moves, hidden quests and so on.
-No grinding up levels to complete the main quest (at least in the first 10 hours) which is a nice change from some mmos where you can have to level up 10 levels just to continue the main story.
-the variety of costumes and hats, though hard to get, make customization fun.
-The decision to opt for text based dialogue is actually a plus for me because i much prefer it to the terrible voice acting i have heard in other mmos such as WildStar.
-Game is around a year old and still updated

There is a big learning curve that look me 1-2 days to get over, but after that,
the Steam Contoller is without doubt the best feeling/working controller in
functionality and feel. However this controller isn't really for the plug and
play type as it's advertised for. For many games, especially non-steam ones,
tuning and button mapping are required for the Steam Controller to either work or just feel right,
but that's the beauty of it: you can completely re-map every button. Because of
that, I would place it in a whole new field from other controllers in
addition to the already alien track pads (which work quite well). The Steam Controller's ability to remap every button gives it the functionality and worth (especially in original PC games)
compared to other controllers as you can literally play any game (as long as it's added to your Steam Library) I would recommend this controller to anyone ready to expand their Steam horizon beyond the desktop (however playing with the Steam Controller at the desktop is also
fun), wanting to add a new method of play outside of the mouse and keyboard,
and someone who is willing to deal with some bumps and challanges in getting it to
work with some games in exchange for great functionality unseen in any other controller.

An extremely solid gem matching puzzle game. You use the gather mode to match gems for resources, and then use those in the battle mode on the upper part of the screen. The game's a bit on the easy side for the first leg of the journey as you have little in your repetoire, but once it gets going it's challenging in a pretty fun way. There does exist the problem of unlucky drops meaning you can't get the mana you need, but it's not common enough to be a major complaint.
Getting expert scores in later levels requires gaming the system a bit, but short of one of the more annoying enemy types in one level, it's usually a case of survival against a pretty tough enemy. If anything, I wish the optional bosses had been more difficult, but the endboss is pretty brutal and an excellent fight to end the game on.
All in all, getting 20 solid hours of gameplay out of some puzzle game I picked up for $10 just because it had pretty pictures is an excellent deal. Buy this game. Bonus points: the story's not bad either, taking the pretty grim idea of the fae rather than friendly faeries.

- Random tech to research. (Technically it's weighted chance, not random, as some things will modify the chance that something appears.) The devs would say this mimics reality where you don't necessarily know where tech will lead you and races develop different tech at different times. What it really does is screw you if don't happen to get the tech you need. In the real world we have both directed research and accidental discoveries, so it'd be great if they could figure out that happy medium.
- The AI is bad, like all 4X games. Nothing says "broken" to me like having good relations with someone who suddenly declares war on you. We've had these kinds of games for 3 decades now, why are we still struggling on the basics of "don't attack your friends"? They need a resource - did they think to *ask* if I'd trade, or is everyone in the future an impulsive, selfish child?

Absolutely charming. A classic that holds up. It isn't immune from the fridge-logic or arbitrary only-the-designer-would-actually-solve-this-without-some-tiral-and-error puzzles seen in pretty much every adventure game. But it has so much humor and cleverness to it that I was able to forgive the game's shortcommings. It also has, easily, the best sword-fighting mechanic in any game I've played.
If you don't like point-and-clicks, this might not convert you because it does not fix the genre's greatest problems. Nonetheless, if you are to try only one adventure game I would recommend Monkey Island or Broken Sword--both have excellent writting and are much more logically grounded that most adventure games I've palyed (though in Monkey Island's case, that doens't mean the same thing it does in Broken Sword's as some degree of absurdity is inherent in Monkey Island's world, it's just that Monkey Island is more internally consistent with it's absurdity than it's cohorts).
The special edition is also particularly fabulous. The voicework is delightful, the artwork lovely, and every detail preserved. Hot-swapping between classic and special edition modes is impresssive; the team was clearly dedicated to preserving the game while also making it more accessible to newcomers. Especially since the entirety of the original game is included within it, this is the definitive edition of Monkey Island.

I really really wanted to like this controller. So much so that I and my wife both pre-ordered one. There are three problems that I had with the controller that I believe steam will fix in future. My recommendation is to wait for the next controller.
Cons:
1) The largest problem for me is that the touch pad on the right side does not work well as a replacement for an analog stick. It can be very sensitive and imprecise. The control works great for games that only require one analog stick.
2) It has batteries. I do not see any reason why these controllers should not be rechargeable.
3) updating the software is not intuitive. The instructions provided do work... after you have opted into something on big picture that I could not find any reference to in the materiel that came with the controller.
While these problem ultimately led me to not recommend this controller I am very likely to recommend what ever comes next  most due to the things I love about it.
Pros:
1) It is easy to customize and gives you a lot of freedom. The touch pads are responsive and the subtle vibration gives great feedback that tracks with your thumb. While the lay out of the shoulder buttons takes some getting use to there is no requirement to adjust how you interact with your triggers.
2) It is as responsive as a console controller with the added bonus of being able to change the layout.
3) Steam is trying something new. Things do not get better with out risk and there are a lot of risks with this controller. I trust steam to adjust what needs to be adjusted.

As one might expect from Paradox Interactive, it is yet another excellent grand strategy game. It's a game where you create your own empire amongst the stars. You will discover anomalies, meet alien races, and come in contact with space entities so vast that they can only be called "leviathans." It is your choice whether you wish to coexist harmoniously with other xenos, or enslave and purge them as you see fit.
Be warned, however. Whilst your empire may rise up to be the supreme overlord of your galaxy, space is a fickle thing. Astronomical numbers combined with astronomical odds can lead to unforeseen consequences...... The aftermath can be devastating for the unprepared player.
As one can expect from the description above, Stellaris provides a multitude of options for the player. Everything from the flavor texts of space encounters to game-changing ascension perks all provide the player with hours of entertainment. One can experiment with many differnet type of empires, changing their playstyle accordingly.
And yet, as all strategy games do, the game has an expiration date. As the player plays multiple games on end, the game starts to lose its luster. The events begin to seem repetitive, and one begins to see the game's limits.
The game truly is amazing. There is no doubt on that matter. However, I do not think its a game that will persevere through the years. It will certainly keep you up all night, but will you keep playing the game after two or three years? I, for one, probably will not.
It might seem unfair to expect a grand stategy game to remain captivating for years on end, but
games do just that. Civilization 5, for example, still keeps me at the desk for hours on end, although my playtime on that must surpass 500 hours.
In retrospect, it seems like I haven't done the game justice on how good it actually is.
If you are a fan of grand strategy, then
Also,
The base game still is quite incredible, but the DLCs effectively bring the game to its full potential.
buy it while its on sale, though, as the entire package does not come cheap. But I guarantee, you will not regret it. I cetainly did not.

Fun game, while it's had it's downsides.  The sheer scale of content being constantly added or worked on by both game designers and mod community alike adds longevity to this game, much like other successful grand strategy 4x games have done.  Yet this game has gone a length further with adding the complexity of species growth an evolving diversity.
It feels as though the designers are doing their best to deliver the best of both world gaming genres, the best elements from turn based civilization style titles, an blending in the RTS styles of Sins of a Solar Empire, which I would surmise given the scale of potential environment as well factoring the multiplayer aspect, an arguably difficult balancing act.  An quite possibly the sole reason why it may feel parts are missing.  To which I'm sure they are.   Sometimes grand ventures require stepping stone processes of fix, balance and tweaking.  Understandably, especially if you don't have a deep resource pocket of triple AAA backers to pull from for development/testing to work into a shorter timeframe launch.
An yet, Paradox has delivered a solid working game from the beginning.  As the time rolls on, the fixes and changes only enhanced the game, as well new content fleshes out the game further.  An the mod community, has amazingly risen to the challenge to address the needed fixes and balances that were missed, or felt could enhance the changes further.
All in all, if you love game series such as civilization, galactic civs, Sins of a Solar Empire an likewise titles,  I would wholeheartedly back this game with a stamp of approval.  Well worth the pricetag, given the endless hours of gameplay, an replayability with friends.

I got mine with the link in the first wave. A lot of people who aren't liking it expect it to be plug and play, which it is not.
I'd think it'd be perfect for PC gamers, because of the tinkering experience, but apparently people just don't want to put in the time to learn a new control scheme.
The first few hours were baffling, confusing, and frustrating.
Once I started getting the hang of what I could do with it, I rapidly started liking it more. The touchpads as a joystick are hard to get used to, and it's like that by default on a lot of titles.
Touchpads as mouse are also hard at first, because it's so different than anything I had played with, but I really enjoyed learning it, it kind of made my brain tickle while I was playing games, as I was focusing so much on what my hands were doing.
I really started liking it once I got used to that. Shooters were more satisfying, because the grip reload was so good, and the pad as mouse was pretty accurate, albeit less than a mouse.
Once I discovered gyro, though, I was in love. Once you get the controller set up the way you want and get gyro going the way you want, it's a completely new experience in gaming.
I'm playing Serious Sam 3 with it, and it's so ♥♥♥♥ing fun. So, I have left trigger soft pull as activate gyro, right grip as reload, left grip as jump, right pad as mouse, left pad as weapon switching, and the others would be what you expect.
You whip around in a not-super-accurate manner with the right pad, it's perfect for movement, and very fast. The second you pull on that left trigger, I have it set to be much much more accurate, think of how bullet hell games are when you're shooting.
People disagree, but once you get it set up the way you like, for me, it's more accurate, and far more immersive than a keyboard and mouse.
Is it for everyone? No, it requires a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of tinkering.
Once you get it going for you though, it's yours.
Think of regular controllers as a prebuilt Dell.
This controller is something you perfect and personalize. Like a computer you built. It's wonderful if you're patient, and are willing to learn an entirely new manner of interacting with playable media.
It's the best controller I have ever used, and I love it.
Edit: pad as joystick with gyro is superb for third person games. Pad as mouse for fps.
Also, if someone reviews it and doesn't use gyro, it's a useless review.
Also edit:  They really push out some fantastic updates, this controller gets better weekly.

Updated review content: After finally getting to level 60 I have to change my review to do not recommend.  Leveling to 60 wasn't too bad, but as I saw in my original review below, nothing special.  The problem is at level 60 quests that were giving you 10-15% of a level each now give about 0.1%.  The solo dungeons available give less than 1% to run the entire thing.  Doing dailies with level 65 mobs that are quite painful to push through give about 3% for 30-60 minutes of work.  But unfun work.  I literally beat on the same enemy for 10 minutes straight to take him down and he was only PART of that quest requirement.  The only way to level is to run party dungeons, but parties don't take people below level 65.  The game does not get better.  All reports indicate level 70+ is even worse.  If it's just grind grind grind and solo grind at that until 65... forget it.  Not the point of an MMO.
It's a free to play MMO with decent graphics that doesn't seem to (I'm only mid 30s in level so far) nickle and dime you for every little think like so many other Asian free to play MMOs do.  There's nothing I've found exceedingly unique or special with this game than so many others.  It has nice convenience features like clicking a quest objective to take you there, easy party finding in most (low level at least) cases, and an active user base.  Again, shocked it doesn't nickle and dime.  There were a number of times I ran into in game things that were free I just KNEW would cost money, like item upgrading and inserting/removing stones that provide bonuses to items.  It's a good diversion for the price.  Nothing spectacular.

Stellaris may be the best entry point into the universe of Paradox games. Grand strategy on a universal scale might seem illogical considering the catalogue the studio has and yet, of all of them, this is the one I find the most fun to jump into and play.
As someone who loves Europa Universalis 4 and has far too long logged on Hearts of Iron 4, the increase in scale actually makes this game more to the point than before. One of the bigger problems of the earlier games comes with how the player approaches them, want to play tall? You can do that here, want to play expansionist? That works too.
In summary, the key selling points to Stellaris are as such:
Large choices for customisation: Your race, your ideas, how you approach building, your ship designs, how you view other species in the galaxy, etc.
Different diplomatic approaches: Crush your neighbours, vassalise and integrate or follow the path to everlasting peace and galactic federations?
Random happenstance: Each game of Stellaris puts players in a different position to start each time you load it up. Locations for planets, resource centres and colonisation options are all randomised each time as well as potential events that can occur.
Multiplayer compatibility: You only have the base version but your friend hosts the game with all of the available content? Guess what, you can play that content. You don't even need it for yourself.
Workshop support: Want some crazy stuff to try? There's mods for that.
The idiom "The sky's the limit" fails to apply here, it's more like the "Universe is your playground", just be very aware, the other kids may play rough.
I thoroughly recommend this title with or without others to play with you.

I honestly can no longer recommend this game to people.
For the longest time I loved playing this game. I still do at the time of writing this review. I was and still am a huge fan of the race/empire creation options and being able to put my new species through the ropes to become an eventual major player in galactic events. The game has its flaws, to be sure. The AI could still use some work and at the time of writing this wars tend to be "All or nothing" affairs that are decided with the outcome of the first one or two big battles, but overall the game has come a long way from where it began.
It isn't the issues with AI or the crawling-pace of the mid-game that is finally turning me off from it though. My major problem is with Paradox and the development team itself.
In 2018 the next major content update, "Cherryh," will be changing up many current game features and functionality in the name of progressing the game forward. In many ways it is arguably no different from their previous updates in adding to the game. But in addition to adding to and changing parts of the game, Paradox will also be taking away current game functionality for the first time.
It can be argued that it is their right and honestly I can and will agree with that. The change in question will also arguably make the game easier for them to take in the direction that the Dev team apparently wants to go with the game. This is also a fact that can not be denied.
The fact that really tears it for me, that I just can not let go, is that they are committing to this level of game-change, which will update everyone's game unless they turn off auto-updating, months after everyone purchased and committed time to playing it. They are taking things that I enjoy out of the game and I don't get a say in the matter if I want to keep getting new content that I do like the look of.
I know that not many people will agree with my issues with the Cherryh update. Indeed the majority of the playerbase doesn't mind at all. But all in all this is the main reason why I can no longer recommend this game to anyone anymore. You never know when something you enjoy in it will be taken from you.

This is the HARDEST strategy game I have EVER played, and strategy games are my thing. This game is made by the same people who made Hearts of Iron IV, which I've played, and let me tell you, THAT game is easier than this one.
Now I won't be surprised if some fat, snobbish Internet Stellaris nerd will probably push up his glasses, sneer and dribble, "No, NOOB, you're just BAD at it!" (tip: if you do that, then you admit to being the stereotype I just described. Best advice; don't.), and you know, you might be partially (like 5%) right, but the game itself is just unbelievably complex, and though it does have a tutorial, the tutorial hardly helps. Another big, big problem is that the AI in this game is just brutally... brutal and highly unbalanced.
Now you would think that after all, I'd vote this game down... well...
If you strive for a serious challenge and aren't some pathetic loser regular who plays this game more than he looks at other human beings, I'd recommend this. I will say that one big positive I have is the just mind-boggling amount of customization and personal preference.
See, HoI4 (Hearts of Iron IV) works with countries; you pick a country that you want to play as. Now since this game is set in space, you have the liberty of choosing who you want to play as, both in cosmetics and gameplay. In cosmetics, you have different (animated) species portraits; you can choose the model of your ships; change the name of your starting planet; so many things. And in the functional side of things, you can use several different policies and government ideologies to provide different bonuses and starting traits.
And this game also has a staggeringly high number of unique random events, such as one of your planets having an earthquake, only for it to be discovered that there's an underground civilization living below the surface of the planet, and numerous others.
So yeah, Stellaris is a great sci-fi game and a masochist's dream, but prepare to have said dreams ground to dust when you try to do the tango with the AI.

Being a sequel/spinoff to Nier, a game I never played, which it itself is a spinoff of another series, I was thrown into a completely new, enthralling world that captivated me with its characters and world building even though I felt lost a few times along the way.
TL;DR version at the bottom.
Set in the year 11945, during the 14th Machine War, Nier: Automata follows the story of three android YoRHa units, 2B, 9S, and A2 in their quest to reclaim Earth from the alien-controlled machines. The game starts with 2B uncovering the secret of the aliens and fighting the powerful machines Adam and Eve. It then shifts gears and retells the whole chapter through 9S’ eyes while uncovering more truths about the humans on the moon and androids themselves. It then shifts gears once more to focus on A2’s story and why she’s a wanted fugitive while also continuing 2B and 9S’ story.
I honestly cannot say anymore otherwise it’ll spoil the fun of the story. All I can say is that the story is full of gut-wrenching twists, comments about our standards of beauty, and existentialism. What I did not like however was how some key story elements were told in a vague and indirect way that had me scouring the Internet to essentially experience the whole story. I guess it is a very Japanese way of storytelling with no concrete answers and comments about the way our society functions.
The story has 26 endings titled A-Z, but don’t let that discourage you! The real meat of the story is told from A-C (F-Z are jokes) with the story diverging to two different endings in D and E. The truth is that “endings” A and B aren’t really endings at all, they’re a prologue to the real game, ending C. There are even opening credits at the beginning of C.
Confused? You should be! It is a Taro Yoko game after all.
A Platinum games masterpiece. A hack ‘n slash JRPG with a plethora of customizable options. From companion pods, weapons, upgrade chips, skills, to the HUD itself, every single moment to moment gameplay is highly customizable.
Combat is one of the most satisfying and diverse I’ve played in a Platinum game with tight melee sword fighting, nice hacking minigames, and a twin stick shooter segments that change the pace from time to time.
Since the game is a JRPG, the game offers 60 optional side quests that are fun and diverse. Some of these side quests add critical background information to the story. In order to experience everything the game has to offer, you’ll probably need to clear 40-50 hours of your schedule to do so.
The highlight of the visual design is probably the phenomenal character design and unique art style. Otherwise, the game suffers from mediocre graphics, muddy textures, terrible drawing distance, and bad performance. I guess the mediocracy was so that the PS4 version can play it at 60fps as well.
One of the best, most memorable soundtracks I’ve heard in recent memory. I remember humming one of the tracks in-class (I hope the professor didn’t notice xD). Voice acting gave life to the machines and I was always loved listening to what they had to say. As for the main characters, all of them sounded great with one outstanding performance by 9S’ voice actor. Kyle McCarley deserves an award.
TL;DR:
Pros:
•	Fun combat
•	2B
•	Plethora of customization options
•	9S
•	Captivating story
•	A2
•	Amazing throwbacks to previous games
•	2B
•	9S
•	A2
Cons:
•	Performance issues
•	Muddy graphics
•	Some convoluted story elements just for the sake of convolution
Overall, Nier: Automata is a game that I see myself playing again in the next few years again and again for its fun gameplay, great characters, and chill soundtrack. The game does have glaring issues though, but I personally found them trivial compared to the rest of things the game does extremely well.
9/10

For a style of game which intends to succeed solely on a player's investment into the story exclusively, it's remarkably bland and uninteresting. More often than not, you'll find yourself faced with quicktime events that offer little to no consequences for failure, dialogue options which offer no impact on the game itself, and, sometimes, choices which at the time seem like they'll influence the game reasonably only to find out the option you didn't choose gets resolved some way or another outside of your experience.
Yet all of this could be acceptable as a part of a game that at least offers an interesting story as the concept of Telltale Games is to have to experience a story which you can hopefully be at least mildly invested in. This fails in a herculean fashion. Characters are presented as important and deep when in reality, they are injected suddenly and unemotionally into the story while the plot itself is generic and often lazily progressed. This means that whenever you're faced with Telltale's trademark "important decision" moments, you really don't have much to go off of emotionally making the choice meaningless and easy.
Even as a children's game, this fails across the board for ham-fisted attempts at sudden and awkward humour, lack of any interesting story or character development, and an overall absence of the emotional investment present in...some...of Telltale's other games, for even games for children can still retain objective elements of entertainment. Believe me, you can find somewhere else to put your money into.

With my first few days with the Steam Controller, it's been a love/hate relationship.
I'll say this first and foremost, it's the first true innovation in gaming in a long time. With that out of the way, I'll discuss the actual device.
Many have said that it feels cheap; and right out of the box and into my hands, I thought so, too. However, during my initial gaming sessions with it, with sweaty hands, rigorous button pressing, and aggressive touchpad swipes, my views completely turned around. This thing holds up well under stress.
Button placement will take some getting used to, of course. The face buttons (A,B,X,Y) are to the left of the left touchpad. Years of using standard console dual stick layouts where the face buttons are to the right have made the transition to the Steam Controller, in this regard, a bit difficult, but not impossible. Everything is within reach, even if the X button is a bit further to reach than I'd like.
The triggers are decent. My favorite are still of the Dualshock 4. With the Steam Controller, both are pressure sensitive and can even act like another button stroke when fully pressed down. It gives a satisfying subtle click when fully depressed. This allows (but not at all limited to) aiming [pulling the trigger down] and shooting [fully depressing the trigger] with the action of one button. It was somewhat of a luxury that I was not expecting. While we're discussing the triggers, let's talk about the bumper buttons. I wasn't as quite impressed with them as I'd hoped to be. They're really, really clicky. It sounds like the keystroke of a mechanical keyboard with cherry blue switches and feel just as stiff. Nonetheless, they're responsive and get the job done, I suppose.
There are two rear buttons comfortably placed where the rest of your fingers would normally go. I loved having them and you can bind whatever your heart's desire is for them. For me, they're perfect for hotkey shortcuts.
The analog joystick feels just as good as any other main console controller. No complaints there.
The left trackpad (RIP left analog stick). This is where most people will give up on the Steam Controller as it takes the most time to get adjusted to. I can't say I hate it, as it's what makes the Steam Controller different. I can't say I love it, because it's still not perfect. There's a plethora of settings you can customize for it to fine tune to your desire--and when I say plethora, I mean it. I've spent quite a while messing around with different settings and still haven't found something that has quite suited me. At the same time, I'm far, far from experimenting with everything you can do with it. If you happen to buy one, give yourself some time to fully explore it.
Is it a replacement for Kb/M? No. Is it a replacement for the controller you're already accustomed to? Maybe. It'll take time with it, that's for sure. But, I do love how you can customize every aspect of it to suit your needs. The haptic feedback is top-notch as well. I really hope to see more developers directly support the device, but even as it is, you can now use a controller for everything in your Steam library, even if it isn't quite perfect. Also, the Steam Controller is still in it's early infancy. There will be updates for sure to come and support will always be there.
In the end, it's really going to take a hands-on experience with it. You'll probably hate it at first, but it grows on you. I'm sure I'll be more fond of it in a month's time.
