This game would have much potential. Practically its a reboot of Primal Carnage, a game that won a Kickstarter campaign, was and was released unfinished on the premise that it will be recieving free updates to the point that it will become a feature complete / bugless game one day. The original Primal Carnage was never finished, and its development team sold the rights to a new team, who are the ones who made this reboot.
The game came out on Early Access, but it left it early, before it was completed, and once again gamers were given the promise that this game will be receiving free content updates with new modes, characters etc. And it does receive them, at least until now. But still, the game feels kind of lacking. Some modes only have 1 map available. But the content updates are not over yet.
Technically the game can be made to look nice. There is something weird though going on. One particular graphics setting seems to not be optimized enough, and that is the lighting quality. At 'medium' quality, the game looks like a dx8 game from 2003, so bad, that on a map that normally its day, its so dark as if its night. At medium setting I get a frame rate of 70s to 90s fps. When I change lighting quality to 'high', the lighting becomes much better, and includes a cool looking sun with sunrays, but framerate drops to 23 ~ 28 fps. The difference between the medium and the high setting is huge in both visual pleasance and frame rate.
The core gameplay idea of the game is very fun, and through many patches, the game's balance is much better than it used to be. This game 'could' offer much fun. And I say 'could', because well, it's too hard to get fun out of it. This game suffers from lacking marketing. There was just a bit press info about it when it was released on Early Access, and back then many people played it, and decided to wait until it leaves Early Access to touch it again. When the game eventually left EA, it didn't received the appropriate press coverage it needed. There have been next to zero promotion for that game, and on Metacritic it only has 2 Critic reviews, so most reviewers didn't even reviewed it.
And unfortunately, when it comes to online games like this, popularity is required to be able to play them and have fun. And that is the biggest negative thing about that game. That there aren't enough people playing it. Whenever I search for servers, there are like 30 of them in total on whole Earth and including all game modes, out of which about 10 have some players playing in them, and 6 out of 10 servers are 'nokill' servers, meaning people join them not to play competitively, but to do dino-acting, where you get banned for killing someone of the other team. The remaining 4 servers are for all other game modes combined, and often you won't find even 1 server with the game mode you want to play.
It's a shame because this game had so much potential, and could be quite fun...
Now do I suggest you to buy this game ?
Well... If MANY people bought it at the same time as you, and the playerbase was multiplied in orders of magnitude, so one can find 2-3 servers for every game mode at any time, at a good ping, well yeah, I would say buy it, because it will be fun! But if you buy it alone, and all else is equal, well, welcome to the club of having a game that could be quite fun but won't give you any, because you can hardly find people in it playing.
P.S. I wish I didn't had to choose between a 'recommended' and 'not recommended', as I would prefer something more neutral. I'd only recommend this game if there is a promotional boom and suddenly its playerbase multiplies 10fold or more. As it is now, I'm sorry, but I can't recommend it.

(2-12-17) So I finished the game via single player and I'm disappointed in the lack of story plot - the ending was very lackluster (in terrms of round and how the game ended).

In regards to the quality of graphics, it's fine. Not praise worthy, but also not terrible. I played the same level using simple and gorgeous and I didn't even care for the difference. Polarity is no Portal but it's a solid game in its own right. I see that some are complaining about its simplicity and its brevity but honestly, those are some of the qualities I like about Polarity. No puzzle is so challenging that it leaves you scratching your head. Each puzzle can be solved in a span of 1 to 5 minutes. It makes the game more of a relaxing experience, whereas, Portal could be relaxing or it could be hectic.
There's little to no story in Polarity but I really enjoyed the TRON-esque asthetic the developers went with. Overall, I found myself enjoying this game and for the price that I paid while it was on sale (I think 99 cents?), I ain't gonna complain about it being short or whatever...
If you like puzzle platformers and you see this one on sale, pick it up.

So, let me start off by saying that while the game does have issues, It's still a great game.
- The story is nice, the auto route system is great to have (I can't stand manually going to every place in every quest).
- The gameplay is pretty good, but can get a bit repetitive at times. Most quest are kill this, find that, same thing.
- However, the story kept it fun enough for me to keep playing. Now, let's move on to the issues.
- Bots, Bots, and more bots. If you can ignore these, than you should be fine. However, the chat is flooded by spam bots.
- Lag. The game suffers from server lag, Probably from all those bots. Changing channels to a channel with less people on it usually helps.
- The game suffers from stutter while loading in things. That doesn't really surprise me though, as many games of this kind have that issue. The game's optimization isn't the best either. The system requirements are far off.
- I played before the steam version came out, and even played in the closed beta. However, I ended up taking a long break from the game, maybe because of some repetitiveness.
- Leveling at first is pretty easy, but once you hit the 40ish point, it gets harder. I currently have a Level 60, and I'm struggling to get even a single level. I would hate to see how hard it is at a higher level.
- The games graphics are pretty good, and it most cases, the game looks beautiful, even without high end textures.
If you're looking for an Anime style MMO, then try the game out. It's free, so you don't lose much by trying it.
I will add more to this review in the future when I progress more.
EDIT: So, I'm back into the game, and time to do a small update:
Leveling is easier than before. I'm not sure what change they made, but whatever they did, it's much better. Before, over half a main area of quests gave me 25% exp at level 62. Now, one quest can give me about 7-10% exp (with XP cards, 20% XP boost). I'm now at 71, and will update this if I get further, and leveling becomes very hard again.
Something I want to add though, even after a year and a half of being inactive, and even made a purchase at one point, I did not get banned. However, I did log in once in a while to keep one of my lower level characters from being deleted.

From my experience so far, I don't really think the Steam controller is your best bet for faster paced first person games (or really any game where you really need to be pin point accurate). Key board and mouse will still be your best bet for those types of games. However if you want to use this for other things like slower paced games or racing games (Steam Controller is probably the best way to play Rocket League, hands down) then the Steam Controller is a great pickup. I have a few games that recommend you use the Steam Controller and I will be trying those out soon. My only big complaint with this hardware so far is that you have to open Big Picture to do really anything relating to the controller. Yes you can just open up a game normally and plug in your Steam Controller, but you won't be able to change any controls mid-game with out opening Big Picture, and trust me you will want to be able to tweak your controls at any point.
A thing I forgot to mention is that the Steam Controller takes a bit to get used to. Rocket League (as I said, using the Steam Controller is my favorite way to play it) took a bit for me to get used to when I first started playing it with the Steam Controller. Granted RL was the very first game I played with the Steam Controller, so that probably has something to do with it. It'll take a bit but when you understand how to use this controller to its full capability then it is totally worth the purchase. Let me reiterate, it will most likely take a while to get used to it and it may be frustrating to use during that time. Make sure to stay calm during that time and change the controls around to make it work the best.
I don't know how it works for games outside of Steam at all as I have not tested that. This controller also works as a mouse outside of Steam. It is very nice to just lean back and surf the web using the controller.
Besides having to use Big Picture, it not being that great for faster paced games, and it taking a while to get used to it, this controller is fantastic. If you use a controller a lot when you play Steam games then pick this up. In my opinion this is the best controller to have for Steam. I definitely recommend this but with a reminder that this might not work the best for everything and takes a while to jump into.

It's good. I love it. Using it for the first time is just as hard as when you first tried to play a FPS with two thumbsticks when you were a kid. But once you learn it, its natural. I'm not even sure if you couldn't play as well as a mouse and keyboard with a year or so's practice. It's much better than a thumbstick controller for shooters, and infinitely better at all others, with the exception of 2D fighters.
But reviews are not about the good, here is where I think it needs improvement. It's 80 percent in the software side of things.
Software:
IT NEEDS UNLIMITED MODIFIERS
Having a single modifier for each input is simply not enough.
Example: for a MOBA mapping I was trying to make, I wanted to have it so that when I select an ability, the camera centers, and the mouse touchpad enters a less sensitive mode with a smaller range of the screen around your character that only extends to the outer range limit of your abilities. The purpose of this being, you want to have the pointer really snappy for moving your character, but less finicky for skillshots.
Let's say I only have 4 abilities bound to the 4 triggers.
Only having one modifier prevents me from being able to have the touchpad enter "skillshot mode" just by pressing one of the ability triggers, and having each trigger be a modifier that makes it enter skillshot mode.
Instead I need to map a skillshot mode modifier to another control completely (say the right grip) and so now when I want to use an ability I need to select the ability with the trigger, hold the right grip to enter skillshot mode, and then fire it off. Considering how many times you use abilities in a MOBA, that one extra action/thing to think about everytime you use an ability really makes a huge difference.
Another example: I wanted to have another mode for the mouse touchpad that snapped it to the minimap and confined its movement to within the minimap. Since there is currently only one modifier per input device, and I am already using a modifier for skillshot mode I can't use the same touchpad for this function, and need to map it to the joystick, or the other touchpad.
I also think that it is vital to have the ability to make modifier buttons toggle switches as well as momentary switches. It would be useful to be able to have toggle functionality on ALL button inputs, but the modifiers are the ones where it is really useful. Back in the day I was hardcore into the DJ Techtools blog, that had an entire community built around creating mappings of Traktor DJ software to various midi controllers. The decision of the team who made Traktor to implement this simple toggle/momentary ability completely changed what was possible for us to do and it will be the same here.
Also having stackable modifiers would be awesome. I.e. right grip makes touchpad do x, left grip makes touchpad do y, right grip+left grip makes touchpad do z.
I know all this sounds complicated, and the average user may not want/need this kind of functionality, but I think that the endgoal of this mappings-sharing network should be to evolve the standard controls that are the best for each genre. And from my experience I think that these standards will require this kind of functionality to be powerful enough to allow the controller to be used for alot of games. It's complicated to make mappings with these functionalities, but not complicated to use them.
I am sure this will come eventually, but having the mappings be able to tie in more intimately with the games themselves would be awesome. To use the MOBA mapping example again, it would be cool if the touchpads could enter different modes depending what kind of ability you were using. I.E. a scroll wheel for aimed skillshots, or just a regular mouse for targeted area-of-affect powers, etc.
A smaller feature that I would like to see is when a touchpad is in button mode, and is in the mode where the buttons are only triggered when you click the pad and not just touch the area, is to have the haptic feedback trigger when you thumb over a button area without triggering the button. Just so that you get a sense that you are on a physical button.
also maybe have the ability to upload a tutorial/explanation video along with your mapping

Previously, at times, I've felt this game hasn't aged well but today, playing it for the first time in >10 years, I take that back.
This game:
It's actually not
horrible to look at - especially given the normalcy of 8-bit etc. experiences, these days.
And the interface etc. was ahead of its time for sure. You will be opening tons of windows but the game also gives you the hotkeys to do that as well as close them fast. ;) Also, logical hotkeys to call up the different views to perform your basic "scan", monitoring your empire. (Think "find idle worker", etc.)
As far as what we think of as being standard these days: bolted-on RPG elements, "progression", tons of customization, achievements (boo hoo!), etc., no, this game has none of it. It's kinda WYSIWYG, like phone games -- and ... y'know ...
games -- used to be. ;P
It's tough to put this game in a box. There are few others like it. It's "RTS", yeah, but the strategic part can be set to move slow like a 4X game (which it also is), and your units/infrastructure etc. is mostly depicted abstractly. There are turns but you control how fast the clock ticks. So yeah, a turn-based RTS. You can run it at ultra-slow speed so it almost feels like a civ game, or crank it up to the point where it basically zips by and you better know your hotkeys. ;)
Here, under the "Gameplay" heading, I do have to be clear about what makes up a lot of, y'know, the gameplay. This is a numbers game. An abstract game. Like any 4x game. A lot of the fun is "in your mind". (I guess that's true of any game, or even existence itself but let's shelve that extended philosophical discussion for the moment...) That being said,
Civ is a recurring theme in this review, and again, the best way I can put it is that this game is more Civ than AoE. You
keep a fast "scan" going like a good RTS, though, if you're into that. Lots of keyboard and mouse activity.
Anyway, when your fleets finally do meet the enemy and engage in space combat, the view/gameplay changes to a 3d tactical sim view where you can control your ships, give them some rudimentary maneuvers etc., and waste the enemy. You can actually micromanage pretty well, not that it's usually very necessary. (There is an instant "auto-resolve combat" feature, also, but you tend to take small but unnecessary losses when you use it -- a couple fighters here and there -- so, I only use it when that won't matter.)
There
a learning curve and the only tutorial is in the manual. But once you get a few concepts clear you'll be off to war!
This game will definitely give you great moments of "wow, I didn't realize [star wars so-and-so] could be such a badass", as well as plenty of "i've never even heard of so-and-so but they're a badass". (Also the occasional "wow, I
expected the AI to show up and ... do exactly what i was planning to do, but better!")
An impressive roster of units, etc., especially capital ships. Lots of EU stuff, including a few things that have (kinda?) been carried over into other games or lore at this point. Liberator Cruiser->Broadside Cruiser comes to mind. And possibly lots of planet names. Not sure on that. The world didn't have the gigantic dumpster of misc. sci-fi canon known as "The Internet" when this game first came out. ;P
~20 years ago ... now that I really think about it, I think this game
my first solid exposure to EU content. and it was actually pretty mind-blowing. Kinda sparked my whole "caring about EU type stuff" for SW and a lot of other games/IPs at all to begin with. So, that's cool, right? ;) I mean .. "x-wing" had tie defenders and whatnot, but this was
. The first place I got used to hearing the phrase "General Skywalker"... "Who is this 'Thrawn' guy and when will we see him in a movie?", etc. ;)
Booted right up on my gg system, Win 10 64-bit. Fullscreen with zero user intervention. I mainly mention it because the only negative review I saw cited this as an issue. Sound, mouse, keyboard, etc., working fine.
Wish they would do a remaster and put achievements tho. ;P
I wouldn't spend crazy $ on this (
, especially, considering I already owned it on disc), but
Final note, though: I say "strategy" games, because, as I covered in "Gameplay", this is technically RTS, but the emphasis is way more on the "S". If you are looking for a "real" star wars RTS, EAW, battlegrounds, force commander are your games. But try this one anyway. ;)

Positives: it didn't crash.  If you like Minecraft, avoid this one.  I played through ep.1, and I'm not planning to continue. For me, Minecraft was great because of the freedoms it gave the player.  The freedom to explore a practically infinite space, an endless treasure hunt to gather materials, and building anything of any size with those materials.  You *played* Minecraft.
Story Mode has none of this freedom.  You're locked into what it shows you, based on few pre-defined choices.  This really is just a choose-your-own-adventure. Once you've made a choice, what comes next is almost entirely out of your hands. There's no exploration, no creative problem solving, no brains required. When you build, it's a specific thing, with materials the game just gives you, no exploration needed. When the game lets you move around, it's in a tiny area, your field of view is limited, and you pass through the area in the one direction the designers have deemed will move the story along.
So if there's none of the freedom, creativity or problem-solving, it must be great to watch, right?  Wrong.  The plot is arbitrary, the characters are boring, the dialogue is shallow, the voice acting is flat, and your options are no more engaging than eeny-meeny-miney-moe.  Story Mode just looks like Minecraft, without actually being Minecraft.

For me, the draw of this game is two big things: you are given enough options during race/empire (or hivemind, republic, etc.!) that I felt really connected to my faction. Your planets will feel important, the races you integrate, subjugate, or exterminate also feel significant. Subfactions that develop within your empire are a real threat and lead to interesting things, and diplomacy with other races can be interesting and lead to some cool scenarios.
The next is that gameplay is so dynamic that each game will feel pretty unique. I like to play with traditional warp lanes (that  create strategic points in the map) and that leads to power struggles over choke points, border issues, etc. If that's not your thing you can play it with open travel.
It's a slick, well functioning space empire sandbox and it just keeps getting better with updates and DLC. Paradox is one of the few companies I will support with DLC since they are (usually) so interesting and have such a positive effect.

Paradox has done it again. This is actually a good introduction to Grand Strategy games, as it is not as grand in terms of complexity as you would normally expect from that genre.
The non-linear research tree, traditions, and highly customizable races make this enjoyable even on repeated playthroughs. While it is otherwise very similar to the Civ-Series, it does has its own unique game mechanics and a late game that is still very engaging, due to varied diplomacy, event chains, and possible end-game crises.

So stellaris as a game all by itself isn't much to look at if you get the core game.  It's a likable game, but the core game is mostly potentially amazing.  What makes this game beyond exceptional is not only the DLC, but more so the massive supporting mod community that makes this game turn into pretty much whatever you want as far as 4x goes.  The only down side is you'll soon find yourself burried in hundreds of mods, choking your pc to death having a great time at wayyyy past bed time, and then the update comes and everything breaks for a few days/weeks depending on what's affected.  that said, I've learned to use that down time to make my own mods for this game and I hope you do too!  It's pretty easy once you get the hang of it, and you can do tons of stuff!  It's pretty great.  All in all, buy this game, all the DLC and play it once through and beat it on vanilla so you understand the gist of it, then run over to the workshop and go crazy.  While the core game is likeable and even a little memorable, when you add all the goodies in, it turns into something special, one of the best games you'll likely play any time soon in the 4x realm.

This is a great game from 1998.  One of the few that is still fun and playable, thank you DosBox.  The controls were a bit strange to learn at first.  If you are a fan of the first Star Wars trilogy released I think you will like this.  It is set in a similar time as the films with the same characters in a Universe that is variable in size and difficulty depending on your choices.
Bottom Line, if you liked the First Star Wars Trilogy beginning with " Episode IV:  A New Hope", odds are you will enjoy this.  The very first moves can be paramount to your success or failure.  You can go fight it out right away, or strategize, recruit, build your forces, engage in diplomacy to recruit systems with industry and then attack in force.  The more system resource points you have, the larger fleet/s you can support.  You can also engage in a campaign of espionage, sabotage, kidnapping or assasination depending on which side you are playing.  You determine where to assign recruited personel.  If they are capable of researching areas in the tech tree, do you assign them to research right away or risk them in use on a mission?  If command capable, do you assign them to command or to missions?  Only you can decide.  To cap it off, you can identify new Jedi candidates and after Luke goes to Dagobah, he can begin to train them, or if you are playing the Empire, Darth Vader can train them almost from the very beginning depending on whether you want Vader to recuit or just train Jedis for the Empire as soon as they are identified.
For a quick victory, the Empire usually has the advantage, for longer games, the Rebel Alliance is the better choice, assuming you max out your research ASAP.
REMEMBER TO SAVE, SAVE, SAVE!
The planets in the universe are always static, but resources, industry, starting locations of your initial characters, and all but one of your starting planets are always randomized with each new game so there is a lot of replayability.
If you are a Star Wars fan, do yourself a favor, buy it on sale and enjoy.
This old game is still one of the best Star Wars game around

This piece of hardware is fantastic!
*Tl;Dr at bottom.
I've spent many hours playing with this since launch, I feel like it's time for me to write a review.
Here are some of the games I've played with this controller:
-GTA5, Rocket League
-MGS PP, Oddworld: Stranger's wrath, RE4, Dead Space 3
-Gauntlet, Bleed
-DFO, Castler Crashers, Battleblock Theater, Broforce
Let me tell you about the shape of this controller, this thing fits snug in the palm of your hands. The first few hours might feel straining on your thumbs but your hand will shape itself perfectly unto this.
To me the two touchpads, Bumpers and trigger feel a little cheap. I got a controller that doesn't read full movements on the right touchpad since day 1. After about a month the triggers feel loose and I hear a rattling now, this controller never fell and I'm generally very gentle with my equipment.
That's about the only negative thing I can think about this controller.
The response, the feel, the gyro, the community and the software is absolutely amazing.
Buttons and Thumbstick
To me everything feels great now, I'm landing crazy combos in DFO, rocket jumping like a champ in Rocket League and clipping necromorphs limbs with tact and precision in Dead Space 3.
Speeding and braking in RL and GTA5 feels great and the Gyro? Oh God the Gyro, bruh.
Haptic is a very neat addition, rumble isn't in the controller but I don't miss it to be honest.
When playing with a KB+Mouse configuration the haptic feedback on the Thumbstick is bestest.
Gyro
The biggest selling point that got me on this controller was the gyro, I love driving games and I really wanted to get the feel of using a steering wheel in GTA5, when I got it working holy heck this controller brought new life into my game.
You can tweak everything to make the steering match your hand movement, 'nuff said.
I tried it out in shooting games, I first got into it when I saw a Community made configuration for RE4 that mimics the Wii controls. A few hours later, I launched CS:GO and tweaked the gyro to point and shoot, it was great. Tried the same thing for Bleed, Gauntlet, How to Survive. The gyro is precise and solid.
The Gyro gave me a case of nostalgia while playing RE4/CSGO, GTA5. It felt magical the same way playing Wii Sports or Metroid on the wii was for the first time. It's refreshing and AMAZING.
Software
The BPM (Big Picture Mode) looks great from my couch, navigating through it with the controller is simple and clean. (Not KH) I spent countless hours tweaking the controls for various games to make it feel "just right".
From trying to point the controller to pull off headshots in CSGO to sliding my thumb to 180 effectively, with enough tweaking this is all very possible. If that's not for you however, there are so many community made configurations.
You can access all of that neat stuff ingame by simply making the press of the Steam button.
So many things you can tweak. You playing MGS PP? you can set a binding so that if you don't push the thumbstick fully while configured with KB+M the input will be W+alt to make walking.
so... 10/10 for that ok.
*
Pros
-Customize everything
-Easy to use UI
-Frequent updates/Community configurations
-GYRO
-Battery lasts forever
-Works with EVERY game RTS/MOBA/Racing/Shooters/Platformers
-Plays well with other Gaming software platforms (Origin, UPlay, DFO thing, Blizzard UI)**
-Plays well with Windows in general, my first time set up was all done on my couch didn't have to get up EVER.
Cons
-The touchpads feel a little cheap, unresponsive.
-When using multiple controllers the Steam controller overrides other controllers, leads to games/Steam not recognizing other controller. (You can fix this, Turn off the Steam Controller and launch the game using another controller. When the game launches you just turn on the Steam controller again.(This only works when I'm using the batteries))
8/10 for me mostly because the overrall build feels cheap to me
I could write much more but I want to get back to playing games.

Ok, first things first, this is not a traditional gamepad.
I have never owned a controller before this one (And yes, I have used other controllers), and as such, it was WONDERFUL. It felt great, the buttons (unlike other people’s opinions) were great to use. I noticed that a lot of people complaining about this were trying to use it as a standard controller. This is not how it was meant to be used, and, as such, how you should never use it.
I noticed that I preferred this to other controllers mainly because I used it differently than other controllers. If you are looking for a normal controller, then buy one. I will explain how they are different, and if anything sounds worse to you, then DO NOT buy this. If you can get over it, don't have much bias as to how controllers are meant to be used, or can get used to features listed here, then this is an awesome piece of hardware, and you should definitely purchase it. Here are the features and how they should be used.
1. The track pad
The track pad is used for the camera or cursor. It is meant for a quick jolt to the side, not for precision. The gyroscope (which most people overlook) should be used for precision. The cursor works fine. Getting used to it takes a day or two, and by then it is precise.
2. The "D" pad
This is NOT a D pad. It functions as two things; a second track pad or another set of buttons (more on that later). The second pad is used mostly for scrolling, and is not really used for much as a track pad (at least for me)
3. The shoulder buttons
These are the main buttons. They are the left click, right click, scope, fire, shortcut, and ext. The abxy are NOT these buttons. You need to get rid of that mentality. The only issue is that the steam big picture uses abxy, however, this will be fixed in the future with big picture control adjustment.
4. The ABXY buttons
These buttons are meant for shortcuts, such as a quick heal, saving, menu, ext. Do NOT make these your main buttons, as they are hard and cumbersome to reach for the majority of your time
If you can get used to using these controls in this way, then this is DEFENETLY the controller that you want to buy. Otherwise, stick with a traditional controller and just use a keyboard and mouse for keyboard and mouse games.

I personally purchased this game. I reviewed it for my 99 Cent Gaming series.
Riot of the Numbers is a game that has me divided (pun intended) on whether I think it's worth the purchase or not. Let me get into the nitty gritty to tell you why.
This game is a platformer where your enemies are numbers, your heroes are numbers, and your weapons are math signs. The goal of each of the Riot of the Numbers' levels (save two boss levels) is to knock down the number from the top center of the screen from whatever it is to 0 which unlucks the door to progress. You start off with a subtraction projectile, an addition stomp, and in some levels you gain the division projectile.
What has me conflicted about this game is just how little there is to do here. I enjoyed the theme surrounding your goals, getting stumped on a few levels trying to figure out who to shoot, who to stomp, and who to spare. I enjoyed having to control two characters at the same time because of the need to focus on who to move and when. Overall, I like what the game brought me.
The issues I have aren't with the gameplay, the controls (although I hope the dev adds controller support at some point), or anything like that. I just wish there was more to it. The game was over before I felt it truly begun. Mechanics like having to divide or controller multiple characters came and went. There were only two boss battles and the last one felt very dissapointing compared to the first, and even more so because it was the final battle. I believe the game could have been something very fun if only there were more. I wanted more chances to rack my brain with the division sign. I wanted to see how multiplication could have thrown things into insanity. What the game had in a good concept was brought down by the lack of content surrounding it.
I have more to say in my video below, and you'll be able to see (and hopefully have read) why it's so hard to say yes or no to this title. I want to say yes because there's nothing inherently wrong with Riot of the Numbers, and I want to say no because I felt like there wasn't enough here for me to really sink my teeth into. That said....if you enjoy what you see on the store page, like a little math challenge to go along with your platforming, and want to have a good 20-30 minute distraction for just under a dollar...is it worth it: yes. For everyone else, it's probably okay to watch someone play it unless the developer decideds to add more, or even do a sequel that adds a lot more to the concept. If either of those things happen, I would love to revisit this game.

Okay, I will admit that I wanted to like this game. And honestly, The core of the game was fun. Its just that it was extremely broken. The Devs need to go back and fix the Frame Rate and the Crashes. And honestly, they need to make the game less confusing. The game may say you need to go to this location, but the game is so spread out there is no knowing where that location is.
I finally had to request a refund when I couldn't figure out where the hotel was on my own. I stumbled into quest blind, not completely knowing why I was there. The controls for driving aren't laid out, and when I say that, I don't mean 'oh I don't know how to turn left and right' because that wasn't an issue. The issue was I couldn't get out of my vehicle on my own without a random quest being there. Since I'm sure there would be a point where there are no location quest but you have to get food for the hotel, that is a serious issue.
The Frame Rate wasn't imposible, I'll say that. But it was slow enough that if I wasn't on my tactical game, zombies would easily come and munch me like a bag of chips. There are many players who would have flipped out faster and gotten themselves killed with that frame rate, So that despreately needs to be fixed.
As for crashes, I only dealt with one before I requested a refund. I was in the middle of a hoard of monsters (not completely sure they were zombies) and I needed to change off my shotgun because I had like 3-4 shots left in it. So I press the convient O button to swap to my chainsaw. The game couldn't have crashed faster. I've read below that there were many more crashes in the game so I didn't put up with it.
Alright, so why the heck did I buy a game with nearly no positive reviews to it?
I really wanted to like this game. I am obsessed with apocalyptic and survival games, as any of my friends they'll tell you the same. So when I saw this, I got excited.
I really like the mechanic where you constantly have to forge for food. I love how you craft weapons, ammo, hotel supplies, and food. I think that is amazing and the things on those list aren't really easy to get. Very fun for hardcore survivalist like me.
I really like how in the beginning the devs give you plenty of ammo to help you get the learning curve. You essentially have no fear of running out of ammo in the beginning, with over 70-100 shots of shotgun ammo, around 200-250 pistol ammo, and 250 chainsaw fuel (I sadly never got to try out the chainsaw as mentioned above when I attempted) the weapons you start with are not top notch. It is a rusty pistol and shotgun. Still they are extremely helpful in the beginning when you are clearing out zombies from the hotel and maybe a couple missions before you actually have to start crafting ammo.
The hotel was pretty nice, for an apocalypse hotel. There were so many issues in the hotel to fix that I got excited, thinking of the time I could have soon fixing up the hotel into a 5 star joint.
Since many of you won't play this, I'll say this, Bruno is the most helpful companion in the game, my opinion. He'll charge zombies, bitting them to death taking almost no damage whatsoever. Very useful with the low frame rate, he'll keep you from being instantly swarmed when you load up the map.
I guess in conclusion, This game would have been amazing. I'm not biased against it. But these errors were right at the start of the game. I had hardly finished my first mission when all this sadly came to a head. I wanted to love this game, But unless the Devs fix these bugs and add in location markers to help players get to places, This game will never gain positive ratings.
One last thing before I go, Only play one day and night to see how it goes for you. The Devs do not give you a time skip button, and at one point try to 'recommend' you to wait it out until morning. Do Not Do This. There is no time skip button, so you are forced to sit there waiting for day to come slowly, which will Wear Down your steam time until the point where Steam will look at your time card when you go to request a refund for it, and they will think you a liar and deny you. Don't get caught in it. Keep to one day and one night to see if you actually like the game.

I like this game.  I really do.
But it is really quite buggy.  Every now and then, the game crashes because of one error message or another, which suggests to me that the level of playtesting involved is inadequate.  It wouldn't be quite so bad if you could save wherever you pleased, but the old fashioned "save point" method makes it pretty frustrating.
If you can get past the bugs, I certainly recommend this game.  Don't let the RPG-maker graphics fool you - it's pretty good.  You upgrade your hotel in a manner that vaguely reminds me of how you upgrade your castle in Suikoden II, and you get to pick and choose to whom you rent.  The different guests offer different services, and there always seems like a LOT to do.  Even the little sidequests, which come and go faster than you can do them all, seem pretty important.  The game has more of a plot than its simplistic writing style would suggest, and the level of inventory management involved appeals to me.
If you can pick it up on sale, it's probably a steal.  I could only recommend it at its list price if the bugs were ironed out.

I literally waited to buy this until I had a new gaming rig. Threadripper 1950X, 1080ti, and there's still a few sections here and there - usually hacking minigames - that lag for literally no comprehensible reason. That was with the FAR Mod, of course; which I would say is damn near essential. Also get an Xbone controller while you're at it. Don't buy this on Steam unless you have an uber mondo rig and are OK with installing a mod. (You can find said mod in the forums)
With performance out of the way, I want to point NieR: Automata's largest flaw: the game's bullet hell system is awful. You can't see the bullets through your own tears. (Oh wait, we already made that joke for UNDERTALE. Damn it.) NieR: Automata plays as a really weird genre mashup. There's at least three different kinds of bullet hell shmup in here (think "Gradius", "Geometry Wars", and "Starfox"), along with 2.5D platforming and 3D PlatinumGames style spectacle fighting. It all changes based on the context of the level, in a way that will eventually make sense as you play through the game. Alongside your YoRHa production model android will be a Pod, which serves as your gun, as well as a user of Pod Programs such as firing a massive laser or summoning a hammer to push enemies back. Gameplay is varied enough to remain interesting despite the open world itself not necessarily holding itself up to, say, Breath of the Wild standards.
But wait, you said something about tears? (And a 2-year-old indie darling everyone hates now?) Well, Yoko Taro is going to tug at your heartstrings, and then tear them out of your body and use them as a makeshift garrote. I can't say much more, because pretty much everything else would constitute a spoiler. Get yourself a copy and play it, and don't stop until Ending [E]. You'll thank me for it later.

I've seen some people say it's too short but I didn't find that a problem. I often get quite disappointed with games that overstay their welcome by adding more and more mechanics that end up not feeling coherent with the main mechanics of the game. That's the problem I had with Portal 2 over the original Portal and I would say Out There Somewhere falls on the side of Portal: it has few mechanics that work very well and that are exploited as much as possible through the course of the game. All the mechanics that get added through the course of the game complement the main teleporting mechanic and get used from that point onwards.
Overall, for its price, it's a must to have in your library. Also, it seems like it's always discounted so more reason to own it.

I'm no professional reviewer. I'm not even a professional Stellaris player (if such a thing exists.) I love space, I love strategy and I love killing dirty filthy xenos. Stellaris is a game about finding new planets, colonizing alien worlds and getting into bad, Sad (!) trade deals. Potentially the worst trade deals in strategy game history. There are many things I would call Stellaris: Good. Bad. Xeno Annhilation Simulator. But overall this game sucked over 560 hours of my life into it before I uninstalled it. As of today, December 10th, 2017, Stellaris is no longer installed, but I am writing a review for it.
Why? I love the game, but I also hate the game. During my first playthrough, I lost in the first 100 years. I was a poorly created nation that I thought would've been fun. This is the reason why it's easy to lose sometimes. There are definitely better Empires that can be created and are usually the "fun" empires to play. While there are offshoots, such as the One Planet Challenge and Inwards Perfection, it's mostly the same monotonous empire type, but that can't stop more roleplaying capabilities. That is a lot of the fun when it comes to Stellaris, is working around a relatively constricted system and making it yours. With mods at your side and a customizable Galaxy, almost any science-fiction empire, coalition, alliance or federation can be played. While the game isn't completely unplayable with mods, there is a reason why I have almost no achievements in Stellaris -- mods disable achievements.
I don't have the greatest PC in the world. It's quite bad actually. After first the 50 years the game starts to slow down, and by the time the massive deathball fleets start slugging it out, it feels like it takes 50 years for the battle to end. Looking at discussions and other player's comments, Stellaris does have issues with performance when it comes to the later years. The difference here is that while my bad PC starts chugging after 50-70 years, better PC's can start chugging after a mere 100 - 150 years, which just by glancing at screenshots and discussions, a lot of players like to go into the 200 and 300 year long campaigns. The longest campaign I've seen went into the 2700's, and the game starts in 2200.
Combat is negligable. It's a matter of who has the largest fleet in the game and comes down to one battle and then becomes either you building up a fleet to take back your captured planets to keep your warscore afloat or moving from planet to planet pumping your warscore up. Although it can be made more interesting, say with friends you intentionally don't have any fleets over 50K fleet power, you can have such a skirmish-based war, but in most conventional wars there is nothing like this. In the upcoming 2.0 update, there are changes coming to this, the idea of a death stack fleet is going to be hard to take away.
Colonizing becomes less of an effort and more of an off-hand thing after the first 30-ish years. You look closely at your colonies and make sure that their needs are tended to for your first five or so colonies. Afterwards it becomes more of a template system applied over planets and using them to produce more ships and armies to conquer more smaller empires and take their planets or make them fight for you.
Exploration is one of the funnest aspects of the Stellaris early game. Getting anomalies, finding new Empires, figuring out who your rivals are, figuring out who your friends are and having your sciENTIST DIE AGAIN BECAUSE OF A FAILED 5% ANOMALY. But this early game is also the most dangerous. Your beginning fleet can be destroyed by the wrong jump into a system with a Leviathan. You can lose your entire science ship fleet in one year. Some slightly larger empire can have a fleet twice the size of yours. Some slightly smaller empire can have a fleet half your size and suddenly look conquerable. Drawing your borders and finding your mid-game is one of the best parts of the game.
The mid-game is when it starts to fall apart and Paradox tries to fix a hole in a tanker with scotch tape. The game starts to slow down. The anomalies start disappearing. The special projects are being researched. The fleets are staring each other down and waiting to fight. Colonies start becoming self-sufficient, and half your colonies are in sectors anyways. While the game starts picking up in diplomacy and war in these parts, the diplomacy is mediocre to say the most and I've already covered the combat. Diplomacy boils down to rivaling your to-be friend's rivals, and sending them some minerals, food and energy monthly for nothing. You then send a non-aggression pact and then a defensive pact. Don't get me started on how the AI declares wars either.
During the late game, things become interesting again. 150-200 years into the game, the legendary and scary Crises start popping up. Everything from the Robotic Contingency, to the interstellar Prethorean Scourge and the devastating Unbidden and their kin. While not exactly an end-game crisis, the War In Heaven divides the galaxy and introduces the galactic powerhouses of the Awakened Empires. All of these breathe new life into the game again, and can be the key to winning the game in a matter of years or fighting a losing war over the course of decades.
Overall, Stellaris is good and bad. I love it so much, otherwise I wouldn't have spent 564 hours on it. I befriended Xenos and I annihilated them. I conquered the galaxy and I helped the galaxy. I lost the game in 10 years and I won the game in 200. I love this game and I hate this game. It's still rough around the edges but is definitely a diamond in the rough. It's a game that, like most Paradox games, still need a couple years before it becomes one of the definitive games in the space 4x genre. I recommend it, but play it later. It still needs a little bit of time to mature.

Hello whoever asked for the steam controller review here we go (sorry for it been late).
The controller arrived 2 weeks before the estimated delivery date so 10/10 on that.
The first time i used the controller i encountered an issue with the gyro i'm not sure why but after putting steam into the beta version (which i recommend if you have the controller)  i got a firmware update and the gyro now works like a dream.
Setting up the controller in games is extremely easy especially if you just use a community config, the menu makes it easy to map the buttons to the keyboard, mouse or controller key which is great, the gyro can be mapped to the mouse or variants of the joystick actions. Also you can use the controller with non-steam games but you need to add them to steam (there is a button in the bottom left of the library where you can add them) the support isnt like steam games in term of community configs but you can still use all of the features like normal steam games.
All the buttons on the controller feel great to use even the a,y,x,b buttons which are the furthest away from you thumbs. The triggers are stiff enough so you control accurately but not to stiff so you have to really pull them, the buttons at the end of the trigger press is good.The bumpers also feel good. the pads are accurate in mouse mode and work the a joystick on that setting, the trackball mode also works well. They are very customisable binding different thinks to a touch or a click or even a double tap. The haptic works well but is loud. The joystick works as you would expect it to, there is a click to the joystick like the xbox 360 controller. the left pad works like a trackpad with all the binds mentioned for the other pad but this pad has an indented cross but if you want to use it like normal it isn't distracting. The paddles on the back are extremely useful for anything like a paddle shifter or as a replacement for the button (simple remapping).
The community configs are extremely helpful and you probably can find what you need in them with only minors tweaks to make it perfect.
Overall if I had to recommend this I definitely would it is a big upgrade from the 360 controller but for shooters i would stick to keyboard and mouse.

I've never written a review about any type of steam product, game or otherwise, but after reading negative reviews I felt I should at least say my opinion.
1. Ignore the people that say they'd rather just stick with the Xbone and PS controller. They are missing the primary focus when it comes to the steam controller, which is an all-emcompassing peripheral. It intends to replace mouse and keyboard, whereas Xbone and PS controller only have functionality for games that support it. Steam controller inputs mouse and keyboard, so by virtue, EVERY game supports it.
2. People say it's too difficult to use, but not true. There is a learning curve because it feels different, just like anything that's new, but it's not difficult. Most everyone I know grew up playing NES, SNES, or Genesis, and we still to this day play games together through Steam. If we can go from using a controller with 2-6 buttons to using an entire keyboard for Age of Empires, we can probably be okay with using the trackpad.
3. Fully customizable. Feels ♥♥♥♥ing great. Playing HOMM3 from the couch and having only useful buttons on the controller is awesome. Playing Portal, Bioshock, L4D, Scribblenauts, whatever, all feels good. It's responsive, it's exactly what you want where you want.
4. People complain that you can't use it as a regular mouse and keyboard without the Steam overlay. Well, yeah. But you can't do that either with Xbone and PS controller. So, just open the steam overlay and in half a ♥♥♥♥ing second you have fixed that problem.
5. Valve claims 80+ hours on 2 batteries. I've not used it 80+ hours, but I've used it at least 30+ and it's still running full battery, so that's pretty neato.
6. Lastly, it's Steam. These are the people that sell games for like, 80% off through the year. If you can spend $100+ on one copy of Halo or one copy of SWBF on a console, $150 on that new Xbone Elite controller, and $10-20 a month for Xbox Live or PS Plus, you can probably give this a try. This is the first edition controller and I expect it only to get better at a fraction of the price.
Cons:
The face buttons. Even the people that love this controller know that it's annoying as hell to reach the "X" button, but eh, I've been able to do it now that I've put in the hours on the controller. Even so, there's other buttons to avoid using the "X" altogether, but like I said, that learning curve goes away and you will finally develop a feel for it.
So this was a cool first post I made. Seriously. Just try it. It feels good and works with every game. I typically like mouse and keyboard better (which I still use from time to time for MMOs or if I'm in the bedroom rather than playing in the living room), but the steam controller is a strong contender and I absolutely love this thing. Maybe not ~better~ than mouse and keyboard, but the best choice in gamepad considering the purpose and intended use of the steam controller.
TL;DR its cool

I'm sure Valve won't read this, but here's my constructive criticism because I want this thing to be awesome:
+ Tons of customization.
+ Trackpads allow for precise mouse-style controls.
+ Grips/Paddles on the back feel like a natural evolution and should be standard in the coming years.
+ Say what you want, batteries are better than battery packs. Just get rechargeables and you're set. They're cheaper and more powerful than any battery pack on the market.
+ 2-stage triggers offer more options than the regular ones.
+ USB cable for wired use / USB dongle for wireless use included.
Alright, now for the far more important part: The negatives
- Face buttons are too small AND concave. They cause physical pain after a while. Either make them larger, or make them flat with rounded edges. They're also far too close to the center, making them weird and uncomfortable to use.
- Analog stick placement is too close to the center as well. Move it more to the side. You can't? Hear me out.
- Trackpads are too large. They don't need to. Make them a bit smaller (maybe half a centimeter in radius). Not only does the deadzone on the right pad prove me somewhat right, but I rarely need the entire amount of space to navigate things. The "d-pad" is a chore to use due to its massive size. By making the trackpads smaller, you'll free up additional space to move the stick and face buttons, or to make the buttons slightly larger. This would solve the issues mentioned above.
- The controller "feels cheap". Pressing any button or trackpad is a rough and rather noisy affair. Console controllers feel way softer and allow for extended use. Please use membranes or (soft and silent) microswitches in future revisions. Pressing the pads regularly causes physical pain and makes my thumbs sore after only half an hour. This is unacceptable considering gamers play games for up to (and over) 8 hours a day (if they have the time, that is).
- Controller integration and customization shouldn't be limited to Big Picture. Add it to the desktop client so we can work on it from a desktop environment (y'know, the thing we're at like 90% of the time anyway). I like quick and easy mouse-controlled customization, not the clunky mess that is Big Picture.
- 2nd-level trigger press needs more resistance. Far too often did I press the final button by complete accident because the resistance was too low. I feel I should be able to rest my finger on it at least a little bit. Sure, it's easy when you try it now and in a safe environment, but things get far more hectic during gameplay. Maybe this is just me though.
- Opional weights would be nice. I find the controller to be a bit too light for my taste (which just adds to the "cheap" feel).
- I think I noticed some mechanical interference while using the trackpads and triggers at the same time. Can't explain it really, sorry. It doesn't impede with gameplay/performance, but it was slightly annoying.
- Left trackpad likes to "spazz" out when I play platformers. Instead of doing something, it would just do nothing at all, letting my character stand in place even though I kept the button pressed. Please look into it by doing some more testing.
Overall, the Steam controller is an innovative little piece of interfacing technology, but it's still a diamond in the rough and needs quite a bit of work. Right now, it definitely doesn't beat the good old 360 controller when it comes to certain games. Fighting games and character action games like Devil May Cry simply work a lot better with a 360 pad. The latter are playable, but you will perform worse or suffer pain from the button presses. The former are next to impossible to play due to the massive, unreliable d-pad (and analog sticks have never been viable, so that's not an option either).
If Valve put their heart into it and treat this thing like a proper alternative to console controllers, they can certainly beat the 360 controller. But as it stands, no console player will convert to Steam machines without feeling alienated by the Steam controller. It does many things right when it comes to PC gaming, but makes far too many compromises (or even sacrifices) with regards to console gaming. Once they manage to iron these out, the Steam controller will become the go-to controller for anyone that plays games on PC. But for now, it's merely an appetizer with an irritating aftertaste.
Recommended because it's heading in the right direction.

I've been using the Steam Controller for 2 days now, in my living room pc, so this isn't a complete review, but more of a first impressions.
First things first, the 1st minutes were rough. I'm actually used to trackballs, so the transition didn't feel alien to me, but when I first plugged it in and started moving the cursor around, it felt very janky. Steam recommended that I used big picture mode, so I did, but no other prompt or guidance was shown. I then minimized it and opened Chrome to access a URL that came with the controller's quick guide, and I saw that a prompt for new firmware should have popped up. I opened up big picture again and this time it said I should use Steam Beta version for the latest controller options, so I did and sure enough the new firmware popped up. After the update, moving the cursor with the right trackpad felt much more predictable. This whole step of updating the firmware would have been easy to miss. Also, it took me a while to realize that I should rotate my finger around the left trackpad to scroll up or down, instead of just going up and down as I think would be more intuitive. All in all, more guidance when the device gets plugged in would be welcome.
After several hours of use (though not enough for a definitive review), my general conclusion is that there is a lot of range in this device's usability across a wide spectrum depending on the game and settings, but at worst - due to its customizability - it's acceptable. It's a very good compromise between a double-joystick configuration and K/M, but can it surpass them individually? Here are my thoughts on that;
- The trackpad surpasses the joystick in precision and speed of looking around, but it's inferior to a dedicated mouse.
- The joystick on the left surpasses the eight directions and singular movement of a keyboard in moving around, like any other controller already did.
- The portability is identical to a regular controller, so it beats K/M handily.
- The amount of keybindings surpasses regular controllers but not the keyboard.
- The customizability of its behavior beats all input methods I had in the past, although some high-end mice should be ahead still.
I wasn't expecting this kind of depth of customization in this iteration of the product, which is very impressive. For instance, the trackpad can behave like a trackball, so by flicking it, the cursor can keep moving as a ball would keep rotating until it stopped. The obvious problem here is that, if you don't feel (or hear) the ball's rotation, how can you tell if it's rotating? Well, by the magic of clever haptics feedback, you actually feel and hear the vibration of the "ball's" rotation. You can also set deadzones, sensitivity, smoothness, and much more.
This depth in customization can be intimidating, but fortunately Steam made it easy on us by providing a list of community setups ordered by popularity; so if you don't want to mess with it but want a tried and true setup for, say, Fallout 4, you just have to select one and you're good to go. I have to say this whole aspect of this device has been very impressive to me.
Now, for the problems with it so far:
The main issue I have with the controller's design is the lack of feedback when your finger is too close to the edge in the right trackpad. This scenario is happening to me very frequently in F4: let's say a dog charges at me; you will have to aim down to hit it, and the closer it gets, the further down you need to go with your finger. Since the trackpad area is very limited you will run out of space very quickly forcing you to reposition your finger in the center to aim further down. If you have a trackball, it's easy to tell when you need to do that because the curvature of the ball makes it impossible for your thumb to keep gripping it after a certain point, but on a trackpad it needs to be obvious when your finger needs to go back to the center. The SC's trackpad has a very subtle edge, which is itself a problem in giving your finger feedback, but worst than that, it will stop registering your finger's input as you get close to it, again with no feedback. This results in you sliding the finger down, expecting the motion to be translated onscreen, but the viewport will stop moving which is extremely uncomfortable. I'd recommend adding an outer ring before the area where inputs stop being registered (or maybe using haptics for that?) so that your finger knows when to reposition in the center.
This other problem is related with the game engine in question, not the controller, but it's something people should know. Fallout 4 doesn't know what the Steam Controller is, and this isn't a problem in itself since the SC is very competent at simulating either a regular controler or K/M, but because F4 only allows for either one of those input devices to be active at any one time, then you need to make a choice of whether the SC will simulate one or the other, so it can't take advantage of both of their strengths (even though it still kinda manages to do so, more on that later). If you set F4 to use a controller, then the SC won't be able to simulate the mouse directly; if you set the game to use K/M, then the SC can't use the analog stick's versatility to move around. In the later scenario, you can still use SC's own stick to move, but it will be simulating WASD resulting in an uncomfortable experience since the stick doesn't stick (no pun intended) to those 8 positions, but the character in the game will. Fortunately, the SC has a solution, and this is where its customization features really impress. If you set F4 to use a controller, the SC will use the left stick as you would expect, and it will attempt to simulate a mouse behavior with the trackpad by sending those inputs to the game as if they came from a regular stick, so basically you can get the best of both worlds even if the game doesn't allow both input methods at the same time. I don't think this extra layer of simulation is as good as direct mouse simulation, but it's hard to say which means that it's pretty damn close.

Seems like nobody really mentioned this, so I will just go ahead with it. I read that this game is full of friendly, helpful people, so I decided to give it a try. I ended up liking the game a lot, however the opinion regarding players couldn't be further from the truth.
Pros:
-Amazing anime style graphics
-Skill customization - change the behavior of skills you already have
-Gliding - fast transport around the map
-Autopath to quest objective - regular quests have this, "hidden" quests do not. You will find both on all the maps.
-Creative missions - take control of npc during a main quest
-Achievements system - you get them for just about every quest you do. The names are creative and it makes the game more fun
-Sub class system - lets you mix 2 classes together for greater variety
-Pets - called Eidelons, they contribute to your damage significantly and you can swap them around based on the situation to take advantage of their special abilities.
Cons:
-Bot heaven - the review I read stated 99/100 players are friendly and helpful. The truth is, 99/100 players are bots. They are complete clones of each other with the same naming convention, yet nobody seems to care about it. You find them everywhere, not difficult to get 5-10 on your screen at a time.
-Players - virtually everoyone ignores you completely. Those that do not only see you as a resource, not a person. There is a system of "loyalty" points and guild points so people only friend you so they can click a greeting button on you once a day for loyalty or that you farm guild points for their benefit. Beyond that, you mean nothing
-Lag - you feel it in every slightly crowded area or town. This is especially noticable with delay on jumping/gliding
-Character appearance - some could say there is a lack of options for character customization. I haven't really run into lookalike characters yet except for bots that all look the same.
-Class balance - some classes are seriously overpowered, just about all players agree on who those are (Ravagers, even after a nerf they are still the most dominant by far)
Conclusion: If you have friends to play with, this game is pretty fun and enjoyable. If you do not and are not a solo player, don't bother, you won't get any help around here.

This is an excellent 4x strategy game.  The gameplay holds up very well, even after almost 20 years.  It's a quisi-real time strategy (RTS) 4x game (outside of the truely real time battles, that is).  I say 'quasi' because, despite being technically real time, it feels more like a hybrid between real time and turn based strategy.  Like an RTS, both players make moves simultaneously, but all moves and locations are descrete (there's nothing between planets).  Also, battles are resolved one at a time, seperately from the rest of gameplay.  The RTS and turn based elements fit together remarkably well create an experience unlike anything else I've played.
I only have two real criticisms: the AI is awful, and the user interface is clunky.  Otherwise, though, it's a great game.

Great idea, horrible execution.I have yet to play a single game that works with this damn thing out of the box.  Since I prefer to not waste my precious gaming time configuring controllers for every game, it is essentially worthless.
Some of the major problems are:
- Inaccurate touchpad in every game I have used it in out of the box
- poorly placed buttons for many games (rocket league)
- Becomes the defualt controller when you REALLY REALLY don't want it to. (Farcry 4, project cars, etc.)
In the games I have configured it to work with, it performs worse than my xbox 360 controller.  This is the case in both Rocket League and GTA V.

The controller takes time to learn, but ends up being the best of M/Kb and controller.  It offers the speed and accuracy of a mouse and keyboard while offering the ability to laze on your couch with some friends while you game, browse the web, etc.  After you learn them, using the touchpads is second nature and about as fast as using a mouse.  The buttons have a nice feel to them, and the haptic feedback is very customizable.  The triggers have a dual stage analog/digital setup (squeezing the trigger allows analog control, but smashing the trigger down to its secondary "click" makes it behave digitally).  Two of the features I think don't ge enough attention are the grip paddles and the gyro control.  The grips feel very natural to squeeze and don't get in the way of anything.  The gyro makes aiming in FPS games very natural and functional.  Competitive players should incorporate it into their configuration.
The controller feels about as sturdy as other gamepads feel, not cheap like some people say.  You have to feel it in your hands to really judge it.  While my hands are small, they don't get sore or cramped even after hours of playing.
Overall the steam controller works for me.  It has a relatively steep learning curve and it's difficult to learn what configurations work in a given game, but after those two hurdles are overcome it becomes second nature to use.

Being a huge fan of the original Primal Carnage, Primal Carnage: Extinction disappoints me. I spent almost 2,000 hours playing the original game, and I have to say that this game isn't fun to play at all. I thought during it's Early Access period that this game would get better, but it really didn't get too much better. The game has horrible balance, hit detection, hitboxes, and dinosaur movement.
The game is also mostly filled with Roleplayers. There is no competitive community for this game like the original game had. Being a competitve player of the original, it just disappoints me to see Primal Carnage: Extinction become the game it is currently. The game seems to mostly revolve around people sitting around in servers and waiting for loot to drop.
The whole game just seems to rely way too heavily on it's economy system. This game seems to be more about Quantity over Quality. Gameplay doesn't seem to be a priority for the developers which is saddening as that's what made the original game so great. The original game had excellent gameplay, and it was much more fun to play. If this game stopped being updated, it'd probably die quicker than the original would. The Saints are back!
Saints Row 2 is set in the fictional city of Stilwater and takes place five years after the original Saints Row, only this time you are in charge of a gang known as the Third Street Saints.
Story: The story has you trying to rebuild the Third Streets Saints gang after it has disbanded. You start off with basically nothing and through a series of varied missions, must take out the opposing gangs: the heavy metal gang Brotherhood,  Haitian Sons of Samedi and the Japanese Ronin. The game has an interesting story which stars memorable antagonists such as the dumb and naive Shogo of the Ronin, to the sadistic General from the Samedi. Each character has traits which standout and are unique only to them. I found myself constantly drawn to the story and eager to see through the next mission to unravel the tale of warring gangs further.
Graphics: The graphics for Saints Row 2 are passable and nothing to write home about. The game originally came out in 2008 so the visuals are dated to be expected. Textures of characters and the environment are somewhat muddy and the colours look bland and do not pop from the screen.
Sound: All characters are voiced extremely well. You can tell what exactly their personality is through their voice and are a joy to listen to, from the always whiny Pierce to the always stoned Shaundi. Each character has their own charm.
Gameplay: I felt that Saints Row 2 was let down abit by it's gameplay. It feels awkward to control your character and sometimes he would go in the direction you had not intended. Also, the car handling is not smooth to say the least. Vehicles turn alot at the slight press of a directional button and they flip too easily as well. I hope that the clumsy controls are fixed in the sequel.
Overall, Saints Row 2 is a fun game with an interesting story about redemption, revenge and warring gangs. It has engaging characters that you care about and if you can get past the clunky controls and performance issues, you will have a good time with the game.

Unlike some of the other reviewers, it did not take long at all for me to adjust to the Steam Controller's functionality. It works great for strategy, point-and-click, visual novels, 3rd person adventure, puzzles, platformers and even racing games. I don't play a lot a FPS games, so I didn't get this controller thinking I'd toast everyone on CS:Go. Nevertheless, it's easy to use, fully configurable for just about everything and even my daughter had no trouble picking it up and playing "Grow Home" with it right away.
It also works well for normal desktop mouse movement and clicking if you happen to be sitting far away from your computer (i.e. for Netflix).
This is a true controller for PC, not a console controller that happens to work with PCs. If you love customization and getting your controller to work exactly the way you want it to, this is the ultimate tool and toy.

It takes some adjusting to because of the track pad on the right side, but, as a console gamer of my entire life, it is an awesome controller. With a few minor adjustments to the sensitivity, it really has no flaws. The fact that you can use it with every steam game is a plus too. If the track pad turns you off about it, try it at a friends house or something because it really is alot better than it sounds and it is not like a laptop touch pad at all thanks to the controller's haptic feedback. I definitely recommend trying this out if you're like me and have always been a console gamer.

The steam controller feels nice in the hands. People who tell otherwise are usually the same people who compare it with their controller they used to play on for many years and didn't give the controller enough time.
The build quality is exactly like other controllers (PS4, Xbox One.) Don't let people fool you who say that it is cheap. It feels very durable.
The X button feels awkward placed (bit too far) but if you have small hands it might be very hard to use for a good while. Test first before you buy.
The only other issue I had were the buttons above the triggers. They felt very stiff compared to other controllers and are awkward when the game maps those buttons to shooting and aiming (like in GTA 5 where the bottom triggers are for driving.) I fixed this by remapping those triggers to the triggers under the controllers.
The haptic feedback feels great for navigating on the touchpads and pushing buttons but I have yet to find a game that support vibrating for gun fire or car crashing (which isn't the fault of the steam controller I suppose. Just that it isn't much supported yet at this time.)
The software functions decently even tho it sometimes feels like a beta. Luckily it's software and can/will get updated as they are doing frequently.
It is decently annoying however that you have to be in Steam Big Picture mode. I am not playing from my couch and would rather have the normal interface for clicking.
Also an annoying this is that you cannot scroll around with the touchpads but only with the joystick. Small but weird as it does work when steam is not activated and the controller acts like a normal mouse.
I also am not sure why but in some games going into steam overlay to change settings or chat to friends you will have to alt+tab out and back in to make the game notice the controller again. Again I am not sure if this is the issue with  Big Picture mode, the controller or the game.
I will have to say that most games works fine with going into Big Picture Mode.
I can safely say that I recommend this controller. It did make my accuracy much better and the remapping isn't far as annoying as some "reviewers" both here and by big "tech" sides made it out to be.
It's my third day and it already feels like a controller I played on for the past decade.
Also the gyroscope and accelerometer makes for fun times in games like GTA and Mario Cart emulators.
It's also very interesting when using it to make macro adjustments in first person shooters as it works well.
But again, if you feel like you have smaller hands, try to find someone to feel the controller out.
Small tip, if you want to play EA games, don't add the game itself to steam but add the Origin client. If you do it this way the controller can use the Battlelog for the last few Battlefield/Medal of Honor titles.
Only issue is that with his work around you cannot set the controller bindings to each game in Origin.

I really, really like this controller. I must admit I was hesitant at first to order it. Even after I opened it and picked it up for the first time it felt... weird. It totally felt like I was holding a controller upside down with how it lays in your hands, there were these hugs paddle buttons underneath, and it had this odd clicky trackpad where my thumb habitually felt around for a joystick. I plugged the tiny USB dongle and it worked, right out of the box! No fuss, no messing around with drivers or anything. Immediately tried it out on Fallout 4 and it worked flawlessly. It took a little bit to realize that I configure the controllers game-specific key binds in Big Picture Mode and the UI was simple and intuitive (try binding jump and sprint to the back paddles, it's life changing.) Found out that this UI will let you rebind a button to any keyboard function allowing full re-mapping for controllers which is a refreshing change. I also tried it out on Binding of Isaac, no complaints or raves for a more arcade type game.
Overall the biggest reason why I've come to love this controller over the past two weeks is the comfort. This is honestly the most natural and comfortable controller I've used. I've shied away from controllers the last few years as joint pain has become a bigger issue (especially as it gets colder) and with this controller it just rests gently in your hands and has allowed me to bind a repetitive and troublesome action like sprinting in Fallout or an FPS to the back paddle putting much less strain on my thumbs and allowing me to comfortably play for much longer.

Pros:

Cons:

So is this game worth getting?
Yes. Despite the length of the game (1-2 hours, give or take) I find that you get quite a lot of enjoyment from it while it lasts.
