First of all, I would like to thank the staff of eq-games to provide me of this key. I hope that the key wasn't meant for writing a review ASAP since I found the code in my mailbox not that long ago and the mail dated back from may. I think I'd rather won this key in a giveaway of some sort on twitch. In any way I'm not going to let that influence my opinion.
Polarity is a first person puzzle game where you are a node inside another persons's network/database/server (it is not clear) and you have to finish the puzzles to collect the data from your victim and to complete the hack. If you are bored with the story itself you can also try out coop mode, which you complete puzzles with two persons even including splitscreen which you can connect controllers so you both can play on the same pc. This sounds like an amazing feature, I enjoyed every splitscreen that you could play and it was an utter shame to remove that on any upcoming game. Also if the main story is finished there are about as many bonus levels to dig into. I did find the concept interesting and they certainly set the bar very high. When I opened the store page this immediately catched my eye: "One of the most fun puzzle/platformers since Portal. Polarity takes it to the next level, demanding all of your wits and reflexes."
That is my main problem with the game, not the fact that it is comparing itself to Portal, but the fact that the execution of this concept is very poor. Okay I agree they have a lot of features to make the puzzles good like colored cubes, lasers, gates, jumping pads that you can rotate, bridges which you need to be the other color to be on top of them, and buttons that rotate a part of the room in front of you, gates that change the color of the object you throw in it or yourself (I don't think you could get in one of em so I couldn't test that). Those features literally made me decide to complete the game because they were pretty well done aside from the chance you may get stuck in an object. As a node you can swap in two colors, red and blue which were meant to make the puzzles more challenging but why limit yourself with only two colors? I think it could be more of a thinking game once you get multiple colors. Not to mention how buggy it sometimes is. The control setting is something you have to take a close look at but even then some glitches happen. For example I have set my forward key to E (standard color swap keys are Q and left ctrl) and whenever I wanted to move in the beginning it swapped my color while moving which made it impossible to complete the puzzles. To solve this I set this key different and that seemed to do the trick. The next problem to me is the fact that they did nothing with the story. They start of with a small intro telling you that you are a node hacking a computer. They could do something with that like make the map the inside of the motherboard or maybe give it a wallpaper with black background and green binary or something like that. Talking about the map that wasn't my favourite feature either. The map could, like I said before, be done better not only in idea but I think they are not familiar to corners. Whenever looking at the ground in the direction of a wall you may see an empty line where a corner should be (for ex Level 9) and sometimes there are corners but they are way too big making it harder to jump over them. Or you can see the floor sometimes not fully connected or stuff like that. The map is also a bit too big in some levels where it could be way smaller but every level had the same width and height of the map. The music was very silent but I didn't mind that because I picked my own music from youtube to play in the background. As for the data you have to collect, for most of the time it is not a challenge at all. Most of the time you just walk around the map a bit and find it convienently being behind a pillar or in the corner or so. I wish they did all the data placement like the few that needed a bit of thinking to get to. I was the least satisfied with the ending, even angry, they could've added a boss battle connecting it with the "story". For example that you as a node get detected by the computer you are infected and you need to escape the level before they erase you but they did nothing instead.
This game definitly has a good concept but the poor execution didn't do well in my book. I consider you only pick this up if you want to play a game just for the puzzles and don't mind the rest of the game.

Developer by Michael Flynn and published by FlynnFour Games, Apocalypse Hotel - The Post-Apocalyptic Hotel Simulator seems to be a RPG zombie game, with a sandbox type of element tied into it as well. The game itself is obviously a RPG Maker game, but it really pushes the engine to what you can actually produce with it.
Apocalypse Hotel - The Post-Apocalyptic Hotel Simulator is a fun and enjoyable game that is based around world building, zombies combined with RPG elements mixed in as well. It seems to be a unique type of zombie game, most zombie games require you to loot things, kill zombie and your main goal is to survive while aquiring missions and such. Although this game does make you loot things and kill zombie your main objective is to build up a hotel as best as you can. It does seem a little strange how something like that can tie into a zombie apocalypse type of game but it is rather unique.
Built up from RPG Maker engine this game really shows you what you can do with the engine if you put your mind to it and put some time into creating a game. The final result of this game is that it is rather enjoyable, and has used most if not all of it's own graphics, character sprites and such.
The gameplay itself is rather simplistic and fun to play around with. It takes a sort of management side of the game as well as looting and gathering resources in order to keep your hotel sustainable throughout the game. Doing things like fixing and repairing the broken pipes and other stuff to keep your hotel in shape.
The games sound and music are something that I think that the game should be able to crisp up a bit more on to be honest. The sounds are just there, obviously nothing too fancy as it is made in RPG Maker. The music I felt could've been a bit more atmospheric at times when you where fighting through a bunch of zombies.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Apocalypse Hotel is the most creative use of RPG Maker that I've yet seen. In this game you play a young adult survivor of a zombie outbreak (yes, again), although in this case the zombies are people that have been killed and brought back to un-life by alien terraforming of Earth. Returning to your childhood home -- a hotel previously run by your parents -- it's your job to survive, and to make the hotel a safe place for other not-yet-zombified guests.
The plot is silly, obviously, but it's meant to be. The tongue-in-cheek style is carried through to other aspects of the game, as well. For example, I couldn't help but laugh when I encountered my first companion.
Graphics - It's RPG Maker, so the main game is pixel graphics all around, but they've been put to good use and nothing looks out of place. The still art (particularly the introduction) is not beautiful, but it gets the job done. In fact, I suspect it's intentionally crude in some places.
Sound - The music is fantastic and in most cases fits the locations perfectly. In particular, the elevator muzak in the hotel had me smiling. Sound effects are nothing spectacular, but they are serviceable.
Gameplay - The controls and action on screen play like any other RPG Maker game, but the unique setting and premise of the game lead to a plot that ties you to your central base (the hotel) and has you venturing out to the zombie-infested surroundings to gather resources, find survivors to become your companions, and complete quests, returning home to recover, craft, and repair and upgrade the hotel. This works well in the early game, but I'm interested to see what will happen once I have fully refurbished my hotel. Will that be the end of the game, I wonder?
The game is in real time with automatic pausing for menus and other interaction. Combat happens whenever you encounter a zombie wandering around and is handled no differently to the rest of the game, so it too is in real time. On the streets there is plenty of cover that can be used to block your simple-minded enemies, who by and large just take the shortest path towards you, unheeding of any barricades. You start with both ranged and melee weapons, so unless you're up against a much faster or more powerful zombie, or you allow yourself to be surrounded, you have a good fighting chance right from the beginning of the game.
I was initially annoyed that all of the outside areas have zombies and mostly random collectible resources that respawn whenever you leave and re-enter the area, but after playing for a while I realised that it's not only more realistic that way, it also keeps you on your toes, making the game more challenging, and allows for loot runs that don't take ages to travel to the furthest corners of the map.
Pros:
+ Enjoyable music that fits the different parts of the game very well (I love the elevator muzak in the hotel)
+ Pretty good pixel graphics
+ Very original use of RPG Maker engine
+ Good sense of humour; doesn't take itself too seriously
+ Extremely responsive developer with a good previous indie game
Cons:
- Buggy with a few grammar errors as well as incorrect information provided on occasion (e.g. no 'o' mentioned on controls screen, while 'e' is mentioned, but doesn't do anything)
- VERY slow/laggy screen update; almost unplayable on some machines that far exceed the stated recommended requirements (this seems to be an issue with some hardware and some RPG Maker games, particularly with the latest version of RPG Maker, and I don't believe it's the developer's fault)
- A bit slow to get into and work out what you're doing to begin with
Apocalypse Hotel is a fun new RPG Maker game that stands on its own, far out from that very crowded group. It has great style and an enjoyable sense of humour, although at the moment it still suffers from RPG-Maker-related performance problems on some hardware and a number of small bugs.

There’s a hotel out in this apocalyptic world in Hotel Apocalypse (no surprise there), a hotel that was once owned by your parents. You go off in search of them at the hotel, but alas they don’t appear to be there. So, in response to this, you’ve just decided to make the world’s first apocalyptic hotel.
Now, before you say anything, I will just mention that I do understand that the game is built in RPG Maker, but that doesn’t make it any less of a good game. Whereas other games in the engine may not be quite up to par, Apocalypse Hotel, along with another one of the developers games built in this engine makes use of their own art assets. The inclusion of their own art assets makes the game so much more interesting to look at when it comes to the visuals, instead of being forced to look at the same grass patch you’ve seen in every rushed out RPG Maker game ever.
On top of the change in visuals, the developer has decided for something other than the typical turn-based combat you would see out of this engine. Instead, the dev has decided to go for action oriented combat that happens in real time. Everything in terms of combat will reveal itself to you the moment you load up the game. Zombies will wander around, you press a button to fire your weapon, and then their health bar drops. Keep doing that until said zombie is down and deceased; permanently! It has to be said, the combat is a nice change from the typical combat you would see from this engine.
To make the combat just that little bit interest, the developer opted in to add a companion system, with the first companion you come across being a zombie dog. And I tell you what, the moment you get that dog, it makes your day’s of zombie killing sooo much easier, that has to be said.
Although, with the change of gameplay, the game does have a level up system for both you and your companions, all of which will level up depending on how much they’ve managed to take down. Levelling up is purely a buff for stats, however, and doesn’t require you to do anything once you’ve levelled up, as you will already have the buff added to the character whom had levelled. Each character in the game can also equip different weapons and items as well, even if they are an undead dog that follows you everywhere out of love and loyalty.
Video games that have the undead in don’t tend to have the best of of storylines, all due to it never really being a focus. Well, with this game the developer has put a little more thought into the story, and I would have to say it pays off. The gist of it: aliens land on Earth, they change the atmosphere to accommodate them, and the majority of humankind just kind of died and was revived as zombies. Initially the plot isn’t anything too special, but with each new piece of story I come across it really brings me to want to find out more about what’s going on in the world.
Apocalypse Hotel may center around you running a hotel, but that doesn’t mean you have to hang around there for the rest of your days. You will be expected to go out often and do quests, as well as finding new items and parts that you can make use of. Those parts you can use for a myriad of things, and not just around the hotel. You’re given the option to build new weapons, ammo, and fix up parts of the hotel to make it more desirable to potential guests.
Obviously, the main chunk of gameplay is keeping the hotel in check. Throughout the hotel you can make improvements all over the place, from restocking the bar, to building the most expensive room imaginable, only for the most prestigious of guests. Thankfully, those guests won’t be staying for free, so they will pay you a regular fee for staying each and every night. The price they are willing to pay will range between each and every guest, so be sure to keep an eye on new potential NPC’s, as they may just be looking to pay more than another individual. Some guests require special rooms, but they tend to be worth it. The reason being is that they will offer something a little more than just the typical fuel that you use for all sorts in the game, like travelling.
Guests may be good for one thing, but they do need to be fed (unfortunately...). So, it is in your place as the hotelier to feed your guests. You can simply do that by going into the kitchen and making some hotel meals out of whatever you can find in the overridden city, but be careful; the more guests, the more mouths to feed, so be sure to keep that in mind.
The city you’re tasked to explore isn’t all empty, as at times you will come across quests that you’ve accumulated over time. These quests tend to range in difficulty, and for the most part will mention whether they’re easy, medium or hard to complete. Quests are your typical fetch jobs that you need to do, but they do end in a reward, so you can’t really complain.
These next few things are rather miscellaneous, but I felt that they deserved some mention. The game has a 24 hour day and night cycle, where every second in real life is a minute in-game, and depending on what time it is, your character will require a light when it is dark out. Trust me, when it’s dark out, you’re a little more reserved when it comes to going anywhere, as it is very difficult to tell where the next attack comes from if it’s not directly in front of you, and that’s just a little bit terrifying. Next up is shadows, and even though you won’t come across them too often, they still look pretty darn good when your character walks past the odd lamp.
With the time I’ve spent in the game I haven’t really come across too many problems so far, but there is one thing that does bug me, and that’s the sound effect you get to hear whenever you save the game. The sound effect is of a zombie growling in your ear, and every single time I hear it, regardless of where I am in the game it makes me think a zombie is right behind, gnawing on my character while I’m stuck saving. It’s never the case, but it’s just a tad annoying to assume as such every time I save.
Overall, the game makes for one very positive experience when you compare it to many other RPG Maker games. But it isn’t just the case of it being a good RPG Maker game, as it is just a solid game on its own. A game where being the hotel manager during a zombie apocalypse is such a bizarre idea, and yet it works and it works well. Couple that with an interesting plot that I really want to see where it ends up, then you’ve got yourself a game that I would personally have to recommend.

This game can be hilarious yet also serious. It is NOT a GTA clone, but it does have similarities. I have played this game from start to finish as well as many activities and other fun things. May I just say one main thing SR2 does better  than GTAV:
GTAV activities include: Tennis, Yoga, Strip clubs, Drinking, Golf, etc
SR2 activities include: Mayhem (where you have to cause as much damage as possible), Insurance fraud (throw yourself into cars to go flying and make money), Fight Club, Attack Helicopter (covering a drug-dealing car from above), Snatch (Oh, how this mode made me cry in my (successful) attempt at getting infinite ammo for the SMG's...), and many more fun and destructive activities. Granted, the SR series does not have as much 'polish', but I still think it is much more fun.
In this game you could be holding an innocent bystander after chucking a sticky bomb on a train. You can then throw this person infront of the train (as it passes), detonate the bomb so the train de-rails and sends itself and the person (and probably multiple cars) flying off a bridge and falling into the sea. All in the space of about a second. There are a hell of a lot of things you can do in this game, all as insane and fun as that. Get the bundle which includes this, SR3 & DLC, and SR4 & DLC. That's what I did (got it off ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) for less than £15 and it has lasted me a long time. Gonna get Gat outta hell when I can :D
Problems though: The cinematics are often out of sync (which really stops any emotion in scenes), The sound quality is often terrible, and often things are out of place (E.G in one scene the phone was stuck on the other side of a guy's hand for me). It is still really fun though, and one of my favourite games.

Stellaris is boring.
Stellaris tries really hard to be a good game.  It checks all the boxes for space based 4X or space based Grand Strategy.  It's got all the bells and whistles you'd expect.  But in the end, it fails to deliver.
No matter how you play, or what race you start as, you always end up in the same repetitive loops, over and over again.  Now, that's not unusual for 4x games, or grand strategy games, but, there's not enough variation to make a difference.  Games like this will usually have a number of different mechanics, which can affect how you play the game.  But in Stellaris, they barely do so.   The apologists will say that you got to approach the game differently, that it requires more patience, and that you should approach it like an unfolding story, rather than a race to the finish.  But in that field, it also fails to deliver - the stories aren't that interesting and aren't that varied, and soon enough you'll be getting the same ones again.
If you want a 4X game, there are much better games out there.  If you want an immersive/emergent story-based grand strategy, there are much better games out there.  This is by far Paradox's weakest game, and it really isn't worth wasting your time on.

I came to Stellaris after having played many games, including 4X games, and including space 4X games. I have to say that it is very well done. The level of detail is great, how everything interacts. The game is also very inspiring, I think it is the one that more closely makes you feel like you are in the Star Trek universe, which I believe must have been one of the intents. Once you get through the initial learning curve and get the hang of it, it becomes highly addictive.
That much said, while the level of detail is on the one hand the good part, it is also the bad part. It is hard, hard, hard to master this game. I have yet to win a game. I have started and dumped a couple dozen games maybe. In each I learn a new something, and next game I play better, just to get my behind handed to me again on a platter for some other reason. I ask a friend who has been coaching me: Why did I fail? It's because you're making too many mines. Oh, OK. Next time I make less mines. Why did I fail? It's because you aren't building enough mines. Huh? Last time you said I was making too many. Oh yes, well it's a balance. Why did I fail? You're colonizing too fast and expanding too much. Oh, OK. Next time I hold back on colonizing. Why did I fail? It's because you're not colonizing enough planets and that limits your fleet size. Wha? Last time you said I was expanding too much. Oh yes, well it's a balance. Gaaah!!
I'm still playing the game and addicted to it and hopefully some day I will win, but it sure isn't for casual players. I wish there was a way to give mixed review recommendations, I would give it two thumbs up and one thumb down.

is a puzzle platformer that'll take you through 22 levels (12 campaign levels and 10 'bonus levels') + 15 local co-op levels (with a horizontal split screen as seen in one of the screenshots).
The goal in each level is to collect 3 items and then find your way to the exit. To reach that goal, you'll need to take blue and red boxes from one point to another. Sometimes you'll need to aim and throw the boxes to their destination. You'll be jumping from platform to platform, sometimes switching your 'polarity' mid-air. Your polarity is a red or blue glow that allows you to pass through force fields of the same colour but prevents you from falling through force fields of the opposite colour. This makes for some interesting mechanics. Unfortunately, it also means that
sometimes becomes a twitchy game when you quickly need to push several buttons  during one long jump or during a series of short consecutive jumps.
The graphics are very basic. They aren't pixel graphics but nonetheless they look quite pixelated when seen up close. However, they serve their purpose here and the 'laser-look' makes up for a lot. I don't just mean the force fields that are made of lasers, but the platforms have a laser-like edge and the walls and the ceilings have laser-like lights drawn through them, too. This livens up a bit what would otherwise be very bland graphics.
The music is subtle. Actually, the music is hardly noticeable. Its volume is too low. You'll need to turn up the volume of your speakers a lot to actually hear it, which makes for tons of fun when another sound pops up, for example a new incoming message, which may startle you and everyone who's in the room with you.
There are little options in the game's menu: you can adjust camera sensitivity and switch music and sound effects on or off. When launching the game, you do get the standard Unity pop-up allowing you to change the resolution, select the overall graphics quality and toggle windowed on or off.
Controls feel a bit clunky from time to time. I used an Xbox controller because that seemed the logical choice for a platformer, but maybe keyboard and mouse makes for a smoother experience, I don't know. A strange thing happened to me when using the controller: when moving the camera left, it kept turning left even when I didn't touch the controller anymore. I had to tap the camera to the right for it to stop. The same thing did not happen when turning the camera right, and this problem doesn't occur when I'm playing other games, so it's a weird bug in
. When trying to find a solution for this problem, I came across posts from people complaining about much worse involuntary movement of the camera and even of the player's avatar, rendering the game pretty much unplayable. So
is not a fully polished game, it seems, and technical difficulties are not out of the question.
has 6 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 just for running the game.
Most of the 10 Steam Achievements are awarded for completing a number of levels successfully. The remaining few achievements are a bit more creative but are easily attained. If you don't have a co-op partner, you can complete the first co-op level by yourself to get that achievement relatively quickly, but you'll be left with two incomplete achievements: one for finishing all 15 co-op levels and one for finishing all the levels of the game, unless you want to take both avatars through each level, one by means of a controller and one by means of the keyboard and mouse.

A classic, and going back, my main complaint, would be that the graphics aren't as clean as they were on the XBox 360, and it's EXTREMELY glitchy on the PC, to the point of invisible helicopters making missions impossible.
Even the makers don't deny that it's very similar to the GTAs, but it doesn't take itself near as seriously, and is all about fun.  It's not as wild as the titles that followed in the series, but, more fun, especially to go back to years later, than any GTA before V.  Tons to do, lots of side missions, good sized maps, and hilarious dialogue keep it entertaining.  Unfortunately, in this early offering, the game doesn't track NPCs or cars well, almost as soon as anything is out of view, it vanishes (kind of a pain when seeking certain cars).
I also wished (before deciding I won't go back to it again) that the DLCs were available, some of those were great, and were referenced in, even integral (like Ultor) to the later games.  Not sure if that counts as a complaint, but would be my only other...
Bottom line, I LOVE the game, still, even when I can play Gat out of Hell instead, but, this copy is far worse than the console ever was.

The controller has its ups and downs. I still can't decide if it's really good or not. I think I'll just make a bullet-list of its good and bad sides and then summarize my short experience with it.
Positive sides:
* Build quality. The gamepad is really, really well made. $50 well spent.
* The stick is the best I've ever tried.
* The trackpads are very responsice and presice. Haptic feedback actually somewhat helps. If anything, you can use the controller as a decent mouse substitute.
* A lot of buttons. I even ran out of ideas of what to bind to which buttons and had some of them not set to anything.
* Extreme configurability. Not only you can bind any controller button to any keyboard or mouse button, but you can also set different behavior to them, like different types of d-pad or mouse/joystick.
Negative sides:
* The left trackpad feels way too big and hence awkward to use, at least at first.
* Position of ABXY buttons also feels very awkward.
* The d-pad shape on the left trackpad doesn't have too much feel to it. I keep seeking the shape with my thumb.
* The trackpad buttons are kinda stiff, which prevents you from making very slight adjustments by fast tapping the button.
* The controller is almost useless without Steam installed and running. You can basically use it only as a mouse, and without even the middle button.
* There's no memory for presets. As soon as you exit Steam, the controller goes back to the default preset, and default presents in Steam and controller itself are actually somewhat different.
* In Linux the controller isn't registered when connected wirelessly unless Steam is running.
* There's no search for community-created presets. You have to manually browse through them to find the one that'll fit your needs. At least they are filtered by games.
I played a few games with it and here's my experience:
* NES games. Like I said, the left trackpad feels awkward to use, and you do not want to use the stick instead of d-pad on any controller. After some getting used to, it performs surprisingly well. Not as good as a controller with an actual d-pad, but manageable. I played some Aladdin (pirate), Chip'n'Dale Rescue Rangers 2 and TNMT: Tournament Fights. I did pretty good, the controller almost didn't stand on my way of playing.
* Painkiller. Impressive performance. More than playable. Of course, mouse and keyboard are still superior, but Steam Controller performs considerably better than any other controller.
* Minecraft. It uses more buttons than Painkiller, but after some getting used to it's playable. I don't think I'll be able to parkour any time soon, but the regular survival is covered so far.
* Deadpool. Feels pretty much like a PS controller, except ABXY buttons' position feels awkward and the camera movement is kinda difficult.
* BattleBlock Theater. No difference from Xbox or PS controller, if you get used to ABXY buttons' position.
Unlike your traditional gamepads, Steam Controller takes a lot more time to get used to, but its flexibility allows you to play in more ways and in more games. You must use Steam and keep it running in order to configure and use it, but it works (or at least it should) in any game or application which supports keyboard, mouse and gamepad in any combination. So far I thing I like it more than dislike it. I need more time to get used to it. Because the controls can be so much different from each other, it'll take getting used to to control scheme for every game individually, at least until I'm comfortable with the controller's layout.
Things I would like to see in the future:
* A Steam-free driver which would allow to use the "extended" default preset.
* A separate small configuration tool.
* Memory for at least one preset aside from the default one.
Is this the best controller ever? Probably not. Is it better than controllers for Xbox or PS? In some ways, yes: you can play a wider range of games more comfortably. In some ways, no: it takes a lot of time to get used to and some controls would feel awkward in some games/situations. It's a neat gadget to have and play with. I think it's $50 (and $30 for shipping) well spent. I would recommend to give it a try for a week or so before deciding if it's good or not.

Overall I'm quite pleased with this controller, but I do see opportunity for improvements. I love to tinker. In fact I assemble and repair computers for a living. Doing so I realize that many people don't like to tinker.
Software:
This controller is very well geared toward those that want to fully tweak everything. At the moment is not so great for those that want something ready to go.
•There are developer recommended layouts available for some games.
•There is a decent amount of community built layouts for many other games. The community is where it is also problematic.
Potential improvements;
•A longer description area,
•rating system,
•and (possibly) a feedback system could go a long way in helping this out.
Firmware:
So far this seems pretty solid. I've ran into only a couple of issues with operability:
•the hard switch from wireless to wired (and back); device ID could be used to maintain a more fluid connection.
•and analog stick emulation on the touchpads. Though, I've had no real need to make use of it, so I currently can't suggest an improvement.
Hardware:
Many of the unique features on this controller aren't entirely new. However, they are well designed. Being a console gamer for more than two decades, I've had some issues adjusting to mouse and keyboard. I had similar reservations about the touchpads (I shudder from bad memories of the SNES touchpad). However, I found myself taking to this quite well.
•Haptic feed is a great feature here. It certainly help to adjust to touchpads, among other benefits.
•Dual stage triggers add more options, but take some practice to adapt a soft touch.
•The grip buttons are a feature that I've felt that should've been on console controllers long ago.
•I'm glad it makes use of the common micro USB, instead of a proprietary connection.
Ideas for the next design;
•This controller would be great with battery charging capabilities.
•Modular components could be an interesting idea, like swapping the button cluster with a D-pad or stick, but I've no idea how to implement that.
Form:
This design works excellently for me.
•It’s lightweight, but still feels somewhat solid.
•The shape feels very ergonomic.
•The layout is mostly intuitive.
•Batteries are well placed and balance the weight of the controller.
For the next generation;
•It would feel a bit better if the button cluster were rotated about 20-30 degrees counterclockwise.
•It could do with a bit more resistance from the full trigger pull bumps.
Game types I’ve worked with this so far:
•3rd Person Shooter/3rd person melee; Warframe
•point and click Role Playing Game; Path of Exile
•Flight sim; Zigfrak (note: I created the only community binding, as yet)
Game types I’ve not yet tested:
•First Person Shooter
•First person RPG
•Multiplayer Online Battle Arena
•Real Time Strategy
•Sports games/ Racing
I’m going to recommend this. None of the cons are really that significant.
•For the price it is definitely worth a try.
•The software will change over time and likely improve.
•As I’ve typed this there has been a firmware update in Steam Beta that allows for mouse zoning on the touchpads. This could be great for RTS.

I was so happy to find this game on Steam. I first purchased it years ago in a game store and it became one of my favorite tycoon games. I'm briefly going to go over some pros and cons.
Pros:
HUGE variety of animals to choose from, both aquatic and terrestrial. You could choose to have a zoo, aquarium, or a combination of the two. Some are available right away, some you have to research in game (you can set how many, if any at all, animals you must unlock by research in freeform mode.) Others are unlocked by completing bonus objectives in the campaign.
Autosave feature
Tutorial, scenarios, and freeform modes
It has a little bit of amusement park tycoon in it. You have a skytrain and a boat ride that you can design however you want. A nice little addition to the game.
You can assign specific zookeepers/marine specialists to specific exhibits, which helps make sure all the animals get the care they need without too much micromanaging.
Finances are easy to manage with various charts and graphs illustrating trends, profits, and expenses. In a pinch and need more money? Grab a loan and pay it back when you can.
Customers and animals are very specific in what they want and need. If someone is unhappy, it's easy to find out why.
Game can be paused or set to one of four different speeds.
The game runs very smoothly on poor graphics cards. On my machine that has one of the worst graphics cards on the market, I experience absolutely no lag. (someone with low RAM or a small hard drive may have trouble, but I'm not sure)
Cons
The graphics are outdated, undetailed, and kind of creepy (the people don't have eyelids). The animal models are decent at least.
The terraformer feature needs some work. Freshwater can only be added at the default level, so if you're using hilly terrain and your exhibits are higher or lower, no fresh water for your terrestrial animals. (Salt water can be added at any level) You can get around this with a water dish, but the animals prefer the stuff they can splash around in. It sounds annoying, but it really isn't  big deal except in some of the scenarios which is easily fixed by leveling everything out.
Some customers will always complain about availability of food and cleanliness of the zoo. You have to learn to accept it, or it gets very annoying. You can keep complaints to a minimum and have a great satisfaction rating in spite of this.
This is the big one for me. Marine specialists do a poor job of keeping the aquatic animals fed, and the animals starve to death as a result. Also, when marine species get ill, it seems impossible to treat them for a similar reason. The marine specialists don't administer the medication, even when the animals are placed in an isolation tank. It's for these reasons that I normally don't bother with species that are 100% aquatic. I'm going to experiment a bit and see if there's something I can do to compensate for this issue, and I'll update if I find anything that helps.
______________________________________
For the price, I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys zoo tycoon games.

I enjoyed this game. The pacing is a little off with the first episode, but it's still pretty fun. Seeing the different possibilities is fantastic. The characters may not shine immediately, but they have a way of growing on you. In any case, the experience is unique. The story mainly picks up in the third episode, though it's accessible right from the get-go.
UPDATE:
I've decided to update this review since episode four is out and the main arc of the story is over. I will say, this game is fantastic! TellTale takes advantage of Minecraft's unique format to create an adventure unique to other point-and-click adventure games, and I hope they find a way to make another season. Here are the weighted pros and cons of this series:
Listing off a con right from the start, Story Mode is a story that takes too long to properly begin. TellTale should have used their first episode to highlight the strengths of their given format, and to a slight extent they accomplish this with unique builds, music, etc.. Though the world itself is well done, this doesn't excuse the characterization, which doesn't shine until later episodes. Moments like finding Reuben, helping Petra, and riding in the Nether are interesting, but not enough so for an immersive experience. This episode doesn't do enough with its elements to pilot the rest of the season.
The episodes that follow are much better. Assembly Required is definitely rushed and by consequence plagued with bugs, but apart from that still serves its purpose and shows off two unique perspectives on Minecraft- an open-world death match and an inventive creation fair. The choices available in this episode are also refreshing, even if they don't impact later episodes by much. Some characters are slightly underutilized, but overall it's a satisfying inclusion.
The Last Place You Look maintains the momentum, introducing an experimental side of Minecraft that manages to carry the atmosphere. The environments are fun to explore, and the buildup to meeting Soren makes for some great interactions. The characters really start to shine here, and the sides of them you can see based on what choices you make are entertaining. The conclusion packs a lot of weight, escalating the stakes and leaving players hungry for more. There are some annoying audio cutoffs which can break the immersion, but that's the extent of the cons.
A Block and a Hard Place is definitely the best episode, calling back to choices made from the beginning and allowing for some unique paths to take. Learning Ivor's motives, trying to bring memories back, and seeing the death of another character are surprisingly emotional moments, highlighted by amazing voice acting. Having the "antagonist" role shifted to another character is a bit odd, yet not entirely unreasonable. Because of the significant amount of people present near the end of the episode, the framerate slightly drops and the game even crashed during my first playthrough. This is the only time I've experienced a technical issue in this episode, which all things considered is probably better than audio cutoffs or any of the problems present in episode two.
Overall, this is a great series, and deserves recognition for an adventurous and imaginative narrative. Why, then, would I not recommend it?
Structurally, this is a great game. It has all the elements of a fantastic TellTale adventure... but it doesn't feel definitive. Many of the elements of this game- writing included- are experimental, since it's TellTale's first time in a long time creating an original story. As an experiment, the game pays off well, and my purchase should be a sign to TellTale that they should continue to experiment until they find that magic number in storytelling for broader audiences. Now that I've become more familiar with TellTale games, however, I realize that they could do better- much better. This is a great idea that does well in several aspects, but simply doesn't carry the weight it should as a definitive story for Minecraft.

text:
Minecraft is a game about creativity. Most people who have played this game aren't familiar with Telltale, as they are more known for making mature games. Most people who see this game would think "OOOH! MINECRAFT 2!", but no. This game has almost no relation to the original Minecraft.
In this game, you play as a character named Jesse, who you can customize (Skin colour, gender). You interact with the environment to collect items, talk to NPCs, and solve puzzles. There are even elements from the original Minecraft, such as crafting and combat. The game follows Telltale's episodic formula, including quick-time events.
Minecraft: Story Mode is a fantastic mixture of a game as creative as Minecraft and Telltale's episodic narritive format. The truth is, the game is not for everyone, if they were expecting the game to be like Minecraft. But if I could recommend any game for people to at least TRY, it's this one. So go ahead, give it a try. I'm sure you'll love it.
I will be reviewing each episode individually. I will try to avoid spoilers, so read on if you want to learn more about the game.
Episode 1: The Order Of The Stone
Release Date: October 13, 2015
Minecraft: Story Mode's debut episode is a joy to play. I remember first picking it up and having the time of my life. This episode is easily the tamest in the series, before the following episodes pick up the intensity. The first episode serves as more of a prologue to the series than anything else, and it truly does not disappoint. The episode is about Jesse and his friends going to EnderCon, an anual event about all things Minecraft, to meet Gabriel the Warrior, one of the four members of the Order Of The Stone. The Order once slew an Ender Dragon, becoming heroes and legends. However, when Jesse and his friends arrive at Endercon, they realize something bigger is going on, and terror and chaos is unleashed, and Jesse and his friends must seek out the Order of the Stone to save the world.
The episode is rather charming in terms of its gameplay. I remember finding the humor in the game very entertaining. One part in particular has you crafting a stone sword, but you can be a rebel and instead craft a level, leading your friend to tease you for being a noob. My favourite chapter has to be the EnderCon chapter, because it ramps up the suspense slowly, but builds up the excitement as well.
All in all, I'd say Episode 1: The Order Of The Stone was my second favourite. Not just because of the originality and the story or even the characters, but because of just how much it makes me want to replay it, to live through those moments I love. For the first episode, it does a pretty great job of getting me hooked.
Episode 2: Assembly Required
Release Date: October 27, 2015
It is generally considered that Assembly Required is the weakest episode in the series. It certainly has a good plot line, but the fact that the episode clocks in at only about an hour in legnth is not very impressive. This does not stop my from enjoying the episode, though.
I wouldn't dare spoil this for you, but the choice that you made at the end of episode one completely affects the story of episode two. You see, Assembly Required branches off into two different stories: one where you go to Boom Town, which is a city full of griefers, and the other where you go to Redstonia, which is a town filled with Redstone Engineers. At the 30-minute mark, though, the two different paths converge and from there the story continues normally. I thought that this was a rather clever idea, and I must say I enjoyed all of the litlle nods to things like griefing and redstoning.
Assembly Required is short, yet fun. I still believe it is the weakest in the series, but I still enjoy it a lot.
Episode 3: The Last Place You Look
Release Date: November 24, 2015
At the episode that I consider the climax, things start to become a bit more emotional, intense, and even a bit disturbing in some cases. Episode 3 revovles around Jesse and his friends having to find the last remaining member of the Order of the Stone, who is currently living in the End. If people thought that the first 2 episodes didn't have a good story, I guarantee that you will think that story gets better.
When I said that it starts to get a bit disturbing, I was mostly talking about the Endermen that live in the End. While in regular Minecraft, these creatures are simply there to steal blocks and stand around, Story Mode really made me feel uncomfortable around these guys. There are moments where Endermen loom right in your face. There are moments where an Enderman jumpscares you. Sometimes, Endermen make unsettling sounds and movements. If a younger child is playing Episode 3, they might want to be accompanied by a parent. I can't guarantee that people will NOT find it too scary, but I do think that Episode 3 is the perfect turning point in the series.
Episode 4: A Block And A Hard Place
Release Date: December 22, 2015
Well, well, well. Here we are. Episode 4. I remember back to the advertisment for this episode, where it exclaimed very sharply, "Are YOU ready to take down the Storm?"  Episode 4 is an emotional joyride, and is easily the best in the series so far.
What makes Episode 4 so good, you ask? Well, for starters, it features a lot of character development. Our characters face hopelessness. As Jesse, it is your job to help your friends, and to lead the group. There were many moments where I felt like I WAS Jesse, because the game does that so well. The episode also has a lot of intensity and twists. The first time I played this episode, I had chills almost the whole way through.
I wouldn't dare spoil the plot, but I will tell you that it revolves around Jesse and his friends going to the Far Lands (Which is a glitch that used to be in Minecraft, being the "edge" of the world) in order to find something that would be their last hope to saving the world. Not only is it intense, but it is very sad. This episode may leave many people crying. I won't tell you why, but just be prepared for it.
So, to sum things up, Episode 4 is really good. Not only is it my favourite episode, but I think that it is one of the best things TellTale has ever made. Holding no regrets there.
Episode 5: Order Up!
Release Date: March 29, 2016

This episode took them a very long time to make, and with good reason. For the most part, they kept the plot, setting and everything about the episode a secret. In fact, the teaser image for the episode used to just be a sign that read "The Next Episode". Now, we finally got to play it, and it surpassed my expectations so much. The episode really does the whole "Minecraft" thing very well.
Set months after the end of episode 4, Jesse and his friends have become idolized across the land. The episode throws you right in. In fact, it doesn't even give you a recap! It just starts you off with an action packed adventure. I don't consider this to be episode 5 of Season 1, but instead episode 1 of Season 2. It reminds me a lot of the debut episode of the series, where it just left me wondering what would happen. And in terms of plot, this one is probably the best.
Something else that is pretty good to notice is that this one is much more interactive than the others. Instead of having a lot of automated things happen on screen, it makes you do a lot more. Telltale games are known for being much more narrative-driven, but I feel that this episode has just enough gameplay that it made me feel incredibly satisfied. For example, there is a segment where you have to make a decision that will take you through two different paths, similar to episode 2, but each path has different styles of interaction. All in all, I think it was a beautiful episode, and I highly recommend it. This concludes my review of Minecraft: Story Mode. I hope it was helpful for you!

Seems like the developer played Portal and got waaaaay too excited to make their own ~exciting first-person puzzle platformer with sterile environments!!~ As it is, the titular mechanic (being able to swap your "polarity" between red and blue, and using this to phase through obstacles of the same color) is used very little, and the only difficulty it adds to the game is trying to swap polarities in midair for platforming purposes. (By the way, first-person platforming is really not enjoyable, especially when the controls handle very poorly.) Indeed, the only challenging puzzle in the entire 90 minutes worth of single-player content, found in Bonus 04, doesn't involve the polarity mechanic at all. It DOES involve lots of clipping, very questionable cube physics (there's no friction between them and moving platforms? pressing a rotate button when they're not in the rotating area makes them fly into the air???), and a plot that's not worth the 20 seconds it takes to click through the expository slideshow. Only buy this game in a bundle, like I did, or if it's 20 cents and you're super desperate for "puzzle" games.

Pro:
Play as empire or rebelion
Both sides have the same buildings and basic ground/space units. All advanced units are fairly differant.
In effect turn based
Mostly space combat. There is only a handful of ground units. Sorry no AT-ST
Many several dozens of heros you can recruit. None effect ground commbat. Space commanders, spies/assassins and diplomats.
Get the emperior + vador or mon mothma + luke.
Each side has real strenghts and weaknesses.
Like some galaxtic conquest games after you have a few dozen systems it become tiering to manage. Luckily you have a whole list of things you can at any time have the computer take over. Good layout of the game buttons
Whole libarary of info about lore or game info or what units do.

Not much replay value each of several set ups are all the same

Absolutely fantastic real-time 4x game, in a category all of its own. This game looses you onto the Galaxy as either Empire or Rebellion in the post Battle of Yavin era (after Episode IV: A New Hope), awarding you full control over well known characters, as well as a slew of expanded universe ones. You will gently direct your faction from your command deck, watching events unfold and little stories being created. That is one of the things that made me fall in love with this game: it sometimes feels like an RPG and it most often feels like a sandbox.
There is a certain apparent simplicity to the game that belies underlying, emergent depth in how your characters develop and how the galaxy changes shape around your actions. Do not be fooled by the dated graphics (the space combat sequences are especially clunky to control), it somehow manages to convey a very authentic original Star Wars feel and your imagination is going to take off and over in the middle of all the little non-animated X-Wing sprites as they swarm an enemy Star Destroyer.
Did i mention you can build a Death Star and blow up planets?
The game, however, will not hold your hand and you are bound to discover all sorts of relatively hidden gameplay elements (Your force users, for instance, can sense force potential in other characters and train them. Sending Jedi Knight Han Solo with a force sensitive Chewbacca as backup and decoy to sabotage an enemy ISD never gets old). Occasionally the UI contributes to the confusion, but nothing that should stop you from enjoying this awesome piece of game.
I sincerely encourage you to give this one a try, if it hasn't already consumed hundreds of hours of your childhood. You are bound to discover one of the best Star Wars games released and an excellent 4x. If only Empire at War was this + updated graphics, it would have been perfect.

So, Stellaris... I've clocked almost 300 hours on it at the time of writing this, and yet I think I've just started to scrape the surface of it. The game has grown a lot since its initial release thanks to the many (free!) content patches alongside with paid DLCs (more on this later). The shortest description of Stellaris I can come up with is "a space empire roleplaying and strategic game, where events can singlehandedly shape the structure itself of your society". You have many aspects to consider, and it's best to describe them by comparing them to other games.
First of all, this is a real time game (or if you really want, you can think of a "day" as a very tiny turn) where a lot of stuff can happen at any point in time: the discovery of a new civilization, either space-faring or not, political crises, a scientific breakthrough that has unintended and unforseen consequences.
You get to personalize your species by selecting a government form (which you can change later in the game if you desire), ideologies, perks that can give you both boosts and penalties and technologies such as the starting weapon type you get; this gives a lot of room for roleplaying and therefore added value for multiple playthroughs.
You have a strategic/management aspect that in my opinion can be somehow reminiscent of Sid Meier's Civilization: You have planets through which you gather resources and build units, and each planet can have strategic resources that can help you expand your empire further; moreover the population of each planet grows (or shrinks!) depending on the amount of food you earn each "month".
The inner works of scientific research are based on a classical research tree divided in three main branches (Physics, Society, Engineering), and at any point in time you can research at least three different options for each of these branches. Research speed is given by the amount of research facilities -- either spaceborne or planet-based -- plus the specializations of your science advisors (more on them later).
Exploration and combat are a lot like Sins of a Solar Empire but do not expect that much micromanagement like in that game, as there are no "special abilities" that you can manually trigger. In exchange for that however you get to have personalized ships, each with its different weapon, armor and shields loadout depending on the techs that you have researched. On a side note, the 2.0 update that is coming within the first half of 2018 is expected to radically change combat for the better, adding more options and more fun things to build and use.
For each of the aspects I've mentioned, the use of leader characters can give you huge bonuses depending on the task at hand: if you for example want to research better ship engines, having a scientific advisor that is expert in Voidcraft will shorten the needed research time by a considerable time, proportionate to their skill level. In the case of sector governors, some will give you discounted prices for building infrastructures while others will give you bonus resources, and so on.
Now, for the less-than-good part: DLCs. DLCs can be a little scarce in content compared to their cost, but fortunately only a few (namely Utopia and Synthetic Dawn, IMHO) I consider critical to enjoy the game as intended. The other expansions are minor when not exclusively cosmetic. The core changes to the game are always part of the free content patches, so even if you decide to go 100% vanilla, you're not being left out by much -- be wary though as in this case, midgame tends to be a bit lackluster. But in any case, there are always mods!
As a final word, what makes the game interesting to me is that each time the game is wildly different because of the insane amount of random events -- some minor, some absolutely massive -- that can happen during a playthrough: each and every game is different.
My vote: 7.5/10 (vanilla game), 9.5/10 (with Utopia + Synthetic Dawn)

Even though I am a supporter of modern RTS, especially indie scene. I would need to be critical and fair on my accessment on this game. So here goes:
It goes without saying that this is one of my few favorite Indie RTS game that featured modern units that do not have fancy gizmo or sci-fi nonsense. I also like how I can customized the units that i needed for combat. I can sent hordes of T-72s to overwhelem my opponent only to get Scud and get a brutal revenge by the oppoenent.
=================================================================
Graphics:
While it is an Indie game, I generally find the graphic is lackluster. The game is graphically very poorly optimized, if you have more than 20 units in one combat, the GT 540M Nvdia graphics card would suffer severe lag and frame rate spike, while the GT 850 Nvida Graphic cards suffer minor frame rate drop and frame jump. I know that many company has seriously optimized their RTS engine to allow 100s of units in one scene with less frame rate issue. Thus this is defenitely something that the DEV need to look out for.
The graphic option is really really sparse, you can only choose: (Low, Normal, High, Ultra) and screen resolution. i do hope the Dev can add more option if possible.
=================================================================
Sound:
I have to be brutally honest, this is probably the worst part of this game. No music, no ambient sound and the voice of each units are generic. Yet it is probably the one thing I can fully understand from a ONE INDIE DEV! So yes this is something that I find it OK!
=================================================================
Gameplay:
While the design is classic RTS style, Unity Engine is not the best engine for RTS. The unit pathfinding can sometimes fustrating, Unit spacing is kinda messy, also in combat, due to pathfinding or AI, unless I micromanage the units, they will go back and forth while not firing weapons. The AI opponent also got this problem as well.
The UI is basic, you know what should be build and it display cleanly. It do not have aesthetic of many RTS, but it gets the job done.
I like the Armory, as it showcase what sort of unit you can pick for your class. I suggest the Dev to provide the description for each individual units, such as history/description of the units to spice it up.
=================================================================
Overall: I do not recommanded if you want full-blown completed RTS, Recommanded if you are into indie RTS

Honestly, I did not know what to expect from this game. It has received very positive praise but it wasn't until I actually started playing that people were calling it a masterpiece.
Roughly 35 hours of playtime, and I am glad I finished it because this game was a real CHORE!
The game does present itself in a very stylistic way that makes itself stand out. I can also point out that the soundtrack is great. There's no doubt about that.
Where the problem lies is the gameplay. There's nothing too major of an issue, but there are far too many small problems with the game that prevent me from enjoying it:
- Stupid sidequests
- Fast travel not unlocked until later
- Enemies keep dodging
- Moments when saving is few and far between
- Graphics aren't even good
- There are certain parts that are infuriating
What makes this really problematic is that the way that the game is structured. You have to play through the game twice, once as 2B (who I disliked because of her personality, by the way!) and once as 9S, in order to get to the 'good stuff'. HOW IS THAT GOOD GAME DESIGN??!?!?! It's like having to go through seasons and seasons of a TV show before something exciting happens, only you HAVE to start from season 1.
Even then, I only kept playing to see what it had to offer, and I was underwhelmed. What is it with Japanese developers and confusing stories? It just dragged on and on and I was not having a good time.
But, here's the icing on the cake: It's not a good port, so it's not even worth playing just for that.
I am honestly confused as to why everyone is calling this a masterpiece, because NieR:Automata is far, far from being a masterpiece.
Yoko Taro, I can see you are trying to be inventive, which is great. Now, how about making a product that is ACCESSIBLE?

This controller is amazing. It feels better than any other gamepad I have used to date. All games, the ones that don't have gamepad support, and even web browsing, feels so natural that you could swear they were made for this controller. I heard people saying it takes time to get used to it, but on me it was almost instant. The moment I got it I was able to play comfortably all the games I have played with it. I will list below the features that make it great:
-Very ergonomic, It is one of the most comfortable controllers I've held in my hand.
-The gamepad build is great. It is even sturdier than my 360 controller.
-The analog stick is a little smaller than the one in other gamepads, but the quality is great. It doesn't drift and it grips to you finger making it easy to use. The haptic feedback also adds a great feel to it even when you use it on non analog inputs like platformers, fighting games, or games that don't have gamepad support.
-Haptic feedback is in almost everything adding a great feel to all the inputs.
-Dual stage analog triggers are much more useful than I expected. In games like Rocket League you can use the analog pull for accelerating and then the final click for activating the boost making it much more intuitive.
-The trackpads are versatile. I usually use the right one to simulate a trackball for aiming or moving the cursor and the left one for additional buttons with the on-screen touch menu were you can bind up to 16 buttons. They also have the best on-screen keyboard for typing I have used on a gamepad.
-The face buttons are smaller than in other controllers, but besides miss-clicking them for the first minutes I used it, I didn't have any issues with them. They feel great.
-With the dual-stage triggers and the back buttons there are games where I completely forget the face buttons since I don't find myself needing them.
-Gyro is probably the most fun feature in this controller. Aiming and steering will never feel the same with another gamepad.
-Customization is extensive letting you configure this controller to fit your style, but if you don't want to mess with that you don't have to worry about it. There are plenty of community presets that are really good, and if there isn't one for a game you want to play the default templates are good enough.
And that is pretty much I guess. I am loving this gamepad. I love it so much that I take good care of it. I put it back on it's box every time I stop using it to make myself sure it is protected, and I usually don't take so much care for my gamepads. That's how good it is.
10/10 - Would buy again.

With that out of the way...
Valve put a lot of effort into the design of this controller. They went through several iterations before finally coming to it's current design. A lot of people there was a long beta test process before this even went on the market. Valve didn't just haphazardly push this out for sale without putting serious thought and engineering into the design.
Compared to other gamepads, the Steam Controller feels solid. It doesn't feel cheap, as other reviews have claimed. There are no rubberizd surfaces except for the single analog stick. The back and sides have a slightly grippy, glossy texture, with a few parts covered in smooth reflective surfaces that retains finger prints.
The dual touch pads function as buttons, and have a satisfying click. The pad on the left is textured with a D-pad cross, while the other is smooth, and both are slightly concave. The Xbox-like A, B, X, Y, buttons are arranged right of the analog stick. They're positiion rather close to the bottom of the controller much like the D-pad and buttons on the Wii-U Pro Controller. The four shoulder buttons don't feel cheap. The top buttons are nice and clicky, while the bottom shoulder buttons are paddles with a short travel distance ending in a nice clicky button that most other gamepad simply don't have. Integrated into the battery cover are two extra buttons underneath the controller. These have a nice click to them and are easily pressed by simply squeezing the wings of the battery cover. The addition of these extra buttons presents all kinds of interesting new control possibilities. The top center has the Steam logo button that turns the controller on and activates Steam Big Picture Mode, and on either side are two extra buttons commonly used for pause and select. On the top between the shoulder buttons is a micro USB port so you can use the controller wired. Since it uses AA batteries, it doesn't recharge when plugged in. This was a wise design decision, since with most rechargable controllers if the battery starts to go out you have buy a whole new controller, and the battery life of the Steam Controller is rather impressive.
Included in the Apple-esque packaging is a fairly standard micro USB cable, the kind you'd get with a smartphone, the wireless dongle, and a weighted USB adapter for the dongle. It has a little bit of heft to it so the weight of the included cable doesn't pull it off your desk like most other USB extensions sometimes do.
You can't just pick this up and start using it like any other gamepad. The Steam Controller was designed first and foremost to deal with a big issue affecting Valve's PC gaming in the living room plans: The fact that the majority of games on Steam only support mouse & keyboard inputs.
On this, Valve has come closer than any other previous attempt I've ever seen to make it "practical" to play PC games on your couch. However, there is a slight learning curve, and it does take patience. This is where the majority of previous reviews fell short. They lacked the patience to really stick with the controller and learn to use it properly. As Yoda once said, "you much unlearn what you have learned". Because the Steam Controller works very differently from most any other gamepad you've ever used before. It also takes a lot of tweaking of the settings, and there are a plethora of settings you can change. Each game in your library maintains it's own separate control profile, so it will work different for each game depending on how you configured it.
To configure the controls you MUST be in Big Picture Mode, a requirement I hope Valve will change since not everyone is using this in their living rooms.
Rumble isn't new, its been around since the days of the N64 and PS1, but it hasn't really changed since those days either. It works via two motors that spin an off-center weight to create a vibration. Haptic Feedback works differently. There are actuators under the two touch pads and buttons on the face of the controller. These can produce vibrations tuned to a much finer level of precision to mimic a variety of different tactile textures and intensities. Valve is making APIs available to game developers so they can tailor haptic feedback for their games to give players tactile information more detailed than what rumble can offer. The addition of this feature was a very smart idea by Valve.
I've seen hundreds of attempts to make it "practical" and easy to play PC games in the living room. None are as elegant as this design. While far from perfect, it is closer to achieving what was once thought nearly impossible than any previous attempt. While the Steam Controller "looks" familiar, once you put it in your hand and try to play a game you discover it is totally unlike any other gamepad you've ever used. Using it effectively requires patience and sometimes a bit of tinkering. This is why it isn't for everyone. The ADHD crowd won't like this controller, but anyone willing to put in the time to master it will wonder how they ever played PC games without it.

I'll be blunt if you were to ask if I were to recommend this as an all-in-one solution to PC gaming control mapping I would say no. However, I have been blown away with my initial experiences with this device.
First I tried it out with a few shooters and it worked far better than I'd hoped. I'm left handed and was worried before it arrived because there was some dribble on google about how the controller wasn't ambidexterous enough, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t basically. You're using the flat of your right thumb for aim and that presented no issue, for the same reason they don't make left handed HOTAS, your mind and body don't need adjustment to benefit fully. If you think otherwise that's your state of mind and it's on you to accept it's your misconception! Initially I played Hard Reset and Shadow Warrior and it felt like they were made for the controller. Obviously not the case but if you told me to play it with a conventional controller I'd have told you to do one. That being said it doesn't hold a candle to KB&M in a multiplayer scenario but if you want to play competitively on PC you're not gonna sit on a sofa. Sorry if I'm ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on Steam Machines but everything has it's place... errrmmm lol if that's you disapointed.
Then I tried Pillars of Eternity to see what the crack was with mouse games. Native Steam controller support and damn fine tbh. The only draw back was I couldn't see a sensible option to turn the sensitivity up so I wasn't constantly dragging the cursor. If that was easily remedied I'd play through the whole game happily on the sofa, making a wholly PC game feel like it belonged on the couch. Imagine that. You can save your control profiles to Steam and make them accessible to everyone and you also can access everybody elses'. Another community fueled endeavour that means we can all scratch each others' backs. Most games are Steam Controller ready thanks to community sharing.
So I say it didn't give me the option to adjust the sensitivity but otherwise that is the pad's strength. Customisation. You can take any game using and control scheme and make it work with the pad. Steam gives you that power, even when the devs phone it in. Logitech did that for me with the X/D switch but this just makes it unconditional, all from the comfort of big screen mode. Again that's quite classy.
If a games got native support that's awesome and it really shines (and this is early days ofc) but the tech in the pad is excellent regardless. I'll keep the old wireless keyboard and mouse to hand for now but this pad really fills a gap with some games. I just hope there isn't a crowd that just expects a steam machine running SteamOS to just boot, run a load of games, require no intervention and just do it's thing from a couch. That's just not what PC gaming was or is. It requires some manipulation and for me it has it's own reward. It's what you make of it though and it can be a lot if you don't expect auto awesome.

Honestly, I'm quite surprised by what seems to be a preponderance of positive reviews. Sure, the controller is novel in that it provides more functionality than any other controller. However, all the numerous features offered fall short of the performance of devices you likely already own (e.g., xbox controller or mouse/keyboard).
If you don't care about your ability to play a game, and merely care about your comfort when doing so (i.e., "I don't care if I suck as long as I can play from the couch")...then you'll love the steam controller. Primarily it comes down to the right track pad. A haptic trackpad just can't have anywhere near the same level of precision as a thumbstick--I found it to be frustratingly clunky.

Since the buttons are extremely tiny, games that make use of mashing them will be harder to play than using an xbox controller.  Games that rely on pretty much the mouse will be difficult as well.  For example, FTL pretty much uses the mouse for selecting everything.  You need to play with the senstivity in that game even though you can pause it whenever you wish.  Impatient players won't play with the settings of the controller but you pretty much need to as it wont work perfectly without the proper configuration.
So keep that in mind before purchasing.  You need to configure each game first in BP mode with a preset list or, making your own.  I reccomend setting most of the heavy use actions to the back buttons.  Not the bumbers, but the back buttons housed near the batteries.  It's a little awkward at first using these buttons to "use" or "jump" functions in first person shooters or 3rd person shooters.  It has to be done however, because the A, B, X, Y buttons are so darn small, that you'll miss them in game half the time.
In conclusion, this controller is where it's at for PC gaming. It doesn't work for every game flawlessly like I originally thought.  And it doesn't have rumble functions nor a rechargable battery (which is unfortunate).  You can tell Valve was trying to save some money but who knows, it's possible the controller was already costing too much to manufacture with the trackpad, that adding rumble support and rechargable batteries would have made this gamepad well close to $100.  It will work best with games that didn't originally support a controller and relied more with kb&m.  Trying to play Fallout 4 with this can be difficult with the senstivity of the trackpad sometimes catching your finger as it hovers above it.  Still, a great product though that PC gamers should be using for a long time.

The Steam Controller is an interesting little beast. Supposedly it is Valve's answer to enable couch gaming for PC gamers. So, let's see if it holds up.
First off, let's talk about the layout. You can see the pictures above to check out the layout, so I'm going to mention the actual use of the thing. The design of the controller makes it fit surprisingly comfortably in your hands, and naturally positions your thumbs by the two large trackpads on the controller.  These trackpads have optional haptic feedback (as does the joystick) which is actually quite nice. The placement of the X/Y/A/B buttons definitely takes some getting used to before you quit hitting the wrong one. The paddles on the back of the controller are fantastic additions, and I use them far more than I thought I would. It's an easy-to-use extra two buttons to bind.
Alright, now onto the stuff people are really curious about. Can the controller really be a decent substitute for a keyboard/mouse combo, or even a 360 controller?
The short answer: It varies by genre.
So I'm going to take some time to talk about the genre's (and list some examples of that genre) I have played:
:  This one took a lot of getting used to. A lot. The track pad doesn't function very nicely as a joystick, so you're mostly left with the option of the mouse/joystick emulation. Which works rather well, thankfully. While you will certainly not be as precise as with a mouse, I found myself performing better with the Steam Controller than a 360 controller. Some people have also claimed to be extremely precise by using the gyro-feature, which I have yet to get working decently.
: Perhaps I need more time, but using the controller with his genre I have had a very hard time keeping up in intense battles. The lack of ability to easily hotkey groups (you can do this, if you tweak your config a bit) is painfully hindering in some games. It's doable, but at times I found it a bit too frustrating.
:  Works just as well as a 360 controller or keyboard/mouse. The only complaint I had here is the camera movement. I have yet to find a configuration I like that makes the camera move as smoothly/quickly as using a 360 controller with a joystick, or a mouse.
:  Works just as well as a mouse and keyboard, no hindrances here at all.
: I was extremely surprised at how well the steam controller works with Pillars of Eternity in particular. It is a fantastic substitute for the keyboard/mouse if you prefer to chill on your couch and play games such as this.
: Works just as good as any other controller. Though not quite as good as a keyboard/mouse if you have inventories to manage (Terraria).
There are several other genres to cover obviously, but these are just the ones that I experienced myself. Overall, here are my feelings:
If you are looking to use the Steam Controller in place of a 360 controller, your results will highly vary. The trackpad just isn't quite there when it comes to emulating a joystick.
Where the Steam Controller really shines is in being a viable substitute for a keyboard/mouse for all those games you have that don't support a controller. Make heavy use of the community controller configurations and you'll be just fine, and find yourself enjoying your city-builders, CRPGs, and various other mouse/keyboard genres from your couch (or just kicking back in your chair, whatever you desire).
Overall, the steam controller can deliver a great experience, as long as you aren't expecting some silver bullet to replace your mouse/keyboard. If you are just looking for something that lets you play the majority of your library comfortably from your couch, then you've just found it.

Ahhhh Dead Rising. Well, Dead Rising is one of my favorite series just to muck about and have lots of fun in, and this game is definitely no exception. Dead Rising 3 is full of fun toys and trinkets to maim and mutilate with, and the map itself is pretty dense. There's lots of enterable buildings, and it feels like you're really in a city. The main character is a pretty goofy young guy, but he's pretty likeable, moreso than the other protagonists of Dead Rising. The story itself is a bit wobbly and isn't that great, but it's pretty alright.
The most fun however is being able to slaughter all the zombies on the streets of Los Perdidos, and it's even better than before. The gameplay has been upped tremendously from Dead Rising 2, where picking up weapons and eating food are much more fluent and everything just flows nicely. There's tons of zombies on screen which is pretty impressive considering none of them look alike. Also there's a sprint button finally so you don't have to leisurely stroll away from your death.
Now all of this is good fun, but there is one giant glaring issue with this game and that's the optimization of this port. I have a stable rig that can run games that are more graphically intense than Dead Rising 3 without a problem, yet I seem to be having tons of framerate and rendering issues. There's lots of pop-up and framerate loss, and sometimes some models don't even show up, so it looks like I'm driving and invisible steam roller. Plus the FOV is horrendous. Hopefully, Capcom will fix this or a modder will come along and make something that will fix these problems (i.e. Dark Souls, Saints Row 2). I would give this port a 9/10 simply because of the fun and bloodshed that this game allows me to have, but sadly because of the terrible optimization and such, It gets a 7/10. Hopefully, if a patch is released that makes the game stable on PC, then it'll bump right back up to a 9.
