This is my personal favorite of the "Sands of Time" trilogy of the Prince of Persia series. The combat is no longer the repetitive string of "do this to X enemy" and instead has a real sense of flow and style to it. The platforming feels more smooth and with a sense of flow to the area. No longer is it one linear path that isn't meant to be backtracked through, there is a way in and out of the area, allowing back and forth travel and exploration of the main game area. The music doesn't fit the feel of the game as well as the original game, or the third game, instead being heavy rock/metal. While I understand this being ridiculous and perhaps annoying, I personally can't get enough of this game's adrenaline inducing soundtrack. Life upgrades have to be earned, no longer being simple passages that must be discovered...instead there is a trap-puzzle given to it, rather than traps with timers being puzzle elements. Getting all of these upgrades unlocks the secondary ending, which is the canon ending for those who are interested in why the main ending doesn't seem to be the one that the third game follows. Sadly, sand tanks are no longer able to be built. Instead, they are rewards for discovering new "time portals", which allow the prince to traverse back and forth in time on the Island of Time, a gameplay mechanic that I found to be an interesting and well used idea.
The large issues stem from the rather nonsensical and needlessly dark/grim storyline that was chosen, and the effort to EARN it's M-rating by being highly skimpy with its women and having blood spurting from...sand creatures? The storyline doesn't make sense except to its own context, where it works fine as a driving narrative of a man attempting to change his fate. The Dahaka, while making no sense in the idea of the game, comes across as a terrifying driving element and antagonist, but the Dahaka as a presence is relatively overshadowed early on by the Empress of Time and the plotline surrounding her attempts to change her own fate. These aside, I would still give this game a try if you enjoyed "Sands of Time" and are looking for a darker and more action heavy twist to the same idea, or even if you just enjoy action platformers.
TL;DR: Game is fun for its gameplay, it's heartpumping music, and its replayibility for exploration and a secondary ending. Where it suffers is lack of a gripping narrative and lack of cohesion to its own setting. Definitely worth playing.
Bear in mind that these above are my opinions, but I feel confident in saying them from my personal experience with the game.

After I completed the first game of this trilogy ( prince of persia: Sands of time ) I was met with kinda meh expectations, the first game had a good story and a beautiful atmosphere but was riddled with a poor combat system, only one boss, incredible lackluster replayability, very short and for the pc version a very bad sound glitch.
But after I started playing the sequel I was met with everything I complained about gone. Subtitles were available, extras and collectibles were abound as well as difficulty settings.
The combat is way better than the first one and the graphics look amazing.
But this game is certainly to be divisive for fans of the Prince of Persia name. We now have a very angry and dark prince who's first word is the B word and it comes out of nowhere, in fact while I do understand that 7 years have passed chased and hunted it still feel very forced, in fact the whole dark tone feels incredible jarring and unecessarily edgy.
This new prince is not very likeable at ALL in fact it's just a no name brute who can platform like the best of them.
The combat has improved a whole lot with more enemies, a whole lot more cool bosses and 1 new time power.
That is however by the end the combat can become a little boring when they start shoving waves after waves of enemies.
What is also apparent ( at least on Hard difficulty ) is that the game is HARD, the platforming and traps for some of the secret life upgrades are really intense and the combat can become very diffcult since enemies now attack without quarter.
I like this change, it made for some intense moments and frustating once too specially the 2 final bosses that I had to abuse the IA to complete the games 2 endings.
There are wesome bloody finishers and the new soundtrack is really heavy metal. There is only 1 song I enjoyed greatly which is the one that starts at the beginning on the boat, the other ones feel very metal generic and none standed out to me.
Now the ambient music is either not there or glitched out, fortunatly the music seems to be the only glitchy aspect in terms of sound, the voices and dialogues work well for the most part ( and even if the don't we have subtitles !! )
The story is also pretty good altough not sure if it's better than the first game, since in the first game you had farah with you almost all the time the banter with them and the noble journey of the prince felt more organic than this one.
Now and this is me nitpicking I feel the game should not have his CANON ENDING as the secret one, since to be able to unlock it you need to find all 9 life upgrades and as well as with the treasure chest for collectibles some of them are really obscure.
This game is not linear unlike the first one this one has a semi metroidvania feel to it, which is not really a  plus, many times you are rerunning the same places just to get further in the story and it can get a little frustating to surpass the same traps in the same locations.
The sequel is also very much longer than the first one, for the first one I clocked 6/7 horus for 100% in the sequel I'm at 19/20 hours for 100%
All in all i loved my time with Prince of Persia: Warrior Within, I love the new combat and the graphics are really good except for the faces, I loved the setting and the story, the replayability in terms of difficulty and collectibles is great, all in all it's a better game.
However the new change of look and feel doesn't suit well, it feels very forced and unecessary. The prince is no longer a likable character and while they did add diffulties and such I still find it hard to believe anyone will want to play the entire thing more than 1 time just because the backtracking and such is very tedious in the later stages of the game also playing on hard the 2 final bosses are ridiculous.
Prince of Persia: Warrior Within gets a 7/10
I enjoyed my time with the game inmensly, the combat is a whole lot better the game plays and looks beautiful and the story is some nice twist.
But the jarring make over, the unlikable hero, the badly balanced 2 last bosses on hard, the tedious backtracking, the forgettable track all takes down what could have been a masterpiece.
Let's see what the next game does for us and if it reaches the high this series deserves.

Skimming through the reviews, it's not hard to figure out that this entry is considered a kind of black sheep in the Sands trilogy. It was a polarizing title back in the day, and it has its fair share of flaws, but the core is solid and there's fun to be had here.
In the presentation department, there were no huge leaps made because this game came out (IIRC) a year after SoT, but there was definitely a huge change in art-style and tone. More gore, more nudity, darker, that was the theoretical basis, but in practice, it comes off as overly edgy and try-hard. The Prince swears and sounds like he's angry (or taking a dump, your pick), the environments are a lot more bleak and deprecated; tribal drumming and Middle-Eastern melodies have been replaced with era-appropriate nu-metal chugging (courtesy of Godsmack) in the sound department. They're good songs, but there are so few that they grow stale fairly quickly - in SoT, the actual number of different pieces was about the same, yet they didn't wear out because they were less conspicuous. Despite there being some criticism of the game's environments being too uniform, I didn't really think so, there is more than enough variety here (gardens, clock towers, castles, caves and so on). The most lamentable thing about this whole direction is that underneath it all, there was a decent story and some neat ideas. It made all the sense in the world to distance the franchise away from the 1001 Nights vibe to a more mature feel, but the problem is that the execution wasn't the greatest.
Speaking of story, I would actually say it is a bit deeper than SoT (let's ignore the presentation and focus on the actual plot). The Prince returns to the island where the Sands were created and tries to prevent the Empress of Time from creating them in the first place. This means messing with the "timeline", the natural order of things, and time doesn't like that, so it sends the Dahaka, the timeline keeper, to mess you up. If this sounds to you like there's time travel involved, well, you're spot on. I was afraid that this would devolve into BioShock Infinite-esque timeline butchering and WTF moments, but luckily it chooses a more "right time, right place" approach and it stops convoluting itself just before it would get lost up it's own rear. The only problem with this is that, like the 2008 reboot, the time travel lends itself to a fair bit of backtracking, and not all of it was necessarily thrilling stuff. The semi-open world design that kicks in can also waste a lot of time because you'll have to return to a hub a few times and the path back can drag on in certain areas. BTW, there are two endings - you get the secret (and IMO, more satisfying one) for collecting all the hidden life upgrades and the Water Sword.
In terms of combat, this game ups the ante quite a bit. I like SoT a lot, but I have to admit the combat got stale pretty fast because it was more or less a matter of spamming that one effective combo until everything was dead. Here, you get a bucketful of combos and the ability to dual-wield weapons. The combo tree is fairly extensive but also quite intuitive and most important of all, the enemy roster has been amped up to include more varied enemies that actually give you incentive to explore your combat prowess, lest you end up a stain on the floor. Spamming one combo won't get you very far, and that's a good thing. My only complaint is that at certain points, fights were really unnecessary and were more of a chore than anything else; these moments are rare, but that doesn't make them any less annoying.
Lastly, I want to talk about the difficulty and platforming. I know there are people who brag about beating this game on super-duper Hard and there are those who will insist that the game isn't *that* hard, but god d4mmit this game is relentless, and not always in a good way. The platforming has some new moves and in general, it's a lot more polished and dynamic than in the first game. However, due to the fact that some of the save points are quite far apart and that sometimes the camera angles aren't the greatest, you might end up replaying a 10min section over and over again. There is a very fine line between challenging, artificially difficult and too easy, and while most of the game falls in the "challenging" department, but some Dahaka segments (where you're basically forced to move fast) and the later part of the game where
, you basically have to speedrun the entire game's geography stand out as firmly in the "cheap/artificially difficult" category.
So, all in all, is it better than SoT or what!? I'd say all things considered, yes, it's a lot richer and more complex, and even though the edgy tone might fall flat, there's a decent story and great (albeit frustrating and relentless) gameplay.

I haven't replayed a game a couple times (A-E) all at once in a while, but this one did it.
First entering the game, the characters seem weirdly contrary. Some of these "combat units" seem more apt at dodging lasers than others (poor D and H units), 2B seemed almost bipolar, and these guys are driven on suicide machines. While the world doesn't really seem all that deep or to make sense for the first few hours, the combat and mechanics are enough to stay interested until the story picks up.
The combat is fast and reactive, intuitive if you have played hack n slash before and easy to learn if not (I had to learn, I'm usually pretty bad at these games). I personally found the game difficult at first, but it didn't feel unfair (especially with such a forgiving dodging mechanic). The seemless switch between close range hack n slash and bullet hell was effective in keeping the combat fun and dynamic. By the end of my first "playthrough", I had gotten pretty good and wanted to see what else lied in the game. Really the story is what drove me to play this over again though.
This is a very complex narrative. While the game can be completed in it's entirety without side missions, each of the side missions adds to the depth of the story, or made me laugh audibly. It will take some time through the game to really understand why the characters are the way they are, especially in respect to some of the "older" characters. However, it was worth every minute. The voice acting was spot on, music was amazing, visual asthetic obviously had care put into it. Heck, there are some parts told primarily in text and I was riveted the whole time.
10/10, will play again.

**This review might contain some spoiler**
Nier: Automata lets u start off by playing as 2B, one of the female protagonists,and u have been provided support by the male protagonist, 9S. Story sets in 9000+ years later from 21st century, where machine lifeforms have invaded, mankind is near extinct, and youre tasked to protect them from being so.
This is a game which the director, Yoko Taro, who might have seemed to cover it with 'Fanservices', but once you have digged enough into the game, you will find that behind all this is a game full of emotions, and entices you to continue exploring the deep plot. You will be surprised by how many ways the game can tell a story, from the weapons, enemies youve fought, etc, all of them have their part in the game, of course some might require you to do some side quest, some  would just need you to progress along the game and they will slowly emerge here and there. At first you might find some of them being rather confusing, but all of them will be addressed in the future part of the game. Some who played other RPGs, might be thinking if side quests in Nier: Automata might be the same old generic ones from other games, let me tell you, absolutely not. The things is side quests in this game comes in all sorts of forms, it can be a puzzle for u to solve it by pushing boxes, it can be a quest where a mother wants u to help find a lost child, or it can be as silly as telling u to find ones follower across the entire map. You arent required to run all the way from point A to point B, as fast travel exist in the game, conveniently helping u to finish quests while maintaining the pace of the game.
Now for the main storyline, Nier: Automata has 26 total endings, 5 of them which are the main endings, being A,B,C,D and E. Others are joke endings that are rather hilarious at sometimes, which might suddenly appear if u accidentally do something stupid, some totally caught me off guard while I was playing, and I thought these are little things that add to a what seems to be GOTY. The main 5 endings all have their own unique way of presenting them (albeit some might say that A and B are repeated), everything slowly accumulates when u play throughout the game until u reach one of the ending, you will be like 'Owh, so this is this, and thats why A was A, or B was B'. You will be shocked as to how well the plot was written, and you will most definitely be satisfied by it. After all this is a Yoko Taro game we are talking about.
Combat system is something also worthy of a praise. You would expect Platinum Games to develop a game with a good combat system, and it delivered, seamlessly. Why? U are given with various types of weapons, 2B utilizies 2 weapons, same as A2, where as 9S only holds one, but comes with an additional ability, hacking. Each of them have a different combo if paired with another type of the weapon, making almost infinite amount of tricks that u can pull off, though sometimes it can come down to you smashing down just a few buttons and youre pretty much good to go, still its fun to play around with different weapon most of the time. Oh did I mentioned hacking? Cause god hacking was probably my favourite aspect of the game. Its like a 8bit game but much much detailed, its not overcomplicated, but before you get a hold onto all types of the enemies, you dont know whats awaiting for you in the hacking game, and transitioning from your combat to hacking is very smooth, they just feel right ( I have no idea how to explain this lul xd). There are also a lot of different ways you fight, being in 3d mode or 2d mode like the arcade games you used to play, even some boxing♥♥♥♥♥♥was involved which was very unique, though short.
Soundtracks. OMFG THEY ARE GOOD. Composed by Keiichi Okabe, I can certainly tell u, that U WILL NOT BE DISSAPOINTED BY HOW GOOD THEY ARE. All of them, literally all of them, fits into the game absolutely perfectly, they just do. They drive your emotions with the game altogether, nothing will feel out of place, its like YOU are the one in the game, not playing it. You actually feel what the soundtracks are trying to convey to you, this isnt those ordinary soundtracks that were like 'its here because its here', they are here because they are the part of the entire game, every single one of the soundtracks has its purpose. Also, most of the soundtracks have different tones for it, they change as the story moves on, or changes as some event happens, to me, this is a very clever implementation.
As for how the game looks, nope, obviously they dont deliver as good as Witcher 3, Horizon Zero Dawn, but still they are decent. The world is well designed, at first it can look rather huge, but after a few hours playing around you will most likely memorize the places.
Also before I forget, voice acting in this game is top notch. I play with japanese voice and english sub, and boi do the voice actors did a amazing job at making all the characters feel alive. 9S and 2B's voice actor in japanese just suite the character so well, they felt real. English voice actors are also very very good, I find 9S's VA in english, Kyle McCarley slightly better than the japanese one, however 2B in english somehow felt a little underwhelming occasionally, but still very good nontheless.
Okay, okay. There must be something negative bout the game that I have to point out, else people would probably start bashing me.
So, performance issues. To me, this is something I find myself scratching my head, thinking as if why people even bother complain about this, even giving negative reviews for the game for this sole reason. Like come on man, it is indeed true that Square Enix has probably abandoned the game, not patching it after X amount of months since its release, but seriously, there are♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of forum/discussion that have pointed out that there is a fan mod that will ultimately boost your performance, LIKE A♥♥♥♥♥♥TON OF THEM IM NOT EVEN JOKING. Its not Yoko Taro's fault that the game isnt optimized, he still needs money to continue making these masterpieces for us, so why cant people bother wasting 5mins of your time, install the fan mod, and VOILA, A LIFETIME EXPERIENCE FOR A 5MINS FIX. And before people question me, let me say this, i play on a god damn ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop with a i3 and a gt720m, yet i still insisted on playing Nier: Automata with a resolution of 800x450 with the lowest possible setting and even with the fan mod, I can barely mantain anywhere around 12-16fps (no im not joking), and finished the final boss fight (ko shi and ro shi) with a 'rock solid' 6fps. If u have a adequate pc spec, anything above 1050/rx560 you should run this game at 1080p smooth framerates well over 30fps (which the game would actually requires to have a decent gameplay).
Nier: Automata is priced at $60, is it worth it? Hell yeah it is. If you only had $60 to play with, what game should you buy? Nier: Automata. No, not even Horizon Zero Dawn, not even anything else. Nier: Automata is where it is at. And mark my words, Nier: Automata will most likely not get the title of GOTY, instead it will be Zelda BOTW, cause we all know the reasons behind that. But once a few years have passed, people will remember BOTW as a very good game, where as Nier: Automata as 'the masterpiece that we wont forget'.
Ill end this with a quote of Jim Sterling.
'If history forgets this game, then ♥♥♥♥ history.'

Ahhhh Dead Rising. Well, Dead Rising is one of my favorite series just to muck about and have lots of fun in, and this game is definitely no exception. Dead Rising 3 is full of fun toys and trinkets to maim and mutilate with, and the map itself is pretty dense. There's lots of enterable buildings, and it feels like you're really in a city. The main character is a pretty goofy young guy, but he's pretty likeable, moreso than the other protagonists of Dead Rising. The story itself is a bit wobbly and isn't that great, but it's pretty alright.
The most fun however is being able to slaughter all the zombies on the streets of Los Perdidos, and it's even better than before. The gameplay has been upped tremendously from Dead Rising 2, where picking up weapons and eating food are much more fluent and everything just flows nicely. There's tons of zombies on screen which is pretty impressive considering none of them look alike. Also there's a sprint button finally so you don't have to leisurely stroll away from your death.
Now all of this is good fun, but there is one giant glaring issue with this game and that's the optimization of this port. I have a stable rig that can run games that are more graphically intense than Dead Rising 3 without a problem, yet I seem to be having tons of framerate and rendering issues. There's lots of pop-up and framerate loss, and sometimes some models don't even show up, so it looks like I'm driving and invisible steam roller. Plus the FOV is horrendous. Hopefully, Capcom will fix this or a modder will come along and make something that will fix these problems (i.e. Dark Souls, Saints Row 2). I would give this port a 9/10 simply because of the fun and bloodshed that this game allows me to have, but sadly because of the terrible optimization and such, It gets a 7/10. Hopefully, if a patch is released that makes the game stable on PC, then it'll bump right back up to a 9.

This review is based on an old CD ROM version I had.
Years ago I nearly lost a friend due to this game. He parked his imperial armada over my fortified rebel planet, and proceeded to lose a star destroyer in an attempt to bombard it. When he decided to maintain the blockade afterwards, I sent commandos onto the fleet to blow up some of his ships. He ragequit, and I am lucky I still have him as a friend.
This is a very nonstandard strategy game. The game is very much tied in with the story and lore of Star Wars. As important as the resources you collect, or the ships you build, are the characters you have and send on missions. Diplomacy, Intrigue, and Sabotage all come into play. If you don't have enough ground troops on a planet who's loyalty is swayed by the other side, you could lose it and all the resources it provides.
It is also great fun for anyone who is familiar with the Star Wars Expanded Universe, as many references to characters, ships, and species are included. The Empire get Noghri Assassin squads, and the Rebels get Bothan Spies. The empire get characters such as Thrawn and Dalla alongside classic characters like Piett, while the rebels get some characters that may have been of questionable loyalty in the books, like Talon Karrde or Borsk Fey'lya. A very fun game even if you just play it for the numerous references!

While I was a fan of its predescecor, Warrior Within came at a huge dissapointment.  If you haven't played a Prince of Persia game, look into the otheres, don't start here.
With that out of the way here are the issues: Combat is attrocious.  The game actually adds to the repetive combat of its predecesor by adding more variety and cutting down on repitition, but that means absolutely nothing when the core balance of combat is thrown off.  The damage the player does is absurd.  I switched difficulty to easy quickly just because of how much damage it would take to kill enemies.  They aren't hard to beat, just time consuming for absolutely no reason.  And even on easy, I was back to having enemies that would take forever.
The other gameplay element Prince of Persia games focus on is the parkour.  Here the core mechanics are actually much better than the original and fun.  HOWEVER (of course this game can't do anything right) the camera controls are downright janky. It's a mixed bag of fixed camera and player control.  You can control it, kinda, but it wants to do its own thing.  And I rarely found what the angles that the game was trying to force on me to be enjoyable or useable.
And as long as we're tallying up the sins.  Warrior Within's aesthetic design is hilarious bad.  It's like Prince of Persia suddenly hit puberty and became an angsty teenager.  The magical arabic vibe is primarily replaced by someone trying to make thier game edgy.  It's dark, everyone is angrier, there are mystifying segments (such as the prologue, you can't miss it) of metal music.  Whoever hired the 13 year old who was in charge of the aesthetics needs to be fired.
The only good things I could say about this game is that it has a nice environment.  But even that is diminished by it being the exact same as last game. The rouge-like exploring in this game is a lot of fun. Opening chests, finding hidden items, blowing up walls. finding keys, discovering secret areas - but there isn't really that many rooms to discover. You visit a couple, boss fight. You visit a couple, boss fight. You need to play the game many times to get the true adventurous experience.
Fortunately, the replayability is where this game shines. All of the rooms, enemies and items are randomly generated, making the game a thrill no matter how many times you play it. Every run you will find a new enemy type, or item, or whatever. The collectibles are so much fun to collect. It is so  satisfying when you find them, and trying to find them all can be a tricky task, but must be rewarding to see your collection full up.
There are other items that can revive health, add extra hearts or give you special abilities. They are cool, but overall feel thrown it to give the game a little more substance. They aren't much help, save for the hearts, and some are just flat out filler; unneccesary or annoying. There was one item, a magic card, which I used in the middle of a boss fight in a panic. It teleported me to another room, where I had to go back to the boss and start it all over again. Just know that that is what the item will do. Some people may like this as it makes the game harder, but personally I find it annoying.
This game is hard, and you will die. A lot. It takes a lot of time to get used to, and its usually the swarm of enemy attacks that will kill you. The enemy/bosses attacks and patterns are really perdictble, though, and you will easily memorise them. Despite that, this game is still a challenge and tough to master.
Overall, a fantastic game with a few annoying flaws, but at the price its at, its a bargain! Definitely pick this up, it can run on almost anything.

Stellaris is one of those games where you have to invest a lot of time and effort into learning how to play, but once you do, you basically have endless possibilities at your disposal. I had the privilege of a good friend of mine teaching me Stellaris. No few words will do the game justice, as there are countless playstyles and experiences to be had. You can do pretty much anything in this game that you would be able to do in another grand strat, plus more.
For instance, you can create your own empire from scratch; custom name, custom appearance, ethos, government ethics and civics, species traits, FTL method, ship appearance, starting weapon technology, city appearance, preferred planet type, and flag. This is my personal favorite part of the game, since you can make your own race of aliens with their own empire and give them a personality of their own.
Want to create a fanatical militarist and authoritarian empire of hegemonic imperialist cockroaches and rule the galaxy with an iron fist? Sure! Want to make a race of xenophilic, pacifist migratory snails that run an egalitarian meritocracy government with a paralimentary system? Why not? How about an empire of decadent, despotic, predadory reptilian slavers that cede planets to integrate other species as slaves into their society? Yeah! What about a race of fanatic pacifist, inward perfectionist pig people with an agrarian idyll who just farm their crops and want absolutely nothing to do with other empires? Totally! Or have you ever wanted to make an empire of vaguely phallic black mushroom people ruled by a hive mind that spreads across the galaxy and consumes other species? Well now you can.
Are you proud of the empires you created? Well, you can create a new one every time and save your old ones either to go back to them and play as them later, or you can make them all spawn into your galaxy at once, and
while you sit back with your intelligent research link robot hive mind and eclipse them all in military technology while building up a fleet big enough and strong enough to crush the entire galaxy.
The best part about Stellaris is really playing with other people. It's fun to see what kinds of races people will make, and how they get used throughout the course of the game to explore, expand, exploit and exterminate other player and NPC empires. There is no end to the fun; you can do anything from forming a federation with other like-minded empires, to finding a planet full of pre-sapient species and uplifting them into primitives, to doing something nasty like
15/10, best grand strategy game I've ever played, and the only one that I actually enjoy. Eat your heart out, Civilization.

This is an Anime style MMORPG. The world you play in is named Azuria, the best work of a deity called Gaia. Somewhere beyond the sky, you find Aura Kingdom. A realm of light and spirit. Beneath is Pandemonium, a hellish place filled with undead and destruction. You find yourself on Terra, where these two realms clash. Terra is a place of wonders guided by Gaia's cubes, conveniently named Cube of Gaia, the mortal's link to the creative force of the universe. Allowing the creative humans, the powerful and pride Makar, ... to use magic, grand them wisdom or power.
The story of the game is (no spoilers) you start with the obligatory, short tutorial. After you've finished it, you wake up in a small town named Port Skandia, memoryless of your past or was the tutorial a glimps of the future, can you change it? During the game powers of good and evil clash and you find yourself in the middle of it. Your duty is, not to choose sides, but to safeguard the people, flora and fauna of Terra.
The game itself is very noob friendly, the main story line exists out of an enormous series of quests, which you will basically follow to level up in a very fast fashion. As in every other MMORPG, there are dungeons, which the main quest line will teach you the basics about. You can also do side quests, which wont give you that much experience, but instead will provide you with supplies or titles to improve your gameplay. The early game, you'll be probably leveling solo, getting used to the more advanced mechanics, the numorous classes and finding friends. Which isn't hard because of the open guild system where everyone can freely join a guild.
The game has a pet system where the pets, called Eidolons, are an extension of yourself. They aid you in battle, grand you passive stats and some can even buff and/or heal you. You get your first Eidolon on account creation and you get two more while doing the quest lines. The other ones you'll have to collect key fragments for to craft their summoning keys.
In general, the game is very fun to play, it looks gorgeous and will never get boring as there is so much content to explore. I have literally played the game for hundreds of hours before linking it to Steam and I still love playing it because the community and the world are still growing and more content gets added every few months. I suggest finding the class best suited for you and referring to the guides found on the aura kingdom forums (link below)

This games feels unfinished an unpolished. It literally feels like I'm playing a university student's project,a demo,a free-to-play Unity game,rather than a fully fledged game.
The game has loads of bugs. Clipping out of boundaries is stupidly easy.
The art style is cheap and lazy, featuring stupidly bland colors.
There is no plot,except for the "Cutscene" that explains that you are a hacker,and explains your goals. By the way, The 'Hacker' thing is a lie. You do absolutely nothing that makes you feel like a hacker. It feels like it's just a cheap excuse to explain the bland color of the levels,the uninspiringly empty and minimalistic design,and the plain use of solid colors.
Textures are horrible and look pixelated when you look closely at them.
Controls aren't bad,except by the fact that the mouse has this weird acceleration that you can't turn off or adjust.
Cubes simply disappear and reappear when the 'Reset Cube' button is pressed,with no animation.
Moving platforms behave weirdly. They just start and stop moving,again,with no animation, this without mentioning that the physics of cubes also behave in a very erratic way when on top of a moving platform.
The UI,once again,features no animation.
Entering or exiting a level also doesn't feature animation. You just hop from the level to the menu,from the menu to the level,because the developer did not even have the audacity to implement a simple fade-in and fade-out
Sound effects are horrible. The sound track isn't bad,though.
The "puzzles"  go from super simple to super confusing,in a matter of minutes of gameplay.
Some of them require you to kill yourself in order to progress. Does that look like good level design for you? It sure doesn't look good for me.
All in all,don't buy this game.It is not worth it's price,not even on sale. It is a shameless waste of time and potential.
If this was a free to play game,or a public alpha,it would be OK,but as a full game,its unacceptable,as it is nothing more than a poorly built 3D game built in Unity,that feels more like a student project,and that being said,there are better student projects out there.

To start, most complaints are from those who hadn't tinkered enough. The lack of any instructions or guides from Valve is disheartening at best :( and the learning curve is pretty steep since its in no way your traditional controller.
HOWEVER this controller is AMAZING for gaming.
Its definetly a game changer as things go, though it will never replace good old fashioned Key/mouse combination gaming, it does a damned good job of replacing classic controllers, and hopefully will set the bar for future console controllers.
The gyro addition, and use, alone makes this thing do amazing things that if Sony had used in their Six-Axis, the PS3/PS4 could be simply ground breaking.
Don't let the list of cons disuade you, its definetly a work in progress at this time, and hopefully most of this will be fixed.
Pros -
+Customizable controls out the wazoo
+Amazingly decent in even FPS games, and can even have a real competitive use in online modes once you get the hang of it (and get a decent configuration setup)
+Gyro that can be always on or part of a mixed control scheme to enhance aiming or driving
couch gaming your PC games with less hassle (if connected to a TV, Shield, or Steam Link)
+alternate controls at the press/hold of a button on the controller gives you TWO sets of possible controls you can swap on the fly.
+Works as a mouse for being lazy on the desktop.
can be setup to work in almost any game.
+Point and click games actually are playable with this!!
+Driving with the Gyro is amazingly accurate, and works better than any steering wheel I've personally ever used. Way better than any traditional gamepad as well, and far beyond better than key/mouse for driving.
Cons-
-STEEP learning curve, this is NOT something your going to master in a few minutes of setting up.
-Default profiles for games that have them aren't very good, and require major tweaks to really get the best out of them.
No guides or documentation for use or setup.
-No real method of knowing the best profiles from the community made ones, it only shows how many people have utilized them, not what people think of them.
-REQUIRES big picture mode, which in its current state is terrible and crashes a LOT. Nice when it -works, but barely functional otherwise. BPM also doesn't like DosBox games and the overlay fails when trying to setup controls and play the game to test at the same time.
-REQUIRES steam overlay to tweak settings.
-No way to use in non-steam games that won't work in steams big picture mode or Steam Overlay. Making the need for some searching to get things working for stuff from Origin (which blocks steams overlay).
-old fashioned batteries.. while not that bad, its a real pain that in this day and age we aren't seeing a decent built in battery (though this does make long term better in terms of when built in batteries fail)
-No documentation as mentioned above, and no basic guide from Valve either in the guides section (that I've found)
-XYAB buttons are in an admittedly odd placement, and small, making them somewhat hard to hit.
-Not entirely as advertised and it DOES NOT work with "Your entire Steam Library", many games simply won't work with it due to Big Picture Mode and Steam Overlay problems.
Overall, while I do say the controller is well worth it, its also possibly worth waiting until the community features and profiles get sorted, as well as BPM to get fixed. All of which should've been done pre-release.
A final note, the controller probably isn't very useful for flying or fighting games IMO. The odd placement of the XYAB buttons, and it just doesn't feel right even if using the gyro to fly.
Other than that, its outstanding in almost everything I've thrown at it.

I have spent a few hours with the Steam Controller and have outlined several of the pros and cons below.
Build Quality:
The build quality leaves something to be desired. This controller is more on par with the Wii U Pro controller in terms of build quality than the PS4 or Xbone controller. It doesn't hold a candle to an Xbone controller in terms of feel and ergonomics, and the smooth shiny plastic feels a little cheap in my opinion. The seams of the controller are a little spaced out which also gives the sense that it is not a "fine-tuned" design. That being said, the controller does not feel flimsy and has a good weight to it. It is a little heftier than a traditional controller if you put batteries in it. The buttons click nicely and feel like they could withstand hundreds of hours of use.
Design:
There are some things that the Steam Controller got very right, and other things that seem like they were compromised in the design process. The track pads work great and feel very nice. The convex shape of the controller naturally positions your thumbs over the track pads. The track pads get a lot of attention, but I want to highlight the rear paddles and the gyroscope. These are the best features of the controller in my opinion.
The paddles are an absolute must have, and competitor controllers are remiss for not including them. Being able to use the right track pad and have a face button mapped to one of the paddles is a convenience that cannot be understated. It's great for mapping sprint, aim, use, etc. They are also clickier than I expected, which is also nice. The gyroscope is great for controlling cameras in first and third person games. I first fell in love with this kind of control playing Splatoon on Wii U, but it works really well in Skyrim and GTA to give you just a little bit of extra control over the camera. These two features allow a level of comfort and usability unprecedented by other controllers. The Xbone Elite controller has paddles, but not a gyroscope: the opposite is true for the Wii U controller (which admittedly has other issues, but the gyroscope is a great feature). No controller I know of features both, and now that the Steam Controller has them, I find that I miss them when using other controllers.
Now for the designs that I think were compromised a bit. First, I have a few criticisms of the analog stick. The analog stick is poorly placed in the bottom left of the controller, and is honestly a bit of a reach. It is not terribly uncomfortable, but it is the thing I had the hardest time adjusting to when using this controller.  Additionally, it is concave rather than convex  which greatly diminishes its quality. The PS4 and Xbone controllers both have convex sticks, and for good reason; they are vastly more comfortable. I can only imagine that future interations of the controller will have a convex stick.
The face buttons are also similarly placed on the opposite side of the controller. However, the placement is not nearly as bothersome as the size: they are very small. Not as small as a 3DS or anything, but they will certainly take some getting used to. Additionally, the A button is placed precariously close to the edge of a bevel on the face of the controller, and your thumb rests rather uncomfortably over the surface of the controller as a result. I recommend for whatever games you can to remap A to one of the paddle grips. Also, the X button is a pretty mighty reach that will take some getting used to. All that being said, my wife who is 5'1" did not complain about the size of the controller, so these spacing issues can certainly be overcome. It seems to me that the traditional size and spacing of these buttons were sacrificed to provide a superior trackpad experience. That being said, this controller is much more comfortable than initial reviews would suggest. I can play it for several hours at a time and not feel any discomfort. The batteries also last FOREVER, even with the gyroscope and haptic feedback on. Very nice and appreciated bonus.
As I mentioned before, the trackpads feel very nice and have a good size to them. One of the greatest features of the trackpads is that they give haptic feedback the whole time you are moving across them. You can also put the trackpads into trackball mode which gives your input some momentum and can be used to "flick" the camera in applicable games. This feels incredibly natural and suprisingly tactile. I must mention though that the left trackpad is no replacement for a d-pad. I would recommend bringing out an Xbone controller for arcade games because the indented cross on the left trackpad is larger than a traditional d-pad (thus more difficult to reach the clickier edges) and hard to keep your bearings with.
The bumpers and triggers feel very nice. The triggers have a soft pull and a hard pull setting that can be mapped separately. This is situationally very useful, but not a feature I use in every game. You can also set it so that the input is "dampened" on the trackpads while pulling one or both of the controllers. I find this to be very necessary in shooters, as pulling the trigger typically results in some unintentional trackpad movement that ruins well-aimed shots.
User-Friendliness:
The main shortcomings of the Steam Controller come from the software. Steam Big Picture mode needs to be run in beta for the controller to properly work with it, which was not adequately explained pre-purchase; and yes, it is almost mandatory to use Big Picture to get the proper Steam Controller experience. I have had several issues where the beta client has crashed when I pressed the home button, which also crashed my game. Also, using the home button sometimes results in a need to alt-tab back into the game after I press it (I saw this with GTA V in particular). This is very inconvenient and breaks the immersive experience of using a controller.

Bindings do not always work properly from the configuration screen and sometimes need to be selected several times. You can remap every aspect of this controller except how it actually works in the Steam client. The track pads do literally nothing while navigating the Steam Big Picture mode. Even in the web browser, I often have to tab out using one of the bumpers and return to the web browser for the trackpads to work for web browsing.  The software needs a lot of tweaks before it is a recommendable experience, in my opinion. Especially if you are trying to sell the experience to a console player, who is used to a relatively seamless experience.
Along the same lines, this controller requires a significant amount of tinkering to get working the way you want it to. It is honestly overwhelming at first. You can change dead zones, the axis at which the track pad registers a horizontal sweep, how the track pad emulates a mouse or a joystick (several options for each). Someone who is used to the plug and play experience of a traditional controller could be turned off by this level of necessary configuration to get things to run smoothly.
Game Support:
This section is very simple. Out of a couple of dozen games I tried, the only game I could not get to work with the Steam Controller was the Binding of Isaac. Games like GTA V, Skyrim, Fez, Psychonauts, even DOTA 2 and CS:GO worked and were actually pretty playable (though your teammates may not appreciate being on your team while you learn your new controller). As mentioned before, you will need to do a lot of tinkering to get things where you want them. Hopefully, the community bindings will start catching on and be a more useful feature.
Conclusion:
The Steam Controller is a nice piece of hardware that is limited by its software. I could go into much greater depth about the insane level of binding customization, but I do not have enough characters. At this point, I can only realy recommend it to people who consider themselves "early adopters".

It takes some getting used to if you're used to a traditional controller - but it's well worth it.
The trackpad is very innovative and way more superior than the traditional thumbstick for aiming/looking.
The first game I had tried with this controller was Far Cry 4, and it amazed me how well the controller worked.
Typically I play stealthy in Far Cry and use the bow for headshots.
With the normal Xbox 360 controller, headshots were somewhat rare because of the lack of precision on the thumbsticks.
However, with the trackpad - I was able to get them no problem.
The trackpad isn't as good as mouse precision, but it's still way better than a controller thumbstick.
The only downside so far is it does take a few minutes to configure the controller before starting a new game.
Most games have community made settings, and Steam provides pre-made templates, but you will always want to fine-tune some of the settings to your liking.
Speaking of fine-tuning, the buttons are extremely configurable.
They can be programmed to do anything your keyboard, or traditional controller can plus more.
Configurations are saved per-game and per-program.
So if you're using the controller to play a game, once you go out of the game - the configurations automatically switch back to your "Big Picture" or "Desktop" configurations.
The controller also has two buttons on the back which are very useful - another feature that traditional controllers lack.
I typically use them as LeftStick-Click or RightStick-Click since pushing down on the trackpad is a bit awkward and typically causes your aim to move.
All and all, it's a great controller.  So far its worked with every game I've played and I've had no real problems as of yet.
I highly reccomend this if you're wanting more accuracy - especially for FPS games.

Hmm... where do I start? The controller is nicely made, seems durable enough and has a great bunch of tech in it, but using it I found that it makes simple things unnecessarily complicated. For example with a regular pad, you can pick it up and jam on a plethora of games that support pads and they just work. However with the Steam Controller you have to do endless fiddling around in settings to get the right feel for it because the base templates are just simply not good enough - even then, once you find a setup that is right for you, it still isn't as straight forward or as comfortable as a standard game pad. A lot of customisation on a per game basis, quite simply undermines the entire point of the controller. It doesn't make anything easier, unless you're lucky and the pad just plays nice with a particular game.
One of the most annoying things for me with this controller was the huge emphasis on Big Picture. I'm a desktop gamer and I don't like having to be forced to use Big Picture, but I have no choice and I understand it is meant primarily for living room gamers, so I roll with it. It's time like these I realise how bad the Steam platform is because instead of one well designed, modernised and unified platform/client, we have one client that splits into two radically different interfaces, one with more features than the other and the other with better support for the Steam Controller - this just alienates desktop PC players but it's no better for those on the couch in the living room either and here's why:
Due to the ridiculous amount of customisation required on many games and the fact that it cannot match the simplicity of a traditional dual analogue stick controller, it falls short in its performance on games that were specifically designed to make use of a traditional twin stick controller and games which use traditional controllers as a secondary - yes in theory you can get better precision with a haptic pad and I won't argue with that, but reliability of input and constant customisation means you'll never get a broad feeling of consistency with aiming and turning in comparison to that of a regular controller.
The area in which the Steam Controller shines is where an analogue stick will fail miserably. Games that have mouse input, such as Sim City (shown in the trailer for the Steam Controller) and games like Civilisation will be a blast to play using the Steam Controller and slowly and more tedious with that of a regular gamepad. However, a traditional controller will destroy Valve's effort in regards to ease of use in FPS games like Call of Duty (since this is primarily focused for the living room, we'll pretend mouse and keyboard doesn't come into the FPS argument) but will fall short of the Steam Controller for mouse oriented tasks. I still think that it'd make more sense to have two pads if you're using Big Picture mode in the living room - one 360 style pad and one Steam Controller. One for FPS and driving. One for mouse-oriented games that require precision. You'd be kidding yourself to think that this is a one-device solution to bridging the gap between mouse, keyboard and controller, because it isn't - regardless of what others might say.
Some people may enjoy customising on a per game basis, but I for one do not. It is a very bold effort from Valve but in practice it just doesn't work unless you use it solely with mouse movement in game and not for camera viewing/aiming in third and first person titles. The emphasis on Big Picture only, with more screwing about if you're a desktop gamer means there is even less reason to get the Steam Controller than the already limited reasons for owning one if you plan to treat your living room PC or Steam Machine (which IMO is also a foolish investment) as a games console - even more stupid is the fact that there is very little in the way of love for those using the Steam Controller on the desktop client because there is absolutely no place other than Big Picture to use the higher functions of the controller and update the firmware - quite ridiculous.
To those who share my concerns, I'd advise you skip this and buy a Xbox One controller for PC and a receiver kit - however you must have Windows 10 to be able to use said wireless receiver - or you can simply use the wired version.
I wish I had more positive review for folks to read and I understand there are those who have bought the device who are naturally going to defend their own interests (and financial investment) and as such thumbs down my review, but that unfortunately doesn't change the reality of the weak points when using this controller. As tempting as it may be to invest in one, I seriously suggest you don't - if you do and you end up regretting it, don't say I didn't tell you so.
It's an investment which will cost you lots of time until the Community Configurations are made actually useful. It works well, but only after hours of tinkering.

All the brilliance of Rising Storm/Red Orchestra 2 now in a Vietnam setting. This doesn't just mean a change in visuals, outfits, and guns, but also special abilities like digging holes to move under the map, radio operation, and of course helicopters.
This game is like a proper sequel to Battlefield: Vietnam, with true evolution in gameplay mechanics which Battlefield never developed due to console focus (dumbing down the gameplay to make it casual, removing modding, removing content and relying on overpriced DLC, disgusting rent-a-server only model). On that note, the makers of Project Reality mod for Battlefield 2 also took matters into their own hands with the game Squad, which is turning out to be a proper modern warfare themed Battlefield game.
In Rising Storm 2: Vietnam, like its predecessors, you have to adjust your weapons for range, manually check your magazine if you want to see how much ammo is in your gun, you can't just fire full auto bursts and expect to kill everything like in Battlefield and other console shooters. You can deploy weapons with bi-pods, choose between different weapon variants e.g. Type-56 vs the S variant vs the AKM. When shot, you bleed and have to bandage yourself, and players can be dismembered. It approaches simulation level mechanics and doesn't shy down much when it comes to vehicles as well, they are much more complex than a mainstream shooter.
So, like its immediate predecessor, this game contains the best infantry shooter gameplay mechanics. You can throw grenades overhand or underhand, you can equip a bayonet and stab foes with a penalty to accuracy, commanders work with radio operators to issue commands and call air strikes, and it has the best sound effects of any war-themed shooter (take it from an audiophile with a 5.1 surround setup). You are issued the equipment soldiers at the time actually used, not like modern Call of Duty games with reflex sights everywhere and worse in Vietnam.
Despite all this, the game modes of Rising Storm 2: Vietnam are typical ones, just like its predecessor. Only two game modes are consistently played: Territory, which is an attack and defend type game mode. One team has to attack and capture objectives, the other has to defend them, whichever team does a better job of controlling the map wins. Respawns work in waves, to simulate reinforcements.
Then there is Supremacy, which is nearly the same as Battlefield's Conquest: both teams battle to capture objective points, holding these positions gains your team points, but the differences are that you can win the match by holding all objectives together for a minute, and you can even capture the enemy's HQ. A bit more unforgiving than Conquest.
Simple game modes, made more tactical by the unforgiving hardcore mechanics. But make no mistake about it, this is not  some complex strategic game nor is it as tactical as Arma can be due to the simpler objectives of Rising Storm 2's game modes. This is a phenomenal war shooter, if only it had an awesome single player campaign though like the classic Call of Duty games... such a campaign with this game's mechanics would be a dream come true, as I don't personally get a whole lot of enjoyment out of PvP shooter game modes as simple as these. But this game will suit a hell of a lot of gamers.
As expected from Tripwire Interactive, this is a true PC game that gives you free reign over your dedicated servers and is moddable. Expect more and more free content, whether official or unofficial, as time passes. This is a war-themed PvP shooter done right, unlike the countless examples of AAA games doing it wrong, scamming you with less content, lower quality content, for a higher price.

Spoilers for my next review: The Binding Of Isaac: Rebirth is one of my favorite games of all time! I’ve spent over 150 hours on it, which is pretty impressive for me, and I often come back to it when I don’t have anything else to do. It is the game I’ve spent the most time with on steam! But something I haven’t done in years before today, is going back to play the game that started it all and answer this simple question: Is the original Isaac still worth playing? Let’s find out!
BTW, this is gonna be a pretty simplified review, since I’m gonna review Rebirth later!
You play as Isaac, a boy who lives with his extremely religious mother. Things were going fine until the mother got in contact with god. God said that Isaac was becoming corrupt, and had to be dealt with. The mother took away all of Isaac’s toys, and even his clothes, but it wasn’t enough. Isaac’s mom locked isaac up in his room, but even after that, it wasn’t enough. God said that she had to sacrifice Isaac. The mother grabbed a knife and walked towards Isaac’s room to do what had to be done. Isaac watched this through a crack in his door, and was terrified. He looked everywhere for a place to hide, and eventually found a trap door to the basement. He jumped down, and the game starts.
Pretty dark story, ain’t it?
This game definitely shows it’s age. It’s not like the flash graphics are bad or anything, but compared to Rebirth, It doesn’t look to good. The only thing I think is slightly better, Is that tinted rocks are easier to spot.
This game runs pretty bad! Even with my new pc, it does stutter a bit. I guess it’s because of the flash engine which doesn’t run well with a game with so much content as this one.
Now this is interesting. It’s so strange to go back and play this game! They’ve changed so much with rebirth and it’s dlcs! okay, where to start. First of all, you can have an infinite number of health in this game. In Rebirth, It will cap at twelve. Secondly, if you spend all your red hearts, even though you still have spirit hearts left, you will die. When picking up an item, you will stand still for a couple of seconds. Secret rooms doesn’t stay open. The list of changes from vanilla to Rebirth goes on and on. I find this a bit hard to play, because of all the quality of life changes made in Rebirth. Even so, it’s still fun to go back and see how it used to be!
The only thing I find vanilla Isaac to do better than Rebirth is the music. I love the music in this game! It’s so nostalgic to me! My favorite song in the entire series is the caves theme. Sure, the music in rebirth is good and all, but I sure miss these ones!
The Binding Of Isaac is a good game, but i just can’t recommend it. Rebirth has all the content this game has, and much more! There’s literally no reason to go back to this game, other than the nostalgia. With that, I’ll give this game a
6/10

With 100+ hours spent in this gem: I can officially say that is worth the "buy".
Not convinced? Let's dig a little deeper...
Stellaris is (as of this review) the latest foray into the genre of grand strategy by Paradox Interactive (more specifically their in-house development studio), and as usual it is excellent at the niche it was designed to fill. It runs great, on systems both new and old, and the DLC scheme isn't punishing to those of us who might not want to spend too much on our games. That being said, some DLCs, especially Utopia, are considered "must-haves" for the features they add.
Best of all is it's moddability, which is absurdly great. It is more than possible to build an entirely new game from the Stellaris framework, and several mods have done just that, most notably the "Star Trek: New Horizons" mod, which is by far the most well made mod for any game published thus far. It's worth a try, even for those who aren't fans of the Trekverse. Other mods, for stellaris base and for ports of Stargate and other titles, are also of good quality, though the Star Wars and Mass Effect modding scene is (as of this review) fairly sparse.
In any case, the drop-in drop-out CO-OP/VS multiplayer functionality that first came to the public eye in Hearts of Iron is a welcome feature, and the quality of multiplayer matches is significantly better than on other Paradox titles. It also has the shallowest learning curve of all the Paradox games, making this a good pick for those who have an interest in "breaking in" to the grand strategy scene.
The Verdict: 95/100
(ST:NH Verdict: 100/100)

Stellaris is the sort of game that's difficult to wholeheartedly recommend, but simultaneously hard to say to pass over. Of all the Paradox games, its vanilla is one of the most fleshed out without any DLC. But you will want, and eventually need, the DLC to fully enjoy the game. Take this into account when buying. On a -50% sale it's only about ~$30-40 dollars with everything, which is not a bad deal for this sort of game. Species packs are decorative fluff that help support the devs, but the others are definitely worth it for mechanics. Also, don't bother with the special editions. There's some neat stuff but not worth the price.
To the game itself, it is not the standard space 4X, especially with the radical changes coming up in the 2.0 update. This is a game about picturing yourself roleplaying an instellar civilization. Min maxing is fun for a bit but the game will simply not be enjoyable after a while because the mechanics aren't tuned towards "optimal" plays. There definitely are best ways to play but it's honestly more entertaining to pick or make a species and go with that. This is the sort of game where you'll want to, on the first few goes, read the flavor text and think about things. Because the mechanics, while fulfilling, are skin deep in a lot of ways: the game currently only allows different flavors of conquest victories and unless you're playing on a small galaxy, that's very unrealistic. This is about making space operas in your head on the backdrop of an engaging 4X game that continues to receive significant updates every two months.
The devs do love this game, and their dedication shows. I'm usually not a fan of the Paradox DLC strategy, but the DLC here truly does feel special and worth keeping this game updating frequently. Leviathans add interesting space creatures to fight, Utopia overhauls the mid and late game with a whole new tech tree, and Synthetic Dawn adds a whole new and customizable machine race options. These do affect the game and make them more enjoyable, unlike some CK II DLCs I could name.
Tl;dr the game keeps getting better, but don't expect this to be master of orion. It is very much a "grand" strategy game, taken from high above while you help fill in the gaps of the story with your own species. This may turn some strategists off but it does make it more welcoming to newcomers. At any rate, you'll definitely get your money back on it.

There is a lot to say about stellaris, and I don't feel like writing thousands of words to convince you how good it is. I don't even know how to begin, as it is quite different from the other 4X existing to date.
Looking at galactic civilization 2 & 3, those two games were more about customizing your ships and less about the complexity of managing an empire. Everything is laid out in the open, leaving choice to the player for which path to take. GCiv 3 is more akin to a giant board game, with many pieces to manage. In comparison, Stellaris has a lot less stuff to handle and will actively reduce the amount of pieces the player has to take care of. You are managing an empire, you should not care about the petty lives of the general populace. Give that job to governors! Obviously, you have to content your people as they will join political factions. Some will want peace, other will be supremacists. Of course, you can promote a faction by spending political influence but that might cost you in expansion.
There is a lot of parameters in Stellaris, a lot of variables that seem innocuous at the first glance but will become important later on. The different governement ethics are diverse enough to create a true sense of diversity, to the point that you might get unlucky and be placed next to a Fanatic Purifiers kind of governement - bunch of xenophobes who will stop at nothing until the whole galaxy is purified from the xeno filth, that means you and everybody else that isn't them. Fast paced short levels with highly responsive controls and a good variety of enemies and obstables to overcome. I like the character animations and the trail left behind while running - they provide great visual feedback to support the sense of speed. Graphics and sound do their jobs. It becomes challenging in the last 10 or so levels, while the first 2 worlds (40 levels + 2 bosses) are rather easy.
Content-wise it's a bit short, such that some of the gameplay elements (like portals and the killing gas floor) could be explored to a much bigger extent. Also, in Super Meat Boy every single level feels like it has a purpose and brings the game forward (by introducing new mechanics or amping up the difficulty and making the player better), while that's not the case in iZBOT - there are several levels in which you just go through without learning anything new or improving.
Overall it's good. I feel it's worth supporting, particularly because of the tight controls and despite its shortcomings - I can see the dev. taking them and making a bigger, better, more inspired and brilliant game (I hope they do).

Rising Storm 2: I AINT SAYIN IM A GENIUS, 2 + 2 IS ON MY MIND
Games based in the Vietnam War have always been a mixed bag given the nature of the war as a whole. Either they were action fests that were vaguely about the war or they spend around 15 years telling you about the war without actually stepping foot on the country in question. But if you're after a realistic first person shooter that allows you to learn that you truly are never too young for Vietnam flashbacks, here you go.
Remember the MkB in Red Orchestra 2? Imagine that but now everyone has the ability to get one. The combat is that frantic mania that has made the Red Orchestra/Rising Storm franchise popular, but now with more shotguns, assault rifles, grenade launchers and napalm. The graphics are very nice even on low and can be customized to whatever flavor you want. And even better, you don't have as much "promising features without delivering" that Red Orchestra 2 had. So the promised Aussies and ARVN are actually coming to/are in the game rather than left on a flash drive in some back office.
There is just a level of combined entertainment and terror to this game that you don't get with other FPS games outside of similar titles like Squad. You can go from mic-spamming Fortunate Son to screaming like a maniac while emptying an M16A1 at angry Vietnamese farmers in the span of a few seconds. It's manic, terrifying and yet still entertaining. Run around with a Russian double barrel shotgun and scream "GO HOME GI", play pilot and blast Wagner or just play to win. This game allows for quite a variety of play styles that other FPS games lack, where being a meme-y♥♥♥♥♥♥actually can help your team. So buy this game, customize yourself with just an undershirt and run across a South-East Asian country with a 50 year old revolver screeching the lyrics to Bobby Fuller.

It's weird, but in a great way... mostly. I love the design, really not sure why only now are we getting a controller that sinks into your palms and makes use of the design of your hands. The touchpad wasn't the massive accuracy upgrade over the joystick that I was expecting, but I'm not dissapointed, I was planning on sticking with mouse and keyboard for competitive games anyway. It was strange to get it working with emulated games, but it works great now, except that the joystick doesn't register, so I have the left touchpad registered as a d-pad with overlapping commands enabled, which works mostly well enough. It's by far the most comfortable controller I've held, and my hands aren't massive, they're quite average sized. One complaint people give is that your hands must be big for it to be comfortable, and I'd disagree, but I see where they're coming from, and wouldn't strongly suggest it for a gamer with particularly small hands. It's higher quality than most people would lead you to believe, I don't find the plastic cheap, and the glossy plastic parts aren't often in contact with fingertips, and they don't 'fingerprint stain' easily like people had anticipated they would. The gyro control is fantastic, no one's disagreeing with that, it's definitely appreciated and very well done. Before the steam controller I used an app that uses the 360 controller as a mouse for a few nifty things like easily browsing the web from my bed using my TV, but the steam controller is far easier to use for this, the design supports desktop navigation incredibly well. Overall, I'd definitely reccommend it, it'll probably get you back into lots of the games you own and have never played, being so new and exciting. Personally, I'm sticking with it, 360 controllers are fantastic, but I won't be going back to them.

TL;DR: This controller does what it advertises. It lets you play all of your Steam games from a couch, or in bed, or wherever a keyboard and mouse aren't comfortable/convenient. However, you need to spend quite a bit of time using and configuring it to feel comfortable with it (10-20 hours). It takes time, sure, but the boon for overcoming the learning curve feel incredible. (BTW, if you need help configuring the controller, check out Woodie's videos on YouTube. His overviews of how to setup the controller for different genres made my transition to this controller much more painless).
Review:
I've used this controlller for around 50 hours across a few differeint games, including Fallout 4, Torchlight 1, and Elder Scrolls Online. Because this controller is so different, it took me a round 5-10 hours to start feeling very comfortable using it, and around 15-20 or so I felt I had more-or-less mastered it. This is the biggest downside of the controller, but like any new input device (whether it be wasd+mouse controls for Quake back in the day, a joystick when you first get into flight/space sims, or using a 3D mouse for CAD for the first time), it takes time to master, but also like other fancy input devices, the benefits of learning how to properly use and configure it are massive.
For games that support mice and controller inputs at the same time, this controller is an incredible improvement over a standard gamepad, even for first person shooters (professional reviews say otherwise, but in every case, they either didn't spend enough time with the controller or didn't discover the gyro settings). Your first few hours will feel clunky, but spend a few hours with Gyro (enabled by right pad touch AND trigger-soft-pull using mode shifting) + right pad, and you will understand the incredible accuracy of this controller. Sure, it's not as good as a keyboard and mouse, but it only has to be better than a gamepad, and it is by a very wide margin.
For games which separate more controls on keyboard than on a gamepad (i.e making E and Enter, Scroll Wheel and Arrow Keys *somtimes* do different actions, when on the controller A and the dpad just do everything), and don't allow mouse inputs while using a gamepad (*cough* Fallout 4 *cough*) it can be a real PITA, and you will most likely have to use mode shifting (such as using a grip or trigger pull to swap between d-pad controls) to make awkward workarounds, but once you make a configuration that works and spend a few hours with it, awkward configs can feel natural and mostly painless. This is much less a problem with the controller and much more a problem with Bethesda's game engine, but it's notable, especially if you are looking to play bethesda games with this controller.
For games that are designed around a controller and don't have tank-controls (so no FPS or third-person shooters), the Steam Controller works well. Dual Stick Shooters are natural, racing games feel fine with normal gamepad controls, and action games also work well in general (though you want have to tweak right-touch settings between Joystick and Mouse-like Joystick if the in camera can't be controlled by a mouse while using a gamepad).
The Steam Controller also works surprisingly well for Keyboard/Mouse over-head action games, though creating and getting used to a profile that works well with these games takes some time. My suggestion: make use of "Touch Menu" for actions which you don't use during combat (in Torchlight, things like Inventory, Character Screen, Map Controls etc,) while mapping your face buttons to your hotbar and your left trigger/right trigger to mouse clicks. On top of that, use BOTH pads to control the mouse, so that you can use extra actions that are set to, say, the joystick while continuing to move around and click. You by no means will probably be able to play games like StarCraft(2) reasonably well with this controller (though it might be possible, there are a LOT of button mappings you'd need to set and memorize for efficient play), but for slower, simpler games like Torchlight, DOTA, or LOL, play fine.
[EDIT: The new Mouse Region mode, which maps a subsection of the screen onto a pad, works surprisingly well for Osu! (mouse-based rhythm game) and will probably help for RTS games using mode shifting (e.x: pressing a button to jump the camera somewhere on the map using the minimap, or for menus, etc. It could be EXTREMELY useful)]
Community profiles are often a good starting point, but in my experience none of them have fit my needs or tastes. Tweaking and twiddling settings are required. If you aren't afraid of configuring your controller settings and experimenting, it won't be afraid to show your its true, glorious gamepad-beating colors. Community profiles are sorted by the number of people using them, and don't have ratings, so sub-par results sometimes reach the top.
Nitpicks: The seams on the side of the controller are a tad annoying (slightly protruding and slightly sharp, like the first runs of Xbox 360 controllers). Clicking the pads requires too much force and make a very loud click, though not using pad click and using high haptic feedback on the left pad helps (I use this for the menus in Fallout 4).

Steam Controller:
A familiar yet different design. The X, Y, A, B buttons are rotated a little different (Further down) then your Xbox controller but close enough to be familiar. The added paddle buttons on the hand grips make the controller feel a bit more fragile even though it probably is not and I am finding them as pretty awesome extra buttons. The right track pad can control the mouse with pretty good precision and the left is like taking the + button on most controls, making it a track pad with a lot inputs based on the direction you press so that's cool. You can also custom load the controller settings for ANY game, as well as pull profiles made by the community. So even games that don't have controller support, can in a way which is really really awesome.
So far I am liking it more then the xbox controller. It also comes with a micro usb that you can plug in directly as well as a wireless dongle that can be used. Updating the steam controllers firmware does require it connecting to a PC (can not be done through steam link)
Cons: Paddle buttons make is a little flimsy feeling until you get used to them, not sure if their are any rechargable battery packs coming out for it like the xbox controllers.
Pros: Customized buttons layouts for any game, new innovative design that is just familiar enough.
Its def unique but not my go to controller.  It takes some time to get used to it but all and all a nice controller.

Edit Feb 2016:
After 3 months of use, I have all but forgotten my Xpad.   I now tend to not play the games which don't suit the Steam controller as I find going back to an Xpad a pain in the butt.  I recently have a session on a PS4 and honestly, the PS controller is just terrible in comparrison.  I didn't realise just how much accuracy the Steam controller provides until I'd gotten used to it then went back to PS/Xpad.
On the negative side, the SC's thumbstick already feels 'gritchy' and starts making a creaky grindy noise during a heavy play session.  Not that I noticed the noise with my headphones on... but the feel is pretty bad.  I upped the sensitivity so I never need to move the stick to it's extremes, and luckily it's more sensitive and accurate than the xpad anyway... so it works alright.
I imagine this may suggest a shortened pad life overall, however.  As it took my xpad a couple of years before it felt so worn.
Battery life is decidedly average.  After having read comments which praised the long battery life, I was disappointed with how often I have to put new batteries in...  I only use high quality batteries.
On the positive side, I get great results from the SC, very much enjoy using it, get less hand cramping than either PS or Xpads and Steam have been very active regarding fixes and updates.
Overall, I'm still pleased with my purchase... and hope that future production/versions will address the less than expected quality of the thumb stick.
