3rd Day Review
Seems well built, certainly better than I was expecting after reading claims of 'cheap feel' from other users.  Doesn't creak like any of the Xpads I've used (many, too many to count) or feel like I could easily snap it like a PS pad.
After about an hour I was kinda disapointed with the way it felt, finding it hard to reach the XABY buttons.  After about 2-3 hours I stopped trying to hold it like an Xpad and suddenly it got much easier.  So easy that I almost felt foolish for finding it a problem in the first place.
I have average size hands for a male with fatter than average thumbs, yet I have no problem finding the correct XABY button once muscle memory had adapted.  I'm nearly 40 so if I can learn I'm sure the younger generations can adapt far more easily (been gaming since I was 7 and have spent far too many hours holding a PS/Xpad)
It's taking me about 30 minutes per session to get my head out of Xpad 'mode' then I get markedly better with it.
Pad response is as close to instant as I can make any observation on.
I haven't tried too many games yet, but I'm coping well on Borderlands 2, though I find the touch pad is lacking in usefulness for a melee build, always in the frantic end of things.  Conversely, as a sniper build it's way more accurate than an Xpad, so long as I can line up shots without being under immediate pressure.  I've not made up my mind about either scenario yet, as I haven't done more than skim the surface of the binding options.  Further review once I've had a few weeks to try and get the best from it.
Whilst the pad never felt too big or clunky, as I have read elsewhere, my Xpad now feels weedy and too compact.  I've played for 5 hours with no noticeable hand cramping or joint pain, and I am honestly surprised because my wrists and fingers are in bad shape after several sport injuries and breakages. So ++ on that score.
Major downside:  Steam Big Picture mode.  It's awful.  Maybe that's harsh?  *I* find it awful.  It feels cumbersome, sluggish, doesn't get me where I want to be in anything like good order.  Terrible interface for setting up group chats and dealing with several chats at once.  Perhaps my bindings are wrong, but I haven't found a way to isolate bindings for specific environments and I CBA changing it every time I need to jump from one task to another, usually just for a few moments.
Really need an option to lock a binding to a given task/game.
For now, screw BPM.  I'm using classic interface with keyboard/mouse for chat and navigation, then pick up the pad at game time (exactly how I used the Xpad)
Overall, I like it but hope to see some practical improvements regarding BPM and bindings for specific tasks. Hence a split score of...
As a gamepad 7/10 (against Xpad 9/10)
As a way to navigate windows/steam 3/10 vs K/M 9/10
Bare in mind, I'm only 3 days in, haven't played with bindings and haven't fully broken away from being used to holding an Xpad... so I can only assume I'll get better with time, and so will my perception of the SC's usefulness.

Had this damn thing in my wishlist for almost two years before finally remembering I need to play it and check it out. Got around to it just the other night and I've got to say... I've played this before. It's essentially Eden Eternal, except the models look a little better.
So you've never played Eden Eternal? Good, don't waste your time. I'll explain for you, by explaining Aura Kindom.
This is, of course, a 3D MMO kind of like what I imagine World of Warcraft must be like. You run around with WASD or you can go full Runescape and click to get anywhere. Also, you can jump. Twice. That would be pretty friggin sweet if the game were based around platforming, but it really seems to only serve two purposes: 1. to make your character clip hilariously on a roof, and 2. to allow you to glide faster than the free mount you're given can run.
You're forced to sit through this really awful tutorial instance where you're given a pretty nifty looking weapon and sweet costume armor so that you can fight a horde of demons. When I started up, something in me said "play a bard this time", so I did. I had pretty high expectations for my new bard, and none of them were met. Instead of strumming hyms of death off of my intricately decorated lyre, I was shooting orbs of light from it. The two skills the game starts a bard off with are also medium range magic attacks. Disappointingly, within ten minutes of gameplay, I discovered that a bard is nothing but a mage whose staff is a lyre. Imagine my disappointment when I wasn't singing the tune of debuff while healing myself and dealing no damage outside of punches and kicks.
So I switched up. I went to the Scythe Magician, because that's pretty cool, right? I love the class who is basically the same concept in LaTale, Phantom Mage. Wrong again, Forte! Back to the literal Hell of a tutorial instance with my twice as big as me reaper weapon. Surely, I thought, if I was doing mad damage as a stratocaster, I should be done with this tutorial in record time now that I have this ginormous weapon!
On Saturday, January 31 at 5:40 CST, Forte wrote: Wrong again, Forte!
I was outputting roughly the same damage as the bard. This tutorial seems to have the character powered up to unreal levels, with 50k HP, crazy armor and weapon, etc... and you mean to tell me that bard and scytheman do the same damage? I understand wanting to make the enemies a challenge, or some other well meaning notion of tutorial... but if this is supposed to be a look at how the class will be if I stick with the game, shouldn't I see real differences? A whole skill bar full of nuts attacks and stuff, at least, instead of the two skills you start the game with... Oh. Right. The combat.
It really isn't my thing. Long past are the days where I could sit at a computer watching my character do stuff, and unfortunately, combat in this game is basically target an enemy, press a skill button, and let your character autoattack. It  honestly feels like I could get up, grab a snack, and come back to find all of the enemies in an area dead by my character's hands without my input or formulating any kind of strategy. Maybe it changes later, but again, I can't see a reason why they would just lie to you about that. This is the first area of the game, where you should be hammering down everything you want the player to know, and since combat is at least 30% of your activities in this game, if it's going to be a deep system, you need to get that out of the way before level 50 when you start fighting something that might actually kill you. The thing that really disappoints me is that the world (especially the pretty crazy looking weapons) and controls really open themselves up for a combat system kind of like Devil May Cry, but it's just generic MMO tripe.
Next up is the quest system. It's basically where the EXP is at, like every MMO ever made. Before playing Eden Eternal, and subsequently this game, I separated quests in MMOs into two categories: Runescape tier and Everything else. Thanks to this one, though, I've got to add a third: X-Legend tier. Most of the quests are "go talk to this guy, go talk to that lady, bring this really generic item to someone", stuff like that. That's pretty typical, honestly, and I don't mind when games throw a few quests out like that, it helps build the world up. The problem comes from being able to click the current task on the quest window and your character automatically goes to that location. Not a marker on the map. Not a GUI marker. You are not only automatically guided to the task, but if it's a person, you automatically speak to them. If it's a monster, you target the closest one for an attack. This, to me, is just unreal. What's the point to this entire, open world you spent so much time on if you're just going to tell the player "it's ok to click one or two things and leave the game to play itself"? It's just not engaging at all. The sense of exploration and adventure is killed by a sparkly little line of magic guidance.
Maybe this kind of game just isn't for me. The aesthetics are nice, the music is a little meh, and the gameplay just doesn't mesh with me at all. In my opinion, spend your time and possibly microtransaction money somewhere else.

For what it was I enjoyed this game. I'll try to break it down.
Gameplay: The character controls are tight, the platforming is tricky yet satisfying and the main game mechanic, the teleport gun, is something I really enjoyed playing around with. That being said the joy ended all too quickly and the main game mechanic wasn't even used in the final boss battle. The game both starts and ends with a bullet hell segment that doesn't fit the rest of the game and I'm scratching my head as to why they were included. My guess is the developer had some code from a previous creation and used it to give the game and intro and outro which I applaud them for recycling code but in this instance it doesn't fit the game.
Story: There isn't much of one from what I saw. The game sets you up with a bad guy and you need to defeat him but beyond this and a few details from the aliens we don't much about this world or the universe it's in. Which is fine but the style seriously had me expecting something more along the lines of Cave Story.
Music: The music will remind you of video games past while still keeping it's own style. Basically, good music if that is a big factor for you.
Replayability: If you're an achievment hound or avid collector then you might end up playing this game through two or three times which leads me to the biggest flaw this game has...
This game can be beat in less than thirty minutes. Without help or anything I managed to conquer this game in under half an hour. This time would be extended would I care to go back and collect everything but there is no reason to besides achievments.
Right as I was getting into the groove of the game it ends...and that's it. I was honestly expecting to chase the bad guy to another planet with different aliens and bigger challenges but such a thing never came. I was sitting there scratching my head expecting more but it never came.
CONCLUSION: This game is fun albeit extremely short space romp that could of used a little more love and attention but if it's on sale and you got a pretty nickely to drop you can find thirty minutes of solid entertainment right here.

One of my favourite games of all time. The real time space battles are really bare bones so you cannot play it for that. You can play it for massive strategy within the Star Wars universe.
If anyone's played the recent boardgame Star Wars:Rebellion it takes themes heavily from this game. You have two different sides with different ways of playing. The Empire can build Death Stars and blow up planets (after a lot of resource/time investment) and the Rebels get a mobile HQ. This is balanced by alignment bars on every planet where you sway the popular opinion to your side.
You have characters to send on missions, along with generic units, that can sabotage, cause uprisings, diplome and assinate other characters. You can use Darth Vader to recruit for example and he can discover a potential force sensitive that you can then train, but it's random so could be anyone. Some characters can research new units.
You build ships, move fleets, assign admirals/generals/commanders, assign ground troops (to ships for invasions or to garrison planets). You send off probe droids to find resource rich planets (Y-wings for Rebels) and hunt for the Rebel base.
Kill/capture two key characters and take the opponent's base is the objective. Simple right? The Empire has the disadvantage of their base always being in the same place, but start off much stronger with star destroyers and probably a more dominant position.
I would say it gets a little easy on the lower difficulties so play on hard and save often!

Truely is one of my favourite Star Wars games and/or strategy games ever.

I first played this game sometime in the early 2000s. It was one of the first games to incorporate (pseudo-)real-time strategy into a turn-based game (much like the Total War series) and offered an enormously large lore and - at the time - rather complex game mechanics (remember, this was two years after the release of Warcraft II). Now, I played it again, mostly out of nostalgia. Even though I cannot recommend it anymore today, it used to be a good game; actually, this makes you realize just how far video games have come over the last 20 years.

This game bring good memories of many sunk hours from my childhood. Basically, this game is a comprehensive Star Wars universe game that range from space battles to diplomatic missions. But I wouldn't say it is for everyone, as the gameplay can be seen as quite tedious for a video game standard - you deal with static images and pop up notifications most of the time. I see this as a strategy game comparable to chess, where the visuals matter less than the information on the board and the options you need to think about. There is a 3D space battle mode, but this hasn't aged well. Controls are clumsy and graphics are very limited (fighters are sprites, and capital ships have a very primitive geometry). Again, this is for those who care less about graphics and interaction and more on how to make strategy decisions in a Star Wars universe.

People who want to get their revenge on a bunch of tiny bears, who should never have been able to overpower a fully armed and operational imperial army... I'm getting sidetracked.
The strategy side is great, playing as the rebels at the beginning, you really are on the backfoot. The Imperials have stronger ships, better troops, juicier core planets. (Hint: Rebels - fighters are you friend, nay your salvation).
Tactical side is old and outdated, tbh it wasnt very good back in the day either. I rarely play it, letting the auto-decider do its thing. This can be a little handicapping as the auto just adds up numbers for who wins, which if you're Rebels puts you at a serious disadvantage. Much like the Total War series, there is fleet combat you could win by playing it instead of auto. Or maybe lessen your losses ( for example facing a fleet with an interdictor, if you play you can focus fire on it blow it try to get some of your ships out. Auto you just die).
Play the from the end of episode IV - A New hope, the way you want to. Fulfil the rebellions goal of toppeling the Empire just like the movies. Or conversly take command of the Empire, and embarass those pillars of the Imperial academy by not being thwarted by a bunch of pint sized care b.... I'm getting side tracked again.
While I really do love this game, I feel for it as well. It has it's faults, which sadly if it was made today would probably be solved by steamworkshop access, this won't happen though with how old it is.
- Tactical combat as mentioned above - Graphically boring, and they clearly had ideas with it that never really got utilised (you can move your ships vertically, but there's no tactical benefit for example), Tactical combat effectively is just biggest ships or group of ships focus fire on single target, rinse repeat and hope you do that before they do.
- Characters/Agents - Characters supremely useful to wnning the game, and could effectively level up. Agents, very little value and couldn't level up. I think with some tweaks on how these types of units were created and level'd (i.e. making it more obvious how they level'd and maybe introducing some form of training mission/facility0 up they could be even more fun to play than they already are. Also actually show what difference having Characters in command positions actually did.
- Ground combat - non-existant, just click invade and hope your troops numbers are bigger than the other guys.
The strategy part of the game though *shrugs* I'd barely change anything about it, I think it stands up to many modern offerings.

Damn it. There are many persistence platformers on Steam these days, and so few of them have the golden ingredients: responsive controls, a good difficulty curve and an interesting setting and/or mechanic. Sadly, this game only has the one, and falls flat on many other respects.
I thought iZBOT was nailed on for being labeled an underrated gem when I first started, and that is almost entirely down to the controls and movement. This game is a dream to play in the mechanical sense. Your robot responds to everything you do, the momentum is satisfying and the jumping arcs make perfect sense. You have total control over your pixelated pipsqueak, and it feels bloody fantastic for the first few levels. One of the only games to attempt to reach for Meat Boy standards, and I sincerely applaud the devs for taking as much time as they evidently did on the tight controls. Unfortunately, that's when the realisation sinks in - the controls are pretty much all this game really has going for it.
It isn't that iZBOT is poor so much as it's lacklustre and uninspired. The environment and level-design are recycled and lazy respectively, with plenty of open space but no reason to explore it. There are collectibles 'hidden' in plain sight, where the only trial is executing the sole method of reaching them. Combining a wall-jump with a double-jump should be a goldmine for interesting levels and puzzle sections, but no such luck here. The difficulty doesn't scale especially well, with two major difficulty spikes that are quite out of kilter with much of the game, but overall it's far from impossible to beat.
Another nitpick is the brevity. Sixty levels, three environments, three bosses, and that's all she wrote. Nothing wrong with that...provided the game hooks its claws into you and drags your dopamine-addled brain back for more fun. Games like Spelunky, INK and others do this despite being as difficult as iZBOT, but I had little desire to go back and speedrun this game, or compete on the leaderboards. I started, but ultimately I just didn't want to - given my obsession with leaderboards, that tells a story.
Devs, please take the exceptional movement mechanics that you've slaved over and create a proper setting around them - I would take your money in a hearbeat. As it is, I reluctantly can't recommend iZBOT. Too many good games out there that are less bland and insipid.

iZBOT is a fast paced 2D fast paced platformer, and follows in the footsteps of games such as Super Meat Boy. This game is.. short I will say, being only three "levels", though each level contains 20 acts and a boss.
The controls are tight and very simple, only requiring two buttons, which can be mapped to whatever you want. Though I do recommend using a controller.
Difficulty does spike up during the last "Level", but first "level" and half of the second "level" you can breeze through with not much trouble.
Graphically the game goes for the whole "retro" style, which I don't mind and works well, and the music is okay, but it does start to become a bit degrading after a while, since each "level" uses only one song and going through 20 acts doesn't help, especially during the last "level".
Oh and as of writing this, the game has had some audio issues, mostly when adjusting the volume. Sometimes you can turn the volume for the music or effects to pretty much nothing, but will end up being really loud. Also if you restart an act or turn off the music from the pause menu, the settings get reset, and there's no way to change it without quitting a level. But hopefully this issue will get fixed in later patches.
There are enemies and hazards you have to watch out for. Enemies are... a thing I guess, ranging from slimes, bats, birds, and crabs. Slimes are usually placed wherever, but for the most part, i have no problem with them. Bats... ♥♥♥♥ them, the hitboxes on them can be way off, and they're really just there to be annoying or to slow you down. For example, one of the acts in the 3rd "level" there are five of them placed near the exit, and are just there to stall, especially when you got to watch out for the hazards.
Speaking of, there are a variety of hazards and other goodies to deal with. One of the more traditional types of hazards being spikes, which my only complaint is that they can blend onto parts of the environment, making them hard to see... especially in the thrid "level". You also have lasers, turrets, homing missles, and spinning fire blades that can instant kill you.
There are these teleporters that appear in some acts, but to be honest, they really have no point being in the game, for the most part. You first see one in the first "level", which at the same time, is also when the game throws in all new hazards and enemies as you progress, but aside from one act, they're useless and aren't necessary to beat the many acts you find them in.
There are three boss battles. They're simple. Can't really say much about them, although the final boss has one of those "race to the end and don't fall behind or else you die" segments, and if you die to the boss, you gotta do it again from the very beginning, since you have to beat an act or boss without dying.
Finally, there's the collectables. Each level and boss battle has a gem you got to collect called "HardToGetium", and as the name implies, they can be "hard to get" for the most part, and can require you to take a different path or hard to reach area to get to them.. oh and you got to do it without dying as well, or else you have to go get it again.
So overall, It's an alright game despite some of it's flaws such as being short, having some audio issues and some of the level designs. But still recommend it!

First it'll be addictive like crack (as you can see from my hours) but it mellows out after a while and you'll eventually start to get bored of it. Instead of leaving it on in the background to buy/ upgrade things, you'll visit it every few days (or weeks) because once you get higher, progress really starts to dwindle to an agonising crawl. The only things that keep me coming back are the events that happen every so often so good job HH.
As of now, I'm pretty much only playing for the events because each event has a different play style which is interesting but otherwise, Earth is unbeatable and Moon takes forever. Achievements are also pretty much unattainable once you're mid/ late game. A downside to Steam is not being able to take advantage of ad multipliers so perhaps it'll be better to check out the website or app.
Once the novelty of the events wear off I'm probably going to stop playing unless HH does something about the horrendously slow progress or adds an incentive to continue.
--Update--
It's been over a year since I've posted this review and here are my closing thoughts. A few months after I posted the review, I finished Earth and the events no longer interested me as they were (and still probably are) basically recycled every year. It's rather sad really, because there was so much potential here. After the Moon and Mars were released, I (and other players) thought we would be given new planets over time and HH would really take advantage of the whole ideal of colonising space. We would go through all the planets, maybe have mini-events or little bonus games on asteroids or meteroids if it was taking a really long time for a new planet to be released, maybe we would go to different solar systems, no one really knew but there were so many possibilities. Instead, none of these happened. Mars was released two years ago.
I recently saw a post on the Adventure Capitalist Facebook page where someone commented and asked if there would be any updates to the end game and HH replied, saying they were focused on having more things for the current planets. ...I don't even how what to think about that. There isn't much more that can be done and it means the loyal players that have stuck through it all from the beginning aren't being rewarded with anything and have no incentive to come back. I really feel like this is the wrong thing to do but at this point it's not really worth making a fuss about. Not to mention that HH has released a few other games in the meantime that they have either seemingly abandoned (Guild Quest) or really screwed over and had everyone start again from scratch (Adventure Communist). I like the games that HH releases but they really need to listen to their users more and to not spread themselves too thin. It's much better to have one solid game than several that have issues.
Anyway, I had a fun run and I haven't played the game in about a year but it looks like no significant changes have been made so it's the end of the game for me.

+ SOME models and textures are better
+ More graphics options
+ More dinosaurs to choose from
Neutral:
= Cosmetics and microtransactions to waste your money on
= Steam Workshop to vote on what you want to waste your money on
Cons:
- Most animations feel choppy and unfinished, while others don't always work
- Quite a few models look poorly designed and textured
- Controls feel clunky and unresponsive
- The community consists of many users that roleplay
To sum it up, I think the devs should've kept working on the original Primal Carnage rather than creating a new title. Both have their own strengths and weaknesses, but Primal Carnage: Extinction feels like a cash grab. I suggest buying the original instead.

Prince of Persia: Warrior Within is the sequel to The Sands of Time. The game returns back with the same familiar controls and gameplay but this time the combat has taken a massive overhaul. There are tons of combos and new attack moves and even secondary weapons to pick up. You also revisit many of the same areas over and over with the time changing from past to present so at times it feels like you're just doing the same thing over and over. Overall though it's a worthy sequel that just improves the combat while keeping the core gameplay unchanged so if you enjoyed the first game then you will enjoy the sequel. Only negatives I can say are the game has turned to use rock music during combat (feels out of place) and also has super annoying game over videos everytime you die. So, make sure to delete the game's intro videos and Game Over videos (GO_.bik in Videos folder).

Look... I guess the game it's fine, I LOVED the first Prince of Persia game (The Sands of Time, not the one from way back in the 90's)
But this game really turned a lot of people around, I think with this game, a lot of people got very upset with the developers for two reasons:
A) They expected the game to carry with the same "tone" from the first game, this game in exchange it's dark, gritty, obscure, gory, etc...
And...
B) A lot of people dislike how tedious the game gets near the end.
Everything ranging from the puzzles to the combat, to the enemies, everything later in the game takes a turn for the worse, the entire pacing of the game gets ruined once that you start having multiple bosses show up continually from one, and another, then you have the game sinking the player in confusing sections where you need to backtrack to specific places around the game, the game has a map which I guess it's supposed to make this complaints nonexistent. but here's the thing, the game's map doesn't work for me, and frankly, tho I can't confirm it, I suppose the game doesn't have anything more than a very basic map that just looks like an early concept art of certain parts around the game, but doesn't really explain where you need to go.
Which really takes me up to the next problem that I have.
The freaking pc port of this game is a mess, the game lacks basic graphic options, something understandable because of the games age, but tedious nonetheless, the game doesn't open up when clicking on "play" inside Steam, instead it throws a screen showing my system specs (24gb ram, gtx 970, i5 6600k), that obviously surpass the system requirements from the game, but since the game doesn't recognize this specs, it simply doesn't allow me to launch my game.
In order to fix this I had to go to the main folder of the game, and launch the game directly from there, while simultaneously keeping the "launcher" with my system specs, running in the background.
It's the only way I got to run the game.
In order to then use my controller, increase the resolution to my screens native one, and skip the five minute cutscenes, I had to download patches, rebind keys, and delete some folders inside the game's directory. It was a process that took me around forthy minutes or so, but it was tedious and more importantly, it was relatively quick, because I knew where to look. (Thank you pcgamingwiki)
After that...
It's a fun game, the puzzles and the combat are great for the most part, climbind around and avoiding deathtraps it's enjoyable and fun, but then the game takes some design choices that in the name of "challenge" end up making the game extremely tedious to play, stuff like getting chased around by an enemy that you have to outrun, only getting the ability to "correct" your mistakes by using a limited supply of "sands of time" which allow you to go back to a specific position before you made whatever mistake got you killed in the first place, only to then having the limited supply of sands of time being the biggest problem of your playthrough, then some enemies that dodge each and every single one of your attacks, or block most of them, while they have attacks that "break" your defence...
It just gets up to a point in which the game breaks it's own flow and ends up making the playing of it, tedious, and annoying, and eventually a section that would usually take you half an hour to complete, ends up taking you two, or three, and then it becomes tedious and annoying, and that frightening question that comes up in a game that clearly bothers you shows it's head.
Is it worth it?
And I don't think it is, the game might have been an incredible game before, and maybe if you can look past the terrible design choices that the game carries, and how horribly some of them have aged, with a terrible camera that switches in the most inconvinient moment making you fall to your death, then maybe you can find some enjoyment from beginning to end, but this is a game that hasn't aged well, I don't mean the graphics...
Who cares about the graphics of a twelve year old game?
But...
It is a game that has design choices, and mechanics, that games have actively been trying to avoid, specifically because of how frustrating they can be.
And I just don't like that, sorry...

You know, this game is kind of the black sheep of the franchise (a franchise that might I add, has been ignored stupidly when it's one of the best Ubisoft has). If you ask fans about it they'll either tell you they love it or they hate it, there doesn't seem to be a middle ground. However I do find it a great game, and as I usually do with my reviews, I'm gonna start with the negative aspects of the game first.
First and foremost, the biggest problem this game has are the glitches and bugs. It's no secret that Ubisoft ♥♥♥♥s up their newer releases but their old games are no strangers to that as well. This game still has quite the number of graphic bugs, collision detection, glitched physics and other crap you might think of. And sure, some are useful like the wall-running glitch that can let you extend your wall-running distance effortlessly, but others are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥that will cause a game over on you, such as going through the floor. It's quite shameful that Ubisoft hasn't and will never fix these mistakes, really. I will also add that the game has no Steam support what-so-ever.
Second, this is something that you can see a lot on Ubisoft games, from both the new and old. If you pick the Hard difficulty, all that will change is the HP of enemies and how much damage they do to you. Come on, that's not difficulty, that's artificial difficulty. And it sucks. Honestly, ignore the Hard difficulty. I went through the game with it and it just makes the game worse, specially when bosses just have too much health and deal too much, while Easy difficulty is programmed for babies.
Third is something that's not a problem with me, but with lots of fans: the setting itself. You see, Sands of Time had a lot of charm on it's style, it was told like a fairy tale and didn't really have much violence; it had a bigger focus on the puzzles and platforming than in combat. Warrior Within flips it over, there's barely any puzzles anymore, platforming has been reworked and it's still there, but combat got a gigantic overhaul and it's the bigger focus. It also went from a faily tale to a violent game in which the main character decapitates, cuts in half and utterly murders most of what's on his way in overly cool ways while the music goes from persian-like music to edgy hard-rock/metal. As I said, it's not really a problem for me, but I know for a fact that a lot of people disliked this game because of it, and you should be aware of it.
Lastly, I can't help it but to think the two female characters in the game got stupidly sexualized for no reason what so ever. Specially Shadde of whatever her name is, literally the first time you see her, it's her gigantic♥♥♥♥♥taking most of the screen. What the♥♥♥♥♥♥
However, looking away from those problems what we got left is a pretty solid platforming game that had some seriously fun combat mechanics, a decent story and catchy music.
The map is pretty cool, and I've always been a fan of it. In the Sands of Time you always went forward and would most likely never visit most of those places again; that ain't happening here, as the Island of Time and it's gigantic damn fortress is well connected and you'll be going from one place to the other. It's sort of like an open world with it's own mini-hub area connecting them all, which I like, andit doubles as good for having both present and past versions of almost all areas, which is really cool when you finally do notice which ones are the same on different times. Though I must question what kind of sense do all of those places make in an in-game prespective, it's impossible to go from one side to the other unless you're some sort of acrobatic monster like the Prince.
I've always liked the story of this game, it's not too deep to get lost on it but it does entertain during the 7-10 hours it takes to go through it. It also likes to make you question what's going on early and give you hints of what happened, and incase you didn't catch it, answer them later near the end. And having two different endings is also cool, the other games also needed something like that.
The combat is absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing Badass. Tons of combos, plenty of weapons, a cluster♥♥♥♥ of ways to deal with an enemy, and it's also quite ♥♥♥♥ing violent and fun to watch. It's certainly a gigantic step-up from The Sands of Time, and I wish Ubisoft didn't just copy it on the sequel (which had almost all the same moves but the gameplay was more stealth focused, which just didn't feel right).
The music, while edgy as hell and really different from the previous game, feels quite fitting in here. The atmosphere is really dark and gritty, having hard-rock/metal for half the soundtrack does wonders.
Do I recommend this game? Certainly. However be aware of two things: First, the price. Ubisoft usually sucks at pricing and a game this old is kinda expensive at it's current price. On a big sale though, it's a great purchase. Second, that you should totally play The Sands of Time first if you haven't yet. Otherwise you won't understand♥♥♥♥♥♥
TL;DR Edition: Great mix between platforming and action-based gameplay with plenty of violence and metal to go along with it. Sure it's edgy as all ♥♥♥♥ but it's also really fun. Story is decent and catchy, the map got a lot of detail, only big negative points being the God-damn bugs.

A fascinating title, Star Wars Supremacy (as the disc I also own says) Is a truly unique little game focussed on themes of  espionage, diplomacy and exploration. If you're planning on playing it, be warned: You'll need to do a quick google search to find and replace the .exe file with a patched one to fix some horrible icon and colour flipping bugs, as well as a window size bug.
You'll be doing this regardless of the version if you want to play this nowadays.
It's graphhically reminiscent of one of those old ROM games, as if you're running an instance of windows 98 with all the windows and such. That said, the UI's design isn't actually bad, just dated.
Mechanically however, I actually think this game is way ahead of its time. Real time battles with (simple) player commands? Check. Espionage, including sabotage, uprisings, assasinations and good ol' spying (among more)? Check. It somehow does diplomacy well too, in a game with only two factions which are permanantly at war, due to needing to sway undecided, or even enemy or rebellious planets over to your side.
It's absolutely something you should play, if only due to how much game is crammed into this tiny, simple package, and how little of it can be found in literally any other title. If this were to be remastered with updated graphics, battle controls and AI (the AI is pretty basic in this game. I recommend multiplayer with a friend for the most this game can offer) it'd blow people away. I'd absolutely rate it with Republic Commando, Jedi Knight and KOTOR as games which could really do with a remaster.

I was the only person at my local store to pre-order it, and I ended up returning it. There is a list of pros and cons, I'll be brief, but... Obviously, all reviews are just opinions.
Pros:
+Extremely customizable
+Long lasting batteries
+Touchpad and control stick textures feel nice
+Feedback is great
+Probably perfect for playing PC-oriented games on your couch
Cons:
-ABXY buttons are -really- small, and I don't even have big hands
-They're also placed very far inwards, hitting them is often a reach
-Ditto for the control stick
-High learing curve with these placements, and uncomfortable after short time periods
-Found the trigger buttons feeling way too light. I'd sometimes be pressing them without noticing it
-Ultimately, if you do all your gaming in front of your PC, I think an Xbox One controller is more than enough; better button sizes, placements, triggers, grip comfort, etc.
TL;DR- Not recommended if you game from your computer. Only recommended if gaming PC-precision type games from your couch/TV/Steam machine, and even then, rather uncomfortable and high learning curve.

I remember liking this game as a kid. Unfortunately, no amount of nostalgia can make up for how truly awful this game is.
By far the biggest issue with the game is over-emphasis on combat. The combat is so repetitive and unsatisfying that you'll look for every opportunity to skip it in order to continue with the platforming elements of the game. On hard mode at least, the enemies have way too much hp, and you can easily find yourself repeating the same attack patterns over and over literally a dozen or more times before the enemy finally falls. And god forbid you're trapped in a group of several enemies. For some reason most of your moves have next to no block recovery, which means you're taking damage one way or another. Even properly timed counter-attacks can result in the enemy still hitting you.
Another major issue is the game is just way too hard for its own good. By midway through the game you're begging for every save point that comes your way. Not only does the game not feature a save-anywhere feature, its checkpoints are virtually nonexistent. This means sometimes you'll lose entire minutes of progress because of a platforming mistake.
Speaking of platforming, it is actually quite good for the most part, very much up-to-par with what you get in the original Sands of Time. However, you'll often get lost and frustrated because of the game's terrible camera angles and misguided use of an open world design that has you backtracking through several areas.
Probably the most aggravating thing about the game is that it's clearly rushed / unfinished. There's a lot of gameplay and graphical glitches that are surprisingly easy to trigger through normal gameplay. Even the way the prince lands on certain beams can provoke glitches where he temporarily appears to be landing on some different type of platform.
Even little details about the game will tend to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. For example, there are time travel portals you can activate. Each portal has 4 switches you have to press to activate them and the order is random. EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. It creates a meaningless guessing game each time and feels utterly pointless.
Whereas the original game feels polished and has a certain charm, this one is just an incomplete mess. The wholy gritty, badass prince vibe they were going with this game falls flat on its face, and is borderline cringy at times.
I can't believe I'm saying this, but even Forgotten Sands is a better game. I would barely place this game above Prince of Persia 2008.

A good example of Star Wars gaming prior to the Prequels, to Disney's purchase of the IP, and the glut of Star Wars merch that resulted each time.
You can say that Rebellion ("Supremacy" on the other side of the Pond) predates both Sins Of A Solar Empire and Galactic Conquest mode from Star Wars: Empire At War as an RT4X game. Sins and EAW are obviously completely different animals, but let's look under the hood:
On one hand, Rebellion's mechanics, and more open-ended interpretation of what was then 21 years of Star Wars canon can convince players they're actually in overall command of the Alliance or the Empire. Every game starts mere days after the Battle of Yavin, and deep, non-linear gameplay lets you rewrite Star Wars history from there; you're building shipyards, factories, defenses, mines and refineries to supply your war effort; you're assigning beloved characters to command fleets, planetary garrisons, or on missions of diplomacy, sabotage, abduction or rescue. The randomized starting conditions of each game are the sprinkles on top.
On the other hand, Rebellion has a crappy UI, and is noticeably poorly balanced (some planetary bombardments, and rescue or sabotage missions often end up annoyingly ineffective humanitarian disasters). Don't expect comfort from your optional control of the needlessly emphasised space battles - they apparently have separate mechanics altogether, comperable to Masters Of Orion for all the wrong reasons.
Get Rebellion for its gravely overlooked place in the history of early Star Wars games, for its depth, and for its tiny, but damn persistant following; DON'T get it for its undercooked interface and design flaws.

I've had this controller since the first wave in October. I've gotten the hang of it, and while I'm fairly comfortable with the touchpads in most games now, I still feel like it's a chore to use at times, and honestly, I'd attribute this to Valve trying too hard to reinvent the wheel. I'm guessing they were attempting to make this controller superior by using the touchpads as opposed to the right-analog stick or the non-touch d-pad. It fails to outperform either.
It's a nice thought when it comes to the d-pad, but it doesn't deliver. It simply isn't good enough. It doesn't feel solid. It doesn't offer any confidence in what direction you're pressing. It would normally be forgiveable if the d-touchpad was smaller, but it's too large, making getting lost on it easy.
Unfortunately, when it comes to the right-touchpad that's supposed to replace the right analog, it's even worse. If the d-pad is easy to lose your thumb's position on, the right-touchpad may as well be pointing you in the wrong direction. It doesn't really redeem itself when it comes to aiming either, as it doesn't substantially improve your aiming in FPS games for example, over a standard analog stick.
What's worse, the construction felt... cheap, to say the least, out of the box. I was willing to overlook this, and it even grew on me down the line, but it has become evident that quality wasn't at the top of the list when the design for this controller was introduced. The left d-touchpad is having issues and spazzing out. Sometimes pressing one direction once will yield multiple inputs, some not even in the same direction. Worse still, the [only] analog stick on this controller seems to also trigger this issue, causing headaches in the middle of a game at times. Mind you, it sits on a desk when not in use. Never dropped it either.
If you're looking for a good controller to use, I'd honestly avoid this one altogether. At $50, it's a steal, just not on your end, unfortunately. Go for an Xbone or 2nd-gen PS4 controller for $10 more, or simply grab an X360 controller, still a much better option than this one, and for less money. I honestly wouldn't be able to look someone in the face while trying to charge them $50 for this controller in its current state/iteration. Back to the drawing board.

Worth every cent - preordered the previews Primal Carnage already + played it a lot, also in the "Primal Carnage Games" (a monthly live-stream competition of clans vs. the developers (hosted in the past)) - this one seams to be just as good;
It's a great game if you want to have fun from time to time for a few hours during a week - you don't have to bother with long-term unlock mechanisms for better weapons, classes etc. - you can just set off and enjoy playing!
That's what i like most, as i don't have that much time anymore and don't want to spend my spare gaming hours for unlocking stuff.
+ PLUS it's a game that courages teamwork - SPECIALLY as humans!
That makes it a great game to play with friends on Skype / TS, or join a clan (if interested; We've got a german group going;)
...there are just too many Role Play servers and not enough Get To The Chopper ones, but that can be also an advantage; If you want to host a server it could find many players (with the right settings;)
Anyway; BUY IT, IF you want to have some hours of fun without bothering about classes & experience an well made asymmetric (guns vs. claws) team-vs-team battle - every Dinos / Humans really plays very different as well + it's best combatting each strengths with your mates / a team - ...well, and of course if you like Dinos ;D
...ah, and btw reacting to some other reviews: I don't think it's unbalanced / the humans have no chance - i myself like to play humans over Dinos e.g. ;) - the Dinos might be more awesome when you first got the game (because that's what makes this game unique) but at long term the humans offer more enhanced tactics + good players cooperate more (yeah, because just with COOPERATION you bet the Dinos, that's the advantage of the humans! - well, let me make that clear; The Dinos are faster & can run away if they want, but the humans can decide where the battle will be fought as the Dinos normally come to THEM, and not the other way around. Though, you can still take a T-Rex down as single human (i prefer the pathfinder for that) if you make advantage of it's slow turnings and run + gun back and forth.)
(...i don't write reviews normally, but just i felt like this (still) underrated game just needs my support;)

When it comes to precision platforming games on Steam the market is stacked. However, that hasn’t stopped a large number of indie developers flooding the market with games of various quality. Sadly it is often the games that are ridiculously bad that get their turn to shine in favor of the more well put together titles that deserve it more. Daniel Spruce released his iZBOT game onto the Steam platform back at the start of September. To this point in time he has ignored the early pleas of the indie bundles world in favor of getting his title into the hands of those who will enjoy it most. A sad consequence of this is that it has remained buried on Steam so it’s about time that it got a little of the spotlight.
I generally read Steam reviews before playing a game to help formulate some idea of what I’m getting myself into. There are a lot of knowledgeable players among Steam’s user base and in part thanks to being able to rate someone’s review contribution you can quickly sort the quality from the muck. If you take a quick browse through iZBOT’s reviews you’ll find that platformer fans have generally similar thoughts on the game. The general train of consensus is that the game is one of the best genre titles to be released in 2015 and that it combines super tight controls with the frustrations and the rage that is generated from the best precision platform titles on Steam such as Super Meat Boy. Those are all things that make platforming engrossing to me.
The aim of iZBOT, much like any platformer, is to defeat each level but you do have an extra challenge per level in getting a gem. This will, most often, slow down your best time (you can defeat each level without getting the gem) but there is an achievement for hunters when you do collect them all, ‘OCD.’ I personally found that this was the most fun in the game for me. I could zip around the levels but if I really wanted a challenge the gem was the real prize. Once you collect the gem you can then restart the level to see how quickly you could have gone had you not bothered to collect the gem. Alternatively, unless you find the gem on your first play through a better idea may be to get the gem on your second attempt.
iZBOT is every bit as precision as Ruxar bills it as being. This is attested to by the Steam reviewers and having played it for myself I can vouch for that fact. Thankfully it controls superbly, at least with an Xbox One controller, making deaths never feel as though you’ve been cheated. It’s a game that I genuinely believe people who are scared of playing platformers could jump into and learn how to play. Therefore iZBOT gets a firm recommendation for all platformer fans.

Everything you expect from a platformer in a neat little package. This definitely isn't a big game. Completing it, getting all gems (although the achievement didn't unlock), and optimizing my time in a few levels took me around 4 hours — and I'm probably somewhere between mediocre and decent at precision platformers.
The controls are tight and responsive, the speed is good, and the levels are well-designed, so you can mostly go as fast as the game allows and not have to wait for moving parts of the level to let you through. And most important of all, it's fair. While you may have to play a level a few times to become familiar with it, the game never just kills you for no reason, and there's mostly no blind drops or anything of the sort. You'll still die probably thousands of times just because you know you can do a level just a liiiiittle faster.
So yeah, if run n' jump precision platformers is your kind of thing, you'll most likely enjoy this — because it's a run n' jump precision platformer and a very decent one at that.
3 very minor things though:
- the bosses are maybe a bit lackluster. You'll be spending most of your in-game time outside of boss fights anyway, so it's not a huge deal really.
- hitboxes seem to be a little bigger than you'd expect. It's something you get used to after a while, but it confused me at first
- the gems seem to only serve to unlock an achievement (which didn't unlock for me for some reason). It'd be super nice if they served some purpose within the game too.
Apart from that, a thouroughly enjoyable platformer that should satisfy the cravings of most platforming enthusiasts for a little while.

The controls in iZBOT are super tight and responsive, allowing you to pull off many manuevers you didn't think possible. If you are into tough platformers with great controls and where you explode a lot, give iZBOT a shot!

iZBOT is a precision platformer by Ruxar. It follows the typical structure of repeatedly reaching the level end while avoiding various enemies and environment obstacles, and offers a reasonably satisfying  experience along the way.
The game is drawn in an adorable pixelated style, and has very retro, 8-bit music to match. But, let's be honest, when it comes to precision platformers, it's all about the controls and the level design.
iZBOT has the tight and predictable controls that you would expect out of this kind of game. No complaints there. When you explode after running into ostrich spit (yup... That's in there) you can bet it's your fault.
As far as level design, there is really only 1 hang up. The game features 3 levels, with over a dozen stages in each level. This is a fair amount of content. I have been playing for about 3 hours and just now reached the final set of stages. Again, no complaints there. My issue in this area is that the difficulty of each stage is more random than progressive. I don't play many precision platformers, so maybe it's standard to throw some really tricky stages in early, and then things suddenly get easier for a while. It seemed a little odd to me.
One thing that iZBOT lacks compared to leading platformers is story. The game features a boss fight at the end of each set of stages. It is never clear why the boss is there, why we are killing it, or what (other than unlocking the door) we get out of the fight. This see like a missed opportunity to flesh out the character a bit and help keep the player interested in completing more stages.
Overall, fans of the precision platforming genre will want to pick up iZBOT, but new players might want to look elsewhere for the most satisfying experience. It can be picked up on Steam for $9.99 US dollars. Disclosure: This review was written on a copy provided by the developer pre-official launch.

TL:DR---One of the best games I have ever had the pleasure to play. Buy this game if you enjoy fast and adrenaline filled combat and an amazing story with well developed characters, sci-fi setting and dialogue. 10/10
Story: 10/10
-I actually truly feel each characters struggle and emotions both through their actions and very well written dialogue. At first the game is a bit confusing with many new ideas and story elements being introduced to you but as the story develops you start to understand and really care for what is going on around the main characters. The main characters (which there are three of them throughout the 25+ hour main story without side quest) really have rich and thoughtful traits to them that feel very unique to both the story and to the constant boring protagonist seen in many videogames today. During times of distress in the story I actually find myself worrying for the amazing characters that you are taking control of. If a storyteller can actually bring out the emotions of everyday life such as joy, rage and sadness, which the creators of this game did masterfully, then that shows the true thought and greatness that resulted from their work.
Gameplay: 10/10
-The combat of Nier:Automata is fantastic with a very reactive focused hack and slash style. There are many various weapons, ranging from greatswords, swords, spears, gloves, guns etc., each with their own unique combos and variants. The speed of the combat feels great, you truly feel your adrenaline kicking as you move across the battlefield at high speeds cutting through countless enemies. Dont be fooled though, even though this game has many hack & slash elements and you may feel like a expert as you are fighting, the game will quickly give you a reality check by pummelling you into the dirt. You have to be smart with many different upgrades and also the real time combat, even though you are fast the enemies are too, requiring you to be efficient in dodging and punishing accordingly. I reccomend starting off in normal difficulty because the spike from normal to hard is high, with enemies going from taking a quarter of your health in a hit, to completely one-shotting you. There are even segments that let you fulfill the dream of getting into a mech suite and fighting a very fun shooter-hell type style of gameplay. Nier:Automata has a very dynamic camera that switches during sections of combat and exploring that feels great, almost as if you are playing a movie. In all, The combat makes you feel as if you are in a film with its very smooth and dynamic sections that constantly vary to help keep it feeling fresh.
Soundtrack: 10/10
-One of the best soundtracks to a game I have ever listened to. Every fight has dynamic music that changes depending on the situation in the story or in the battle. The compositions are almost celestial, with a distressful tone that connects with the theme of the story that is also accompanied by an angelic female vocalist that steals the stage (or battlefield?).
Optimization: 10/10
-I played Nier:Automata with a gtx 1080, i7 4770k and it ran perfectly at all ultra setting with virtually no frame drops besides the cutscenes that are unfortunatley locked at 30 frames but doesn't detract from the story or gameplay at all. As long as your computer is atleast mid tier then you should have no problems running this game and keep it looking good. As far as bugs or issues that came with release, I have experienced NO crashes or bugs that I have noticed and definitley DID NOT experience any game breaking bugs or crashes throughout my 25+ hours beating the game.
Final Note:
---If you are a fan of high speed sci fi action with an amazing story and characters then this game is a 100% buy, please support the developers that released a optimized full package and put so much effort, thoughfulness and creativity into their game that is not seen in this industry often.

I have seen a lot of reviews complaining about crashes, so the first thing I will say is that 6 hours in (At time of writing) I haven't had any crashes. The game runs perfectly fine on max settings. I run a gtx 780 and I5 4670. If the game crashes after you alter the frame rate settings that is your own fault, the game has an fps cap for a reason, and as capcom said, uncapping it will make it very unstable. The game runs at a constant frame-rate with no screen tearing for me, and while it isn't the prettiest game, it isby no means ugly, and there is often times hundreds of zombies on screen at once, with explosions and bullets and blood flying everywhere.
On to the game itself, I enjoy it so far. The boss fights are a pain, but mowing down zombies, leveling up, unlocking new areas and weapon combinations, and playing with the vehicles is very fun. Unless you are a completionist, the game is not very long however. While there is a 6 day time limit on the game that is constantly ticking down, I finished chapter 4 (out of 7) by the time night came around on the first day, about 5-6 hours into the game. If you only did the story, It will likely take you less than 10 hours to beat. However, with all of the collectibles and side missions and activites, that number about doubles. If you count the nightmare mode and mini dlc campaigns, it just about doubles again. So overall you have somewhere between 10-40 hours depending on how much of the game you feel is worth playing.

The Melee combat feels weighty and meaningful, and there are a lot of different animations for the different weapons, so you don't just see the character doing the same thing over and over with a different model in his hand. The ranged combat is decent, but is underused because you can't earn nearly as much xp with a gun as you can with a combo weapon. Overall, I would give this game an 8/10, being fun and for me personnally, I will definietly get my money's worth of time out of it.

Next, I received a message saying an AI won by owning over 40% of planets, although it clearly showed I had 71/1235 to their 63/1020.  I decided to play it through as I had a drake and about a 400k fleet to play with.  I went up against a 105k and two 50ks.  I paused and checked our loadouts and I was surprised that they were nearly exact, except I had scale armor.  The AI fleet had no leaders, and I had two high level admirals.  The AI destroyed my fleet and lost only 50 corvettes and 18 battleships.  Now, before you start thinking 'this guy must have done something really stupid'.. understand that I've been playing strategy games since before the PC was invented, I worked on fighter jets in the military, and I'm a data intelligence architect; I'm not stupid.  I do understand that software updates occur and unbalance the game and it's hard to find every bug, but Stellaris is broken like non-alcoholic beer.. it's cold and tastes good, but then nothing happens... it's a big buildup for nothing but disappointment.  I might wait for a few patches and try again, but at this point I would tell anyone who asked that this game had great potential, but turned out to be a waste of time and money.

Before I get into the review, I just want to give my gaming background. Why? Because your experience as a gamer will greatly affect your first impressions with the steam controller. I've been gaming on consoles since the NES days. In 2011, I switched to PC and never looked back. I witnessed the birth of analog sticks and 3d games alike. I experienced many versions of a gamepad up until today, where we have the rock solid Xbox pad which has been perfected over the years and has not seen an equal...until the steam controller showed up.
My experience in a nutshell.
Day 1: Unboxed and got it working within seconds. First game? Fallout 4. After hours of tweaking and getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me, I was ready to rage-return the controller. I kept my cool and went at it the next day.
Day2: Watched some youtube videos and did some research. Got better at tweaking the controls and using it in general.
Day3: I am a PC gaming god with the steam controller. I will NEVER use analog sticks again. An xbox controller can only dream of the accuracy a trackpad has to offer.
The learning curve is steep, for sure. Both in learning to use the software and even more so in trying to undo YEARS of muscle memory with analog sticks and even the idea of what a "proper" controller should be. Once I got over the hump, everything just clicked. I can't really explain it. It's like those blurry pictures of what appears to be digital noise, but if you stare long enough a 3d image pops out at you.
The haptic feedback felt gimmicky at first. But eventually you realize it's importance. It turns a lifeless flat touchpad into something with tangible feedback. It gently sends signals through your fingers to your brain, indicating sensitivity thresholds you've set or even angular directions, which is important on a circular trackpad. It's fine work by valve.
I won't get into many more details or I'd be typing for days. The bottom line is this: If you're a PC gamer there's no reason you shouldn't pick one of these up and give a shot. My only advice is to have patience and approach the controller with an open mind. You WILL get frustrated at first, but eventually, you'll just "get it" and you'll never look back.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED
My ONLY gripe with it is the need to use Big Picture mode. This is only justifed while gaming from a couch on a steam machine. For the rest of us gaming on our PC's, well, Big Picture is just awkward as hell. It was clearly designed to be viewed from a distance...on a TV. Not sure why we HAVE to use it on our monitors to take advantage of the steam controller. Hopefully, Valve acknowledges this soon.
Innovation, future and precision. These are the 3 words I'd use to wrap up this review.

I use the Steam Controller for my living room PC from my sofa where my choice is XBOX 360 controller or... well... nothing. Basically the exact use-case this is for.
There's a learning curve for this, building up whole new muscle memory for the 'trackerball' style of camera movement but it came pretty quickly and I'm getting better and more accurate with it every time.
The build quality feels great to me. It feels solid and well built. I love the haptics.. I actually really love playing on this controller just to hear and feel the little ticking noises. The wireless connection is solid and doesn't drop out or jam like every other wireless device in that room - otherwise it'd be useless.
The grip buttons underneath the controller are godly and I can easily see that feature appearing on lots of other controllers in the future. Being able to 'jump' and 'use' without taking your thumb off the camera trackerball thing is spooky but very natural.
Two features that would make this perfect:
The driver/controller thing needs to be decoupled from the Steam application so that it can safely be run with administrator privileges on windows. Otherwise you're stuck running Steam as administrator in order to use it outside of Steam. (I actually do not want to use Steam Big Picture at all because it's not really The Full Steam)
That driver/controller app? It should also let you use an on-screen keyboard anywhere. The onscreen keyboard right now is just in Big Picture mode in Steam which is basically pointless. I want to use this controller to completely control my entire PC not just one particular app.
absolutley brilliant, well worth the money, reccomend to anybody, and it is very easy to use.

Great for: Shadow of Mordor, Batman, Dark Souls, Grow Home.  Anything where using a stick to turn a camera felt dumb, but moving a guy with keys felt less analog and skillful than a stick.
I also really like it for playing mousepad style games on my laptop (xcom, invisible inc).
You have one more analog control than an xbox 360 controller, and so games like Lunar Flight, Sublevel Zero (both where you have 6 axis to control) you can really do justice to them with this.
There are simply more controls and possibilities than the 360 controller too - I liked being able to get everything I wanted bound.
Once a game is how you want it via the software in big picture mode - you can run a game from the non-big picture mode method - and the last profile used for the steam controller for the game will be loaded.  I like this a lot.
Using it on the desktop in Windows is nice and it dynamically switches between your Windows desktop settings and games, again regardless of whether big picture is open.
Loved that the controller can be wired or wireless too.
Worked out the box with no drivers for me, first thing it did when I opened big picture mode up was update it's firmware.
I do not recommend it for games where you really want two sticks (ie simple twin stick shooter) - here an xbox pad is more immediate.
I do not recommend it for an fps (payday 2, L4D 2) where the mouse and keyboard is simply more immediate and accurate.
I like it for more hybrid games.
I found it best in games that allow mouse keyboard AND a controller at the same time.  Examples Spintires, Sublevel Zero - here I have both mouse and joystick at once on the controller.
Where this was not possible, I found I prefered setting the game to use mouse and keyboard - then creating a profile to 'analogise' that onto the controller (example Cyptark, Full mojo rampage) than setting the game to expect an xbox360 controller and just have the steam controller mimic it.
Getting started with a new controller takes several hours, getting used to it probably takes weeks..  Wish some of the gaming press could be bothered with more than a quick pre release try out and write off.  Personally after a few evenings of tweaking settings I find it to be perfect for any game that is good but not quite right with either mouse or a controller.  I love tweaking settings - so it's fun for me.  For other people, there is a growing library of presets.  It will be bewildering a first.
The software in big picture is amazing - I always wanted have that level of control for any controller.  Deadzones, antideadzones (which allow 'unarcadey-ing' a lite-flightsim into much more tapered gradual controls) - as well as second functions (boost anyone?) when the stick is pressed to maximum.  The amount of control that can be dialed in is daunting - but becomes intuitive

The steam controller has a very high learning curve and takes about a month to fully retrain the muscle memory to adapt to new button layouts.
The trackpad is very responsive, but this is where the problem arises. The trackpad is very fast in regards to NON accurate movements. Simply, a player can move from point A to point B very quickly, however, the accuracy varies and is not consistent, due to the nature of a trackpad.
Also, I do realize there is a gyroscope, but stafing using the left thumbstick and using the gyro at the same time, causes the player to decrease in usage of the left thumb. Simply, the brain wlll have a difficult time in accomplishing both of the preceding ideas. There is an article on this, entitled, "Multitasking and Academic Performance" I wrote my Master's thesis on this ^-^.
At first, I was very annoyed by the non accurate trackpad. However, I soon realized that the xbox and playstation controllers that I loved so much were so accurate, because I have been using it for over 10 years!!!!! I went back and reanalyzed the comments made years ago regarding the PS one's controller when they decided to use the analog joystick, comments were mediocre at best, but as years passed, the XBOX and PLAYSTATION controllers became the standard by which all controllers follow.
At the same time, I can see that making players adapt to a product is not a good idea. The product should adapt to players! Simply, why would I buy something that will take months to adapt to? when I already have a controller that I've been using for ten years go to waste.
Recommendations:
1) Keep the touchpads, but give us, the PLAYERS, the option to use a physical analog stick for our right thumbs. For example, give players the ability to swap out mechanical parts, such as the trackpad for an analog stick if we choose to do so.
2) As a matter of fact, give us the ability to interchange all mechanical positions of the controller to our liking. That way players can adjust every physical aspect of the controller.
3) Find a way to add an analog stick in addition to the two trackpads.
4) Realize that gamers have been using the analog stick for a very very very long time. Give us that ability ^-^ please for the love of GOD.
5) If everything you read here does not follow through. For the love of god, VALVE, Find a way to make the trackpads more accurate in regards to small movements.
LASTLY, I apologize for any grammar errors, syntax, and strange usages of diction. It is 6:09 a.m. I am up reading, and my steam controller was right next to me. Therefore, I decided to write about my thoughts regarding the Steam controller.

I expect the game to sell well and may even be their biggest selling game to date due to the IP; and that worries me because I don't want to see Telltale leave behind a formula that I enjoy in favor of bigger profits.
This is not a game for grown-ups like The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us or Game of Thrones. I would struggle to even recommend it to anyone with kids, Minecraft lovers or not because it's just not very entertaining.
